t.weltenburg am galget kleinkastell@48.9,1:
The Danube does something unexpected just upstream of Kelheim. Instead of wandering across flat Bavarian farmland, it cuts straight through a band of white Jurassic limestone, squeezed between cliffs that rise steeply from the water. This is the Weltenburg Narrows, and on the hill above the abbey at Weltenburg, at the spot called Am Galget, the Romans put a small fort to watch the river and the frontier.

The fort was part of the Raetian frontier, the line of the Roman Limes where the Danube itself served as the border. The remains today are mostly earthworks and ground traces rather than standing walls, so this is a place you visit for its position and story more than for masonry. Stand up here and it becomes obvious why soldiers were posted: the river, the gorge and the land beyond all lie open. A few minutes away, down at the water, Weltenburg Abbey has been a Benedictine house for well over a thousand years, its church a riot of late Baroque by the Asam brothers, and its brewery is reckoned one of the oldest monastic breweries in the world. The dark beer in the beer garden is the local sacrament.

The classic way to see the gorge is by boat from Kelheim, which takes you past the rock formations that locals have given names over the centuries. On the bike, the road to Weltenburg is a dead end of sorts, so the ride is about getting there and back through the wooded hills of the Altmühl and Danube country. The roads around Kelheim, Essing and Riedenburg are gentle and well surfaced, with river views and plenty of bends through beech woods. Summer weekends bring crowds of day-trippers, cyclists and coaches, so a weekday or an early start makes a real difference.

Kelheim, about five kilometres away, has fuel, shops and everything else you might need. Above the town on the Michelsberg stands the Befreiungshalle, a huge round hall built for King Ludwig I to commemorate the wars against Napoleon, and it is worth the short detour for the view alone. In late autumn the woods turn gold and the river mist lingers well into the morning, which makes for beautiful but damp riding.
t.watchtowers wp 15 11 to 15 26 and fortle:
The Altmühl valley in Bavaria is one of Germany's best kept riding secrets, a winding river valley cut deep into Jurassic limestone, lined with juniper heaths, rock towers and castles. Near where the valley meets the Danube, the Roman frontier, the Raetian Limes, ran across the land, and the stretch of watchtowers and small forts numbered WP 15/11 to 15/26 lies in the wooded hills here, between Riedenburg, Dietfurt and the Danube town of Vohburg.

The Raetian Limes was a continuous barrier, at first a wooden palisade and later a stone wall, running across southern Germany to the Danube, where it ended near Eining. Watchtowers stood along it at regular intervals, and soldiers in them could signal to each other and to the forts behind. Today, most of what survives is in the form of low earthworks, foundations and lines in the forest, sometimes with a reconstructed tower or information board. The frontier is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire site. It is a place for the imagination as much as the eyes.

The riding is lovely in a relaxed way. The roads along the Altmühl between Riedenburg, Dietfurt and Kelheim follow the river through the valley with gentle bends and views of cliffs and castles. Riedenburg has three castles on the heights above it, including Rosenburg, which has a falconry show. Side roads climb out of the valley onto the Jura plateau, crossing forests and fields with long curves and very little traffic. Surfaces are generally excellent, as you would expect in Bavaria, but watch out for cyclists on the valley roads in summer, when the Altmühltal cycle path is busy.

Riedenburg, about eleven kilometres away, has fuel, cafés and restaurants. Dietfurt is famous for an odd local custom: it calls itself Bavarian China, and its carnival includes a Chinese-themed parade. The Bavarian beer gardens around here are the obvious place for lunch, with a roast pork and a dark beer. Autumn, when the beech woods turn and mist lingers in the valley, is beautiful but sometimes chilly in the mornings.
t.fort site and civil settlement of pfoerr:
Between Ingolstadt and Kelheim, the Danube flows through a broad, flat valley in Bavaria, with hop gardens, fields of maize and asparagus beds on its banks. Pförring is a small market town on the north bank, with Neustadt an der Donau and Vohburg on the other side. In Roman times, this was the frontier: the Raetian Limes ended at the Danube just downstream, and the Romans built a fort here, known as Celeusum, with a civil settlement outside its walls.

The fort at Pförring housed a cavalry unit and guarded a crossing of the Danube and the road along the river. The surrounding settlement, where traders, craftsmen and soldiers' families lived, grew up next to it. Today, the site is mostly fields, and the outline of the fort can be seen in places as slight earthworks, with information boards explaining what stood there. The fort is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire site. A few kilometres downstream, at Eining, the fort of Abusina has well-preserved stone foundations and is one of the most visited Roman sites in Bavaria.

This stretch of the Danube is also known for the Hallertau, the world's largest hop-growing region, which lies just to the south. In late summer, the hop gardens, with their tall poles and wires, are full of green cones, and the smell of hops hangs in the air. Neustadt an der Donau has a spa, Bad Gögging, with thermal baths that the Romans also used.

The riding here is flat and pleasant, along the Danube and through the farmland, with gentle curves and little traffic on the smaller roads. For more interesting riding, head north into the Altmühl valley and the Franconian Jura, with its limestone cliffs, castles and winding roads, or south into the rolling hills of the Hallertau. The surfaces are generally excellent.

Neustadt an der Donau, about seven kilometres away, has fuel and all services, as does Vohburg. Local food includes the white asparagus of Abensberg in spring, Bavarian roast pork, and the beer of the region, brewed with the local hops. Spring and late summer, when the hops are ready for harvest, are the best times to visit.
t.laghetto della costa@45.3,11.7:
The Euganean Hills rise abruptly from the flat plain south-west of Padua, a cluster of volcanic cones covered in vineyards, chestnut woods and olive groves. Arquà Petrarca, a medieval village on the southern slopes, is where the poet Petrarch spent his last years and died in 1374; his house can still be visited. Close by, in a small hollow between the hills, lies the Laghetto della Costa, a tiny lake that hides a big secret.

In the mud at the bottom of the lake, archaeologists found the remains of a Bronze Age pile-dwelling settlement, with wooden posts, pottery and other objects preserved in the wet sediment. It is one of the sites included in the UNESCO-listed Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, inscribed in 2011, which covers more than a hundred sites in six countries. There is little to see at the lake itself, but the setting, a quiet pond surrounded by trees and hills, is lovely, and finds from the area's prehistoric sites are displayed in regional museums such as the one at Este.

The Euganean Hills have long been known for their thermal springs. Abano Terme and Montegrotto Terme, on the eastern side of the hills, are among the largest spa resorts in Europe, with hot mud and water used since Roman times. Battaglia Terme, nearby, has a castle-like villa, the Catajo, with frescoed halls. Monselice, a few kilometres away, is a town with a castle and a sanctuary on its hill.

The riding in the Euganean Hills is excellent. The roads that wind around and over the hills, through vineyards and woods, toward Teolo, Torreglia, Cinto Euganeo and Arquà, are twisty and scenic, with little traffic. The hills are small, so you can cover a lot of ground in a short time. The surfaces are generally good. The roads on the plain are flat and busy.

Monselice, about four kilometres away, has fuel and all services. Local food includes the wines of the Colli Euganei, especially the sweet Fior d'Arancio, and jujube broth, a liqueur made from jujube fruit in Arquà Petrarca. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer on the Venetian plain is hot and humid.
t.skocjan caves@45.7,14.0:
Underneath the sleepy stone villages of the Slovenian Karst, a river called the Reka plunges into the earth and carves one of the largest underground canyons known anywhere. The Škocjan Caves, a UNESCO site since 1986, are the reason the word karst became the scientific name for this kind of limestone landscape everywhere in the world. Inside, a narrow footbridge spans the Reka gorge far above the roaring water, the chamber walls disappear into darkness, and the scale is so huge that your mind struggles to accept it is all underground.

The guided tour takes a couple of hours and is well worth it; the temperature in the caves stays cool all year, so bring a layer even on a hot day, and the paths are damp and steep in places. Outside, the trail around the collapsed dolines of Velika and Mala dolina shows where the cave roof fell in long ago, and the tiny village of Škocjan clings to the rock above them. Swallows, bats and the sound of running water fill the air.

The Karst plateau is a lovely place to ride. Narrow roads connect stone villages through oak scrub, sumac that turns scarlet in autumn, and dry stone walls, with vineyards growing the dark local Teran grape and smokehouses curing pršut ham. Corners are tight, surfaces mostly good, traffic light away from the main roads, and the views stretch toward the Adriatic around Trieste. Be warned about the bora, the cold northeasterly wind that can blow here with frightening force, especially in winter, rocking a bike sideways on exposed stretches. Spring and autumn are perfect, summer is warm but rarely brutal up here.

Divača, three kilometres away, is a small town with fuel, a supermarket and simple places to eat; Sežana, about eleven kilometres away, is larger and has more choice. The motorway between Ljubljana and the coast passes close by, and remember that Slovenian motorways require a vignette, motorbikes included. Lipica, home of the Lipizzaner horses, is a short ride away, and so is the Vilenica cave, one of the oldest show caves in Europe. Finish the day in a family farm tavern with a glass of Teran and a plate of pršut and cheese, and you will understand why people who come here once usually return.
t.hirschleitengraben wachtturm@48.3,14.2:
Just west of Linz, the Danube narrows and the steep, wooded slopes of the Kürnberger Wald rise from its southern bank. In the Roman period this river was the frontier of the empire, and the soldiers who guarded it built a chain of forts and watchtowers along the bank to watch for raiders crossing from the north. The Hirschleitengraben watchtower is one of these, a small Roman tower in a side ravine of the forest, part of the Danube Limes, which UNESCO listed in 2021 as one of the great frontiers of the Roman Empire. Its remains are modest, but the position, looking over the river toward Puchenau and the hills of the Mühlviertel, makes the purpose clear.

The Kürnberger Wald is a popular recreational area for the people of Linz, with paths through beech and oak forest, and there are legends connecting it with the Nibelungenlied, the epic of the Burgundian heroes, whose journey down the Danube passed through this region. In spring the forest floor is covered with wild garlic, and the smell fills the air.

The riding along the Danube here is gentle and scenic, with roads on both banks following the river through villages and fields. Upstream, the Danube valley becomes more dramatic, with the famous Schlögener Schlinge, a tight double meander through steep forested hills, and the roads on the north bank climb up into the Mühlviertel, a rolling upland of granite, forests and farms with plenty of curves. Traffic around Linz can be heavy, especially at rush hour, and Austrian motorways require a vignette, motorcycles included. The Danube cycle path is very popular in summer, so expect many cyclists on the riverside roads.

Linz, about five kilometres away, is a lively city with all services, from fuel to motorcycle shops. Its cultural scene is surprisingly modern, with the Ars Electronica Center and the Lentos art museum on the riverbanks, as well as a charming old town around the main square. Local specialities include the Linzer Torte, one of the oldest known cake recipes, made with nuts and redcurrant jam, and hearty Austrian dishes like schnitzel and dumplings. Wilhering Abbey, a short ride upstream, has one of the most beautiful rococo churches in Austria.
t.rose island@47.9,11.3:
Lake Starnberg, south-west of Munich, is the lake where Bavaria's Fairy Tale King met his end. Ludwig II drowned in its waters near Berg in 1886, in circumstances that are still debated, and a cross stands in the lake where his body was found. On the opposite shore, near Feldafing, lies the small Roseninsel, or Rose Island, the only island in the lake. Ludwig's father Maximilian II had a little villa built there, surrounded by a rose garden, and Ludwig used it as a retreat, sometimes meeting his cousin, the Empress Elisabeth of Austria, known as Sisi, who spent her childhood at nearby Possenhofen.

The island is also listed by UNESCO for a much older reason. Around its shores lie the remains of prehistoric pile dwellings, part of the transnational World Heritage site of Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps. You will not see them, as they lie under water and mud, but they show that people lived on and around the island thousands of years before the kings.

Getting to the island is part of the charm. A small boat runs across the narrow strait from the shore near Feldafing in the warmer months, and the crossing takes just a few minutes. The villa can be visited on guided tours, and the rose garden is in full bloom in early summer. The park around Feldafing, with old trees and lakeside paths, is a lovely place to walk.

The roads around Lake Starnberg are pleasant but busy, particularly on summer weekends, when half of Munich heads out to the lakes. Traffic jams, cyclists and pedestrians are common, and speed limits are low and enforced. The real riding lies further south, towards the Alps: roads lead to Kochel, the Walchensee and the Kesselberg, a twisty mountain road that is a favourite of riders but has seasonal weekend restrictions for motorbikes because of accidents and noise. Check the current rules before planning a route.

Fuel and supplies are easy to find in Starnberg, Tutzing and Pöcking, all close by. Lakeside beer gardens serve Bavarian food, roast pork, sausages and pretzels, under chestnut trees. Sit by the water with a cold drink, and watch the paddle steamers glide by.
t.villa pisani ferri@45.4,11.4:
Andrea Palladio was still a young architect, not long out of his training as a stonemason, when the Pisani brothers, members of a powerful Venetian family, asked him to design a country house at Bagnolo, near Lonigo, in the late 1530s or early 1540s. The result, now known as Villa Pisani Ferri, is one of his early villas, a solid, symmetrical house with a grand central hall and a facade facing the river, part of the UNESCO site of the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto. Visits depend on the owners' arrangements, so check ahead if you hope to go inside.

Palladio's villas were not just luxury retreats. They were working farm estates, built at a time when Venetian families were investing in agriculture on the mainland, and they combined elegant living quarters with barns, stables and storage. Their classical forms, inspired by ancient Roman temples and houses, influenced architects for centuries, from England to the United States.

Lonigo, a short distance away, is a market town with a large church, a historic horse fair and, on the hill above, the Rocca Pisana, a villa built by Vincenzo Scamozzi, Palladio's pupil, for the same family. To the north-east rise the Colli Berici, a range of low limestone hills with vineyards, olive groves, caves and small villages, famous for their wines, including the local red variety called Tai Rosso.

The riding in the Colli Berici is delightful. Narrow roads climb and twist through the hills, with views over the plain towards the Alps on clear days and quiet villages to pass through. Traffic is light, though cyclists are common on weekends. On the plain, roads are flat and straight, sometimes busy with trucks. Fog is common in autumn and winter, and summer can be hot and humid, so spring and early autumn are the best times to visit.

Lonigo, about three kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a plate of bigoli, thick spaghetti traditionally served with duck sauce, or baccalà alla vicentina, salt cod slow-cooked in milk and served with polenta, washed down with a glass of local wine.
t.villa angarano@45.8,11.7:
Bassano del Grappa sits where the river Brenta leaves the mountains and spreads onto the Venetian plain, and its symbol is a covered wooden bridge, the Ponte Vecchio, designed by Palladio in the sixteenth century and rebuilt several times since after floods and wars. On the right bank of the river, just outside the town, stands Villa Angarano, a country house whose two long colonnaded wings were designed by Palladio, while the central residence was built later, in a different style, by the Venetian architect Baldassare Longhena. The villa is still a working wine estate and belongs to the UNESCO site of the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto.

Bassano is a town to linger in. Its streets are lined with arcades and painted facades, and by the bridge stands a distillery making grappa since the eighteenth century, where you can taste the strong grape spirit standing at the counter. In spring, Bassano is famous for its white asparagus, served with boiled eggs and a simple dressing. The bridge was also a key point in the First World War, and the alpine troops who fought nearby are honoured throughout the town.

Above Bassano looms Monte Grappa, a massive mountain at the edge of the Alps that was the scene of bitter fighting between Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces in 1917 and 1918. At the summit, over seventeen hundred metres high, stands a huge memorial and ossuary containing the remains of thousands of soldiers. The road up from Romano d'Ezzelino, known as the Cadorna road after the general who built it, climbs in a long series of hairpins with views over the plain, and it is a classic motorcycle ride.

To the north, the Valsugana follows the Brenta into the mountains towards Trento, with a fast main road and quieter roads along the river. The roads around Bassano can be busy, and the climbs to Monte Grappa are popular on weekends with cyclists and riders, so take care on blind bends. Weather in the mountains changes quickly, and the top can be cold and foggy even in summer.

Bassano has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants. Stand on the old bridge with a glass of grappa or a mezzo e mezzo aperitivo, and watch the river rush by beneath you.
t.villa cornaro@45.6,12.0:
Piombino Dese is a quiet village on the flat plain between Padua and Treviso, the kind of place you pass through on the way to somewhere else. Stop on the main road, though, and look at the house set back behind its lawn. Villa Cornaro was designed by Andrea Palladio in the early 1550s for Giorgio Cornaro, a member of one of the grandest Venetian families, and its central portico rises in two storeys of columns, one loggia stacked on another like a temple front on a temple front. On the garden side the same double loggia faces a long lawn. It is one of the most copied houses in architectural history, and echoes of it can be seen in country houses across England and in mansions of the American South. The villa is part of the UNESCO site of the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto, and it opens to visitors on certain days in the warmer months.

Unlike some of Palladio's farm villas, this one sits right in the village, facing the road, as if it wanted to be seen. Inside, the rooms are decorated with stucco and statues added in later centuries, and the proportions are as harmonious as the facade promises.

The surrounding countryside is the flat heart of the Veneto, crossed by irrigation channels, fields of maize and soya, vineyards and lines of poplars. Castelfranco Veneto, a short ride north, is a walled town with a moat and a red brick tower, birthplace of the painter Giorgione, whose mysterious altarpiece hangs in the cathedral. The town also gives its name to a speckled variety of radicchio, cream-coloured with red flecks, a winter favourite in local kitchens.

The riding here is flat and straightforward, honestly more about getting from one beautiful town to another than about the road itself. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads, with trucks and impatient drivers, and fog is common in the autumn and winter. For more interesting riding, head north to the hills around Asolo, with their winding lanes and views over the plain.

Trebaseleghe, about four kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, with fuel and shops. Try a risotto with radicchio, or a plate of local cured meats with a glass of Prosecco from the hills to the north, served at a village trattoria.
t.watchtowers wp 15 8 to 15 10@48.9,11.4:
The Raetian Limes, the eastern stretch of Rome's frontier in Germany, was built differently from its western counterpart. Instead of a wooden palisade, the Romans eventually raised a stone wall here, running for over a hundred and sixty kilometres across what is now Bavaria, towards the Danube. Locals later called it the Teufelsmauer, the Devil's Wall, convinced that only a demon could have built something so long. Watchtowers stood along it every few hundred metres, and the group between WP 15/8 and 15/10, in the hills between Greding and Dietfurt, is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire. In places, low remains of the wall and towers can be traced in the forest and fields.

The area lies within the Altmühltal Nature Park, one of Germany's largest nature parks, a landscape of limestone plateaus cut by deep valleys, with juniper heaths, rocky cliffs and quiet villages. The Altmühl river winds slowly through it, and at Solnhofen, to the west, quarries of fine limestone have yielded the famous Archaeopteryx fossils, the feathered link between dinosaurs and birds. The limestone was also used for lithography printing stones around the world.

To the south-east, at Kelheim, the Danube cuts through a narrow gorge, and Weltenburg Abbey, on a bend of the river, has a Baroque church and one of the oldest monastic breweries in the world. Greding has an almost complete medieval town wall with towers, and Dietfurt holds a famous Chinese-themed carnival every year, a local tradition with a curious history.

The riding is excellent. Roads wind through valleys and over plateaus, with plenty of bends, gentle climbs and little traffic away from the main routes. Surfaces are generally good. Watch for cyclists, especially along the Altmühl, and tractors in the fields. Wildlife crosses frequently, and fog can fill the valleys in the mornings in autumn. Summer weekends bring more traffic and police checks.

Greding, about fourteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and inns. Try a Bavarian lunch, roast pork with dumplings, or a plate of local trout, with a beer from one of the many small breweries in the region, saving the beer for when the bike is parked for the night.
t.villa barbaro@45.8,12.0:
At the foot of the Asolo hills, near the village of Maser, a long, golden villa looks out over the plain with the mountains behind it. Villa Barbaro was designed by Andrea Palladio in the 1550s for the brothers Daniele and Marcantonio Barbaro, cultivated Venetian patricians, and it is one of his most perfect works, combining a central house like a temple with long arcaded wings for farm buildings. Inside, the rooms are covered with frescoes by Paolo Veronese, among the finest of the Venetian Renaissance: painted landscapes, mythological figures and trompe l'oeil doors with servants peeping through, a game of illusion that still surprises visitors. Behind the villa, a nymphaeum with statues and a pool sits against the hillside, and nearby stands the Tempietto, a small round church also designed by Palladio. The villa is part of the UNESCO site of the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto, and it remains a working estate producing wine.

Asolo, a few kilometres west, is a charming hill town once ruled by Caterina Cornaro, the Venetian-born queen of Cyprus, and later beloved of poets and travellers. To the east, the Prosecco hills of Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, a World Heritage site since 2019, roll in steep, vine-covered ridges, a landscape of hogback hills and tiny villages.

The riding is delightful. Narrow roads climb and twist through the hills above Maser and Asolo, past vineyards, woods and villas, with views over the plain. The Montello, a long wooded hill to the south-east, has a grid of quiet roads and memorials to the battles of the First World War, fought along the river Piave nearby. The Prosecco roads are steep and winding, busy with cyclists and visitors on weekends, especially in autumn during the harvest. Surfaces are generally good, but narrow sections and tight bends demand care.

Cornuda, about three kilometres away, has fuel and shops. Try a glass of Prosecco Superiore from the hills, or the villa's own wine, with a plate of sopressa, a local salami, and polenta, or a risotto with local mushrooms in autumn. An afternoon at the villa, followed by a ride through the hills to Asolo, makes a perfect day.
t.fort site of burgsalach@49.0,11.1:
The small fortlet at Burgsalach stood on the Raetian Limes, the eastern section of Rome's frontier in Germany. Dating from a late phase of the frontier, it had walls of stone and was compact and well defended, more like a small castle than the usual timber watchtower, and its name lives on in the village of Burgsalach nearby. The outline of the walls can still be traced on the ground, and like the rest of the frontier it is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire. Here, in the hills of Middle Franconia, the Raetian Limes was not a palisade but a stone wall, which local legend later attributed to the Devil himself, calling it the Teufelsmauer.

The area is part of the Franconian Jura, a limestone plateau with dry grasslands, juniper heaths, beech forests and deep valleys. To the south, the Altmühl valley cuts a winding course through the Jura, with rock formations and cliffs, and it is one of the most scenic river valleys in Bavaria. The region around Solnhofen, nearby, is famous for its fine limestone, quarried for lithographic printing and the source of the Archaeopteryx fossils.

Weißenburg in Bayern, eight kilometres away, is a delightful old town with medieval walls and gates, and its Roman past is impressive: the remains of a fort, a reconstructed gate, Roman baths and a museum displaying a treasure hoard of silver and bronze objects found in a garden in 1979. The riding is pleasant, with country roads crossing the Jura plateau, gently rolling, with good surfaces and little traffic. The Altmühl valley roads are more scenic, with tight bends and views of the cliffs, but busier in summer with cyclists and tourists.

Weißenburg has fuel, supermarkets and a good choice of restaurants and beer gardens. Franconia is known for its breweries, and many villages have their own. Try Schäufele, roast pork shoulder with crispy crackling, Franconian sausages with sauerkraut or Karpfen, fried carp, in the months with an R. On a summer evening, a beer garden under chestnut trees is hard to beat.
t.villa godi malinverni@45.7,11.5:
Every great architect has to start somewhere, and Andrea Palladio started here. Villa Godi, built for the Godi brothers in the late 1530s and early 1540s at Lugo di Vicenza, is considered his first villa, and you can already see the ideas that would make him famous: a clear, symmetrical plan, a central hall flanked by rooms in harmonious proportion, and a building set carefully into the landscape, here on a terrace looking out over the plain. It is still a little stern compared with his later villas, but the frescoes inside, by painters such as Giovanni Battista Zelotti, are lively and colourful. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto.

The villa sits at the foot of the Asiago plateau, where the Venetian plain meets the first slopes of the Prealps. The hills around Breganze are covered in vineyards, producing Torcolato, a sweet golden dessert wine made from dried Vespaiola grapes, as well as reds and whites. Above, the Asiago plateau was the scene of fierce fighting during the First World War, and its forests and meadows are dotted with trenches, forts and memorials. It is also the home of Asiago cheese, sold fresh or aged in every village.

For riders, the climb from the plain to the plateau is the main event. The road from Thiene or Lugo via the Costo is a series of tight hairpins, with views back over the plain, and other roads climb steeply through the forest to the plateau. Up there, the roads are fast and open, crossing meadows and forests, with little traffic outside weekends. In winter, snow covers the plateau, and the roads can be icy.

Lugo di Vicenza is a small village with a few cafés, and Breganze, five kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Thiene, a little further, has a larger choice. Try bigoli, thick spaghetti, with duck sauce, or polenta with local cheese and mushrooms, and a glass of Breganze wine if your ride is over. A slice of Asiago cheese and a crusty roll make a good lunch on the go.
t.villa chiericati@45.5,11.6:
Villa Chiericati stands in the flat countryside east of Vicenza, at Vancimuglio near Grumolo delle Abbadesse, a cube of pale plaster with a deep, columned portico that looks as if a Roman temple has been grafted onto a farmhouse. That is precisely what Palladio intended. Designed in the 1550s for Giovanni Chiericati, it is often cited as one of the first villas in which he gave the main façade a full temple front, an idea he would repeat, refine and make famous, and which architects copied for centuries afterwards, from English country houses to the American South. Like the other Palladian villas of the Veneto, it is part of the UNESCO site that includes the city of Vicenza.

Vicenza, a short ride west, is Palladio's city. Its Basilica Palladiana, a medieval town hall wrapped in a double loggia of arches, dominates the main square, and the Teatro Olimpico, his last work, has a stage set of streets receding in perfect perspective, built in wood and stucco. The city also has a famous villa just outside town, La Rotonda, perched on a hill with four identical porticoes. South of Vicenza, the Berici hills are dotted with villas, vineyards and caves, and the road along their eastern edge, the Riviera Berica, is a pleasant ride.

The riding here is mostly about the plain: flat, straight roads between fields of maize and vines, with towns and villages close together and frequent roundabouts. Traffic can be heavy around Vicenza and on the main roads, but the minor roads are quieter. The Colli Berici offer more interesting riding, with short climbs and tight bends through woods and vineyards. Summer is hot and humid, with mosquitoes in the evenings; winter brings fog that can be thick enough to stop you in your tracks.

Torri di Quartesolo, two kilometres away, has fuel, shopping centres and services. Vicenza has everything you could want. The city's signature dish is baccalà alla vicentina, dried cod slow-cooked in milk and served with polenta, and you should try the wines from the Colli Berici, such as Tai Rosso, a light, fruity red.
t.see@47.8,13.4:
At the southeastern tip of the Mondsee, where the lake narrows toward the Attersee and the cliffs of the Drachenwand and the Schafberg crowd in on both sides, lies a hamlet with the shortest name you will find on any map: See. Just offshore, in the shallow water where the lake drains, divers found the remains of a prehistoric pile-dwelling settlement, and the finds were so characteristic that archaeologists named a whole Neolithic culture after the lake: the Mondsee culture, known for its decorated pottery and early copper working. The site is part of the UNESCO listing of Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, and as with most of them, there is nothing to see except the water, which is part of the point.

The Mondsee is one of the warmest lakes in the Salzkammergut, and in summer its shores are busy with swimmers, sailors and stand-up paddlers. The town of Mondsee at the northern end has a grand baroque basilica, made famous by the wedding scene in The Sound of Music, and a lively square with cafés. The Drachenwand, the dragon wall, rises above the western shore, with a via ferrata that attracts climbers from all over.

The riding is classic Salzkammergut. The road along the southern shore of the Mondsee is narrow and twisting, squeezed between the lake and the cliffs, with tunnels and great views, and it leads on to the Attersee, where the road follows the shore through villages and orchards. Over the Scharfling pass, a short climb takes you to St Gilgen and the Wolfgangsee. Traffic can be heavy in summer, with tourists, cyclists and caravans, and the police are vigilant about noise and speed. Spring and autumn are quieter and often clearer.

There are no services at See itself, but Unterach and Mondsee, a few kilometres away, have fuel, shops and restaurants, and Gmunden, about thirty kilometres off, is the largest town in the area. Lakeside inns serve Reinanke, a whitefish from the lake, often smoked or fried, and Kaiserschmarrn, a fluffy shredded pancake with plum compote. After a hot day, a swim in the lake is one of life's simpler pleasures.
t.fort site and civil settlement of koschi:
North of the Danube, on the edge of the Franconian Jura, the Romans built a string of forts behind the Raetian frontier to guard the river valley and the roads leading to it. Kösching, today a market town near Ingolstadt, was the site of one of them, an auxiliary fort with a civilian settlement around it, home to craftsmen, traders and the families of soldiers. Little is visible today, as the modern town has grown over it, but the site is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire. The Danube valley was a busy corridor in Roman times, and remains so today.

Ingolstadt, a few kilometres away, is a city of contrasts. It was a Bavarian fortress town and the seat of the first Bavarian university, founded in 1472, where, in fiction, Mary Shelley's Victor Frankenstein created his monster. It was also here, in 1516, that the Bavarian Purity Law was proclaimed, decreeing that beer could only be made from water, barley and hops. Today, Ingolstadt is best known as the home of Audi, whose headquarters and museum, the Audi museum mobile, display the company's history from early cars to racing machines, including some lovely old motorcycles from the brands that merged into Auto Union.

The riding is varied. The roads along the Danube are flat and fast, with views of the river, but to the north, the Altmühl valley offers more interesting riding, with curves, cliffs and pretty villages. A little to the east, the Danube cuts through a narrow limestone gorge near Kelheim, and at its entrance stands Weltenburg Abbey, home to one of the oldest monastery breweries in the world. The road to it is narrow and busy in summer, but well worth it.

Kösching, Gaimersheim and Vohburg are small towns with fuel and shops, and Ingolstadt has everything. Try a Weißwurst, a white veal sausage eaten before noon with sweet mustard and a pretzel, or a roast pork with dumplings and gravy. And of course, a beer, brewed according to the Purity Law, preferably in a beer garden under chestnut trees, but only when your riding is done.
t.watchtowers wp 14 63 to 14 78 including:
Between Greding and Eichstätt, the Raetian Limes runs across the high Franconian Jura plateau, and the names on the map, WP 14/63 to 14/78, are archaeologists' shorthand for a sequence of Roman watchtower sites along this section of the frontier. The Raetian Limes was the wall part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes, inscribed by UNESCO as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire. Here, the Romans built a stone wall rather than the timber palisade used further west. Locals later called the remains the Teufelsmauer, the Devil's Wall, believing nothing human could have built it.

Today the line is a low bank through fields and woods, marked in places by reconstructed tower footprints or signboards, and a walking and cycle route follows it. To see more, head to Kipfenberg, where a Limes museum explains the frontier, or to the reconstructed Roman fort at Pfünz near Eichstätt, which gives a vivid impression of a garrison post above the Altmühl valley.

The Altmühl valley is the real star for riders. The river winds through a deep, wooded limestone gorge with white cliffs, junipers and castles perched on crags, and the road along it from Kipfenberg to Eichstätt and on to Dollnstein is one of the most pleasant in Bavaria. Climbs out of the valley onto the plateau are short and twisty, and the plateau roads are fast and open, with villages of stone houses topped by slate-like limestone roofs. Weekends bring cyclists and canoeists, so take care on narrow bends.

The Altmühltal is a nature park, and its quarries at Solnhofen and around Eichstätt have produced some of the most famous fossils in the world, including the Archaeopteryx. The Jura Museum in Eichstätt shows a specimen. Fuel and food are easy in Greding or Eichstätt, a Baroque bishop's town with a cathedral and a university. Bavarian beer gardens along the river provide shade and a cold drink on a hot afternoon, and spring and autumn bring the clearest light to the valley.
t.fort site and civil settlement of pfunz@:
Above the village of Pfünz, on a spur of white Jura limestone looking down into the Altmühl valley, the Romans built a fort they called Vetoniana. Today a reconstructed gate and a stretch of wall stand on the hilltop, and from up there you understand the choice at once: the valley floor curls below you, the river meanders slowly, and anyone moving along it would have been seen hours before they arrived.

The fort belonged to the Raetian section of the Limes, the long frontier that ran from the Rhine to the Danube, and Pfünz guarded the hinterland a little south of the wall itself. Its end was violent. During the Germanic raids of the third century the garrison was overrun, and excavations found clear traces of a sudden attack. Below the fort lay the civil settlement where traders, craftsmen and soldiers' families lived, now just meadows and a few marked outlines. It is a quiet, slightly melancholy place, best visited when nobody else is there, which is most of the time.

The Altmühltal Nature Park is one of the great motorcycling valleys of Bavaria without being famous for it. The road between Eichstätt and Kipfenberg follows the river in long, flowing bends past juniper heaths and pale crags known as the Twelve Apostles further upstream near Solnhofen. Side roads climb out onto the Jura plateau through beech woods and drop back down in tight turns. Watch for cyclists on the valley route, which is one of Germany's most popular bike paths, and for gravel thrown onto the bends by farm traffic. Spring and early autumn are ideal; summer weekends get busy with canoes and campers.

The rock is the thing. This is the same fine-grained limestone that gave the world Archaeopteryx, found in the quarries around Solnhofen and Eichstätt, and you can see fossils in the museum at the Willibaldsburg, the fortress above Eichstätt. The town itself, five kilometres away, is the obvious place for fuel and lunch: a compact baroque bishop's seat with a cathedral, a university, plenty of beer gardens and the honey-coloured squares the Italian-trained architects left behind after the Thirty Years War. Fill up there, because Pfünz itself is a village with a church and not much else.
t.fort site and civil settlement of ruffen:
There is nothing to climb at Ruffenhofen, and that is the clever part. The Roman fort here, on gently rising ground above the Wörnitz near Weiltingen and Wittelshofen, has never been rebuilt in stone. Instead, the outline of the walls, gates and the buildings of the settlement around it has been traced across the fields with hedges, trees and mown strips, so the whole place reads like a plan drawn in plants. From the little viewing hill you can see the shape of a garrison that has been underground for seventeen centuries.

The fort sat just behind the Raetian Limes in western Middle Franconia, a cavalry and infantry post watching a frontier that was then the edge of the empire. Geophysical surveys mapped it in remarkable detail without much digging, and the Limeseum next to the park explains what they found with a refreshingly modern touch. It is worth an hour, especially if you have been riding past Limes signs all week without quite knowing what you were looking at.

The country around is soft, rolling farmland, wide skies and small villages with steep red roofs. The great landmark is the Hesselberg, the highest point in Middle Franconia at 689 metres, a long whaleback hill that rises out of the plain a few kilometres to the south and can be seen from everywhere. A small road climbs most of the way up, and from the top the view runs across the Ries crater towards the Swabian Jura. Local roads here are narrow and well surfaced, with sudden ninety-degree bends at field corners and the occasional tractor; they reward a relaxed pace.

For fuel and supplies, Wassertrüdingen is nine kilometres away and Dinkelsbühl, about fifteen to the west, is the better reason to make a detour: one of the best preserved medieval towns in Germany, with an intact ring of walls and towers on the Romantic Road. Weiltingen and Wittelshofen are small villages with a church and an inn rather than a full service stop. On a summer evening the light across the planted fort turns gold, the swallows hunt low over the hedges, and the only sound is the wind in the wheat. Hard to imagine a legionary feeling quite so peaceful here.
t.castellaro lagusello fondo tacoli@45.4,1:
South of Lake Garda, the land rises into a series of low hills, the moraines left behind by the glacier that carved the lake. Among them, in a hollow, lies a small heart-shaped lake, and on a ridge above it stands the walled village of Castellaro Lagusello, one of the most charming in Lombardy. The lake and its marshes are a nature reserve, and on its shore, at Fondo Tacoli, archaeologists found the remains of a Bronze Age pile dwelling settlement, part of the UNESCO group of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps.

The village itself is a medieval fortified hamlet, with walls, a tower gate and a castle that later became a villa. The houses inside are small and carefully restored, and the views over the lake and the surrounding hills are lovely. The morainic hills around are full of history: a few kilometres north lie Solferino and San Martino, where in 1859 French and Piedmontese armies defeated the Austrians in a battle so bloody that it inspired Henri Dunant to found the Red Cross. The ossuary chapel at Solferino and the tower at San Martino are moving memorials.

The riding in the morainic hills is a delight. Small roads wind over the hills and through the vineyards, with constant changes of direction and gradient, and views of the Garda and the Alps to the north. Traffic is light, except on summer weekends when visitors head to the lake. The roads can be narrow and occasionally gravelly, and agricultural traffic is common. Spring and autumn are best, with mild temperatures and beautiful light.

The villages around, such as Monzambano, Cavriana and Pozzolengo, are small but have fuel and basic services, and Valeggio sul Mincio, eight kilometres away, is a larger town. Valeggio is famous for its tortellini, called nodi d'amore, love knots, and the nearby village of Borghetto, with its water mills on the Mincio, is very pretty. The local wines include Lugana, a white from the southern shore of the lake. On a summer evening, the lake below Castellaro is calm and the frogs begin to sing.
t.okitsu miya yohaisho@33.9,130.4:
Some holy places are meant to be seen from a distance. Off the coast of Munakata, in Fukuoka Prefecture on the island of Kyushu, the island of Okinoshima rises from the Genkai Sea about sixty kilometres offshore. It is a sacred island where rituals were performed from the fourth to the ninth century, and tens of thousands of offerings, including mirrors, jewels and gold rings, were left on its rocks. Ordinary visitors are not allowed to land, so on the island of Oshima, closer to the mainland, stands the Okitsu-miya Yohaisho, a hall from which worshippers can pray towards Okinoshima across the sea.

The sites form the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Sacred Island of Okinoshima and Associated Sites in the Munakata Region, inscribed in 2017. The Munakata Taisha shrine consists of three parts: the Okitsu-miya on Okinoshima, the Nakatsu-miya on Oshima and the Hetsu-miya on the mainland. Strict rules still govern Okinoshima: women have traditionally been forbidden from landing, and men who were permitted to land, on a limited basis, had to purify themselves in the sea first.

Getting to the Yohaisho means taking the ferry from Kōnominato port in Munakata to Oshima, a short crossing. On the island, roads are narrow and quiet, winding along the coast and over the hills, with views across the sea. On clear days Okinoshima is visible on the horizon. On the mainland, the coast road along the Genkai Sea passes beaches, pine forests and fishing villages. Remember that Japan drives on the left, and that roads are well maintained but speed limits are low and strictly enforced. Typhoons can disrupt ferries in late summer and autumn.

Oshima is small, with a few shops and restaurants near the port; fuel is easier to find on the mainland in Munakata or Fukutsu, so fill up before crossing. The Hetsu-miya on the mainland has a museum displaying the offerings found on Okinoshima, which are designated national treasures. Fresh seafood is excellent here, especially squid and sea bream. Standing at the Yohaisho, looking out over the sea towards an island few can visit, is a strangely moving experience.
t.marmolada@46.4,11.9:
The Queen of the Dolomites, they call her, and the Marmolada earns the title: at 3,343 metres, Punta Penia is the highest summit of the range, and its northern flank carries the largest glacier in the Dolomites, while the south face drops away as a sheer wall of pale limestone. That glacier is shrinking fast, and in July 2022 a large section of it collapsed, killing eleven climbers, a tragedy that brought the effects of climate change home to everyone who loves these mountains.

The Marmolada saw some of the strangest fighting of the First World War. The front line between Italy and Austria-Hungary ran across the mountain, and Austrian troops dug a network of tunnels and shelters inside the glacier itself, the so-called City of Ice, where soldiers lived for months. Remains of the war still emerge from the melting ice. A museum at Punta Serauta, reached by the cable car from Malga Ciapela, tells the story.

The Passo Fedaia, at 2,057 metres, crosses the northern foot of the mountain, linking Canazei in the Val di Fassa with Malga Ciapela and the Agordino. The western side is gentle, passing the turquoise Lago di Fedaia reservoir with the glacier above, while the eastern ramp is one of the steepest pass roads in the Alps, a long, straight climb at gradients well into double figures. It is a challenging ride in both directions. The Sottoguda gorge below was badly damaged by the Vaia storm in 2018. The pass can close in winter and after heavy snow, and summer weekends bring heavy traffic and many cyclists.

Canazei, eight kilometres away, is a resort village with fuel, hotels and restaurants, and it makes a good base for exploring the Sella group and the passes around it, such as the Pordoi and the Sella. Malga Ciapela and Rocca Pietore on the east side have basic services. Ladin culture is strong in the valleys, with its own language and traditions, and the food mixes Italian and Tyrolean influences: canederli, dumplings, and polenta with venison. Early in the morning, the glacier catches the first light and the lake is still.
t.schlogen kastell@48.4,13.9:
The Danube here performs one of its most famous tricks. Forced by hard granite, the river makes two tight hairpin turns, the Schlögener Schlinge, doubling back on itself in a loop so neat it looks drawn with a compass. From the viewpoint on the wooded slope above, a short walk from the road, you look down on the river curling around a forested spur, and it is one of the classic images of Upper Austria.

The Romans knew this place well. The Danube was the frontier of their empire, and at Schlögen, on the south bank, they built a small fort to watch the river and the crossing. Its foundations were excavated and are partly visible near the hotel and campsite on the riverbank, and the site is part of the Danube Limes World Heritage Site. A bath house belonging to the fort has also been found. In those days the north bank, now the Mühlviertel, was barbarian territory, and the soldiers here looked across the water at forests they did not control.

Riding to Schlögen is half the pleasure. The B130 follows the south bank of the Danube through the gorge, a quiet, scenic road with gentle curves along the water. The north bank, in the Mühlviertel, is reached by small ferries that cross the river at several points, and the roads up there wind over a high granite plateau of fields, forests and villages, with lovely views back down into the valley. The roads climbing up from the river are steep and twisty, great fun on a dry day. The Danube cycle path runs right through, so expect plenty of cyclists in summer.

The nearest fuel is in the larger villages on the plateaus and in towns such as Eferding or Rohrbach, so plan accordingly. Kirchberg ob der Donau and Neukirchen am Walde are small villages with basic services. The Mühlviertel is known for its hearty food, such as dumplings, roast pork and bread made from local grain. In the morning, mist often fills the gorge and slowly lifts to reveal the river, a sight worth getting up early for.
t.watchtower wp 13 54@49.1,10.8:
Gunzenhausen is a small town in Middle Franconia, on the Altmühl river, and the Roman frontier ran right through it. Watchtower WP 13/54 stood within what is now the town, and the course of the frontier is traced through the streets. It is unusual to find the Roman frontier in an urban setting, and it is a nice surprise as you wander the streets.

The Raetian Limes, the section of the frontier in Bavaria, was a stone wall rather than a palisade, and it ran from the Danube near Kelheim westward through Franconia to meet the Upper Germanic Limes near Lorch. Gunzenhausen was on its line, and the town has made the most of it, with markers along the line and Roman finds in the local museum. Later the town was a residence of the margraves of Brandenburg-Ansbach, and its old centre has fine baroque buildings.

The area around Gunzenhausen is known as the Franconian Lake District, the Fränkisches Seenland, a series of artificial lakes created from the 1970s onwards to manage water and provide recreation. The Altmühlsee, right next to the town, is a large shallow lake with a bird island and beaches, popular in summer. The riding here is gentle: flat or rolling roads around the lakes and through farmland, with some more winding routes in the hills of the Altmühl valley to the south-east. Summer weekends bring crowds to the lakes.

Gunzenhausen has fuel, shops and restaurants, and its market square is pleasant for a break. Franconian food is hearty: Schäufele, roast pork shoulder with crackling, Bratwurst and dumplings, washed down with local beer from small breweries. The Brombachsee, the largest of the lakes, is a short ride south and has swimming beaches and boat trips. In the evening, the light over the Altmühlsee is lovely, and the birds on the island make a constant chatter.
t.tombola@45.2,11.2:
In the flat, fertile plain south of Verona, near the town of Cerea, a low rise in the fields called Tombola hides the remains of a Bronze Age settlement. The site is listed among the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it belongs to a group of wetland villages that once stood among the marshes of the Valli Grandi Veronesi, a large area of wetland that was drained and reclaimed over the centuries.

The Veronese lowlands were once a land of rivers and swamps, and the prehistoric settlements here were built on the edges of the wetlands, on platforms or islands, to take advantage of the water and the fertile soil. The marshes were drained in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and the landscape is now one of fields, canals and farms. Cerea is known for its furniture industry, with many workshops and showrooms, and the area around it produces rice, used in the local risotto all'isolana.

The riding here is flat and straightforward, with long straight roads across the plain, lined with poplars and canals. It is not exciting, but it is relaxing, and the light over the fields can be beautiful in the early morning or evening, with mist rising from the canals. The plain is hot and humid in summer, with mosquitoes, and foggy in winter. The Euganean Hills and the Berici Hills, to the east, offer more interesting riding, with winding roads through vineyards and villages, and the Palladian villas scattered across the countryside are worth seeking out.

Cerea, a town of thirteen thousand, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Casaleone and Asparetto are smaller villages nearby. Verona, about forty kilometres north, is one of the most beautiful cities in Italy, with its Roman arena and medieval centre. The local food includes risotto all'isolana, a rice dish with pork, and pandoro, the Christmas cake of Verona. Riding across the plain in the evening, with the sun setting over the fields and the church towers silhouetted against the sky, has a quiet charm.
t.villa saraceno@45.3,11.6:
In the countryside south of the Berici Hills, near the village of Agugliaro, Villa Saraceno is one of the simplest and most elegant of Andrea Palladio's villas, built in the mid-sixteenth century for Biagio Saraceno, a Vicentine nobleman. It is a compact building with a classical portico of arches and a triangular pediment, set among farmland, and it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto.

Palladio's villas were designed not only as country residences for the Venetian nobility but also as working farms, and Villa Saraceno is a good example of this, with barns and outbuildings around it. Inside, the main rooms are decorated with frescoes. The villa was restored by the Landmark Trust, a British charity that rescues historic buildings and lets them as holiday accommodation, so it is possible to stay in it, though visits for the public are limited to certain days.

The riding around Villa Saraceno is gentle and pleasant. The roads cross the flat farmland of the lower Vicentine plain, with canals and poplars, and climb into the Berici Hills to the north, with winding roads through vineyards, woods and villages. The Euganean Hills, to the east, offer more winding roads and spa towns such as Abano Terme. The Palladian villas are scattered across the countryside, and a tour of them by motorcycle makes a lovely day. Summer is hot and humid, and spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Noventa Vicentina, three kilometres away, is a town of seven thousand with fuel, shops and restaurants, and Agugliaro and Campiglia dei Berici are smaller villages. Vicenza, about twenty-five kilometres north, is the city of Palladio, with the Basilica Palladiana and the Teatro Olimpico. The local food includes baccalà alla vicentina, stewed salt cod with polenta, and the wines of the Berici Hills, such as Tai Rosso. Standing in front of Villa Saraceno in the evening light, with the fields around it, you understand Palladio's vision of harmony between architecture and landscape.
t.albing legionslager@48.2,14.6:
There is almost nothing to see at Albing, and that is exactly what makes it a good story. Under these fields near the confluence of the Enns and the Danube lay one of the largest Roman military bases ever built in what is now Austria, a full legionary fortress raised in the later second century, around the time of the Marcomannic Wars, when Rome was fighting hard to hold the Danube against peoples from the north. It was planned on a grand scale and then, it seems, given up very soon after, probably because the site was too exposed to floods. The legion moved a few kilometres south to Lauriacum, the camp at today's Enns.

Aerial photographs and surveys have traced the outline of walls, gates and barracks under the crops, so when you stand at the edge of a field near Sankt Pantaleon you are looking at a ghost the size of a small town. It is part of the Danube Limes UNESCO site, along with many far more visible remains, and it rewards a bit of imagination more than a camera.

The ride around here is gentle and open. Flat farmland runs down to the Danube with its power station and locks, and the roads are fast, mostly straight and well surfaced, with gusty wind from the west on many days. North of the river the land climbs into the granite hills of the Mühlviertel, where you will find far better curves, while south of Enns the roads begin to roll toward the foothills of the Alps. Across the Danube stands Mauthausen, whose concentration camp memorial is a sober and important place to visit if you have the time and the frame of mind.

For practical matters, ride to Enns, about six kilometres away. It is a proper town with fuel, shops and cafés around a main square dominated by a tall sixteenth-century city tower, and it likes to call itself the oldest town in Austria on the strength of a town charter from 1212. The museum there tells the story of Lauriacum and makes Albing make sense.

Come in early summer when the barley is up and low evening sun brings out faint crop marks in the fields; with a bit of luck you might spot the lines yourself. Otherwise, enjoy the irony of a mighty fortress that the river beat before any enemy could.
t.kalkalpen urlach@47.8,14.2:
Somewhere in these forests a beech tree has been standing since before anyone thought to draw a border here, and the Kalkalpen National Park exists largely to keep it that way. This is the largest protected forest area in Austria, spread across the limestone ranges of the Sengsengebirge and the Reichraminger Hintergebirge in Upper Austria, and parts of it belong to the UNESCO listing of ancient and primeval beech forests of Europe. Urlach lies on the edge of that wild country, in the folds above the Steyr valley between Molln and Windischgarsten.

You do not ride into the park proper; the roads stop at its edge and the interior belongs to walkers, chamois, red deer and woodpeckers. What you do ride is wonderful in its own right. The Steyrtal road follows the river through a valley of green pools and limestone gorges, and the side roads toward Molln and up toward the Hengstpass climb through forest with tight bends, narrow lanes and patches where shade keeps the tarmac damp long after rain. Watch for forestry trucks and gravel on the inside of corners, and for cyclists who know these roads as well as you do.

Molln is the nearest village with real services and has a curious claim to fame: it has been a centre of Jew's harp making for centuries, and the little twanging instruments are still produced there. Windischgarsten, on the other side, sits in a wide green basin at the foot of the Pyhrn and is the more convenient place for food, rooms and petrol. For a bigger town, Micheldorf and Kirchdorf on the Krems valley side are about eleven kilometres off.

The smell is what stays with you: wet limestone, resin, wild garlic in spring and, in autumn, the dry sweetness of beech leaves turning copper. The streams here run clear and cold over white gravel, and the national park visitor centres in Molln and Windischgarsten explain why so many rare beetles, owls and orchids still live here.

Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with fewer people and the beech canopy at its most dramatic. In midsummer, thunderstorms build over the limestone peaks in the afternoon, so plan your ride for the morning and leave the evening for a cold drink in the valley.
t.watchtowers wp 12 69 to 12 85@48.9,10.2:
In the forests near Ellwangen the Roman frontier changes character. Here the Upper Germanic Limes, with its timber palisade and ditch, meets the Raetian Limes, which the Romans eventually built as a stone wall, and the stretch of watchtowers numbered 12/69 to 12/85 runs through the farmland and woods east of the Jagst. Archaeologists number the towers with slashes and digits, which makes them sound like spare parts, but each one was a small stone or timber post with a few soldiers watching the border, passing signals along the line. Together they form part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

Not far away at Rainau-Dalkingen is one of the most remarkable remains of the whole Limes, a monumental gateway where the frontier was crossed, now protected under a modern glass building. Rainau-Buch also has a reconstructed fort area by a lake, and the Limes Museum in Aalen, about fifteen kilometres to the west, explains the frontier with real finds and models. Between them, the walking paths follow the line of the old wall through meadows and forest.

Ellwangen itself is a charming small baroque town of around twenty-five thousand people, with a basilica, a hilltop palace and, on the hill opposite, the pilgrimage church of Schönenberg, a fine landmark from many directions. It has everything a rider needs: fuel, food, cafés and a market square for people-watching. Westhausen and Hüttlingen are smaller but useful too.

The riding in the Ostalb is relaxed and rolling. Roads sweep through farmland and forest, with long views and gentle gradients. Surfaces are generally good, traffic light outside the main roads, but farm vehicles, cyclists and deer in the forest at dusk are part of the mix. Head south toward the Swabian Jura and the Härtsfeld for more relief, steeper valleys and the limestone escarpment above Aalen.

Come in late spring when the fields are bright with rapeseed, or in autumn when the forests turn golden. The light here is soft, the air smells of cut hay and pine, and the line of the Limes is often visible as a low ridge in the fields. Walk along it for a few minutes and consider how much effort an empire put into watching a border that was, for most of its length, simply forest.
t.dolomiti di brenta@46.2,10.9:
The Brenta Dolomites stand apart from the rest of the Dolomites, a separate range west of the Adige valley, and they look as if they were carved by someone with a taste for drama: sheer walls, needle-sharp spires and long ledges of pale limestone glowing pink at dawn and dusk. The range is part of the Dolomites UNESCO World Heritage site, listed in 2009, and it is protected within the Adamello Brenta Nature Park, home to brown bears, which were reintroduced here from Slovenia around the turn of the millennium.

Molveno and its neighbour Andalo are resort villages, busy with walkers and climbers in summer and skiers in winter, and the lake is one of the most beautiful in the Alps, with clear water reflecting the peaks. San Lorenzo in Banale, to the south, is a village of old stone farmhouses, quieter and more traditional. The famous via ferrata routes of the Brenta, iron-cable climbing paths, cross some of the wildest ledges in the range.

The riding here is superb. Roads climb from the Adige valley through the Rocchetta gorge and up to Andalo and Molveno, with tight hairpins and views over the lake. To the west, Madonna di Campiglio and the Campo Carlo Magno pass offer more curves, and to the south the roads through the Giudicarie valleys lead toward Lake Garda. Surfaces are generally good, but traffic can be heavy in high season, and cyclists are everywhere.

Molveno and Andalo have basic services, including cafés, restaurants and accommodation, but for a reliable choice of fuel and supermarkets, plan around Mezzolombardo, about sixteen kilometres away, or the larger resort towns. Local food includes canederli, bread dumplings, polenta with mushrooms or game, and cheeses from the mountain pastures. A glass of Teroldego, the red wine from the Rotaliana plain near Mezzolombardo, is a fine reward.

Come in late spring or early autumn, when the peaks are clear and the crowds thin. In midsummer, afternoon thunderstorms are common. Ride up to Molveno at dawn or dusk to see the Brenta turn pink above the lake.
t.villa foscari@45.4,12.2:
Locals call it La Malcontenta, the unhappy woman, and the stories about who she was are better than any of them can prove. The legend says a Foscari wife was banished here for her bad behaviour in Venice; the duller truth is that the name probably came from the area or a nearby canal long before the villa existed. Either way, the house Andrea Palladio built for the brothers Nicolò and Alvise Foscari around 1560 is one of his masterpieces, a temple-fronted block raised on a high base above the Brenta canal, looking out over the water like a Roman villa that had wandered down to the lagoon. It forms part of the UNESCO listing of the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto.

The Riviera del Brenta, the stretch of canal between Padua and Venice, was where Venetian patricians built their summer houses, and dozens of villas line the water at Mira, Dolo and Stra. Boats still carry visitors along the canal, through old locks and past swing bridges, on a route that the old burchiello passenger barges used to follow. Inside La Malcontenta, frescoes by Battista Franco and Giovanni Battista Zelotti decorate the halls, and the garden facing the canal is a calm place to sit.

Riding here is flat and often busy. The road along the canal is lovely to look at but crowded with traffic, cyclists and lorries heading for Mestre and the port of Marghera, and the many bridges, traffic lights and speed limits keep the pace slow. If you want curves, head south-west to the Euganean Hills beyond Padua, where volcanic cones covered with vineyards and chestnut woods offer short, twisty roads and thermal spa towns.

Mira and Mestre are both close, with all the fuel, shops and food you could want. Along the canal you will find trattorias serving Venetian cooking: bigoli in salsa, thick pasta with anchovy and onion, sarde in saor, sweet and sour sardines, and risotto with whatever the lagoon provides. Venice itself is a short hop away, though the bike stays on the mainland; Tronchetto and Piazzale Roma have car parks, and from there you walk or take the boat.

Spring and early autumn bring the kindest light on the canal, when the villa's white columns glow and mist rises off the water in the morning. Summer is hot, humid and generous with mosquitoes. Arrive on a weekday morning, stand at the water's edge and admire one of the most perfectly balanced buildings ever made.
t.fortified city of peschiera del garda@45:
Water surrounds Peschiera on every side, and that was the whole idea. The town sits where the River Mincio flows out of the southern end of Lake Garda, and in the sixteenth century the Republic of Venice turned it into a star-shaped fortress with massive pentagonal walls, bastions and moats fed by the lake and the river. Later the Austrians made it one of the four corners of the Quadrilatero, the defensive square of fortresses that guarded their hold on northern Italy in the nineteenth century. In 2017 Peschiera became part of the UNESCO listing of Venetian works of defence between the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, alongside Bergamo, Palmanova and fortresses on the Adriatic.

Walking around the walls, crossing the bridges over the canals and watching the boats slip out onto the lake, you get a vivid sense of a town that was built to resist cannon fire. Today the old barracks house shops and restaurants, the harbour is full of pleasure craft, and the lakeside promenade is lively on summer evenings.

The riding around Peschiera is a game of two halves. The lake roads, especially the Gardesana along the eastern shore, are beautiful but very crowded in summer, with slow traffic, buses, cyclists and pedestrians. South of the lake, the Mincio valley is a much quieter delight: gentle hills covered with vineyards, small roads through villages and the medieval village of Borghetto, with its fortified bridge and mills, just below Valeggio sul Mincio. Valeggio is famous for its tortellini, small hand-made pasta known locally as nodi d'amore, love knots.

Peschiera has fuel, shops and food in abundance. The local white wine is Lugana, made from vineyards on the southern shore of the lake, fresh and mineral, a perfect match for lake fish. Try grilled lavarello or perch fillets with risotto. Amusement parks nearby attract big crowds in summer, so expect traffic jams on the main roads at weekends.

Come out of season if you can, in spring or late September, when the lake is calm, the hills green or golden and the crowds thinner. Walk the walls at sunset, when the light turns the water pink and the fortress glows warm, and you will see why so many armies wanted this place.
t.villa pisani@45.2,11.5:
Montagnana is one of the best-preserved walled towns in Europe, with its entire ring of medieval brick walls, towers and gates still standing around the old centre, and just outside the eastern gate stands a villa by Andrea Palladio. Villa Pisani at Montagnana, built for Francesco Pisani in the 1550s, is a two-storey palace with a classical façade facing the road, part of the UNESCO listing of the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto. Unlike most of Palladio's country villas, it sits right at the edge of town, more urban palazzo than farmhouse, and its elegant columns make a striking contrast with the rugged walls nearby.

The town itself deserves a slow look. The walls run for about two kilometres, with twenty-four towers and two great fortified gates, the Rocca degli Alberi and the Castel San Zeno, and the cathedral in the main square holds paintings by Veronese and others. Montagnana is also famous for its prosciutto, the Veneto Berico-Euganeo ham, sweet and delicate, which you can taste in local shops and trattorias.

The riding in the plain around Montagnana is flat and straight, with fields of maize and soy, poplars along the canals and small villages with tall bell towers. It is easy, pleasant riding but not exciting. For curves, head north-east to the Euganean Hills, a cluster of volcanic cones rising abruptly from the plain, where twisting roads climb through vineyards and chestnut woods to villages like Arquà Petrarca, where the poet Petrarch spent his last years, and the walled town of Este.

Montagnana has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the historic centre has several cafés and bars. The surrounding area is known for its wines, especially from the Colli Euganei, and for dishes like bigoli pasta with duck sauce, risotto and grilled meats.

Come in spring or early autumn, when the light on the brick walls is warm and the fields green or golden. Summer can be hot and humid, and fog often blankets the plain in winter, creating a mysterious, muffled atmosphere. Walk the circuit outside the walls at sunset, then cross the road and look at Palladio's villa in the evening light, a calm statement of classical order beside the battered medieval brick.
t.onga river pumping station@33.8,130.7:
Steel needs water, a great deal of it, and in the early twentieth century the new Imperial Steel Works at Yawata in northern Kyushu needed more than the local streams could provide. The answer was this pumping station on the Onga river at Nakama, built in 1910, which drew water from the river and sent it through pipelines to the steel works. Remarkably, it is still in operation more than a century later. The red brick building with its tall windows is part of the UNESCO listing of Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, alongside shipyards, coal mines and iron works that tell the story of Japan's dramatic transformation into an industrial power.

The pumping station sits in a quiet riverside setting, with the brick building against green banks and the wide Onga river flowing slowly toward the sea. Visitors can see it from an observation area across the river; it is a working facility, so access is restricted. The building's style, with its Western-inspired design, shows how Japanese engineers absorbed and adapted technology from Europe.

The Onga valley runs through the old Chikuho coalfield, which supplied fuel to the steel works and was one of Japan's most important mining regions until the mines closed in the second half of the twentieth century. In nearby Tagawa, the paintings of coal miner Yamamoto Sakubei, depicting life underground, are recognised on UNESCO's Memory of the World register. The region is now quieter, with towns, rice fields and low wooded hills.

Riding in Japan means driving on the left, strict speed limits and courteous, orderly traffic. Roads in this area are mostly urban and suburban, with traffic lights, convenience stores and petrol stations everywhere. Expressways are fast but tolled. For more interesting riding, head for the hills of the Kitakyushu Quasi-National Park or the coast of the Genkai Sea to the north.

Nakama has plenty of fuel, food and convenience stores, and Kitakyushu, the big city nearby, has everything. Try local ramen with rich pork broth, a Kyushu specialty, or a bowl of udon in a small shop. Come in spring for cherry blossom along the river, or autumn for clear skies and comfortable temperatures. Summers are hot and humid, with typhoons possible. A brick pumping station may not sound like a highlight, but this one is a living piece of the industrial age.
t.watchtowers wp 14 1 to 14 27 including t:
Here the frontier changes character. West of the Franconian lakes the Romans built the Raetian Limes not as a palisade but, in its final form, as a stone wall, a metre or so thick and perhaps three high, running across Middle Franconia toward the Danube. Medieval villagers who found its rubble in their fields had no idea who had built it and called it the Teufelsmauer, the Devil's Wall, which tells you how thoroughly the empire had been forgotten. The watchtowers numbered in this section sat along that wall in the farmland around Pfofeld and Gunzenhausen, close to where the line crosses the Altmühl valley.

The landscape today is softer than the history. Pfofeld is a small village on a low plateau, and just to the north-east lies the Brombachsee, one of the reservoirs built from the 1970s onward to move water from the wet south of Bavaria to the dry north. The result is an unexpected lake district: sailing boats, sandy beaches, cyclists in matching jerseys and, on hot weekends, a fair amount of traffic around the shore roads. Weekday mornings are another story, with mist on the water, herons in the reeds and long empty lanes through pine woods and pasture.

For riding, think flowing rather than technical. The country roads between Pfofeld, Absberg and Gunzenhausen roll over gentle hills with occasional surprisingly tight bends at village entrances, and the surfaces are generally good. Watch for farm machinery in harvest season and for tractors dragging mud onto the tarmac after rain. The Altmühlsee near Gunzenhausen adds more water to the views, and the Altmühl valley further south becomes properly dramatic with limestone cliffs, if you have time to extend the day.

Gunzenhausen is the practical anchor: a town of some sixteen thousand with fuel, supermarkets and an old centre where a few stretches of the medieval walls survive. Franconian food is hearty and cheap by German standards, so a plate of Schäufele with dumplings and a local beer is a fine reward for the end of a ride, provided someone else is doing the riding afterwards. Along the Limes itself, look for the information boards and a reconstructed section or two of wall and tower around Gunzenhausen; they help you picture how the frontier once looked, a pale stone ribbon cutting straight across the fields you have been riding through all afternoon.
t.villa pojana@45.3,11.5:
Andrea Palladio could make a farmhouse look like a temple, and at Villa Pojana he did it with remarkable restraint. Built in the mid-sixteenth century for Bonifacio Pojana, a nobleman with military ambitions, the villa stands in the village of Poiana Maggiore in the flat country south of Vicenza. Its facade is almost bare: a great arched entrance framed by a Serlian motif with round windows, a pediment above, smooth plaster walls. The interior has frescoes by artists of the time. Like other Palladian villas of the Veneto, it counts as one component of UNESCO's inscription of the city of Vicenza and the villas around it.

The Basso Vicentino, the southern part of the province, is a land of fields, canals and poplars, flat as a table and crossed by rivers that flood in wet years. The Berici hills rise to the north, a cluster of low wooded hills with villages and vineyards, while to the south-east the Euganean hills can be seen on clear days. Montagnana, a short ride away, is one of the best-preserved walled towns in Italy, with its brick walls and towers intact, and it is known for its sweet prosciutto. Noventa Vicentina, the nearest larger town, has a grand villa now used as its town hall.

The riding here is easy and relaxing. The roads run straight between fields, with gentle bends around villages and along canals, and traffic is generally light. It is not a place for corners, but the Berici hills offer some twisty climbs and pleasant ridges if you want to work the bike. Summer is hot and humid, and mosquitoes are a feature of the evenings. Fog is common in late autumn and winter, sometimes very thick, so take care. Watch for tractors and cyclists on the narrow roads.

Noventa Vicentina has fuel, shops and cafés. The local food is rich: bigoli pasta with duck sauce, baccalà alla vicentina, salt cod slowly cooked in milk and onions, polenta and wines from the Berici hills, especially the red Tai Rosso. The villa's opening times vary, so check before you go. Take time to stand in front of the facade and appreciate its simplicity, which feels almost modern. Palladio used very few elements, and every one of them counts.
t.venice and its lagoon@45.4,12.3:
Venice is the only great city in Europe where your motorcycle is entirely useless.
