The road ends at Piazzale Roma, at the end of a long bridge across the lagoon, and from there on, everything happens on foot or by boat. The city and its lagoon are listed by UNESCO as a whole, a recognition that the islands, the canals, the salt marshes and the fishing villages form a single living system, shaped by over a thousand years of human effort to keep the sea out and the city afloat.

The ride in is part of the experience. The Ponte della Libertà, built in the 1930s next to the older railway bridge, carries you across the open water from Mestre, with the city rising ahead, its towers and domes catching the light. At Piazzale Roma and the nearby Tronchetto island there are multi-storey car parks, some with space for motorcycles, but they fill up fast in summer and are not cheap. If you want to keep riding, the car ferry from Tronchetto to the Lido lets you take your bike to the long island that separates the lagoon from the sea, with roads, beaches and the old Venice Film Festival buildings.

Once on foot, Venice is a labyrinth of narrow streets, bridges and squares, and getting lost is the whole point. The Grand Canal, St Mark's Square, the Rialto bridge and the Doge's Palace are the obvious highlights, but the quieter districts, Cannaregio, Castello, the Giudecca, are where Venetians still live. The islands of the lagoon, Murano with its glass, Burano with its colourful houses and lace, and Torcello with its ancient cathedral, are reachable by vaporetto, the water bus.

Fuel is available in Mestre and on the mainland; there is none on the main islands. Venetian food is distinctive: cicchetti, small snacks served with a glass of wine in bacari, sarde in saor, sweet and sour sardines, risotto with cuttlefish ink and liver with onions. Coffee at the counter is cheap; coffee at a table on St Mark's Square is a famous extravagance. Come out of season if you can, in late autumn or winter, when mist lies on the canals and the city is quieter. And remember that your bike is waiting for you at Piazzale Roma, and the mainland roads are wide open.
t.linderhof castle@47.6,11.0:
Of all the palaces King Ludwig II of Bavaria dreamed up, Linderhof is the only one he saw finished, and it is the one he actually lived in for long periods. Hidden in the Graswang valley in the Ammergau Alps, it is a small, extravagant rococo villa inspired by Versailles, with gilded rooms, a hall of mirrors and a dining table that rose from the kitchen below so that the shy king could eat without seeing servants. The park around it is full of follies: a Moorish kiosk, a Moroccan house and, most famous of all, the Venus Grotto, an artificial cave with a lake, a shell-shaped boat and coloured lighting, built so Ludwig could imagine himself in a Wagner opera. Linderhof belongs to the group of Ludwig's palaces recently listed by UNESCO.

The valley is narrow and wooded, with mountains rising steeply on both sides. Ettal, a few kilometres east, has a huge baroque Benedictine monastery whose monks brew beer and make a herbal liqueur. Oberammergau, beyond, is famous for its passion play, performed by the villagers every ten years since the seventeenth century, when they vowed to do so if spared from the plague, and for its painted houses and woodcarvers.

The riding is superb. The road from Ettal through the Graswang valley past Linderhof continues over the border into Austria, past the Ammerwald and down to the Plansee, a stunning lake of turquoise water surrounded by mountains, and on to Reutte. It is one of the classic rides of the Bavarian Alps, with curves, forests and views, but it is popular, and on summer weekends it is busy with cars, motorcycles and cyclists. Police controls are frequent, and noise is a sensitive topic in these valleys, so ride sensibly. In winter, snow can make the road difficult.

Oberammergau, eight kilometres away, covers fuel, food and a bed for the night. Bavarian food is hearty: roast pork with dumplings, Weisswurst for breakfast, pretzels and beer in a beer garden. The monastery at Ettal has a pleasant inn. Arrive early at Linderhof to avoid the crowds, visit the palace and the grotto, then sit in the park and look at the fountain shooting its jet high into the air; Ludwig liked his fantasies big.
t.parco pluritematico@46.2,10.4:
Valcamonica holds one of the largest collections of prehistoric rock carvings in the world, some three hundred thousand figures pecked into the smooth glacier-polished rocks of the valley over thousands of years, from hunters and deer to warriors, ploughs, houses and mysterious symbols. It was the first Italian site to be listed by UNESCO, in 1979. In the upper valley, near Sonico, a few kilometres south of Edolo, a multi-themed park around the rocks of Còren de le Fate, the fairies' rock, offers carvings, nature trails and an insight into the life of the valley.

The valley of the Oglio river cuts deep into the Alps of Lombardy, between the Adamello massif with its glaciers to the east and the Orobie Alps to the west. Edolo is the main town of the upper valley, at a crossroads of mountain routes, with roads leading north to the Tonale pass and Trentino, and west to the Aprica pass and Valtellina. Sonico is a small village with stone houses, and the slopes around are covered with chestnut woods, larches and pastures, with waterfalls tumbling down from the heights.

For riders, this is a dream location. From Edolo, the Passo del Tonale, at over eighteen hundred metres, is a fast and scenic climb, while the Passo dell'Aprica leads into the Valtellina. A little further north, the Mortirolo, one of the hardest climbs in cycling, offers a narrow, steep and twisty road with countless hairpins, and the Gavia pass, over two thousand six hundred metres, is a legendary high road, narrow and spectacular, usually open only in summer. Watch for cyclists, livestock and sudden weather changes. The high passes close in winter.

Edolo, three kilometres away, can handle fuel, meals and lodging. Food in Valcamonica is mountain fare: casoncelli, stuffed pasta with butter and sage, polenta, cheeses such as Silter, and cured meats. The wines of Valtellina, made from Nebbiolo grown on steep terraces, are close by. Visit the rock carvings in the morning, when the low light brings out the figures, and then ride up to a pass in the afternoon; you will be following, in a way, the paths of the people who carved these rocks.
t.regensburg ostliche canabae@49.0,12.1:
Marcus Aurelius had the legionary fortress of Castra Regina built here, on the northernmost bend of the Danube, and its north gate, the Porta Praetoria, still stands in Regensburg's old town, built into later buildings, with a foundation inscription dated to AD 179. Outside the fortress walls, the canabae, the civilian settlements where traders, craftsmen and soldiers' families lived, spread along the river, and the eastern canabae are a piece of the World Heritage property for the Danube Limes. Regensburg's medieval old town, built on top of the Roman city, has its own UNESCO listing.

Regensburg is one of the best-preserved medieval cities in Germany, with towers built by rich merchant families, a Gothic cathedral and a maze of narrow streets. The Stone Bridge, built in the twelfth century, crosses the Danube on sixteen arches and was a marvel of its time. Next to it, the Historische Wurstkuchl, a small sausage kitchen, has been serving grilled sausages with sauerkraut and sweet mustard for centuries. A short ride downstream, the Walhalla, a neoclassical temple built by Ludwig I of Bavaria to honour great Germans, stands on a hill above the river at Donaustauf.

The riding is enjoyable. The roads along the Danube are flat and scenic, and to the north, the Bavarian Forest offers twisty roads through hills and forests. The Altmühl valley to the west has limestone cliffs and gentle curves. The old town of Regensburg is mostly pedestrian, with cobbles, and parking for motorcycles is limited, so it is best to park outside and walk. Traffic around the city can be heavy. Weather is continental, with hot summers and cold winters, and fog along the river in autumn.

Regensburg has filling stations, supermarkets and inns. Bavarian food is hearty: sausages, pork knuckle, dumplings and beer from the local breweries. The city has a lively student life and many cafés. Walk through the old town to the Porta Praetoria, run your hand along the Roman stones, then cross the Stone Bridge and buy a sausage at the Wurstkuchl; it is the same view of the river and the cathedral that travellers have enjoyed for eight hundred years.
t.watchtowers wp 12 86 to 13 5 including f:
Near Rainau, not far from here, the Romans built a monumental gate in the Raetian Limes, a showpiece entrance probably connected with a visit by the emperor Caracalla in the early third century. Today the Limestor Dalkingen is protected under a glass and steel shelter, an impressive sight. The watchtowers numbered in this section, around Stödtlen, Wört and Tannhausen, were part of the same frontier, which ran here as a stone wall across the hilly country between the Ries crater and the Swabian Forest, toward the Danube.

The landscape is the Virngrund, a large forest area of spruce and beech, with clearings, ponds and small villages. Ellwangen, to the west, is a charming baroque town with a castle and a pilgrimage church on a hill. Dinkelsbühl, about ten kilometres to the north-east, is one of the best-preserved medieval towns in Germany, with its walls, towers and gates intact and its streets lined with half-timbered houses. Every July, it celebrates the Kinderzeche, a festival that commemorates how the town's children saved it from destruction during the Thirty Years' War, according to legend.

The riding is pleasant and relaxed. The roads through the forest are gentle, with curves, hills and long straights, and the surface is generally good. Traffic is light outside the towns. The Romantic Road, a tourist route through Franconia and Swabia, passes through Dinkelsbühl, and it is busy with coaches in summer, so the side roads are often more enjoyable. Watch for wildlife, especially deer at dawn and dusk, and for tractors. Weather is continental, with warm summers and cold winters.

The villages around the watchtowers are small; for fuel and services, Dinkelsbühl and Ellwangen are the best options. Food here is Swabian and Franconian, with roast pork, dumplings, carp from the local ponds and good beer. Dinkelsbühl's old town has many inns and cafés. Visit the Limes gate at Dalkingen to see the scale of Roman ambition, then ride through the forest along the line of the wall, and finish with a walk through Dinkelsbühl's medieval streets.
t.sciliar catinaccio@46.5,11.6:
Watch the Rosengarten at sunset from the valley of Bolzano and you will understand the legend. As the sun goes down, the pale dolomite peaks glow pink, then red, then purple, a phenomenon the Ladin people call enrosadira. According to the old story, King Laurin of the dwarves had a magnificent rose garden here, and when he was captured by enemies who had spotted his roses, he cursed the garden so that no one would see it by day or by night. He forgot the twilight, and so, for a few minutes each evening, the roses bloom again on the rocks. Together with the Sciliar, or Schlern, the great flat-topped massif to the north, the Catinaccio forms one of the components of the Dolomites UNESCO World Heritage site, listed in 2009.

The Sciliar is a symbol of South Tyrol, its sheer walls and rounded summit visible from all over the region, and local legend held that witches gathered on its plateau. Below it spreads the Alpe di Siusi, the Seiser Alm, the largest high-altitude meadow in Europe, carpeted with flowers in early summer. Between the two massifs, the valleys of Tires and the Eggental lead into the heart of the mountains.

The riding is world-class. From Nova Levante, Welschnofen in German, the road climbs past the Lago di Carezza, a small lake of extraordinary colours with the Latemar reflected in its water, to the Passo di Costalunga, the Karerpass, at 1,745 metres, before dropping into the Val di Fassa at Vigo. The Passo Nigra, a narrower road, links the Tires valley with the Costalunga, with tight bends and views of the Rosengarten walls. From the Fassa valley, the great Dolomite passes, Sella, Pordoi, Fedaia, are within easy reach. Surfaces are generally excellent, but traffic in summer can be heavy, with cars, buses, cyclists and other bikes, and speed limits and noise restrictions are strictly enforced.

Nova Levante and Vigo di Fassa have fuel, shops, restaurants and plenty of accommodation. The local food is a blend of Tyrolean and Italian: canederli, speck, apple strudel, and polenta with mushrooms. The passes are usually open from late spring to autumn, but snow can fall at any time at altitude. Early morning and late afternoon offer the quietest roads and the best light.
t.watchtowers wp 15 1 to 15 7@48.9,11.4:
In Bavaria, the Roman frontier changed character. Instead of the wooden palisade used in the Upper German section, the Raetian Limes was eventually built as a stone wall, known locally as the Devil's Wall, because medieval people could not imagine anyone but the devil building something so long. The stretch between Watchtowers 15/1 and 15/7 crosses the hills around the Altmühl valley, near Kipfenberg and Kinding, and the line of the wall can still be traced in places as a low ridge in the forest. It is part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes World Heritage site.

Kipfenberg, in the valley below, has a Roman museum, the Römer und Bajuwaren Museum, with finds from the area and displays about life on the frontier. The town also claims to be close to the geographical centre of Bavaria, marked by a stone in the hills. A reconstructed wooden watchtower stands near Erkertshofen, giving a sense of how the frontier looked.

The Altmühl valley is one of the most beautiful landscapes in Bavaria, a deep, winding valley carved through the limestone of the Franconian Jura, with white cliffs, juniper heaths, castles and small towns. It is a nature park, popular with canoeists, cyclists and walkers, and the slow, meandering river is lined with willows and meadows. The limestone here is famous for its fossils, and the quarries around Solnhofen and Eichstätt have yielded specimens of Archaeopteryx, the feathered dinosaur.

The riding is excellent. The roads along the valley follow the river with gentle bends and views of the cliffs, while the roads that climb onto the plateau above have steeper gradients and tighter turns. Traffic is light on weekdays, busier at weekends with tourists and cyclists. Surfaces are generally good. Watch for farm traffic, gravel and wildlife, especially deer at dawn and dusk.

Kipfenberg, Greding and Beilngries have fuel, shops and restaurants; Greding also has a well-preserved medieval wall. The region is known for its beer, brewed in small breweries in many villages, and for hearty Bavarian food, such as roast pork with dumplings and Altmühltal lamb. Spring and autumn are lovely; summers are warm, and winters cold, with fog in the valleys.
t.fort site of oberhochstatt@49.0,11.1:
Not every Roman fort on the frontier was a great stone fortress. Some were small, temporary or quickly abandoned, and the fort site of Oberhochstatt, on the high plateau above Weißenburg in Bavaria, seems to have been one of these, a modest garrison post on the Raetian Limes. There is little to see today beyond a field, perhaps an information board and the outline of the defences in the grass. But the landscape around is full of Roman history, and the town of Weißenburg, a short ride away, is one of the best places in Germany to experience it.

Weißenburg was the site of the Roman fort of Biriciana, and its reconstructed north gate stands in a park on the edge of town, giving a vivid sense of the scale of the defences. Nearby, the remains of the Roman baths are among the best preserved in southern Germany, protected under a modern roof. In 1979 a local gardener digging in his vegetable patch found a hoard of Roman treasure, including bronze statuettes of gods, silver vessels and votive plaques, now displayed in the town's Roman museum. Weißenburg itself is a lovely old town, with walls, towers and half-timbered houses, and a fortress, the Wülzburg, on a hill above.

The landscape around is a mix of the Franconian Jura, with limestone hills, juniper heaths and forests, and the Franconian Lake District, a group of artificial lakes created in recent decades to balance water supply in Bavaria. The Altmühlsee and the Brombachsee, to the west, are popular for swimming, sailing and cycling in summer.

The riding is pleasant and varied. The roads on the plateau are straight and open, with long views over fields and forests. The roads that descend into the valleys of the Altmühl and the Schwäbische Rezat are more winding, with good bends and views. Traffic is light, but watch for farm vehicles, cyclists and deer. Surfaces are generally good.

Weißenburg has fuel, shops and restaurants; the villages around have inns and small shops. Try a beer from a local brewery, and Franconian specialties such as Schäufele, roast pork shoulder with crackling, or Nürnberger sausages. The weather is continental, with warm summers and cold winters; spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding.
t.fort site and civil settlement of aalen@:
The largest Roman cavalry fort north of the Alps stood on the site of today's Aalen, in the eastern Swabian Jura. It was home to a regiment of a thousand horsemen, the ala II Flavia, the most prestigious cavalry unit on the Raetian frontier, and its walls enclosed a huge area, with barracks, stables, granaries and a headquarters building. Beside it grew a civilian settlement, with traders, craftsmen and families. Today the site is home to the Limesmuseum Aalen, one of the most important museums of the Roman frontier in Germany, with excavated foundations, reconstructions and a rich collection of finds. It is part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes World Heritage site.

The museum is excellent, with displays about the soldiers, their horses, their equipment and their daily life, and outside in the archaeological park you can walk among the remains of the headquarters and see a reconstructed section of the barracks. In summer, Roman festivals bring re-enactors in armour and costume.

Aalen is a lively town at the edge of the Swabian Jura, the Schwäbische Alb, a limestone plateau that runs across southern Germany. Its old town has half-timbered houses and a market square. Nearby, the Tiefer Stollen is an old iron ore mine that you can visit by mine train, and part of it is used for therapy for respiratory conditions. Oberkochen, just south, is home to the optics company Zeiss.

The riding is excellent. The Swabian Jura is one of the best riding areas in southern Germany, with winding roads through valleys and over the plateau, past castles, caves and small towns. The roads around the Kocher and Brenz valleys, and towards Heidenheim and Schwäbisch Gmünd, are particularly good, with many bends and varied scenery. The Albtrauf, the steep escarpment along the northern edge of the plateau, offers dramatic climbs and views. Traffic is moderate, and surfaces are generally good, but watch for farm vehicles, cyclists and speed cameras.

Aalen has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try Swabian specialties: Maultaschen, large pasta pockets filled with meat and spinach, or Käsespätzle, egg noodles with cheese and fried onions. The weather on the Alb is cooler and windier than in the lowlands, with snow in winter. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding.
t.villa trissino@45.4,11.4:
A Palladio villa that was never finished can be more interesting than one that was. At Meledo, a hamlet in the municipality of Sarego south of Vicenza, Andrea Palladio drew up grand plans for the Trissino brothers in the mid-sixteenth century: a central block topped by a dome, with long curved colonnades stretching out like arms toward the river. Only a fragment was built, and what you see today is a modest farm building and some remains incorporated into later structures. Yet the design, published in Palladio's Four Books of Architecture, became one of his most influential, and the site is part of the UNESCO listing of the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto.

The Trissino name carries weight in Vicenza. Gian Giorgio Trissino, a humanist scholar and poet, was the man who spotted the talent of Palladio, then a young stonemason called Andrea di Pietro, and gave him the classical name by which he became famous. The villas of the Veneto were country estates for wealthy Venetian and Vicentine families, combining farm and residence, and Palladio's genius lay in making working farmhouses look like Roman temples.

The ride through this corner of the Veneto is easy and pleasant. The flat plain south of Vicenza is crossed by straight roads lined with poplars, canals and vineyards, with the Monti Berici rising to the east and the foothills of the Lessini to the north. The Berici hills offer the best riding nearby: narrow lanes that climb and twist through woods and vineyards, with small villages and views over the plain. Surfaces are generally good, but lanes can be narrow, and agricultural traffic is common. Spring is lovely, with fresh green fields and wisteria, and autumn brings the grape harvest.

Fuel is easy to find in Montebello Vicentino or Lonigo, the nearest larger towns. Food in the area is excellent: try bigoli pasta with duck sauce, baccalà alla vicentina, or the local Durello sparkling wine from the hills to the north. Park near the villa, take a look at what remains, and imagine the grand structure Palladio had in mind. Then head to one of the completed villas nearby, such as Villa Pojana, to see his vision fully realised.
t.water management system of augsburg@48.4:
Augsburg was a Roman town, a medieval free imperial city and the home of the fabulously rich Fugger banking family, but the thing that held it all together was water. Over the centuries, the city built an intricate network of canals fed by the Lech and Wertach rivers, water towers, pumping stations and fountains, supplying clean drinking water to the citizens and power to mills and workshops. The system was so advanced that UNESCO inscribed it in 2019, recognising twenty-two sites, from the water towers at the Red Gate, dating back to the fifteenth century, to the great Renaissance fountains dedicated to Augustus, Mercury and Hercules on the main street.

Walking through the old town, you constantly cross canals, some running openly between houses, others hidden under streets. The Lech quarter, with its narrow lanes and old craftsmen's houses, is especially charming, and the Fuggerei, the world's oldest social housing settlement, founded by Jakob Fugger in 1516, still houses residents for an annual rent of less than one euro, along with a few prayers for the founder. The Eiskanal, built for the canoe slalom events of the 1972 Olympic Games, is also part of the water story.

Riding into Augsburg means dealing with city traffic, trams and cobbles in the old town, so it is best to park on the edge and walk. The surrounding countryside offers much more pleasant riding. To the west, the Westliche Wälder nature park has quiet roads through forests and small villages, with gentle hills and curves. To the south, the Lech valley leads toward the Alps, and on clear days you can see the mountains from the higher ground. The roads are generally excellent, but traffic can be heavy around the city.

Augsburg is a city of over a quarter of a million people, with fuel, cafés, beer gardens and restaurants of every kind. Try Swabian specialities like Spätzle and Maultaschen, or a Weißwurst breakfast if you are early enough. Walk along the canals, look at the water towers at the Red Gate, and stand by one of the great bronze fountains on Maximilianstrasse. It is a city that wears its history lightly, and the water is what makes it come alive.
t.the dolomites@46.6,12.2:
North of Cortina d'Ampezzo, the valley narrows between walls of pale rock, and the road toward Dobbiaco threads through a landscape that looks almost too dramatic to be real. Here, between the Cristallo group to the east and the high plateaus of Fanes and Sennes to the west, you are in the heart of the Dolomites, the mountains UNESCO inscribed in 2009 for their extraordinary beauty and geology. The rock is dolomite, a magnesium-rich limestone formed from ancient coral reefs in a tropical sea some two hundred and fifty million years ago, and the way it catches the evening light, turning pink and orange, has a name of its own in the local Ladin language: enrosadira.

The area was the front line between Italy and Austria-Hungary during the First World War, and the mountains are still riddled with tunnels, trenches and fortifications, some of which can be visited. Cortina itself, a stylish resort town, hosted the Winter Olympics in 1956 and shared the 2026 Games with Milan. The Ladin culture of the valleys, with its own language and traditions, gives the region a distinct identity, and the food blends Italian, Austrian and Alpine influences.

The road here, the SS51, climbs from Cortina over Passo Cimabanche, a gentle pass at around 1,530 metres, and descends past Lago di Landro, with stunning views of the Tre Cime di Lavaredo, toward Dobbiaco in the Puster valley. It is a fast, flowing road with long curves rather than tight hairpins, but traffic in summer can be heavy, with camper vans, cyclists and tourist cars. The more famous Dolomite passes, such as the Falzarego, Giau and Tre Croci, are all within reach and offer some of the best riding in Europe. Many high passes are closed in winter, and summer weekends bring crowds and police controls.

Cortina, about nine kilometres away, has fuel, cafés and restaurants, as does Dobbiaco to the north, which is smaller but well supplied. Try canederli, the bread dumplings of the Tyrolean tradition, or casunziei, a local beet-filled pasta. Pull over at Lago di Landro, where the Tre Cime rise behind the lake, and take a few minutes to look. The light, the rock and the silence are worth every kilometre.
t.passau haibach burgus@48.6,13.5:
Passau sits where three rivers meet, the Danube, the Inn and the Ilz, and from the high point of the Oberhaus fortress you can see their colours run side by side before mixing: green from the Inn, blue-grey from the Danube, and dark from the Ilz, which flows down from the Bavarian Forest stained by peat. The Romans knew this spot well. They had a fort here called Batavis, named after a unit of Batavian soldiers from the Rhine delta, and another at Boiotro across the Inn, and along the Danube downstream they built small fortified towers called burgi to watch the river and signal to each other. One of these late Roman burgi stood near Haibach, and its remains are part of the Danube Limes, inscribed by UNESCO in 2021 as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

The Danube was the frontier of the empire in this region for four centuries, and the burgi of the late period, in the fourth century, reflected a more defensive posture, as pressure from Germanic peoples increased. Today the river flows peacefully past wooded slopes, with cruise boats, cyclists on the Danube cycle path, and fishermen on the banks. Passau itself, with its baroque cathedral and one of the world's largest church organs, is a lively university town.

Riding along the Danube east of Passau is a joy. The roads on both banks follow the river through a narrow, wooded valley, with gentle curves and views of the water, and lead toward Austria and the Schlögen loop, where the river makes a dramatic hairpin through the hills. North of Passau, the Bavarian Forest offers more challenging riding, with climbs, tight bends and dense woods. Traffic in the valley can be busy in summer, and cyclists are everywhere on the riverside paths and lanes, so stay alert.

Passau, about five kilometres away, is a town of around fifty thousand people with fuel, cafés, beer gardens and restaurants, and Salzweg, just north, is another option. Try Bavarian dishes such as roast pork with dumplings, or fresh fish from the river. Stop by the river near Haibach, look at the flowing water, and think of the Roman soldiers who watched over it, peering across at the dark forests on the far bank. Then ride into Passau and climb up to the fortress for the view of the three rivers.
t.dolomiti friulane e d oltre piave@46.3,1:
The Friulian Dolomites are the quiet cousins of the famous peaks around Cortina, and that is precisely their charm. West of the Tagliamento, between the Piave and the Friulian plain, these rugged limestone mountains rise in jagged ridges and pinnacles, with deep valleys and very few roads. They are part of the UNESCO Dolomites site and form the Parco Naturale delle Dolomiti Friulane, a wild area of forests, gorges and rock towers, including the extraordinary Campanile di Val Montanaia, a needle of rock standing alone in a high valley like a stone bell tower. Chamois, ibex, golden eagles and marmots live here, and the silence on the high trails is profound.

The valleys carry a painful memory. On 9 October 1963, a massive landslide from Monte Toc fell into the reservoir behind the Vajont dam, just west of Erto and Casso, and a wave of water overtopped the dam and swept down into the Piave valley, destroying the town of Longarone and killing nearly two thousand people. The dam itself survived and still stands, an eerie concrete wall above a valley filled with rubble. Visits are possible, and the story is told with great honesty at memorials in the area.

The road through the Val Cellina and over the Passo di Sant'Osvaldo, from Cimolais and Claut to Erto and down to Longarone, is a great ride: narrow, winding, with tunnels, hairpins and views of the mountains and the old dam. Surfaces can be uneven, and some tunnels are narrow and poorly lit. To the north, the road from Forni di Sopra over the Passo della Mauria toward Cadore is another fine route, with good curves and little traffic. Weather can be unpredictable, with sudden storms in summer, and snow at higher elevations from autumn to spring.

Cimolais and Claut are small villages with a few bars, shops and restaurants, but fuel is limited, so fill up in larger towns such as Maniago or Longarone before heading into the mountains. Local food includes frico, a crisp cheese and potato dish, and polenta with game or mushrooms. Stop at the visitor centre in Cimolais, then ride on to the Vajont dam and stand on the crest above the valley. It is a sobering place, and the mountains around it are beautiful.
t.fort site and civil settlement of boehmi:
The Altmühl valley is one of the most beautiful river valleys in Bavaria, and near the village of Böhming, a short way upstream from Kipfenberg, the Romans built a small fort to guard the point where their frontier, the Raetian Limes, crossed the river. The Limes here came down from the plateau, crossed the valley and climbed again on the other side, and the fort, with its civil settlement, controlled the crossing and the route along the river. Little is visible today beyond outlines in the fields and a few marked spots, but a stone inscription found here and the finds displayed in the Roman and Bavarian museum in Kipfenberg bring the site to life.

The Altmühl valley cuts through the limestone of the Franconian Jura, and the landscape is dramatic for southern Germany: steep slopes covered in juniper heath, white limestone cliffs, and the slow, meandering river below. This is fossil country too. The quarries of Solnhofen and Eichstätt, not far away, produced the famous Archaeopteryx fossils, the feathered dinosaur-bird, and the Jura Museum in Eichstätt displays one. Kipfenberg, with its fairy-tale castle on a rock above the river, is said to lie close to the geographic centre of Bavaria.

Riding through the Altmühltal is a joy. The roads follow the river through the valley, with gentle curves, good surfaces and constant views of the cliffs and the water, and side roads climb onto the plateau with steeper gradients and tighter bends. The valley is popular with cyclists and canoeists, so watch out for both in summer. On the plateau, the roads become straighter and more open, crossing fields and forests. The valley can be misty in the morning, especially in autumn, when the colours are wonderful.

Kipfenberg, a few kilometres away, has cafés, guesthouses and small shops, while Greding, Eichstätt and Gaimersheim offer fuel and more services. Bavarian food is hearty: try roast pork with dumplings, sausages, or freshwater fish from the river, with a local beer if you are done riding. Stop by the river near Böhming, look up at the slopes where the Limes once climbed, and enjoy the peaceful valley. Then head to Kipfenberg for the castle and the museum.
t.watchtowers wp 13 6 to 13 12@49.0,10.4:
Along the Wörnitz valley in western Middle Franconia, near the village of Weiltingen, the line of the Raetian Limes cuts across the countryside, and the places where Roman watchtowers once stood are numbered by archaeologists in a dry sequence: WP 13/6, 13/7, and so on. In Raetia, the frontier was not a palisade, as in Upper Germany, but a stone wall about three metres high, and local people called its remains the Teufelsmauer, the Devil's Wall, believing that only the devil could have built something so long and straight. Today, you may see a low bank in a field or a line of trees following the old route, and in some places the foundations of towers have been marked or reconstructed.

The countryside around Weiltingen is a gentle landscape of fields, meadows and small woods, with the Wörnitz meandering through the valley. Dinkelsbühl, a few kilometres to the northwest, is one of the best preserved medieval towns in Germany, with intact walls, towers and gates, and half-timbered houses lining its streets. It lies on the Romantic Road, the tourist route from Würzburg to Füssen, and draws many visitors in summer. The area was largely spared destruction in the Second World War, which is why its old towns survive so well.

The riding is quiet and pleasant. Back roads link the villages along the Wörnitz and over the gentle hills, with good surfaces, light traffic and enough curves to keep you interested. The roads toward the Hesselberg, the highest point in Middle Franconia, climb a little more, and the views from the top are wide. Traffic is heavier on the Romantic Road near Dinkelsbühl, especially with tourist buses and camper vans. Spring brings green fields and blossom, autumn brings misty mornings and golden woods.

Weiltingen and nearby Wilburgstetten are small villages with a few shops and an inn, while Dinkelsbühl, about ten kilometres away, has pumps, coffee, proper meals and accommodation. Franconian food is hearty: try Schäufele, roast pork shoulder with a crispy crust, or bratwurst with sauerkraut, and maybe a local beer at the end of the day. Stop near the line of the Limes, look across the fields, and imagine the stone wall running into the distance, with towers at regular intervals and soldiers watching.
t.fort site and civil settlement of elling:
Ellingen is a small town that punches well above its weight. Its centre is dominated by a vast baroque palace built by the Teutonic Order, the German crusading knights who later became a religious and administrative order, and who ran a commandery here for centuries. The palace, with its church, courtyards and gardens, is far grander than you would expect in such a small place. Just outside the town, the Romans had an earlier presence: a fort called Sablonetum stood here on the Raetian Limes, with a civil settlement beside it, guarding the frontier as it crossed the countryside north of Weißenburg. Its outline has been marked in the fields, and it is part of the World Heritage site of the Upper German-Raetian Limes.

Weißenburg, a few kilometres south, was a major Roman centre. The fort of Biriciana has a reconstructed north gate, and the remains of large Roman baths are protected under a modern roof. In 1979, a gardener digging in Weißenburg found a hoard of Roman treasure, including statuettes of gods, which is now displayed in the town's Roman museum. The medieval town, with its walls and gates, and the Wülzburg fortress on a hill above, add to the appeal.

The riding here is relaxed and scenic. The roads around Ellingen and Weißenburg run through gentle hills, fields and forests, with good surfaces and light traffic. To the north and west, the Franconian Lake District, with the Altmühlsee and the Brombachsee, offers lakeside roads and summer swimming. To the south, the Altmühl valley and the Franconian Jura provide more dramatic scenery, with limestone cliffs, juniper heaths and winding roads. Weekends bring more traffic, especially around the lakes.

Ellingen has a few cafés, inns and shops, and Weißenburg, about four kilometres away, has fuel, restaurants and supermarkets. Ellingen also has a well-known brewery, and Franconia has more breweries per head than almost anywhere in the world, so if you are finished for the day, a local beer is a must, preferably with a plate of sausages or roast pork. Visit the palace, look at the Roman fort outline, and then ride to Weißenburg to see the baths and the reconstructed gate. It is a rich slice of history in a small area.
t.oratory of st michael@45.4,11.9:
In the old centre of Padua, near the medieval tower that later became an astronomical observatory, a small oratory hides one of the city's quieter treasures. The Oratory of St Michael contains frescoes painted by Jacopo da Verona at the end of the fourteenth century, scenes from the life of the Virgin populated with recognisable citizens of Padua dressed in the fashions of the day. It is one of eight sites inscribed in 2021 as Padua's fourteenth-century fresco cycles, the group that also includes Giotto's Scrovegni Chapel.

Padua was an extraordinary place in that century. The Carrara lords who ruled the city patronised painters who pushed far beyond the flat, gold-backed images of the past, and the frescoes scattered across Padua show the start of a new way of seeing space and people. The city's university, founded in 1222, is one of the oldest in Europe; Galileo taught there, and its botanical garden, laid out in the sixteenth century, is a World Heritage Site in its own right. The great Basilica of Saint Anthony draws pilgrims from all over the world.

As a riding stop, be realistic: this is the middle of a busy city. The centre has restricted traffic zones with cameras, the ring roads are congested at peak hours, and scooters, bicycles and trams all compete for space. Park on the edge of the old town and walk. In return you get one of the most enjoyable cities in Italy for a long lunch, with arcaded streets, the vast market squares around the Palazzo della Ragione, and a spritz culture that Padua claims as its own.

The rewarding riding starts twenty kilometres south-west, where the Euganean Hills rise abruptly out of the plain. These volcanic hills are small but full of roads that twist up through vineyards and chestnut woods to villages like Teolo, Arquà Petrarca, where the poet Petrarch spent his last years, and the old spa towns of Abano and Montegrotto. The bends are tight and the surfaces sometimes patchy, and cyclists love these hills as much as riders do, so watch every blind corner on weekends.

Fuel is easy everywhere around Padua outside the centre. Summer in the Veneto plain is hot and humid, with thunderstorms on many afternoons, so spring and autumn are more comfortable for riding the hills.
t.fiave lago carera@46.0,10.8:
Lago Carera is barely a lake any more: a damp, reedy hollow and peat bog below the village of Fiavè, in the Giudicarie valleys of western Trentino. Yet in the Bronze Age this was a lakeshore crowded with houses on wooden piles, and the waterlogged peat preserved their timbers, tools and food remains for three and a half thousand years. Fiavè is one of the pile-dwelling sites of the transnational World Heritage Site covering prehistoric settlements around the Alps, and a museum in the village shows what came out of the bog.

The landscape is a broad, open upland of meadows and forest, with the walls of the Brenta Dolomites rising to the north and the gentler ridges above Lake Garda to the south. This is the Bleggio area, famous for its walnuts, and the region of San Lorenzo in Banale nearby is known for ciuìga, a smoked sausage made with turnip. It is a quiet, farming country, much less crowded than Garda only twenty minutes away.

For riders the best approach is from Riva del Garda or Arco, climbing past Tenno and its turquoise lake to the Passo del Ballino, then down into the valley of Fiavè. It is a lovely road: steep, twisting hairpins above the lake, then a flowing run through forest and meadow with excellent surfaces and much less traffic than the roads around Garda. From Fiavè you can continue to Ponte Arche, home of the Comano Terme spa, and on through the Sarca gorges to Tione or towards Molveno and the Brenta.

Weather in the Giudicarie is mountain weather. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms that build over the Brenta and can drench the valleys within minutes, while spring and autumn have crisp, clear mornings with fog in the hollows. In winter, snow and ice are common on the higher stretches, and Ballino, while not high by Alpine standards, can be icy in shade.

Fiavè is a small village, so for reliable fuel go to Ponte Arche or down to Arco, nine kilometres away as the crow flies but further by road. Arco also has a beautiful old centre under a castle on a cliff, plenty of cafés and the whole climbing and cycling culture of the northern end of Lake Garda.
t.rio delle foglie@46.4,11.4:
Rio delle Foglie is the Italian name for the Bletterbach, a gorge that cuts deep into the plateau above the Adige valley, south of Bolzano, near the villages of Aldino and Redagno. It is part of the Dolomites World Heritage Site, inscribed in 2009, and it is one of the best places in the Alps to read the history of the Earth in rock. The stream has carved down through hundreds of metres of layers, from volcanic porphyry at the bottom through red sandstones to the white dolomite of the Corno Bianco at the top, spanning tens of millions of years.

Walking in the gorge is like walking through a geology textbook. The red sandstones contain fossilised footprints of reptiles that lived before the dinosaurs, plant fossils and ripple marks from ancient rivers. A visitor centre in Aldino explains it all, and trails lead down into the gorge and up to the top of the Corno Bianco. It is a fine walk in sturdy shoes, with waterfalls, rocky steps and a cool, damp atmosphere in summer.

The riding around here is classic South Tyrol. From the Adige valley at Ora, a road climbs in hairpins up to Aldino and on to the plateau, with views back over the valley and vineyards. From there, roads lead to the Passo di Lavazè and the Passo degli Oclini, both relatively low and quiet passes through forests and meadows, and on to Nova Ponente and the Passo di Costalunga, with views of the Latemar and the Catinaccio. The asphalt is usually excellent, though cyclists and caravans are common in summer, and the curves can be tight.

The plateau is a farming landscape of meadows, forest and scattered farms, with the Dolomites rising to the east. In spring the meadows are full of flowers, and in autumn the larches turn golden. Weather can change quickly, with afternoon thunderstorms in summer and snow at higher elevations from November to April.

Fuel is available in the valley at Ora or Laives, ten kilometres away, and in some villages on the plateau. Food is a mix of Austrian and Italian: speck, dumplings, apple strudel and pasta. A stop at a mountain inn for a plate of knödel and a glass of local wine, with the peaks turning pink outside, rarely disappoints.
t.hallstatt dachstein salzkammergut cultur:
Salt made all of this. Long before anyone thought of postcards, people were tunnelling into the mountain above Hallstatt for it, and finds from the prehistoric mine and its cemetery were so rich that archaeologists named a whole phase of the European Iron Age, the Hallstatt culture, after a village you can walk across in ten minutes. The Hallstatt-Dachstein / Salzkammergut cultural landscape, inscribed in 1997, takes in the lake, the village, the salt mountain, the limestone massif of the Dachstein and the valleys around Gosau, Bad Goisern and Bad Aussee.

Limestone dominates everything: cliffs, caves, sinkholes and water that runs green and astonishingly clear. In the valleys the air smells of cut hay and woodsmoke; up high, of stone and snow.

Riders have two classic roads here. The Pass Gschütt climbs from Bad Goisern to Gosau, where the Vorderer Gosausee holds the Dachstein in its reflection on a calm morning, and continues down towards Abtenau. The Pötschen pass, on the main road from Bad Goisern to Bad Aussee, is broad, fast and well cambered, with a viewpoint at the top. Both are busy on summer weekends with caravans and coaches, and both deserve an early start. Rain is a regular visitor; the Salzkammergut catches every Atlantic front that reaches the northern Alps.

Hallstatt village has become a victim of its own beauty, swamped by day visitors in high season, with traffic and parking controlled through a tunnel that bypasses the centre. Park outside and walk, or come in the evening when the coaches have gone. The charnel house beside the Catholic church, with its painted skulls, says a lot about how little flat ground there is here. Fish from the lake, especially the local whitefish called Reinanke, often turns up grilled on menus.

Bad Goisern, ten kilometres or so away, is a good, unpretentious base with fuel and shops, and Bad Ischl further north, the imperial spa town where Emperor Franz Joseph spent his summers, has cafés with cakes worth riding for. In winter, snow and ice make the passes demanding, and Gschütt can be properly wintry well into spring.
t.wallsee kastell@48.2,14.7:
Wallsee is one of those Danube villages that people cycle through on the long riverside path without guessing how much history sits under their tyres. A castle rises on a rock above the river, and beneath and around the village lie the remains of a Roman fort that guarded this stretch of the Danube frontier. It is part of the Danube Limes World Heritage Site, inscribed in 2021, which follows the river from Bavaria through Austria to Slovakia, a line of forts, watchtowers and towns that held the northern edge of the empire for centuries.

There is not much Roman masonry to see, but the setting makes the point. The river is broad here, and from the high ground above it you can see a long way upstream and down, perfect for watching boats and anyone trying to cross. The later castle uses the same logic, and has dominated the village since the Middle Ages.

Wallsee lies in the Mostviertel, the cider country of Lower Austria, named after Most, the fermented juice of pears and apples. In April the old pear trees that line the roads and fields burst into white blossom, and the whole landscape looks like it has been dusted with snow. Farm inns serve Most with cold meats and bread, and in autumn you can buy fresh juice and fruit at the roadside.

The roads around here are gentle rather than dramatic, rolling through farmland and orchards, with views of the river and, on clear days, the Alps to the south. The main road along the Danube is pleasant, and the bridge at Wallsee or nearby crossings lead to the north bank, where the hills of the Mühlviertel and the Strudengau gorge downstream offer more curves. Watch out for cyclists on the riverside roads, especially in summer.

Wallsee itself is a small market village; for a wider choice of fuel and services, Perg, eleven kilometres away across the river, is a straightforward option, and Amstetten to the south has more. The power station at Ybbs-Persenbeug downstream and the town of Grein, with its old theatre, make good stops if you are heading east along the river.
t.limessection between watchtowers wp 13 4:
In the rolling country of Middle Franconia, between Gunzenhausen and Wassertrüdingen, the Raetian Limes ran as a stone wall rather than a wooden palisade. Local people later called its remains the Teufelsmauer, the Devil's Wall, believing no human could have built such a long barrier. The section near watchtower WP 13/40, close to Arberg and Ornbau, is part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes World Heritage Site, and in places a low bank of stones in the fields and woods still marks the line.

The Raetian Limes ran from the Rhine-Danube watershed to the Danube near Regensburg, protecting the province of Raetia. Its stone wall, about three metres high, was a late addition, built in the early third century, and watchtowers stood along it at regular intervals. Gunzenhausen has a reconstructed section and a small museum, and a long-distance cycle and walking route follows the line.

The landscape is gentle, with fields, forests, small rivers and villages with half-timbered houses and onion-domed church towers. To the south rises the Hesselberg, the highest point in Middle Franconia, a long, flat-topped hill with views over the countryside. The Franconian Lake District, a group of reservoirs built in recent decades, including the Altmühlsee and the Brombachsee, has turned the area into a holiday region, with beaches, sailing and cycling.

Riding here is relaxed, with quiet country roads, gentle curves and little traffic outside the lake area in summer. The roads around the Hesselberg and the Altmühl valley are particularly pleasant, and the old towns of Dinkelsbühl and Rothenburg ob der Tauber are within easy reach.

Wassertrüdingen, eight kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and Gunzenhausen offers more services. Franconia has more small breweries than almost anywhere on earth, and the food is built to go with the beer: Schäufele, roast pork shoulder with crackling, dumplings and sausages. Many villages still have their own brewery tavern, and finding one is half the fun.
t.city of vicenza and the palladian villas:
Andrea Palladio was a stonemason from Padua who became the most copied architect in history, and Vicenza is where he did it. Walk the main street, Corso Palladio, and you are moving through his workshop: palace after palace designed for the local nobility in the sixteenth century, with columns, pediments and proportions that ended up on English country houses, American plantation homes and Washington government buildings. The city and the villas scattered across the surrounding countryside were listed together by UNESCO for exactly that reason.

Start at the Piazza dei Signori, dominated by the Basilica Palladiana. It was not a church at all but the medieval town hall, and Palladio's contribution was the double loggia of white stone he wrapped around it. A short walk away is the Teatro Olimpico, his last project, finished after his death by Vincenzo Scamozzi, with a fixed stage set of streets painted and built in forced perspective that still fools the eye. Then ride up to Monte Berico, the hill just south of the centre, where the basilica terrace gives the best view of the red roofs with the Alps behind on a clear day.

From the foot of that hill a lane leads to La Rotonda, the villa everyone knows even if they do not know its name: a square house with a dome and four identical porticoes, built so its owner could look out over the countryside in every direction. It is the start of a beautiful ride. Head south along the Riviera Berica and into the Colli Berici, small limestone hills crossed by narrow, wriggling roads, vineyards and cherry orchards, with villages that seem to have been forgotten by the motorway just a few kilometres away.

Practicalities are simple in a city of over a hundred thousand people. Fuel is everywhere on the ring roads. The historic centre is a limited traffic zone with cameras at the entrances, so park on the edge and walk in rather than risk a fine arriving by post months later. Summer can be oppressively humid on the Venetian plain; spring and early autumn are kinder.

Eat what the Vicentini eat. Baccalà alla vicentina, dried cod slow-cooked in milk and served with polenta, is the city's signature, and bigoli, thick fresh pasta often served with duck ragù, is the classic first course. A glass of local wine from the Berici hills finishes the argument for staying the night.
t.villa thiene@45.6,11.6:
Quinto Vicentino is a quiet farming town on the flat plain just north-east of Vicenza, and its town hall happens to be a villa by Andrea Palladio. Villa Thiene was commissioned in the sixteenth century by the brothers Marcantonio and Adriano Thiene, members of one of the most powerful families in Vicenza, and Palladio drew up a grand design for it with courtyards and wings that would have spread across the fields. Only part of that plan was ever built. What stands today is a solid, rather austere block, and the council offices are inside it, which gives the place a pleasingly everyday feeling.

That unfinished quality is part of the interest. Palladio's villas were not just country retreats for the wealthy; they were working farms, centres of estates that the Venetian nobility developed as the Republic of Venice turned from the sea toward the land in the sixteenth century. The barns, granaries and dovecotes were meant to sit alongside the owner's rooms in one harmonious composition. At Quinto you can see how such a scheme was supposed to begin, and imagine the rest.

The surrounding countryside is pancake-flat, a patchwork of maize fields, irrigation ditches, poplar rows and small rivers like the Tesina, which slides past the town. This is not curve country, and nobody pretends it is. What it offers instead is easy riding on small roads between villages with campaniles that you can see from miles away, and the chance to tick off several Palladian villas in a single morning. Villa Emo at Fanzolo, Villa Badoer at Fratta Polesine and the cluster around Vicenza itself all fit into a day's riding across the Veneto plain.

The best time is spring, when the fields are green and the air is still fresh, or autumn, when the maize has come in and the mist sits low in the morning. Summer days can be heavy and humid. The town is small, under two thousand people, but Monticello Conte Otto, five kilometres away, and Vicenza itself have plenty of fuel stations, and you are never far from a bar for a coffee and a tramezzino.

If you want the full Palladio story with grand interiors and frescoes, ride on to one of the villas that are open as house museums. If you want to see how his ideas became part of the furniture of daily life, stop here, park outside the town hall and look at it for a while.
t.schlogen vicus@48.4,13.9:
The Danube does something remarkable at Schlögen. Forced by hard granite, the river makes a tight double hairpin, the Schlögener Schlinge, turning back on itself twice in a deep, wooded valley in Upper Austria, and the view of it from above is one of the most famous in the country. A short walk from the river up through the forest leads to the Schlögener Blick viewpoint, where you can see the river coiling below like a green-brown snake between steep slopes.

Down by the water, at the village of Schlögen, the Romans built a small fort and a civilian settlement, part of the Danube frontier that ran through the province of Noricum. Excavations have uncovered the remains of a bath house, which can be seen in a protected building near the river, and the outline of the fort. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire – The Danube Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2021, and a quiet, evocative place, with the river slipping past only a few steps away.

The riding here is a pleasure. The B130 runs along the northern bank of the Danube from Passau toward Aschach, a road through a narrow valley with the river on one side and forest on the other, with gentle curves and good surfaces. On the south bank, narrower roads climb up onto the plateau, with steep, winding sections and views back over the valley. The ferries across the river at several points add to the fun: small boats that carry a few cars and bikes across in minutes. Traffic is usually light, though cyclists on the Danube cycle path are numerous in summer.

Above the valley, the Mühlviertel to the north and the Innviertel and Hausruck to the south are rolling, rural regions with small villages, farms and forests, and excellent small roads for exploring. Mornings in the valley are often misty, especially in autumn, and the mist burning off over the river is a beautiful sight.

Facilities in Schlögen are limited to a hotel, a campsite and a few restaurants by the river. The nearest towns with fuel are a short ride away on the plateaus above the valley, and the larger town of Wegscheid in Germany is about twenty kilometres away, so it is wise to fill up before descending into the valley. Try a plate of fresh fish from the Danube or a Mühlviertel speciality, such as dumplings, with a glass of local cider, Most, a traditional drink of the region.
t.fort site and civil settlement of theile:
The Romans called it Iciniacum, and for a century and a half it was home to a cavalry unit guarding the Raetian frontier in what is now Middle Franconia. The fort at Theilenhofen, near Gunzenhausen in Bavaria, lay just behind the Limes, the frontier wall that here was built of stone, running across the landscape from the Danube toward the Main. Today there is little above ground, but information panels by the site and the line of the fort traced in the fields help visitors picture it. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2005.

The countryside around Theilenhofen is gentle and rural, with fields, woods and villages of red-roofed houses, and the Hahnenkamm hills rising to the south. A few kilometres to the north, the Franconian Lake District, the Fränkisches Seenland, is a group of artificial lakes created from the 1970s onward to transfer water from the Danube basin to the dry north of Bavaria. The Altmühlsee and the Großer Brombachsee are now popular for swimming, sailing and cycling, and their shores are lined with beaches, campsites and cafés.

For riders, the area offers relaxed riding on quiet roads through rolling farmland and forests, with gentle curves and good surfaces. To the south, the Altmühl valley, part of the Altmühltal Nature Park, is a beautiful, winding valley with limestone cliffs, juniper heaths and small towns, and the roads along it are a pleasure. To the west, the Hesselberg, the highest point in Middle Franconia, rises from the plain, with views from the top over the countryside. Traffic around the lakes can be heavy in summer, especially on weekends.

Gunzenhausen, a town of over sixteen thousand people about seven kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and an old town with a market square and a tower that was part of the town walls. The line of the Limes passes close to the town, and walking and cycling trails follow it through the countryside.

Franconian food is hearty and delicious: try Schäufele, roast pork shoulder with a crispy crackling, served with potato dumplings and gravy, or Bratwurst from Nuremberg, small sausages grilled over beech wood, and wash it down with a glass of Franconian beer from one of the many small breweries in the region, or a dry white wine from the vineyards of Lower Franconia. The best time to ride here is from late spring to early autumn, when the lakes are at their liveliest.
t.regensburg gro prufening kastell und vic:
There is not much to see at Großprüfening, and that is worth knowing before you arrive expecting walls. The Roman fort and its civil settlement lie on the western edge of Regensburg, close to where the Naab flows into the Danube, and what survives is mostly under fields and houses, known from excavation and aerial photographs rather than from standing masonry. The site is part of the Danube Limes, the river frontier that UNESCO listed in 2021, and its value is in the position: a garrison watching a river junction, a natural route north into what the Romans considered barbarian country.

The real Roman prize is a few kilometres downstream. Castra Regina, the legionary fortress founded under Marcus Aurelius in 179 for the Third Italian Legion, became the core of Regensburg, and pieces of its wall and the Porta Praetoria still stand in the old town, built into later houses as if nobody ever thought twice about it. The medieval city that grew on top is one of the best preserved in Germany, with the cathedral, the Stone Bridge over the Danube and the old sausage kitchen beside it that has been grilling for centuries.

Nearby, the former Benedictine abbey of Prüfening has a Romanesque church with remarkable twelfth-century wall paintings, which makes a calmer stop than the crowded centre. Sinzing, across the river, is a commuter village with a petrol station and a bakery or two, which is really all you need at the start or end of a day.

The riding around here is better than the flat Danube plain suggests. Head up the Naab valley and the road follows the river through wooded limestone country, with cliffs above the water and small villages every few kilometres. Westward, the Altmühl and the Danube gorge at Weltenburg are within easy reach, and the roads through the Jura there are twisty, scenic and busy with motorcycles on sunny Sundays. Eastward the Danube opens out into the Gäuboden, Bavaria's grain basket, where the land is flat and the riding becomes transport rather than pleasure.

Regensburg itself has fuel, food and every kind of rest you could want. Leave the bike outside the pedestrian centre and walk; the old town is compact, and an hour among its towers and lanes is a fine reward for a morning in the saddle.
t.krokar@45.5,14.8:
Krokar is one of the last true virgin forests in Europe, a reserve of beech and fir on a steep slope above the Kolpa river in southern Slovenia, where humans have never logged or managed the woods. Trees grow, fall and rot as they have done since the end of the Ice Age, and the result is an extraordinary tangle of giant trunks, dead wood and fresh saplings, home to fungi, beetles and birds that need old, undisturbed forest. Since 2017, Krokar has been part of the UNESCO site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe. The reserve itself is strictly protected and not open to visitors; you can walk along its edge, but the heart of it is left alone, which is precisely the point.

The surrounding Kočevje region is one of the most heavily forested parts of Europe, and it is famous for its brown bears. Slovenia has a healthy bear population, and the Kočevje forests are the core of their range, along with wolves and lynx. You are unlikely to see one from the road, but they are there, and locals are matter-of-fact about them.

The region also has a melancholy history. For six centuries it was home to the Gottscheers, a German-speaking community settled here in the Middle Ages. In 1941, under an agreement between Hitler and Mussolini, almost all of them were resettled elsewhere, and after the war the area was largely emptied. Many villages were abandoned and swallowed by the forest; their churches and cemeteries can still be found among the trees.

The Kolpa river forms the border with Croatia, and in summer it is one of the warmest rivers in Slovenia, with clear water, pebble beaches and swimming spots where locals spend lazy afternoons. The road along the river is narrow, quiet and winding, following the valley through small villages and forest, with Croatia on the other bank. The roads through the forest between Kočevje and the Kolpa climb over wooded ridges with good surfaces and very little traffic, though logging trucks appear without warning.

Kočevje, about thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel, shops and restaurants. Delnice, on the Croatian side, is another option. Slovenian motorways require a vignette, including for motorcycles; the minor roads here do not.
t.villa caldogno@45.6,11.5:
Villa Caldogno is one of the quieter Palladian villas, standing in a park on the edge of the town of the same name, a few kilometres north of Vicenza. Andrea Palladio designed it in the mid-sixteenth century for the Caldogno family, and it shows his early style: a compact, symmetrical block with a triple-arched loggia in the centre, a pediment above, and no unnecessary decoration. Inside, the main hall and rooms are covered with frescoes by Giovanni Antonio Fasolo and Giovanni Battista Zelotti, depicting scenes of country life, banquets, games and love, painted with charm and humour. Like the other villas of the Veneto, it belongs to the UNESCO listing of the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas.

The villas were country houses and working farms at the same time. Venetian noble families, as Venice turned from the sea to the land in the sixteenth century, invested in agriculture on the mainland, and Palladio gave them buildings that combined the dignity of a classical temple with the practicality of barns, stables and storerooms. His ideas, spread through his books, influenced architecture from England to the United States, where Jefferson's Monticello owes him a clear debt.

Vicenza itself is the city Palladio shaped, with the Basilica Palladiana on the main square, the Teatro Olimpico and street after street of palazzi. It's worth a half day, but leave the bike outside the restricted traffic zone.

North of Caldogno, the plain gives way to the foothills of the Alps, and the riding becomes excellent. The road up to the Asiago plateau climbs from the plain in a long series of hairpins, the Costo, to a high plateau of meadows and forests, scene of fierce fighting in the First World War, where war memorials and trenches are scattered through the woods. Monte Grappa, to the east, is another great climb, with a huge war memorial at the summit. Both roads are popular with riders and cyclists, so ride with care on weekends.

Caldogno has fuel and cafés; Vicenza has everything. The area around Breganze, on the edge of the hills, produces Torcolato, a sweet wine from dried grapes, and Asiago cheese comes from the plateau above. Have a plate of baccalà alla vicentina, the city's famous dried cod dish, with polenta.
t.botanical garden@45.4,11.9:
The Orto Botanico of Padua was founded in 1545 by the university, which needed a place to grow medicinal plants for the study of medicine, and it is the oldest university botanical garden in the world still in its original location. Its layout has hardly changed in nearly five centuries: a circular wall enclosing a square divided into quarters, with geometric flowerbeds, fountains and gates, a symbolic representation of the world. One of its most famous inhabitants is a palm tree planted in 1585, known as Goethe's palm because the poet studied it during his Italian journey in 1786 and drew from it ideas about the metamorphosis of plants. The garden was listed by UNESCO in 1997, and a modern greenhouse, the Garden of Biodiversity, now sits beside the historic garden, showing plants from different climates around the world.

Padua is a university city, and it feels young and lively, with students filling the squares in the evenings for a spritz. The university, founded in 1222, is one of the oldest in Europe; Galileo taught here, and the anatomy theatre where students watched dissections is still there in the Palazzo del Bo. A short walk from the garden, the Basilica of Saint Anthony draws pilgrims from all over the world, and the Prato della Valle, an enormous elliptical square surrounded by a canal and statues, is one of the largest squares in Europe. The Scrovegni Chapel, painted by Giotto in the early fourteenth century, is the city's supreme treasure; visits are timed and must be booked ahead.

Riding in Padua is like riding in most Italian cities: chaotic, with trams, cyclists and scooters everywhere, and restricted traffic zones in the historic centre where unauthorised vehicles are fined by camera. Park outside the centre and walk.

The best riding is to the southwest, in the Euganean Hills, a group of volcanic hills rising abruptly from the plain about twenty kilometres away. The roads wind around and over them, through vineyards, chestnut woods and medieval villages like Arquà Petrarca, where the poet Petrarch spent his last years. The surface is generally good, the bends are tight and frequent, and the views over the plain are lovely. Spa towns like Abano Terme sit at the foot of the hills.

Padua has fuel, garages and all services. Try the bigoli, thick pasta, and a glass of wine from the Euganean Hills.
t.frassino@45.4,10.7:
Just outside Peschiera del Garda, at the southern tip of the lake, the Sanctuary of the Madonna del Frassino stands among vineyards and fields. According to legend, in 1510 a farmer working in his vineyard was threatened by a snake, prayed to the Virgin and found a small statue of the Madonna in the branches of an ash tree, frassino in Italian. The snake disappeared, and the sanctuary was built on the spot. Today it is a Franciscan church and convent, with a cloister and a collection of votive offerings left by the grateful over the centuries.

Peschiera itself is a fortress town, surrounded by water. The Venetians built a star-shaped fortress around it in the sixteenth century, with walls rising from the lake and the Mincio river, and the town is part of the UNESCO listing of Venetian Works of Defence, alongside Bergamo and Palmanova. Later, it formed part of the Austrian Quadrilateral, a system of four fortresses defending the Habsburg possessions in northern Italy.

The area also has much older history. The lakeshore was home to prehistoric pile dwellings, and the site of Lucone, in the hills to the west, belongs to the UNESCO-listed Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps. South of the lake, the morainic hills left by the glacier that carved Lake Garda roll towards the plain, and among them, near Solferino and San Martino, the bloody battle of 1859 between the Franco-Piedmontese and Austrian armies was fought. The suffering of the wounded so shocked the Swiss businessman Henry Dunant that he wrote a book about it, which led to the founding of the Red Cross. There is a museum, an ossuary chapel and a monument at Solferino.

The riding around the lake is busy in summer, with heavy tourist traffic on the shore roads, but the hills to the south offer quieter roads through vineyards producing Lugana, a white wine, and the Custoza wines on the Veronese side. The Mincio valley, running south to Mantua, has a cycle path and gentle roads through fields and villages like Borghetto, with its old mills.

Peschiera has fuel, cafés and restaurants. Come in spring or autumn, when the lake is calm and the roads are emptier. In July and August, the shore roads around Garda are a traffic jam.
t.longobards in italy places of the power@:
Cividale del Friuli was founded as Forum Iulii, a market town established by Julius Caesar, and it gave its name to the whole region of Friuli. In 568, when the Lombards crossed the Alps and invaded Italy, Cividale was the first city they took, and it became the seat of their first duchy. The Lombards ruled much of Italy for two centuries, and Cividale preserves some of the finest traces of their culture. The Tempietto Longobardo, a small eighth-century chapel overlooking the river, holds a row of stucco female saints of extraordinary grace, among the most beautiful works of art of the early Middle Ages. It is the centrepiece of the UNESCO listing of the Longobards in Italy, Places of the Power, along with sites from Brescia to Benevento. The National Archaeological Museum displays jewellery, weapons and grave goods from Lombard tombs.

The town is built on the edge of a gorge cut by the Natisone river, and the Ponte del Diavolo, the Devil's Bridge, spans it in two high arches resting on a rock in the middle of the stream. Legend says the devil built it in exchange for the soul of the first to cross; the townspeople sent a cat. The river below is a vivid green, and on hot days locals swim in its pools.

Cividale is surrounded by the vineyards of the Colli Orientali del Friuli, which produce some of Italy's finest white wines, along with Ramandolo and Picolit, sweet wines from nearby hills. The town is also known for gubana, a spiral pastry filled with nuts, raisins and grappa, sold in every bakery.

The riding is excellent. East of Cividale, the Natisone valleys climb into the hills along the Slovenian border, an area with a Slovene-speaking community, small villages and quiet, winding roads through forests. The road over to Kobarid, in Slovenia, follows the Natisone and crosses the border into the Soča valley, where the Battle of Caporetto was fought in 1917; the museum in Kobarid is one of the best First World War museums anywhere. Monte Matajur, rising above the valleys, has a twisting road to near its summit, with views over the plain to the Adriatic.

Cividale has fuel, cafés and restaurants. Try frico, a crisp, rich cake of potato and Montasio cheese, the very definition of Friulian comfort food.
t.itsukushima shinto shrine@34.3,132.3:
The great orange torii gate of Itsukushima, standing in the sea off the island of Miyajima, is one of the most famous images of Japan. At high tide, it seems to float on the water; at low tide, you can walk out across the sand to its feet. The shrine behind it is built on piers over the bay, a series of halls and corridors painted vermilion and white, connected by boardwalks, so that it too seems to float when the tide is in. A shrine has stood here for well over a thousand years, and its present form owes much to Taira no Kiyomori, the powerful warlord who rebuilt it in the twelfth century. The island itself has long been considered sacred, so much so that in the past, births and deaths were not permitted on it. The shrine was listed by UNESCO in 1996, and the torii was restored a few years ago after a long period under scaffolding.

Miyajima is a short ferry ride from Miyajimaguchi, on the mainland southwest of Hiroshima. The simplest approach for a rider is to park at the terminal and cross on foot; the island is small and walkable, and its narrow streets are crowded with visitors. A small visitor levy is collected when you board the ferry. Tame deer wander everywhere, and they will eat your map, your ticket and your lunch if you let them. Above the town, Mount Misen rises steeply, reached by a ropeway and a walk, with views over the islands of the Inland Sea.

The local specialities are oysters, grilled on the street, and momiji manju, small cakes shaped like maple leaves and filled with sweet bean paste. Hiroshima's okonomiyaki, a savoury pancake layered with noodles, is worth seeking out on the mainland.

The roads around Hatsukaichi and along the coast are busy, with traffic lights and urban sprawl, but inland the hills of western Hiroshima prefecture offer quiet, winding mountain roads through forests and small villages. Japan drives on the left, and the speed limits are low and enforced.

Hatsukaichi and the Miyajimaguchi area have fuel, convenience stores and restaurants. Come early in the morning or stay into the evening, when the day-trippers have left and the shrine is lit up; check the tide tables to see the gate at high water.
t.idrija kamst water pump with the rake wa:
Idrija sits at the bottom of a narrow, steep-sided valley in western Slovenia, and for about five hundred years the town made a living from the red mineral cinnabar, the ore of mercury. The mine at Idrija was one of the largest mercury mines in Europe, second only to Almadén in Spain, and the two sites share UNESCO World Heritage status. The Kamšt is the best monument to that history: a huge wooden waterwheel, more than thirteen metres across, built in the late eighteenth century to drive pumps that kept the mine from flooding.

The wheel is fed by the Rake, a long channel carrying water from the surrounding hills to the town, an engineering feat of its time that tells you how seriously Idrija's miners took the problem of water underground. The mine's tunnels are open to visitors with a guide, and the town museum, in a castle above the centre, adds the stories of miners' families, mercury, and the lace-making that grew up alongside the mine. Idrija lace is still made, and the town celebrates it every June with a festival. For food, try žlikrofi, small potato dumplings that are protected as a local speciality, usually served with a meat sauce or on their own with a little bacon.

The roads into Idrija are what make the ride. From Logatec and Vrhnika you climb through forest and drop into the Idrijca valley, with long curving bends, sections of tight hairpins, and views down into green gorges. The road to Cerkno and the one toward Žiri are both rewarding, with good tarmac, moderate traffic and a steady stream of corners that suit a bike well. Weekends bring cyclists and other riders, so stay on your side of the line, and be careful with gravel on shaded bends after rain. Spring and early autumn are best, when the beech woods are bright and the light is clear.

Idrija is large enough for fuel, groceries and cafés, and there are plenty of places to sit down by the river. A day here works well when you walk the old town on foot, so park near the centre and leave the helmet behind for a couple of hours.
t.kalkalpen hintergebirg@47.7,14.5:
The Kalkalpen National Park is the largest forest wilderness in Austria, and the Hintergebirge is one of its quiet corners, a limestone mountain range in Upper Austria with steep wooded slopes, deep valleys and very few roads. It is a landscape of beech, spruce and fir, with some of the oldest unmanaged beech forest in the Alps, so valuable that it is included in the UNESCO listing of ancient beech forests of Europe. Walking in it feels like walking in the Europe before the roads.

Wildlife is the great attraction. Lynx, reintroduced in this region, are rare and secretive, but chamois, red deer and roe deer are common, and capercaillie and black woodpeckers live in the forests. Rivers run clear and cold through limestone gorges, and the water is some of the cleanest in the country. In the old days this was timber country, with logs floated down the streams to the sawmills and forges of the Enns and Steyr valleys, and the trails and small dams from that era are still visible if you know what to look for.

The roads are the main constraint. The area around the park has fine riding, with the long valleys leading toward Windischgarsten and the Pyhrn corridor offering smooth bends, gradual climbs and views of limestone cliffs, but the interior has few roads open to traffic, and some forestry tracks are closed to motor vehicles. Respect all signs, because the park authorities take restrictions seriously, and expect to turn back if a barrier appears. Weather in the mountains can change fast, with afternoon storms in summer and early snow in autumn, so check forecasts before heading out.
