Windischgarsten, about ten kilometres away, has fuel, food and rooms, with a pleasant village centre and hotels used to hikers and cyclists. A plate of Knödel or a slice of curd cheese cake from a local inn is the right reward after a morning on the road. If you prefer a quieter evening, the smaller villages nearby, such as Spital am Pyhrn, offer guesthouses and a more rural feel. Early October, when the beech leaves turn orange and the air is crisp, is the best season, although late spring has its own charm.
t.episcopal complex of the euphrasian basi:
Poreč sits on a little limestone peninsula on the western coast of Istria, and the old town still follows the grid the Romans laid down, with the Decumanus running straight down the middle. The Euphrasian Basilica is tucked a few lanes from the main street, behind a quiet atrium, and it is easy to walk past if you are looking for something grand from the outside. Inside is the reason it earned its UNESCO listing: a sixth-century church, built under Bishop Euphrasius, that kept its Byzantine mosaics through a millennium and a half of earthquakes, Venetian rule and tourism.

The apse is the part to stand in front of. Gold tesserae, a Virgin and Child enthroned between angels, the bishop himself holding a model of his church. Under the floor and around the complex there are older layers, the remains of earlier prayer rooms and Roman houses, because Christians here had been meeting in a private house long before anyone built a basilica. The bell tower can be climbed, and from the top you read the whole peninsula, red roofs, marina and the flat blue Adriatic.

For a rider, Poreč itself is a place to arrive on foot. The old centre is mostly closed to traffic, so leave the bike at the edge of town and walk in, and do it early, because by midday the cruise-ship crowd of the coast has found the Decumanus. Fuel is no problem here, with a town of ten thousand people, and there are plenty of cafes along the waterfront promenade where a coffee costs what you would expect for a tourist port.

The better riding starts when you leave. Head inland and the land lifts into the green and red Istrian interior, small roads between vineyards, olive groves and hilltop villages like Motovun and Grožnjan, where the corners are tight but the surface is usually decent and traffic thins out quickly once you are a few kilometres from the coast. Funtana to the south and Tar to the east are the nearest small neighbours, both useful for a quiet back road rather than the busy coastal route. Summer weekends are crowded and hot, so spring and late September are kinder, when the stone is warm and the light slants gold across the apse mosaics and the vineyards alike.
t.palazzo de la ragione chapel of the cara:
Padua's Palazzo della Ragione is the big hall that sits between the two market squares, Piazza delle Erbe and Piazza della Frutta, and it has done that job since the early thirteenth century, when the city was a self-governing commune and wanted a building big enough for its courts. The enormous upper hall, with a roof shaped like an upturned ship's keel, is said to be one of the largest medieval halls in Europe, its walls covered in astrological frescoes and a giant wooden horse standing at one end. Downstairs the arcades still house butchers, cheesemongers and cafes, which is the best sign that the building has remained a living part of town.

The chapel in the label presumably belongs to the Carraresi, the family who ruled Padua in the fourteenth century before Venice absorbed it, and their taste can still be seen across the old centre. The university, one of the oldest in the world, was founded in 1222, and Galileo taught here for eighteen years. Students are why the lanes around the squares are lively into the night, with spritz bars filling the pavements by early evening.

For riders, Padua is a day of walking and eating, not riding. The centre is a limited traffic zone, so leave the bike on the outskirts, where there are paid parking areas for motorbikes, and walk in. Padua is a big city with all services, so fuel and coffee are never a problem, but the ring roads and the Veneto plain around it are flat, busy and not fun. If you want a ride, go south-west to the Euganean Hills, a cluster of old volcanic cones rising abruptly from the plain, with winding roads, vineyards and medieval villages like Arquà Petrarca, where the poet Petrarch spent his last years and died in 1374.

The Euganean roads are narrow and twisty, with a few hairpins and surprisingly steep gradients, and cyclists use them in numbers, so stay patient on weekends. The best seasons are spring and autumn, with clear air from the Alps and the hills at their greenest or golden.
t.scrovegni chapel church of the eremitani:
Giotto painted the Scrovegni Chapel in about two years, between 1303 and 1305, and it changed how Europeans drew people. Before him faces were icons; here they are tired, tender, furious, ashamed. The chapel was commissioned by Enrico Scrovegni, whose father Reginaldo was a moneylender so notorious that Dante put him in hell. Enrico built the chapel beside the family palace, so the story goes, to ease his father's soul, and the result is a small brick box covered inside with a blue ceiling of gold stars and thirty-odd scenes from the lives of Mary and Christ, ending with a vast Last Judgment on the west wall.

Visits are strictly timed. You wait in a climate-controlled room for a quarter of an hour so the air in the chapel stays stable, then you are let in for a short slot, which means booking ahead is wise, especially in spring and early autumn. Next door is the Church of the Eremitani, built by Augustinian friars in the thirteenth century, with a great wooden ship-keel ceiling. In March 1944 an Allied bombing raid destroyed the Ovetari chapel here, along with the early frescoes of the young Mantegna. Fragments were painstakingly recovered, and what you see now is a patient jigsaw, which gives the church a sad, serious dignity.

Padua is a big city with all the services a rider needs, so fuel and food are simple, though the centre is a restricted traffic zone and the best plan is to park at the edge and walk the short distance. Do not try to ride through the lanes by Prato della Valle at midday, because the one-way pattern and the trams are baffling.

For the ride out, the ride list pairs this stop with Palladio's Villa Saraceno at Agugliaro, which lies south-west of Padua on the edge of the Berici hills, a gentle land of flat fields and low wooded ridges. The roads between are quiet country lanes through vineyards and maize, with some traffic on the provincial roads and fog in late autumn and winter. Spring and early autumn offer the best light, and a spritz in the old squares after the chapel visit is a fair reward.
t.nakatsu miya@33.9,130.4:
Munakata Taisha is not one shrine but three, spread across the sea off northern Kyushu, and Nakatsu-miya is the middle one. The boat leaves from the little harbour of Kōnominato and takes roughly a quarter of an hour, crossing water that was once the main sea lane between Japan and the Korean peninsula. Shrines were built at three points along that lane to protect sailors, and the middle one honours the goddess Tagitsuhime.

The island is small, quiet and rich in forest, with camellias and old trees around the shrine, and deer and cats wander the paths. On the far side is a place where worshippers pray toward Okinoshima, the sacred island further out, which is closed to ordinary visitors and has been for centuries, a place where sailors left offerings of mirrors, gold rings and carved gems that now fill a museum on the mainland. Ōshima is the closest an ordinary person can get to that old idea of the sea as a holy road.

For a rider the real appeal is the coast. The road along the Genkai Sea, with its views of islands, small fishing harbours and pine-covered headlands, is one of the best easy rides in northern Kyushu. The surface is excellent, the bends are smooth and the traffic is light outside holidays, though summer weekends fill the beaches and the road. There is a ferry timetable to respect, and weather can cancel crossings, so check before you set out, and leave the bike on the mainland, since you walk on the island.

Fuel is no trouble. Koga and Nishifukuma, with populations of forty to sixty thousand, are close, and the roadside stations on the coast sell fresh fish, rice balls and strong coffee. The other half of this ride heads for the Imperial Steel Works at Yawata, in Kitakyushu, the plant that powered Japan's industrialisation, and the contrast between the island shrine and the blast furnaces makes the day. Late April and October are lovely, with clear light and mild sea air.
t.hetsu miya@33.8,130.5:
Hetsu-miya is the third of the Munakata shrines, and the only one you can drive to. Munakata Taisha honours three goddesses, the daughters of the sun goddess Amaterasu in the old myths, and each lives in a different place along the sea lane between Japan and Korea: one on the remote island of Okinoshima, one on Ōshima and one here on the mainland, at Tashima, beside a calm pine grove close to the shore. The grounds are plain, with a simple wooden hall and an air of sea and pine, and in autumn a festival draws crowds and boats.

The real wonder is in the museum next to the main shrine, the Shinpōkan, which holds the offerings from Okinoshima, tens of thousands of objects, many of them left by travellers and envoys from the fourth to the ninth centuries. Bronze mirrors from China, glass cups from Persia, gold rings and carved ornaments show how far this sea road reached, and the whole treasure has been declared a national treasure. Okinoshima itself, the sacred island, was added to the UNESCO list in 2017, and its entry is so strictly limited that almost nobody is allowed to land.

Munakata is a modest city, and Koga and Nishifukuma to the east and west are bigger towns of forty to sixty thousand where you will find fuel and supermarkets. The area is easy to reach from Fukuoka, about an hour away by road, and the coastal route is pleasant, running past fishing harbours, beaches and low hills with the shapes of islands offshore. The surface is excellent, the traffic is light and the road bends gently, so it is relaxed riding, not a technical challenge.

The ride list also takes you to the Imperial Steel Works, in the Yawata district of Kitakyushu, which was one of the foundations of Japan's rise as an industrial power. After the quiet of Tashima, with its pines and mirrors, the blast furnaces are a jolt, but that contrast is the point. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the first days of May are lively with festivals. Stop for grilled fish or a plate of local sashimi at one of the harbours.
t.historic centre of cesky krumlov@48.8,14:
Český Krumlov is shaped by a river. The Vltava makes a series of tight S-bends in a rocky valley in south Bohemia, and the old town sits in one of the loops, with a castle on a cliff above it, so that the whole place feels like a stage set. The castle is the second largest in the Czech Republic, with a round tower painted in Renaissance style, a bridge across the moat where brown bears live, and a Baroque theatre from the seventeenth century that still has its original stage machinery. The town was owned by the Rožmberk family and later the Schwarzenbergs, and the painter Egon Schiele lived here for a time in 1911. UNESCO listed the historic centre in 1992.

The centre is a tangle of cobbled lanes, with red roofs, gabled houses and little squares, and it is mostly closed to cars, so leave the bike in a car park at the edge and walk in. Fuel is available in town, which has about fourteen thousand people, and Kájov, a small village nearby, is quieter. Summer fills the streets with tourists, so go early or stay overnight to see the town in the evening, when the lamps are lit and the crowds have gone. Rafting down the river in an old canoe is a local summer ritual.

For riding, the Bohemian Forest, the Šumava, is the real reward. The roads around the Lipno reservoir and up into the hills run through spruce woods and meadows, with smooth surfaces, moderate bends and light traffic, and they cross into Austria with no border checks within the Schengen area. The ride list pairs this with the Enns Gräberstraße, a Roman cemetery road in Upper Austria, and a day that crosses both countries gives a feel for the old frontier between the Roman empire and the northern tribes.

Try roast pork with dumplings and cabbage, a thick garlic soup in a bread bowl and a glass of local beer, which is excellent. May to October is the best season, with September offering the quietest roads. Winter brings snow, and the town looks even better in white.
t.regensburg kumpfmuhl kastell und vicus i:
Kumpfmühl is an ordinary southern suburb of Regensburg, with apartment blocks, a church and a quiet street grid, and under it lies one of the earliest Roman forts on the Danube. The fort, built in the first century, guarded a crossing of roads south of the river, and it was succeeded by the large legionary camp, Castra Regina, which gave the city its name after the late second century. A civil settlement, a vicus, grew beside the fort. Finds from it fill cases in the city's museums, and little shows above ground. The honest summary is that this is a stop for people who like their history thin and imaginative.

What Regensburg does offer a rider is a remarkable city, one of the best-preserved medieval centres in Germany, and a place where you can park the bike and walk for half a day. The old town sits where the Regen meets the Danube, with a twelfth-century Stone Bridge, a Gothic cathedral with twin spires, and narrow streets lined with tall tower houses that the old patrician families built to rival each other. A sausage kitchen beside the bridge claims to be among the oldest restaurants in the world, and you will smell it before you see it. UNESCO listed the old town in 2006.

The ride in from the south is not much to write about, since it is suburban streets, ring roads and traffic lights. If you are heading here from the Altmühl valley or the Bavarian Forest, the better moments come earlier, on the roads that climb over the Jura limestone ridges and descend into the Danube basin. Regensburg is a city of one hundred and thirty thousand, so fuel, parking and food are never an issue, though the centre is pedestrian and tight. Leave the bike at a garage or in one of the outer lots and walk in.

The Danube here is wide and calm, and cyclists run along its banks. A summer evening on the north bank in Stadtamhof, with beer and the old bridge lit, is a good reward for a day on the road. Early spring and autumn are best, because midsummer crowds fill every terrace and the centre is hot and dense. Kumpfmühl is the starting line, and the city is the finish.
t.fort site and civil setllement of weisse:
Weißenburg in Bayern is the best Roman stop in this part of Franconia, and the fort here, known in antiquity as Biriciana, was a serious place. It stood on the Upper German-Raetian Limes, which UNESCO listed in 2005, and it held a cavalry unit at its height. Today you can walk the reconstructed gate and walls and then visit the Roman baths, which are among the best preserved in southern Germany and sit under a modern roof beside the old town. In 1979, builders found a hoard of bronze and silver objects buried in the fort's grounds, the Weißenburg treasure, which includes ceremonial armour, and it is now one of the key finds of Roman Bavaria.

The town itself is a pleasant surprise, a walled medieval town of seventeen thousand people with towers, half-timbered houses and a main street of cafes and bakeries. Above it stands the Wülzburg, a massive Renaissance fortress that later served as a prison. Weißenburg also has a long tradition of brewing and a local appetite for pork and dumplings, in the Franconian way. Fuel and supermarkets are easy to find, and parking near the old town is straightforward for bikes.

The riding around here is gentle and varied. The Altmühl Valley Nature Park lies just south, with limestone cliffs, river meanders and long smooth curves, and to the north the Franconian Lake District offers flat, quick roads between reservoirs and farmland. Ellingen, a short run away, has a baroque palace of the Teutonic Order in a very tidy small town. Roads are well surfaced and traffic is moderate, though weekends in good weather bring plenty of cyclists and day trippers.

For the stop, spend time at the baths first, because they make the Romans real, then climb the street to the old town for coffee. If the day is hot, the shade of the medieval gates is welcome. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with the fields in bloom or golden. After a morning here, you will notice the Limes everywhere in the countryside, a long, quiet line that once marked the edge of an empire.
t.old town of regensburg with stadtamhof@4:
The first thing to do in Regensburg is to cross the Stone Bridge on foot. It dates from the twelfth century and, for a long time, was the only fixed crossing of the Danube for hundreds of kilometres, which is why the city grew rich on trade. Merchants, crusaders and pilgrims passed over it, and the arches still carry the tourist traffic. At the far end lies Stadtamhof, an island of narrow streets and low houses between two river channels, which was once a separate town and still feels slightly apart. UNESCO listed the old town and Stadtamhof in 2006, and the city has one of the largest medieval centres in Germany.

The other face of Regensburg is imperial. From 1663 until 1806 the Perpetual Imperial Diet, the parliament of the Holy Roman Empire, met here, and the old town hall still shows the chambers. The cathedral of St Peter, in Gothic style with twin spires, anchors the skyline, and inside there is some remarkable stained glass. Around it the streets are lined with patrician towers, built by merchant families as status symbols, and a few survive at full height. Roman walls remain in the foundations, since this was the camp of the Third Italic Legion.

For a rider, the town is for walking, not riding. The centre is a maze of one-way streets and pedestrian zones, so park at the edge, perhaps near the river on the north side, and walk in. With one hundred and thirty thousand inhabitants, fuel and workshops are easy to find on the outskirts. The approach roads from the north, through the hills of the Bavarian Forest foothills, are the better riding, with climbs and long curves. The Danube valley road upstream to Kelheim and the Danube gorge at Weltenburg is a good half-day excursion and a quiet one on weekdays.

Eat on the river, near the bridge, where you can watch the water move. The local sausages with sweet mustard and sauerkraut are the classic order. Early morning, before the tour groups arrive, gives you almost empty streets and warm light on the pale stone. In winter, the Christmas markets fill the squares, but the cold and the cobbles make the bike a bad idea.
t.lagazzi del vho@45.1,10.4:
Four thousand years ago people built a village on stilts at the edge of a marsh here, and the muck preserved it. The Lagazzi del Vho site, near Piadena in the Po plain, was a Bronze Age settlement raised on wooden piles above a wetland, and thousands of its timbers, pots and tools lay waterlogged in the mud until archaeologists recovered them. It is one of the prehistoric pile dwelling sites around the Alps that UNESCO listed in 2011, and Italy has several. You will not see houses, since the evidence lies buried, but you will see a flat green plain that was once water, and a good museum in the town explains the finds.

The country is the heart of the Po valley, the great flat basin between the Alps and the Apennines, drained by the Oglio river. It is a land of poplars, maize, irrigation ditches and long straight roads, and in winter it is famous for fog so thick that you can lose the bonnet of a car. The villages are built of warm red brick, with a church and a square, and farms still keep pigs and dairy cattle. Cremona, famous for violins, lies to the south-east, and Mantua, with its Gonzaga palaces, is not far.

Sabbioneta, the ideal town named in the ride titles, is a short ride away and one of the oddest places in Italy. Vespasiano Gonzaga built it in the late sixteenth century on a perfectly planned grid with a theatre, a gallery and a ring of walls, and it was meant to be a perfect Renaissance capital in miniature. It never grew into the capital he dreamed of, and today it is a quiet, almost empty little town in the fields. UNESCO listed it together with Mantua in 2008.

Riding here is flat, quiet and pleasant, on small roads between fields, with canals and the odd levee. Expect farm traffic, crosswinds and mist in the mornings. Fuel is easy in Piadena, with a few thousand people, and Asola is a bit bigger. The food is rich: salami and cotechino, mostarda, a sweet and sharp fruit relish, and tortelli di zucca, the pumpkin-filled pasta of Mantua. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and midsummer is hot and thick with mosquitoes. Take a short walk on the edge of the marsh, if there is a path.
t.litzlberg sud@47.9,13.6:
Attersee is the largest lake lying entirely within Austria, and the water is so clear and clean that boats seem to hang over their own shadows. It lies in the Salzkammergut, the lake district east of Salzburg, ringed by forested hills and with the limestone wall of the Hollengebirge at its southern end. Litzlberg sits on the western shore, a short way from Seewalchen, where the lake narrows and the shoreline is a mix of meadows, reed beds and villas with boathouses. It is a place that people have lived since the Stone Age, and the lake bed here holds the remains of prehistoric pile dwellings that are part of the UNESCO listing for such sites around the Alps.

Nothing of the pile dwellings can be seen from the shore, because the posts and the debris of daily life lie preserved in the mud under the water, a fragile record that is better left in place. What you can see is the later history of the place, and in particular the summers of Gustav Klimt. The painter spent many holidays on the Attersee from 1900 to 1916 with the Floge family, and the lake and its surroundings feature in many of his landscapes, with their square canvases and shimmering colours. Several of the views he painted, including the little castle of Kammer, can still be recognised, and the sense of a summer idyll is still strong.

The riding around the lake is a classic of the Salzkammergut. The road loops around the shore through lakeside villages, with views of the water and the mountains, and then climbs through meadows and woods. The surfaces are smooth, the bends are gentle and the traffic is heavy on summer weekends, so the best time to ride is a weekday morning in May or September. In summer, the lake is warm enough for swimming, and the water temperature on a hot day can reach the mid-twenties.

Seewalchen, three kilometres away, has fuel, a supermarket and cafes, and Attnang-Puchheim, a bigger railway town, is to the north. Local fish from the lake, such as Reinanke or char, is served smoked or fried at lakeside inns, and the local cake and coffee are excellent. Wear layers, because the weather in the Alps can change quickly, and bring a swimsuit.
t.kalkalpen bodinggraben@47.8,14.4:
Where the Pyhrn pass road drops from the Totes Gebirge toward the Enns and the Steyr valleys, Austria keeps one of its most important pieces of old forest. Kalkalpen National Park covers a large area of limestone mountains, gorges and woodland in Upper Austria, and its beech forests are among the last in Europe where trees have been left to grow, fall and rot undisturbed. They are part of a UNESCO listing called the Ancient Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, a strange name for what is, in the end, a green cathedral of grey trunks and soft, filtered light.

Bodinggraben is a narrow valley that leads into this country, a wooded ravine with a stream at the bottom and steep slopes of beech, spruce and fir on each side. In such places the forest has a particular feel, thick with moss, mushrooms and fallen logs, and full of the sound of water. Lynx have been reintroduced to the area, and while you are unlikely to see one, black woodpeckers, three-toed woodpeckers and capercaillie are among the birds that live here. In autumn, the beech leaves turn a deep copper, and the whole valley glows.

The ride is a delight, with plenty of choice. The road from Windischgarsten climbs through meadows with views of the Warscheneck and the Totes Gebirge, and the Pyhrn route itself has been a main way over the mountains since Roman times, used by merchants, pilgrims and armies. The tarmac is good, the bends are moderate and the scenery changes constantly, from farmland to forest to bare rock. Cattle graze in high pastures, and traffic is generally light apart from weekends. Weather in the Alps is variable, with sudden rain and fog, and snow can linger into April.

Windischgarsten, seven kilometres away, is a small resort town with fuel, shops and cafes, and Spital am Pyhrn, a little further, has an old collegiate church. Local cheeses, smoked meats and dumplings are all good, and a hearty Kasnocken makes a good lunch. Trails lead into the park from several points, and if you leave the bike for a walk, you will understand why people feel protective of this forest.
t.benedictine convent of st john at mustai:
In the high, narrow Val Mustair, at the point where Switzerland meets South Tyrol and the Stelvio national park, there is a Benedictine convent that was founded, according to tradition, by Charlemagne himself around the year 800. Whether or not the emperor's role is exactly as the legend has it, the convent of St John is certainly Carolingian, and it keeps the largest cycle of Carolingian wall paintings anywhere. The figures, painted in the early ninth century, cover the walls of the church in red, yellow and green, in a lively, slightly naive style, with scenes from the life of David and the story of Christ, and later Romanesque frescoes were painted over them in places. UNESCO listed it in 1983.

The convent is still home to a community of Benedictine nuns, and the church is open to visitors, with a museum in the old tower that explains the history and the restoration work. It is a modest, quiet place with white walls, grey roofs and the mountains standing behind it. The valley's language is Romansh, a descendant of Latin that is spoken by only a few tens of thousands of people, and you will see it on signs and hear it in the shops. A slice of Engadine nut cake in the village is the proper reward.

This is outstanding riding country. The Ofen pass, at 2,149 metres, climbs from the valley through the Swiss National Park to Zernez, with long, flowing bends and larch forest, and the Umbrail pass, at 2,501 metres, is the highest paved road in Switzerland, joining the Stelvio road above Bormio. The Stelvio itself, at 2,757 metres, with its dozens of hairpins, is just across the border, but all of these passes are closed by snow from late autumn until late spring, so check before you go. Summer weekends are very busy.

Tubre, across the border in Italy, and Mustair itself are small, and fuel is better bought in Mals, a larger town in South Tyrol a short ride away, and in the valley's main villages. Prices are lower on the Italian side. Bring warm clothes, because the passes are cold even in July, and carry some cash in both euros and francs.
t.rock drawings in valcamonica@46.0,10.3:
Valcamonica is a long, deep Alpine valley running north from Lake Iseo towards the Adamello and Tonale mountains, and for something like eight thousand years people have been scratching pictures on its rocks. The Camunni, an Iron Age tribe, carved most of them, but the tradition began in the Neolithic and carried on through the Roman period and into the Middle Ages. The result is one of the largest collections of petroglyphs in the world, well over a hundred thousand figures by the common estimate, and in 1979 it became the first site in Italy to be given World Heritage status.

The images are simple and astonishingly alive. There are stick-figure warriors with round shields, deer hunted by dogs, ploughs drawn by oxen, huts on stilts, and the so-called Camunian rose, a looping symbol that is now the emblem of the Lombardy region. Some rocks show a village, drawn almost like a map. The carvings were pecked into smooth glacial sandstone, polished by ice in the last glaciation, and the best of them are in open parks near Capo di Ponte, where paths run through chestnut and oak woods and the rock surfaces rise like grey whales from the moss. Go on a bright morning if you can, because low raking light makes the engraved lines stand out. Breno, close by, is the valley's main town, with a hilltop castle and enough shops, cafes and petrol stations to sort out any practical need.

The valley is good riding in its own right. The main road follows the Oglio river through a wide, green floor with steep wooded sides, villages with tall bell towers and farms on terraces, and at the top the road reaches Ponte di Legno, from which two great Alpine passes open up. The Gavia, a narrow, high and sometimes terrifying climb, and the Tonale, an easier wide road across to Trentino, are both within reach. Another famous test, the Mortirolo, leaves the valley side near Monno, and its gradients that cyclists talk about in hushed voices. High passes carry closures in winter, and even in June they can hold snow, so check before you commit.

Late spring and September are the sweet times, with clear air and fewer visitors. In midsummer the traffic of holidaymakers heading for Lake Iseo and the mountains thickens along the valley floor. Polenta, cured meats and casonsei, filled pasta from the Brescia area, are what you will find on local menus.
t.the imperial steel works@33.9,130.8:
Japan's modern industry has a birthday, and in Kitakyushu they celebrate it with a rusting blast furnace. The Imperial Steel Works at Yawata began producing iron in 1901, a state-run enterprise financed with money from the war indemnity that China paid after the First Sino-Japanese War, and it was built to give a country that had just opened to the world its own supply of steel. German engineers advised on the early design. The works grew into the heart of the northern Kyushu industrial belt, and Yawata became a city that smelled of coke and smoke for most of a century.

UNESCO included the site in the Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution in 2015, a group of twenty-three components that traces how Japan went from feudal domains to a major industrial and naval power in barely fifty years. The old Higashida blast furnace, dating from 1901, stands near the present works and is the best-known feature, a tall dark cylinder with pipes and stairs, preserved as a memorial. Today it is surrounded by parks, shopping malls and a former theme park site, a strange mix of heritage and ordinary life.

Kitakyushu sits at the northern tip of Kyushu, facing the Kanmon Strait, the narrow channel that separates the island from Honshu. Ships squeeze through day and night, and the Kanmon Bridge and the tunnels beneath carry road traffic. The ride into the city is not a scenic one, with expressways, interchanges, factories and housing blocks, and the riding is best treated as a way to reach the interesting parts. Fuel, food and everything else are easy in a city of nearly a million people. The nearby Mojiko district has restored brick buildings from the days of the port's glory, and a ferry crosses the strait to Shimonoseki, famous for its fugu, the pufferfish served by specially licensed chefs.

For better riding, head south into the hills of the Hiko mountains or east along the coast towards Oita, where the roads loosen up. Weekday mornings are easier than weekends in the city, and the air is clearer in spring and autumn. If you care about the story of industry, this is a place to stand and imagine the roar of the furnaces, which once lit the night sky of Kyushu.
t.idrija old town@46.0,14.0:
Mercury is a strange thing to build a town on. In 1490, according to the story, a local cooper was soaking a tub in a spring when he noticed a gleaming liquid metal in the bottom, and the find was the start of one of the biggest mercury mines in the world. Idrija, a small town in a narrow valley in western Slovenia, became rich on the metal, which was used for medicine, mirrors, gold extraction and later for gunpowder detonators. The mine ran for about five hundred years until it was closed in 1994, and together with the mine at Almaden in Spain, Idrija was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 2012.

The old town is a compact cluster of tall houses and miners' buildings around the river, dominated by Gewerkenegg Castle, a sturdy sixteenth-century building that was once the mine's administration and storehouse and now houses the municipal museum. Part of the mine is open for visits, and you can go down a tunnel in a helmet and walk through the old workings, which include a small chapel and a Miner's House. The town also has a lace-making tradition that began in the seventeenth century, when miners' wives made lace to earn money, and the Idrija School of Lace still teaches the craft. The local dish, Idrijski zlikrofi, are small dumplings filled with potato and herbs, protected by a European label, and you can try them in almost any local restaurant.

The roads to Idrija are one of its charms. From Ljubljana, the route runs through Vrhnika and Logatec, then climbs into forested hills, and the road down into the valley winds through steep woods with tight curves and views across the narrow valley. The surface is generally good, but traffic can be heavy with trucks and commuters, and there are speed cameras. From Idrija the roads climb to the Cerkno hills and the Idrijca valley, with curves, hairpins and scenery that Slovenian riders love. Spring and autumn are the best times, when the beech forest is bright green or burnt orange. Winter brings ice and snow.

Idrija has about six thousand people, so fuel, shops, restaurants and rooms are all easy to find. The Krokar forest reserve, on the ride, is a rare patch of virgin beech and fir woodland in the Kocevje region, wild and quiet, and a world away from the mine.
t.herrenchiemsee new palace@47.9,12.4:
King Ludwig II wanted to build Versailles on an island, and for the most part he did. The New Palace on Herrenchiemsee, the largest island in the Chiemsee, is his answer to Louis XIV, a Bavarian homage to the French sun king that took years to build and was never finished. Ludwig spent barely ten days there in total. The money ran out, the king's reputation among his ministers fell, and in 1886 he was dead in Lake Starnberg under circumstances people still argue about.

You cannot ride to the palace. Boats from Prien am Chiemsee, about four kilometres from here, run across the water, and the island itself has no cars. So the day works like this: park or leave your bike in the Prien area, take the ferry and enjoy a walk through the lime-tree avenues to the front of the palace. The Hall of Mirrors is longer than the one in Versailles, which was not an accident, and the guided tour covers the rooms that Ludwig actually finished. The kitchens and staircase were left half done, and you can see the difference.

The riding around the Chiemsee is the Bavarian sort you plan a weekend around: gentle roads along the shore, big views south to the Chiemgau Alps, and a good chance of a sky that changes by the hour. The lake is nicknamed the Bavarian Sea, and the weather on it can turn quickly, with afternoon thunderstorms in summer. Traffic is heavy at weekends, especially on the road into Prien, so mornings on weekdays are the civilised hour. Prien am Chiemsee, with about 10,000 people, is the sensible place for fuel, food and a bed.

Nature fans should look at the lake in a wider sense. The Chiemsee is a basin gouged out by an Alpine glacier, and its shallow margins are good for reed birds. The lake is also known for its Chiemsee Renke, a whitefish served smoked or fried in the lakeside inns. Late afternoon from the shore, with the mountains going blue behind the island, is the picture most people remember.
t.abtsdorf iii@47.9,13.5:
The Attersee is the biggest lake in the Salzkammergut, and Abtsdorf sits on its western shore, a settlement so small the label can get away with a Roman numeral. In this case the III means a third spot among a cluster of lake access points, so what you are really visiting is the shoreline between Attersee village and Weyregg, where the water is startlingly clear and the mountains stand up behind the opposite bank.

That clarity is not an accident. The Attersee is deep and fed by cold mountain water, and for a long time it had a reputation as one of the cleanest large lakes in Austria. Swimmers and sailors have used it for generations. Gustav Klimt spent many summers on its shores, and some of his best-known landscape paintings were made on the lake and around Litzlberg, a short way along. You can see why a painter would sit here: the surface changes from steel to turquoise in half an hour as the clouds move.

For riding, the road along the lake is the attraction. It runs close to the water in places, with enough small bends and rises to keep you awake without needing anything dramatic, and the views open onto the Höllengebirge range to the east. Summer weekends can be busy with cars and cyclists, so weekday mornings or the shoulder seasons are kinder. In July and August thunderstorms build over the mountains in the afternoon and the temperature can drop a good deal in minutes, so keep a thin waterproof in the bag.

You will find small cafés and lakeside restaurants in Attersee and Weyregg, and the lake has public swimming spots dotted along the shore. For fuel, however, the villages here are small, so plan on Sankt Georgen im Attergau, about six kilometres away, or the larger town of Attnang-Puchheim some 19 km to the north, which has the full set of shops and filling stations. The lake fish, especially Reinanke, a type of whitefish, is on every menu in season and is simple and good. This is a place to slow down, with Salzburg just under an hour away and the mood of the Salzkammergut all around you.
t.parco comunale di sellero@46.1,10.3:
Valcamonica is the valley of the rock carvings, and Sellero is one of the places where you can walk among them. For about eight thousand years, from the Stone Age to Roman times, the people who lived here, especially the Camuni of the Iron Age, hammered and scratched pictures onto the smooth glacier-polished rock: hunters, deer, warriors, farmers, ploughs, huts and strange symbols. The valley holds hundreds of thousands of them, and in 1979 it became Italy's first UNESCO World Heritage Site. The municipal park at Sellero preserves a group of engraved rocks in woodland above the Oglio river, so you walk on a path and find the carvings on bare sheets of stone among the trees.

What makes the carvings compelling is that they are not formal art. They show what people cared about: weapons, farming, ritual scenes, and the occasional picture of a house or a dancing figure. After rain the lichen and wet stone make them easier to read, and low raking light helps too, so early morning or late afternoon is the time to look. Be gentle, stay on the paths and never rub or touch the surface, as the engravings are fragile.

The valley is a fine ride. Valcamonica runs north from Lake Iseo for about 80 km, with the Adamello massif on one side and the Orobie Alps on the other. The main road is a busy valley road with traffic and a lot of small towns, so most riders use it as a connection to the passes: the Tonale at about 1,880 metres to the north-east, and the Gavia, a much more demanding high pass beyond Ponte di Legno, which is closed in winter and often opens only in early summer. Snow and fog can arrive quickly at height, so take layers.

Sellero is a small village of about a thousand people, with Cedegolo and Capo di Ponte a few kilometres away. Capo di Ponte has the largest cluster of carvings at Naquane and a number of simple places to eat. For fuel the valley towns have stations, but do not count on a small village, so top up in Capo di Ponte or farther down the valley around Darfo Boario Terme, which is the larger town. Try casoncelli, the local filled pasta with sage and butter, and a glass of Franciacorta if you are heading toward the lake.
t.holasovice historic village@49.0,14.3:
Holašovice looks like a village painted from memory by someone who loved it. A long rectangular green sits in the middle, with a pond and a small chapel, and around it stand more than twenty farmhouses with gabled fronts in rich, ornate plasterwork, some in white and pale yellow and some in soft blue. The style is called folk Baroque, or peasant Baroque, and the houses were mostly built in the nineteenth century, when wealthy farmers dressed their gables in a local version of the grand style of the cities. It has been on the UNESCO list since 1998.

There is a story behind the survival of this place. Holašovice was in the Sudeten border region, where Czech and German speakers had lived side by side, and after the Second World War the German population was expelled. The village was left to decline and was close to the sealed border of the Iron Curtain, and many buildings were abandoned, but neglect also meant that nobody modernised them. After 1989 the village began a careful restoration, and now it is a living place again, with a few cafés and guesthouses. The big event is the Holašovice Peasant Fair in July.

The country here is gentle South Bohemia, a landscape of ponds, meadows, birch and pine woods, with the line of the Šumava mountains on the horizon. The roads are narrow and quiet, with a fair amount of cyclists, and surfaces are mostly decent, though patched in places. It makes a lovely afternoon loop out of Český Krumlov, about 20 km away. The best light is late in the day, and May, with its apple blossom, and September are very good.

For fuel and larger shops, České Budějovice, a city of about 96,000 people, lies only about 15 km away, and Křemže, a small town nearby, has the basics. Local food includes roast pork with dumplings and sauerkraut, carp from the region's ponds, especially around Christmas, and the beer of Budweis, the original Budweiser Budvar. Walk the green, look at the details on the gables and notice how quiet it is. Tourists come, but the village does not feel staged.
t.straubing kastell st peter@48.9,12.6:
In 1950, workmen digging in a Straubing suburb found a hoard that stunned archaeologists: a collection of Roman parade armour, helmets with face masks and decorated metal pieces, buried in the third century, probably to hide them from invaders. The Straubing Roman treasure is now one of the most important finds of its kind north of the Alps, and it is displayed in the Gäubodenmuseum in the city. The fort at St Peter, on the eastern edge of town, was part of the same Roman presence. Straubing was Sorviodurum, a Roman town with several forts on the Danube frontier, and this was one of several forts there.

Today the site is marked by St Peter's church and its old cemetery, one of the oldest in Bavaria, with wrought-iron crosses and a chapel. The church stands close to the old Roman camp, and Roman finds have come out of the ground around it. It is a quiet corner, away from the bustle of the town centre, and worth a short stop for the atmosphere of its old graves.

Straubing sits on the Danube in the fertile Gäuboden plain, one of the best farming regions in Bavaria, with wheat, sugar beet and corn spreading to the horizon. The riding is flat and easy, along river roads and straight lanes between fields, with the Bavarian Forest rising to the north-east and offering more rewarding bends. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads, and in August the Gäubodenvolksfest, a huge beer festival, fills the town with visitors. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons.

Straubing has about 45,000 people and everything a rider needs, with fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés and a pretty central square with a tall town tower. A plate of roast pork with dumpling and a Bavarian wheat beer is the obvious meal, or fresh river fish. The old town is pleasant to walk through, with arcaded houses and a Gothic church. If you carry on to the next watchtower of the Limes, the Danube road eastward gives a calm and easy ride, with the river on one side and the fields on the other.
t.fort site and civil settlement of eining:
The Danube here is already a serious river, and about two thousand years ago it was the edge of the Roman Empire. Abusina, the Roman fort at Eining, stood on the south bank, where a small tributary joins, and its soldiers watched the Germanic lands across the water. The site lies in a bend a few kilometres from Neustadt an der Donau, and what remains are the foundations of a fort that was rebuilt several times, and of a civilian settlement, with a bath house, whose walls you can see outlined in the grass. The fort ended its life in the fifth century, in the unsettled times when Rome let go of the frontier.

It is a quiet site, partly covered by a small village and a church, with a reconstructed section of wall and an information trail. What strikes you is the openness, with fields on all sides and the river nearby, and the sense of a long and lonely posting. The Raetian frontier is part of the UNESCO listing for the Roman limes, and Abusina is one of its better-known forts in Bavaria.

Just a few kilometres upstream the Danube cuts a narrow gorge through the Jurassic limestone, the Donaudurchbruch near Kelheim, with white cliffs on both banks. Weltenburg Abbey, one of the oldest monasteries in Bavaria, sits at the entrance and brews a well-known dark beer, with a beer garden by the river. Boats run through the gorge from Kelheim, and the road along the river is a lovely ride, with curves between the cliffs and the trees.

Neustadt an der Donau, with almost 13,000 people, and Abensberg, nearby, have fuel, supermarkets and cafés. Abensberg is the heart of the Hallertau, the world's largest hop-growing region, and in late summer you ride past fields of tall hop poles, covered in bright green vines. A tower by Friedensreich Hundertwasser at the Kuchlbauer brewery is a surprising sight in the countryside. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, and weekends in summer can be busy with cyclists on the Danube path. Stop for a beer and a pretzel and look at the water.
t.villa piovene@45.7,11.5:
Palladio designed villas the way other architects write poetry, with proportion, rhythm and an ear for the landscape, and Villa Piovene at Lugo di Vicenza is one of his early ones. It stands on a slope at the foot of the Venetian pre-Alps, north of Vicenza, a stern box of pale stone fronted by a tall flight of steps and a temple-like portico of Ionic columns. The house was meant to be seen from below, rising out of the garden like a small temple, and the effect is of calm authority. Palladio is said to have designed it in the 1540s for the Piovene family, who were wealthy merchants and landowners.

The villas of the Veneto were working farms as well as country houses, with granaries, stables and dovecotes, and the owners spent the summers supervising harvests and entertaining friends. Palladio's villas, together with his palaces in Vicenza, are listed by UNESCO, and the architecture has been copied for centuries, from English country houses to the plantations of Virginia and the White House.

This is an easy, rolling ride. The country between Vicenza and the Asiago plateau is a patchwork of vineyards, orchards and cherry trees, with small villages and church towers, and the land rises in folds to the high ridges of the Alps. Breganze, five kilometres away, is the centre of a wine district known for its Torcolato, a sweet golden wine made from dried grapes, and for the red wines of the hills. From here, roads wind up toward the Asiago plateau in tight hairpins through pine woods, a classic ride for those who enjoy mountain bends.

Lugo is tiny, with barely a couple of thousand people, so for fuel and shopping head to Breganze or Thiene. The villa is private property and opens to the public only on limited occasions, so you are likely to see it from the road or the garden gate, and it is wise to check before you go. Spring and early autumn suit it, with soft light and clear air, and weekends bring a lot of cyclists on the quiet roads.
t.mantoue@45.2,10.8:
Mantua rises out of three artificial lakes formed by the river Mincio, a Renaissance city set in the flat Po plain, and in summer the air carries the smell of water and reeds. The Gonzaga family ruled here for almost four centuries, and they turned a modest town into one of the most brilliant courts in Italy. In the Ducal Palace, a labyrinth of hundreds of rooms, Andrea Mantegna painted the Camera degli Sposi, a small chamber whose ceiling shows an illusionistic oculus with faces and cherubs peering down. Not far away, the Palazzo Te, built for Federico Gonzaga by Giulio Romano, is a pleasure villa with playful frescoes of giants falling.

The poet Virgil was born in a village near Mantua, and Verdi set his opera Rigoletto here. The city is listed by UNESCO along with Sabbioneta, a small planned town built by another Gonzaga in the sixteenth century. Mantua was also a place of tragedy: in 1630 imperial troops sacked it and plague followed, and the court never fully recovered.

The ride into Mantua is flat, along long, straight roads across the Po valley, past maize fields, poplars and irrigation canals. The land is unremarkable for riding, and fog can be dense in winter, but the great pleasure is the final approach along the causeways between the lakes, where herons stand in the shallows and the towers of the city rise ahead. Summer evenings bring clouds of mosquitoes, so keep your visor down. The centre has restricted access, with cobbled streets, so park outside and walk in.

Mantua has about forty thousand people, so petrol and a meal are easy to find. Local dishes include tortelli di zucca, pumpkin-filled pasta with amaretti, and sbrisolona, a crumbly almond cake. The Mincio cycle path to Peschiera on Lake Garda is popular, and a boat trip on the lakes is pleasant. The best light comes in April, May and late September, with mist lying on the water at dawn.
t.parco nazionale delle incisioni rupestri:
Valcamonica is a long, narrow valley that runs north from Lake Iseo into the Alps, and for about eight thousand years people have been carving pictures on its rocks. The Camuni, an Iron Age people, left the most, but the earliest carvings belong to hunters of the end of the ice age, and the latest belong to medieval travellers. In all, there are hundreds of thousands of figures, scratched or pecked into smooth glacial sandstone: deer, warriors, ploughmen, huts, maps, dancers and strange sun-like symbols. In 1979 it became the first site in Italy to be placed on the World Heritage list.

The national park at Naquane, near Capo di Ponte, is the place to see the carvings, with paths winding through chestnut woods between big polished slabs. The famous Rosa Camuna, a swirling flower-like symbol, has become the emblem of Lombardy. Close by is the Seradina-Bedolina park and a handsome Romanesque monastery, and the valley is dotted with castles and chapels. Walking among the rocks, with sun on the stone and a smell of resin, is oddly intimate, as though the artists had just stepped out.

The valley is also an excellent starting point for riders. Capo di Ponte lies on the road to Edolo, where the great passes begin: the Passo del Tonale to the north-east, the Aprica to the north, and the Gavia and Mortirolo for serious mountain riders. Roads rise through forests of fir and pine, with tight hairpins and fine views over snow-streaked peaks. Surfaces are generally good, but passes close in winter, and the high ones are often open only from June to October. Weekend traffic builds, with cyclists and motorcyclists out in force.

Capo di Ponte is a small town with only basic services, and the nearest larger town is Darfo Boario Terme, twenty kilometres south, where you will find fuel, supermarkets and hotels. Local food is mountain fare, with polenta, cured meats, casoncelli pasta and strong cheeses. Opening times for the park vary, so check before you set out, and wear shoes with good grip on the stone.
t.padua s fourteenth century fresco cycles:
Giotto's chapel in Padua is smaller than most people expect, a plain brick hall tucked behind the Arena gardens, and the first surprise is that you are rationed. Visits are timed and short, and groups wait in a climate-controlled room first so that the breath and humidity of too many people do not harm the paint. Then the doors open and the walls turn blue. Around 1305 the banker Enrico Scrovegni commissioned Giotto to cover the whole interior with the lives of Mary and Christ, and what he painted, people with weight, faces with feeling, a sky that behaves like a sky, changed the course of European painting.

Padua holds more than that one room. The city's fourteenth-century fresco cycles also include the Baptistery by the cathedral, covered in a dome of paradise by Giusto de' Menabuoi, the Oratory of San Giorgio, the Eremitani church and the great hall of the Palazzo della Ragione. They were recognised by UNESCO as a group in 2021, and walking between them is a good way to see a city that was once a rival of Venice and one of the great intellectual centres of Italy. Its university dates from 1222 and Galileo taught here for eighteen years. The basilica of Saint Anthony, simply called il Santo, draws pilgrims from all over the world, and the vast oval of Prato della Valle makes a pleasant place to sit among statues and canals.

For a rider, Padua is a city to park and walk. The centre has restricted traffic, so use the car parks near the Scrovegni and walk in, and book the chapel in advance. The landscape around is flat, but only a few kilometres south-west rise the Euganean Hills, a cluster of old volcanic cones covered in vineyards, chestnut woods and villas, with narrow winding roads that climb to hilltop villages such as Arquà Petrarca, where the poet Petrarch spent his last years. The roads are tight, sometimes rough, and busy with cyclists on weekends.

Fuel and food are no trouble in a city of two hundred thousand, and the local specialities include risotto with spring vegetables, bigoli pasta and a good spritz in the evening. Spring and autumn bring clear light, and fog in winter turns the plain into a grey room.
t.villa valmarana zen@45.6,11.6:
Not every Palladian villa sits on a hill with a view. Villa Valmarana at Lisiera lies on the flat Vicentine plain east of the city, among fields of maize and soy, irrigation ditches and poplar rows, and it was built for a family whose wealth came from the land itself. Palladio designed it in the middle of the sixteenth century, and it belongs to the family of villas around Vicenza that UNESCO lists together with his town palaces. The house follows his idea of a working farm dressed as a Roman temple: a central block with a portico, flanked by long service wings, the barchesse, that once held grain, tools and animals.

What to take from it is that Palladio was a practical builder as much as a poet. The long wings were barns and granaries, the cellars stored wine, and the owner could walk from his front door to the field without leaving the composition. The villa stands in a village so small it barely registers on the map, Lisiera, with a few houses and a church, and the nearest sizeable place is Monticello Conte Otto, a few kilometres away, with Vicenza itself beyond. The house is private and visits are limited, so check ahead and expect to see it from the road.

Riding on this plain is gentle, direct and sometimes dull. Roads run dead straight along canals and field edges, with sharp right-angle turns at farm tracks, and in winter fog hangs thick for days. In summer the maize stands head high and blocks the views at every junction, so approach crossings carefully. The pleasure is in what lies beside: Vicenza's arcaded streets and the Basilica Palladiana, a short ride off, and the low Berici Hills to the south, with winding lanes and hilltop sanctuaries such as Monte Berico. Those roads are better for riding than the plain.

Monticello Conte Otto has petrol stations and a few places to eat, and Vicenza has everything. Try baccalà alla vicentina, the local salt cod stewed in milk and onions, and a glass of Durello or Garganega. Spring brings blossom, and September brings the harvest and the light.
t.parco archeologico comunale di seradina:
Seradina is the part of Valcamonica that shows how the Camuni told stories. On a broad slab of polished sandstone, shaped by a glacier and now shaded by oak and chestnut, a crowd of tiny figures has been pecked into the surface: men ploughing with oxen, hunters stalking deer, warriors with round shields, huts on stilts and fields marked out in squares. The scenes were carved over many centuries by people who lived by farming and herding, and they read like a diary of an Alpine community from the Bronze and Iron Ages. Nearby, the Bedolina rock holds a famous design often described as a map, a network of lines, dots and little houses that seems to record fields and paths.

The park lies on the slope above the river Oglio, on the west side of the valley, opposite the sacred mountain of Concarena, whose pale limestone peak rises to over two and a half thousand metres and was probably a place of worship in the same ancient times. Some carvings seem to have been aligned with it. The area around Capo di Ponte also has a Romanesque church, San Siro, perched on a rock, and the monastery of San Salvatore, founded by monks from Cluny in the eleventh century.

Riders find the valley both a destination and a doorway. The road along the Oglio is a straightforward valley road, with trucks and traffic lights in the towns, but from Edolo the great Alpine passes begin. Tonale, Aprica and, for more demanding riding, Mortirolo and Gavia, which are narrow and steep and open only in summer, all lie within a morning's ride. In summer weekends the valley is busy, and in winter ice closes the passes. The park paths are short, but steep and slippery after rain, so decent boots are worth wearing.

Capo di Ponte has a handful of shops and trattorias, and the closest large town for fuel and supplies is Darfo Boario Terme, some twenty kilometres south, though smaller villages along the valley have petrol stations. Local fare is hearty: polenta, venison, pizzoccheri and casoncelli. The park has opening hours and a small entrance fee, which vary by season.
t.shimbaru nuyama mounded tomb group@33.8,:
In Fukuoka prefecture, on the shore of the Genkai Sea, a group of burial mounds records the power of the Munakata clan, the family who were priests and sea-lords of the strait between Kyushu and Korea. Shimbaru-Nuyama is a cluster of tombs from the fifth and sixth centuries, small and large mounds scattered over a low ridge, and it belongs to the World Heritage listing for Okinoshima and the associated sites of the Munakata region, inscribed in 2017. Okinoshima is a remote island in the channel where ritual offerings were made for centuries to pray for safe voyages, and no women are allowed to land, and men must purify themselves in the sea before setting foot on it.

The mounds on the mainland belonged to the clan that managed those rituals and the sea routes. Grave goods found in the area show contacts across the water, with mirrors, gold rings and glass beads from the continent. Munakata Taisha, the great shrine of the clan, still stands, with three sanctuaries for the three goddesses of the sea, and it draws crowds to pray for traffic safety, including blessings for cars.

The country here is quiet farmland and low hills with the sea close by. The main coastal road, Route 3, is busy and flat, with long stretches of shops and car dealerships, while side roads run among rice fields and persimmon orchards, past small shrines. A bit further north the coast offers fine views over the Genkai Sea, with its rocks and pine trees, and the drive along it is relaxed rather than twisty. Summer is hot and humid, typhoons come in late summer, and winter brings cold winds from the north-west but little snow.

Nishifukuma, the nearest sizeable town, has fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and the cities of Fukuoka and Kitakyushu are close. The seafood here is outstanding, and sashimi, grilled squid and mentaiko, spicy pollock roe, are local favourites. The museum in Munakata gives a good introduction to the story of Okinoshima. Visiting hours vary, so check before you go.
t.plecnik s zale garden of all saints@46.1:
It is the city's central burial ground, laid out on the eastern edge of town, and in the late 1930s the architect Joze Plecnik added a series of chapels, arcades and entrance structures that turn it into a quiet landscape of white walls, columns and calm courtyards. He called it the Garden of All Saints, and the name fits. Plecnik was Slovenia's great architect of the twentieth century, a man who also shaped the bridges, markets and riverbanks of Ljubljana, and his works in the city were added to the UNESCO list in 2021.

What you notice first is restraint. The buildings are simple, in pale stone and plaster, with colonnades and rhythmic repetition rather than decoration. Plecnik mixed classical forms with Slovene vernacular, and the result feels both ancient and modern. Visitors walk slowly here because the place tells you to. Remember that this is a working cemetery, so keep your voice down, park the bike outside, and take your helmet and boots off the path.

Ljubljana is a gentle city for riders. The old town around the Ljubljanica river is mostly pedestrian, but the surrounding streets are quiet by European standards, and the city is compact enough that you can see most of what matters in an afternoon. The Triple Bridge, the market colonnade, the National and University Library and the embankments of the river are all Plecnik's work. The castle on its hill looks down over the red roofs. Trzin, a smaller town to the north, is close, but Ljubljana, with more than two hundred and seventy thousand people, has fuel, workshops and hotels in abundance.

This sits on a ride that heads north towards Klagenfurt across the Karawanks, so you are close to the mountain roads of the Julian Alps and the Austrian border. Slovenia uses an electronic vignette on motorways, which you must buy before you use them, and speed limits are strictly enforced. Spring and autumn are the best times, with clear air and few crowds. In early November, on All Saints Day, the cemetery is lit by thousands of candles, a very moving scene.
t.abtsdorf i@47.9,13.5:
Abtsdorf lies on the western shore of the Attersee, the largest lake in the Salzkammergut, a region of lakes, forests and limestone peaks east of Salzburg. The water is remarkably clear, a deep blue-green that looks almost Mediterranean on a bright day, and the lake is about twenty kilometres long, which makes it a gentle place to ride beside. The towns along the shore, Attersee and Weyregg among them, are small and old-fashioned, with sailing clubs and cafes that open onto the water.

The site called Abtsdorf I is one of the prehistoric pile dwelling settlements around the Alps that UNESCO listed in 2011. About five thousand years ago, people built houses on timber piles at the edges of lakes here, and the wet mud has preserved wood, tools and plant remains in remarkable condition. At the Attersee, the remains lie under water and in the lake bed, so there is little to see on the surface. It is a place for the imagination, and for reading about the people who lived on stilts above the shallows in the Neolithic and Bronze Ages.

The riding along the lake is pleasant rather than dramatic. The road follows the shore through villages and orchards, with views across the water to the Hollengebirge, a limestone wall on the far side. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, with cyclists, tour buses and day trippers, so go early or on weekdays. The mountains behind the lake offer more fun, with roads climbing towards Mondsee and the Wolfgangsee. Weather can turn quickly in the Alps, and afternoon thunderstorms in summer are common.

For fuel, look to the larger places at the northern end of the lake, since the villages along the shore are small. The lake has a long association with art. Gustav Klimt spent summers near Litzlberg in the early twentieth century and painted many of his landscapes here, and the square format of those paintings suits the view. Take a swim if the weather allows. The water is clean and cool, and the shoreline is well suited to a quiet pause.
t.enns canabae nordwest@48.2,14.5:
Enns claims to be the oldest town in Austria, and it has some evidence. The town received city rights in 1212, but people have lived here since long before that. The Romans built a legionary fortress on this spot, called Lauriacum, in the second century, and it was home to the Second Italic Legion, one of the units that guarded the Danube frontier. The civilian settlement that grew up outside the walls, known as the canabae, held traders, craftsmen and families, and the whole complex became a major provincial centre.

Lauriacum was important in the later Roman period, too. Christianity took hold early here, and a basilica stood on the site of what is now the church of St Laurentius. Tradition associates the area with Saint Florian, a Roman officer who was martyred in the early fourth century and whose name is given to the famous monastery of St Florian not far away. The legion left, the empire shrank, and Enns fell into the hands of Bavarian and Frankish rulers. It became a border town between Upper and Lower Austria, a position that left it with an old defensive character.

Today Enns is a pleasant town of about ten thousand, with a long main square, a city tower built in the sixteenth century, and cafes where people sit and talk. Fuel and food are easy here, so it works well as a stop on a ride through the Danube valley. The river Enns, which comes down from the Alps to join the Danube nearby, is the old boundary and gives the town its name.

The riding between Linz and Enns is gentle and flat, with farmland, small villages and views of the Danube plain. South of Enns the hills begin, and roads head into the foothills of the Alps with a little more interest. The Limes route is a good excuse to explore. In summer the flatlands can be hot and busy, and in autumn the mist settles in the river valleys and the light turns soft. Take time to walk the main square.
t.linz siedlung martinsfeld@48.3,14.3:
Linz sits on the Danube about halfway between Vienna and Passau, and its history goes back to the Romans, who built a fort here called Lentia. The site of the Roman settlement lies under the old town, near the castle and the main square, and the remains of the civilian settlement spread to the surrounding districts. Martinsfeld, where this stop is placed, lies close to the centre, and the old church of St Martin nearby is one of the oldest surviving churches in Austria, with parts of its walls dating back more than a thousand years.

The city has had many lives. It was the home of the composer Anton Bruckner, who worked as organist at the cathedral, and of the astronomer Johannes Kepler, who lived here for over a decade and wrote key works on planetary motion. Industry arrived in the twentieth century, with steelworks and chemical plants, and it gave Linz a rough reputation that the city has worked to shed. Today it is known for culture, with the Ars Electronica centre on the river, and for the Linzer Torte, a lattice-topped almond and jam tart said to be one of the oldest cakes in the world.

Riding in and around Linz is not difficult. The Danube valley is wide, the roads are well signed, and the city has everything a traveller needs. With over two hundred thousand people, it has plenty of fuel stations, workshops and hotels. The best views are from the Postlingberg, a hill north of the river that is reached by a steep tramway and gives a fine view over the city and the plain. North of the river the countryside rises into the Muhlviertel, with granite hills, forests and quiet lanes that are a pleasure on a motorcycle.

Traffic can be heavy at rush hour, and the bridges become bottlenecks. Weather is continental, with cold winters and warm summers, and fog is common in the river valleys in autumn. Take time to walk across the Danube on the old bridge, and look at the arcades of the main square. It is one of the biggest in Austria, with colourful baroque houses on every side.
t.regensburg legionslager i@49.0,12.1:
Regensburg exists because of a decision made in the year 179. The emperor Marcus Aurelius was fighting the Marcomanni and other tribes across the Danube, and a new legionary fortress was needed on the northern frontier of the province of Raetia. The site chosen was a bluff on the south bank of the Danube, near the point where the river Regen comes in from the north. The fortress was named Castra Regina, the camp by the Regen, and the Third Italic Legion, raised by Marcus Aurelius himself, was stationed there.

The camp was large, a rectangle of about five hundred and forty by four hundred and fifty metres, with stone walls, towers and four gates. Inside were barracks, a headquarters building, a hospital, baths and workshops, and thousands of soldiers lived within its walls. Outside, a civilian settlement of traders, craftsmen and families grew up, and in time the whole complex became the centre of a thriving town. The outline of the camp is still visible in the street plan of the old city, and some Roman stones survive in later buildings.

The old town of Regensburg, with its medieval bridge, cathedral and merchants' towers, is one of the best-preserved in Germany, and UNESCO listed it in 2006. The Danube Limes, of which Castra Regina was a part, was listed in 2021. The city has about a hundred and thirty thousand people, and Reinhausen, across the river, is a suburb. Fuel and food are easy to find, and the old town is a fine place for a long lunch.

For riders, Regensburg is a gateway between the Danube valley and the hills of Bavaria. East of the city, the Danube gives way to the Bavarian Forest, with quiet roads that wind through spruce woods, and west, the Altmuhl valley offers fine riding too. In the city itself, the old town is compact and cobbled, so park the bike on the edge and walk. Early autumn is a lovely time to come, when the light is golden and the evenings are warm.
t.regensburg legionslager vi@49.0,12.1:
Across the Danube from Regensburg, on the high ground to the east, stands the Walhalla, a Greek temple in the middle of Bavaria. King Ludwig I had it built in the 1830s and 1840s as a hall of fame for great Germans, and its white marble columns, set on a hill above the river, look odd and wonderful. It is a short ride from the old Roman camp, and the two make an interesting pair, the Roman soldier's frontier and the nineteenth century's dream of antiquity.

The Roman camp itself, Castra Regina, lay on the south bank, on a low terrace above the river. Its walls, gates and streets were laid out on a grid, and the northern wall ran close to the Danube, with a view across the water to the barbarian lands beyond. Today the Roman layers lie beneath the old town, but they show in the plan: the street called Unter den Schwibbogen follows the line of the northern wall, and the Porta Praetoria, the northern gate, survives in part in the old town.

Riding out to the Walhalla is a pleasant afternoon. The road runs along the north bank of the Danube through Donaustauf, a small town with a castle ruin above it, and climbs to the monument through woods of beech. The surface is good, the bends are easy, and traffic is moderate, though weekends can be busy with visitors. The view over the Danube valley from the steps is wide and calm, with barges moving slowly along the river.

Regensburg has plenty of fuel and food, and Reinhausen, a suburb on the north side, has a few stations. If you want a snack, the historic sausage kitchen near the stone bridge grills small bratwurst over beechwood and serves them with sauerkraut and sweet mustard, and has done so for centuries, so it says. Wine from the hills around is light and crisp. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the air is clear and the crowds are smaller. Climb the steps slowly and look back at the river.
t.bad gogging heilbad@48.8,11.8:
Bad Gogging is a spa town, and it has been one for nearly two thousand years. The Romans found hot sulphur springs here, in the Danube plain between Abensberg and Neustadt, and built a bathhouse beside the fort of Abusina, a short distance away. The spring water still rises, smelling of eggs, and the modern spa uses it for treatments. Excavated Roman baths are displayed in the town, and the heating channels and pools give a good idea of how the Romans relaxed after a day on the frontier.

The spa came back into use in the 1960s, when drilling for oil in the Danube plain found warm sulphurous water at depth. Since then Bad Gogging has become one of Bavaria's thermal resorts, and its hotels and clinics fill the streets around the spa gardens. The town's pride in its Roman past is clear. The Danube Limes, of which this is a part, was listed by UNESCO in 2021.

The countryside here is the Hallertau, the largest hop growing region in the world, and in late summer the fields are full of tall green hop plants on high wires, with a heavy resinous smell. Roads run straight across the plain with slight rises and falls, and the villages are Bavarian, with onion-domed churches and beer gardens. Abensberg is known for its beer and for a tower designed by Friedensreich Hundertwasser at a brewery. A short ride east, the Danube squeezes through the gorge of Weltenburg, where an abbey stands on the bank.

Neustadt an der Donau and Abensberg, both about twelve thousand people, have fuel and shops. Try the local beer, a hearty meal of roast pork and dumplings, and the Bavarian soft pretzel. Weather is moderate, with warm summers and cold winters. In late summer, when the hops are ready, the area is at its best, and the light is golden. A swim in the thermal water is a good way to end a day on the bike.
t.regensburg legionslager iii@49.0,12.1:
The first thing you see in the old town of Regensburg is stone. The Steinerne Brucke, the stone bridge, was built in the twelfth century and was for hundreds of years the only bridge across the Danube for a long distance, so trade routes ran through the city. It made the town rich, and the merchants built tall towers and patrician houses in the streets by the river. The whole old town survived the Second World War almost untouched and was listed by UNESCO in 2006.

Below the medieval layers lies the Roman fortress of Castra Regina, and walking the streets, you can feel the earlier plan. The old city centre is a dense grid, narrow lanes and open squares, and some of the straight streets follow the lines of the Roman camp. The Romans left walls, gates and a few reused stones, and the Porta Praetoria is the best-known fragment. After the Romans left, Bavarian dukes ruled from here, and later, between 1663 and 1806, the Imperial Diet sat in the city.

The cathedral, with its twin spires, is the great Gothic landmark, and it is the home of the Domspatzen, a boys' choir that is nearly a thousand years old. The old town has more than a thousand listed buildings, and cafes and beer gardens everywhere. Regensburg is also known for its sausages, and for a sweet mustard that is served with them. Beer drinkers should try the local Bavarian lagers and wheat beers.

For the rider, the city is compact and friendly, but the old town is largely pedestrian, and cobbles are slippery when wet. Park on the edge and walk, since Regensburg is easy to see on foot. Fuel is easy to find, with stations on the ring roads and in Reinhausen. The Danube cycle path draws cyclists, so take care on the riverside. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with comfortable temperatures and good light. Evening on the bridge, with the river below, is a fine thing.
t.regensburg gro es graberfeld@49.0,12.1:
Romans buried their dead outside the city walls, along the roads, so that travellers would pass the tombs and remember the names. West of the fortress of Castra Regina, beside the road that led towards Augsburg, lay a very large cemetery, and the burial field has been found and excavated bit by bit as the modern city expanded. Thousands of graves have been recorded, with both cremation and burial, and the finds include pottery, glass, coins, jewellery and tombstones that tell us who lived and died here.

The inscriptions are the best part. Many of the stones record soldiers of the Third Italic Legion, with their age at death, their length of service and the name of the heir who paid for the stone. Other stones belong to merchants, freedmen and women. They have simple names and simple wishes, and they come from many parts of the empire. Regensburg's museums hold a good collection, and the pieces make a surprisingly human link to the people who lived on this stretch of the Danube.

Today the cemetery lies under streets and gardens, and there is little to see on the surface. It is a place for the imagination. The district is now part of the busy western side of the city, close to the main station and the ring roads, so the ride in is through modern suburbs. Once you reach the old town, a short walk leads to the Roman wall remains and to the museums.

Regensburg has about a hundred and thirty thousand people, and fuel, food and parking are easy on the edge of the centre. Reinhausen, across the river, is a quieter district with small cafes. The Danube here runs wide and green, and the cycle path along the bank draws walkers and cyclists in summer. If you have time, ride out to the Danube gorge at Weltenburg, a short way upstream, where the river cuts through a wall of limestone, and a monastery sits at the bend. Autumn is the best time, with clear light and mellow colour.
t.watchtowers wp 13 37 to 13 40@49.1,10.6:
In this corner of Franconia, the Roman frontier is a straight line. From the Danube near Eining the Raetian Limes ran north and then swung west across a quiet landscape of low hills and fields, and in the section near Wassertrudingen, the line is as ruler-straight as anything the Romans ever built. Here the frontier was a stone wall, unlike the timber palisade further north, and it ran between towers numbered by archaeologists. The group 13/37 to 13/40 is a short stretch of that wall and its watchtowers.

The wall was built in the early third century, and its purpose has long been debated. It could not stop a determined army, but it controlled trade and movement, and it let the Romans watch for raiders.
