Local people later called it the Devil's Wall, because they thought nobody but the devil could have built something so long and straight. It was abandoned in the middle of the third century, when the Alamanni overran the area, and the stones were reused for farms and churches. UNESCO listed the Limes in 2005.

What remains is a low bank of rubble in the fields and woods, and the foundations of the towers. The landscape is gentle, with cereal fields, meadows and patches of pine, and a few hills like the Hesselberg, the highest point in the area, rise in the distance. Villages are small and farm based, with brick and half-timbered houses, and the roads between them are quiet and well surfaced. Traffic is light, and the bends are mild.

Wassertrudingen has about six thousand people and fuel, a bakery and a couple of inns, and Gunzenhausen, a bit further, is a larger town with everything you need. The region produces carp from small ponds, and local menus often feature it, along with Franconian beer and sausages. Weather is moderate, with warm summers and cold winters, and in spring the rapeseed fields glow yellow. Take a walk along the line of the wall, and think about the soldiers who stood on this low ridge looking north into country that offered nothing but trouble.
t.regensburg legionslager v@49.0,12.1:
Johannes Kepler died in Regensburg in November 1630, nearly penniless, having ridden here to try to collect money the emperor owed him. He is one of the great figures of European science, the man who worked out that planets move in ellipses, and his death in this city is a reminder of how much the town meant in his time. He was buried in the cemetery of St Peter, but the grave was lost when the cemetery was destroyed during the Thirty Years War. A memorial temple stands in a park by the old town, and the small house where he spent his last days is now a museum.

Regensburg had a long run as an imperial city. From 1663 to 1806, the Perpetual Imperial Diet, the parliament of the Holy Roman Empire, met in the old town hall, and the city filled with diplomats, courtiers and servants. The meeting room, the Imperial Hall, can still be visited, along with the old interrogation chambers beneath it. The whole assembly was a slow, ceremonial machine, and the city's streets and inns bear traces of it.

The old fortress of Castra Regina lay under all this. The Roman soldiers who built it in 179 are now far behind the layers of Kepler and the emperors, but their street grid is still there. The Danube Limes, of which it was a part, was listed by UNESCO in 2021, along with the old town in 2006.

If you arrive on a motorcycle, the ring roads lead easily to the old town, where you can park near the edge and walk. Regensburg has about a hundred and thirty thousand people, so fuel and food are plentiful. The Danube is the central feature, with the stone bridge and the island district of Stadtamhof, now a pleasant place for cafes. Take your time to look at the Imperial Hall, then sit by the river with a drink and think about the long chain of people who passed this way. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.regensburg westliche canabae@49.0,12.1:
Where there is a fort, a town grows beside it, and at Regensburg the civilian settlement beside Castra Regina was called the canabae. The west side was the busiest, with workshops, taverns, houses of merchants and families of soldiers who were not allowed to marry officially while in service. The road from the west, the route from Augsburg and the Alps, entered here, and wagons unloaded at the edge of the camp. It was a noisy, smoky, practical place of potters and smiths, bakers and traders.

Archaeology has found many traces: pottery kilns, wells, cellars, floors and thousands of small objects, from brooches to gaming counters. The finds suggest that people came from different regions, with a wide range of tastes and trades. The settlement continued after the legion left, and the Roman population mixed with Germanic newcomers. By about the year 700, the Bavarian dukes were making Regensburg their residence, and Saint Boniface organised the bishopric here in 739.

The district today is part of the old town, with narrow lanes, Gothic houses, and the long, tall front of the cathedral. The Danube is close, and the stone bridge is only a short walk away. Regensburg survived the war with little damage, and the old centre is an unusually intact mix of medieval and later buildings. UNESCO listed the old town in 2006, and the Danube Limes in 2021.

For riders, the old town is for walking, and the bike is best left near the edge. The city has about a hundred and thirty thousand people, so fuel, food and workshops are plentiful. Reinhausen lies across the river, with its own quiet streets. From here you can go east along the Danube into the Bavarian Forest, or west along the Altmuhl towards Eichstatt, both fine riding country. Autumn is lovely, and the evenings are good for walking along the river.
t.regensburg niedermunster legionslager@49:
The Niedermunster is one of the oldest churches in Regensburg, and it stands on the site of the Roman headquarters building. It was part of a women's abbey, founded in the Middle Ages, and the Romanesque church that stands today is a plain, solid building with a tower. Below it, excavations have revealed the foundations of the Roman building, with floors and walls, and beneath those, early medieval graves. It is one of the few places where you can see the layers of the city in one spot.

The abbey was a rich foundation, and its abbesses were powerful, answering only to the king. The cathedral stands next door, with its twin spires, and the whole district is a quiet corner of the old town, with cobbled lanes and old houses. Roman, Bavarian and medieval Regensburg all meet here, which is why archaeologists have worked on it for decades. The finds include coins, inscriptions and fragments of wall painting, and the story that emerges is of a city that never entirely died after the legion left.

Regensburg itself was listed by UNESCO in 2006, and the Danube Limes in 2021, so there is an official recognition of its importance. The city is a fine place to wander, with squares, towers, and the views of the river. A good bakery or cafe is never far, and the beer is worth tasting. Bavarian cooking here leans on roast pork, dumplings and cabbage, and it suits a cool day among old stones.

If you come on a motorbike, treat the old town as a place to explore on foot. The city has about a hundred and thirty thousand people, so you will find fuel on the ring roads, and Reinhausen, across the river, has stations too. The roads to the east, into the Bavarian Forest, are full of quiet curves, and to the west, the Altmuhl valley is lovely. Autumn is best, and morning is quietest. Light a candle in the cathedral if the mood takes you.
t.regensburg legionslager vii@49.0,12.1:
For nearly two centuries, one of the most powerful families in Europe lived in what had been a monastery in Regensburg. The Thurn und Taxis family ran the imperial postal service of the Holy Roman Empire, and when the Imperial Diet settled in the city in the seventeenth century, the family came too. In 1812 they acquired the abbey of St Emmeram and turned it into a palace, and it is still the home of the family today, a vast complex of cloisters, ballrooms and gardens beside the old town.

The Roman story lies just beneath the surface. St Emmeram stands near the line of the Roman camp, and the area around it was a cemetery and settlement in antiquity, then an early Christian burial place. The abbey church is one of the finest in Bavaria, with an interior of exuberant baroque decoration by the Asam brothers, who covered the walls with gilded stucco. The crypt is far older, and holds the tomb of Saint Emmeram, a missionary bishop who died in the seventh century.

The old town around the palace is a pleasure to wander, with its tall merchants' houses, the stone bridge, the cathedral and a lot of cafes and bookshops. The Danube Limes and the old town are both UNESCO World Heritage sites. Bikes are best left on the edge, since the central lanes are cobbled and often closed to cars, and the city has plenty of parking near the ring road.

Regensburg has about a hundred and thirty thousand people, so you will find fuel, food and repairs without trouble, and Reinhausen, just over the water, has its own small centre. Beer is excellent, and the Christmas market in the palace courtyard, held in the weeks before Christmas, is one of the most famous in Germany. If you visit in summer, there are open-air concerts. Spring and autumn give you the best light. A ride out of the city to the north leads into rolling Upper Palatinate country, quiet and green.
t.regensburg legionslager iv@49.0,12.1:
A legionary in Castra Regina had a life of drill, labour and waiting. He served for twenty-five years, was paid in coin, was fed on bread, porridge and a little meat and wine, and he could not marry legally while in service. The soldiers of the Third Italic Legion spent much of their time building: roads, bridges, brick kilns and the camp itself. Their stamps appear on tiles and bricks all around the area, which is how historians know where they went. When there was no war, there was always another ditch to dig.

The camp was laid out in the standard way, with a main street from gate to gate, a headquarters building at the centre, barracks in long rows, granaries, a hospital and a bathhouse. Sixty centuries of eighty men each made up a legion, give or take, though the real figures changed over time. The north gate, the Porta Praetoria, faced the Danube and the barbarian lands beyond, and its massive masonry is one of the few Roman structures you can still see standing in Bavaria.

Today the old town has covered all this, but the shapes survive. Streets follow the old lines, and walls rise on old foundations. UNESCO listed the old town in 2006 and the Danube Limes in 2021, and the city's Roman museum tells the story of the legion with finds from the area. It is a fine place to spend an hour on a wet day.

For riders, the Altmuhl valley to the west is a great reward. The river winds through a limestone gorge with cliffs and old towns, and the road follows it, with easy bends and good views. Regensburg has about a hundred and thirty thousand people, and fuel stations are on all the main roads. Reinhausen is a smaller district across the river. Try the local Bavarian roast pork and beer, then sleep well. Autumn is the best time, with soft light and few tourists.
t.regensburg legionslager viii@49.0,12.1:
The Danube gorge at Weltenburg is the best reason to ride south from Regensburg. About forty kilometres upstream, the river hits a wall of Jurassic limestone and, instead of turning aside, cuts straight through it in a narrow defile with cliffs on both sides, some of them over a hundred metres high. At the entrance to the gorge sits Weltenburg Abbey, one of the oldest monasteries in Bavaria, founded around 700, with a baroque church by the Asam brothers and a brewery that claims to be the oldest monastery brewery in the world.

You can reach the abbey by road, or by a small boat from Kelheim that takes about thirty minutes through the gorge, and it is a fine trip on a clear day. Above Kelheim stands the Befreiungshalle, the Hall of Liberation, a giant round monument built by King Ludwig I to commemorate the defeat of Napoleon. The Altmuhl joins the Danube at Kelheim, and the roads along both rivers are among the best in the region.

From Regensburg, the road follows the Danube upstream through farmland and small villages, with the river appearing and vanishing between trees. The surface is good and the bends are easy, but traffic is heavy on summer weekends, with cyclists and day trippers. The gorge road itself is narrow and can be slow. In spring, the meadows are bright green, and in autumn the beech forests on the cliffs turn red and gold.

The Roman legionary camp at Regensburg that began this journey lies behind you, and it is worth remembering that the Romans too used the river as a highway and a boundary. The Danube Limes ran along the south bank here, with forts at Abusina, near Eining, a short way upstream of Weltenburg. Regensburg has fuel on every ring road and plenty of cafes, and Reinhausen, across the water, has its own pleasant streets. Fill up before the gorge. Drink a beer in the abbey garden, and watch the boats.
t.watchtower wp 13 50@49.1,10.7:
In the middle of Franconia lies a string of lakes that did not exist fifty years ago. The Franconian Lake District was created by dams on the Altmuhl and other rivers, to hold floodwater and feed the Main-Danube canal, and the biggest of these lakes, the Altmuhlsee, lies right beside Gunzenhausen. Birds love it. The lake is a protected area for waders and ducks, and storks nest on the rooftops in the nearby villages.

The Roman frontier passed through here as well, on its long journey from the Rhine to the Danube. At tower 13/50 the Limes ran across a landscape of low hills and farmland, and the marks it left are faint: a swelling in a meadow, a stretch of overgrown wall in a wood. It was once a stone barrier, and local people long believed that it was the work of the devil. UNESCO listed the Limes in 2005.

Gunzenhausen, a town of about sixteen thousand people, has a pretty market place with half-timbered houses and a Roman history of its own, as a fort stood nearby. It has fuel, food and rooms, and Muhr am See, a small village on the lake, offers cafes by the water. Riding around the lake is gentle, with flat roads, good surfaces and plenty of cyclists in summer. The wider area, between the Altmuhl and the Hahnenkamm hills, has quiet roads through woods and fields.

Franconian food is hearty, with sausages, roast pork, dumplings and carp from local ponds, washed down with beer. Weather is mild, with warm summers and cold winters, and in winter the lake can freeze. Spring is lovely, with blossom and fresh green, and autumn brings mist on the water. A walk along the lake shore in the early morning, with the light low and the birds active, is one of the best ways to start a day.
t.regensburg legionslager ii@49.0,12.1:
Regensburg stands where three rivers meet. The Regen comes in from the north and the Naab arrives just upstream, and together they join the Danube at the city. The Danube itself reaches its northernmost point here, after flowing northeast from its source in the Black Forest, before it turns southeast towards Vienna and the Black Sea. A town on a bend, with a crossing and a confluence, was always going to matter, and the Romans noticed it.

The legionary camp of Castra Regina was placed on a gravel terrace above the south bank, safe from floods, with the river at its back and the northern frontier before it. Behind it ran the road south to the Alpine passes and Italy. The river was a highway for boats carrying grain, wine and military supplies, and a ford and bridge crossed the Danube here. In the Middle Ages, merchants took over the tradition, and the city grew rich on the salt trade and on the long stone bridge.

Today the confluence is a pleasant place to walk. You can follow the Danube bank from the old town to the point where the Regen joins, watching the green water of one river merge with the brown of another. Cycle paths run along both banks, and boats leave from the quays for trips along the river and through the gorge at Weltenburg. The old town and the Roman remains are on the UNESCO list, along with the old town since 2006 and the Danube Limes since 2021.

For riders, Regensburg is a convenient and relaxed city. It has about a hundred and thirty thousand people, and fuel, food and workshops are easy to find, with Reinhausen across the river for a quieter option. The roads north follow the Regen into the Bavarian Forest, with quiet curves through spruce woods, and south the Danube plain is flat and fast. Early morning on the riverbank, with mist on the water, is the best moment.
t.villa valmarana bressan@45.6,11.6:
Palladio had a way of making a house look like a temple, and his clients were happy to pay for it. Andrea Palladio, born in Padua in 1508 and trained in Vicenza as a stonemason, designed dozens of villas for the landowners of the Veneto, using the proportions of ancient Rome to give their country houses a sense of order and dignity. The Villa Valmarana, at Monticello Conte Otto, just north of Vicenza, dates from the middle of the sixteenth century and is one of the buildings that UNESCO lists with the city of Vicenza and the Palladian villas of the Veneto. It stands in a field, with a pedimented front and neat flanks, and the loggia is the sort of space that makes you want to sit down and read.

The countryside around is flat, fertile and busy, a landscape of fields, rows of poplar and small factories, with the hills rising in the north. The area is one of the wealthier parts of Italy, and the roads are full of vans, lorries and commuters. Monticello Conte Otto has seven thousand people and fuel, bars and bakeries. Vicenza, a few kilometres south, has more.

The reason to come to this stop is the road north. Beyond Thiene and Schio the Asiago plateau rises in a series of hairpins that are among the most popular in northern Italy, with forests, meadows and war memorials from the First World War. The Pasubio, a rocky mountain with a famous military road, is nearby. The Altopiano is a place of cheese and honey, and the mountain air feels very different from the plain.

The ride continues to Molina di Ledro, in the Trentino, where the lake has a reconstructed prehistoric village on stilts, part of another UNESCO listing for the pile dwellings around the Alps. The contrast of a Renaissance villa and a Bronze Age lakeside makes for an interesting day.

Try baccalà alla vicentina, the local dish of dried cod stewed in milk, served with polenta, and a glass of wine from the nearby Breganze hills. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the plain is clear and the mountains are sharp on the horizon.
t.villa trissino@45.6,11.5:
Gian Giorgio Trissino was a poet, diplomat and amateur architect, and in the 1530s he had a clever idea. He saw a young stonemason working at his villa in Cricoli, on the edge of Vicenza, and decided to turn him into an architect. He gave the man a classical education, took him to Rome to study the ruins, and gave him a new name, Palladio, after Pallas Athena and the angel in his own epic poem. The stonemason was Andrea di Pietro della Gondola, and he became the most influential architect in the history of the West. The villa at Cricoli, where it all began, is a modest building of the early sixteenth century with a loggia and a tall, plain front.

Palladio's villas, scattered across the Veneto, are part of a UNESCO listing together with the buildings in Vicenza itself. Villa Pojana, at Pojana Maggiore, which is on this ride, is one of the best, with elegant rooms and decoration. The city of Vicenza, a short distance away, is where Palladio's buildings cluster most thickly. The Basilica, the Teatro Olimpico, with its theatrical stage of an ancient city built in wood and stucco, and the palaces along the Corso Palladio give the city a distinctive grandeur.

The riding here is a modest matter. The roads around Vicenza are flat, straight and busy, with trucks and commuters. For a more rewarding ride, the Colli Berici, a range of low hills south of the city, offer lanes between vineyards, olive groves and cypress, with sudden views of the plain. The surface is good, the bends gentle, and there are villas and trattorias at every turn. Monte Berico, with a hilltop basilica, gives a view over the city.

Vicenza, with a hundred and seven thousand inhabitants, has plenty of fuel, parking and places to eat. Motorcycle parking is available in the old town, but the traffic zone means you should check where you can ride. A plate of bigoli with duck sauce and a glass of local red make a good lunch.

Spring is lovely, with blossom on the hillsides. Autumn brings mist, and the city is quieter after the summer.
t.kolisca na igu@46.0,14.5:
The oldest wheel in the world was found in a peat bog in Slovenia, and the bog is the Ljubljana Marshes. Archaeologists working here in 2002 pulled out a wooden wheel with its axle, dating from around 3100 BC, which is now in the city museum in Ljubljana. The find was made close to the village of Ig, a few kilometres south of the capital, where for centuries people built houses on stilts above the wet ground. The pile dwellings at Ig, called Kolišča in Slovenian, are one of the settlements that UNESCO lists among the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps.

The marsh, the Barje, is a flat expanse of meadows, ditches and reed beds, with lines of poplar and the occasional farmhouse. It was once a lake, and the peat that formed over the centuries preserved wood, tools and pottery in remarkable condition. In winter, the mist lies across it, and in summer the meadows are full of flowers and butterflies. The houses on stilts are gone, but the museum in Ljubljana and a small site near Ig tell the story, and a walk on the dyke paths gives a feeling of the setting.

Riding here is easy and unhurried. The roads across the marsh are straight and flat, with a few sharp bends where they cross ditches. Behind the village, the land rises to Krim, a forested mountain of just over eleven hundred metres, with winding roads and wooded slopes that are fun on a bike. The Iška gorge, a few kilometres farther, has a narrow road that follows the river through steep rock walls. Traffic is light, apart from commuters in the morning and evening.

A vignette is required for motorcycles on Slovenian motorways, and you can buy one online or at a fuel station before entering. Ig has two thousand people, and fuel is available there or in Ljubljana, which has two hundred and seventy-two thousand and is only nine kilometres away. Try a buckwheat dish, such as žganci with sour milk, or a plate of cured ham and local cheese.

The best seasons are spring and autumn. The ride continues to Trieste, in Italy, over the limestone plateau of the Karst.
t.lugana vecchia@45.5,10.6:
Lake Garda's southern shore is a landscape made by ice. At the end of the last glaciation a huge tongue of ice pushed out of the Alps and left behind a ring of moraine hills, curved like an amphitheatre, with the lake in the middle and the Po plain beyond. The shallow bay near Sirmione, where the lake meets the low land, was settled very early, and Lugana Vecchia is one of the prehistoric pile-dwelling sites around the Alps that UNESCO has grouped together as a World Heritage Site. Villages of timber houses on stilts stood in the shallows or on the shore here in the Bronze Age, and the wet ground preserved wood, textiles and tools that would have rotted elsewhere.

Be honest about what you will see: there is almost nothing visible, because the remains lie under water or under the mud of the lake shore, and the archaeology is to be understood rather than looked at. The Lugana area is also the name of a famous white wine, made from the Turbiana grape on the pale clay soils behind the shore, with a fresh, mineral taste that goes well with lake fish. Cellars around Sirmione, Peschiera and Desenzano open for tastings, and the vineyards in autumn turn a rich gold.

Riding around the southern lake is easy and pleasant. The roads are flat or gently rolling, well surfaced and signed, and the views over the water are good. Traffic, however, is thick in summer, particularly at weekends, with tourists and queues for Sirmione, which is reached by a narrow causeway to a long peninsula with a medieval castle, the Scaligero fortress. Go early in the morning or in the shoulder seasons, April to June or September and October, to avoid the crush. Further inland, the moraine hills offer winding lanes through vineyards and olive groves.

The history of the area goes well beyond prehistory. Nearby San Martino della Battaglia was the scene of a bloody fight in 1859 during the Second Italian War of Independence, fought on the same day as the battle of Solferino, and a tall memorial tower stands on the ridge. Sirmione, with nearly seven thousand people, has fuel stations on the approach roads, and Peschiera and Desenzano have more. Eat risotto with perch or a plate of lake sardines, and drink a glass of local Lugana in the shade of a vine.
t.the gastaldaga area and the episcopal co:
Cividale del Friuli sits where the Natisone river leaves its green valleys and meets the Friulian plain, in the far north-east of Italy, a few kilometres from the Slovenian border. Julius Caesar is said to have founded it as Forum Iulii, which later gave the whole region its name, and in 568 the Lombards, a Germanic people who invaded Italy, made it the seat of their first duchy. UNESCO lists seven Lombard sites across Italy together, and Cividale holds several, among them the Gastaldaga area, where the royal governor, the gastald, had his residence, and the episcopal complex with its cathedral, baptistery and museum. The label cuts off its words, but those are the two places it means.

The remains here are fragments, but what fragments. The Christian Museum keeps the altar of Duke Ratchis, carved in the eighth century with Christ in a mandorla held by flying angels, in a flat, spirited style that is not quite Roman and not quite Byzantine. The Baptistery of Callixtus is an octagonal font under a canopy of columns, and in the Archaeological Museum you will find Lombard grave goods, including gold crosses, brooches and weapons. The most remarkable building is the Tempietto Longobardo, a small chapel above the river, with a frieze of stucco saints that look like a row of calm, large-eyed women in processional robes.

Cividale is a lovely town to arrive in on two wheels. The Devil's Bridge, a high stone arch over the green gorge of the Natisone, was rebuilt after being blown up in the First World War, and legend says the devil built it in a night in exchange for the first soul to cross. East of town the Natisone valleys, known as Slavia Friulana, run up towards Slovenia on narrow, winding roads through chestnut woods, with villages where Slovene dialects are still spoken. The roads are twisty and quiet, with some rough patches and occasional gravel, and the climbs reward you with views of the Julian Alps.

The town has about nine thousand people, so fuel and a mechanic are no problem. Try gubana, the local spiral pastry stuffed with nuts, raisins and grappa, and a glass of Ramandolo or Picolit, the sweet wines of the Friulian hills, or a dry Friulano. Each September the Mittelfest brings theatre and music into the squares. The best seasons are spring and autumn, and if you stay overnight, wander the old streets after dark when the crowds have gone.
t.tenguiwa@34.2,130.1:
Tenguiwa is a rock, and it is a rock with a long reputation. It stands in the sea near Okinoshima, the sacred island that lies about sixty kilometres off the north coast of Kyushu in the Genkai Sea, midway between Japan and Korea, and it belongs to the World Heritage listing of the Sacred Island of Okinoshima and Associated Sites in the Munakata Region. The name means the Tengu's rock, after the long-nosed goblin of Japanese folklore, and it is one of a few small islets and reefs that rise around the main island, used by sailors as marks and treated with respect as part of the sacred place.

Okinoshima is one of the most restricted places in Japan. Since the fourth century, people crossing the sea between the mainland and Korea and China made offerings here to the goddesses of the Munakata shrine, asking for safe passage, and they left mirrors, gold rings, beads, weapons and fine objects, some of which came from as far as Persia. More than eighty thousand items have been found, all classed as national treasures, and the island has been called the Shosoin of the sea. Today no one may land except a single Shinto priest on a rotation, women are not permitted, and men who visit once a year, on the day of a memorial ceremony in late May, must strip and purify themselves in the sea before stepping ashore. Visitors are not allowed to take anything from the island, nor to speak of what they see.

For an ordinary rider, the experience is therefore from afar. The nearest ways to feel the place are on the mainland, at the shrine of Munakata Taisha, whose Hetsu-miya sits near the town of Munakata, and on Oshima, a small island reachable by ferry, where the Okitsu-miya worship hall faces the open sea and, on clear days, Okinoshima itself can be seen as a faint shape on the horizon. The coast road along the Genkai Sea through Munakata and Fukutsu is a pleasant run, with fishing ports, pine groves and sea views.

Fuel and food are in Munakata, and the ferry terminal has a small shop and a restaurant that serves fresh fish. Check ferry timetables in advance, since weather in the strait can cancel crossings. Summer is hot and humid, with typhoon risk in late summer and autumn, and the best months are April to June and October.
t.koyajima@34.2,130.1:
Koyajima is one of the small rocky islets that lie in the sea around Okinoshima, in the strait between Kyushu and the Korean peninsula, and like its neighbours it is part of the World Heritage listing of the sacred island and its related sites. It is a barren place, with bare rock and sea birds, and nobody lives here. The islets near the main island were treated as part of the sacred zone, and sailors steering across the Genkai Sea used them as marks and as places to ask for protection.

The Genkai Sea is rough, cold in winter and subject to strong currents, and it has swallowed a great many ships. The Munakata fishing communities have lived beside it for over a thousand years, and the shrines along the coast at Munakata and on Oshima are dedicated to three goddesses who protect travellers on the water. The priests who lived at Okinoshima held rituals before and after each crossing, and the ancient envoys to China and Korea made offerings before leaving.

On the mainland, the coast road from Fukuoka to Kitakyushu is a pleasant ride, with sea views, pine trees and small harbours. Munakata Taisha is a major Shinto shrine, with a modern treasure hall displaying the finds from the island, including gold rings, glass beads and a Sasanian cut-glass bowl, and a visit there is the best way to see the objects without the restrictions of the island. The shrine is quiet, beautifully kept and shaded by old camphor trees. Parking for motorcycles is available, and entry to the grounds is free, with a modest fee for the treasure hall.

Fuel and food are in Munakata, which has convenience stores, fuel stations and restaurants serving grilled fish and sashimi, and there are small ports with ferries to Oshima. Check the timetables, because the sea can be rough and ferries are cancelled at short notice. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the air is clear and the sea calm, and typhoons are a concern from August to October. In May, on the anniversary of a naval battle that took place in these waters in 1905, a ceremony is held on Okinoshima with a small number of men permitted to attend.
t.himeji jo@34.8,134.7:
Himeji Castle is the one that survived. Japan has a lot of reconstructed keeps, concrete inside and gift shop on the ground floor, but the big white donjon here is the real thing, largely as it stood in the early 1600s when Ikeda Terumasa rebuilt the place on the hill. It came through the bombing of 1945 and the Kobe earthquake of 1995 with the timbers intact, and it has been a World Heritage site since 1993. The plaster is so brilliantly white that people call it Hakuro-jo, the White Heron, and on a clear morning from the east side you can see why: the roofs stack up like a bird lifting off.

The city around it is big, nearly half a million people, so this is a place for a slow arrival. Come in on the old Sanyo corridor early, park the bike at one of the lots near the station end of the avenue that runs straight to the castle gate, and walk the last stretch. The avenue is wide and dead flat, the castle sits at the end of it like a punchline. Fuel and everything else are in town; you will not be short of anything within a few minutes of the walls.

Inside, the keep is a maze of narrow stairs and wooden floors polished by four centuries of socks, and the defensive design is genuinely clever: winding approaches, hidden gun ports, gates that make you turn sharply under fire. The castle was never actually besieged in anger, which probably explains why so much of it is still standing. Next door is the Koko-en garden, a set of walled gardens in the Edo style, good for twenty quiet minutes if the crowds on the castle stairs have worn you down.

For food, look for Himeji oden, which the locals eat with a ginger-spiked soy dip rather than the usual mustard, and for anago, the sea eel of the Seto Inland Sea, grilled over charcoal. Both are simple things done properly. If you have an afternoon spare, the ridge of Mount Shosha rises behind the city with the old temple complex of Engyo-ji on top, reached by ropeway and a short walk through cedar forest.

Riding out, the Harima plain is flat and busy, with traffic lights and trucks, so the pleasure is in what you stopped to see rather than the tarmac. Spring brings the cherry blossoms around the moat, and November can set the maples on fire; summer is hot and humid enough that the tall white walls feel almost like a refrigerator by comparison.
t.okinoshima@34.2,130.1:
You cannot visit Okinoshima, and that is the whole point of it. This small rocky island sits in the Genkai Sea, about sixty kilometres off the coast of northern Kyushu, and it has been a sacred site for around sixteen hundred years. Sailors crossing to Korea and China used to stop here to pray for safe passage, and they left treasure: mirrors, gold rings, glass from Persia, offerings that archaeologists have found in the thousands, so many that the island is sometimes called the Treasure House of the Sea.

Today the island belongs to the Munakata Taisha shrine, which treats it as the dwelling of a goddess. The rules are strict and well known. Women have never been allowed. Men who visited used to strip and purify themselves in the sea before setting foot ashore, and nobody was allowed to take anything away, not even a blade of grass, and nobody spoke of what they saw. Since 2018 the island has been closed to the public entirely, apart from the one priest on duty at a time and a single ceremony in late spring, and it was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 2017.

For a rider the practical story is on the mainland. The coast near Munakata, northeast of Fukuoka, is pleasant riding: low hills, sea views, small fishing ports, and the main shrine buildings that make up the other components of the site, including a remote worship hall on the island of Oshima, reached by ferry. Fukuoka is a big city with fuel, food and an excellent ramen culture, and from there the roads along the Genkai coast are easy, quiet outside the summer weekends.

If you want to look at the island, the best idea is the distant one: from Oshima's viewing hall on a clear day you can just make out the shape of Okinoshima on the horizon. That is as close as most of us ever get, and the effect of being so near to something so firmly closed is more powerful than many places that are open to everyone.
t.sacred island of okinoshima and associat:
For about five hundred years, roughly from the fourth to the ninth century, people sailed out into the Genkai Sea to leave offerings to the three goddesses of Munakata, and what they left is why this World Heritage site exists. The sacred island of Okinoshima is only part of it. The listing also includes the Munakata Taisha shrine complex on the mainland and on the island of Oshima, and a field of burial mounds called Shinbaru-Nuyama, where the Munakata clan, the local sea lords who ran these rituals, were buried.

The mainland part is open and easy to enjoy. On the coast of northern Kyushu, in the countryside between Fukuoka and Kitakyushu, you can ride the minor roads along the shoreline, with views of low islands, fishing harbours and calm bays. The shrine called Hetsu-miya has a broad wooded precinct and a hall for worshipping the goddesses of the sea, and there is a museum, the Shinpokan, which keeps the treasures excavated on Okinoshima: gold rings, glass cups, mirrors from China and the Korean kingdoms, a whole shipping history of the East China Sea displayed in cases. It is well worth an hour, especially if you want to understand what the island really was.

The burial mounds, a short ride away, are low and grass-covered, the sort of place where a plain-clothed dog walker is more likely to be met than a tourist. Nothing here is theatrical, which is exactly why it works: you are in a landscape lived in by one clan for centuries.

For logistics, the nearer towns are well stocked with fuel and food, and the Fukuoka region is famous for its eating. Order a bowl of tonkotsu ramen in Hakata, or look for mentaiko, the spicy cod roe, and grilled seafood on the coast. If you are curious about the sea itself, ferries cross from the small port of Konominato to Oshima in a few minutes.

The best season is spring or autumn. In typhoon months the Genkai Sea is rough and ferries are cancelled, while winter winds come hard from the northwest and make the coast road a cold one.
t.mikadobashira@34.2,130.1:
A pillar, a monkey and a goblin: the rocks around Okinoshima have the kind of names that sailors give to things that frightened them. Mikadobashira is one of a small cluster of sea stacks that rise out of the water close to the sacred island, along with Kozaru-jima and Tengu-iwa, and they count as part of the World Heritage listing. Together they work as a natural boundary to the holy ground, jagged rock where the swell breaks white even on calm days.

The sea here is the Genkai Sea, a part of the Tsushima Strait, the narrow and dangerous passage between Kyushu and Korea. For centuries ships crossed it on their way to Silla and Tang China, and Okinoshima was their landmark, the last piece of Japan and the first. Those rock pillars would have been visible long before the island itself, and a wrecked ship here was a common story. Offerings made on the island were meant to buy safe passage. In 1905, the Japanese fleet fought and destroyed the Russian Baltic fleet in these same waters, an event so loud that people on Okinoshima reportedly heard the guns.

You cannot land at these rocks, and you cannot ride to them. For a rider the practical business is on the Munakata coast of northern Kyushu, where there are good coastal roads, small harbours and a calm, unhurried fishing country. Fukuoka is the big city nearby, with all the fuel, food and repair shops you could want. From the shoreline at Oshima, reached by ferry, and in clear weather, you might catch the pale line of the island and perhaps its outlying rocks on the horizon.

Respect is the order of the day. Fishermen and shrine priests have kept to the rules here for generations, and the idea of a place that can be seen but not touched is one of the strongest things about it.

If you plan to look, go on a clear winter or autumn morning, when the air is sharp and the visibility long. Summer haze and typhoon swell hide the sea beyond the nearest few miles.
t.gorenja kanomilja kanomilja or ovcjak wa:
Idrija is a small town in a narrow valley in western Slovenia, and for five hundred years it was one of the richest places in Europe, because under it lay mercury. The ore was found in 1490, and the mine became the second biggest in the world, after Almaden in Spain, and employed generations of miners. The two together were listed as a World Heritage site in 2012. Mercury was vital for extracting gold and silver, and for mirrors, medicines and later industry, and the Habsburg emperors treasured Idrija. The miners' wives and daughters made lace to earn money, and Idrija lace is still made today, taught in a school, and a local pride.

The hills around Idrija are steep and wooded, cut by narrow gorges and dotted with small farms. Gorenja Kanomlja, the point on the map, is a village in the hills near the town, and the label refers to a wall or wall-like feature, possibly part of a late Roman defensive system, the Claustra Alpium Iuliarum, a line of barriers, towers and forts built across the passes of the eastern Alps between the third and fifth centuries to guard the road into Italy.

The riding is excellent. From Ljubljana the road to Idrija climbs through Vrhnika and Logatec, and then twists down into the valley, with forest, small villages and wonderful curves. Beyond Idrija, minor roads head up toward Cerkno, near which lies the Franja Partisan Hospital, hidden in a gorge during the Second World War. Surfaces are generally good but narrow, with sharp bends and occasional gravel. Traffic is light. Idrija has fuel, cafes and shops, and the larger villages have basic supplies.

Slovenia uses an electronic vignette for motorways, with a separate cheaper category for motorcycles, but you can avoid the motorways entirely on this route.

Try zlikrofi, small dumplings filled with potato and herbs, a dish unique to Idrija with protected status, and a glass of local wine. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and summer can bring thunderstorms.
t.church of st michael@46.0,14.5:
Five thousand years ago, someone in the marshes south of Ljubljana made a wheel, and it is still here to prove it. In 2002, archaeologists working in the peat at Stare gmajne found a wooden wheel with its axle, made of ash and oak, which turned out to be about five thousand one hundred years old, the oldest known wheel of its kind in the world. It is now in the City Museum in Ljubljana, but it was found in the Ljubljana Marshes, the Barje, a broad, flat, wet plain between the city and the hills, which was once a lake. In the Neolithic and Copper Age, people built villages on stilts above the water, and the wood, preserved in the waterlogged peat, has survived for millennia. The pile dwellings of the Barje were included in the UNESCO listing of Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, in 2011.

The label points to the Church of St Michael, which stands in the marshes on a slight rise, one of the small village churches that dot the Barje. In autumn, mist lies on the fields, and the whole plain turns silver.

The Barje is a nature park, a place of drainage ditches, meadows, reeds and birds, with corncrakes, lapwings and storks in spring and summer. The Ljubljanica river, which winds through it, was drained and channelled in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, but the water still returns in wet years.

For riders, the plain is easy and flat, with quiet country roads and cycle tracks, and in a few kilometres the hills begin, with winding roads toward Krim and the Iska gorge. Ljubljana, only four kilometres away, is a delightful capital of around 270,000 people with plenty of fuel, repair shops and cafes, and a car-free old town with Plecnik's bridges and the dragon on the Dragon Bridge.

The best seasons are spring and autumn. Summers are warm, with thunderstorms. Winters bring fog and frost. Try a plate of Carniolan sausage, Kranjska klobasa, with mustard and fresh bread, in a local inn.
t.bormio@46.5,10.4:
Bormio lies in a high valley of Lombardy, a town of narrow lanes, stone arches and church bells at around 1,200 metres, with mountains rising steeply on every side. It has been a spa since Roman times, and the warm springs that bubble up from deep in the rock still feed thermal baths where you can soak after a long day. In winter it is a ski resort with a long tradition, and the famously steep Stelvio downhill run, used for World Cup races, starts above the town.

The history of the place runs deep. Bormio sat on a trade route linking northern Italy with the Alpine passes and Switzerland, and Venetian and Milanese merchants passed through. The Valtellina, the valley below, is known for its wines, made from the nebbiolo grape grown on steep terraces, and for bresaola, the air-dried beef. Local dishes in Bormio include pizzoccheri, buckwheat pasta cooked with cabbage, potatoes and melted cheese, and the town's winter carnival and old stone fountains give it character.

The Stelvio Pass is the reason many riders come. At about 2,758 metres it is the second highest paved pass in the Alps, and the road from Bormio climbs through galleries and tunnels, then flings itself up in dozens of hairpins to a crest of snow, cafes and souvenir stalls. The Bormio side is generally smoother and wider than the famous series of hairpins on the Prato allo Stelvio side. Traffic is heavy in summer, especially at weekends, so go early. The pass is typically closed from late autumn to late spring, and the weather can turn cold and foggy even in July.

Bormio has fuel stations, supermarkets and lodging at all levels, and San Nicolò, a short ride down the road, also has services. Fill the tank before the climb, since the top has none. Dress in layers, because the temperature drops sharply with altitude, and enjoy a cup of hot chocolate at the summit.
t.keutschacher see@46.6,14.2:
Keutschacher See is one of the warm little lakes of Carinthia, tucked into the rolling moraine country south of the Wörthersee, where glaciers of the last ice age left a jumble of hills, hollows and water. It is small and shallow, with reeds at the edges and pine and beech woods around it, and in summer it warms to a temperature that makes the Alpine lakes a few valleys away seem Arctic. Locals swim from jetties and lawns, and the nearby village of Keutschach am See is a quiet place of fewer than five hundred people.

The surprise is below the surface. Around the shores of the Alps, from about 5000 to 500 BC, people built their houses on wooden piles near lakes and bogs, and the waterlogged mud has preserved timbers, tools and pottery in remarkable condition. Keutschacher See is one of the Austrian sites included in UNESCO's listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. There is little to see from the shore, since the remains lie under water and silt, but the knowledge that Bronze Age families lived here lends the gentle landscape a deeper time.

The ride around here is soft and pretty rather than dramatic. Narrow, well-surfaced roads wind through farmland and woods with views toward the jagged Karawanks, the range that forms the border with Slovenia, and the traffic is light outside holiday weekends. From here, many riders cross the mountains to Slovenia, where the ride continues to the Idrijska Bela valley and its old timber-flume reservoir, built to float logs to mines. Late spring and early autumn are the sweetest seasons, when the water is calm and mist lies on the lake in the morning. Thunderstorms in summer can arrive quickly.

There are inns and lakeside cafes serving trout and Carinthian dishes such as Kasnudeln, cheese-filled pasta parcels with a crimped edge. Pack swimming gear, since a dip in the lake is the best way to end a day in the saddle.
t.enns st laurenz@48.2,14.5:
Enns claims to be the oldest town in Austria, and it has the paperwork to prove it. The town received its city rights in 1212, and long before that, the Romans built a legionary fortress here named Lauriacum, one of the major bases on the Danube frontier. A civilian settlement, the canabae, grew up outside its walls, and the church of St Laurenz stands on part of that ground, with a basilica that has Roman-era origins and layers of medieval rebuilding.

The place has a moving association with Saint Florian, a Roman official who, tradition says, was martyred at Lauriacum in AD 304, drowned in the Enns river with a stone tied to his neck for refusing to renounce his faith. He is now the patron saint of firefighters in Austria and across Central Europe, and the great abbey of St Florian, not far away, is named for him. The town centre has a broad main square, pastel-coloured houses and a freestanding city tower, built in the sixteenth century, with a clock face you can see from every corner.

The river Enns is the boundary between Upper and Lower Austria, and just upstream of the town it joins the Danube. The countryside here is flat and farmed, with rich fields and orchards, and the ride out toward Linz, about twenty kilometres to the northwest, passes along the Danube plain. The Danube cycle path is busy, so cyclists share the roads on summer weekends. Surfaces are good and traffic is moderate, though the main roads are busy at rush hour. A short distance away is Mauthausen, where another concentration camp memorial stands, a sombre reminder of the region's twentieth-century past.

Enns, with nearly ten thousand people, has fuel stations, bakeries, cafes and a handful of inns, and Ennsdorf, just across the river, is smaller. Try local cider, known as Most, a speciality of the region, and a slice of Linzer Torte once you reach Linz. In late spring the orchards are in blossom, and the evening light on the square is a good time for a coffee.
t.allgau high roads@47.7,11.7:
Bad Wiessee lies on the western shore and Tegernsee town on the eastern side, with the mountains of the Mangfall range dropping steeply into the water behind them. It is a place where Munich's money goes for the weekend, and the villas and boat houses show it, but it is also a real valley with cows, hay meadows and a long history.

That history starts with the Benedictine monastery, founded in the eighth century, which still stands on the lake's eastern shore. Its church towers and the former abbey, later a residence of the Bavarian dukes, give Tegernsee town a calm and slightly grand appearance. The brewery in the old buildings serves beer and Bavarian dishes in a courtyard in the open air. The writer Ludwig Thoma lived and wrote here, and the Tegernsee valley has been a retreat for artists and royals ever since the nineteenth century.

Riding out of here is a pleasure. A lake-side road leads south through Rottach-Egern and on to Kreuth, where the valley narrows and the road climbs through spruce forest to the Austrian border at the Achenpass, and on toward the Achensee. Bends are smooth and well graded, and the surface is generally excellent, though weekend traffic, cyclists and sightseers can fill the road, so early starts are far better than midday. Bavarian and Tyrolean authorities pay attention to motorcycle noise, so keep the revs reasonable through villages. Autumn is gorgeous, with golden larches and sharp clear air.

Bad Wiessee has fuel, and it sits only a few kilometres from Tegernsee, so this is the sensible place to top up before heading into the hills. Cafés and bakeries in both towns serve strong coffee and sweet pastries. The weather in the Alps is moody, with afternoon storms in summer and snow on the heights from October, so look at the sky before setting out. If the day is clear, take the cable car on the Wallberg for a view across the whole lake.
t.rothenburg ob der tauber@49.4,10.2:
Rothenburg ob der Tauber looks like a film set because, for a long time, it had no choice. The medieval town stands on a ridge above the Tauber valley in Franconia, enclosed by an almost complete ring of walls with towers and gates, and its timber houses, steep roofs and cobbled lanes have survived because the town lost its wealth after the Thirty Years War and could not afford to rebuild. It was too poor to modernise, and so it stayed old. Today it draws visitors in large numbers, and the main streets can be packed with tour groups by mid-morning.

There are stories attached. One of the best known, the Meistertrunk, tells how the town was spared in 1631 when the mayor accepted a challenge from the enemy general to drain a large tankard of wine in one go, and did it. A play about the event is staged each year. In the church of St. James there is a carved altar of the Holy Blood by the sculptor Tilman Riemenschneider, a masterpiece of late Gothic woodcarving. In March 1945 an air raid destroyed about forty percent of the old town, and it was rebuilt with the help of donations from around the world, which explains the many plaques on the walls.

For riders, Rothenburg is a starting point on the Castle Road, which crosses Franconia toward Bamberg by way of small towns, castles and wooded hills. The roads are quiet and smooth, running through farmland and orchards, with gentle curves and views over open country. Surfaces are good, and the biggest hazards are agricultural vehicles and the odd tour coach. Spring blossom and autumn colour are lovely, and summer weekends are busy.

For fuel and food, the town has what you need, but the old centre is largely closed to cars, so park outside and walk in. A walk along the top of the town wall, which is free, gives the best views over the roofs. Sweet Schneeball pastries are sold in every bakery, and the Franconian wine from the surrounding valleys is worth trying. Evenings, after the tourists have gone, are the time when the lanes feel like they did centuries ago.
t.berchtesgaden@47.6,13.0:
Berchtesgaden sits in the far southeast corner of Germany, in a pocket of Bavaria that pokes into Austria, and the mountains here do not bother to be modest. The Watzmann, at 2,713 metres Germany's second highest mountain, stands above the valley in a long ridge, with the pale wall of the Hochkalter opposite. The town is the end of the German Alpine Road, which runs from Lake Constance, and it feels like the end of the line, with the peaks closing in on all sides. For centuries the local economy rested on salt, and the salt mine, worked since the sixteenth century, is open to visitors who put on miners' clothes and slide down the wooden chutes.

The area has a heavy twentieth century history as well. On the Obersalzberg above the town, the Nazi leadership built a compound with Hitler's residence, and the Documentation Centre there explains the story honestly and in detail. The Kehlsteinhaus, the so-called Eagle's Nest, built on a ridge top as a gift for Hitler, is reached by a narrow road and a lift cut into the rock, and it is now a restaurant with views. Many visitors find the contrast between the beauty of the scenery and the history uncomfortable, which is probably appropriate.

Nature is the main reason to come. The Königssee, a deep green fjord-like lake south of the town, is reached by electric boats that glide below cliffs of grey rock to the pilgrimage chapel of St. Bartholomä, with its red domes. The Berchtesgaden National Park protects the high country around it, with chamois, marmots and golden eagles. For riders, the Roßfeld panoramic road, a toll road that climbs to a high ridge above the valley, offers some of the best views in the region, and nearby roads wind through meadows and forest. Surfaces are good, but traffic is heavy in summer, particularly at weekends.

Fuel, food and accommodation are all available in town, though prices rise in high season. Cafés and inns serve local dishes such as Kaiserschmarrn, a sweet shredded pancake with fruit, and cold Bavarian beer, and the evening light on the Watzmann is a quiet reward at the end of a long ride.
t.bolzano@46.5,11.4:
Bolzano lives with two languages and does so with a certain comfortable pride. It lies in a wide valley at the meeting of three rivers in South Tyrol, surrounded by steep slopes of vines and apples, with the pink limestone peaks of the Dolomites rising to the east. Until 1919 it belonged to Austria, and German is still the first language of most people in the province, though Bolzano itself is mostly Italian-speaking. Signs are in both, the cooking mixes dumplings and strudel with pasta and espresso, and the city feels like a conversation between two cultures.

The most famous resident is the oldest. Ötzi, the man in the ice, is a natural mummy about five thousand three hundred years old, found in 1991 by hikers in the glacier on the Italian-Austrian border. He lies in a cold, dim chamber in the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology, together with his clothing, copper axe and bow, and the museum does a marvellous job of explaining how he lived, and probably died, from an arrow wound. In the old town, arcaded streets and Gothic churches surround Walther Square, named after the medieval poet Walther von der Vogelweide.

For riders, Bolzano is the start of the Great Dolomites Road, which runs about a hundred and ten kilometres east to Cortina d'Ampezzo. The route climbs first through the Val d'Ega past Lake Carezza, in front of the Latemar peaks, crosses the Karer Pass at about 1,750 metres, and continues to the Pordoi Pass, above 2,200 metres, and the Falzarego Pass, above 2,100. The road is smooth and engineered with a series of hairpins that make it popular with riders. At sunrise and sunset the rock faces glow with a deep pink called enrosadira, a sight that stays in memory for a long time. Summer weekends bring heavy traffic, so aim for weekdays and early starts.

Fuel and repair shops are all easy to find, and the city has an excellent range of restaurants. Try speck, the smoked ham, and canederli dumplings, and cool down with a glass of local white wine. Summers in the valley are hot, but the mountains are fresh, and snow can close the highest passes from late autumn to spring.
t.enns canabae nordost@48.2,14.5:
Enns calls itself the oldest town in Austria, and it has a very good case, since a Roman settlement stood here long before there was an Austria to speak of. Roman Lauriacum was a legionary base on the Danube frontier, and around the fort grew what the Romans called the canabae, a sprawling civilian settlement of traders, craftsmen, veterans' families, innkeepers and anyone else who made a living from the soldiers. This corner of the map marks the north-eastern end of that civilian quarter.

Look at the ground and you will find little. Roman Enns lies under modern houses, gardens and fields, and archaeologists have worked out the layout mostly from excavated walls, graves and bits of pottery. The ordinary pattern is plain: strips of workshops along the roads leading out from the camp, a mixture of timber and stone houses, and cemeteries outside the settlement along the highways. That all belongs to the frontier of the empire, the Limes, which runs along the Danube and has been added to the UNESCO list. For a rider, the lesson is that the great river was once the edge of the known world, and the land south of it was Rome.

The modern town is a pleasant one. A long main square is lined with painted houses and dominated by a tall tower from the sixteenth century, with a clock face and a pointed roof, and there are fine cafés beneath it. The Enns river, which gives the town its name, forms the old boundary between Upper and Lower Austria. A little way off, in the district of Lorch, stands the basilica of Saint Laurence, built over older foundations and with a small museum explaining the Roman past.

The roads in the area are mostly flat and fast, running along the Danube plain through farmland and small villages, with the odd tighter section where the land rises toward the hills. This is not a route for corner hunters. It is a place to understand history by riding through it. Enns has nearly ten thousand people and plenty of fuel and food, and Linz lies about twenty kilometres away to the west if you need anything larger. Come in spring or autumn, and take your time at the museums and the river.
t.enns legionslager nordecke@48.2,14.5:
When the Roman army reorganised the Danube frontier after the wars against the Marcomanni in the later second century, a legion was posted here, the Second Italica, with a base large enough to hold several thousand soldiers. Fortresses of this kind were laid out to a standard plan, a rectangle with rounded corners, four gates, a main street and a headquarters building at the centre, so a soldier transferred from another province would know where to find the bath house without asking.

The Danube lies just north, and the river was as much a part of the defence as the walls. Patrol boats moved up and down, watchtowers were strung along the bank, and the traffic of goods ran in both directions. Lauriacum later became the capital of the province of Noricum Ripense, a sign of how important the frontier region had become. The best-known figure from this world is Florian, a Roman official said to have been put to death here around the year 304 for refusing to give up his faith, and thrown into the Enns with a stone around his neck. He became a patron saint of Upper Austria and of firefighters, and many village churches carry his image with a bucket of water.

What remains is subtle. Parts of the fortress walls were found under the town and some are shown in the local museum, while the shape of the camp survives in the street pattern, a quiet echo of a Roman plan. Few visitors come with high expectations, and that suits the place. It is a fine example of how history is often not a monument but a trace in the layout of a town.

The riding is straightforward: flat roads along the Danube plain, a short hop to the Autobahn, and quieter lanes through farmland if you prefer. Enns has everything practical, with fuel stations on the main roads, bakeries in the centre and cafés on the square. A few kilometres east lies the Enns river mouth, where the clear, cold water of the mountain river meets the broad, slower Danube. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the light is soft on the fields.
t.enns canabae sudwest@48.2,14.5:
The southwestern edge of Roman Enns is the part that faces the way to Linz, and it is a good place to think about what a frontier town was actually like. The civilian settlement around the legionary fortress spread out along roads in every direction, and the western side held a mix of workshops, houses and burial grounds. Roman law kept the dead outside settlements, so the tombs lined the roads leading out, which is where later farmers kept turning up stone coffins and funerary inscriptions with the plough.

Daily life in a place like this was a mixture of the military and the commercial. Soldiers needed boots, belts, pottery, wine and entertainment, and the canabae supplied all of it. Families formed, since legionaries were not allowed to marry officially but often did anyway, and many children grew up in the shadow of the barracks. When the empire collapsed in the west, the settlement shrank but never wholly vanished, and a church dedicated to Saint Laurence continued the Christian tradition. The modern town grew up around the medieval centre rather than the Roman one, which explains why the traces lie in odd corners.

You can ride this edge of town easily. A mixture of quiet roads, main roads and cycle paths lead west toward the Danube and Linz, and the land is largely flat and agricultural. Close to the river, there is a good chance of wind, and in autumn mist lies along the water for hours after dawn. This ride later heads toward the great bend of the Danube at Schlögen, where another Roman fort once watched the river, and the scenery becomes more dramatic with wooded slopes and narrow roads.

Fuel and food are easy in Enns, which has just under ten thousand people. Several petrol stations are on the main roads, and the town centre has bakeries, cafés and inns serving schnitzel, dumplings and Danube fish. The Ennshafen port area nearby is industrial, with silos, cranes and barges, a reminder that the river is still a working one. Spring brings blossom on the orchards, early summer is warm with long evenings, and autumn is the best time for a slow ride with clear light.
t.innsbruck@47.3,11.4:
Innsbruck sits in a bowl. The Inn river runs through the middle, the town name means bridge over the Inn, and on both sides steep limestone mountains rise almost from the streets. To the north the jagged Nordkette stands over the rooftops, and a funicular and a cable car carry you from the old centre to over two thousand metres in about twenty minutes, so that you can drink a morning coffee in town and an afternoon coffee among the rocks.

The old town is compact and colourful, with arcaded houses, narrow lanes and a small balcony roofed in gilded copper tiles that Emperor Maximilian ordered around the year 1500, now known as the Golden Roof. Maximilian was fond of this place and is buried, in a manner of speaking, in a vast tomb in the Hofkirche, surrounded by life-size bronze figures of ancestors and heroes. In the modern era the town hosted the Winter Olympics in 1964 and 1976, and the ski jump at Bergisel, redesigned by Zaha Hadid, stands above the town as a dramatic curve of steel and glass.

Innsbruck is the great crossroads of the Alps for riders. South of it the Brenner road leads to Italy, passing under the tall bridge called the Europabrücke, and the old pass itself, at about thirteen hundred and seventy metres, is one of the lowest crossings of the main Alpine chain, which is why it has been used since Roman times. West, the road goes into the valleys of the Ötztal and Kühtai, where the climbs are steeper and the passes higher. Traffic in the valley can be heavy, particularly lorries on the Brenner corridor and holiday queues at weekends, so leave early.

Fuel and food are plentiful in a city of well over a hundred thousand. Station prices on the motorway are higher than in town, and Austrian vignette rules apply on motorways, so check that you have one. Föhn winds can bring warm air and startling clarity, with the mountains looking close enough to touch, and they sometimes bring headaches and gusts too. Spring and autumn are quieter, summer is busy but lovely, and winter belongs to the skiers.
t.campolongo pass@46.5,11.9:
Campolongo is the quiet pass in a family of loud ones. At 1,875 metres it links Corvara in Alta Badia with Arabba and the upper valley of Livinallongo, and on the Sella Ronda it is the stretch that most riders ride without thinking, between the more famous climbs of Pordoi and Gardena. That undersells it. The road winds up through pasture and scattered spruce from Corvara with a long, relaxed run of hairpins, and from the top the whole of the Sella massif stands over you, a pale, castellated block of limestone that looks as if it was built rather than eroded.

The Dolomites were once the floor of a warm tropical sea, and the rock shows it: pale dolomite and limestone, formed from corals and shells, lifted and carved into pinnacles that glow pink and orange at sunset, the famous enrosadira. UNESCO listed the range in 2009. The valleys here are Ladin-speaking, with a language of their own that is neither Italian nor German, and you will see bilingual or even trilingual signs. Corvara and Arabba are ski towns first, so in summer they are slightly sleepy, with cable cars carrying walkers and bikers up the slopes.

The area has a harder history as well. In the First World War the front between Austria and Italy ran right through these mountains, and the nearby Col di Lana, close to Arabba, was the site of a famous mine explosion in 1916 that blew the summit apart. Old trenches, tunnels and rusting wire still scar the ridges, and open-air museums trace some of them.

The riding is superb but the weather deserves attention, since afternoon thunderstorms in summer build quickly over the Sella and can leave the road greasy. Start early. The pass is usually open from late spring to autumn, though snow can close it outside that window. Traffic, particularly on weekends, can be heavy with cars, cyclists, and other motorcyclists, and the speed limits are watched. A mountain hut near the summit usually serves coffee and strudel, and that alone justifies a pause.
t.bernina pass@46.4,10.0:
The Bernina Pass is the stark one. At 2,330 metres, it has no forest, no village to speak of, and almost no vegetation to soften the view: just two small lakes, a scatter of buildings at the Ospizio, a railway line, and mountains that look like they were left half-finished. It is also a true divide. Water from one side of the summit lake eventually reaches the Inn and the Danube, and then the Black Sea, while water from the other side flows south to the Po and the Adriatic. Lago Bianco, the milky-green reservoir on the summit, drains toward Italy, and Lago Nero, a little further north, toward the Inn.

The road climbs from the Engadin side near Pontresina in easy, open curves, then drops south toward Poschiavo in a long run of switchbacks and tight bends, with the climate changing noticeably as it descends from alpine tundra to chestnut and vines near Tirano. The surface is good and the corners are well signed, but the pass is exposed to cold, wind and fog, even in summer, so a layer under your jacket is wise. Snow can arrive early and linger, and while the road is kept open for much of the year, check conditions in winter and spring.

Next to the road runs the Bernina railway, whose red trains carry the Bernina Express from Chur to Tirano. It is the highest adhesion railway in the Alps, meaning it climbs without cogs, and it was listed by UNESCO with its companion Albula line in 2008. You may find yourself riding beside a train for miles, a good game to play. Above the pass, Piz Palü and the Bernina massif carry glaciers that have shrunk visibly in recent decades. The Diavolezza cable car, just north of the pass, climbs to a ridge with a close view of the ice.

Poschiavo, about ten kilometres south, has a pump, and Pontresina to the north has more, while Tirano across the Italian border is the nearest town of any size. The Ospizio has a place for a coffee, a hot soup or a slice of nut cake, which is the proper reward for the climb. Ride early in the day to avoid the traffic, and expect to find the light flat and clear and the air thin and cold.
t.bamberg@49.9,10.9:
Bamberg is one of those German cities that came through the twentieth century almost undamaged, so its old centre feels more like a seventeenth-century drawing than a place that has been repaired. It was listed by UNESCO in 1993, and it is easy to see why: it stretches across seven hills, like Rome, with the cathedral and the old bishop's residence on the highest, the Regnitz river looping through the middle, and rows of half-timbered houses and fishermen's cottages along the water. The little town hall sits on an artificial island in the river, reached by bridges, and has frescoes that seem to spill out over the walls.

The city owes its shape to Emperor Heinrich II, who made it a bishopric in 1007, and the cathedral that he founded still holds his tomb and the famous Bamberg Horseman, a medieval stone rider whose identity is still debated. Later, the prince-bishops added baroque palaces. Perhaps the best-known local product, though, is smoked beer, or Rauchbier, with a flavour like a campfire sausage in a glass. Whether you love it or not, it is a point of local pride, and several old breweries and taverns still serve it from wooden barrels, along with hearty Franconian food like pork roast with dumplings.

For riders, Bamberg is the northern end of the Castle Road section from Rothenburg ob der Tauber. The road gets here through gently rolling Franconian farmland, with wooded ridges, orchards and small villages built around church spires and castles. The surface is generally good and the bends are easy rather than dramatic, so the pleasure is steady and unhurried. To the east, the Fränkische Schweiz, the Franconian Switzerland, has more twisting roads, rock formations and cave systems, and it is worth an extra day if you have one.

The city has about seventy thousand people, so fuel, parking garages and services are plentiful, though the old town is a maze of one-way streets and pedestrian zones. Leave the bike in a car park at the edge and walk in. The 'Little Venice' fishermen's quarter is best at sunset, and autumn is a lovely time, with harvest festivals and lighter crowds. Weekends in summer can be busy, so book rooms ahead.
t.salzburg@47.8,13.1:
Salzburg owes its name and its wealth to salt, the white gold that was mined in the nearby hills and floated down the Salzach river for centuries. The prince-archbishops who ruled the city used that income to turn it into a baroque stage set, with domes, fountains and palaces crowded below the mighty fortress of Hohensalzburg, which looks down from its rock over the old town. The city is also the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, born in 1756 in a narrow house on the Getreidegasse, and every summer the Salzburg Festival fills the squares and churches with music.

As a base for a ride into the Salzkammergut, the lake district to the east, it could hardly be better placed. Within half an hour of leaving the city, the land begins to rise, and the first lakes appear: the Fuschlsee, then the Mondsee with its distinctive twin-towered abbey church, and on to the Wolfgangsee, where the village of St Gilgen is Mozart's mother's birthplace. The roads that link them are smooth, with relaxed curves, glimpses of water between the trees and mountains that rise in the distance, some still streaked with snow into June. The best times are late spring and September, when the crowds have thinned and the light is warm. In summer, the lakeside roads are busy with cars, buses and bikes, so start early.

The city itself is walkable, and an hour of wandering is a good start. The Mirabell Gardens, with their dwarf statues and views toward the fortress, and the cathedral square are classic stops. The film The Sound of Music was shot here in 1964, and coach tours still follow its locations, though locals have rather mixed feelings about its fame. For something local, try Salzburger Nockerl, a huge, fluffy sweet soufflé said to represent the hills around the town, and a coffee in one of the old coffee houses is hard to beat.

Salzburg has more than enough of everything practical, with fuel stations on the ring roads and in the suburbs, repair shops and every kind of lodging. Remember that Austrian motorways require a vignette, which can be bought at petrol stations, and that motorcycles have their own cheaper version. Bring waterproofs, because the region catches a lot of rain, locally known as Schnürlregen, a fine, steady drizzle that can last all day.
t.pordoi pass@46.5,11.8:
Pordoi is the high point of the Sella Ronda, a pass of 2,239 metres between the Fassa valley and Arabba, and for many people the one with the best view in the Dolomites. The road climbs from Canazei in about thirty hairpins to the saddle, where a big car park, a few restaurants and the cable car to Sass Pordoi cluster beneath the pale cliffs of the Sella massif. On a clear day, the rock turns pink and gold at dusk, the effect known locally as the enrosadira.

The Dolomites are made from an ancient coral reef lifted from the sea, which is why the mountains look so unlike the Alps further west: pale, vertical and fretted with towers. During the First World War the Austro-Hungarian and Italian armies fought here on the very peaks, and tunnels and trenches still scar the rocks, particularly on nearby Marmolada. The Pordoi road was built in the early twentieth century and has been a motorcyclists' favourite since the first bikes could climb it.

The ride is excellent but crowded. In July and August, weekends bring an endless stream of motorbikes, cyclists and campervans, and the best time is early morning or an evening in September, when traffic has thinned and the larches begin to turn gold. The surface is good, the bends are nicely engineered, and you can link it with the Sella, Gardena and Campolongo passes in a classic loop of about fifty kilometres. Police and local authorities have at times introduced limits and noise controls in the area, so ride considerately.

Canazei, a town of around a thousand people at the bottom, has fuel, hotels and food, so use it before the climb. At the top, a plate of local speck, canederli dumplings and a strudel, with a mountain-hut coffee, takes the edge off the cold. Snow can fall on the pass in any month, and the road is closed in winter, normally from late autumn to late spring, so check conditions. Wear warm gloves even on a hot day in the valley.
t.gavia pass@46.3,10.5:
The Gavia is one of those passes that people talk about in lowered voices. At 2,621 metres it is among the highest paved roads in the Italian Alps, linking Bormio in the Valtellina with Ponte di Legno in the Val Camonica, and it crosses the rugged, rocky heart of the Stelvio National Park. The summit is bare and wild, with snow patches into July, two small lakes, the dark Lago Nero and the pale Lago Bianco, and a stone refuge, Rifugio Berni, with a restaurant and a view across the glaciers of the Ortler-Cevedale group.

The road is narrow, steep and rough. The western side, climbing from Santa Caterina Valfurva, has gradients up to eighteen percent, lots of blind hairpins and almost no barriers over the drop, and the surface patches and potholes are the norm. On the eastern side, from Ponte di Legno, the climb is a little more forgiving, but still narrow, with passing places that the bus drivers and campers use with practiced calm. Meeting a coach on a hairpin can require reversing. Weather changes quickly at this altitude, and the pass is closed by snow from late autumn until early summer, usually reopening in June.

The Gavia has a famous history in cycling: in the 1988 Giro d'Italia, a blizzard struck as the riders crossed the pass, and Andy Hampsten of the United States attacked in the snow to win the stage and eventually the race. It also has a darker history: the area was a front line in the First World War, when Italian and Austro-Hungarian troops fought at extraordinary altitudes, and the remains of trenches and barracks can still be found on the surrounding peaks.

The nearest petrol is at Bormio or in the valley towns, and Ponte di Legno, with about thirteen hundred residents, may have it, but fill up before the climb and do not trust the gauge. Food is simple and hearty, with polenta, venison stew and pizzoccheri, buckwheat pasta from the Valtellina, served at the refuge.

Go early to avoid traffic and afternoon thunderstorms. Bring a warm layer even in August, because the temperature at the top can be close to freezing, and wear gloves. Take your time, ride within your limits, and the Gavia will reward you with one of the best days in the Alps.
t.canazei@46.5,11.8:
Canazei is a small Ladin town at the head of the Val di Fassa, and the first impression is of towering rock. The Marmolada, the highest peak in the Dolomites at 3,343 metres, rises to the south-east with its glacier, while the cliffs of the Sella group fill the northern horizon, huge walls of pale dolomite that glow pink and orange at sunrise and sunset. The Dolomites were declared a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2009, and no one who stands here is likely to wonder why.

This is Ladin country, and the old language, related to Romansh and Friulian, is still spoken in the valley, with signs in Italian, German and Ladin. Canazei is a ski town as much as a summer one, with a lively main street of hotels, shops and restaurants, and the cuisine mixes Tyrolean and Italian: speck, canederli dumplings, polenta, strudel and rich soups.
