The mountains were also a front line in the First World War, and the Marmolada glacier held an entire network of tunnels and barracks, the so-called Ice City, where Austrian and Italian soldiers lived in the ice. In July 2022, part of the glacier collapsed, killing several climbers, a reminder of how fast the high mountains are changing.

The riding is why most people are here. From Canazei, roads climb to the Passo Pordoi at 2,239 metres, with dozens of hairpins and a huge view, and to the Passo Sella and Passo Gardena, forming the famous Sella Ronda loop around the massif. The surface is generally excellent, but the passes are narrow, popular and crowded, with cyclists, motorhomes and fellow bikers. On certain days in summer and autumn the passes are closed to motor traffic for cycling events, so check the calendar before planning. The best hours are early morning and evening, and September, when the crowds thin and the larches turn gold.

Canazei has fuel and shops, but fill up in the valley rather than counting on the passes, where petrol is scarce and expensive. There are plenty of hotels, hostels and rifugi, and booking is wise in July and August. Weather is changeable, with sunshine, cloud and thunder in the same afternoon, so carry waterproofs and wear a warm layer for the high passes.

Take the loop in either direction, but start early, and stop at the summit of the Pordoi for a coffee and a long look at the Marmolada.
t.brescia@45.5,10.2:
Brescia is one of those Italian cities that is much better than its reputation. It lies at the foot of the Alps, on the edge of the Lombard plain, with the Garda and Iseo lakes close by and the Val Trompia and Val Camonica running north into the mountains. It has Roman remains, including a temple and theatre on the slopes beneath the castle, as well as a medieval and Renaissance heart. The Santa Giulia monastery, now a museum, is a UNESCO site, and the castle on the hill above gives a wide view across the rooftops.

For motorcyclists and car people, Brescia means one thing above all: the Mille Miglia. That race, run between Brescia and Rome and back on public roads from 1927 until 1957, made the city a pilgrimage point for enthusiasts. It was stopped after a fatal accident, and today it lives on as a classic-car rally every spring, when the town fills with beautiful old machines. There is a museum devoted to the race in a former monastery, and the route is a good reason for the ride that starts here.

Arriving or leaving by road means dealing with a busy industrial city, with a good deal of traffic around the ring roads and the A4 motorway. Tram-free but full of one-way streets, the old centre is a limited traffic zone, the ZTL, so do not ride into it without checking, as cameras issue fines. Park on the outskirts and walk in. Early morning is the best time to leave, with mist sometimes lying over the plain and the air cool.

Fuel and food are no trouble, since Brescia has a population of nearly two hundred thousand and plenty of everything. The local table is hearty, with casoncelli, a stuffed pasta served with butter and sage, and spiedo, a slow-cooked skewered meat dish, as signature dishes. The wines of Franciacorta, a sparkling wine region just to the west, are among Italy's best.

Late spring and early autumn are the finest times to be here, with warm days and clear views toward the mountains. It is a good city to start a long run south toward Rome, and a pleasant one to come home to.
t.munich bavarian alps@48.7,11.5:
South of Ingolstadt on the Danube plain, the ground is so flat that the horizon becomes the main landscape feature. This stop lies between Manching and Ingolstadt, in a region once covered by the great Donaumoos, a peat bog drained in the eighteenth century under the Bavarian elector Karl Theodor, who wanted farmland and settlers. The road network that crosses the old moor is neat, straight and carefully ditch-lined, with fields of maize, wheat and sugar beet standing behind.

Manching has a history much older than the roads. The Celts built a huge fortified settlement here, an oppidum, in the last two centuries before Christ, one of the largest in Europe, with ramparts that ran for kilometres. Today the town is better known for its military airfield and aerospace industry, but the Celtic past still lingers in the museum, which is worth a look if you like objects with stories. Ingolstadt, seven kilometres away, is a large city with over a hundred thousand people, home to Audi, a medieval wall, and the claim to be where the Bavarian beer purity law was issued in 1516.

For a rider, this is a start, not a destination. Fuel and food are easy in Manching, and Ingolstadt has everything you could need. The roads near the Danube are good for covering ground quickly, but they are also busy with commuters, so a morning start before the traffic builds is a good plan. The Danube floodplain nearby has paths and beech woods if you want to walk for ten minutes before you mount up.

The reward for a start like this comes later, when the road turns south and the first hills of the Alpine foreland rise ahead. The contrast makes the mountains look taller than they are. Check your luggage, fill the tank and enjoy the rare luxury of flat tarmac, because you will want to remember it when the hairpins begin.
t.rosenheim@47.9,12.1:
Rosenheim is the main town of the Inn valley south of Munich, a city of around sixty thousand people at the point where the Mangfall flows into the Inn. Its name means rose home, though the town grew rich on something less romantic: salt. For centuries salt from Bad Reichenhall travelled here through a pipeline of wooden pipes, was boiled in local pans and loaded onto boats on the Inn, and the merchants who handled it built the arcaded houses around Max-Josefs-Platz that still give the old centre its look. Television viewers may know it from a detective series, but the real thing is livelier and less murderous.

For a rider, Rosenheim is a hub. The A8 runs past on its way between Munich and Salzburg, the Inn valley road leads south toward Kufstein and the Tyrol, and the Chiemsee lies about twenty kilometres to the east. You will find several fuel stations, supermarkets, cafes and restaurants, and a station with fast trains to Munich. It is the ideal place to fill the tank, eat breakfast and check your route before heading up into the mountains.

The traffic is the price. On a Friday afternoon in summer, the roads into the city and the motorway ramps can be crowded with holidaymakers, so aim to start early or come back late. The old centre is pleasant for a stroll, with the Mittertor gate, the Marienplatz and a few churches, and the riverside paths offer a green escape. From the bridge over the Inn you can see the Alps rise to the south, a reminder of why you are here.

Nature has a say, too. The Inn is a fast, milky green river carrying meltwater from the high Alps, and in spring it can run high and loud. To the south the Wendelstein and Kaiser mountains frame the horizon, and on a clear day the peaks look close enough to touch. Rosenheim is a good beginning and a good ending, comfortable in both roles.
t.munich bavarian alps@48.8,12.5:
Straubing lies a little to the northeast, and this stop sits in the great grain country around it, the Gäuboden. It is some of the most fertile land in Bavaria, a broad plain between the Danube and the Bavarian Forest covered in deep loess soil laid down by wind in the ice age, and the locals call it the breadbasket of the state. The villages of Leiblfing, Mengkofen and Geiselhöring each have a church with an onion dome and a ring of large farms. In summer the fields stand tall and golden, and the whole area smells of dust and warm straw.

For riders, this is a place of long straight roads and wide horizons. The land is flat, with scarcely a bend, and the surface is good, so progress is easy but a little monotonous. The most important thing is to watch the wind and the farm traffic: tractors with wide trailers appear without warning, and in harvest season the roads can be littered with chaff. Visibility is good, and you can see a long way ahead, but patience is a virtue.

Geiselhöring is the largest place nearby, with nearly seven thousand people, a railway station and the usual shops, bakeries and fuel stations. Mengkofen, a bit smaller, also has services, and Leiblfing, though tiny, has an inn. For a more substantial stop, Straubing, with its handsome old town and tall city tower, is only a short ride away, and every August hosts the Gäubodenfest, one of the biggest folk festivals in Bavaria.

The swim marker suggests a quiet lake or river bank nearby, and the Danube and Isar both lie within a few kilometres, along with a number of gravel pit lakes that have become local bathing spots. Be careful of currents on the rivers and ask a local about safe places. On a hot afternoon, a dip and a nap in the shade of an alder are an excellent way to end a day on the plain.
t.landsberg am lech@48.1,10.9:
Landsberg am Lech sits on a bend of the river with a medieval gate, a tilted market square and a history that began with salt. In the twelfth century Henry the Lion, the Duke of Bavaria, built a toll station here on the Lech to tax the salt traders who were bringing their loads from Reichenhall to Swabia, and the town grew up around it. The Bayertor, a tall, ornate gate of the fifteenth century, still stands at the end of the old town, and its roof is covered in glazed tiles that sparkle after rain. The Lech itself tumbles over a weir in the middle of town, a lively sound that follows you through the streets.

For a rider, Landsberg is a pleasant, practical stop. It has over twenty-seven thousand inhabitants, with fuel stations, supermarkets, cafes and a good selection of restaurants. The Hauptplatz, with its fountain and painted facades, is a lovely place to sit with a coffee, and the streets around it have small shops and bakeries. The town lies on the Romantic Road, the tourist route from Würzburg to Füssen, so it can be busy on summer weekends, especially around the market square.

The artist Hubert von Herkomer, who was born in a nearby village and went on to become a celebrated painter in Britain, left his mark on the town in the form of a studio and a concert hall, and the whole place has a slightly bohemian air. The river valley is also a good place for walking, with paths along the banks and a few quiet pools where the green Alpine water slows down.

South of Landsberg the roads begin to lift toward the Alpine foothills, and on a clear day you can see the far line of the mountains from the hill above town. Neuschwanstein lies about sixty kilometres south, and this is the natural base for a day trip. In the evening, when the light turns golden and the swifts wheel around the towers, the old town is hard to leave.
t.klagenfurt@46.6,14.3:
Klagenfurt has a dragon, and the dragon is the first thing to see. The Lindwurm fountain on the Neuer Platz, carved from a single block of local stone in the late sixteenth century, is the symbol of the city, and the legend says a monster once lived in the marshes here before the founders drained them. The city of ninety thousand people is the capital of Carinthia, built on flat ground just east of the Wörthersee, with the long wall of the Karawanks to the south marking the border with Slovenia. Robert Musil and Ingeborg Bachmann were both born here, an unexpected literary pedigree for a quiet provincial capital.

The setting is the real draw. Carinthia is Austria's warmest corner, with lakes that reach swimming temperature by early summer, and the Wörthersee is the largest, a few kilometres west of the centre. On the south shore the pine-covered slopes drop to the water, and the north shore is lined with old villas. The Alps on all sides give the region a bowl-like climate that is dry and bright for much of the year, though thunderstorms in July can be sudden and loud.

For a rider, Klagenfurt is a base rather than a destination. The old centre is compact, with arcaded courtyards and a pedestrian zone that is easy to enjoy on foot. The riding starts on the edges. South of the city the road climbs towards the Loibl Pass, a steep, narrow crossing into Slovenia that tops out at around 1,360 metres and goes through a short tunnel under the crest; the tunnel was dug during the war by forced labourers from a nearby concentration camp, and a memorial stands on the Carinthian side. In the other direction, the Wörthersee roads, the Gailtal and the Nockalm Road all start within easy range.

Fuel is plentiful, with stations all over the ring roads, and cafes fill the main squares. For lunch, order Kärntner Kasnudeln, the local filled pasta with a distinctive crimped edge, served with butter and salad. Cross the border and you will need a vignette for Slovenia's motorways, but not on the Loibl itself, and in spring you should expect snow on the high crest into April.
t.linz@48.3,14.3:
Linz sits on the Danube like a working city that has learned to dress for dinner. For most of the twentieth century it was an industrial town, famous for its steelworks and chemical plants, and for being the place people drove through on the way to somewhere better. Then it reinvented itself as a centre of media art, with the Ars Electronica Center on the north bank and a string of modern buildings along the river, and in 2009 it was a European Capital of Culture. About two hundred thousand people live here, making it the third city of Austria.

History is layered. The Romans had a fort called Lentia on this bend in the river, and the Habsburg emperor Friedrich III held court here in the fifteenth century. Johannes Kepler taught at the school in Linz and worked on his third law of planetary motion while living in the city in the 1610s and 1620s, and Mozart wrote his Linz Symphony in a few days in 1783 while staying as a guest. Anton Bruckner was organist at the old cathedral, and the concert hall on the river bears his name. The Linzer Torte, a latticed almond and redcurrant tart, is among the oldest named cakes in the world, and every cafe in town will have it.

For a motorcyclist, the interest is in the roads out of town. East along the south bank, you ride into the Danube limes, the line of Roman forts and watchtowers, passing places such as Enns, with its Roman and medieval remains, and Wallsee, with its castle above the river. North across the bridge, the land rises into the Mühlviertel, a quiet granite plateau of woods, farms and winding lanes, almost empty of tourists. The Pöstlingberg, with its twin-towered pilgrimage church, is reached by one of the steepest adhesion tramways in the world and gives a fine view of the river and the Alps.

Fuel is straightforward, with stations on every approach. Go in May or September when the days are warm and the riverside meadows are open, and keep an eye on city traffic and tram tracks, which are slippery in the wet.
t.arlberg return option@47.1,10.2:
Anton, where the road begins its climb. It is one of the oldest crossing points in the Eastern Alps, used since the Middle Ages by traders and pilgrims, and the name itself is thought to come from the dwarf pines, the Arlen, that grow on the slopes. A hospice was built on the pass in the fourteenth century to help travellers survive the winter, and the cult of St. Christopher that grew up there is still remembered in the name of the village below.

The ride is easy and enjoyable rather than frightening. The road is wide, the surface is excellent and the bends are steady, with a couple of tighter hairpins on the Vorarlberg side as the road drops to Langen and Bludenz. From St. Anton the road climbs gently through meadows and larch woods, and in early summer the slopes are bright with alpine flowers. The pass stays open all year, though winter brings heavy snow and chains are sometimes required. The Arlberg road tunnel, opened in 1978, bypasses the pass for fourteen kilometres but charges a toll, so most motorcyclists on a sunny day prefer the old road.

St. Anton is the cradle of modern alpine skiing. Hannes Schneider founded the first ski school here in the early twentieth century and developed the Arlberg technique, which spread around the world. The village is still a major winter destination, and it is quiet in summer, which makes it a good place for a long lunch on a terrace. You can find fuel in St. Anton or in the smaller villages of the Stanzer Valley, while Landeck, about twenty-seven kilometres east, is the bigger town if you need a wider choice.

From the pass, the Flexen road leads off towards Zürs and Lech, a spectacular stretch with galleries cut into the rock, though it is closed when avalanches threaten. The Arlberg is also the watershed between the Rhine and the Danube, so rain falling here may end up in the North Sea or the Black Sea. Weather can turn fast, with cold rain at the top while the valley basks, so pack a layer.
t.ofenpass approach@46.6,10.3:
The Ofenpass, which the Romansh call Pass dal Fuorn, climbs through the only national park in Switzerland. The park was founded in 1914 and the road is the single way to see it by bike, so the rules matter: stay on the road, stop only where parking is allowed, and leave the ibex, red deer and marmots to their own devices.

From Zernez in the Engadine the road rises through Scots pine and then mountain pine into a high, open valley, with the peaks of the park rising on either side. Bends are generally moderate and the road is wide, in good shape, and rarely crowded. On the far side it drops through the Val Müstair, towards the Italian border at Tubre, a quiet, pastoral valley with Romansh villages and terraced fields. Ibex and red deer graze at the roadside in the early morning and evening, so slow down when you see animals.

Müstair, at the bottom of the descent, has the Benedictine convent of St John, a UNESCO World Heritage Site that contains one of the best-preserved sets of early medieval frescoes in Europe, dating back to about the ninth century. It is worth the extra kilometres. Further on, the Stelvio pass climbs from the Italian side, a very different and far more famous road, with dozens of hairpins and many visitors.

Fuel is available at Zernez, but not within the park, so make sure the tank is full before you start. The pass is open all year round in normal conditions, though snow can close it for short periods in winter. Summer thunderstorms build in the afternoon, and the temperature changes quickly, so dress in layers. Mobile coverage is thin, and nobody will hear you if you break down, so carry what you need.
t.gardena pass@46.5,11.8:
Gardena Pass joins two Ladin valleys: Val Gardena on the north side, with Selva and Ortisei, and Alta Badia on the south, around Corvara. At roughly 2,100 metres it is one of the four passes that circle the Sella massif, and the road runs between the great rock walls of the Sassolungo and the Sella, with their pale dolomite faces that glow pink at sunset.

The riding is good: smooth tarmac, well-engineered bends and a gradient that never gets nasty. From the north the road climbs out of Selva in a series of broad hairpins, passing hotels, ski lifts and small chapels, and from the south it drops away through meadows towards Corvara. It is a busy road, especially in July and August, when cars, camper vans, coaches, cyclists and other bikes share the same ribbon. The best time is early morning or late afternoon, when the crowds thin and the light turns the rock to colour.

The Dolomites were once the floor of a tropical sea, and the white rock you see is the remains of ancient coral reefs, lifted and carved by ice. The peaks were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009. The people of these valleys speak Ladin, a Romance language descended from Latin and unrelated to Italian or German, and you will see bilingual signs in three languages. Food is a mix of Tyrolean and Italian: speck, dumplings, polenta, and apple strudel, served in mountain huts with long wooden tables and a dizzying view.

Passes in the Dolomites sometimes have restrictions on motor traffic for a morning or two in the summer to give cyclists some peace, so check local notices if you arrive on a quiet weekday. The pass is normally closed in winter by snow, though the main roads are cleared quite early in spring.
t.val gardena overnight base@46.6,11.7:
Val Gardena is the valley where the Dolomites speak Ladin. The language, a Romance tongue descended from the Latin of Roman soldiers, survives here in a handful of valleys, and in villages like Selva, Santa Cristina and Ortisei you will see three sets of names on every sign: German, Italian and Ladin, so Selva is also Wolkenstein and Sëlva. The altitude of 1,560 metres puts you in Selva, at the top end of the valley, where the road to the Sella and Gardena passes begins and the walls of the Dolomites are close enough to touch.

The scenery is enormous. The Sassolungo, the Langkofel, rises straight above the valley to 3,181 metres, a vast comb of pale rock that flushes pink at dawn and dusk, the famous enrosadira. The Sella massif, a great flat-topped block, stands to the east, ringed by passes. The Dolomites were named a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2009, and a few minutes in the valley explain why. Meadows in June are full of flowers, and in autumn the larches turn the lower slopes gold.

For a rider, this is the base for the Sella Ronda, the loop around the Sella massif by four passes: Gardena, Campolongo, Pordoi and Sella, each with its own character. The roads are narrow, twisting and well surfaced, with hairpins that climb and drop beneath huge cliffs, and in summer they fill with motorcyclists, cyclists and coaches, so an early start is worth it. The Gardena Pass, at about 2,121 metres, is the first climb from the valley. Mornings are clear and crisp, and afternoon thunderstorms are likely, so get over the passes before lunch if you can.

Ortisei, the larger village down the valley, has fuel and shops, and is the best place to fill the tank. Ortisei is also the centre of the region's woodcarving tradition, and shops sell carved saints, nativity figures and toys, some of them very fine. For dinner, eat canederli, bread dumplings in broth, with speck, Schüttelbrot, a crisp rye bread flavoured with fennel and caraway, and a glass of South Tyrolean red. The valley is quiet at night, with starry skies, and the hotels are small and family-run. Passes close with snow from late October to spring, so check conditions.
t.fluelapass high section@46.8,10.0:
The scenery is stark: bare rock, screes, snow patches and a handful of small, dark lakes, with the Flüela Wisshorn and the Schwarzhorn rising on either side. Davos, the highest town of its size in the Alps, is ten and a half kilometres away, and Zernez about twelve.

For a rider, the pass is excellent. Coming from Davos, the road climbs through the Flüelatal in a series of well-engineered bends, with views opening out over the valley and then the dramatic, treeless upper section. The surface is generally good, the barriers are solid and the gradient is steady. The descent towards Susch is steeper and more exposed, with tighter hairpins, a few narrow places and an old hospice at the top, a plain stone building that has sheltered travellers for centuries.

The pass is closed in winter, normally from about November to May, because of heavy snow and avalanche risk, and a late spring or early autumn storm can shut it for a day or two. Weather at this height can change fast, with cold wind, low cloud and sudden sleet, even in July. Keep a warm layer and gloves in the top case, because the pass is a good fifteen degrees colder than the valleys.

Davos, in its high valley at over fifteen hundred metres, is known for the World Economic Forum, for the tuberculosis sanatoria that made it famous in the nineteenth century, and for winter sport. Thomas Mann set his novel The Magic Mountain in a Davos sanatorium, and the town still carries some of that air. Fuel and food are plentiful there and in Zernez or Susch on the far side. For the best ride, go early, when the light is raking and the tarmac is empty.
t.dinkelsbuhl@49.1,10.3:
Dinkelsbühl is the one that makes people stop talking mid-sentence when they ride through the gate. A complete medieval wall rings the old town, with towers, a moat of lawns and a maze of lanes of gabled houses painted in butter and rose, and the whole thing came through the Second World War largely untouched. It lies on the Wörnitz in western Bavaria, a town of about twelve thousand people on the Romantic Road, which makes it a natural place to start or end a day on that famous route.

The Romantic Road is a marketing name from the 1950s, devised to lure visitors to the old towns between Würzburg and Füssen, and it is more a string of lovely places than a thrilling ride. Between towns the roads are gentle and wide, with long, easy curves through rolling Franconian farmland, hop fields and orchards. Traffic is steady, and speed limits are meant. The pleasure here is in the pace and the stops, not the corners. Go early on a weekday in May or September, and you will have the lanes nearly to yourself.

The minster of St George, a late Gothic hall church, rises above the market square with a single tall tower, and its interior is wonderfully light, with slender pillars holding up a net vault. Dinkelsbühl's great annual event is the Kinderzeche in July, a children's festival that recalls a legend from the Thirty Years' War, when the town's children are said to have persuaded a Swedish commander to spare the place. The story is probably more charming than true, but the pageant, with costumes, music and a lot of beer, is one of the best of its kind in Germany.

Eating is easy. Local inns serve Franconian classics, such as roast pork, dumplings and sauerkraut, and a good deal of the local beer. A walk along the walls at dusk, when the lamps come on and the swifts circle the towers, costs nothing and repays the effort. Fuel is available at the edge of town, and the larger towns of Ansbach and Crailsheim lie on either side. Park outside the walls, as the centre is partly pedestrianised and the cobbles are unkind to a loaded bike.
t.nordlingen@48.9,10.5:
Nördlingen sits in the middle of a hole in the ground, and the hole was made from space. About fourteen and a half million years ago, a meteorite crashed into this part of southern Germany and left a crater about twenty-five kilometres wide, the Ries, now a gently bowl-shaped plain of fields, villages and low hills. Nördlingen was built inside it, in a perfect circle, and the medieval wall that surrounds it is almost round, the only fully preserved ring wall in Germany that you can walk along the top of. The walk takes about an hour.

The tower of St George's church, called the Daniel, rises ninety metres above the market square, and you can climb its stairs for a view over the red roofs and out across the rim of the crater. The church walls are made of suevite, a rock formed by the impact, which contains tiny diamonds, too small to see and too small to sell. A night watchman still calls out from the tower every half hour on summer evenings, a custom that dates back centuries. In 1970 the Apollo 14 astronauts came here to study impact geology before flying to the Moon.

The Romantic Road passes through, and Nördlingen is one of its best stops, with half-timbered houses, small squares and a cheerful, unpretentious atmosphere. The riding between Dinkelsbühl and Nördlingen is quiet, along minor roads over open farmland and through small villages. Surfaces are generally good, bends are broad and easy, and the main hazards are tractors and the wind, which sweeps freely across the crater plain. The edge of the crater is a low rim of hills, and you can see it from several vantage points.

Wallerstein, four kilometres away, has a striking rock outcrop with a former castle site and a fine Baroque church. Nördlingen has fuel, bakeries and a good choice of restaurants, and menus here lean on Swabian and Bavarian staples, from Spätzle to roast pork. The town is small enough to walk across in twenty minutes, so leave the bike at a car park outside the wall and wander in. Evening is best, when the tour groups have left and the stone glows in the low light.
t.walchensee@47.6,11.3:
Walchensee is one of the deepest and clearest alpine lakes in Germany, lying at about eight hundred metres in the Bavarian Pre-Alps, with a surface the colour of turquoise glass on a good day and dark green on a stormy one. The lake is surrounded by forested mountains, with the Herzogstand and the Heimgarten rising to the north, and it has a calm, almost Scandinavian look in the early morning.

The approach is the thing. From Kochel am See, the B11 climbs the Kesselberg in a series of hairpins and tight curves, rising about two hundred metres in a few kilometres, with the old road snaking up through beech forest. The gradient is steady, the surface is generally good, and the road is a classic for riders, which is also its problem: it is crowded at weekends, the noise is a source of friction with locals, and restrictions on motorcycles have been introduced and changed in recent years. Check the current rules before you go and expect speed limits and police checks on busy days.

The lake is also home to a major hydroelectric scheme. In the early twentieth century, the engineer Oskar von Miller realised that the water of Walchensee could be dropped about two hundred metres down to the Kochelsee, and the power station that he built opened in 1924. It supplied electricity to Munich and the railways for decades, and it still operates, a remarkable piece of engineering hidden in the hillside. The painter Franz Marc lived in nearby Kochel, and his bright, colourful animals are celebrated in a museum in Kochel itself.

The water is clean and cold, and in summer it is popular for windsurfing and sailing, since the afternoon wind is reliable. Swimmers should expect a chill, even in August. The village of Walchensee has fuel, cafes and a few small guesthouses, and Kochel and Mittenwald offer more choice. Go early in the morning, when the lake is still and the road is empty, and you will understand why people queue for this place.
t.tegernsee@47.7,11.8:
Tegernsee is a lake town in the Bavarian foothills, at the eastern edge of the Tegernsee valley, with the lake in front and steep, forested mountains behind. The Benedictine monastery that gave the place its name was founded in the eighth century, and its church and cloister still dominate the shore, though the buildings are now partly a secondary school and partly a brewery tavern, the Bräustüberl, where locals and visitors share long tables and big pretzels in the courtyard. It is a lively place on a sunny afternoon, with a crowd of beer drinkers, cyclists and bikers.

The town has about thirty-eight hundred inhabitants, and the neighbouring village of Rottach-Egern, a little over two kilometres away, is bigger and smarter. Fuel, cafes and shops are easy to find, though parking in summer is a struggle. The lake itself is clean and relatively warm for an alpine lake, and the promenade is a pleasant place to walk. The Wallberg, a mountain above Rottach, has a cable car, and a long toboggan run in summer.

The ride along the Bavarian Alpine Road follows the lake and then climbs into the mountains, with long, flowing bends, glimpses of blue water, and meadows full of cows. The road surface is good, and the traffic is thick on summer weekends, with buses and cars crawling along the shore. Early morning, before the day trippers arrive, is the time to ride, when the mist lies on the lake and the peaks stand out clear. Further south, the road leads to Kreuth and the Achenpass on the Austrian border, a winding, forested route that is a pleasure on a quiet day.

The valley was long a retreat of the Bavarian royal family, whose summer residence was in Tegernsee, and in the twentieth century it became a favourite of writers and artists. Ludwig Thoma, the satirist, lived and died in Rottach, and his house is a memorial. The lake is surrounded by well-to-do villas, and prices are high, but the beer at the Bräustüberl is reasonable and the view is free. Take time for a walk along the shore, and leave the bike for an hour.
t.milan northern italy@46.1,10.0:
The Orobie Alps rise steeply on the southern side of the Valtellina, and this part of the valley, around Chiuro and the side valleys that drop into it, is one of the least visited corners of Lombardy.

Valtellina's terraced vineyards are a sight in themselves. Over centuries, farmers built stone walls up the steep slope to create narrow shelves for vines, and the terraces now extend for dozens of kilometres, a landscape so remarkable that it is protected as a heritage site in its own right. The grape is Nebbiolo, known locally as Chiavennasca, and the wines, with names such as Sassella and Grumello, are elegant and long-lived. Teglio, nearby, is the home of pizzoccheri, buckwheat pasta cooked with cabbage, potato, butter and cheese, which is perfect after a cold ride.

The roads into the side valleys are often steep, narrow and twisty, with hairpins that climb through woods and meadows to small mountain villages. In autumn the larches turn gold and the whole slope glows, and in spring the meadows are covered with wildflowers. Surfaces can be broken by frost and rock fall, so watch for gravel on the corners, and expect cyclists, because the valley is a favourite training ground. The big names, such as the Stelvio and Mortirolo, are not far away, which makes this a fine base.

Sondrio, fourteen kilometres away, has the fuel, shops and restaurants that a rider needs. The town is the capital of the province, with a handsome old centre and a castle, and is also the place to taste bresaola, the air-dried beef that is a speciality of the valley, and bitto, a strong cheese made in the high pastures. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and good light, while in summer the valley can be very hot and the traffic heavier.
t.stelvio pass@46.5,10.5:
Few roads in Europe have a reputation as large as the Stelvio, and for once it is deserved. At 2,757 metres, it is one of the highest paved passes in the Alps, and the road up from the Trafoi side is a staircase of forty-eight numbered hairpins stacked against the mountainside, while the Bormio side has about forty of its own, longer and more open. Engineers of the Austrian empire built it in the 1820s to link Lombardy with the Tyrol, under the direction of Carlo Donegani, and it was meant for horse-drawn carts, which explains why the bends are so tight.

The riding is a pleasure and a test. The surface is generally good, but the road is narrow, with buses and campers taking up the full width on the hairpins, so you ride carefully and look well ahead. The best moments come on the stretches between hairpins, where the road opens out, and the view down the valley, with the pale ribbon of tarmac folded back and forth, is an image you will remember. The summit is a busy place in summer, with souvenir stalls, sausage vans and a crowd of motorbikes. To the south-west stands the Ortler, at 3,905 metres the highest mountain in the eastern Alps, and glaciers glitter above the road.

The pass was a front line in the First World War. Italian and Austro-Hungarian troops fought at extraordinary heights, in trenches and tunnels cut in the ice, and relics still turn up as the glaciers shrink. The Giro d'Italia has crossed the Stelvio many times, and the highest point of the race is named after Fausto Coppi. At the top, a short road leads off to the Umbrail Pass and Switzerland, a quieter, partly unpaved alternative.

Plan carefully. The pass is usually open from around late May or June until October or early November, depending on snow, and it can close at short notice. Weather changes quickly, with cold, rain and even snow possible in July, so carry warm layers. Start early, before the traffic builds, and you may have the hairpins nearly to yourself, with the light low and golden on the rocks.
t.arabba@46.5,11.9:
Arabba is a small village in the heart of the Dolomites, and a crossroads of passes. It sits at about 1,600 metres on the upper Cordevole river, at the foot of the Pordoi, the Campolongo and the Fedaia, and its position makes it the natural halfway point of the Sella Ronda, the circuit around the huge Sella massif. The mountains here are the pale, jagged towers that make the Dolomites famous, and the whole range was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009.

The village belongs to Livinallongo, a Ladin-speaking valley whose people have their own language, a relic of the Roman era, and the signs are often in Italian, German and Ladin. In the First World War, the front line ran through the valley, and the summit of nearby Col di Lana was blown up in a mine explosion in April 1916 after a long underground battle. Today the mountain is called the Col di Sangue, the blood hill, and there are memorials and trails for walkers.

The road in each direction is a delight. The climb north from Arabba to the Campolongo is short and open, a handful of hairpins with views of the Sella walls, while the road south to the Pordoi climbs in a long series of switchbacks. To the south-east the white mass of the Marmolada, the highest mountain in the Dolomites, rises above the valley, and its glacier is visible on a clear day. In winter this is a ski resort, with lifts rising directly from the village, and in summer the pastures are full of cattle and wildflowers.

Practical matters need some thought. Arabba is small, and while it has a handful of hotels, bars and shops, you should not count on fuel here, so fill up in Cortina or Corvara, or in Canazei on the other side of the Pordoi. In summer, the passes are crowded with motorbikes and cars, especially at weekends, and a morning start is a great help. The roads are generally open from late May to October, depending on snow, and the weather can change fast. A hot chocolate or a bowl of barley soup at a mountain hut is a classic Dolomite treat.
t.passo pordoi@46.5,11.8:
The Pordoi Pass is the highest on the Sella Ronda, at 2,239 metres, and the road from Arabba climbs it in thirty-three hairpins that are among the most photographed in the Alps. The road is wide, the surface is generally excellent and the bends are well graded, so it is one of the most enjoyable climbs in the Dolomites, a place where you can find a rhythm and let the bike dance. At the top you come out beneath the vertical cliffs of the Sella, with the Marmolada glacier shining to the south-east.

The summit is a small, busy world, with a few hotels, a souvenir shop or two, a row of motorbikes and a cable car that rises to nearly three thousand metres on the Sass Pordoi, the summit plateau of the Sella. On clear days the views from the top are staggering, stretching over hundreds of peaks. Just below the pass, a large German war cemetery, built in the 1950s, holds the remains of thousands of soldiers from the two world wars, and the low stone building, set among the rocks, is a quiet, moving place that is worth a visit.

The pass was crossed by traders and pilgrims for centuries, and the modern road dates from the late nineteenth century, when the Dolomites became a destination for early tourists. It was a stage in the Giro d'Italia many times, and cyclists, especially in summer, fill the road, so you should expect to share it and take care when overtaking. In summer weekends the traffic can be heavy, with many motorbikes, and a start at dawn will give you a very different experience.

Fuel is the thing to note. There is none on the pass itself, and the nearest stations are in Canazei, about three and a half kilometres away on the south side, and in Corvara and Cortina, so make sure you have enough. Mountain huts serve coffee, strudel and polenta with cheese, and a stop for something warm is worth it. The pass is generally open from late May to October, and the weather can bring rain, cold wind or snow, even in summer. The light at dawn and dusk, when the Sella glows orange and pink, is something you remember.
t.trento@46.1,11.1:
Trento lies in the Adige valley with the Dolomites standing over it, a mid-sized Alpine city of about eighty thousand where Italian and Austrian history meet. Until 1918 it belonged to the Habsburgs, and before that it was a prince-bishopric, and you can still feel the north-south seam in its architecture, its apple orchards and its habit of doing things properly. Rock walls rise on both sides, and in winter the valley floor can sit in shade by mid-afternoon.

Everyone with a history book knows the name from the Council of Trent, the long church council held here between 1545 and 1563 that shaped the Catholic response to the Reformation. The sessions took place in the cathedral and in Santa Maria Maggiore, and the city has quietly traded on it ever since. In the centre, the Fountain of Neptune stands in Piazza Duomo, the Castello del Buonconsiglio sits beside the old walls with its frescoed Torre Aquila, and the modern MUSE science museum, designed by Renzo Piano, stands on the site of an old factory by the river.

From a rider's point of view, Trento is a gateway rather than a destination. The road up Monte Bondone from the city climbs through hairpins toward a ski area and botanical garden, a quick way to feel the Alps after a morning in town. To the east lies the Valsugana, to the west the Val di Non with its apple orchards, and north the road toward Bolzano and the Brenner. Traffic in the valley is heavy at rush hour, and trucks use the Adige corridor in numbers, so leave early or late.

Fuel and food are no problem in a city this size. Look for strangolapreti, bread dumplings with spinach, canederli in broth, and local wines such as Teroldego and Trentodoc, the sparkling wine made in the traditional method. Parking in the old centre is restricted, but the edges are workable for bikes. Winter brings ice on shaded bends in the surrounding hills, so late spring through early autumn is the comfortable window.
t.hagi proto industrial heritage hagi cast:
Hagi is a castle town on the Sea of Japan coast, in the far west of Honshu, and a place where a small, quiet town changed the country. It was the capital of the Choshu domain, and in the nineteenth century young samurai from here played a leading part in bringing down the Tokugawa shogunate and starting the Meiji era. Several of the figures who later led modern Japan, including Ito Hirobumi, the first prime minister, came out of this town's circle.

What survives gives a strong sense of that time. The old castle town of Hagi has streets of white plastered walls and tiled gates, with orange trees leaning over the lanes, because the samurai families were encouraged to plant citrus. The Shokason Juku, a small wooden schoolroom, is where Yoshida Shoin taught the future reformers before he was executed in 1859. The castle itself was dismantled in the 1870s, and only the stone walls and the moat remain, with the bay and the green hill of Shizuki behind. Also on the list of heritage sites here are the reverberatory furnace and shipyard remains, which show the early push toward industry.

Hagi is also known for Hagi ware, a soft, pale pottery whose glaze develops fine cracks with use, treasured by tea masters. The seafood is excellent, with fresh squid and fish from the nearby Japan Sea coast, and the town has several small museums and shops selling pottery. The delta of the Abu and Hashimoto rivers gives it an unusual shape, a flat triangle between water and hills.

For riding, the coastal road, Route 191, runs along the sea cliffs with islands offshore and wide views, with little traffic outside holidays. Winter weather on this coast is grey and windy, with occasional snow, and summer typhoons can bring heavy surf. Spring and autumn are the best times. Fuel is simple in the town, and there are plenty of places to eat. Allow a slow morning among the old walls.
t.fukuoka@33.6,130.4:
Fukuoka is the big city of Kyushu, home to about one and a half million people, and it feels closer to Seoul and Shanghai than to Tokyo in the way it turns its face to the sea. The harbour of Hakata has been a gateway to the continent for two thousand years, and a gold seal found nearby, dated to the first century AD, is said to record a gift from the Chinese emperor. In 1274 and 1281 the Mongols landed here with huge fleets, and the stone wall built to resist them survives in places.

The city's food scene is its most obvious pleasure. Hakata ramen, with its cloudy pork-bone broth and thin straight noodles, is the local religion, and in the evenings the yatai stalls set up along the river on Nakasu island, offering ramen, skewers and oden under red lanterns. Mentaiko, spicy pollock roe, is another speciality, and the fish, fresh from the Genkai Sea, is outstanding. The summer Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival in July sees teams of men race giant floats through the streets at dawn.

Nearby shrines carry weight too. Munakata Taisha, whose outlying shrine on Okinoshima island across the water has been a sacred site for centuries and whose Okitsu-miya Yohaisho sits on the coast for worship from afar, guards sea voyages. Women have never been allowed on the island and men must purify themselves in the sea. Dazaifu, to the south, honours the scholar Sugawara no Michizane and draws students before exams.

Riding in Fukuoka itself is urban, with expressways and heavy traffic. The coast toward Itoshima, west of the city, is the reward: sea views, small beaches and cafes, and roads that wind through low hills. Fuel is plentiful. Summer is hot and humid, and typhoons arrive in late summer and early autumn. Spring and late autumn are the best times for riding, with clear skies.
t.shuseikan@31.6,130.6:
Kagoshima lies under a volcano, and that explains almost everything about it. Sakurajima, the smoking mountain across the bay, erupts often enough that locals carry umbrellas against falling ash, and its cone dominates every view. The city of more than half a million people sits on the bay of Kinko, with the volcano just a short ferry ride away, and the warm climate gives it palm trees and an air of the south.

Shuseikan is the reason the city matters in industrial history. In the 1850s, Shimazu Nariakira, the lord of Satsuma, started an ambitious programme to build Western-style industry, with a reverberatory furnace, a glass workshop, a cannon foundry and a spinning mill, all gathered at this site on the shore. The factory complex was one of the first in Japan, begun even before the Meiji Restoration, and the remains are part of the Meiji Industrial Revolution World Heritage group. The old spinning mill building, one of the earliest Western-style factories in the country, still stands, and the Shimazu family's garden, Iso Garden, adjoins it, with a view across the bay to Sakurajima.

The riding in the area is a pleasure. The coastal road along the bay gives long views of the volcano, and the Sakurajima road circles the mountain with ash-covered fields and hot springs. Roads are narrow in places and ash on the surface can be slippery when wet, so keep your speed measured. Typhoons arrive from the south in late summer, and the temperature is mild in winter.

Food is part of the pleasure. Kagoshima is famous for kurobuta, black pork, and for satsuma-age, deep-fried fish cakes, and its sweet potato shochu is the local drink. Fuel is easy in the city, and ferries to Sakurajima run all day and night. Walk the grounds of the garden and take your time with the old buildings. The volcano, grumbling on the horizon, adds a sense that nothing here is quite permanent.
t.shuseikan sekiyoshi sluice gate of yoshi:
Water was the engine of Shuseikan, and the Sekiyoshi sluice gate is part of the story of how it was supplied. The factory complex that Shimazu Nariakira founded in the 1850s on the shore of Kagoshima Bay needed power for its machinery, and the answer was a canal that carried water from a river in the hills north of the city. The sluice gate controlling the flow still survives, a modest stone structure beside a stream, and it forms part of the World Heritage listing of Meiji industrial sites.

It is not a spectacular place, and that is part of its charm. The surroundings are quiet suburban hills, with small fields, tea bushes and woods of cedar and camphor. You can stand by the channel and listen to the water, thinking of the workers who built the system with hand tools, long before modern machinery. The Satsuma domain was determined to catch up with Western technology, partly in response to the shock of the British bombardment of Kagoshima in 1863, and projects like this show the pace of that ambition.

The roads to the site are narrow, often only one lane wide, with sharp corners and little signage, so a motorcyclist should go slowly and expect to meet local cars. The soil here is volcanic, and ash from Sakurajima settles on the surface after eruptions, which makes roads slick when damp. Tall bamboo groves and old stone walls line the lanes, and the light under the trees is green and soft.

Kagoshima is the nearest city, about seven kilometres away, with plenty of fuel and food. This is a place to visit in the morning, when it is calm and cool, or late in the afternoon. Wear sensible shoes if you plan to walk along the channel. In the rainy season, from late May to June, the paths can be slippery. A short stop here adds depth to a day of exploring the bay's industrial history.
t.hiroshima@34.4,132.5:
Hiroshima is a city that has made peace its work. On 6 August 1945 the first atomic bomb used in war was dropped here, and most of the city was destroyed. The skeletal dome of the former Industrial Promotion Hall, now the Genbaku Dome, stands by the river as it did then, preserved in ruin, and the Peace Memorial Park beside it holds a museum, a cenotaph and the Flame of Peace. It is a serious place and deserves unhurried time, and visitors are quiet there.

The city itself is now lively, with more than a million people, broad avenues, trams that rattle through the streets and a cheerful food culture. Okonomiyaki here is layered rather than mixed, with noodles and cabbage and egg on a hot plate, and the oysters from the bay are famous. The city lies on a delta, with seven rivers dividing it into islands, and bridges and riverside walks make it easy to explore. The castle was rebuilt after the war, and Shukkeien, a small garden, gives a calm hour.

Beyond the city, the Seto Inland Sea offers some of the best riding in western Japan. The island roads across the Shimanami Kaido, with bridges linking small islands toward Shikoku, are famous with cyclists, and the quiet coastal roads give views of fishing boats and orange groves. Miyajima, the sacred island with its floating torii gate, is a short ferry trip from the western edge of the city, and deer wander the streets there.

Fuel is plentiful, though the centre is dense with traffic. Expect trams, which sometimes share lanes, and watch the rails when wet. Spring and autumn are comfortable, while summer is hot and humid, with a rainy season in June. The mountains inland, toward the Chugoku range, offer twisty roads and few cars, a good contrast to a day among memories.
t.shuseikan terayama charcoal kiln@31.7,13:
Charcoal does not sound like a monument, but at Terayama it was part of a project to modernise a whole domain. The Shimazu lords of Satsuma needed fuel for the furnaces at Shuseikan, and charcoal was made in kilns on the wooded hills north of Kagoshima, then carried down to the factory by cart. The remains of a kiln here, part of the Meiji industrial heritage listing, show how a traditional craft was bent to the service of the new age.

The setting is the point. You are in the hills about ten kilometres from the city, in woods of cedar, oak and camphor, where the air smells of damp earth and leaf mould. The kiln is a stone-lined structure half dug into the slope, and you can see how the charcoal was baked slowly in the absence of air. Tucked in the trees, it feels like a place rarely visited, though a signboard explains its role. The rest of the heritage is down on the coast, so this is the quiet, rural counterpoint.

The road is narrow and winding, partly shaded, with mossy stretches that can be slippery after rain. The ash from Sakurajima settles across this whole area, and the roadsides are dusted grey after a big eruption. There is little traffic, and the farms and tea plantations are charming. Weather changes quickly in the hills, with morning mist and sudden showers in the rainy season. In autumn the air is clear and the leaves turn.

Services are in Kagoshima, with fuel stations along the main roads, not up in the hills, so fill up before leaving the city. Take water. A picnic lunch bought from a bakery or convenience store works well, since there is nowhere to eat nearby. The pleasure of a visit lies in the stillness and in the feeling of finding a small piece of history away from the crowd.
t.dinosaur colorado@40.2,-109.0:
The little town of Dinosaur, Colorado, has streets named for its famous residents: Brontosaurus Boulevard, Stegosaurus Freeway, Triceratops Terrace. It lies in the arid country of the far north-west corner of the state, just east of the Utah line, in the Uinta Basin, a land of red rock, juniper and dust. The surrounding hills are banded in pink, grey and rust, and the sky is huge. Rangely, about twenty-four kilometres east, is the nearest sizeable settlement and the practical place for fuel and supplies.

The town earned its name from the nearby Dinosaur National Monument, a vast tract of canyon country along the Green and Yampa rivers, where in 1909 the paleontologist Earl Douglass found a rich bed of dinosaur bones in the Utah side. The quarry, near Jensen, still shows a wall of fossils, hundreds of bones of long-necked sauropods embedded in a tilted sandstone face. The monument also protects spectacular river canyons, whose rapids attract rafting parties, and the Harpers Corner Scenic Drive, a long, high road that ends with a view down into the canyons of the Green and Yampa.

For riders, the Dinosaur Diamond is a long loop of highways across Colorado and Utah, linking fossil sites and old mining towns. The roads are mostly wide and open, with huge views, little traffic and long distances between services. Highway 64 runs between Dinosaur and Rangely, while Highway 40 heads west into Utah. Heat in summer is fierce, with temperatures well over thirty-five degrees, and winter brings snow and wind. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Carry water and extra fuel range; towns are far apart, and cell coverage is patchy. The sunsets across the desert are some of the best in the West, with the rock glowing in red and orange. Keep an eye out for deer, pronghorn and the occasional wandering cow. The visitor centre in the monument offers maps and a good introduction to the geology, and the night skies, far from city lights, are spectacularly full of stars.
t.solden@47.0,11.0:
Sölden lies at about thirteen hundred metres in the Ötztal, a long Tyrolean valley that runs south from the Inn into the high, glaciated mountains on the Italian border. In winter it is one of Austria's big ski resorts, and in summer it is a base for hikers, cyclists and riders heading for the Timmelsjoch. The village is a bit loud and a bit brash, with large hotels and plenty of apres-ski, but the setting is genuinely impressive, with peaks above three thousand metres on all sides and a river running clear and fast below.

The valley has a famous visitor in the museum record. In 1991 hikers found a mummified man in the ice of the nearby Similaun, a Copper Age hunter who had lain there about five thousand years. Known as Ötzi, he is now displayed in Bolzano, but the Ötztal still takes pride in the find, and the story gives an extra dimension to the quiet peaks above the village. Sölden also appeared in a James Bond film, which locals will mention if you give them a chance.

Riding out from here is the point. Ride south and the road climbs through Zwieselstein and Obergurgl, which is among the highest parish villages in Austria, then goes over the Timmelsjoch at about 2,474 metres into Italy. It is a toll road and closes in winter, normally opening in early summer and staying open until the first heavy snow in autumn. The bends are well engineered and wide, the surface is good, and the road switches from forest to bare rock in a matter of minutes. Tourists and cyclists share it, so be patient on the lower sections.

Sölden has several filling stations and plenty of food, from simple bakeries to heavy Tyrolean fare of Kasspatzln and dumplings. The valley also offers the Aqua Dome thermal spa at Längenfeld, which will do wonders for tired shoulders after a long day in the saddle.

Mornings are calmest, and crowds thin out by evening. Early in the season, you may find snow banks beside the road at the top, while in September the larches turn gold and the light is superb.
t.timmelsjoch@46.9,11.1:
Timmelsjoch, at 2,474 metres, is a border pass between Austria and Italy, linking the Ötztal valley with the Passeier valley, and it is one of the great high Alpine roads. The Italians call it Passo del Rombo. It opened in 1968 as a toll road, built partly to connect the two sides of the old Tyrol, which had been divided after the First World War, and it remains a toll road today, with a charge for motorbikes collected on the Austrian side.

The ride from the Austrian side begins at Sölden, a big ski resort, and climbs through Hochgurgl and Obergurgl, among the highest villages in the Alps, then above the tree line into bare rock and scree. Hairpins and long, open bends lead to the pass, where a modern museum and a viewing platform stand. The air is thin and cold, and snow can lie on the verges well into June. The pass is usually open from late spring or early summer until October, but it closes in winter and can shut at short notice in bad weather.

The Italian side drops into South Tyrol through a series of tight hairpins and narrow tunnels cut into the rock, with sheer drops and views down into the Passeier valley. The surface is generally good, but the narrow bends and sudden fog call for care. The valley below, with its apple orchards and stone farmhouses, is the homeland of Andreas Hofer, the innkeeper who led the Tyrolean uprising against Napoleon's forces in 1809 and was executed in Mantua in 1810, becoming a folk hero.

The pass is popular with riders, and on a fine summer weekend it can be crowded, with long queues of bikes and cars. Early weekdays are better. Dress for cold, with a windproof layer and warm gloves, because even in August the summit can be near freezing, and a descent into wet cloud is chilly.

Fuel is available in Sölden on the Austrian side and in St. Leonhard in Passeier or at the bigger town of Vipiteno, about twenty-six kilometres away, on the Italian side. There is nothing at the pass itself, so fill the tank before the climb. Bring your passport or ID card, since the border is open but may be checked. The restaurants near the summit serve South Tyrolean dishes such as dumplings, speck and strudel.
t.german alpine@48.3,11.8:
Flat as a table and wide as the sky, the land around Moosinning and Oberding is the gravel plain northeast of Munich, a former marsh called the Erdinger Moos that was drained over a century ago and is now mostly fields, villages and the long concrete ribbon of Munich Airport. For a rider coming back from the Alps on the German Alpine Road, the mountains are simply gone, and the horizon is a line of trees, a church spire and the occasional aircraft banking in.

The German Alpine Road itself is a long tourist route that runs along the northern edge of the Alps from Lindau on Lake Constance to Königssee near Berchtesgaden, about four hundred and fifty kilometres in all. The eastern portion, part of which this ride follows, passes lakes and meadows and the foothills of the Chiemgau, and has a few real highlights, but this last leg is strictly commuting country. Roads are straight, speed limits are strict, and much of the traffic is airport-related, so expect delivery vans and taxis.

If you want some relief, Erding is close and has a handsome old town with a long main street and a famous wheat beer, Erdinger Weissbier, which is brewed here. It also has one of the largest thermal spas in Europe, popular with Bavarians after a cold weekend. Freising, to the west, has an old cathedral hill and is the seat of an ancient bishopric; Bavarians say Munich owes some of its faith and brewing to this town.

Small towns here are well supplied. Moosinning and Oberding have little of interest beyond the practical, but Erding and Freising have filling stations, supermarkets, bakeries and cafes, and the airport region has twenty-four hour fuel. The Isar and the Strogen canals add a few green corridors for a short walk.

Because the land is so level, the wind can be sharp in spring and winter, and fog sometimes settles over the Moos in autumn mornings, cutting visibility. In summer, the evening light across the fields is warm and soft, and the Alps will sometimes reappear, rows of pale teeth to the south, as a reminder of where you have been.
t.grossglockner@48.0,11.3:
Starnberg sits at the northern end of the Starnberger See, the big, elongated lake south of Munich, and the dot lands in the lakeside commuter belt between the town and Pöcking. It is wealthy country. The shoreline is lined with villas and old summer houses, the roads are quiet, and the Alps appear on clear days as a long white wall above the water, with the Zugspitze and the Karwendel easy to pick out.

For a rider, the lake is the first and last taste of the mountains. The road along the western shore leads through Possenhofen, where the Empress Elisabeth of Austria, known as Sisi, spent much of her childhood in the Wittelsbach family's summer home. On the eastern side, near Berg, a cross stands in the water where King Ludwig II was found drowned in 1886 after being declared unfit to rule, an event that remains one of Bavaria's great unsolved stories and draws many visitors. Both are easy to reach along quiet lakeside lanes.

The riding here is leisurely. Traffic can be heavy at weekends, with cyclists, joggers and cars looking for parking, and speed limits are strictly kept. In summer the lake draws crowds; on a weekday morning or late in the evening, it is calmer. The roads away from the shore climb gently through meadows and woods, and the views over the water are good from several high points.

Fuel is easy in Starnberg, which is a proper town of over twenty thousand people, with supermarkets, bakeries and cafes. There is a steamer service on the lake, and the lakeside promenade has beer gardens where you can sit with a view of the water. A small portion of fish, perhaps a Renke from the lake, is the local specialty.

On the larger ride, the contrast could hardly be bigger. The Grossglockner is at 3,798 metres the highest peak in Austria, and its high road climbs to over 2,500 metres with a toll. Here, the highest point is a bench by the lake.
t.tegernsee and@48.2,12.0:
East of Munich the Alps vanish from view, and the landscape becomes one of gravel terraces, fields of wheat and rapeseed, and little towns clustered around onion-domed churches. The dot sits in the Erding district, near Buch am Buchrain and Pastetten, where the main business is farming and where the roads are straight and the villages have a tidy, prosperous look. It is the tail end of a long day that took in the Chiemgau and the Tegernsee valley.

The upper part of the ride has a good deal of history. Tegernsee's monastery was founded in the eighth century, and later became the summer residence of the Bavarian royal family, the Wittelsbachs, whose former abbey now houses a brewery and restaurant by the lake. The Chiemsee, often called the Bavarian Sea, holds the island of Herrenchiemsee, where King Ludwig II built a palace modelled on Versailles but never finished it. At Sudelfeld, a high pass road between Bayrischzell and Oberaudorf, the road climbs to about eleven hundred metres and offers wide views over the Inn valley.

Back in the lowlands, the character changes. The roads are open and fast, and the speed limits are low in the villages, so ride with some restraint. In spring the yellow of the rapeseed makes a striking contrast with the distant mountains, and in autumn the fields are brown and the air has a sharp smell of woodsmoke and harvest. Fog can settle in the shallow valleys, and early mornings can be wet and cold even in summer.

Buch am Buchrain and Pastetten are small, so for fuel and shops head for Erding, a few kilometres to the north, or Markt Schwaben, which has a railway station, supermarkets and plenty of cafes. Bavarian bakeries open early and are an excellent source of breakfast, with fresh pretzels and Leberkäse rolls.

The sun sets late over the plain in summer, which means you can usually enjoy the last stretch of the ride in a warm, golden light, with the faint outline of the Alps still visible to the south.
t.bormio overnight base@46.5,10.4:
It is a small town with an old centre of stone houses, narrow streets and a clock tower, and it has been a spa town since Roman times, drawing on hot springs that still feed the baths.

Everything starts here. The Stelvio Pass, at 2,758 metres, climbs from Bormio in a series of hairpins to one of the highest paved roads in Europe, and the Gavia Pass leaves from Santa Caterina Valfurva, about fifteen kilometres away, and reaches 2,621 metres on a narrow road with few barriers on the west side. Livigno, over the Foscagno and Eira passes, is another day's ride. The roads are usually open from late May or June to October or November, depending on snow, and early starts help to avoid the crowds and the afternoon storms. Surfaces are generally good, though the Gavia can be rough and narrow, so meeting a coach is an adventure.

Bormio has a long mountaineering and skiing tradition. It has hosted World Cup races for years, and the Olympic downhill races of 2026 were held on its slopes. The town is also known for its food, especially pizzoccheri, buckwheat noodles with cabbage, potatoes and cheese, and bresaola, air-dried beef from the valley. The local cheese, Bitto, is made in the high pastures.

Fuel is available in Bormio, with stations on the main road, and it is wise to fill up before heading into the mountains, as the passes have none. Tirano, thirty-two kilometres to the south-west, is the nearest large town, and the Bernina railway runs from there across the border to Switzerland.

Slip into the thermal baths in the evening if your legs allow it, or at least walk the old streets. The valley is quiet after the day-trippers leave.
t.santa maria@46.6,10.4:
Santa Maria is the main village of the Val Mustair, a quiet Swiss valley that runs east from the Ofen Pass toward the Italian border, and the place where the road to the Umbrail Pass begins. It lies at roughly 1,400 metres, among meadows and pine forest, with a few traditional Romansh houses with deep window reveals and painted sgraffito decoration on their walls. The people here speak Romansh, a Latin-derived language that survives in only a few valleys of Switzerland.

The label suggests fuel, and that is the right way to think about this stop. It is the last settlement before the Umbrail Pass, a narrow, spectacular road that climbs steeply toward the Stelvio, and a sensible place to check the fuel level before the climb, since prices on the Swiss side are in francs and typically higher than in Italy. Fuel may also be available in Mustair, a few kilometres further east, and in the Italian villages down the valley, such as Tubre.

Just down the road in Mustair, the Benedictine convent of St John is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with Carolingian frescoes that date back to around the year 800, among the best surviving examples of early medieval wall painting in Europe. It is well worth an hour, if you can spare it.

The Umbrail road itself rises in a series of hairpins to about 2,500 metres, where it meets the Stelvio road near the Italian border. The road is paved but narrow, and it is closed during winter, usually opening in late spring after the snow has been cleared. The weather up there is often cold, windy and changeable, even in summer, so bring warm layers and gloves.

The valley is rich in wildlife, with chamois and ibex on the high slopes, and eagles circling overhead. The air is clean and cool, and the nights are cold. A coffee in the village before the climb is a good way of gathering yourself for what lies ahead.
t.prato allo stelvio@46.6,10.6:
Prato allo Stelvio, or Prad am Stilfserjoch in German, is a village of around two and a half thousand people in the Val Venosta, in South Tyrol, at 915 metres above sea level. It is the doorstep of the Stelvio Pass from the eastern side, and the place where most riders who approach from the Vinschgau valley fill up, have a coffee and gather their courage. Almost everyone speaks German first and Italian second, and the village looks more Austrian than Italian, with painted house fronts and flower boxes.

The valley itself is a rain-shadow, one of the driest in the Alps, and the sunny slopes are covered with apple orchards that bloom white in April and carry red fruit in autumn. The apples of the Val Venosta are sold all over Europe. Along the road toward Spondinig you pass the pale marble quarries at Laas, where white marble has been cut for centuries and used in buildings around the world.

From the village, the Stelvio road begins immediately, climbing through forest and past the hamlet of Gomagoi, and then rising in a famous sequence of forty-eight numbered hairpins on this side to the summit at 2,757 metres, one of the highest paved passes in the Alps. The tarmac is generally good, but the road is narrow and busy, with coaches, cyclists and fellow riders, so patience is needed. The pass is open usually from late May or early June until October, depending on snow, and it is worth checking before setting out. It can be cold and windy at the top even in summer.

There is fuel in the village, and it makes sense to fill up here, since the road ahead is steep and prices on the pass are higher. Several bakeries and cafes serve South Tyrolean breakfasts, with speck, rye bread, strudel and strong coffee, and the portions are generous.

Start early, before the traffic builds up, and you will have the first hairpins to yourself with the sun just reaching the upper valley.
t.cortina d ampezzo@46.5,12.1:
The peaks of the Tofane, Cristallo, Pomagagnon and Sorapiss surround it, and the whole area is part of the UNESCO Dolomites World Heritage Site. The town has about five thousand residents, and many more in the holidays, with elegant shops, bars and a long history as a mountain resort.

It sits on the Great Dolomites Road, which runs from Bolzano to Cortina over the Costalunga and Pordoi passes and the Falzarego Pass, which at 2,105 metres leaves Cortina to the west. Further afield, the Passo Giau at 2,236 metres, the Tre Croci and the road to Misurina and the Tre Cime di Lavaredo are all close. These are some of the most beautiful mountain roads in Europe, with hairpins, tunnels and walls of rock, and the surface is generally good. They are also popular, so weekdays and early mornings are best, and in July and August the passes can be crowded. The roads are normally open from late spring to October.

Cortina hosted the Winter Olympics in 1956 and is a co-host of the 2026 Games, and its Olympic past is visible in the ski jump, the ice stadium and the old bobsleigh run. Films have often used it, including a James Bond adventure, For Your Eyes Only, and an early Pink Panther film. The culture is Ladin as much as Italian, and the Regole d'Ampezzo, an ancient communal body, still manages much of the pastureland and forest.

Fuel is available in Cortina, with stations on the main road, and it is wise to fill up before the passes. The town has plenty of food: casunziei, a beetroot-filled pasta, and Tyrolean-style dishes like canederli dumplings and venison are common, and cafes serve excellent pastry and hot chocolate.

Sit on a bench in the main street at the end of the day. The rock walls turn pink and gold in the evening, a spectacle the Dolomites call the enrosadira.
t.merano@46.7,11.2:
Merano has a climate that surprises people. Sheltered by high mountains on three sides, it has mild winters and warm summers, and palm trees, cypresses and even a few vines grow in the town, which sits at about three hundred metres where the Passer river joins the Adige.

The Timmelsjoch and Jaufen loop starts and ends here, and it is a superb day. The Passeier valley road climbs from Merano to St. Leonhard, where it splits: one fork climbs to the Jaufen Pass, at 2,094 metres, and the other continues up to the Timmelsjoch, at 2,474 metres, on the Austrian border. The Timmelsjoch road is a tolled high alpine road, and it is usually open from about June to October, while the Jaufen stays open longer but can be closed after snow. Surfaces are good, bends are many, and the views are wide. Traffic is heavy on summer weekends, so start early.

The Passeier valley is the birthplace of Andreas Hofer, the innkeeper who led the Tyrolean uprising against Napoleon's forces in 1809, and his farm, the Sandhof, is a short way up the valley. In Merano, the Kurhaus, the long promenades along the river, and the gardens of Trauttmansdorff Castle, where Empress Elisabeth stayed in 1870, recall the town's days as a spa for the Habsburg aristocracy. The thermal baths are modern, and the old town has arcades with cafes and shops.

Fuel is easy in Merano, which has stations and supermarkets, and it is wise to fill up before the passes. The food is a mix of Tyrolean and Italian: speck, a smoked ham, Schüttelbrot, a crisp rye bread, apple strudel and dumplings. In autumn, Törggelen, the tradition of eating roast chestnuts and new wine in farm inns, is at its best.

Walk the river promenade in the evening. The apple orchards and the lights of the town below the mountains are a fitting end.
t.passo giau@46.5,12.1:
Giau is one of those passes that makes you slow down on purpose. At 2,236 metres it crosses between the valley of Selva di Cadore and the Cortina side of the Dolomites, climbing out of dark spruce forest onto an open saddle of short grass, boulders and scattered chalets, with the jagged ridge of Ra Gusela and the table-like top of Nuvolau rising to the north. The villages below, Selva di Cadore and Colle Santa Lucia, are tiny and Ladin-speaking, and the ancient Ladin culture of these valleys gives this part of the Dolomites a different flavour from the German-speaking Alto Adige on the far side of the range.

The road is narrow, and the hairpins come one after another on the southern climb, tight enough that first and second gear are the right choices. The surface is generally good, though frost heave leaves a few ripples, and on a summer weekend you share it with cyclists and cars. Early morning is by far the best time, when the light slants across the rocks and the meadows are still wet. By afternoon cloud often builds around the summits, and thunderstorms can roll in quickly, so keep an eye on the sky and have a waterproof layer within reach.

At the top, a small refuge sells coffee and simple food, and marmots whistle from the slopes and sometimes pose near the car park. The flowers in July are extraordinary, especially gentians and orchids. The mountain called Croda da Lago stands a little further to the east, a hanging wall of rock above a small lake that makes a rewarding walk if you have time. In the First World War, this front line ran through these peaks, and the remains of trenches and tunnels can still be found on the surrounding mountains.

The pass is normally snow-free from early summer into October, but check before you go, because heavy snow can close it earlier or later. Cortina d'Ampezzo, nine kilometres away, has several stations, and it is the sensible place to fill up before heading back to Falzarego.

Finishing here feels fitting. After the long climb and the views, the descent to the valley and a plate of pasta in Cortina is the perfect reward.
t.tirano food@46.2,10.2:
Tirano sits at the foot of the Bernina route, near the Swiss border, and it is the one place in Italy where a train runs along the street. The red carriages of the Rhaetian Railway start here and climb over the Bernina Pass into Switzerland on a line that is listed by UNESCO, and the Bernina Express leaves from a station just a few steps from the town centre. Watching the little train rattle between parked cars on the main road is one of those charming oddities that make you smile.

The town has about eight thousand people, which means fuel, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat. Its main sight is the Basilica of the Madonna di Tirano, a handsome Renaissance church built after a vision of the Virgin Mary was reported here in 1504, with a grand facade and a plain square in front. Each September a big pilgrimage fills the streets. It is also a good place to try the local cooking: the Valtellina is known for buckwheat dishes, mountain cheeses and bresaola, and the red wines of the terraced slopes above the Adda river.

For the rider, Tirano is the crossroads of three great mountain roads. To the north, the road climbs to the Bernina Pass, at 2,328 metres, with long curves and views of glaciers, and into Switzerland. To the west, the valley leads toward Sondrio, and to the east the Aprica pass rises toward Edolo. Bormio, with the Stelvio and Gavia passes, is a short ride further up the main valley, so this is a natural food stop on a serious pass day.

The valley is narrow and the traffic can be heavy, particularly lorries on the main road, but side roads climb quickly into forest and meadow. Weather in the Alps changes quickly, so check conditions for the high passes and keep waterproofs handy. The southern slope here is warm and sunny, often a good deal warmer than the high passes above.

Order a plate of local pasta, find a table in the sun, and let the engine cool. Whatever the timetable, give yourself an hour here, because the rest of the day is demanding.
t.holm@65.2,12.1:
Holm is where the road meets the water. Terråk and Vik, small settlements in the municipality of Bindal, lie to the south and east.

The riding here is slow and scenic. The road follows the coast, with ferries linking its sections, and the bends are tight in places, with narrow roads between rock and water. The surface is good, but the ferries impose a rhythm, and timetables matter: arrive early in summer, since queues build and cars may be left behind. The summer light is long, and the sea is often calm. Rain and wind can arrive suddenly, and fog sometimes hides the islands.

Helgeland has a powerful mythology. The mountain of Torghatten, further north, has a hole through it, about 160 metres long, which legend says was made by an arrow shot by a troll chasing a maiden, and the Seven Sisters, a row of jagged peaks, stand on the coast near Sandnessjøen.
