Leka island, offshore, has a rare geological formation of rocks from the earth's mantle. Fishing villages with red boathouses, called rorbuer or naust, line the shores, and sea eagles are common.

Fuel is not easy to find, so fill up before arriving, with Kolvereid to the south or Brønnøysund beyond the ferry as the nearest places with a good choice. The ferry kiosks sell coffee, waffles and hot dogs, and local cafes serve fish soup. Carry a card, as the ferries take payment by card or online.

Stand on the deck on the crossing. The coast opens up in a way a road cannot show.
t.bronnoysund@65.5,12.2:
Brønnøysund is the largest town on this part of the Helgeland coast, with a little over four thousand residents and a harbour full of fishing boats and ferries, and it works as the commercial and administrative heart of a scattering of islands. The place has an airport, a long bridge that carries the main road across the sound, a busy waterfront and the practical comforts a rider needs after the ferries: fuel, supermarkets, cafes, and hotels with a view of the water.

The big landmark lies a short ride to the south of town: Torghatten, a granite mountain with a hole right through it. The tunnel is roughly a hundred and sixty metres long and some thirty-five metres high, and you can walk through it. Norwegian legend says a troll named Hestmannen chased a girl across the sea and shot an arrow at her, and that a king threw his hat to save her. The sun rose, everyone turned to stone, and the hat became the mountain with the arrow hole through it. Geologists give a different account, in which the hole was cut by waves at a time when the sea stood higher, at the end of the Ice Age.

For a rider this is coastal Norway at its most rhythmic, with Rv 17, the Kystriksveien, hopping from island to island on ferries and bridges. The roads are narrow, usually well surfaced, and change character at every crossing, from open skerry landscape to forest and mountain. The ferries are part of the fun, and the timetables matter, so check them and allow for a wait in summer. Weather comes in fast off the Norwegian Sea, and the same view can be sharp and sunny at breakfast and grey and wet an hour later.

The Arctic Circle lies not far to the north, so in midsummer the light never really goes, and a ride at midnight under a pink sky is possible. Local seafood is a good choice, and fish soup or fresh cod need no explanation. Take fuel in town, since the stations on the smaller islands are sparse and sometimes unmanned.
t.reine@67.9,13.1:
Reine is one of those places that looks unreal in photographs and looks better in life. A cluster of red and ochre fishing cabins, the rorbuer, stand on stilts at the edge of a narrow fjord, with the sheer spire of Reinebringen rising straight behind them, and the whole scene sits at the southern end of the Lofoten archipelago, a long wall of peaks that rises out of the Norwegian Sea well inside the Arctic Circle. Only a few hundred people live in the village, and in summer the number of visitors dwarfs them.

The fishing is what put Reine on the map. For a thousand years cod have come to spawn off Lofoten in winter, and the fishermen hang them on wooden racks to dry in the cold wind, producing stockfish that was exported to Italy and Portugal for centuries. The racks are still there, and so is a certain smell in the air in spring, which you either like or you do not. The Reinebringen mountain has a stone stairway, built by Nepalese Sherpas in recent years, which takes a lot of the damage out of the climb and gives you the view everyone wants.

The riding on the E10 along the islands is as good as Norway offers. The road hops between islands on bridges and causeways, passes through tunnels, and drops to the water at every bay, with mountains close on the left and the sea on the right. The corners are open and the surface is generally good, but the road is narrow, caravans are common in summer and the wind can be fierce on the bridges. Weather swings quickly, with sun and rain in the same hour, so keep the rain gear to hand. In midsummer the sun does not set, and a ride at one in the morning is a strange and beautiful thing.

Services are thin here, and Reine has only small shops and cafes. Fill the tank in Leknes or at one of the larger stations to the north before you head into the southern islands. Book accommodation ahead in July and August, because rooms vanish, and consider September, when the crowds are gone and the northern lights begin to appear.
t.glomfjord@66.8,13.9:
Glomfjord sits at the end of a short fjord arm in Nordland, on the Helgeland coast just south of the Arctic Circle, and it is a company town in the way that only Norway can manage: a place built around hydropower, in a landscape that looks as if it were designed for a postcard. The power station was built in the early twentieth century to use the water from the mountains, and an industrial plant followed, so a village of about twelve hundred people stands where the steep slopes meet the water.

The place has a dark episode in its past. In September 1942 a small group of British and Norwegian commandos sabotaged the power station in Operation Musketoon, an attack that damaged the plant and the German war effort but cost most of the raiders their lives after they were captured and executed. The story is told locally, and a short visit to the village makes more sense once you know it.

The landscape around is the real draw. Above the village lies the Svartisen glacier, the second largest in mainland Norway, and a boat or a short drive from the area gets you to its tongue, a fading blue wall that has retreated noticeably in recent decades. The riding on Rv 17 is the sort that Norwegians call the coastal route, the Kystriksveien, a succession of ferries, tunnels, bridges and fjord arms, with spectacular views over islands and mountains, and with a ferry timetable that organises your day. The road surface is good, the speed limits are low and the tunnels are long and damp, so keep your visor clear.

Fuel and food are limited in Glomfjord itself, so check your tank when you pass through. The nearest larger centre is Ørnes, a short drive to the north, and it has a petrol station and a few shops. In summer the long days give you plenty of time. The air here is damp and clean, and after rain the waterfalls come down the mountain slopes in white threads. Finish the day with a walk by the water and a bit of fish, since you will have earned it.
t.bovec@46.3,13.6:
Bovec sits at the head of the Soča valley, in a wide bowl of green meadows ringed by limestone walls that look as if they were stacked there deliberately. Kanin rises to the south, the high Julian Alps close in to the east, and the river that gave the valley its name runs cold and unbelievably turquoise just down the road. It is a small town of around sixteen hundred people, but in summer its population of kayakers, rafters, paragliders and riders makes it feel much larger.

The Soča is the star. Its colour comes from glacial minerals and the clean limestone it flows through, and it is cold enough in all but the hottest weeks to make you gasp. The upper valley is one of the best whitewater areas in Europe, and the little town is a base for rafting, canyoning and kayaking. Even if you do none of this, the viewpoints along the road are worth the pauses.

History hangs over the place. During the First World War the Isonzo front, as the Italians called it, ran through here, and twelve battles were fought along the valley between 1915 and 1917. At nearby Kobarid, ten kilometres down the road, a good museum tells the story, and Ernest Hemingway used the retreat from Caporetto in A Farewell to Arms. Bunkers, tunnels and chapels still scatter the hillsides. It is sobering to ride through such calm beauty and then remember how much happened here.

The roads from Bovec are among the best in Slovenia. To the north, the Vršič Pass climbs to 1,611 metres through about fifty hairpins, many of them cobbled on the northern side, so it needs care in the wet. It is usually closed in winter. To the west the Predel pass crosses to Italy and Tarvisio, an easier road with long bends and mountain views.

Fuel is found in the valley, with larger supplies in Tolmin down the road, and it is wise to top up before the passes. Food is generous: look for the local Bovec cheese, a hard sheep cheese, the thick bean soup called jota, and fresh trout from the river. Afternoon thunderstorms can roll in quickly during summer, so start the passes early.
t.landeck@47.1,10.6:
Landeck sits at the meeting of valleys in the Tyrolean Alps, where the Inn river swings from its long upper valley into a gorge and the Sanna comes tumbling down from the Arlberg side. At around 800 metres, it is a modest height for the Alps, but the mountains rise steeply on all sides, and the old castle on its rock above the town gives the place the look of a doorway. Burg Landeck dates from the thirteenth century and now houses a museum. The town has about 7,700 people, and the old centre is small, with painted houses and cafes.

Landeck has always been a crossroads. The Via Claudia Augusta, the Roman road from Italy to the Danube, came through over the Reschen Pass, and later salt, wine and cattle moved the same way. Today the roads from here lead in every direction: east along the Inn toward Innsbruck, south to the Reschen Pass and Italy, and west over the Arlberg to Vorarlberg. Zams, next door, has a cable car to the Venet, a peak with views over the valley, and a pilgrimage and hospital tradition going back to the nineteenth century.

For riders, Landeck is a perfect base. The Arlberg road, with its famous passes, climbs from St Anton, and the Flexen road beyond cuts through galleries and cliffs to Lech and Zürs, with views over a mountain basin. The Silvretta High Alpine Road, a toll road to the west, climbs to a reservoir and a pass of about 2,000 metres. Surfaces are generally excellent, and the bends are a joy, but high passes can close with snow from late autumn to late spring, and summer weekends bring heavy traffic and tour buses. Tyrol takes noise seriously, with restrictions for loud exhausts on some roads, so ride considerately.

Practically, Landeck has fuel stations, supermarkets and many guesthouses and restaurants. Tyrolean food includes Gröstl, a pan of potatoes and meat, Kaspressknödel, cheese dumplings in broth, and apple strudel. Parking is easy in the centre, though some bays require a ticket. If you plan a high pass, fill the tank here and bring warm layers, since temperatures drop sharply with height. Early morning light on the peaks is spectacular.
t.walchensee and@48.3,11.6:
The nearest bigger town is Freising, perched on the Domberg above the Isar, with a cathedral and a brewery at Weihenstephan that claims to be the oldest in the world, running since 1040. That claim is proudly defended, and the brewery's tavern is a pleasant stop for a Bavarian lunch.

The plain is called the Münchner Schotterebene, and it was created by meltwater rivers pouring gravel out of the Alps. Under the surface lies a huge aquifer that feeds the city's drinking water. Peat bogs, the Moos, once covered the hollows, and were drained in the nineteenth century to create farmland, so the fields here are black soil and the villages have names ending in moos. The Echinger Lohe, a patch of rare heath near Eching, preserves a bit of the original landscape. The Isar and its side channels run quietly through woods and meadows.

The Walchensee and Kochelsee, named in this stop's label, lie far to the south in the Alps, and this is the other end of a long loop. Back on the plain, the roads are straight and fast, with the main risk coming from boredom and tractors. Surfaces are good, and traffic is dense around the airport and the autobahn junctions. Crosswinds can be strong in the open, and in autumn fog lies heavy on the fields in the morning. For a quieter route, follow the small roads along the Isar through Freising and Moosburg, where the river is lined with trees.

Practically, fuel stations are near every junction, with supermarkets and bakeries in all the towns. The airport area has hotels and restaurants. Freising has a lively old town, with cafes and breweries, and the cathedral hill makes a pleasant walk. Beer gardens are the best places to eat, with roast chicken, pretzels and cold beer, and some serve in a self-service style where you can bring your own picnic. Parking for motorcycles is plentiful, and the S-Bahn from the airport runs to central Munich.
t.kochelsee lakeside@47.7,11.4:
Kochel am See lies right at the point where the Bavarian flatlands end, as if somebody had stood the Alps up against the lake. The Kochelsee is a small, deep glacial lake of a few kilometres' length with reed beds along the north shore, and behind the village the ground rises sharply to the Herzogstand and Heimgarten, two wooded ridges that give the lake its backdrop. The village has about four thousand people, a handful of cafes, a promenade and, if you ride south from Penzberg, the first real sense of arriving in the mountains.

The painter Franz Marc lived nearby, at Ried, and there is a museum devoted to him in Kochel, set on the hillside above the lake. Marc was one of the founders of the Blue Rider group and painted his famous blue horses in this country; he was killed at Verdun in 1916, aged thirty-six. The light on the lake on a still morning, when the water goes grey-green and the mist rises from the reeds, is easy to link to those paintings. A short way east, Benediktbeuern has a large Benedictine monastery whose abbey church is one of the finest baroque buildings in the region. Carmina Burana, the medieval songs, were found there in manuscript form.

For riders the fun starts just beyond the village. The Kesselberg road climbs from the lake toward Walchensee in a tight series of bends, some of them quite steep, and has a reputation among Munich riders that goes back decades. It is also a road where local authorities have at times restricted motorbikes, notably on weekends and holidays for noise reasons, so check the current rules before you plan a Sunday there. Early weekday mornings are the best time, with cool air and few cars. Take care in the shade, where damp stays long after rain.

Kochel has petrol stations and bakeries, and for a larger choice of shops Penzberg, eleven kilometres north, is the place, a former coal-mining town that has reinvented itself. The lake is good for swimming in summer, with a public beach and shallow water that warms more than the high lakes, though water temperature is still cool. In autumn the beech forest on the slopes turns copper, and on the clearest days after rain the whole range stands sharp above the water.
t.walchensee road@47.6,11.3:
The Walchensee is one of the deepest and clearest Alpine lakes in Germany, and the road along its eastern and southern shore is one of the most photographed in Bavaria. The water is a turquoise that looks almost Caribbean when the sun hits the shallows, and it is fed by cold springs, which keep it chilly all summer. Around it rise forested slopes, the Herzogstand to the north and the peaks of the Karwendel and the Estergebirge to the south, so the lake sits in a bowl, with its surface often creased by wind.

That wind is the lake's trademark. In summer the thermals draw a steady breeze along the water in the afternoon, and the lake is a favourite of windsurfers and kitesurfers, whose coloured sails dot the surface. For a rider the wind means gusts that push across the road on the exposed stretches, and the bike will feel it. The road itself, the B11, is smooth, with long bends and short straight sections close to the water, and the lake appears and disappears between trees. There are a number of pull-offs, though on summer weekends they fill early and the road gets busy with cars and cyclists.

Something remarkable lies under the mountain above. The Walchensee power station, built in the 1920s, uses the drop of about two hundred metres from the lake down to the Kochelsee to generate electricity, and it was a major engineering project of its time, associated with the engineer Oskar von Miller. You can visit the plant in season, and the pipes running down the hillside are visible from the road above Kochel.

The nearest towns are not on the lake: Schlehdorf, with its handsome church and a convent on a hill above the Kochelsee, is about seven kilometres away, and Murnau am Staffelsee, with nearly twelve thousand people and the fuel and supermarkets you want, is thirteen kilometres off. Murnau was the home of the painter Gabriele Münter, whose house became a gathering place for the Blue Rider painters. A small village on the Walchensee itself offers cafes with lake views and a plate of grilled lake char, a regional speciality. Come early in the day, before the beach crowd arrives, or late in the evening, when the lake loses its wind and turns to glass.
t.jachenau valley@47.6,11.5:
Not many people know the Jachenau. It is a long, narrow side valley that runs east from the Walchensee region to the Isar, shut in by forested ridges and farmed by a few families on meadow terraces, and it has the quality of a place that the main roads missed. Lenggries, with its nine thousand inhabitants, is the nearest real town and the place for petrol, bakeries and shops, about eleven kilometres to the east.

The road through the valley is quiet, narrow and wonderfully varied, winding between meadows with a small stream beside it, and rising and falling over little saddles. Surfaces are mostly good, though patched, and there are places where the asphalt narrows enough for only one car. Weekday mornings are very quiet, but on summer Sundays the road sees local bikers and cyclists who know the valley, so expect to meet someone around a bend. Cows sometimes wander near fences, and the grass verges are mown late, so watch for hay on the road in summer. The rewards are small and constant: timber barns with weathered shingles, a wooden bridge, a cross at a junction, and the sound of the stream.

The Jachenau has a certain independence. It was once an isolated community with its own customs, and its inhabitants are known for a distinctive dress. Forestry and cattle farming are the main livelihoods, and the woods on the slopes are managed for timber that was once floated down the Isar on rafts.

The surrounding mountains hold good walking, and the Walchensee, a short ride to the west, brings the crowd back. For fuel, remember that the valley has none, so fill up at Kochel or Lenggries. The best season is late spring and early summer, when the meadows are full of flowers, and early autumn when the light is gold and the larches begin to turn. If it rains, the valley stays damp and the cold comes down from the hills, so pack a warm layer.
t.bad tolz food@47.8,11.6:
Bad Tölz is the market town of the Isarwinkel, a place of seventeen thousand people on the Isar river with the Alps standing behind it, and it is the sort of town where a motorcyclist can eat very well. The old main street, the Marktstraße, climbs gently from the river and is lined with houses painted in bright colours and decorated with gables and painted fronts, a pattern that Bavarian towns have followed for centuries. It is a spa town in a modest way, known since the nineteenth century for the iodine-rich springs that gave it the name Bad, and people still come here for the cure.

Television viewers in Germany know the town as the setting of a police series, The Bull of Tölz, and the film crews are part of the local colour. Among music lovers the Tölzer Knabenchor, the boys' choir, has an international reputation. The best known local tradition is the Leonhardifahrt, held every November, when decorated horse carriages take part in a procession up to the chapel on the Kalvarienberg in honour of Saint Leonard, patron of livestock. The hill with its chapel is a short climb and gives a good view over the town to the mountains.

For food, the Marktstraße has a cluster of traditional inns and bakeries, and you can expect the usual Bavarian menu of roast pork, dumplings, sausage salad and Kaiserschmarrn, the shredded pancake with plum compote that no mountain meal ends without. There are also ice cream cafes by the river. Lunch on a terrace here is a fine reward after the bends of the Kesselberg or the Jachenau. Parking in the centre can be tight on weekends, and the street is steep and sometimes cobbled, so a heavy bike needs care when turning.

Practical things are easy: Bad Tölz has petrol stations at its edges, supermarkets, and a railway to Munich. The Isar here is wide and green, with gravel banks, and in summer people swim and picnic along its edges, though the current is strong and cold. The ride from here toward Munich on the old roads through Holzkirchen or along the Isar is smooth and easy. Time your visit for a weekday if you can: on sunny weekends the town fills with day-trippers and the queue for a table can run long.
t.kochelsee@47.7,11.4:
Kochel am See lies at the foot of the Alps, where the Bavarian lowlands finally give way to mountains, and the Kochelsee fills the basin in front of it with a sheet of green-blue water about six hundred metres above the sea. The town has about four thousand people and a long lakeside promenade, with the first big peaks rising behind. The painter Franz Marc, one of the founders of the Blue Rider group, lived in the village of Ried, just outside, and the Franz Marc Museum on the hill above the lake holds a lovely collection of his work and that of his circle. Marc died at Verdun in 1916.

The lake's other great neighbour is the Walchensee, which lies about two hundred metres higher on the other side of the Kesselberg ridge. In the 1920s, the engineer Oskar von Miller used that height difference to build a hydroelectric power station at Kochel, where water drops from the upper lake through pipes down the mountainside. The Kesselberg road climbs the same slope, and it has been an important route since the Middle Ages. Behind it rises the Herzogstand, a peak of 1,731 metres with a cable car and a famous view.

For riders, the Kesselberg road, the B11, is the classic. It leaves the lake shore in a series of bends and hairpins, climbs through beech and spruce forest to the high pass and then drops to the Walchensee with views of the water and the peaks. The surface is excellent, but the road is narrow in places, steep, and busy on summer weekends with motorcycles, cars and cyclists. Noise limits and local restrictions apply, so watch the signs. Fog can hang on the lake in the morning, and the first autumn frosts can leave ice in the shade. Spring and autumn weekdays are best.

Practically, Kochel has fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and many inns and cafes, and in summer boats run on the lake. Schlehdorf and Großweil, nearby, are small villages with limited services. A swim in the lake is cold but refreshing, and a slice of cake on the terrace is a Bavarian tradition. Parking for bikes is plentiful, and the walk along the shore is flat and easy.
t.chiemsee shore@47.9,12.4:
The Chiemsee is the biggest lake in Bavaria, so big that Bavarians call it the Bavarian Sea, and from the shore near Gstadt and Prien it looks like one, a wide pale expanse with the Alps behind it. Two islands sit in the middle. The Herreninsel carries the palace that Ludwig II began building in the 1870s as his copy of Versailles, never finished, and the smaller Fraueninsel has a Benedictine abbey that was founded in the eighth century and is still occupied by nuns. The islands are reached by ferry from Prien, and on the road to the pier, a little steam railway runs from the town to the harbour, an old-fashioned way to start an excursion.

For a rider the shore is more an interlude than a thrill. Roads around the lake are flat, with roundabouts and long straight stretches between villages, and in the summer season traffic can be heavy with holidaymakers. But the views are lovely. Reed beds, sailing boats, the white sails and, to the south, the long serrated line of the Chiemgau Alps with the Kampenwand as the best known peak make a classic Bavarian postcard. Prien am Chiemsee, with ten thousand inhabitants, has petrol, supermarkets and lakeside cafes, and Gstadt is a quiet village on the north shore.

The lake is good for swimming, and in July and August the water gets warm enough for a proper dip, with public bathing places along the shore. A towel in the pannier is cheap insurance. The fish of the lake, particularly the Renke, a kind of whitefish, are served smoked or grilled in the island inns and the lakeside restaurants, and it is a speciality worth trying, with a pretzel and a glass of apple juice spritzer.

Bear in mind that on fine weekends the area gets very crowded and parking by the shore is difficult. If you want the lake at its best, come on a weekday evening in early summer, when the day-trippers have gone and the water reflects the pink light on the mountains. In autumn the fog often lies over the lake in the morning and the sun burns it off by noon, which gives photographers a very good hour.
t.aschau mountain view@47.8,12.3:
Aschau im Chiemgau lies at the mouth of the Prien valley, where the river leaves the mountains for the plain, and it has the best view of the Kampenwand, the jagged limestone ridge that stands over the Chiemsee region. The summit reaches about 1,670 metres, and a cable car from the village takes walkers to the top. Seen from the road at the right time, with low sun on the pale cliffs and shadows in the gullies, it is a classic Bavarian skyline. The village has about five thousand people, a few shops and a petrol station, with Frasdorf, three thousand people, just along the road.

Above the village stands Hohenaschau Castle, a large and imposing building that was long the seat of the lords of the valley, and is today used as a holiday home. The village itself is known in German foodie circles for its fine dining, though a rider in leathers will be just as happy with a plate of dumplings in a Gasthof. The valley road, which continues south through Sachrang to the Austrian border, is a very pleasant ride with soft bends, forest, and a stream beside it, and it is far quieter than the road to Kufstein.

Weather in the foothills changes quickly. A clear morning can turn to cloud by noon, and the Kampenwand then disappears, so take the photograph when you have it. In the spring, when the snow lies on the upper slopes and the meadows below are bright green, the contrast is striking. Autumn is also good, with the larches turning and the air clear after a cold front.

The pastures near Aschau are grazed by cows with big bells, and farmers sell cheese and bacon at the gate. If you stop for a snack, make it something local: a Brotzeit plate, with bread, cheese and cold meat, is a reliable meal. Fuel is not an issue in the village, but on the road south toward the mountain valleys there is nothing, so fill the tank if you are heading toward Austria. The road is open year round, but snow can close side routes in winter.
t.miesbach return roads@47.8,11.8:
Miesbach is the main town of the Oberland district of the same name, a place of about eleven thousand people on the Schlierach river, where the foothills rise from the plain. It sits in the Leitzach valley country that links the lakes of Schliersee and Tegernsee with Munich, and the roads leading out of it, to the capital to the north and to the lakes to the south, are among the pleasantest in Bavaria for a return ride. The town has everything you could need: petrol stations, supermarkets, bakeries, banks and a railway to Munich.

The town carries the character of the region. It is a centre of Bavarian dress tradition, and many people here still wear Tracht, the regional costume, on festival days. Hausham, a neighbour, was a coal-mining town until the 1960s, and the old pit closed in the second half of the twentieth century. The miners' houses and the old workings give a different side to a region that tourists see mostly as cows and onion domes. A bakery in Miesbach, with a good selection of pastry and a cup of strong coffee, is the best way to begin a stop.

Heading home, the road through Holzkirchen, a gentle route with rolling hills and long open bends, makes for an easy ride toward Munich. The surface is mostly good, and the views of the Alps behind you, in the mirror, are fine in the evening light. Traffic builds on Sunday evenings when the lake visitors return, and the autobahn gets busy, so the country roads are often faster than the motorway. Watch for speed cameras near the villages and in some of the longer stretches.

In terms of season, late spring is hard to beat: the meadows are full of flowers, the hills are green and the peaks still carry snow. Summer weekends bring many riders, cyclists and cars, and on a hot Sunday the roads around Schliersee can be packed. In autumn the Föhn brings clear, warm days and colours. By late October the first frosts can leave ice on the shaded corners in the early morning, so take the first hours of the day gently.
t.ammergau@47.8,12.0:
Irschenberg is the hill that every driver on the Munich to Salzburg motorway knows, the long ridge where the road crests and the whole Alpine front suddenly appears, a row of grey peaks across the green foreland. On a clear day, the view from the old church on the hill, the pilgrimage church that is the village landmark, takes in the Wendelstein, the Kaisergebirge and the faraway Zugspitze.

Bad Aibling is a spa town, with a park and a thermal bath fed by mineral springs and, from the nineteenth century, a mud treatment from the local peat. The Mangfall river runs out of the Tegernsee through a deep gorge and across a wide, flat valley, and the land here is a patchwork of meadows and moor, with the famous Rosenheim basin to the east. The soil is damp and green, the farms are big, with wide-eaved wooden houses and flower-hung balconies, and onion-domed churches stand in every village.

The Ammergau mountains, named in this stop's label, lie to the west, a very different part of the Alps with Ludwig II's Linderhof palace and the Ettal monastery. Here, in the east, the riding is gentler. The roads cross the low hills of the foreland, with quiet bends, farm lanes and glimpses of the mountains, and the surface is generally excellent. Traffic is heavy on the autobahn and the main road, so the back roads through Irschenberg and Hausham are better. Cold air pools in the hollows on autumn mornings, and the first snow dusts the peaks in October.

For practical matters, fuel stations are in Bad Aibling and Bruckmühl, with supermarkets and bakeries, and a number of inns and cafes in the villages. Gasthäuser serve Bavarian roast pork with dumplings, weisswurst in the morning and strong local beer. Parking is easy, and the spa town makes a good place for a gentle stroll. Bring a jacket, because even in summer, evenings turn cool.
t.forggensee view@47.6,10.7:
From the shore above the Forggensee you can see Neuschwanstein, white and improbable on its rock, and behind it the mountains of the Ammergau Alps fold into Tyrol. Few views in Germany are so famous, and few so likely to be crowded, so the advice is to come early. The castle was built by King Ludwig II from 1869, was unfinished when he died in 1886, and opened to the public within weeks. Hohenschwangau, the yellow castle below it, was where he grew up. Tickets for the interiors are sold for timed entry and fill up in summer, so this is a place to admire from the road if you did not plan ahead.

The Forggensee itself is a reservoir, made in the 1950s by damming the Lech, and it has an odd feature: in late autumn it is drained, and the lakebed becomes a grey plain, only to be refilled in spring. In summer it is the largest lake in the area, with a smooth turquoise surface, sailing boats, a passenger ferry and a few beaches where swimming is allowed. The water is clean and cold, and the shoreline, with Schwangau on one side and Füssen to the east, is busy with cyclists on the lake path.

Füssen, with nearly fourteen thousand people, has fuel stations, supermarkets and a handsome old town that climbs a hill to a castle of the Augsburg bishops, with a monastery, St. Mang's, on the river below. The town was a centre of lute and violin making from the Middle Ages, and there is a museum on the subject. It also sits on the line of the Via Claudia Augusta, the Roman road that crossed the Alps here from Italy to the Danube. A coffee and a slice of cake in the old town's narrow streets is a good way to rest the legs.

For riding, the approach from the north through the Allgäu foothills is lovely, with rolling meadows and views of the peaks ahead. The roads near Schwangau are heavily used by coaches, so ride patiently and watch for pedestrians crossing near the car parks. The best light on the castle comes in the morning, and on a clear day in autumn, with the first snow on the peaks, the picture is fine.
t.neuschwanstein view area@47.6,10.7:
Everyone knows the picture: white towers on a limestone crag, forest below, flat land stretching away to the north. What the postcards do not tell you is how many people are in the picture's foreground. The village of Schwangau and the car parks around Hohenschwangau fill with coaches from about ten in the morning, so if you want to see the castle with some room to think, arrive early or come late and treat the visit as a shoulder-season pleasure.

Ludwig II began Neuschwanstein in 1869, as a private fantasy of medieval knighthood and Wagnerian opera, on a hill facing the older castle of Hohenschwangau where he had grown up. He lived in it only for a few months before being declared unfit to rule in 1886 and dying in Lake Starnberg under circumstances that are still argued about. The castle was opened to paying visitors within weeks of his death, which is perhaps the most Bavarian irony available. The view you want is from the Marienbrücke, a steel bridge over the Pöllat gorge, with the waterfall below and the castle across the void. It is a short walk uphill from the village, and in winter the path can be icy.

For riding, the surroundings are better than the sight itself. The land here is where the Alpine foreland meets the first real wall of mountains: the Tegelberg rises behind, the Forggensee reservoir spreads to the north, and the Lech river leaves the mountains at Füssen. Roads over the border to Reutte and the Tyrol begin a few minutes away, and the rolling farm roads toward Roßhaupten and Lechbruck are quiet, curvy and framed by the Alps on one side. In clear autumn light with the cows still out, they are some of the nicest low-speed riding in Bavaria.

Füssen, just under four kilometres away, is a proper town with fuel, cafés and a handsome old centre under the High Castle; it was a hub for lute and violin makers in the late Middle Ages and still has a reputation for instruments. Schwangau itself is small, and prices around the castle car parks reflect captive customers. Eat in Füssen instead.

Motorcycle parking exists near the ticket centre, but the road up to the castle itself is closed to private vehicles. Plan on walking, on shoes with grip, and on some patience with selfie sticks.
t.pei enberg hills@47.8,11.1:
Peißenberg is a town on a hill, and the hill is the thing. The Hoher Peißenberg rises to just under a thousand metres, isolated from the Alps behind it, so that it stands like a lookout over the whole of the Pfaffenwinkel, the Priest's Corner, the pilgrim country between the Lech and the Loisach. From its top you see the lakes, the Ammergau mountains and the line of the Zugspitze in the distance. The road up is steep and short, with a good surface, and parking near the summit is limited.

On top stands a pilgrimage church, built in the early seventeenth century and one of the best known in Upper Bavaria, with a baroque interior. Next to it, there is also a weather station that has been recording since 1781, one of the oldest mountain weather stations in the world with an unbroken record, which today is operated by the German weather service. A beer garden near the top serves a view of the Alps along with a plate of local sausages. The stone terrace is windy and cool, so bring a jacket.

The town below carries a different history. Peißenberg was a coal-mining town, and the pits there worked for more than a century before the last one closed in 1971. The miners' colony and the mining museum are part of the town's memory, and you can see how the work made the place. Today it has twelve thousand inhabitants, petrol stations, supermarkets and a mixture of old and new, and it is the nearest source of fuel for a long way.

Polling, a few kilometres off, is a small village with a former Augustinian monastery that holds a library hall, a rococo room with a ceiling painted with allegories and tall shelves of old books, which is worth a stop if it is open. The riding in this corner of Bavaria is soft and rolling, with farmland, small lakes and views that open and close. Weekends bring cyclists and walkers, and in autumn the Föhn clears the air and the mountains seem near. Mornings are best, when the mist lies in the valleys and the hill rises out of it.
t.motovun@45.3,13.8:
Motovun rises out of the Mirna valley like a stone crown on a green hill, a walled town at about two hundred and seventy metres with a church tower on top and a ring of ramparts around it. From the road below, as you approach through the vineyards and oak woods, it looks almost too neat to be real, and you are very likely to stop for a photograph before you even reach the gate. It is one of the best known of Istria's hill towns, and for good reason.

The town's history is Venetian. The ramparts and the loggia date from the centuries when Istria belonged to the Republic of Venice, and the lion of St Mark appears on the gate and the walls. A walk around the top of the walls gives a long view over the valley, with its patchwork of vines, olive groves and fields, and on a clear day you can see the hills of the Učka range and even, far off, the glitter of the Adriatic. Every summer the town hosts a film festival, which fills the streets with visitors for a week or so.

The area is known for truffles, which grow in the oak forests of the Mirna valley, and a huge white truffle found here in 1999 made headlines around the world. Truffle dishes appear on every menu, from pasta and eggs to steak and cheese, and the local wines, Malvazija, a crisp white, and Teran, a dark and tart red, go well with them. Restaurants around the town serve them, with prices that reflect their fame, and a simple plate of fresh pasta with truffle is a classic Istrian lunch.

The ride up to Motovun is a pleasure, with a winding climb in a series of bends through the trees, and the roads in the valley are quiet, smooth and well kept. Cars are not allowed in the centre, and visitors park below the walls, so you walk the last stretch. Buzet, about fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with a proper range of services, including fuel, while Karojba, a few kilometres off, is a smaller option. Summer is hot and busy, and spring and early autumn are the best times to visit.
t.godoysund near bodo@67.1,14.0:
Whichever way you read it, the setting is the same: low islands, skerries, fjord arms and snow-streaked mountains standing right up from the sea.

It helps to know that you are well north of the Arctic Circle, which the coast road crosses at the Helgeland ferry link near Jektvik. In midsummer the sun does not set at all in this latitude, and the light at midnight turns the water a pale, rosy gold. In winter the opposite is true, and the northern lights draw visitors to the coast. The weather swings between the two with little warning, and a cold wind off the Norwegian Sea can arrive on a sunny day.

The coastal road, the Kystriksveien, is one of the great slow rides of Europe. It threads along fjords, crosses on ferries and takes bridges between islands, with long bends and gentle gradients rather than hairpins. Ferries are part of the rhythm, and you should check timetables because they are not frequent, particularly outside summer. Just east of Bodø is Saltstraumen, where the tide forces enormous volumes of water through a narrow strait several times a day, producing whirlpools and one of the strongest tidal currents in the world. It is worth timing your visit for the changing of the tide.

Fishing is the old economy here. Cod, drying racks and old fishing stations tell the story, and the Lofoten stockfish trade that made Bergen rich started along this coast. You will see red and yellow houses on stilts at the water's edge, with boats pulled up beside them, and eagles circling above. Sea eagles are common, and you may spot one over the sound.

Fuel is thin on the ground in this part of Norway. Inndyr is small, and the reliable choice is Bodø, about twenty-two kilometres away, where you will find stations, cafes and shops. Fill up there and buy lunch, because small shops on the coast keep short hours.

Plan to finish with a meal of fresh fish in Bodø and a walk along the harbour in the late light.
t.bodo@67.3,14.4:
Bodø is a young city with an old burn scar. On 27 May 1940, German bombers destroyed most of the town centre during the campaign for northern Norway, and the replacement was built in the plain, practical style of the postwar years. It is not a pretty place in the postcard sense, but it is a sensible, friendly one, with about thirty-four thousand people, a harbour full of boats and mountains standing in a ring on the far side of the water.

Its true magic is its position, north of the Arctic Circle on a headland facing the Lofoten islands. In early summer the sun stays above the horizon for weeks, and in winter the sky puts on the northern lights. The cathedral, completed in the 1950s, stands apart from its bell tower, which looks like a separate building altogether, and the Norwegian Aviation Museum is a good place on a wet day. Bodø was a European Capital of Culture in 2024, and it has been busy ever since.

Out of town, the real star is Saltstraumen, about thirty kilometres away, where the tide forces vast amounts of water through a narrow channel and produces whirlpools you can watch from the bridge. It is regularly described as one of the strongest tidal currents in the world, and you can time your arrival with a tide table. Sea eagles gather there, and so do anglers. Further afield, the Svartisen glacier tumbles from a high ice cap not far to the south, and the Lofoten ferry leaves from the harbour for a crossing of a few hours.

For a long ride east towards the Swedish border, as this route does, the roads are gentle at first, then climb through birch and pine into high, open country. Traffic is light, bends are long and easy, and the main danger is reindeer, which stand on the tarmac as though it were their right. Mosquitoes in July are fierce, so stop with care. Weather can swing from sun to sleet in an hour.

Fuel is easy in a town of this size, with stations across Bodø, and it is the place to fill up and eat before heading inland. The roads beyond are long and the services sparse.

Finish the day on the waterfront, with fish and a late sun that does not seem to want to go down.
t.kobarid@46.2,13.6:
Kobarid is a quiet little town in a loud history. In October 1917, in what the Italians know as Caporetto, Austro-Hungarian and German troops broke through the Italian lines on the Isonzo front in the twelfth battle of the river, and the retreat that followed became a byword for catastrophe in Italy. Ernest Hemingway used it as the backdrop for A Farewell to Arms. For two and a half years before that the valley had been a front line, with thousands of men dying in the mountains above, and the town now holds one of the most thoughtful war museums in Europe, which was named European Museum of the Year in 1993.

A hill above the town carries the Italian ossuary, a circular church in pale stone that holds the bones of more than seven thousand soldiers, and it is a sombre and impressive place. A walk up to it takes ten minutes and gives a view of the whole valley. Down by the river, the Napoleon Bridge, a stone arch over a deep emerald gorge, is a gentler sight, and a short walk takes you to the Kozjak waterfall, which drops into a rocky basin. The Soča itself, one of the most vivid rivers in Europe, runs the colour of glass-green jade, with marble trout in the pools.

The riding in the Soča valley is wonderful. The road from Kobarid up to Bovec is a mix of rolling curves and faster stretches, with the river shining below and the limestone peaks of the Julian Alps above. Surfaces are generally excellent, though in summer the traffic can be heavy with cyclists, campervans and tourists. In winter, ice lingers in the shade of the gorges. Spring brings snowmelt, and the river runs full and loud.

The town has a handful of good restaurants and a bakery, and the local speciality is a walnut-filled pastry called Kobariški štruklji. Fuel is limited, so fill the tank at Tolmin or Bovec. Cividale in Italy is about twenty kilometres west, across the border, and the crossing is open and easy. On a warm evening, with a glass of wine on a terrace and the mountains going pink above the roofs, Kobarid is hard to leave.
t.tolmin@46.2,13.7:
Tolmin sits at the meeting of two rivers, the Soča and the Tolminka, in a broad green bowl where the Julian Alps begin to soften toward the Friulian plain. It is the main town of the middle Soča valley, a place with three and a half thousand people, a handful of shops, a market and a cheerful, workaday air, and it makes a good base for riders in the region. Kobarid lies up the valley, Kanal further down, and the Italian town of Cividale del Friuli is beyond the hills to the west.

The big attraction is Tolmin Gorge, a short drive from the town. The Tolminka and the Zadlaščica have carved a deep, narrow canyon in the limestone, and a path with bridges and steps runs through it, past a spot called the Devil's Bridge, a natural stone arch high above the water. It is a half-day walk in beautiful, dripping, cool shade. The valley's cheese, Tolminc, is a hard, sweet, nutty cheese made in alpine dairies and protected by a designation of origin, and it is worth buying a wedge for the saddlebag.

Tolmin has a more dramatic history than its calm appearance suggests. In 1713 peasants of the district rose in rebellion against their feudal lords, and the revolt was bloodily put down. In the First World War the town lay close to the front line and was shelled repeatedly, and most of it was rebuilt afterward. Today the main street has a pleasant, unhurried feel.

The road along the Soča valley from here is superb. It winds north to Kobarid and Bovec through narrow gorges, wide meadows and little villages, and south toward the lake at Most na Soči. The curves are smooth and open, the surface excellent, and the views are dazzling. Early morning is best, before the cyclists and the heat. Fuel is available in Tolmin itself, and there are supermarkets, bakeries and cafes where you can sit with a coffee and a pastry. Be aware that summer afternoons can bring sudden storms, and the rivers rise quickly when the rain comes down.
t.estes park@40.4,-105.5:
Elk wander through the streets of Estes Park in autumn as if they had a lease on the place. During the rut, in late September and October, bulls bugle on the lawns and golf course, and visitors line up with cameras at a respectful distance, while the town itself, sitting at around 7,500 feet in a mountain bowl where the Big Thompson and Fall rivers meet, carries on with its cafes, fudge shops and outdoor stores. It is the eastern gateway to Rocky Mountain National Park and the starting point for Trail Ridge Road.

The Stanley Hotel, a white Colonial Revival building on a hill above town, opened in 1909 and was built by the inventor F. O. Stanley, who came to Colorado hoping the mountain air would cure his tuberculosis. Stephen King stayed there with his wife in 1974 and the visit inspired The Shining, which is why the hotel now runs ghost tours. The film that followed used a different building for its exteriors, but the story clings to the hotel all the same.

Trail Ridge Road, US 34, climbs out of Estes Park into the park and across the Continental Divide, reaching 12,183 feet, the highest continuous paved highway in the United States. For about eleven miles it runs above the treeline, over open tundra where marmots whistle, elk graze in summer and the wind blows hard. Bends are broad, climbs are long, and the drop-offs are steep, with few guardrails in places. The road usually closes in mid October and reopens around Memorial Day, though snow can close it at any time, and in summer a timed-entry reservation for the park is often required, so check the park's website.

Everything you need is in Estes Park, which has just over six thousand year-round residents and many more visitors. Take on fuel in town, because there is none on the road itself. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in July and August, with lightning exposed on the tundra, so aim to cross in the morning. Dress for a temperature drop of twenty degrees or more between town and summit. The ride rewards early starts, light traffic and a hot drink at the visitor centre on the way down.
t.beppu@33.3,131.5:
Beppu steams. Walk down almost any street in this city on the east coast of Kyushu and you will see white plumes rising from vents, drains and rooftops, because the ground below is boiling. With some two thousand hot-spring sources, among the most of any place in Japan, Beppu produces more hot water than almost anywhere in the world, and the city is organized around it, with public bathhouses, steaming ponds and a faint smell of sulfur everywhere.

The best-known attractions are the Jigoku, the Hells, a group of spectacular hot springs meant for viewing rather than bathing. One is a bright, blood-red pond; another, a milky, cobalt-blue; another spouts a geyser at intervals. Locals cook with the steam, using it to steam vegetables, eggs and pudding at the Kannawa district, a method called jigoku-mushi. At the old Takegawara bathhouse, built in 1879, you can be buried in warm sand, a Beppu specialty, and the experience is oddly relaxing.

Geography makes the riding. Behind the city rise the volcanoes of the Beppu-Yufuin region, including Mount Tsurumi, and the road known as the Yamanami Highway climbs from here through highland grassland toward Mount Aso, the huge caldera in the heart of Kyushu. The route offers wide views, open ridges of silver grass and gentle curves, and the surface is generally good, with relatively little traffic outside holidays. The area around Yufuin, a hot-spring town with a lake and a lively tourist street, makes a pleasant stop.

Beppu is a city of over a hundred thousand, so fuel, convenience stores and restaurants are everywhere, and Oita, a short ride south, is bigger still. Local food includes toriten, a fried chicken dish, and dango-jiru, a dumpling soup. The best months are April for cherry blossom, and October and November for color on the mountains; summer is hot and humid, with typhoon risk in late summer and autumn. Winter brings occasional snow on the high roads, which can close them, and the steaming town is a pleasure at that time of year.
t.postojna@45.8,14.2:
Postojna is a small town on the Karst plateau of south-western Slovenia, and almost everyone who comes here has one purpose: the cave. The Postojna Cave system, carved by the Pivka river through limestone, runs for more than twenty kilometres, and part of it is visited by an electric train that carries you deep into the mountain before you walk through halls of stalactites and pale columns. It has been a tourist attraction since the early nineteenth century, one of the oldest in Europe. The temperature inside hovers around ten degrees all year, so bring a warm layer even if you arrive in a heat wave.

In the dark pools of the cave lives the olm, a pale, blind salamander that can survive for years without food. Locals call it the human fish because of its skin colour, and in the old days people believed it to be a baby dragon, a story the Slovenes seem to enjoy. A few kilometres away, Predjama Castle clings to the mouth of a cave in a sheer cliff, the stronghold of a robber knight, Erazem, who is said to have held off a siege for a long time thanks to a secret passage.

For riding, this is limestone country, with rolling forested hills, sinkholes and plateaus. The roads to the Vipava valley and the coast are scenic and fun, with sharp bends, though the surface can be slippery in wet weather. The wind called the bora blasts down from the hills in winter and can be fierce, particularly on the motorway near Razdrto and on exposed viaducts. Check the forecast and keep a firm grip if it is gusting.

Slovenia requires an electronic vignette for motorways. Fuel is available in Postojna itself, a town of about nine thousand, which has stations by the main road and supermarkets. Order pršut, the dry-cured Karst ham, and a glass of teran, a tart red wine from the region, before you head down to the sea.
t.koper@45.5,13.7:
Koper is the main port of Slovenia, on a short stretch of the Adriatic between Italy and Croatia, and it has the air of a town that was Italian for centuries and still remembers. Under Venice it was known as Capodistria, and the old centre has the classic Venetian look: a square lined with a Gothic loggia, the Praetorian Palace in pale stone, a cathedral, a campanile you can climb for a view over the bay and the red roofs. Italian is still widely spoken, and on signs you will see both languages.

The container port is just beside the old town, and cranes stand against the hills like giraffes. It is easy to ignore, and the coast beyond is lovelier than you might expect. Short rides lead to Piran, a jewel of a town on a headland, and to the salt pans of Sečovlje, where salt has been harvested in the old way for hundreds of years. The Istrian hinterland, with olive groves, vineyards and hilltop villages, rises behind the coast and has some of the best roads in the area.

On the bike, the lanes through the hills toward Grožnjan, Motovun and the Rižana valley are twisty and often quiet, with excellent views over the sea in clear weather. The surface is generally good on main roads and patched on small ones. In winter and early spring the bora wind can howl across the passes, and in summer the coast road fills with traffic and parking is hard to find. Early morning is the time to ride.

Koper has all the fuel and food you could want, and the old town is a fine place to sit with a coffee or an ice cream. Local specialities include fresh fish, seafood risotto, Istrian olive oil, and the white wine Malvasia and the red Refošk. The Italian border is close, and the Croatian border is only a short distance south, so keep your passport handy for crossings that sometimes see spot checks.

Late spring and September are ideal, when the sea is warm and the roads are free.
t.labin@45.1,14.1:
Labin crowns a hill in eastern Istria, three hundred-odd metres above the Adriatic, and you reach it by climbing a sequence of bends through scrub oak and cypress. The upper town is a knot of Venetian-era lanes, with pastel houses, stone doorways and a church tower, set around a small square, and from the terraces you look straight across the Kvarner gulf to the islands of Cres and Krk. Below, down a twisting road, lies Rabac, a former fishing village turned family beach resort.

The old town has a deep and surprising history. Labin was for centuries a rough-edged mining area; the coal pits in the Raša valley below fed the Habsburg and then the Italian economy, and the miners were poor and fiercely organised. In 1921, as fascism rose in Italy, they rose in what is called the Labin Republic, an armed strike that lasted for several weeks and is remembered as one of the first anti-fascist uprisings in Europe. The theologian Matthias Flacius Illyricus, a leading figure of the early Lutheran Reformation, was born here in 1520, and the house associated with him is a small museum.

Riders will like the winding roads that link Labin to the coast and the interior. The route down to Rabac is a succession of tight bends with sea views, and the road along the Raša bay passes inlets and old mine villages. Surfaces are generally good, though minor roads in the hills can be rough, and in summer you share them with tourists on rented scooters. To the north, Mount Učka rises to roughly fourteen hundred metres, with a narrow road to a high viewpoint.

Labin has a few thousand people, which is enough for fuel stations and supermarkets, and a handful of cafes on the hill. Istrian cooking runs strongly to truffles, wild asparagus, homemade pasta, and the red Teran wine. Come in May or September, when the sea is warm and the roads are quiet, and leave the bike below if you plan to wander the cobbled upper town.
t.opatija@45.3,14.3:
Opatija became fashionable almost by accident. In 1844 a wealthy merchant from Rijeka built a villa among the laurels on this sheltered stretch of the Kvarner coast and called it Villa Angiolina, after his late wife. Within a few decades the Austrian Southern Railway had arrived, doctors were recommending the mild climate, and the resort had become the seaside playground of the Habsburg empire. Grand hotels in cream and ochre went up along the shore, with balconies, domes and palm gardens, and the Viennese aristocracy came to take the sea air and be seen.

That elegance remains. The Lungomare, a coastal promenade of about twelve kilometres, runs from Volosko to Lovran along the rocks, past villas, bathing platforms and the famous bronze statue of the Maiden with the Seagull. The town itself is small, under eight thousand people, and dignified, with a good selection of cafes and cake shops that suit a rest after a hard ride.

For motorcyclists, Opatija is a gateway to two very different roads. Behind it, the mountain of Učka rises steeply, and a narrow road climbs to a viewpoint at about fourteen hundred metres with panoramic views of the islands, the gulf and the Istrian peninsula. It is a series of tight bends through beech wood, and it can be cold and windy at the top. Along the coast, the old coastal road runs south toward Lovran, whose chestnut festival fills the streets in October, and north towards Rijeka, a busy port city with heavy traffic.

Fuel is easy in and around Opatija, but prices on the coast tend to be a little higher than inland. Parking in summer can be tricky, so aim to arrive early. The tunnel under Učka is a toll route, but the mountain road is free.

Spring, with camellias in flower, and autumn are the best times; in July and August the coast road is crowded and the heat is intense. Winter days are often mild and quiet, with the mountain sometimes dusted with snow.
t.kagoshima@31.6,130.6:
Kagoshima faces an active volcano. Sakurajima rises from the bay barely four kilometres from the centre of the city, its flanks scarred with old lava flows and its summit often trailing a plume of ash, and the locals live with it as others live with weather. A ferry crosses to the island every few minutes through the day and night, and on the far side you can ride a loop road around the base of the mountain, past lava fields and small farms where radishes and mandarins grow in the black soil. On windy days the ash drifts over the city and settles on cars, pavements and rooftops, and residents have special bags for sweeping it up.

The city has a proud and slightly rebellious character. It was the capital of the Satsuma domain, whose samurai played a key role in the overthrow of the shogunate in 1868 and the creation of modern Japan. Saigō Takamori, the great Satsuma leader who later led a rebellion against the new government and died on Shiroyama hill above the city in 1877, is still a hero to people here. The Sengan-en garden, built by the Shimazu lords, borrows the volcano as its backdrop.

For motorcyclists, Kagoshima is a good place to arrive and a great place to leave from. Roads north climb into the Kirishima mountains, with crater lakes, steam vents and forested passes, and long smooth bends that suit a big bike. South, the Satsuma peninsula road leads to Ibusuki, where you can be buried in warm volcanic sand at a seaside bath. Volcanic ash on the road is slippery, particularly when damp, so treat any grey dust with caution.

Fuel is easy, with stations in all directions, and attendants in many Japanese stations will fill your tank for you. Do not miss the local black pork, the sweet-potato shochu, and the ramen. Spring and autumn are best; summer is hot and humid, with typhoons from August into early autumn.
t.st anton am arlberg@47.1,10.3:
St Anton is the village where alpine skiing as the world knows it was invented, or at least codified. In the 1920s, the local ski teacher Hannes Schneider, building on the Arlberg technique, taught generations of skiers to turn on steep slopes, and his school became famous across Europe. Today, the village of fewer than two thousand people sits at the head of the Stanzer valley in Tyrol, at about 1,300 metres, with the great ridge of the Arlberg massif rising on all sides. In winter it is one of the liveliest ski resorts in the Alps, famous for its steep terrain and noisy, lively après-ski.

Summer is quieter, and for riders, perhaps better. The valley is green, the high meadows are full of flowers, and the streets are calmer, with a few shops open, a clutch of good restaurants, and cafes with terraces. The old railway station is a handsome landmark, and the Arlberg rail tunnel, finished in 1884, opened the region to the world. The road tunnel beneath the pass, nearly fourteen kilometres long, opened in 1978 and carries the main traffic, and a toll is charged to use it. Most riders choose the old road over the pass, which is free and much prettier.

The village has fuel, shops and plenty of places to eat, and it is the best base for the surrounding roads. Going west, the pass road climbs to the Arlberg Pass and then to Lech and Zürs. East, the road runs down the valley to Landeck, about twenty-three kilometres away, with the Inn valley beyond. Tyrol's food is hearty, with Kaiserschmarrn, a shredded pancake with raisins and fruit compote, Tiroler Gröstl, a pan of potatoes, bacon and egg, and Kasspatzln, small cheese dumplings. After a day's riding, they are exactly right.

The weather here is mountain weather. Mornings can be clear and cool, and afternoons bring cloud and thunderstorms, especially in July and August. Snow can come early in autumn and linger late in spring, and the high roads are closed in winter. Be ready for cold at the passes, even if it is warm in the village.

Parking in the centre is easy outside the ski season, and a walk along the main street, with the mountains above, is a good way to stretch. The cable car to the Valluga, a high summit, offers wide views.
t.arlberg pass@47.1,10.2:
Few passes in the Alps have a better claim to being a true divide, because the Arlberg is where the water decides its direction. Rain falling on the western side flows into the Rhine and from there to the North Sea, while on the eastern side it joins the Inn and the Danube and ends in the Black Sea. At 1,793 metres, the pass marks the border between Tyrol and Vorarlberg, and it has been crossed since the Middle Ages, though for centuries it was a difficult and dangerous route.

Near the top, the little hamlet of St Christoph preserves an old story. In 1386, a man named Heinrich Findelkind founded a hospice here for travellers lost in the snow, and the brotherhood he started, the St Christoph Brotherhood, still exists. The hospice rang a bell in bad weather to guide people through the storm. Today, the area is a quiet ski settlement, with a few hotels and a small church, and the monument to the hospice stands by the road.

Since the road tunnel opened in 1978, most traffic has gone under the mountain, and the old pass road is a quiet delight. It climbs from St Anton in a series of long bends, with good surface and clear views, past pastures and rocky slopes. On the western side, the road drops through woods toward Langen am Arlberg and Klösterle, and then to the Klostertal valley. Traffic is light, apart from cyclists, who are numerous in summer. Corners are generally easy, with the occasional tight turn, and the road is wide enough to be comfortable.

The pass is open all year, but winter is another matter. Snow and ice can close the road, and avalanche control may stop traffic for hours, so check conditions before heading out in the cold months. Even in summer, clouds can sweep in, and a mild day can turn cool and wet. The pass can be windy, and the high pastures have a chill that hints at the glaciers far above.

There are no big services at the summit, though the nearby hotels at St Christoph serve coffee and meals. For fuel, use St Anton, about three and a half kilometres away, or Landeck. Carry a layer, and enjoy the quiet.
t.flexen pass@47.2,10.2:
Flexen Pass is the road to Lech and Zürs, two of the most glamorous ski villages in the Alps, and it is a piece of engineering as much as a mountain road. At 1,773 metres, it links the Klostertal valley with the high basin of the Lech, and it was built at the end of the nineteenth century to give the villages a year-round connection. The route runs along a steep, rocky slope, with galleries and tunnels cut through the cliffs to protect it from avalanches, and there are places where the road seems to cling to the face of the mountain.

The ride up from Danöfen is a series of tight bends, with steep gradients and rock walls, followed by a dramatic stretch through the galleries, some open on one side to give views into the valley. Be careful of the sudden change from light to dark, and of the narrow lanes in the tunnels. The surface is good, but the road is slow in places, and traffic can be heavy in the high season, with buses and cars. The road is closed from time to time in winter, when the avalanche danger is high, and sometimes in heavy snow, with long waits. Check before setting out in cold weather.

Beyond the top, the road descends toward Zürs, a high village with hotels and ski lifts, and then on to Lech. Lech has become famous as a smart resort, frequented by European royalty, with expensive hotels, chalets and boutiques, yet the village retains a calm, traditional character, with a wooden church and a river running through. The skiing in the area is part of the Arlberg system, one of the largest ski areas in Austria, and in summer, the same slopes are used for walking and cycling.

The landscape is rocky and wild, with grey limestone and green pastures, and snow often lies high in the gullies well into the summer. The air is crisp, and the light is bright. In June, the meadows are filled with alpine flowers, and in autumn, the larches turn gold.

Lech has a station, but prices are high, and the nearest big town is Bludenz, about twenty-six kilometres away. Klösterle, close to the western foot, has a few basic services. The best time to ride is early in the morning, before the traffic builds, and the best season is summer.
t.lech@47.2,10.1:
Lech sits in a high bowl of the Lech valley in Vorarlberg, at around fourteen hundred and fifty metres, with grey limestone peaks of the Arlberg on every side. It is known mainly as a ski resort, one of the most exclusive in Austria, and in winter the narrow village fills with fur coats and champagne, but in summer it is quiet, green and full of cowbells. The village was settled in the fourteenth century by Walser people, German-speaking farmers from the Valais in Switzerland who moved to high valleys across the Alps, and their wooden houses and chapel give it character. The river Lech, which rises nearby and flows north into Bavaria, is one of the last wild rivers in the Alps, with gravel banks and braided channels in its lower reaches.

For riders, Lech is the end of a fine road. The Flexenpass, at around seventeen hundred and seventy metres, links the Klostertal with the Lech valley, and the road is carved into the rock on the steep slope, passing through galleries and tunnels built to protect it from avalanches. The ascent from Stuben has tight hairpins and a pleasing rhythm, and the views from the top over the Rote Wand and the green basin below are superb. The surface is good, and traffic is moderate, though weekends can bring a convoy of cars and bikes. The pass is closed in winter, usually until late spring, and sudden avalanche closures can happen even in early summer, so check conditions.

North of Lech, the road continues along the river toward Warth and the Hochtannberg Pass, with long views and gentle bends, a route that combines mountain scenery with smooth tarmac. Weather in the Arlberg is changeable, with cold air, fog and showers in the afternoon, so carry a waterproof.

Fuel in Lech itself is limited, so fill up in Bludenz or Landeck, or in the valley below, and use the village for lunch. Austrian mountain cooking, with Kässpätzle, cheese dumplings in a pan with fried onions, is the thing to order. The best months are late June to September.
t.pass museum@46.9,11.1:
The Timmelsjoch is one of the great high roads of the Alps, linking Sölden in Austria with the Passeier valley in South Tyrol, Italy, and the museum at the top tells the story of how it came to be. At 2,474 metres, the pass crosses the border in a high, bare landscape of rock and scree, with a few small lakes and the occasional patch of snow in summer. The road was built in stages in the middle of the twentieth century, to link two valleys that had been separated by the mountains for centuries, and its construction was a major effort, with workers battling the weather and steep terrain.

The pass has a long history as a smugglers' path and trade route. Before the road, people crossed here on foot or with pack animals, carrying goods, livestock and, in hard times, contraband. The region has a rich and complicated past. After 1919, South Tyrol became part of Italy, and the border dividing the old Tyrol shaped lives on both sides. The Passeier valley is the homeland of Andreas Hofer, the innkeeper who led the Tyrolean uprising against Napoleon's armies in 1809, and who remains a symbol of Tyrolean independence. His birthplace, at St Leonhard, is a short distance down the valley.

The museum at the pass offers information about the road, the border and the people who crossed it, and the building has a viewing terrace. Next to it stands a customs station from earlier days. A cafe nearby serves hot drinks and snacks in season, and the views from the terrace over the surrounding peaks are superb.

For a rider, the Timmelsjoch is a pleasure, with long, flowing bends, good tarmac and splendid views. The Austrian side climbs in long hairpins from Sölden, and the Italian side drops through tunnels and bends into the valley. It is a toll road, and a fee is charged at the border station. It is closed in winter, usually from late autumn to early summer, and is subject to closure at short notice in bad weather. Cold winds and sudden storms are possible at any time of year, so carry warm and waterproof clothing.

Fuel is not available at the pass. Sölden, about ten kilometres on the Austrian side, has stations, as does the Passeier valley below, and Vipiteno is the nearest bigger town on the Italian side, though it is a long way off. Fill up in the valley, and bring cash for the toll.
t.st leonhard in passeier@46.8,11.2:
St Leonhard in Passeier lies in the Passeier valley of South Tyrol, where the river Passer tumbles down from the high Alps toward Merano through a corridor of apple orchards, steep meadows and farms that cling to terraces. The village is small and wooden-balconied, with a church tower and a handful of inns, and the people speak German with a Tyrolean twang, though the signs are Italian as well, as it is San Leonardo in Passiria on the map. The valley belongs to Italy, but its heart is Tyrolean, a fact that locals do not forget.

The great local hero is Andreas Hofer, born in 1767 at the Sandhof, an inn a short distance from the village. An innkeeper and cattle dealer, he led the Tyrolean uprising of 1809 against the Bavarian and French armies, winning several battles on the Bergisel above Innsbruck before the cause collapsed. He was betrayed, captured and shot in Mantua in 1810, and became a symbol of Tyrolean freedom. A museum at the Sandhof tells his story, and his name appears on pubs, statues and songs across the region.

For riders, St Leonhard is the foot of two notable passes. Southward, the road leads to Merano, a spa town with palm trees and a mild climate, but northward it climbs to Moos, then the Timmelsjoch, at about twenty-four hundred and seventy metres, crossing into Austria's Ötztal. The Timmelsjoch is a toll road, with a good surface, long ramps and hairpins that open to wide views of rock and snowfields, and a museum of the old mountain trade at the top. It is closed by snow from late autumn to late spring. The Jaufenpass, around two thousand metres, links the valley with Vipiteno, with a smooth rhythm of bends through spruce forest.

Fuel is easy to find in the larger villages of the valley, and Merano and Vipiteno are the main towns. The weather in the Alps changes fast, with cold and fog at the top even in July, so pack a warm layer. The best months are June to September. Local food, such as speck, dumplings and apple strudel, makes a sound reward at an inn after the ride.
t.stanzach@47.4,10.6:
Stanzach is a small village in the Lechtal, the long valley of the Lech river in Tyrol, and the river is the making of it. The Lech here is still wild, with a broad bed of pale gravel, braided channels and shifting banks that change after every flood, and conservationists have protected it as part of the Tyrolean Lech Nature Park, because few Alpine rivers still run free in this way. Kingfishers, dippers and the rare little ringed plover nest on the gravel, and in spring the water is the colour of milky jade. Hikers on the Lechweg, a long-distance footpath, pass through the village.

The village itself is little more than a cluster of farmhouses and a church, with painted facades and flower boxes, and is a classic Tyrolean settlement, quiet and tidy. A few guesthouses offer bed and breakfast, and a bakery or two has fresh bread in the morning. In the Middle Ages this valley was a trade route and a place for timber rafting, with logs floated downstream to the plains, and the old rafting trade left traces in names and customs.

For riders, Stanzach is the start of the Namlos Valley road, a narrow, lightly used route that leaves the main road and climbs a side valley in a series of bends through spruce and pine forest, past waterfalls and old farms, toward Namlos and Berwang. It is a road for taking slowly: the width is limited, the surface can be patchy with gravel on corners, and cows and cyclists share the tarmac. In return it is peaceful, and the views of the limestone peaks of the Lechtal Alps are magnificent. In spring, meltwater turns the side streams into torrents, and in winter the road may be closed or icy.

Weather can change quickly in the mountains, with afternoon showers in summer. The best months are June to September, when the roads are clear and the valley is green.
t.namlos@47.4,10.7:
Namlos is a village at the head of a long, quiet side valley in the Lechtal Alps of Tyrol, and the road that leads to it is the reason to come. It is one of the smallest places on the map, a handful of farms and houses at an altitude of more than a thousand metres, with steep forested slopes and limestone peaks around. There is no through traffic, because the valley ends in a cul-de-sac of mountains, apart from the road across to Berwang, which makes it a ride that few visitors know about.

The road, which leaves the Lech valley near Stanzach, follows the Namlos stream up a narrow gorge. It is a twisting, single-lane road in places, with passing places, steep slopes, and a surface that is mostly good but can be patched and broken in the spring. The corners are tight, and you need to take them slowly, because you never know what lies around them, whether it is a tractor, a herd of cows or a cyclist. The reward is the quiet, the trees, the sound of water, and the sense of a place that has been left alone.

The Lechtal Alps are part of a nature park, one of the largest in Austria, which protects the wild upper Lech river, one of the last free-flowing rivers in the Alps. The gravel banks and braided channels are a rare habitat, supporting birds such as the little ringed plover and plants that depend on the shifting riverbed. The meadows in the side valleys are full of wildflowers in June and July, and the forests hold deer, chamois and, in the high crags, ibex.

Farming here is traditional, with hay cut by hand on the steepest slopes, and cows driven up to the alpine pastures in summer. The cheese made on these alps is excellent, and a mountain inn may offer a plate of cheese and bacon with dark bread.

Services are minimal in the village itself, and fuel is not available. Reutte, a town of about seven thousand to the north, and Imst, to the south, have proper stations, and it is wise to fill up before you climb. Carry water, a rain jacket and a little cash. Early morning and late afternoon are the best times, and snow can close the road in winter.
t.berwang@47.4,10.7:
Berwang sits on a high, sunny terrace above the Lech valley, at about 1,300 metres, a village of wooden chalets and green meadows, with the long ridge of the Lechtal Alps behind and the great bulk of the Zugspitze, Germany's highest mountain, visible to the north-east. It is part of the Zugspitz Arena, a ski and hiking region that spans the border of Tyrol and Bavaria, and the village is a good deal busier than its neighbour Namlos, with hotels, a few shops and lifts.

The mood is quiet and rural. In summer, cows graze on the meadows, and walkers set out for the ridges, while in winter, snow covers everything and the village becomes a small family ski centre. Berwang has a modest charm, with a simple church and a long main street, and the houses are decorated with painted shutters and window boxes full of geraniums. The people here are proud of their alpine traditions, and in spring and autumn, the cattle drives from and to the high pastures, with the cows decorated with flowers, are a spectacle.

The road from Namlos to Berwang, a pass of sorts, climbs through forest and open meadows, with good views and gentle curves, and is a quiet link between two valleys. Down the other side, the road drops toward Bichlbach and Heiterwang, passing the lake of Heiterwang, which is warm enough for swimming in summer. It is easy riding, with fair surfaces and moderate traffic, though in the high season, cyclists and walkers share the road, and the occasional tractor slows the pace. Weather in the area can change quickly, and fog and rain are common in spring and autumn.

For the curious, the region has fine history close by.
