The castles of Neuschwanstein and Hohenschwangau, built for the Bavarian kings in the nineteenth century, lie just across the border near Füssen, about thirty kilometres away. The Fernpass, a major route between Bavaria and the Inn valley, passes nearby, and Ehrwald, at the foot of the Zugspitz, has a cable car to the summit.

Reutte, nine kilometres away, is the nearest large town, and has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. The village itself has a few places for a coffee and cake, and a hearty mountain lunch. Fill up in Reutte before heading into the hills, and bring a layer, as the evenings are cool.
t.reutte@47.5,10.7:
Reutte lies in a broad basin where the Lech valley opens and the mountains step back, a town of under seven thousand in the Außerfern, the part of Tyrol that is cut off from the rest of the province by the Alps and is connected more easily with Bavaria than with Innsbruck. For centuries the town was a stop on the trade route between Italy and southern Germany, and it grew rich on the carriage trade and on the road that crossed the Fern Pass. Its long main street, Untermarkt, still has old merchants' houses with painted facades and ornate oriel windows, and the market feel remains.

Above the town, on the ridge, stand the ruins of Ehrenberg, a castle that once guarded the road to the pass, built in the Middle Ages and extended over centuries. Its crumbling walls are linked by a modern footbridge, the Highline179, a suspension bridge about four hundred metres long, which hangs high over the valley between the ruins and a neighbouring fortress, and is among the longest of its type in the world. You can walk across it, with a view of the valley far below, and the wire mesh underfoot lets you see through.

For riders, Reutte is a crossroads with excellent roads in every direction. North, the border with Germany is a few minutes away, with Füssen and the fairy-tale castle of Neuschwanstein about twenty kilometres off, though the route is often crowded with tourists. East, the Fern Pass road climbs to a small, green lake and over the divide toward Imst, with long bends and fine views. West, the road follows the Lech into the Lechtal, and south-west, the Tannheimer Tal is a flat, wide glacial valley ringed with peaks, one of the prettiest in the Alps. Surfaces are generally excellent, and traffic is moderate except on summer weekends.

Fuel is easy in Reutte, which has several stations and supermarkets, so it is the place to fill up before the mountain roads. The Plansee, a clear, green lake a few kilometres west, is good for a rest and a swim in warm weather. Spring and autumn are quieter and lovely, while winter brings snow and the need for caution.
t.spittal an der drau@46.8,13.5:
Spittal an der Drau lies in the broad valley of the Drau in Upper Carinthia, at the foot of the Goldeck mountain, and it is the main town of the region, a busy crossroads of roads and railways between Salzburg, Villach and the Italian border. Its centrepiece is Schloss Porcia, a Renaissance palace of the sixteenth century, built for a wealthy nobleman, Gabriel von Salamanca, and later passed to the Porcia family, whose name it carries. The courtyard, with its three storeys of graceful arcades in pale stone, is regarded as one of the finest Renaissance courtyards north of the Alps, and in summer it is used for open-air theatre and concerts.

The old centre is small but pleasant, with pastel houses, arcaded shops and a pedestrian street, and a few cafes where locals meet in the afternoon. A little to the north-west lies the Millstätter See, a long, clear lake that is warm enough for swimming in summer and is ringed by villas, beaches and the resort of Seeboden. Above the town, a cable car climbs the Goldeck to a viewing platform and hiking trails, with views across the Drau valley to the Hohe Tauern and the Carnic Alps.

For riders, Spittal is the start of the road up to the Katschberg. The route follows the Lieser river, then climbs over the pass, at about sixteen hundred and forty metres, into Salzburg's Lungau region, with a good surface, regular bends and a rhythm that suits a smooth, steady ride. The motorway runs under the mountain through a tunnel, which leaves the old road quiet. The pass is usually open all year, though snow and ice are possible in winter. Beyond it, the road continues toward Obertauern and the Radstädter Tauern, a classic Alpine crossing.

Fuel is easy in Spittal, a town of nearly thirteen thousand, with stations along the main roads and supermarkets, so it is the place to fill the tank before the pass. Local food includes Kärntner Kasnudeln, large, crimped dumplings filled with cheese and herbs, which are served with melted butter. The best months are June to September, when the lake is warm.
t.katschberg pass@47.1,13.6:
The Katschberg is a modest pass in height, at 1,641 metres, but a serious one in character, since the old road over it has some of the steepest gradients on a main route in Austria. It links Carinthia with the Salzburg region of Lungau, crossing the ridge between the Lieser valley and the upper Mur, and for centuries it was an important crossing for traders and pilgrims. Today, most traffic uses the long tunnel beneath it, part of the Tauern motorway, which leaves the old road quiet and a good deal more rewarding.

The climb from the Carinthian side is steep, with sustained gradients that make a heavy bike work, and a series of tight bends through spruce forest. At the top, the landscape opens into a high basin of meadows and woods, with a small ski resort, a few hotels and a chapel. On the Salzburg side, the road drops into the Lungau, a high, quiet region of wide valleys and old villages, often called the Austrian Siberia because it gets very cold in winter. Frost can occur here in any month, which is a good reason to wear a warm layer.

Lungau has its own traditions, and one of them is the Samson parade, in which huge figures of the biblical giant are carried through the villages by men in costume during the summer festivals, accompanied by brass bands. It is recognised by UNESCO as part of the world's intangible cultural heritage, and it is a joyful, slightly surreal sight. The Mur river, which rises in the nearby Tauern mountains, flows through the region and on to Slovenia and Croatia.

Nature is abundant. The forests hold red deer and capercaillie, and the high pastures are full of alpine flowers in early summer. The air is clear, and in autumn, the larches turn gold on the slopes. The weather can change quickly, and snow can close the road in winter, or make chains necessary.

Services at the pass are limited, though a few hotels serve coffee and food in season. For fuel, St Michael im Lungau, about five kilometres from here, has stations and shops, and Spittal an der Drau, thirty kilometres away on the Carinthian side, is much larger. Rennweg, closer to the pass, has a few basic services. From here, the road continues toward Obertauern and its high pass, making a fine loop.
t.mauterndorf@47.1,13.7:
Mauterndorf sits in the Lungau, the high, bowl-shaped basin in the far south-east corner of Salzburg province, where the Taurach river collects itself before heading north. You arrive here with the Niedere Tauern behind you and the Katschberg ahead, and the basin floor is already over a thousand metres up, which is why winters here are properly cold and why the light on a clear September morning feels so thin and bright.

The village is dominated by its castle, a medieval pile that has been owned by Salzburg's archbishops, a string of noble families and, in the early twentieth century, a wealthy doctor who restored it and brought up his godson there. That godson was Hermann Göring, which is the sort of footnote the village tends to mention quietly, if at all. The castle today is open to visitors, and the old market square below it, with its painted facades and fountain, is a pleasant place to park the bike and walk in boots that are slightly too warm.

Mauterndorf is a crossroads rather than a destination in itself. The old trade road over the Radstädter Tauern runs north from here, and the road east climbs to the Katschberg pass, about 1,640 metres, on its way into Carinthia. Both are well graded and easy to enjoy: wide enough for a bit of rhythm, steep enough to keep you honest on the hairpins, and usually busy with campervans in July. If you want the road to yourself, aim for the early part of the day or the weeks either side of the main holiday rush.

For practical matters, the village is small, about twelve hundred people, so treat fuel as something to confirm rather than assume. Sankt Michael im Lungau, five kilometres away, is the larger neighbour and sits on the Tauern motorway, which makes it the safer bet for a full tank before the passes. For food, this is potato country: the Lungauer Eachtling, a local potato variety, turns up on menus in dumplings and dishes that taste far better after a cold ride than they sound.

Stay a little longer than you planned if the weather is clear. The ring of high peaks around the basin catches the evening light well, and the air smells of cut grass and woodsmoke, which is about as good as a rest stop gets.
t.obertauern@47.2,13.6:
Obertauern is not so much a village as a ski resort that happens to be built exactly on the summit of a pass. At 1,738 metres on the Radstädter Tauern, the buildings crowd along the road in a long ribbon, hotels and chalets pressed tight to the tarmac because there is simply nowhere else to put them. In summer it is quiet, a bit hollow, with shutters half closed and the cable cars still. In winter it is one of the snowiest places in Austria, and the road itself stays open through the whole season, usually with chains required for cars and, for you, a firm decision to stay at home.

The crossing has been in use for a very long time. Romans used a route over these mountains, and medieval traders carried salt, wine and iron across them, so what you ride today follows a path that has been worn in for two thousand years. The modern road, the B99, was engineered with that history in mind: it is a proper mountain road with generous radii, a couple of long runs of hairpins on each flank and a surface that tends to be good, though the freeze and thaw leave the odd patch to watch for on the shaded sections.

Fans of a certain age will know the place from the film Help!, because the Beatles came here in 1965 to shoot the snowy scenes. Locals have not forgotten it, and the connection still gets a mention in the resort's marketing, even if the motorcycles on the terraces today outnumber the people looking for John, Paul, George and Ringo.

Fuel is the one thing the pass does not guarantee. Zederhaus and Forstau are the nearest villages, both small, and the real choices for a full tank are Mauterndorf on the south side or Radstadt and Bischofshofen on the north. Fill up before you go up. Coffee and a hot meal, on the other hand, are easy; the resort's hotels and cafes are built for people who arrive cold and wet, and they handle riders without fuss.

Come on a dry weekday morning if you can. The upper part of the road has big open views of bare rock and grass slopes, the wind can pick up quickly at the summit, and a light jacket under your shell will earn its keep even in August.
t.radstadt@47.4,13.5:
Radstadt is a little walled town in the Enns valley, on the border of Salzburg and Styria, and it is one of the few places in Austria where the medieval town walls are still standing in good order. Towers, a moat and long stretches of wall from the thirteenth century enclose a rectangle of narrow streets with painted houses, a parish church and a market square, and the gates are still the way in. The town held out against a siege of rebellious peasants during the uprising of 1525 and 1526, when the countryside around the Salzburg lands rose against its prince-archbishop, which is the proudest story of the place.

The mountains around are the other half of the character. To the south, the road climbs toward Obertauern, a ski resort at the top of the Radstädter Tauern pass, which carries the old road over the Alps toward Carinthia. Obertauern is known for reliable snow and, to film fans, for the scenes shot there in 1965 for the Beatles film Help!, which brought a touch of the sixties to the pass. In summer the village is quiet, with cowbells and the smell of cut hay.

For riders, the Tauern road is the highlight. It leaves the Enns valley and climbs in a series of wide bends and several hairpins through spruce forest to the pass, at about seventeen hundred and forty metres, then drops into the Lungau, with a smooth surface and a steady gradient that makes it a favourite among motorcyclists. Weekends see plenty of bikes, so there can be congestion on the climb, and the pass can have snow from late autumn to spring. Fog and sudden showers are common, so carry a rain layer.

Radstadt has a handful of fuel stations on the road through the valley, plus supermarkets and bakeries, and it is a sensible place to fill up before heading over the Tauern. The nearest larger town is Bischofshofen, nineteen kilometres away. Local cafes serve coffee and cake, and in the small restaurants you can try Pinzgau-style dishes with cheese and dumplings. The best months are June to September.
t.partenen@47.0,10.1:
Partenen is the last proper village at the head of the Montafon, the long valley that runs south-east from Bludenz toward the Silvretta range. After here the valley narrows, the trees close in and the road starts to climb toward the high lakes. It is a small place, a scatter of farmhouses and guest houses along the Ill, with the mountains standing so close that the sun arrives late and leaves early.

Most riders know Partenen as the gate to the Silvretta High Alpine Road. The toll booth sits just up the hill, and the ride begins in earnest as soon as you pass it, with a long climb of tight, regular hairpins that gain height quickly through spruce forest and then out into open ground. It is one of those roads that is more satisfying going up than coming down, because the bends are cut into the slope with generous room and the surface is smooth enough for a smooth line. Out of season the road is closed by snow, so check the dates before planning a day around it.

Next to the village stands a small cable railway, the Vermuntbahn, which carries hikers up to the Vermunt reservoir, and above that there is a network of hydroelectric works that has shaped this valley since the early twentieth century. Water is the main economy here besides tourism: the Illwerke built dams and power stations through the Montafon, and much of the electricity that lights western Austria has passed through these slopes. It is easy to miss from the road, but the pipes, tunnels and reservoirs are all part of the landscape you are riding through.

The Montafon has a character of its own, with dark timber houses, steep farm meadows and a dialect that visitors from Vienna struggle with. You can eat well in Partenen, with hearty mountain food, strong coffee and, if you are lucky, a slice of cake that has clearly been made that morning.

For fuel, do not count on the village. Gaschurn, a few kilometres back down the valley, is the more reliable stop, and Schruns further down is larger still. Fill before you climb, because the next sure thing is on the other side of the pass, and Galtür is not big.
t.bielerhohe@46.9,10.1:
The Bielerhöhe is the high point of the Silvretta High Alpine Road, a broad saddle at 2,032 metres where Vorarlberg meets Tyrol and where the water changes its mind about where it wants to go. Rain that falls on the western side runs into the Ill and the Rhine, eventually reaching the North Sea; rain on the eastern side drains into the Trisanna, the Inn and the Danube, and finally the Black Sea. Standing at the top, with a lake beside you, it is satisfying to know you are on a European watershed.

The lake is the Silvretta reservoir, held back by a rockfill dam, and its still surface mirrors the peaks on a calm morning. The big mountain across the water is Piz Buin, at 3,312 metres the highest in Vorarlberg, and around it the Silvretta glaciers are shrinking each year, though from here they still look convincingly white against the grey rock. A footpath runs along the dam and down towards the Wiesbadener Hütte, and you can see walkers setting off on routes that continue into Switzerland.

The road was opened in the 1950s, built primarily to serve the hydroelectric project, and it still feels like a utility road with ambitions. There are around thirty hairpins on the Montafon side, laid out with a clear logic, and the east side drops more gently toward Galtür and the Paznaun valley. Tolls are collected, traffic is light by Alpine standards, and the surface has the slightly polished feel of a road that is well looked after. It closes with the first serious snow and reopens when the plough has done its work, normally from late spring to autumn.

Weather here is not to be trusted. The altitude means that a warm day in the valley can be five or six degrees colder at the summit, the wind blows hard off the water, and clouds can arrive from nowhere. Dress for a mountain top even if the morning looked mild.

There is a hotel-restaurant at the top, which is useful for a coffee and a hot meal while you warm your hands. Galtür is the closest village with services, and the larger choices, Gaschurn and Landeck, are further away than you might think when the tank is low. Davos lies to the south-west on the Swiss side, across several mountain ranges and a border that is not a short detour.
t.galtur@47.0,10.2:
Galtür stands at about 1,600 metres at the head of the Paznaun valley, and the first thing you notice is a concrete wall. It is long, curved and tall, and it was built after the avalanche of February 1999, when a wall of snow roared down into the village and killed thirty-one people. The wall now shields the centre, and a museum beside it, the Alpinarium, tells the story of the disaster and, more broadly, of living under snow. It is a serious place, and a thoughtful stop even for riders who normally only want coffee.

The village itself has recovered with quiet dignity. The church, the old farmhouses and the gardens still have the look of a high mountain community, and the rhythm of the place is set by the seasons: ski traffic in winter, hikers and riders in summer, and a lull in November when everything shuts for a rest. The Trisanna river runs beside the village, a pale grey-green stream fed by glaciers that you can see from the road in clear weather.

The riding here is the eastern half of the Silvretta High Alpine Road. Coming from the Bielerhöhe, you descend a gentler, wider road than the Montafon side, with longer straights between the bends and big views down the valley. Out of the village, the road continues toward Ischgl and Landeck along the Trisanna, a fast, pleasant run with a few tunnels and some tight stretches where the valley closes in. In the evening the shadows lengthen early, so you may be riding in cold air long before sunset.

It is worth remembering how remote Galtür feels. It has a population of under eight hundred, and though it is not a small village in tourist terms, with plenty of beds, it is a long way from any large town. Ischgl is nine kilometres down the valley and has services, but anything bigger means a drive to Landeck or over the border. Check your fuel before committing to the high road.

Eat at one of the traditional inns if you can. Tyrolean dishes like Kaspressknödel, cheese dumplings in broth, are the right size for the end of a cold day, and the beer, brewed somewhere down the valley, is honest and cold.
t.innerkrems@47.0,13.8:
Innerkrems is the top end of the Krems valley, a scatter of farms, hotels and ski lifts at around fifteen hundred metres in the Nockberge, the rounded green mountains of western Carinthia. Unlike the sharp limestone of the Dolomites or the glaciated peaks of the Hohe Tauern, the Nocks are soft, grassy domes, shaped by ice and worn smooth, and they roll away in every direction like waves frozen in place. They are protected as a biosphere reserve, a landscape of alpine pasture, dwarf pine, lakes and stone huts that is among the gentlest in the Alps.

The great road here is the Nockalmstraße, the Nockalm Road, a toll route built in the 1980s to make the highland accessible without wrecking it, thirty-odd kilometres long with more than fifty hairpins. It runs between Innerkrems and Ebene Reichenau, climbing to the Eisentalhöhe, the highest point at about two thousand and forty metres, with views across the domes to the Hohe Tauern on the horizon. Marmots whistle in the screes, golden eagles circle, and cattle and sheep graze on the high pastures. The toll is charged per vehicle, with motorcycles paying a lower fee, and the road is usually open from May to October, depending on snow.

Riding it is a delight. The surface is smooth and well maintained, the bends are well engineered with good visibility, and the gradient is moderate, so it is a road to enjoy rather than endure. The road is popular with riders, so avoid peak weekends in July and August if you want space, and watch for cyclists, who also love it. Weather at altitude changes quickly, with fog, wind and cold even in summer, so carry layers. In early summer, patches of snow may linger by the road.

The mountain huts serve simple food, such as Kasnudeln and soup, and a glass of Almdudler, an alpine herbal soda. The best months are late June to September, when the pastures are green and the weather mostly stable.
t.eisentalhohe@46.9,13.8:
At 2,042 metres, the Eisentalhöhe is the highest point on the Nockalm Road, and it earns the title in a gentle way. There are no needle peaks here, no glaciers hanging on a cliff. The Nockberge are rounded, grassy mountains, the sort that look like sleeping animals under a blanket, and the road crosses them in a succession of curves that feels almost private, as if the mountains had been designed for riding.

The route is a toll road, opened in 1981 after years of argument between those who wanted a tourist highway and those who wanted the high pastures left alone. Today the Nockberge is a biosphere park, and the road is the compromise: a ribbon with fifty-two hairpins that gives access to alpine meadows without cutting them to pieces. Cattle graze on the slopes through summer, sometimes wandering across the tarmac, so a bit of attention in the bends is sensible. In late June the grass is green and full of wildflowers, in September it turns a golden brown, and by October the road may already be closed.

The Zirbe, the Swiss stone pine, is the tree of these mountains. Its wood has a sweet, resinous smell that locals prize for furniture and for bedrooms, and its twisted shapes in the high pasture mark the treeline. If you stop and breathe, the air up here has a faint pine scent mixed with cut grass and sun-warmed stone.

From the summit, the view is a long, slow roll of ridges extending in every direction, with the Hohe Tauern further away to the west and the Carinthian lakes somewhere beyond the haze to the south. On a clear day it is wonderful, and in cloud it is a lonely place, so go when the forecast is kind.

Petrol is not sold on the summit, and the nearest service stations are in the valleys: Radenthein, about fourteen kilometres away, is a modest town, and Spittal an der Drau is the bigger one on the Drau river. Top the tank in the valley first, since this is a ride that takes longer than the map suggests. The huts along the road serve food and coffee, and some do a very good Kaiserschmarrn, the shredded pancake that Austrians believe is a complete meal.
t.schiestelscharte@46.9,13.8:
A Scharte is a notch in a ridge, and the Schiestelscharte, at about 2,024 metres, is one of the notches the Nockalm Road threads through on its way across the Nockberge. It sits only a little lower than the Eisentalhöhe, a few kilometres away, and the two are often grouped together, but the character is different: the Schiestelscharte feels more exposed, with the hillside opening out suddenly and the road swinging round the shoulder of a ridge.

Riding it is a pleasure in the same way that a good stretch of coastline is a pleasure, because the road keeps offering something new without requiring anything demanding. The bends are wide and well banked, the surface is smooth, and the gradient is moderate, so you can concentrate on the views. In the early morning the light comes in low from the east and the slopes are striped with shadow, and in the late afternoon the grass turns a warm gold. There is very little traffic at either end of the day.

The area is protected as part of the Nockberge biosphere park, and the pastures are still worked by farmers who bring their cattle up each summer. You might see a herd wandering across a slope, hear bells in the distance and, if you stop, catch the faint smell of dung and hay that belongs to every Alpine pasture. The soil here is mostly crystalline rock, which gives the landscape its soft contours, quite unlike the sharp limestone of the Dolomites or the Salzkammergut.

Keep an eye on the weather. At this altitude the clouds can sit down on the ridge and the temperature falls fast when they do. The road is a toll road and closes for the winter, normally from the first heavy snow until late spring, so check before you travel.

Radenthein, about twelve kilometres away, is the closest town of any size, and Döbriach on the Millstätter See has a few services. For anything larger, Spittal an der Drau is the destination. Mountain huts along the road serve coffee, soup and cake, and a quick stop at one of them is the best way to warm up before the descent, when the road drops through the forest and the air gets noticeably warmer.
t.ebene reichenau@46.8,13.9:
Ebene Reichenau lies in the Gurk valley of Carinthia, at the lower gate of the Nockalm Road, and it is where the toll booth sits across the road, with a car park and a cafe beside it. The village is small, with wooden farmhouses and a church spire, and the fresh air, the sound of a stream and the smell of mown hay make it feel far from anywhere. It lies at about eleven hundred metres, so the climb to the top of the Nocks, which begins right behind the village, has about a thousand metres of height to gain.

This side of the biosphere reserve has a different feel from Innerkrems. The first hairpins climb steeply through spruce forest with little to see but trunks and sky, then break out onto open alpine pastures, where the road swings in great loops across grassy slopes and the distant peaks come into view. Sheep bells, wooden fences and old hay huts add to the picture. Everything is on a gentle scale, and the road is wide enough for two vehicles. The rolling shape of the Nocks gives the sense of riding on the back of some enormous sleeping animal.

Nearby, the pass of Turracher Höhe, to the east, is another well-known road, famous for its steep gradients and the little lake at the top. To the south, Bad Kleinkirchheim is a spa and ski resort with hot springs and a golf course, with roads leading down toward Villach and the Italian border. In this area, the Alpine climate means cold nights, thunderstorms in the afternoon and fog in the early morning. Check the forecast before you pay the toll, since riding the Nockalm in cloud is a waste of the view.

There is no reliable fuel in the village, and the nearest large town is Lind, twenty-five kilometres away, so top up beforehand, in Feld am See or in Bad Kleinkirchheim. The cafe by the toll booth serves coffee and cake, and local farm shops sell cheese and bacon. The best months are June to September, with peak colour in early autumn when the larches turn gold.
t.fuschlsee@47.8,13.3:
Fuschlsee is the first lake you meet when you ride east out of Salzburg toward the Salzkammergut, and it makes a good first impression. It is small, about four kilometres long, and its water is so clean and clear that it has a reputation as nearly drinkable. The shore is lined with forest and a few elegant buildings, with hills rising behind, and on a calm morning the whole scene sits in the water like a second world turned upside down.

The village of Fuschl am See has about fifteen hundred residents and a lakeside promenade, and it is also the home of the Red Bull company, whose headquarters are a modern building a short distance from the water. That is a curious contrast with the old castle, Schloss Fuschl, a former hunting lodge that is now a hotel and stands on a small peninsula, looking as if it has been waiting for a film crew since the 1950s.

The road here, the B158, is a mix of fast, flowing sections and slower village stretches. It rolls along the lake with gentle curves and small climbs, and on a weekday morning it is a delight, with the water flashing through the trees. At weekends and in July and August it can be slow, with caravans, cyclists and day-trippers from Salzburg. If you can, go early or go late, or time your visit for the weeks in May and September when the weather is still good and the crowds have not arrived.

You can swim from public access points on the lakeshore in summer, and the water is cold enough to wake you up even in August. There are cafes by the water, mostly informal, which do coffee and cake and a decent fish sandwich. Local trout and char are the specialties, caught in the lakes of the region.

For fuel, the village is small, but Salzburg is only about nineteen kilometres away, with every service you could want. Hallein is another option to the south. Fill the tank before you go too deep into the lake district, because the roads past St Gilgen and on to Bad Ischl are scenic but not densely served.
t.rovinj@45.1,13.6:
Rovinj was an island once, and it still behaves like one. The old town sits on a rounded rock, a peninsula that was joined to the mainland by filling in a channel in 1763, and every street climbs steeply toward the top, where the church of Saint Euphemia stands with its tall bell tower. The tower, about sixty metres high, was modelled on St Mark's campanile in Venice, and it is topped by a copper statue of the saint that turns with the wind. From the foot of the hill, the town looks like a pile of pastel-coloured houses, red roofs and narrow lanes tumbling into the harbour.

The Venetians ruled Rovinj for more than five hundred years, from the late thirteenth century until the fall of the republic in 1797, and the town still has a strong Italian flavour. Many of the street signs are bilingual, Italian is widely spoken among locals, and the old customs of fishing and boat-building continue in the harbour. The wooden fishing boats called batanas, flat-bottomed and painted in bright colours, are on the local heritage list, and an eco-museum celebrates them. Saint Euphemia, whose marble sarcophagus is said to have drifted ashore here in the ninth century, is still the town's patron.

The streets of the old town are cobbled, steep and slippery, and no place for a motorcycle, so park at the edge and walk. The best views are from the harbour, from the church terrace, and from the Golden Cape, or Zlatni Rt, a forested peninsula south of the town with pine woods, picnic spots and rocky coves for swimming. In summer the town is packed with visitors, and the narrow alleys fill with artists selling paintings, cafés and ice cream stalls. Early morning and evening are the best times, and spring and autumn are much quieter.

The riding in the Istrian interior is excellent, with good roads, little traffic and a gentle rhythm of hills, vineyards and olive groves. From Rovinj, roads lead inland to villages such as Bale and Svetvinčenat, with their old walls and loggias. Istria is known for its truffles, olive oil, and wines, particularly the white Malvazija and the red Teran, as well as prosciutto and fresh seafood. Cafés and konobas, the small family taverns, line the harbour and the back streets.

Rovinj is a proper town with about thirteen thousand people, and it has fuel stations, supermarkets and all services. Fill up here before heading into the hills, where villages are small and stations are sparse.
t.groznjan@45.4,13.7:
Grožnjan, called Grisignana in Italian, is a hill town with fewer than a thousand people, and it has been rescued from decline by an unusual idea. After the Second World War and the departure of much of the Italian population, the village was left half empty and crumbling. In the 1960s, artists were invited to take over the abandoned houses as studios, and the town became a colony of painters, sculptors and potters. A summer music school, run by Jeunesses Musicales, brings young musicians from around the world, and in July and August the narrow streets fill with the sound of violins, pianos and singing from open windows.

The town sits on a ridge about two hundred and fifty metres above the valley of the Mirna river, with a long view across rolling green and brown hills toward the Adriatic and, on clear days, the Alps. Its old walls, gate and loggia date from the Venetian period, when Istria was part of the republic's territory, and the church and bell tower in the centre are simple and handsome. The stone houses along the cobbled lanes are now galleries and craft shops, selling paintings, ceramics and jewellery, as well as truffle products and local wine. The pace is slow, and the atmosphere is relaxed.

The roads leading up to Grožnjan are among the best in Istria for riding. They wind through woods of oak and hornbeam, past vineyards and olive groves, and across the open plateau, with gentle curves and smooth surfaces. Traffic is light, except at weekends in summer, when day visitors arrive. The village itself is closed to cars, so you park at the edge and walk. The inland hills are cooler and quieter than the coast, and in autumn the vineyards turn red and gold. Spring brings fresh green and wild flowers, and the evenings are mild.

The surrounding landscape is the heart of truffle country. The forests of the Mirna valley, near Motovun, produce the white truffle, which is hunted by trained dogs in autumn, and the black truffle, found in summer. Restaurants in the area serve truffles with pasta, eggs and local cheese. The wine here is mostly Malvazija, a crisp, aromatic white, and Teran, a robust red.

For fuel, Buje, about six kilometres from the village, has a station and a few shops, and Umag on the coast is a larger town with supermarkets. Grožnjan has a few cafés and konobas, though opening hours depend on the season. Visit on a weekday if you can, in the evening when the light is best.
t.porec@45.2,13.6:
Poreč finishes the Istrian ride on the west coast, and it does it with a small old town laid out on a peninsula by the Romans. The grid of streets is still there: the Decumanus, the main street, runs straight along the spine of the old centre, and it is paved in smooth worn stone that is slippery after rain, so walk rather than ride. With about ten thousand residents, Poreč is big enough to have everything a rider needs, and since it is a top holiday destination, in high season it is also loud, crowded and slow.

The reason to linger is the Euphrasian Basilica, a sixth-century church that survives with its Byzantine mosaics intact, and for that reason is a UNESCO World Heritage site. The gold mosaics of the apse are dazzling and the atrium is quiet. Venice ruled this coast for centuries, and you see it in the little palaces and the Gothic windows along the lanes. Local life sits on the waterfront, where fishing boats have to compete with ferries and pleasure craft for space.

Having ridden through the red-earth hills of the interior, you notice how different the coast feels: pine trees, limestone, a flat blue Adriatic and warm air that smells of resin. The coastal road north and south is busy in July and August, with caravans and tourists on rental scooters, and you will want to ride early. Inland, a few kilometres away, the traffic thins to almost nothing and the villages like Tar and Funtana give you a view of how Istria used to be: stone houses, vineyards, fig trees.

Practical things are easy. Poreč has fuel stations on its approaches, supermarkets, and a long line of restaurants where Istrian staples turn up: fresh fish, truffle pasta, the local prosciutto and a dry Malvazija white wine. Prices are higher on the waterfront and kinder a street back. Late September is a good moment to arrive, when the sea is still warm, the crowds have gone home, and the grape harvest begins in the hills behind you.
t.san martino di castrozza@46.3,11.8:
San Martino di Castrozza lies in a green basin in the Trentino Dolomites, at about 1,450 metres, with the Pale di San Martino rising behind it in a wall of pale, jagged rock. The Pale group is one of the most dramatic in the Dolomites, a high limestone plateau with towers and spires that glow pink at sunrise and sunset, the enrosadira that people travel far to see. The town grew up as a mountain resort in the nineteenth century, and today it is a base for walkers, climbers and skiers, with hotels, cafes and a small church dating from the earlier hospice that once stood here for pilgrims and travellers.

The town sits on the road between Primiero and the Rolle Pass. It is an old route, used for centuries to move cattle and timber, and the hospice was founded to give shelter to people crossing the high ground. Siror, Tonadico and Fiera di Primiero lie further down the valley, and these villages keep the older stone-and-wood look that tourist development has smoothed in San Martino itself. The nearest bigger towns with a full range of services are found in the valleys, though San Martino has fuel and supplies.

The riding here is a pleasure. Up toward Passo Rolle, at about 1,980 metres, the road climbs through spruce forest with long, well-surfaced curves and open meadows at the top, where the view back to the Pale is stunning. In the other direction, the road drops down through the Primiero valley with a series of bends that keep a rider busy. Traffic builds in July and August, especially at weekends, and bikers share the road with cyclists and campervans, so early starts are rewarded.

Rolle is generally open from late spring to autumn, although snow can close roads early in the season or late in the year, so check conditions. Mountain huts nearby serve polenta, cheese, speck and strudel, and the local dish canederli, bread dumplings in broth, is hearty after a cold ride. Stay in the evening if you can, because the mountains change colour as the sun goes down and the town falls quiet.
t.falcade@46.4,11.9:
Falcade is a ski village at the head of the Biois valley, in the Veneto side of the Dolomites, and it has the slightly sleepy, practical feel of a place that is much busier in January than in June. The valley is narrow and green, with steep forested slopes and, rising behind, the pale walls of the Pale di San Martino and the Marmolada group beyond. Villages along it, such as Canale d'Agordo, a few kilometres down, are small and traditional, with wooden balconies, stone fountains and churches with onion-domed or pointed towers. Canale d'Agordo is also the birthplace of Albino Luciani, who became Pope John Paul I in 1978 and died after only thirty-three days.

For riders, Falcade matters because it is the junction between two excellent passes. Heading west, the road climbs steeply to Passo San Pellegrino, while north-west the road to Passo Valles winds up through forest and meadow toward the Paneveggio area. The surface is typically good, the bends are well-engineered and the gradients are steady, but the Dolomite weather can be changeable and thunderstorms in the afternoon are common in summer. Traffic is moderate during the week and heavier at weekends and in August. Early morning rides are the most pleasant, with mist in the valley and the first sunlight on the rock.

The village has the services you might expect of a ski town: bars, bakeries, supermarkets and restaurants, and you can find simple Dolomite food such as polenta, venison, cheese and the dumplings called canederli. A sit-down lunch is easy. It is also a good place for a bed if you want to ride the passes at both ends of the day. There is fuel in the valley, but if you are in doubt, Agordo, to the south, is the larger town with several stations, and it is wise not to start a pass with the tank low.

In summer, the cable car in Falcade runs up towards the peaks, giving walkers quick access to alpine trails, and in winter the village comes alive with skiers. The lower slopes are dotted with old farmhouses and haybarns, and in June the meadows are full of wildflowers.

If you arrive in the evening, linger a moment on the main street. The light on the peaks as the sun sets is the sort of thing the Dolomites do very well.
t.passo valles@46.3,11.8:
Passo Valles is the quiet pass of the Dolomites, a ridge crossing at just over two thousand metres between Falcade and the high forests of Paneveggio, and it has none of the crowds of its famous neighbours. There are no cable cars, no big souvenir stalls and few buses, just a road that climbs steadily through spruce forest, emerges into open pasture and tops out in a landscape of grass and stone. A small refuge or bar is sometimes open near the top, but services are minimal, so bring what you need.

The road is a pleasure to ride. From the Falcade side it climbs in a rhythm of long bends, with enough hairpins to be interesting and enough straight to rest, and the surface is generally smooth and well-kept. The gradient is not extreme, and the pass is open to riders of all abilities who stay sensible. Look out for cyclists, cattle and mountain weather. Snow closes the road in winter, usually from late autumn until late spring, and even in summer the pass can be wrapped in cloud while the valley is sunny.

On the far side, the road runs down into Paneveggio, a forest of spruce that is famous in Italy as the wood from which violins were once made. The trees here grow slowly and evenly in cold conditions, giving the timber the tonal qualities that instrument makers prize, and local stories link the forest to Stradivari, though like most good legends it has more charm than evidence. The ridges of the Pale di San Martino rise to the south, and the pointed Cimon della Pala is sometimes nicknamed the Matterhorn of the Dolomites.

The nearest stations are in the Biois valley around Falcade and Canale d'Agordo, and the larger centres of Agordo and Sedico further south, and on the other side, Predazzo or Moena. Start with a full tank, because the stretch between is longer than it looks on the map.

It is a pass for early mornings and weekdays. If you arrive when the mist lifts from the forest and the light slants over the pastures, it will feel like the Dolomites before the world found them.
t.passo rolle@46.3,11.8:
Passo Rolle is one of the great classics of the Dolomites, at 1,989 metres, and the reason is not just the road but what it looks at. As you reach the top, the Pale di San Martino rear up on the southern side in a wall of pale, jagged rock, with the Cimon della Pala and the rounded Cima Vezzana lighting up in the sun. The pass connects the Fiemme valley around Predazzo with the Primiero valley and San Martino di Castrozza, and has been a crossing for centuries, used by traders and shepherds long before the road was paved.

The riding is excellent. From the Predazzo side, the road climbs through dense spruce forest with long, flowing bends and a handful of hairpins, then opens onto meadows near the top. The tarmac is good, the gradients are manageable, and the views get bigger as you rise. On the south side, the descent towards San Martino di Castrozza is exhilarating, with the great wall of rock looming ahead. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, with motorcycles, cars, cyclists and campervans sharing the road, so go early or choose a weekday if you can. Weather can change fast, and fog or storms often build in the afternoon.

The top of the pass has a hotel, a couple of bars and a car park, and there is a chair lift station nearby. Coffee and a slice of apple strudel are the natural order of business, and the buzz of other riders compares notes on lines and weather. Local specialities include polenta, cheese, mushroom dishes and speck, and prices are what you would expect of a popular Alpine pass.

Moena, about twelve kilometres away, is a larger resort town with services, and Feltre is the bigger town to the south. It is best to top up before you go over the pass, since the roads connecting are long.

This region was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire before 1918, and the front line of the First World War ran through these mountains, so the landscape is marked by trenches, forts and memorials. A quiet moment at the pass, looking at the peaks, is a good reminder of the history.
t.predazzo@46.3,11.6:
Predazzo is the largest village in the Val di Fiemme, and it has a surprisingly special place in the world of geology. The valley lies in Trentino, between the pale limestone Dolomites and the darker volcanic rock of the Latemar and Monzoni areas, and Predazzo sits on the line where these meet. Geologists have studied the rocks here since the early nineteenth century, and there is a small museum, the Museo Geologico delle Dolomiti, that explains how ancient seas, volcanoes and later uplift built the mountains. With about four thousand people, the village is large enough for fuel, supermarkets and several hotels.

The Val di Fiemme has its own history. For centuries it was governed by the Magnifica Comunità di Fiemme, a medieval community that managed the forests collectively, and its spruce was prized for violins; Stradivari is said to have chosen wood from this region. Today the valley is known for cross-country skiing, including the Marcialonga race, and for the long summers on the high pastures. The architecture is a mix of Alpine and Italian, with painted house fronts and church towers with onion roofs.

As a finish to the Rolle and Valles ride, Predazzo makes a very good landing. After the open meadows and hairpins of the passes, you come down through forest into a valley with a clear river and a lively main street. The road from Passo Rolle descends steadily, with curves that run out into easier stretches as you near the valley floor. The Valles Pass, at around 2,000 metres, is another gem, quiet and with less traffic than the better-known routes, though it can be rough in places after winter.

Food is straightforward and good. Try canederli, barley soup, local cheeses, and if you are lucky a plate of game with polenta. The evening air is cold enough for a jumper even in July. Early autumn brings golden larches and fewer people, which makes it a favourite season for riders who dislike crowds. Leave a night for Predazzo, and the next morning the Lagorai and Latemar will look like a different range.
t.trafoi@46.5,10.5:
Trafoi is the last village before the Stelvio gets serious. It sits at about fifteen hundred metres in a narrow valley in South Tyrol, and above it the wall of the Ortler massif rises in a dazzling block of snow and ice, the highest peak in the Eastern Alps at 3,905 metres. German is the first language here, with Italian a close second, and the church, the wooden balconies and the dumplings on the menu all say Tyrol rather than Lombardy. A short walk up the valley takes you to the Three Holy Springs, a pilgrimage spot where, the story goes, the Virgin appeared to a local shepherd girl in the nineteenth century, and a small chapel has stood beside the water ever since.

For riders the village is a staging post. From here the road climbs to the famous series of hairpins that lead to the Stelvio Pass, which at 2,757 metres is the second-highest paved pass in the Alps. The road was built in the 1820s by the Austrian Empire, to link its Tyrolean lands with Lombardy, and it was engineered by Carlo Donegani. The numbering of the bends, forty-eight in all on the Prato side, is a local tradition that every rider recognises. Coming up from Prato allo Stelvio, you pass through Trafoi on the way to the first of them, and the real work begins just above the last houses.

The weather decides everything. The pass is usually open from about late May or June until October, but snow can close it at short notice even in summer, and a bright morning in the valley often becomes fog, rain or hail at the top. Traffic in July and August can be enormous, with buses, cyclists and groups of motorbikes sharing narrow bends, so leave early or ride on a weekday. If you wait until midday, the queue can be longer than the view.

This is a good place to prepare. There are hotels, gasthofs and cafes in the village, with soup, cheese dumplings and apple strudel on offer, and a stop here before the climb is a good idea. Fuel is less certain. Prato allo Stelvio, about ten kilometres down the valley, has stations and larger shops, so fill there rather than hoping to find something on the mountain.

The Stelvio National Park lies all around, a protected area of glaciers, larch woods and alpine meadows where ibex and marmots live, and in the quiet hours you might see both.
t.passo sella@46.5,11.8:
Passo Sella is the pass that puts you in the middle of the Dolomites rather than at the edge of them. At 2,240 metres it connects the Val di Fassa with the Val Gardena, and it sits in a saddle between two of the great massifs of the range. To the north rises the huge, flat-topped block of the Sella group, a fortress of pale rock with vertical walls, and to the south, almost close enough to touch, are the pointed towers of the Sassolungo, called the Langkofel in German, which look like the fingers of a stone hand raised to the sky.

The road is a joy, with a perfect surface and a rhythm of bends that rises through the larches and then out into open pasture and rocky slopes. There are enough hairpins to feel like proper mountain riding, and the gradient is steady without being hard. The view at the top is the reward, where the whole panorama opens on both sides of the saddle. The pass is part of the Sella Ronda, a circuit of four passes around the massif that is a rite of passage for riders and cyclists, and in high season the road is correspondingly busy, so an early start pays off.

There are several refuges and cafes at the top, with terraces facing the rocks, and stopping for a coffee or a bowl of soup is part of the experience. The prices are mountain prices. The Ladin culture, the ancient language and traditions of the region, is visible in the place names, and in the Fassa and Gardena valleys you will hear Ladin spoken alongside Italian and German. The mountains saw heavy fighting in the First World War, and traces of those years are still found on the slopes.

Canazei, about three and a half kilometres down the Fassa side, has stations and shops, and so does Selva on the Gardena side. Plan to fill before you climb, as it is easy to burn more than expected in the thin air and the stop-start of the traffic.

The pass closes in winter, usually from autumn to late spring, and in summer the weather can change quickly, with afternoon storms common. A light waterproof and gloves are a good idea even in July. The best times are early morning, when the mountain light is clear, and the late afternoon, when the rock glows pink.
t.selva di val gardena@46.6,11.8:
Selva is the top of the Val Gardena, a long, green valley in South Tyrol that cuts into the heart of the Dolomites, and it is the place where winter sport, woodcarving and the Ladin language all meet. The village lies below the Sella massif and the jagged spires of the Sassolungo, and its houses are strung out along the stream, with meadows climbing to the forest on either side. It is known in German as Wolkenstein, after a castle ruin up the valley, and in Ladin as Sëlva, and the three names on the signs tell you something about the place before you have left the bike.

Val Gardena has been a woodcarving valley for centuries. Local families, with so little arable land and long winters, took to carving religious figures, toys and decorations, and sold them across Europe. The craft is still alive in the shops of Selva and Ortisei, with carved saints and wooden animals in the windows. The valley also hosts the famous Saslong ski course, where World Cup downhill races are held every winter, and in summer the ski lifts carry walkers and mountain bikers to high meadows.

For riders, Selva is a junction. From here, you can climb to Passo Gardena on one side and Passo Sella on the other, and the two together make half of the Sella Ronda circuit. The roads are well surfaced, with a mix of hairpins and flowing bends, and the views of the rock walls are spectacular. In summer, traffic can be heavy, and the passes fill up with bikes and cars on fine weekends, so a weekday is better. Afternoon thunderstorms are possible. The valley road is also pleasant, running down towards Ortisei and Bressanone through forests and meadows.

The village has everything a rider needs. Fuel is available in the valley, with several stations along the main road, along with supermarkets, bakeries, restaurants and hotels. A plate of canederli, dumplings made from stale bread and speck, or a bowl of barley soup is a good way to warm up, and Italian coffee is excellent as always. Many hotels cater for riders, with garages and drying rooms, and booking ahead in summer is a good idea.

Bressanone, about nineteen kilometres away, is the nearest large town and has a lovely old centre with a cathedral and arcades, and is worth a detour if you have a spare afternoon.

If the weather turns, there is plenty to do in the village, and the rock walls above give a dramatic backdrop whether they are in sunshine or cloud.
t.passo gardena@46.5,11.8:
Passo Gardena, at 2,121 metres, links Val Gardena with Alta Badia, and it is one of the four passes that circle the Sella massif. It does not have the drama of the Stelvio or the fame of the Pordoi, but it has a distinctive character: a wide, open crossing of grass and scree between the Sella on one side and the jagged Cir peaks on the other, with the road threading through a landscape that feels more intimate than grand. The Italian name is Passo Gardena, the German Grödner Joch, and in Ladin it is Jëuf de Frara.

The riding is superb. From the Selva side, the road climbs in a series of gentle bends and a few hairpins through spruce and then open pasture, and the surface is smooth and the gradient moderate. At the top, the road turns across a broad plateau before descending towards Corvara in a long series of bends with views across the Alta Badia valley. It is a pass that rewards a relaxed pace, so you can look around as well as at the road. In the morning, the light on the east-facing rock walls is warm and golden, and in the evening the shadows come early.

At the pass itself there is a handful of hotels and refuges, with a car park and terraces overlooking the meadows. Coffee, strudel and a view are the usual order of business. Cattle graze on the high pastures in summer, and sometimes wander onto the road, so keep an eye out. Walkers can follow trails from the car park into the high country, with rock formations and views in all directions.

Fuel is not available on the pass. The nearest options are down in Selva, about four kilometres away, and Corvara on the other side, so plan accordingly. Bressanone is the bigger town for any major services, but it is a fair distance away.

The Ladin people have lived in these valleys for a very long time, and their language, a Romance tongue related to Romansh in Switzerland, is protected and taught in schools. You will see it on road signs and menus, and it adds a layer of interest to the ride.

The pass closes in winter and usually reopens in spring, and even in summer, a check of the weather is wise.
t.corvara@46.6,11.9:
Corvara is the heart of Alta Badia, a village of tall chalets and church spire in a bowl of meadows with the Sella massif looming to the south and the Puez-Odle range to the north. It is one of the most popular ski resorts in the Dolomites and, in summer, one of the best bases for riders, because four passes meet within a short ride. It is also the start and finish of the Maratona dles Dolomites, a famous one-day cycling event, and on race weekends the whole village fills with cyclists in bright kit. Ladin is the local language, and signs are often in three languages, which gives the place a distinctive, mixed identity.

The riding around Corvara is as good as it gets for a lover of mountain roads. Heading south-west, the road climbs to Passo Campolongo, while to the north-west it climbs to Passo Gardena, and farther on lie the Pordoi and Sella. The surfaces are excellent, the bends well-engineered, and the views of the rock walls are constant. In summer the roads are busy, particularly on weekends and in August, so early starts and weekdays make life easier. Afternoon storms are a feature of the weather, building quickly in the heat, and the temperature at the passes can be much lower than in the valley.

The village is well provided with hotels, restaurants and shops, and the food is a happy mix of Tyrolean and Italian traditions, with dumplings, polenta and pasta all on the menu. Dolomite cooking is rich and filling, and after a day on the passes it is welcome. Pastries and good coffee are available at every turn. Fuel is available in the valley, and there are stations along the main road, but they are not everywhere, so it is best to fill before you set off on a long loop around the Sella.

Corvara also has a long history of mountain tourism, with the first ski lifts built in the early twentieth century, and the cable car to the high plateau of the Sella is a favourite with walkers. In summer, the meadows are full of wildflowers and the cow bells ring across the valley.

The best times to come are June, when the meadows are in bloom, and September, when the crowds have thinned and the air is crisp and clear.
t.passo campolongo@46.5,11.9:
Passo Campolongo is the low, easy member of the Sella Ronda family, at 1,875 metres, and it is the one that most riders cross without much ceremony. It joins Corvara in Alta Badia with Arabba in the Livinallongo valley, and the road climbs through meadows and spruce, with views of the Sella to one side and, on a clear day, the glacier of the Marmolada in the distance. The name means long field, and it describes the pass well: a broad, gentle grassy saddle rather than a sharp notch in the rock.

The road is smooth and well-engineered, with a series of wide bends and a few hairpins, and it is one of the easiest passes in the Dolomites to ride. This makes it popular with all kinds of traffic, from cyclists and motorcyclists to coaches and campervans, and on summer weekends it can be busy. The descent towards Arabba is long and gentle, with open views over the valley. In winter the pass is usually open for the ski traffic, as it is a major link between ski areas, though ice and snow can make conditions difficult.

This was once the frontier country of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and Livinallongo, which the Germans called Buchenstein, was part of the Tyrol until 1918. The war left deep scars on the area, and the mountain of Col di Lana, close by, was the site of fierce fighting and underground mining. Memorials and open-air museums can still be found in the area, and the story is told with respect and sadness.

The nearest petrol stations are in Corvara and in Arabba, so it is best to fill before you set off. Arabba is a small ski village with hotels and restaurants, and it makes a good lunch stop on a loop.

The area is rich in mountain flowers in June and July, and cows graze on the pastures, so take care on the road. Weather can change quickly, so a waterproof layer is a good idea, even on a sunny day.
t.salo@45.6,10.5:
Salò is a lakeside town on the western shore of Lake Garda, tucked into a deep bay that protects it from the worst of the wind. It has a long, elegant promenade, a cathedral with a Gothic facade and the kind of old arcades that make you want to sit with a coffee. The town is known for the violin maker Gasparo da Salò, who worked here in the sixteenth century and is considered one of the founders of the modern violin. For a very different reason, it is also remembered as the seat of the Italian Social Republic, Mussolini's puppet state, from 1943 to 1945.

With around eight thousand people, Salò has everything a rider needs: petrol stations, supermarkets, bakeries and plenty of places to eat by the water. The nearby town of Roè Volciano has more shopping and services. The Gardesana Occidentale, the road along the west shore, begins here and runs north, a famous route with tunnels carved into the cliffs and views over the water. Early in the day it is a joy; at weekends and in summer, it fills with cars, campervans and cyclists, and a leisurely pace is the only sensible one.

Garda is Italy's largest lake, formed by a glacier, and its climate is mild enough that lemon trees, olives and oleander grow along the shore. The wind pattern is well known: the Peler blows from the north in the morning, and the Ora arrives from the south in the early afternoon, making the lake a favourite for sailors and windsurfers. Spring can bring surprising squalls, and storms in summer build quickly over the mountains at the north end, so keep an eye on the sky.

The route that leaves Salò toward the hills behind the lake offers a quiet alternative. Narrow roads climb through olive groves and small villages, with a very different feel from the busy shore. The food is lake fish, such as lavarello and trout, with olive oil from the local groves, which is among the lightest in Italy. Start here early, have a proper breakfast on the front, and watch the first light turn the lake silver before the day's traffic begins.
t.gardone riviera@45.6,10.6:
Gardone Riviera is where Lake Garda decided to be elegant. It sits on the western shore, a few kilometres from Salò, in a sheltered bay with a mild climate that made it a favourite winter resort for the Austro-Hungarian and German aristocracy in the late nineteenth century. Grand hotels with wrought-iron balconies still line the lakefront, and palms, cypress and magnolias grow in the gardens, giving the place a faintly Mediterranean look even though the Alps are close behind. The botanical garden, founded by Arturo Hruska in the early twentieth century, collects plants from many climates and is a pleasant shady escape on a hot day.

The most extraordinary place in town is the Vittoriale degli Italiani, the house and estate of the poet and soldier Gabriele D'Annunzio, who lived here from 1921 until his death in 1938. It is part museum, part mausoleum and part fever dream, a collection of rooms, gardens and monuments that includes the prow of a warship set into the hillside. D'Annunzio was a poet, a war hero and an early supporter of Mussolini, and the place reflects his flamboyance and ego. Whatever you think of him, it is unforgettable.

Riding on the western shore of Garda is a mixed pleasure. The Gardesana Occidentale, the main lakeside road, is spectacular, passing through tunnels cut into the cliffs with the blue water below, but it is also busy, particularly at weekends and in summer, with heavy traffic and slow-moving lorries. Overtaking is limited, and the tunnels can be loud and dark. Early morning is best, or late autumn and early spring, when the crowds have gone and the light is clear. In the afternoon, a wind called the Ora blows up the lake from the south and gives sailors their best sport.

The services are excellent. Gardone has hotels, restaurants and cafes along the waterfront, with fresh lake fish, risotto and local olive oil on the menu. Salò, three and a half kilometres to the south, is a larger town with fuel, supermarkets and a handsome promenade, and was briefly the capital of Mussolini's puppet republic in the last years of the war.

If you have time, take a short ride up into the hills behind the lake, where the roads are quiet and the views of the water are lovely. In the evening, the lakefront is a good spot to sit with a spritz and watch the lights come on.
t.limone sul garda@45.8,10.8:
Limone sits on a ledge between the lake and the cliffs, at the northern end of Lake Garda's western shore, and for much of its history it was reachable only by boat. The mountains rise almost sheer behind it, and the old town is a tangle of narrow alleys that run down to a small harbour. It is famous for lemons, though the name may come from a word for boundary rather than from the fruit, and the terraced lemon houses, called limonaie, with their stone pillars and wooden frames covered in glass in winter, are still visible on the hillside. In the nineteenth century, Limone shipped lemons to the cold cities of northern Europe.

The road to the village is a story in itself. The Gardesana Occidentale, which runs along the shore, was blasted through the rock in the early twentieth century, and the stretch near Limone passes through a long series of tunnels with windows cut into the cliff. The riding is dramatic, with the lake glittering below and the rocks above, but it is also slow, with heavy traffic in summer and few chances to overtake. The surface is generally good. Be careful in the tunnels, where the light changes abruptly, and watch for cyclists and pedestrians in the village.

Limone is a place for a walk and an ice cream, rather than a long visit on the bike. The lanes are crowded in summer and the parking is limited, so it is best to leave the bike in the lot at the edge of town and wander. The shops sell lemon products, from soap to liqueur, and the waterfront has cafes where you can sit with a coffee and watch the ferries come and go. Fuel in the village is limited, so fill before arriving, or in Riva del Garda, about nine kilometres to the north, which is a larger town with stations, supermarkets and a pretty old centre.

The climate is mild, with a Mediterranean feel, and olive and lemon trees grow here despite the proximity of the Alps. The best months to visit are April to June and September to October, when the weather is warm but the crowds are smaller.

From Limone, the road to the Tremosine plateau begins, and it is one of the great detours of the lake. If you have a taste for narrow roads and big drops, that is where the day really gets interesting.
t.strada della forra@45.8,10.8:
The Strada della Forra is the sort of road that makes people look at a map twice. It leaves the lake shore near Limone and climbs through the gorge of the Brasa stream to the Tremosine plateau, cut into the vertical rock, with the cliff wall on one side and a very long drop on the other. It was built in the early twentieth century to link the isolated villages of Tremosine, which until then were almost cut off from the rest of the world, and it is remarkable that anyone thought to build it at all. Narrow tunnels, overhanging rock and tight bends make it one of the most dramatic roads in Italy.

For a rider, it is thrilling but demands attention. The road is narrow, in places barely wide enough for two cars to pass, with several short tunnels that are almost one lane. Blind corners and oncoming traffic, including buses, are normal. The surface is generally fair but there can be loose stone and damp patches, and the gorge is shaded and cool even in summer. Speeds should be low, partly because the road demands it, and partly because there is simply too much to look at. Sometimes the road is closed after rockfall or storms, so check before you commit.

At the top, the plateau of Tremosine opens out into a quieter country of villages, meadows and sweeping views over the lake. The village of Pieve is the main centre, and at its edge is a terrace built out over the cliff, a glass platform nicknamed the Terrace of Thrills, which hangs more than three hundred metres above the water. It is not for those afraid of heights, but the view down the lake to the south is one of the finest anywhere.

There is little in the way of services on the road itself. Pieve has cafes, a few restaurants and basic shops, and the lake terrace has a bar that serves coffee and light meals. Fuel is the main issue. There is none in the gorge, and the nearest large town in the data is Riva del Garda, about fourteen kilometres away, so fill there or in one of the shore villages before you climb.

If the road is busy, take your time and enjoy it. It is best ridden early, on a weekday in spring or autumn, when the light is soft and the tourists are few. The ride down again is a different experience, with the lake spread out below like a blue floor.
t.tremosine@45.8,10.8:
Tremosine is not so much a village as a plateau hung on the cliffs above the western shore of Lake Garda, a scattering of hamlets spread across a terrace roughly 400 metres above the water. The main settlement, Pieve, sits on the edge, with a terrace that overlooks the lake from a height that makes the stomach lurch. Across the water lies Malcesine, and in the evening the lights of the east shore twinkle. Nearby Gardola is the administrative centre of the commune. The area is tiny in population, with only a few hundred people in each village, so fuel is not something you can count on up here.

The famous way up is the Strada della Forra, a road cut in the early twentieth century through a narrow ravine from Limone and the lakeshore. It was called by Winston Churchill, according to local lore, the eighth wonder of the world, though that attribution is hard to prove. The road is narrow, carved into the rock, with overhangs above and a drop to a gorge below, and a series of short tunnels. It is tight enough that large vehicles can struggle, and you may meet a bus coming the other way, so keep to your side and go slowly.

The riding on the plateau itself is quieter and less dramatic, but rewarding: narrow lanes among pastures and woodland, small chapels and views on all sides. The surface is mostly good, though gravel appears in places, and the gradient is steady. It is the sort of place where the best thing to do is stop at a cafe terrace over the cliff and watch the paragliders drop from the edge. A few viewpoints, including the Terrazza del Brivido, a glass-floored platform, give a sense of the drop.

Fuel and supplies are best taken in Salò or on the lakeshore before you climb, as the nearest big pumps are down at the lake. The local cooking is mountain-style: polenta, cured meats, game and cheese, with lake fish near the shore. Summer weekends are busy, spring and autumn are calm, and a clear morning in October, with fresh air and gentle light, is hard to beat.
t.santa caterina valfurva@46.4,10.5:
Santa Caterina Valfurva is a small ski village at about 1,700 metres in the Lombard Alps, at the head of a valley that ends against the glaciers of the Ortler-Cevedale range. It lies inside the Stelvio National Park, and the air has that thin, clean mountain bite, with larch and spruce on the slopes and the peaks of the Gran Zebrù and the Cevedale shining white in the distance. In winter it is a quiet, serious skiing resort. In summer it belongs to walkers, climbers and the riders who come to tackle the road above it, the Gavia Pass.

The Gavia is one of the toughest and most atmospheric paved passes in the Alps. Rising to 2,621 metres, it begins just above the village and climbs in a narrow ribbon, with sections barely wider than a car, steep gradients and stretches without guard rails. The surface is mostly paved and decent but has patches that are rough or broken after winter, and the road is single-lane in places, with passing bays. The descent on the Ponte di Legno side is a long, bumpy, exposed run. The pass is only open from about June to October, and snow can fall in any month, so check conditions before you go. Fog, rain and sudden cold are common, and the temperature at the summit can be a shock after the valley.

The Gavia has a place in cycling history. In 1988, a blizzard struck the riders of the Giro d'Italia on the climb, and the stage became a legend of cold, suffering and heroism. Even in summer, standing at the top and looking at the grey lakes and rock, you can imagine how brutal it must have been. Near the summit, a mountain refuge serves hot food and drinks, and walkers use it as a base for high routes.

In the village, you will find a few hotels, restaurants and shops, with hearty mountain food such as pizzoccheri, buckwheat pasta with cheese, cabbage and potatoes, and bresaola, the air-dried beef of the Valtellina. A warm meal here is a good idea before the climb. As for fuel, the village is small, so it is best to fill in the larger centres down the valley, such as Bormio, before heading up. Tirano, about thirty-four kilometres away, is the bigger town on the way out of the valley.

This is a place for early starts. Ride in the morning, when the air is clear and the road is quiet, and keep a layer in the top box for the summit.
t.ponte di legno@46.3,10.5:
Ponte di Legno takes its name from the wooden bridge that once crossed the Oglio river here, and it is the last proper village before the road leaves the Val Camonica and heads up into the high mountains. It sits at about 1,260 metres, and it is surrounded by the peaks of the Adamello and Ortles-Cevedale groups, with the Tonale Pass just to the east and the Gavia pass to the north. The village is a ski and walking resort, and it keeps a handsome old centre of stone houses beside a modern strip of hotels and cafes. The nearby hamlets of Temù and Vezza d'Oglio are smaller still.

For a rider, this is where preparation counts. The Gavia Pass, at 2,621 metres, is one of the highest paved roads in Italy, and it has a reputation. The road from the Ponte di Legno side is narrow, with steep gradients, tight hairpins, little or no barrier in places and sections of rough surface. It is closed in winter, usually opening in late spring or early summer after snow clearing, and it can close again at the first autumn snowfall. Check conditions before you go. The Giro d'Italia has crossed it, famously in 1988 in a blizzard.

Ponte di Legno has fuel stations and shops, and since the pass has no supplies at the top, fill up and take some water. The village is also a convenient place for a hot lunch before or after the climb, and local cooking features polenta, cured meats, cheese and berries from the woods. The nearby Stelvio National Park, one of Italy's largest, protects chamois, ibex and golden eagles, and in the early morning you may see wildlife on the road verges.

Weather is the constant theme. Mornings tend to be clearest, and afternoon cloud and thunder build over the mountains in summer, so start early. Even in July, it can be near freezing at the top, so carry layers. The ride finishes here with the sort of tiredness that comes from concentration and altitude, and a quiet evening in the village feels earned.
t.carezza@46.4,11.6:
Lago di Carezza has a reputation for being the most beautiful lake in the Dolomites, and in good light it earns it. It sits at about fifteen hundred metres in a forest of spruce below the jagged crest of the Latemar and the great towers of the Rosengarten, and its water is a deep, shifting emerald that changes from green to blue to turquoise depending on the sky and the angle of the sun. The German name is Karersee, and the Ladin name is Lec de Ciareja. Local people call it the rainbow lake, and there is a legend to match.

The story goes that a water nymph lived in the lake and a sorcerer fell in love with her, and that in trying to win her he disguised himself as a merchant. The nymph's friends saw through him, and in his rage he tore a rainbow from the sky and threw it into the lake, where its colours broke into pieces and gave the water its shades. It is a charming tale and it fits the view. The lake has no visible inflow or outflow, which only adds to the mystery, and its level changes with the seasons.

The ride up from Bolzano to Carezza follows the Val d'Ega, or Eggental, through a narrow gorge and then a green valley with orchards, farms and woods. The road is well surfaced, with moderate bends and gentle gradients, and the views of the Latemar grow steadily. It is part of the Great Dolomites Road, which links Bolzano with Cortina. The area is busy in summer, and the car park at the lake fills with coaches and cars, so early morning and late afternoon are better. A path leads from the road to a boardwalk and viewing platforms around the water, and a short walk gives different views of the mountain reflection.

Please stay on the paths. The lake is fragile and swimming and wading are not allowed. A nearby hotel and a cafe provide coffee and food, and the village of Nova Levante, about three and a half kilometres away, has more choice, including fuel, shops and restaurants. Bolzano, further down the valley, is the larger city.

The best time to see the colour is on a clear, calm morning, before the wind ruffles the surface, and in autumn the larches around the lake turn gold, which makes a lovely frame.
t.passo costalunga@46.4,11.6:
Passo Costalunga, known in German as the Karerpass, is the saddle at 1,752 metres that carries the road from the Bolzano side into the Val di Fassa. It is not a spectacular pass in itself, with its broad, wooded crossing and gentle slopes, but it sits at the foot of some of the most famous mountains in the Dolomites, and the view from the pass is one of the best things about it. To the south rise the Latemar, a ragged crest of pale rock, and to the north the Rosengarten, or Catinaccio, with its pink and orange towers.

The Rosengarten has its own legend. King Laurin, a dwarf ruler of the mountains, had a magnificent rose garden that he protected with a spell, and when he was captured by a knight he cursed the roses so that no one would see them by day or night. He forgot the twilight, so at dawn and dusk the rock still glows rose-red, a phenomenon known in the Dolomites as the Enrosadira. It is a beautiful effect, and the best place to see it is from here or from the shore of Lake Carezza on the northern side of the pass.

The road over the pass is part of the Great Dolomites Road, which was opened in 1909 to connect Bolzano with Cortina d'Ampezzo, one of the earliest tourist routes through the mountains. It is easy riding, with a good surface, flowing bends and moderate gradients, and it is a wonderful warm-up for the bigger passes. Traffic can be heavy in July and August, and the road is often busy with coaches and cyclists. In winter, the road is plowed and usually open, though snow and ice can make it tricky.

The pass itself is a lovely place for a break. There are a couple of hotels and cafes at the top, and pastures where cows graze and walkers set off into the forest. Moena, on the Fassa side, is a larger village with fuel and food, and it is only about five kilometres down. Nova Levante, on the other side, offers the same, so it is easy to fill before you climb.

The Ladin and German cultures meet at this pass, and you will see both languages on signs and menus. Try the local cheese and speck, and in autumn the pastries made with apples from the Bolzano orchards.
t.passo giovo@46.8,11.3:
