The Jaufenpass, which Italians call Passo Giovo, is a good road that gets very little attention because the roads next to it are so famous. It crosses the ridge between the Sterzing basin and the Passeier valley at 2,094 metres, and it does so with no tolls, no crowds and no fuss. The road climbs from Vipiteno through dark spruce forest, with a clean surface and bends that keep coming, and then emerges above the tree line into open pasture and rock. At the top there is a small restaurant and a car park, and the view down the other side is long and green, with the Texel group of mountains standing in the distance.

The Passeier valley, on the far side, has its own place in the history of the Tyrol. It was the home of Andreas Hofer, the innkeeper who led the Tyrolean uprising against Napoleon's Bavarian allies in 1809, and who was captured and shot in Mantua the following year. He remains a hero in the region, and his farm in the valley is a museum. The road down takes you through orchards and villages toward Merano, and the further you go, the warmer the air becomes, with apples, vines and even palms in the gardens at the bottom.

The riding is a pleasure. On the north side the road is steep and twisty, with enough hairpins to keep you busy, and on the south side the bends are longer and smoother. The gradient is relentless in places, and in wet weather the forest sections can be slick with needles and moisture. Traffic is lighter than on the Brenner or the Timmelsjoch, though cyclists and campers use it on summer weekends. The pass is usually open from late spring to early autumn, and it can be closed or require care after heavy snow.

There is a small hut at the top for coffee and a simple meal, and the Ratschings ski area and its summer lifts lie a short way to the side. Fuel is the main thing to plan. Vipiteno, about ten kilometres away, is the bigger town and has several stations, while the Passeier valley has pumps in St Leonhard. Fill before you go, since the climb itself has no services.

Tyrolean weather can change quickly, so bring a layer, especially if you are crossing in the afternoon. In the early morning, the forest is still and the road is empty, and it is easy to see why local riders keep this one quiet.
t.vipiteno@46.9,11.4:
Vipiteno, called Sterzing in German, is a small walled town that has been collecting travellers for a very long time. It stands on the old route over the Brenner, where the road from the Eisack valley opens out into a broad basin before climbing to the pass, and it grew rich on trade and, in the late Middle Ages, on silver mining in the surrounding hills. The result is a main street that looks like a film set, with a long, curving line of arcaded houses in pastel colours, oriel windows, wrought-iron signs and, at one end, the Zwölferturm, a tall tower from the late fifteenth century that is the town's emblem.

The town is officially bilingual, though German is the everyday language, and you will see both on every sign. The food is Tyrolean, with dumplings, speck, goulash and apple strudel in every restaurant, and the beer is good. It is a pleasant place for a slow lunch or a coffee under the arcades, with the town hall and the old customs houses to look at. The Pfitsch and Ridnaun valleys open off the basin and lead to quiet mountain scenery for those with time to spare.

For a rider, Vipiteno is mostly a junction and a service stop. The A22 motorway takes most of the traffic over the Brenner these days, which leaves the old state road relatively quiet, and from here you can head west over the Jaufen Pass to Merano, east towards Bressanone and the Pustertal, or north toward Austria. The roads out of town are well surfaced and the gradients fairly gentle until the passes begin. In winter, snow comes early and stays late, so check conditions before you set out.

The town has everything you need. There are fuel stations on the main road, supermarkets, banks, bakeries, pharmacies and a good choice of hotels, and prices are lower than in the resorts higher in the Dolomites. It is a good place to stay if you are crossing the Alps and want a quiet evening. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends and during holiday periods, but the town centre is mostly pedestrianised.

Walk the length of the main street at least once, under the tower and out the other side. The mountains at the end of the street are close and dramatic, and in the evening the light on the pastel facades is excellent.
t.selva di cadore@46.5,12.0:
Selva di Cadore is a quiet village on the road between two big names, in the Fiorentina valley, with Monte Pelmo on one side and the great wall of the Civetta on the other. It is not a place that most people choose as a destination, and that is part of its appeal. A handful of houses, a church, a few hotels and a ski lift sit in a green bowl, and above them the Pelmo, with its flat, throne-like summit, dominates the view. The mountain is known locally as the throne of God, and when the light catches it at the end of the day, it is easy to see why.

The village belongs to the Ladin cultural area, and the neighbouring Colle Santa Lucia, only a couple of kilometres away, is one of the Ladin-speaking communities that keep their language and traditions alive in the face of Italian and German. The Dolomites were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009, and this part of the range, with its high walls and its pale rock, is one of the finest.

The riding is excellent in both directions. Heading east from Selva, the road climbs towards Passo Giau, at 2,236 metres, with long sequences of hairpins through meadows and then open rock, and the summit area is a high saddle with a cluster of huts and spectacular views. It is one of the finest passes in the Dolomites and the road, though narrow in places, is well surfaced. From there you can continue to Passo Falzarego and loop back via Cortina or the Livinallongo valley. In the other direction, the road climbs over Passo Staulanza, below the Pelmo, and down to the Zoldo valley. Traffic is moderate, though weekends in July and August bring more bikes and cyclists.

Weather in these mountains can change quickly, with morning sunshine turning to afternoon thunderstorms, and snow can close the higher passes from autumn to late spring. At the top of the Giau, the wind can be cold even in summer, so bring a windproof layer.

There is little in the village itself, though there are a couple of cafes and small shops, and local dishes such as casunziei, a stuffed pasta with beetroot, or polenta with mushrooms are worth trying. Fuel is limited, and the larger town of Cortina d'Ampezzo, about twelve kilometres away, has stations and plenty of services, so fill there before heading for the high passes.

Late June brings flowers to the pastures, and September offers crisp air and golden larches on the slopes.
t.el salto@23.8,-105.4:
El Salto is a lumber town in the pine forests of Durango, high in the Sierra Madre Occidental, and it is the point where the road from Durango begins its descent toward the Pacific. The altitude is well above two thousand metres, and you feel it in the cool, thin, resinous air. Sawmills line the approach, logging trucks grind up and down the highway, and the smell of cut timber and woodsmoke is part of the place. The name means the jump or the waterfall, and the little cascade nearby is the origin of it. Nobody comes to El Salto for the architecture, but it is a useful, friendly town and a good place to prepare.

Prepare you must, because west of here lies the Espinazo del Diablo, the Devil's Backbone, one of the most famous roads in Mexico. The highway to Mazatlán twists down the spine of a narrow ridge with deep barrancas on both sides, hundreds of bends, tunnels and long bridges, and the views, when the cloud lifts, go on for ever. Up around El Salto the road is more forgiving, with pine and oak, wide curves and long, climbing sweepers. The surface can be broken by logging trucks, and diesel patches sit in the bends. In winter there can be snow and ice, and fog at any time of year, so check the weather and leave early.

The Devil's Backbone was a feat of engineering in its day. The highway, finished in the 1990s, replaced a notoriously slow and dangerous mountain road, and it opened the western slope to trade. You will see crosses and shrines along the bends, a reminder of the old road's toll. Truckers use the lay-bys, and ride-outs of the sort we like are a normal sight on weekends.

El Salto is big enough, with about twenty-four thousand people, to have fuel stations, small restaurants and shops, and you should fill up here because the stretch ahead has few services. Eat well before you leave: a plate of carne asada, beans and tortillas will keep you going. In the dry months the days are mild and the nights cold, so a warm layer is no luxury.
t.cabo san lucas@22.9,-109.9:
Cabo San Lucas sits at the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula, where the Pacific meets the Gulf of California, and it announces itself with a curving rock arch called El Arco at the very end of the land. The town has about sixty-eight thousand people, many of them working in tourism, and it is loud, bright and busy, with marinas full of sport-fishing boats, bars and resort hotels. In the nineteenth century it was a modest fishing and canning village, and the transformation into a major resort took place from the 1970s, when the Transpeninsular Highway was completed, finally linking the tip of Baja with the border.

That is the ride's story. Highway 1, the Transpeninsular, runs about 1,700 kilometres from Tijuana to Cabo, through desert, cactus forest, mountains and coastal flats, and it is a classic adventure road. Cabo is a satisfying place to finish: warm water, cold beer, and fish tacos. The last stretch, from La Paz and Todos Santos, is a pleasant run through desert scrub and along the Pacific, with cardón cactus, some surfers and old mission towns. Todos Santos is worth a stop for its art galleries and the Hotel California, which claims, without much evidence, to have inspired the song.

Practical matters are easy here. Fuel is everywhere in town, there are plenty of hotels and workshops, and the roads around are in good shape. Heat is the enemy in summer, from June to October, when temperatures are extreme and humidity is high, and hurricane season brings risk of storms. The best months are November to April, with warm days and cool evenings, and whales can be seen offshore from December to March, as grey and humpback whales visit the warm waters.

The water around Cabo is rich with marine life, and the Los Cabos area is known for marlin, dorado and sea lions that bask on the rocks near the arch. A boat ride to see the arch is popular. Watch your belongings in crowded areas, and expect higher prices than elsewhere in Mexico. A sunset on the beach near the rocks, with the Pacific swell rolling in, makes a good ending to a long road.
t.fort collins@40.6,-105.1:
Fort Collins is a university town of about a hundred and sixty thousand people at the foot of the Rockies in northern Colorado, with Colorado State University at its heart and a well-preserved Old Town of brick buildings, trees and fountains. It is a famously bicycle-friendly place, and also a famous place for beer: New Belgium, Odell and dozens of smaller breweries started here, and the craft beer scene is serious. It has a relaxed, outdoorsy feel, and a motorcycle is very much at home.

The town began as a military camp on the Cache la Poudre River in the 1860s, and the name of the river tells its own story: French trappers in the 1820s are said to have buried a cache of gunpowder along its banks during a snowstorm, hence Cache la Poudre, hide the powder. The river rises high in the mountains of Rocky Mountain National Park and runs down through a rugged canyon, and it is Colorado's only designated Wild and Scenic River. It is a lively stream, with rapids that are popular for rafting in early summer.

The Cache la Poudre Scenic Byway begins here and follows Highway 14 up the canyon, with the river rushing beside the road. The ride is a delight, with tight bends, rocky walls and forest, and plenty of pull-outs along the river. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, with rafters, fishermen and cyclists, and rockfalls and flash floods occasionally close the road. After the canyon, the road climbs through pine and aspen to Cameron Pass, at over ten thousand feet, and then drops into the broad, empty bowl of North Park.

Everything you need is available in Fort Collins, including fuel, food and repair shops, and the town is a good place to spend the night before the ride. Services up the canyon are few, with a couple of small stores and lodges, so be sure to fill up. Mornings are cool and clear, and thunderstorms build in the afternoon, so aim to cross the pass early. Autumn colour, with golden aspen in late September, is the highlight of the year. Winter snow can close the pass.
t.poudre canyon@40.7,-105.6:
The Cache la Poudre is the only river in Colorado with National Wild and Scenic status, and Highway 14 spends a good thirty miles of its length following the water up into the mountains. The name is French, from the early trappers who, according to the story, buried a stock of gunpowder somewhere along its banks in the 1820s after a blizzard forced them to lighten their loads, and called the place the hiding place of the powder.

The canyon starts a short way north-west of Fort Collins, where the plains suddenly give way to rock, and from there the road runs close to the river in a winding course between granite walls. In the lower reaches the bends are tight, with overhanging cliffs and little shoulder, and the speed limit is often low for good reason. Further up, the canyon widens into pine and aspen forest and the river slows into pools and riffles, popular with anglers and rafters in early summer when snowmelt is high. Bighorn sheep appear on the cliffs, and in winter the river steams in the cold.

Riding the canyon is a pleasure of rhythm rather than speed. It is a road for cruising, with a steady stream of cars, bicycles and rafting vans, so it is better on weekdays. Rockfalls and washouts can close sections, wildfire has marked the upper canyon in recent years, and flash floods in the burn areas are a real hazard. In winter the shaded sections ice early and stay icy.

Fort Collins, at the bottom, has everything, and Estes Park is a long ride over the mountains. If you are heading west, the sensible approach is to fill up in Fort Collins, carry water and a warm layer, and keep going through Cameron Pass to Walden, where the next real services are.
t.cameron pass@40.5,-105.9:
The top of Cameron Pass is a quiet, broad saddle at 3,132 metres between the Never Summer Mountains to the south and the Medicine Bow Mountains to the north, with spruce and fir all around and snow lingering in the shaded hollows well into summer. It is a gentle sort of summit, and the sign that marks it seems almost shy. A few hundred metres away, the land begins to fall westward into North Park, a vast open basin that feels as though it belongs to another state.

The ride up from the east follows the Cache la Poudre River through its canyon, then leaves the water and climbs through dense forest in a sequence of bends that grow longer and more open as you rise. From the pass, the road drops to the Colorado State Forest and then out into the sagebrush plains. It is a calm, easy road for most of the year, but it is open in winter, which means snow, ice and avalanche control are all live issues. In summer, the weather is pleasant in the morning and stormy by mid-afternoon.

The pass is known for moose. They were introduced into the state forest in the 1970s, and a healthy population has settled in the willows and beaver ponds, particularly around the Michigan River valley. Seeing one is possible and slightly nerve-racking, as a moose is large, unpredictable and not much impressed by a motorcycle. Go slowly at dusk and dawn. The pass is also a gateway to excellent walking, with lakes and meadows reached by short trails from the roadside, and the high peaks to the south hold snow until July.

The name honours General Robert Cameron, a leader of the Union Colony at Greeley in the 1870s, who explored the route. The road itself was improved as a state highway in the twentieth century. Estes Park is listed as the nearest town, about thirty-five kilometres off as the crow flies, but the practical neighbours are Fort Collins to the east and Walden to the west, each a long way. The pass itself has toilets and a few parking spots, and nothing else.
t.walden@40.7,-106.3:
Walden sits in the middle of North Park, an enormous high basin in northern Colorado, ringed by mountains, and it is one of the most remote little county seats in the state. About six hundred people live here, at around eight thousand one hundred feet, in a village of low buildings and wide streets, with sagebrush and hay meadows stretching away on every side. The Medicine Bow Mountains to the north and the Never Summer range to the south frame the view, and the wind is a constant companion.

North Park is a ranching region, with cattle grazing on the meadows, and a national wildlife refuge protects wetlands where ducks, geese and sandhill cranes gather. It also has the distinction of being the moose capital of Colorado. In the late 1970s, wildlife managers released a small number of moose into the basin, and the population thrived in the willow thickets, so you have a good chance of seeing a moose near the road, especially at dawn or dusk. A visitor centre in town explains the story.

Arriving here from the Poudre canyon, you cross Cameron Pass at over ten thousand feet, where the road drops from the forest into the park, with a sudden sense of space. The descent is gentle, with long bends, and in front of you lies a broad bowl, with the peaks around its edge. The road is generally good, but wind and weather can be severe, and ice and snow can appear very early or very late in the year. The cold here is serious, and winter nights in the park are among the coldest in Colorado.

Fuel is available in Walden, along with a few cafes and motels, but it is a small place and hours are short, so arrive with a reasonable tank. The nearest big town is a long distance away, so plan carefully, especially if the weather is bad. Wildlife is common, and elk, deer and pronghorn graze near the road, so keep your speed moderate at dusk. The best time is from late June to September, with wildflowers in the meadows, and golden aspens in the autumn, along the roads.
t.cody@44.5,-109.1:
Cody was founded by a man who understood the value of a story. William F. Cody, Buffalo Bill, the scout and showman whose Wild West show toured America and Europe in the late nineteenth century, helped establish the town in 1896 on the Shoshone River in north-west Wyoming, and he built a hotel here, the Irma, named after his daughter. The cherry-wood bar in the Irma was a gift from Queen Victoria, so the story goes. Today Cody has about ten thousand people and calls itself the Rodeo Capital of the World, with a rodeo every night in summer.

The Buffalo Bill Center of the West is a collection of five museums under one roof, covering Plains Indian cultures, Western art, natural history, firearms and Cody's life, and it is one of the best museums in the region. The Shoshone River runs through a red-rock canyon just west of town, near a huge concrete dam that was the tallest in the world when it was built in 1910, and the road to Yellowstone follows it through tunnels in the rock.

The Chief Joseph Scenic Byway heads north-west from the area, following a route taken by the Nez Perce in 1877, when about eight hundred men, women and children fled from the US Army across Idaho, Montana and Wyoming in an attempt to reach Canada. Chief Joseph, their principal spokesman, became famous for his dignity and eloquence. The road climbs over Dead Indian Pass, at over eight thousand feet, with a view into the canyon of the Clarks Fork, a deep, narrow gorge, then runs along a high plateau to Sunlight Basin.

You should fill the tank in Cody, since services on the byway are few and far between, and the nearest fuel beyond is a long way north-west. Take warm clothing, as mountain weather is changeable, and watch for wildlife: moose, elk, deer and bears all live here. Summer is the best time, with wildflowers in the meadows, but the road may close in winter. Cody has a good selection of restaurants and steak houses, and a plate of local beef, grilled over an open fire, is well deserved.
t.dead indian pass@44.7,-109.4:
The summit of this road is a high, windy shoulder at about 2,450 metres, with a view that drops away to the west over the Clarks Fork valley and the red and grey peaks of the Absaroka Range, and the name on the sign is a hard one. The pass is part of the route taken in 1877 by the Nez Perce, who were fleeing the US Army across Idaho, Montana and Wyoming in a desperate attempt to reach Canada, and the name reflects an incident in that flight. The name has been the subject of debate for years, and it is a reminder that the landscape carries painful history.

The Chief Joseph Scenic Byway, Wyoming Highway 296, climbs here from the Cody side, and the ascent is steep. The grade reaches ten percent in places, with tight switchbacks, narrow lanes and big drops, and the road then plunges down the other side into Sunlight Basin. It is a spectacular ride, but demanding, and caravans and large trailers are advised to avoid it. The surface is generally good, with the occasional patch of loose gravel, and traffic is light. The road is closed by snow in winter and usually opens in late spring, and snow can return at any time, even in June or September.

The scenery is the reward. The view from the top takes in layered volcanic cliffs, forested slopes, wide meadows and the long ridge of the Absarokas, with clouds throwing moving shadows across the valleys. The air is clear and cool, and it smells of sage and pine. Elk, mule deer and the occasional black bear graze along the road, and dawn and dusk are the best times for wildlife.

Cody, about thirty-five kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town. It was founded by William F. Cody, the showman Buffalo Bill, in 1896, and has a fine museum complex devoted to the West, along with petrol stations, restaurants and motels. Take a layer, since wind and altitude can make it chilly. Allow time for the descent, and use engine braking on the long grades.
t.sunlight basin@44.8,-109.5:
Sunlight Basin is a broad, green valley hidden behind a mountain, and you arrive in it by dropping off the top of Dead Indian Pass and rounding a bend. Suddenly the road levels, the sky opens, and the land spreads out in ranch meadows with Sunlight Creek winding through willows, and big red cliffs and grey ridges standing guard. It is cattle country and dude-ranch country, still sparsely settled, with scattered cabins, fences and hay barns, and its beauty is the kind that makes you slow without knowing why.

The valley sits in the heart of the Absaroka Range, a high, rugged volcanic region east of Yellowstone, and the rocks here are the debris of ancient eruptions, giving the cliffs their red, yellow and brown colours. Sunlight Creek runs down to the Clarks Fork, and the bridge where Highway 296 crosses its gorge is among the highest in Wyoming, spanning a deep, narrow canyon where the creek drops in a thin white line. Stop and look over the rail if you have a head for heights.

The riding is a pure pleasure. After the steep descent from Dead Indian, the road runs along the valley floor in gentle curves and easy straights, with long views and the smell of sage and hay. The surface is good, the traffic light, and the main hazards are cattle on the road, deer at dusk and the occasional tractor. In summer the days are warm and the nights cool, and in autumn the aspens along the creek turn gold, making the ride glow. Snow closes the upper road in winter, and the basin is nearly cut off for months.

The region has a long history as the hunting ground of the Crow and the Shoshone, and as part of the route taken by the Nez Perce in 1877. Later it was settled by ranchers, and some of the oldest dude ranches in the West were founded here, taking in wealthy easterners who came to ride horses and fish. Today a few lodges and ranches offer meals and beds, though hours and availability vary with the season.

Fuel is the thing to plan. There is none in the basin, and the nearest town is Cody, about fifty kilometres away, so fill up there. The road continues to the Chief Joseph byway's far end near Crandall and the Beartooth Highway, where services are also limited. Bring food and water, and enjoy the quiet.
t.sella pass@46.5,11.8:
The Sella Pass is the one the Dolomites are famous for, even if the locals would argue that every pass here is. At 2,244 metres, it connects the Val Gardena with the Val di Fassa, running between the sheer grey towers of the Sassolungo, or Langkofel, on one side and the great fortress mass of the Sella group on the other. The rock is dolomite, a pale limestone that glows pink and orange at sunset, an effect the Ladin people call enrosadira, and the setting is the sort of place where cyclists weep and motorcyclists forget to ride.

The road up from the Fassa side begins at Canazei, about four kilometres away, and climbs in a series of long, graceful bends, with meadows and pine forest giving way to bare scree and rock. On the way down toward Val Gardena, hairpins tighten and the surface is generally excellent. The gradient is steady, the corners are readable, and the traffic, especially on summer weekends, is heavy with cars, campervans, cyclists, and other bikes. Early morning is the quiet time, and the light on the rock is superb.

Culture here is a mix of three worlds. This is Ladin country, where a Romance language older than Italian is still spoken in the valleys, and the region has swung between Austria and Italy over the last century. The First World War front passed through the Dolomites, and traces of it survive in tunnels, trenches, and fortifications all over the mountains. The pass is also the start and finish of the Sellaronda, the loop around the Sella massif that skiers ride in winter and cyclists and motorcyclists tackle in summer.

Fuel is best in the valley towns. Canazei and Campitello have stations and shops, and Selva in Val Gardena on the other side has more, though prices are higher than in the lowlands. At the pass itself, there are refuges and cafes serving coffee, strudel, and hearty mountain food, and they make a welcome stop. Snow can close the road in winter and in late spring, and thunderstorms can build over the peaks in summer afternoons. Bring warm gloves, because even in August the wind at the top is cold.
t.arabba overnight base@46.5,11.9:
Arabba is a small village in the Livinallongo valley, at about sixteen hundred metres, and for a motorcyclist it is one of the best places in the Dolomites to sleep. It lies at the foot of the Pordoi, Campolongo and Falzarego passes, close enough to the Marmolada, the highest peak in the range at about 3,340 metres, to see the glacier on a clear day. Cable cars climb from the village in winter and summer, the slopes behind are green with meadows and grazing cows, and when the day-trippers leave the passes in the evening, the place settles into quiet.

The culture here is Ladin, a Romance language descended from the Latin spoken in the Alps, and you will see bilingual signs and hear it in the shops. Livinallongo, or Fodóm in Ladin, was part of Tyrol until 1918, and the mountains around were the front line in the First World War, when Austrian and Italian troops fought across the peaks and tunnelled into the rock. The Col di Lana, nearby, was mined and blown up in 1916. Many of the trenches and tunnels can still be walked, and the old forts and shelters are scattered across the passes.

The roads out of Arabba make this a great base. Pordoi climbs in a long chain of hairpins toward the Sella massif, with the pass at about 2,240 metres. Campolongo brings you down toward Corvara, and Falzarego climbs toward Cortina. The surface is good, the bends are plentiful and well engineered, and the views of the pale, jagged rock are the main distraction. Go early, because by ten the roads are busy with cars, buses and cyclists. In summer, there are car-free days on parts of the Sella Ronda, so check the calendar. Passes close in winter, usually from late October to May, so plan your season, and carry warm layers because the weather changes quickly.

Practical matters are simple enough. Arabba has hotels, guesthouses and restaurants, serving polenta, venison, cheese dumplings and good local wine. Cortina d'Ampezzo, about twenty kilometres away, is the largest nearby, with several stations.

Park the bike, walk to the edge of the village, and watch the light go pink on the rock.
t.falzarego pass@46.5,12.0:
Falzarego Pass is a high, rocky saddle at 2,105 metres on the road between Cortina d'Ampezzo and the Livinallongo valley, and the first thing you notice is how much of the landscape is made of ruin. Not buildings, but rock: the walls of the Tofane and the Cinque Torri, the tower-like peaks to the east, and the great scree slopes beneath them. Near the summit is the lower station of the cable car that rises to the Lagazuoi, a summit with a view over half the Dolomites.

The pass has a grim history. During the First World War, the line between Italy and Austria-Hungary ran along these ridges, and soldiers on both sides spent years in tunnels dug into the mountains, fighting as much against the weather as each other. Tunnels, trenches, and gun emplacements remain on the Lagazuoi and the Cinque Torri, and an open-air museum preserves some of them. The mountain is heavily visited, but the silence of the old galleries, cold and dripping, is a reminder of what happened there.

The riding is a pleasure. From Cortina, the road climbs steadily through forest and then open pasture, with long bends and good surface, and it feels natural, with views opening onto the pale towers. The descent toward Livinallongo is steeper, with tight hairpins, and the traffic can be heavy in July and August. The pass is generally open from late spring to autumn, though snow can fall early, and winter may close it intermittently. Morning is the best time for the light and the quiet.

Cortina d'Ampezzo, about ten kilometres to the east, is the biggest town nearby, with fuel, restaurants, and shops, and it is the sensible place to fill up. Smaller places along the way, like Livinallongo and Colle Santa Lucia, have limited facilities. At the pass itself you will find refuges, a hotel, and a cable car station, and a plate of pasta or polenta with a coffee works well after the climb. Wind and cloud can arrive suddenly, so carry a warm layer and a waterproof, even on a clear day.
t.valparola high road@46.6,12.0:
Valparola is the pass that most people drive without registering, because it comes straight after Falzarego and shares its scenery. At 2,192 metres it is actually higher, and it is the quieter of the two, a gentle crest in a landscape of green pasture and pale rock, with a small lake beside the road and a stone fort standing at the summit. The fort, Tre Sassi, was built by Austria-Hungary before the First World War and was shelled by Italian artillery in 1915. It is now a museum, and the walls still show the scars.

The road branches from the Falzarego route a few kilometres on, and heads north-west toward Armentarola and the Val Badia. It is a relaxed road, with long, open bends, little gradient, and good surface. It does not have the drama of the Falzarego hairpins, but it has a kind of calm, the quiet of high pasture, with cattle bells and larch trees. Motorcycles are plentiful, and the traffic can be slow in summer, but the views are never far from perfect.

The geology is dolomitic, but the vegetation is richer than on the harder passes. Alpine meadows bloom in July with gentians, arnica, and orchids, and the air smells of cut hay and resin. Marmots whistle from the scree, and in the evening, chamois can sometimes be seen on the slopes. It is easy to spend an hour here without doing much at all, and the little lake is a pleasant place for a sandwich.

For fuel, Cortina d'Ampezzo is about twelve kilometres away, and Corvara and La Villa, on the far side, have smaller stations. Livinallongo, to the south, is also a small place. There is little in the way of services on the pass itself, apart from a refuge and the museum. The best season is from June to September, when the road is open and the weather is warm, though afternoon thunderstorms are common. In autumn, the larches turn gold, and the traffic thins, so it may be the best time of all.
t.corvara food base@46.6,11.9:
Corvara sits in a bowl of green pasture at the head of the Alta Badia, ringed by the great limestone walls of the Sella group and the Puez, and it has the compact, sunny confidence of a place that has been hosting travellers for a long time. It is a Ladin village, and in the signs, the church, and the farmhouses with their carved balconies, you can see how the Dolomites have kept a culture of their own. The sound of Ladin, a Romance language with hints of German and Italian, is still heard in the cafes.

Corvara is a good place to eat well. The food of the Dolomites mixes Tyrolean and Italian traditions, and menus here run to canederli, the big bread dumplings, casunziei, half-moon pasta stuffed with beetroot, polenta with mushrooms, and apple strudel with cream. Local producers offer cheese and cured meats, and the coffee is Italian in strength. A proper meal here is a pleasure that can turn a couple of hours into half a day, and it is worth allowing for that.

The roads around it are among the best in the Alps. From Corvara you can ride over the Campolongo Pass to Arabba, over the Gardena Pass to Val Gardena, or toward Falzarego and Valparola, and all of them have good surface, steady gradients, and views that make you slow down. The corners range from open sweepers to tight hairpins, and the traffic is heavy on summer weekends but manageable early or late. Winter closes some passes, and snow can fall in any month at altitude.

Fuel is available in Corvara and the nearby villages, though small stations may have limited hours, and it is sensible to fill the tank when you can. Cortina d'Ampezzo, about twenty kilometres away, is the largest town in the area, and has everything a traveller needs. Rest in the sunshine on a terrace if the weather is fair, and keep a warm layer for the evening, when the temperature falls quickly. The light at dusk, when the Sella walls turn pink, is something to remember.
t.building remains of south of pfahlheim@4:
The name of the village gives the game away. Pfahlheim, a part of Ellwangen in the Ostalb, takes its name from the Pfahl, the stake line, which is what generations of farmers called the Roman frontier that ran through their fields. Here, at the edge of what is now Baden-Württemberg, the Upper German Limes and the Raetian Limes met, and the building remains south of the village are one of many small components of the UNESCO-listed Upper German-Raetian Limes. The frontier ran almost dead straight across this country for long distances, ignoring hills and streams in a way that still baffles people. There is very little to see on the ground today, perhaps a low bank or a signboard, but the line can be traced by eye if you know where to look.

To make sense of it, ride a few kilometres west to Rainau-Dalkingen, where the remains of a Limes gate have been protected under a modern glass structure, and to the Limes park at Rainau-Buch, with a reconstructed fort outline and a lake. The Aalen Limes Museum, built on the site of the largest cavalry fort north of the Alps, is also within easy reach.

The Ostalb landscape is gentle and rural, a rolling patchwork of fields, meadows and woods with small villages and onion-domed churches. The roads are quiet, mostly well surfaced, with gentle curves and good sightlines, though tractors and cyclists are common. Further west, the Swabian Jura rises into steeper country with cliffs and castles, including the Hohenstaufen and the Hohenrechberg, two conical hills crowned with castle ruins that gave the Staufer emperors their name and their home ground.

Ellwangen, nine kilometres away, is a fine Baroque town with a castle, a Romanesque basilica and the pilgrimage church of Schönenberg on a hill above. It has fuel, shops and plenty of places to eat. Swabian food is filling and comforting: Maultaschen, Spätzle with cheese, roast pork and cider. Spring, when the fruit trees blossom, and autumn, when the woods turn golden, are lovely times to ride here.
t.villa badoer@45.0,11.6:
Fratta Polesine is a quiet village in the Polesine, the flat, fertile land between the Adige and the Po in the south of the Veneto, and its pride is a villa by Andrea Palladio. Villa Badoer, built in the 1550s for Francesco Badoer, a Venetian nobleman, stands on a raised platform above the surrounding fields, with a temple-front portico, curved colonnades sweeping out on either side to farm buildings, and a grand staircase. It was the first of Palladio's villas to use the curved barchesse, and it is part of the UNESCO-listed City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto. Inside, the walls carry frescoes, and the villa houses a museum about the Polesine and its history.

The Venetian nobility built villas like this one not as idle retreats but as working estates, the centre of farms reclaimed from marsh, and the Badoer family were part of that great project of land reclamation. The Polesine has always lived with water: the Po flooded catastrophically in 1951, forcing the evacuation of tens of thousands of people.

Fratta Polesine is also the birthplace of Giacomo Matteotti, the socialist deputy murdered by fascists in 1924 after denouncing electoral fraud in parliament. His house is a museum, and his memory is honoured across Italy.

The riding here is flat, open and relaxing. Roads follow canals and riverbanks, through fields of maize, wheat and sugar beet, poplar rows and farm buildings. Traffic is light, but watch out for tractors, cyclists and fog, which can be thick in autumn and winter. The Po delta, to the east, is a vast wetland of lagoons, reed beds and channels, rich in birds. Lendinara, seven kilometres away, has fuel and services, and Rovigo is the provincial capital. Try the local dishes, such as risotto, fish from the rivers and lagoons, and the sweets of the Polesine.
t.villa forni cerato@45.7,11.6:
Not every Palladian villa is a palace. Villa Forni Cerato, in Montecchio Precalcino north of Vicenza, is a small, modest building, a cube with a simple loggia and pediment, built in the mid-sixteenth century for Girolamo Forni, a timber merchant and amateur painter. Its attribution to Palladio has been debated, but it is included in the UNESCO-listed City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto, and its compact harmony shows how Palladio's ideas worked even at a small scale. It is privately owned and not always open, so check before planning a visit.

The countryside here is the high plain north of Vicenza, between the Astico and Brenta rivers, a landscape of fields, vineyards, poplar rows and small towns, with the Alps rising abruptly to the north. Sandrigo, two kilometres away, is famous for one dish: baccalà alla vicentina, stockfish slow-cooked in milk and oil and served with polenta, celebrated every year with a festival. Nearby, Breganze is known for its wine, especially the sweet Torcolato.

The riding gets serious just to the north. The Asiago plateau, reached by the Costo road from Piovene Rocchette, a climb of many hairpins, is a high plateau of meadows, forests and cheese dairies, scarred by First World War trenches and memorials. To the east, Monte Grappa, another battlefield, is reached by spectacular roads with views over the plain. Marostica, with its walled town and the human chess game held on its square in September every other year, and Bassano del Grappa, with its covered wooden bridge and grappa distilleries, are both nearby.

Sandrigo and Thiene have fuel and services, and Vicenza, the city of Palladio, is a short ride south. The plain is busy and built-up, with lots of traffic and speed cameras, so the best riding is in the hills. Spring and autumn are ideal, while summer can be hot and hazy on the plain.
t.molina di ledro@45.9,10.8:
In 1929, when the level of Lake Ledro was lowered to feed a hydroelectric plant, thousands of wooden posts emerged from the mud near Molina di Ledro. They were the remains of a Bronze Age pile-dwelling village, inhabited some four thousand years ago, and the finds included pottery, tools, weapons, and a canoe. Molina di Ledro is part of the UNESCO-listed Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, and the Museo delle Palafitte, on the lake shore, displays the finds alongside reconstructed huts on stilts.

Lake Ledro is a small, clear lake in a green valley above Riva del Garda, surrounded by forests and mountains. It is popular for swimming, kayaking and walking, and in summer its shores are busy with families from Trentino and beyond. The water is colder than Garda, and the air fresher, which makes it a welcome escape from the heat of the lake below.

The ride up from Riva is famous. The old Ponale road, carved into the cliffs above Lake Garda in the nineteenth century, was once the only route, and it is now closed to motor traffic and used by cyclists and walkers. The modern road, the SS240, climbs through a long tunnel and then along the valley, an easy ride with views back toward the lake. Beyond Ledro, the road continues through the Val di Ledro and down to the Valle del Chiese, then on toward Lake Idro and Brescia, a lovely route with forests, villages and few cars.

The area is a paradise for riders, with the Garda roads, the Tremosine plateau and its terrace road, the Passo del Tonale and the roads of the Brenta Dolomites all within reach. Riva del Garda, six kilometres away, has fuel, food and lodgings, though it is busy in summer. Try the local trout, carne salada, Trentino cheeses and the olive oil of the Garda. Spring and early autumn are best, when the roads are quieter and the weather mild.
t.historic centre of the city of salzburg@:
Salzburg's old town is a stage set that happens to be real. Squeezed between the river Salzach and the steep rock of the Mönchsberg, it packs baroque domes, church towers and tall merchants' houses into a few dense streets, while the white walls of Hohensalzburg fortress sit high above everything like a lid on a jewellery box. The city has around a hundred and fifty thousand people, yet the centre still feels small enough to cross on foot in twenty minutes.

Its wealth came from salt. For centuries the prince-archbishops controlled the mines at nearby Hallein and Bad Reichenhall, and they spent the money on making their capital look like Rome north of the Alps. The cathedral, the squares around it and the Residenz date largely from the ambitious seventeenth-century rebuilding. Mozart was born on Getreidegasse in 1756, and the yellow house is now a museum, though the narrow lane with its wrought iron shop signs is half the attraction. Every summer the Salzburg Festival fills the city with music, and in December the Christkindlmarkt in front of the cathedral smells of mulled wine and roasted almonds.

Riding into the centre is not the point; much of the old town is pedestrian, parking is limited and the one-way system rewards local knowledge. Leave the bike on the edge, at a garage or a designated motorcycle bay, and walk. Remember that Austrian motorways and expressways need a vignette, which you can buy digitally or at fuel stations near the border. The real riding starts once you leave town. The Salzkammergut lakes lie to the east, Berchtesgaden and the Rossfeld panorama road a short hop south across the German border, and the Grossglockner road within an easy day.

Fuel and food are no trouble, with stations on every main road out of town. For a break, cross the river to the Mirabell gardens, or climb to the fortress for a view over rooftops to the Untersberg. Then try a Salzburger Nockerl, a soufflé shaped like three snowy peaks, which is as close to edible scenery as Austria gets.
t.mantua and sabbioneta@45.2,10.8:
Approach Mantua from the north across the causeway and you see why it was so hard to conquer: the city rises from water on three sides, encircled by lakes formed from the river Mincio, its domes and towers reflected in the still surface. For nearly four centuries it belonged to the Gonzaga family, who turned a marshy town into one of the most brilliant courts of the Renaissance, and Mantua is listed by UNESCO together with Sabbioneta, the small ideal city that a branch of the same family built some thirty kilometres away.

Inside the Ducal Palace, a sprawling complex of courtyards and halls, the Camera degli Sposi painted by Andrea Mantegna is one of the treasures of Italian art, with its trompe l'oeil ceiling where figures peer down through a painted opening to the sky. At the other end of town, Palazzo Te, designed by Giulio Romano as a pleasure palace, has a room where giants seem to crash down around you. The Roman poet Virgil was born near Mantua, and the city has a calm, cultured air, with arcaded streets, bicycles and squares made for long dinners.

Sabbioneta was built in the late sixteenth century by Vespasiano Gonzaga as a planned town: star-shaped walls, a grid of streets, a theatre, galleries and palaces, all designed to express Renaissance ideas about the perfect city. On a weekday it can be almost silent, which makes it rather wonderful.

The ride between the two crosses the Po plain, flat and fertile, with poplar plantations, rice fields, dykes and farmhouses. Straight roads, dusty in summer and shrouded in fog in winter, are punctuated by sharp corners at field boundaries. Mosquitoes can be fierce on summer evenings near the water. Mantua's centre has limited traffic zones, so park outside the core and walk. Fuel and food are easy in Mantua; for lunch, order tortelli di zucca, pasta filled with pumpkin, amaretti and mostarda, a sweet and savoury mix that sums up the city's character, or risotto alla pilota with sausage, from the rice country just outside the walls.
t.le colline del prosecco di conegliano e:
These are not soft, rolling wine hills. Between Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, the foothills of the Pre-Alps rise in steep hogback ridges, sharp crests of rock running east to west, with vines clinging to slopes so steep that much of the work is still done by hand. Grass-covered terraces called ciglioni hold the soil in place, and the result is a patchwork of vines, woods and small villages that UNESCO listed in 2019.

The grape is Glera, the base for Prosecco Superiore, and the wineries here range from tiny family cellars to grand estates. The Strada del Prosecco, opened in 1966 as Italy's first official wine road, winds through the hills linking them. Look for the Molinetto della Croda, a seventeenth-century mill by a waterfall near Refrontolo, and the small lakes of Revine to the north. Vittorio Veneto gave its name to the decisive Italian victory of the First World War in 1918, and the town has a museum dedicated to it.

For riders, the region has two personalities. In the hills, the roads are narrow and sinuous, flowing from one viewpoint to the next with constant changes of gradient, perfect for a relaxed pace and plenty of stops. Just to the north, the Passo San Boldo climbs from Tovena in a stack of hairpins and tunnels carved into the rock, built by the Austro-Hungarian army in a matter of months during the war; it has an alternating traffic light system and height limits, and anyone who loves unusual roads should ride it at least once. Beyond lie the Dolomites, within easy reach.

Vittorio Veneto, a town of around twenty-five thousand, is the obvious place for fuel and services, as is Conegliano to the south. Look for osterie that serve spiedo, meat roasted slowly on a spit, or a plate of soppressa salami with polenta, alongside a cold glass of Prosecco. The best months are spring and autumn, when the vines are green or gold and the summer heat has eased.
t.hiroshima peace memorial@34.4,132.5:
The skeleton of a dome against the sky, the twisted steel frame of what was once an elegant exhibition hall, is one of the most recognisable images of the twentieth century. On 6 August 1945, the atomic bomb exploded almost directly above this building in central Hiroshima. Almost everything around it was destroyed, but part of its walls and dome remained, and after long debate the city chose to preserve the ruin exactly as it was. It was listed by UNESCO in 1996 as the Hiroshima Peace Memorial, also known as the Genbaku Dome.

The building was designed before the war by a Czech architect, Jan Letzel, as the Hiroshima Prefectural Industrial Promotion Hall. Today it stands beside the Motoyasu river at the northern edge of the Peace Memorial Park, with the cenotaph, the Children's Peace Monument hung with strings of paper cranes, and the museum, which is harrowing but essential. Many visitors come away silent. The city around it, rebuilt from ashes, is a lively, friendly place with trams, broad avenues and a famous baseball team, the Carp.

Riding in Japan is orderly, careful and often slow in towns, with frequent traffic lights and strict speed limits. Foreign riders need an international driving permit of the right kind, and expressways carry tolls. From Hiroshima, the coastal roads along the Seto Inland Sea offer beautiful views of islands and bridges, and the Shimanami Kaido, the bridge route linking islands across to Shikoku, starts not far east; the expressway over the bridges is open to motorcycles above a certain size, while smaller bikes use dedicated lanes. Inland, the Chugoku mountains have quiet, curvy roads through forests and small farming villages.

Fuel stations are everywhere, many with attendants. Parking for motorcycles in the city is in designated spaces, so look for them rather than leaving the bike on the pavement. Hiroshima has its own style of okonomiyaki, layered pancakes with cabbage, noodles and pork, cooked on a hot plate in front of you, and it is the perfect meal after a heavy day. The island of Miyajima, with its floating torii gate, is a short ride and ferry away.
t.oberranna kleinkastell@48.5,13.8:
The Danube between Passau and Linz is one of the loveliest stretches of the whole river, and near Oberranna, on the Upper Austrian bank, it flows quietly between steep wooded slopes, dark and almost gorge-like. Here, beside the water, archaeologists found a small Roman fort, a Kleinkastell, part of the Danube Limes that guarded the northern frontier of the province of Noricum. Its remains are now protected under a modern shelter, and it forms part of the UNESCO listing of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire along the Danube.

The fort was small, holding perhaps a few dozen soldiers to watch the river and the road along it, and its walls and towers have been preserved to a surprising height, giving a real sense of its layout. A short distance downstream is the abbey of Engelszell, the only Trappist monastery in Austria, where the monks brew beer and make liqueurs, and further along, the river makes its famous loop at Schlögen, a tight bend where the water reverses direction around a forested spur. A viewpoint above the loop is one of the classic sights of the upper Danube.

Riding along the Danube here is relaxed and beautiful. The road on the southern bank follows the river closely, with gentle curves, views across the water and small villages with inns and moorings for river cruise boats. Side roads climb away from the river into the Innviertel and the Sauwald hills, with sharper bends, farm traffic and wide views. Ferries cross the river at several points, linking the two banks and making for interesting loops. Be aware of cyclists, especially in summer, as the Danube cycle path is one of the most popular in Europe.

The nearest towns are small, with limited services, but Engelhartszell and other villages along the river have fuel stations or are close to them, and Passau, a little upstream, has everything you need. Riverside inns serve local fish such as pike-perch, as well as Austrian classics like schnitzel and roast pork. Remember that Austrian motorways require a vignette, though you will hardly need them here.
t.parco comunale di luine di darfo boario:
Valcamonica, the long valley of the Oglio river north of Lake Iseo, holds one of the largest collections of prehistoric rock carvings in the world, with hundreds of thousands of figures pecked into smooth glacier-polished rocks over thousands of years. It was the first site in Italy to be listed by UNESCO, in 1979. The Luine park, on a wooded hill above Darfo Boario Terme at the southern end of the valley, is one of the places where you can see these engravings up close, with paths leading between rock surfaces covered in figures of animals, people, weapons and mysterious symbols.

The carvings at Luine are among the oldest in the valley, and some may date back to the end of the last Ice Age, while others were made in later periods. The most famous symbol of Valcamonica, the Camunian rose, a curving, four-armed design, has been adopted as the emblem of the Lombardy region. Walking among the rocks, often in dappled shade under chestnut trees, you get a sense of a sacred landscape, used and reused over countless generations. Darfo Boario Terme itself is a spa town, with thermal baths and a park with Art Nouveau buildings.

For riders, Valcamonica is a gateway to some of the best roads in the Alps. The valley road runs north towards Edolo and the Passo del Tonale, and side roads climb to the Passo del Vivione, a narrow, dramatic pass with tight bends and huge views, and to the Passo di Crocedomini and the Gavia, high passes with spectacular scenery, though they are often closed in winter and can be challenging, with narrow sections and steep drops. To the south, the road along Lake Iseo offers gentle curves and lake views.

Darfo Boario Terme has around fifteen thousand people and plenty of fuel, shops and restaurants. The valley is known for its cheeses, such as Silter, and for casoncelli, stuffed pasta served with butter and sage. Try a glass of wine from the nearby Franciacorta region, famous for its sparkling wines. Visit the rock carvings early in the day, when the low sun makes the engravings easier to see.
t.puez odle puez geisler poz odles@46.6,11:
Above Selva in Val Gardena and the villages of Val Badia, the Puez-Odle massif shows the Dolomites at their most theatrical: the jagged spires of the Odle, or Geisler, piercing the sky like a row of broken teeth, and behind them the Puez plateau, a strange high desert of grey scree, layered rock and hidden lakes. The area is a nature park in South Tyrol and one of the nine components of the Dolomites World Heritage site, listed by UNESCO in 2009 for its exceptional landscapes and geology.

The Dolomites are the remains of ancient coral reefs and tropical seas, lifted up by the collision of continents and carved by ice and water into towers, walls and plateaus. On the Puez plateau, you can see the layers of rock like the pages of a book, recording millions of years of the earth's history. The valleys below are home to the Ladin people, who speak their own Romance language, Ladin, and have kept their traditions, from wood carving in Val Gardena to distinctive costumes and festivals. In summer, the meadows are full of flowers and cows, and in winter, the area is one of the most famous ski regions in the world.

For riders, the passes around the Puez-Odle massif are legendary. The Passo Gardena, at 2,121 metres, links Val Gardena with Val Badia, and the Passo Sella and Passo Campolongo complete the Sella Ronda, a loop around the Sella massif that is one of the classic motorcycle rides of the Alps. The roads are well maintained, with hairpins, steep climbs and spectacular views, but in summer, traffic can be heavy, with cars, buses, cyclists and other motorcyclists, and the authorities have discussed restrictions to reduce congestion and noise. Ride early in the morning or late in the afternoon for the best experience.

Selva and the other villages have fuel, restaurants, cafés and hotels, though prices can be high. Ladin and Tyrolean cuisine is hearty: try canederli, bread dumplings with speck or cheese, or schlutzkrapfen, half-moon ravioli filled with spinach and cheese, and finish with apple strudel. Weather in the mountains can change quickly, with afternoon thunderstorms in summer, and the passes can be closed by snow from autumn to spring.
t.villa emo@45.7,12.0:
Andrea Palladio built villas for the Venetian nobility as working farms, not just as country houses, and Villa Emo at Fanzolo is perhaps the purest example of that idea. Completed around 1560 for the Emo family, it stands at the centre of a flat, fertile estate, with a long, symmetrical central block flanked by two arcaded wings, the barchesse, which housed the farm buildings, storage and dovecotes. The ramp leading up to the front door was used for threshing grain. Inside, the rooms are decorated with frescoes by Giovanni Battista Zelotti, mythological and allegorical scenes that bring colour and life to the classical architecture. The villa is part of the UNESCO listing of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto.

The Emo family owned the villa for more than four centuries, which is part of the reason it has survived so well. The surrounding fields are still farmed, and the long straight avenue leading to the villa gives a sense of the original layout, with the house at the centre of a carefully planned agricultural landscape.

The riding around Fanzolo is flat and easy, through the plains of the Treviso province, with long straight roads, fields of maize and vines, and small towns and villages. It is not dramatic, but the mountains are never far away. To the north, Monte Grappa rises from the plain, with a famous road that climbs to the summit and the vast war memorial there, the scene of heavy fighting in the First World War. To the north east, the Prosecco hills around Valdobbiadene and Conegliano offer winding roads through vineyards, with views over the plain.

Castelfranco Veneto, about seven kilometres away, is a walled town with a fine cathedral, which houses a famous altarpiece by Giorgione, the Renaissance painter who was born there. It has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the local speciality is radicchio, especially the variegated Castelfranco variety, speckled with red. Asolo, a hilltop town north of the plain, is another lovely place to visit, with views over the countryside. The weather in the Veneto is hot and humid in summer, with occasional thunderstorms, so the early morning is the best time for riding.
t.san sivino@45.5,10.6:
On the western shore of Lake Garda, between Manerba and Moniga, the little bay of San Sivino hides something very old under its shallows. People lived here in the Bronze Age in villages built on wooden piles at the water's edge, and the remains of their posts, tools and pottery survive in the mud of the lake. The site is one of the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps that UNESCO listed in 2011, a series of more than a hundred sites spread across six countries. There is nothing to see above the water, but knowing that the shore was settled thousands of years ago adds a quiet depth to an afternoon by the lake.

The area is the Valtènesi, a gently rolling stretch of hills between the lake and the moraine country to the west, covered in vineyards and olive groves. The local wine is the Chiaretto, a pale, fresh rosé that is perfect on a hot afternoon, and the olive oil from the Garda shores has its own protected designation. Above Manerba, the Rocca di Manerba, a limestone promontory crowned with the ruins of a castle, rises steeply above the lake, with a nature reserve, walking paths and a spectacular view over the water and the islands.

Riding around Lake Garda is a mixed experience. The lakeside roads are beautiful but often crowded, especially in summer, with heavy traffic, slow-moving cars, buses and cyclists. The smaller roads through the Valtènesi hills are more relaxed, winding between vineyards and villages, with views over the lake. Further north, the road along the western shore, the Gardesana Occidentale, runs through a series of tunnels and galleries cut into the cliffs, with dramatic views, though it can be very busy. Early mornings and evenings outside the peak season are the best times to ride.

Manerba del Garda, Moniga and Solarolo are small towns with shops, cafes and restaurants, and fuel is available along the main roads. Sirmione, at the southern end of the lake, is a famous resort on a narrow peninsula, with a moated castle and the remains of a large Roman villa, though it can be overwhelmed by visitors in summer. The beaches around San Sivino are good places for a swim, with clear water and views of the Rocca.
t.remains of hara castle@32.6,130.3:
On a headland overlooking the Ariake Sea, at the southern tip of the Shimabara Peninsula in Nagasaki prefecture, the grassy ruins of Hara Castle mark the scene of one of the darkest episodes in Japanese history. In the winter of 1637 to 1638, thousands of peasants, many of them Christians, rose up against heavy taxation and religious persecution, and took refuge in the abandoned castle under the leadership of a charismatic teenager, Amakusa Shirō. The shogunate besieged the castle for months with a huge army, and when it finally fell, almost all the defenders, including women and children, were killed.

The rebellion led the shogunate to tighten its ban on Christianity and to close Japan to most foreign contact for more than two centuries. Those who kept their faith did so in secret, becoming the Hidden Christians, and the remains of Hara Castle are part of the UNESCO listing of Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region, added in 2018. Today the site is quiet, with stone walls, grassy terraces, a few monuments and a statue of Amakusa Shirō, with views over the sea to the hills of Amakusa.

The Shimabara Peninsula is dominated by the volcano Unzen, which rises in the centre, its slopes covered in forests and dotted with hot springs. In 1991, a pyroclastic flow from the Fugen-dake peak killed more than forty people, including journalists and volcanologists, and the area still bears the scars of that eruption. The road that climbs to the Unzen hot spring town and the Nita pass offers some of the best riding in the area, with tight bends, steep gradients and spectacular views over the sea and the volcano.

The coastal road around the peninsula is gentle and scenic, with little traffic and views over the sea. Shimabara, about twenty kilometres away, is the main town, with a reconstructed castle, carp swimming in the town's canals, and fuel and shops. Ferries run from Shimabara across the Ariake Sea to Kumamoto, a convenient way to continue a trip through Kyushu. The local speciality is guzoni, a hearty soup with rice cakes, said to have sustained the rebels during the siege.
t.limessection between watchtowers wp 13 5:
In the fields near Wilburgstetten, in the west of Franconia, a low ridge runs across the landscape, overgrown with grass and bushes. It looks like nothing much, but it is the remains of the Raetian Limes, the stone wall that marked the frontier of the Roman province of Raetia in the second and third centuries. Unlike the Upper German Limes to the north west, which was mostly a palisade and ditch, the Raetian section was eventually built as a continuous stone wall, more than a hundred and sixty kilometres long. Local people later called it the Teufelsmauer, the Devil's Wall, believing it could only have been built by supernatural forces. The section between watchtowers here is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site.

The frontier crossed the valley of the Wörnitz near here, and the river, slow and winding through meadows and woods, is a pleasant companion for a ride. Upstream lies Dinkelsbühl, about eight kilometres away, one of the best-preserved medieval towns in Germany, with a complete ring of walls, towers and gates, and streets of half-timbered and gabled houses. It sits on the Romantic Road, the famous tourist route through Bavaria from Würzburg to Füssen, and every summer it celebrates the Kinderzeche, a festival commemorating a legend from the Thirty Years' War, in which the town's children are said to have saved it from destruction.

The riding in this part of Franconia is gentle and pleasant, with quiet roads through rolling hills, fields, forests and villages. The roads are well surfaced and well signposted, with little traffic outside the main routes. The Romantic Road itself can be busy with tourist coaches in summer, but the minor roads that run parallel to it are much quieter. To the north, Rothenburg ob der Tauber is another medieval gem, and to the south east, the Nördlinger Ries, a huge crater formed by a meteorite impact millions of years ago, has the walled town of Nördlingen at its centre.

Wilburgstetten, Mönchsroth and Weiltingen are small villages with basic services, while Dinkelsbühl has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants and beer gardens. The local food is hearty Franconian fare, with roast pork, dumplings and sausages, and the local beers are excellent. The weather is continental, with warm summers and cold winters.
t.villa serego@45.5,10.9:
Andrea Palladio built many villas around the Veneto, but the one at Santa Sofia di Pedemonte, in the Valpolicella just north-west of Verona, is the oddball of the family. Commissioned by Marcantonio Serego in the mid-sixteenth century and never finished, it has none of the smooth classical calm of the Rotonda. Instead its courtyard is lined with giant Ionic columns built up from rough, rusticated blocks of local stone, as if the building were half turning back into the hillside. Only part of the planned design was completed, and the effect is wonderfully strange.

The villa stands among the vineyards of one of Italy's great red wine districts. Valpolicella's grapes, Corvina above all, are dried on racks for months before pressing to make Amarone, dense and powerful, and its sweet cousin Recioto. Many of the wine estates in the area are housed in old villas and farm courts, and the stone used throughout the valley, the pink and white limestone of the Lessini hills, gives the villages a warm colour. Verona itself, with its Roman arena and medieval bridges, is close enough to see from the higher slopes.

The riding is better than you might expect for a wine district. Small roads wind between the vineyards and villages of Negrar, Fumane and San Pietro in Cariano, and from here you can climb north into the Lessinia plateau, where hairpins lead up to high pastures, ancient stone huts and views over the Adige valley to Lake Garda and the Alps. Down in the valley traffic can be heavy around Pedemonte and on the main road into Verona, especially at rush hour. Autumn is the season, when the vines turn and the smell of fermenting grapes drifts over everything.

Fuel and shops are easy to find in Pedemonte and Arbizzano, both close by, and Verona has everything. The villa is a working estate and visits are not always possible, so look before you plan the stop around a tour. For food, try risotto all'Amarone or pasta e fagioli, and keep the tasting for the end of the day. Verona's summer opera season in the arena is worth planning a night around.
t.the monumental area with the monastic co:
The centre of Brescia holds two thousand years of layered history within a few hundred metres. Along the old Roman main street, the Capitolium temple raised under Vespasian still lifts its columns above the forum, with a Roman theatre beside it, and a short walk away the monastery of San Salvatore and Santa Giulia spreads its cloisters and churches over the site of Roman houses. The monastery was founded in the eighth century by Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards, and his wife Ansa; their daughter Ermengarda, rejected by Charlemagne, is said to have ended her days here.

Together these monuments form part of the World Heritage listing for the Lombards in Italy, and the Santa Giulia museum is one of the most rewarding in northern Italy. Inside are Roman mosaics, the extraordinary jewelled cross of Desiderius, and the bronze Winged Victory found in the Capitolium in 1826, recently restored and displayed in its own temple room. On the hill above the city, the castle on the Cidneo looks out over the plain and the foothills of the Alps.

To a motorcyclist, Brescia means one thing above all: the Mille Miglia, the legendary road race that started and finished here from 1927 to 1957, sending cars racing to Rome and back on public roads. Its spirit lives on in the vintage event that still leaves the city every year, and the museum dedicated to it sits in an old monastery on the eastern edge of town. Riding in the city is the usual urban grind of traffic lights, buses and limited-traffic zones in the centre, so park and walk. Out of town, Lake Iseo, the vineyards of Franciacorta and the Valtrompia and Valcamonica roads into the mountains are all within easy reach.

Brescia is a big city with fuel and services everywhere. The food is hearty Lombard fare: casoncelli pasta with butter and sage, polenta, and spit-roasted meats, with Franciacorta sparkling wine to wash it down. The monastery and museum deserve at least two hours, and summer heat in the city can be oppressive, so a morning visit followed by an afternoon ride to the lakes makes a good plan.
t.sakitsu village in amakusa@32.3,130.0:
A small Gothic church with a spire stands right at the water's edge in Sakitsu, a fishing village tucked into an inlet on the southern coast of Amakusa's Shimoshima island. It looks almost Breton, a surprise in rural Kyushu, and the story behind it is one of the most moving in Japanese history. When Christianity was banned in the early seventeenth century, the people of Sakitsu kept their faith in secret for over two centuries, disguising prayers and objects as Buddhist or Shinto practice, and using things from their own fishing life, such as abalone shells whose inner patterns recalled holy images, as objects of devotion.

The church was rebuilt in the 1930s on the site of the village headman's house, where the authorities once forced villagers to trample on images of Christ and Mary to prove they were not Christians; the altar is said to stand where those trampling ceremonies took place. Sakitsu is part of the World Heritage listing of the Hidden Christian sites of the Nagasaki region. Amakusa was also a heartland of the Shimabara rebellion of 1637 and 1638, a peasant uprising led by the teenage Amakusa Shiro that ended in a massacre and hardened the persecution.

Getting here is a lovely ride. From the Kyushu mainland, the Amakusa Five Bridges carry the road across islands and straits, and then smaller coastal roads wind around inlets, through fishing villages and over wooded headlands, with views across the sea to other islands. Traffic in Japan drives on the left, roads are well maintained but often narrow, and speed limits are low and enforced. Typhoon season in late summer can bring heavy rain and strong winds, so spring and autumn are the best times.

Fuel and food are easy to find in Ushibuka and Hondo, the main towns of the islands. Sakitsu itself has a small information centre and a few places to eat, including fresh seafood from the local fishermen. The village is still lived in, so visit quietly and respect the residents, especially around the church, which is still used for worship and asks visitors to behave with respect during services.
t.wallsee kleinkastell@48.2,14.7:
Wallsee is the kind of Danube town you only notice if you slow down: a market square, a big castle on a rock above the river, and a long, quiet waterfront where the cycle path runs past willows and moored boats. Beneath the streets lie the remains of a small Roman fort, one of the posts that lined the river frontier of the province of Noricum, and archaeologists have also traced a larger fort nearby. Both are part of the Danube Limes World Heritage listing inscribed in 2021, though above ground the medieval and Baroque town has long since taken over.

Wallsee sits right on the boundary between Lower and Upper Austria, at the northern edge of the Mostviertel, the country of perry and cider. Old pear trees line the lanes and stand in the meadows around the farmsteads, white with blossom in April, and the region has signposted a Moststraße, a road of cider taverns and farm shops. A little downstream, the Danube enters the Strudengau, a narrow wooded gorge where whirlpools and rocks once terrified boatmen; Grein, with its castle and tiny old theatre, is the main town there.

For riders, the roads on the south bank wind through the rolling Mostviertel hills between farms and orchards, with gentle curves, good surfaces and little traffic. Cross the river at the power station or by ferry and the north bank opens up the Strudengau and the climbs into the Mühlviertel, with tighter bends and forest. On summer weekends you will share the riverside roads with many cyclists, and some sections have low speed limits. Spring blossom and the colours of October are the high points.

Perg, on the north side, is the nearest town of five thousand people and has fuel and shops; Amstetten, to the south, is larger. Wallsee itself has a few inns and cafés, and a glass of Most with a Brettljause, a board of cold meats, cheese and spreads on dark bread, is the local answer to a long day in the saddle. The castle is private, but its silhouette over the river at sunset is free for everyone.
t.lone valley@48.6,10.2:
The Lone is a small river in the Swabian Jura, east of Ulm, that often vanishes underground in dry weather, slipping into the limestone and leaving its bed empty. Its quiet valley, flanked by wooded slopes and limestone cliffs, holds caves where some of the oldest figurative art in the world was found. In the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave, fragments of a figure carved from mammoth ivory were pieced together into the Lion Man, a being with a human body and a lion's head, around forty thousand years old. In the Vogelherd cave, tiny ivory animals, a horse, a mammoth, a cave lion, emerged from the sediment.

These caves, together with others in the nearby Ach valley, were inscribed by UNESCO in 2017 as the Caves and Ice Age Art in the Swabian Jura. The Archaeopark at Vogelherd lets you walk up to the cave and see some of the finds, and the Lion Man himself lives in the museum in Ulm. Standing at the mouth of a cave where people sat by the fire and carved these figures while mammoths roamed the valley below is a humbling experience.

The landscape is gentle and rural, with fields, meadows and patches of beech forest on the plateau, and the Lone valley winding through it. The roads are smooth, quiet and mostly straight, with some pleasant curves where they dip into the valley or climb back onto the plateau. Traffic is light except near Ulm and on the main roads, and the riding is relaxed rather than thrilling. Late spring and early autumn are lovely, and the valley is particularly beautiful in the soft light of evening.

Langenau, a market town seven kilometres south, has fuel and a supermarket, and Niederstotzingen, a little closer, covers the basics. The Archaeopark at the Vogelherd has a café with a terrace overlooking the valley, and the village inns serve Swabian classics: Maultaschen, the large pasta parcels filled with meat and spinach, Käsespätzle with fried onions, and lentils with sausages. Ulm, half an hour away, is the place to meet the Lion Man in person, and its minster has the tallest church spire in the world, with a dizzying staircase for anyone whose legs survived the ride.
t.enns graberstra e@48.2,14.5:
Enns claims to be the oldest town in Austria, on the strength of a charter granted in 1212, but its roots go much deeper. Just outside the modern town lay Lauriacum, a Roman legionary fortress that housed the Second Italian Legion and grew into one of the most important places on the Danube frontier, with a civilian town, temples and, as the Gräberstraße name suggests, roads lined with cemeteries. The Romans buried their dead along the roads outside settlements, and excavations here have found hundreds of graves, stones and offerings. The site is part of the Danube Limes World Heritage listing.

Christianity left its mark too. Saint Florian, a Roman officer, was drowned in the Enns river in 304 for refusing to give up his faith, and the great Augustinian monastery of St. Florian, a few kilometres away, stands over his supposed grave; the composer Anton Bruckner was organist there and is buried beneath the organ. In Enns itself, the tall Stadtturm stands in the middle of the main square, and the basilica of St. Laurenz in the suburb of Lorch is built over Roman and early Christian remains. Across the Danube, the memorial at Mauthausen, a former Nazi concentration camp, is a sobering reminder of a much darker chapter.

The riding around Enns offers variety. The town sits where the Enns river meets the Danube, and roads follow both valleys: south, along the Enns, towards Steyr and the mountains of the Kalkalpen national park, with winding roads and dramatic scenery; east and west, along the Danube, through farmland and villages. Traffic can be heavy near Linz and on the main roads, but the side roads are quiet and scenic.

Enns is big enough for fuel, banks and a choice of restaurants, and its main square, with the tall Stadtturm in the middle, is a good place to sit in the sun with a coffee and a slice of Linzer torte, the latticed jam tart from the city just up the road. The town museum holds many of the finds from Lauriacum, including tombstones from the roads of the dead. Allow half a day for St. Florian if you can; the abbey's library and Bruckner's organ are extraordinary, and the drive there is a short, pleasant run through farmland.
t.idrija smelting plant@46.0,14.0:
In 1490, so the story goes, a tub-maker soaking a wooden vessel in a spring found shiny drops of liquid metal at the bottom. It was mercury, and the mine that grew from that discovery at Idrija, in the hills of western Slovenia, became the second largest mercury mine in the world, operating for five centuries. Together with Almadén in Spain, it was inscribed by UNESCO in 2012. The smelting plant, where the ore was roasted to release the mercury vapour, was the heart of the operation, and its buildings and furnaces now tell the story of the industry and its toll on the workers.

Idrija is a compact town in a deep valley of the Idrijca river, surrounded by steep, forested hills.
