Besides the mine, it is famous for lace, idrijska čipka, made with bobbins by local women since the seventeenth century, when miners' wives supplemented their income with it, and for žlikrofi, small dumplings filled with potato and herbs, protected as a traditional speciality. The castle of Gewerkenegg, which housed the mine administration, now holds the town museum, and the Anthony's shaft, one of the oldest entrances to the mine, can be visited.

The roads around Idrija are a delight for riders. The Idrijca valley road winds along the river through narrow gorges, and the routes over the hills to Cerkno, Žiri and Logatec offer endless corners, climbs and descents, through forests and small villages. Tarmac is mostly well kept, and once you leave the valley floor you may not meet another vehicle for long stretches. Remember that motorcycles need a vignette for Slovenian motorways. May and late September are ideal; high summer can be sticky down in the gorge.

Idrija is a small town but a complete one, with fuel, shops and several gostilnas, the traditional Slovenian inns. Order žlikrofi with a rich meat sauce called bakalca, and look in at the lace shops, where the patterns are fine enough to need a magnifying glass. The mine tour through the Anthony's shaft is well done and gives a real sense of the conditions underground, and the castle museum explains how mercury from these hills travelled across the world. On the edge of town, the Divje jezero, the Wild Lake, is a small, intensely green karst spring that sometimes surges up after rain.
t.watchtowers wp 12 60 to 12 68@48.9,10.1:
The Roman frontier wall known as the Limes ran for more than five hundred kilometres across what is now southern Germany, from the Rhine to the Danube, and near Aalen it passed through the Kocher valley and over the hills of the Ostalb. Along its length, watchtowers were built at regular intervals, numbered by archaeologists in sequence: WP 12/60 to 12/68 are a group of tower sites near Hüttlingen, mostly now visible as low mounds or reconstructed foundations. The Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes was inscribed by UNESCO in 2005 as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

Aalen, a few kilometres away, was home to the largest Roman cavalry fort north of the Alps, garrisoned by a unit of a thousand horsemen, and the Limesmuseum there displays the finds and tells the story of life on the frontier, with reconstructions and a park on the site of the fort. The Kocher river flows through the valley, and the Ostalb, the eastern part of the Swabian Jura, rises around, a landscape of forested hills, juniper heaths and limestone cliffs.

The roads here are a pleasure: quiet, well surfaced, with gentle curves through the valleys and over the hills. The Deutsche Limesstraße, a signposted touring route, follows the line of the frontier through the region, and the roads of the Ostalb, through forests and villages, offer good riding. Traffic is light except near the towns, and the scenery is varied and attractive. The Ostalb is at its best in early summer, when the juniper heaths are in flower and the evenings stay light until late.

Hüttlingen, just down the Kocher valley, can fill the tank, and Aalen, a town of nearly seventy thousand people, covers everything else. The Limesmuseum deserves a couple of hours, with its full-size reconstructions, cavalry equipment and the outline of the vast fort laid out in the park. Swabian inns in the area serve Zwiebelrostbraten, roast beef under a heap of fried onions, with Spätzle on the side, and the local beers from small breweries in the Ostalb are excellent. Aalen's old town, compact and pleasant, makes a good evening stroll after a day on the road.
t.watchtower wp 14 28@49.1,11.0:
Near the Franconian town of Pleinfeld, the Raetian Limes, the stone wall that marked the frontier of the province of Raetia, crossed a landscape of woods, fields and small rivers, and a watchtower stood here, one of hundreds along the line. Watchtower WP 14/28 is now a low mound or reconstructed foundation, but it is part of the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes World Heritage listing. The frontier here was a stone wall, known locally as the Teufelsmauer, the devil's wall, because medieval villagers could not believe that humans had built it.

A few kilometres to the south, the town of Weißenburg was the site of a Roman fort called Biriciana, and its Roman baths, among the best preserved in Germany, and its museum, displaying a hoard of Roman treasure found by a gardener in 1979, are well worth a visit. North of Pleinfeld, the Franconian lake district, a series of artificial lakes created from the 1970s onwards, offers beaches, sailing and swimming, and the Brombachsee is the largest of them. Ellingen, nearby, has a magnificent Baroque palace, built by the Teutonic Order.

The riding here is relaxed and pleasant, through rolling farmland, forests and villages, with lakes and rivers adding variety. The roads are well surfaced and quiet, with gentle curves, and the Altmühl valley, to the south, offers more dramatic scenery, with limestone cliffs and winding roads. Traffic is light except near the lakes in summer.

Pleinfeld, a couple of kilometres off, sells petrol and provisions, and Weißenburg and Gunzenhausen offer more choice. The Franconian lake district, built from the 1970s onwards, has beaches, boat hire and cafés along its shores, and a swim in the Brombachsee is a fine way to end a hot day. Franconia is famous for its many small breweries, and a Schäufele, roast pork shoulder with crackling and dumplings, with a local beer in a village inn, is the regional classic. Ellingen's palace, Weißenburg's Roman baths and the Roman treasure in the town museum are all within half an hour.
t.watchtowers wp 13 16 to 13 36 including:
The Raetian Limes ran across southern Franconia as a stone wall, and between Wassertrüdingen and Gunzenhausen it climbed over low hills and crossed the valleys of small rivers, with watchtowers at regular intervals. The group from WP 13/16 to 13/36 includes the sites of several towers and a fortlet, now visible as low mounds and foundations, sometimes with reconstructions, and they are part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes World Heritage listing. In the woods and fields, a line of stones or a slight bank may mark the course of the wall.

The landscape around here is gentle and rural, with the Hesselberg, the highest hill in Middle Franconia, rising to the north-west, and the Ries, a vast crater formed by a meteorite impact around fifteen million years ago, to the south. The medieval town of Nördlingen, in the centre of the crater, has a complete circuit of walls, and the stone of its church tower contains tiny diamonds formed by the impact. Dinkelsbühl, to the west, is one of the best preserved medieval towns in Germany.

For riders, this is easy country: quiet roads through farmland, forests and villages, with gentle curves and little traffic. The Romantic Road, a famous touring route, passes through Dinkelsbühl and Nördlingen, and the roads around the Hesselberg and the Ries crater offer views and variety. It is the sort of riding where you find yourself humming in the helmet.

Wassertrüdingen, a small town seven kilometres west, can supply petrol and a snack, and Gunzenhausen and Dinkelsbühl offer more. The villages have inns serving Franconian food and beer from local breweries, and Dinkelsbühl and Nördlingen have many restaurants and cafés in their medieval centres. Climb the Daniel, the tower of Nördlingen's church, for a view across the rim of the crater, or walk the complete circuit of the town walls. The Hesselberg, with its open summit, offers a wide view over the region and is a popular spot for paragliders and walkers.
t.sneznik zdrocle@45.6,14.5:
Ždrocle is a fragment of primeval beech forest on the slopes of Snežnik, the big karst mountain in the far south of Slovenia, close to the Croatian border, and it is one of the components of the great European UNESCO listing of ancient and primeval beech forests. That listing stretches from the Carpathians to Spain, but here you are in its Dinaric heart, where beech, fir and maple grow on a chaotic surface of limestone sinkholes, sharp ridges and hollows full of moss. Snežnik itself rises to just under eighteen hundred metres and holds its snow late, which is how it got its name.

This is one of the wildest corners of Central Europe. Brown bears live in these forests in good numbers, along with wolves and lynx, and the karst underneath swallows rivers and spits them out again elsewhere. In autumn the beech woods go gold and copper; in summer they are cool and green even when the coast below is baking. There is no tourist infrastructure to speak of at the reserve itself, which is entirely the point.

Riding here is about forest roads, many of them gravel, which wind for miles through the woods between Ilirska Bistrica, Leskova Dolina and the Croatian side. Some are graded and fine for a road bike taken slowly; others are rough, rutted, and remote, with no phone signal and logging trucks that come round corners fast. On asphalt, the roads around Ilirska Bistrica and down towards Rijeka and Klana have plenty of curves, quiet traffic and broad views of the Brkini hills. Bear in mind wildlife on the road, especially deer at dusk.

Snežnik Castle, on the far side of the mountain in the Lož valley, is a fairytale little Renaissance castle worth the detour, and Cerknica's famous disappearing lake is not far beyond. Leskova Dolina is a tiny hamlet with nothing much; fill up in Ilirska Bistrica, the nearest town with services and a few places to eat, or across the border in Rijeka. Water in the karst disappears underground, so carry some on any forest excursion, and let someone know where you are going if you leave the asphalt.
t.sabbioneta@45.0,10.5:
Sabbioneta is a Renaissance experiment: a whole town built from scratch in the second half of the sixteenth century by Vespasiano Gonzaga, a soldier, scholar and minor prince of the great Mantuan family, who wanted a capital laid out according to the ideals of the age. He got it. Inside its star-shaped walls the streets run in a regular grid, and in a few hundred metres you pass a ducal palace, a long gallery built to show off his collection of ancient sculpture, a summer palace, and one of the earliest purpose-built theatres in Europe, the Teatro all'Antica, designed by Vincenzo Scamozzi. Sabbioneta and Mantua were listed together by UNESCO in 2008 as two contrasting visions of the Renaissance city.

When Vespasiano died in 1591 without a male heir, his town lost its reason to exist and simply stopped. That is why it survives so completely, a tiny place of fifteen hundred people inside walls built for a court. Walking through it on a weekday afternoon can feel eerily like walking onto an empty stage set.

The landscape is the lower Po plain, flat as a billiard table, cut into fields of maize, tomatoes and poplar plantations, with irrigation canals everywhere and the great river itself just to the south. The riding is straight and easy, on roads lined with plane trees or running along the top of embankments, and in summer the heat can be oppressive and the mosquitoes ferocious near the water. In autumn and winter thick fog settles over the plain, sometimes for days, which makes riding genuinely dangerous; if the forecast says nebbia, believe it.

Casalmaggiore, six kilometres away on the Po, is the nearest town with a decent choice of fuel stations, shops and places to eat; Sabbioneta itself has a few cafes and trattorias. This is good food country. Try tortelli di zucca, pumpkin-filled pasta with a hint of mostarda and amaretti, and the cured meats of the area, culatello and salame, with a glass of chilled Lambrusco from just across the river in Emilia. Then ride along the embankment at sunset, when the poplars throw long shadows across the fields.
t.city of verona@45.4,11.0:
Verona is where the north of Italy starts to feel like the south, and where history piles up in layers so thick that you trip over them. The Roman amphitheatre, the Arena, still dominates Piazza Bra and still hosts opera in summer, with tens of thousands of people sitting on stone steps two thousand years old. The Adige river swings through town in a double bend, crossed by bridges including the Ponte Pietra, part Roman and rebuilt after the Germans blew it up in 1945. And of course there is Juliet's balcony, which was added to a medieval house in the twentieth century to satisfy visitors searching for the Shakespeare story; people queue to rub the breast of her bronze statue for luck.

The city's real heyday came under the della Scala family in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, whose fortress of Castelvecchio, with its red-brick bridge over the Adige, now houses an excellent art museum. Their extraordinary Gothic tombs stand in a little courtyard near Piazza dei Signori. UNESCO listed the whole city in 2000.

Riding into Verona is not a joy. The centre is a limited traffic zone with cameras, the ring roads are busy, and summer heat makes stop-start traffic very uncomfortable. Park on the edge and walk. The real riding lies just outside the city: north into the Valpolicella, where narrow roads climb through terraced vineyards and cherry orchards to villages making Amarone, or further up onto the Lessinia plateau, with high pastures, stone huts and views over the whole Po plain on clear days. To the west, Lake Garda is less than forty kilometres away, and the Monte Baldo roads above its eastern shore are some of the best in the region.

Fuel is plentiful on the ring roads, less so in the centre. Verona eats well: try risotto all'Amarone, bigoli pasta with duck, or pastissada, a slow-cooked horse stew that is a local tradition, and the pandoro cake that was born here. Summer evenings, when the Arena lights up for the opera and the squares fill with people, are the best time to linger, but book a room well in advance during the festival season.
t.lucone@45.6,10.5:
Lucone is a small basin in the green hills of the Valtènesi, just west of Lake Garda, and it is one of the sites in the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. Once there was a little lake here, and during the Bronze Age people built villages of wooden houses raised on piles along its shore. The lake later turned to marsh and peat, which preserved the timbers, pottery and organic remains in waterlogged conditions for thousands of years. What you see today is a gentle, wooded hollow among vineyards and fields, and you need some imagination; the finds are in the archaeological museum in nearby Gavardo.

The countryside around it is some of the most pleasant in Lombardy. The Valtènesi rolls softly down to the lake shore between Salò and Desenzano, with vineyards, olive groves, cypress trees and little villages of warm stone. The local wines are the light red Groppello and the pale pink Chiaretto, perfect for a hot afternoon, and the olive oil from the Garda shore is excellent. Polpenazze del Garda, the nearest village, has a castle on a hill and a few places to eat.

The riding is gentle and very pretty. Narrow roads wind through the hills between villages, with short climbs and dips, views across the lake to Monte Baldo and the Sirmione peninsula, and the occasional tight bend in a village centre. The main lake road, the Gardesana Occidentale, is busy in summer with tourist traffic and cyclists, and its tunnels further north towards Limone are famous but often crowded. In the Valtènesi itself traffic is light outside the high season, though tractors and wine-estate vans are common in the harvest.

For fuel, Prevalle and the larger towns around Salò and Desenzano have plenty of stations. The lake beaches at Manerba and Moniga are a short ride away if you fancy a swim, and the Rocca di Manerba, a headland with ancient ruins, gives one of the best views over the lower lake. Spring and early autumn are ideal, with the light soft and the crowds thinning out; July and August can be hot and hazy, with frequent evening thunderstorms rolling down from the Alps.
t.archaeological area and the patriarchal:
Aquileia today is a village of fewer than three thousand people in the flat farmland of Friuli, near the head of the Adriatic, but two thousand years ago it was one of the largest and richest cities of the Roman Empire. Founded as a Latin colony in 181 BC to guard the northeastern approaches to Italy, it grew into a great trading port, connected to the sea by a river and a canal, through which amber, wine, oil and glass moved between the Mediterranean and the lands beyond the Alps. Attila sacked it in 452, and many of its people fled to the lagoons, where their descendants helped found Venice and Grado.

The basilica is the reason to come. Founded in the fourth century, it was rebuilt several times, and the present church, with its tall Romanesque bell tower, stands over one of the largest and most beautiful early Christian mosaic floors in the world. It was uncovered in the early twentieth century, and you walk above it on glass walkways, looking down at fish, birds, shepherds, Jonah being swallowed by a sea monster and donors' portraits, all in tiny coloured stones, all over sixteen hundred years old. UNESCO listed the archaeological area and basilica in 1998.

Around the village the excavated ruins of the Roman city are spread through the fields: the forum, a row of columns along the old river port, house foundations and a cypress-lined cemetery. A good museum holds the finds. The atmosphere is quiet and rural, nothing like the crowds of Pompeii.

The riding around here is flat and straightforward, across the Friulian plain with its maize fields, vineyards and long straight roads lined with poplars. South of Aquileia a causeway road crosses the lagoon to Grado, an old island town with a beautiful little cathedral, fresh fish and beaches. The wind, especially the bora from the northeast, can be strong and sudden. Cervignano del Friuli, six kilometres north, is the nearest town with a full choice of fuel and supermarkets. The local wines of the Aquileia DOC, refosco and friulano among them, are well worth a glass.
t.unfriedshausen@48.1,11.0:
Unfriedshausen is a hamlet in the rolling farmland west of the Ammersee, part of the municipality of Geltendorf in the Landsberg district of Bavaria, and if you have never heard of it, you are in good company. This is the gentle, prosperous countryside between Munich and Augsburg, a patchwork of fields, meadows, spruce woods, onion-domed churches and farmhouses with balconies full of geraniums, and it is the kind of place where the main event of the day might be a tractor crossing the road.

The village name sounds almost like unpeace in German, which is fitting enough, because the Lech plain just to the west has seen its share of war. In 955, somewhere on the Lechfeld south of Augsburg, Otto the Great defeated the Magyars in a battle that ended their raids into Western Europe and helped him become emperor. Augsburg itself, about twenty-five kilometres to the northwest, is one of Germany's oldest cities, founded by the Romans, and its water management system, a network of canals, water towers and fountains drawing on the Lech and Wertach rivers, was added to the World Heritage list in 2019.

The riding around here is relaxed rather than thrilling. Country roads link villages like Weil, Scheuring and Egling, with gentle curves, small hills and long views to the Alps on clear days, especially when the föhn wind blows from the south and the mountains seem close enough to touch. Traffic is light on weekdays, busier on weekends when Munich residents head for the lakes. Watch for farm machinery, mud on the road during harvest and cyclists, who are everywhere in Bavaria.

There is not much in Unfriedshausen itself; Geltendorf, seven kilometres away, has a station and basic services, and the larger towns of Landsberg am Lech, with its medieval old town and the Lech weir, and Fürstenfeldbruck have everything. The Ammersee, a short ride east, has lakeside beer gardens, boats and the monastery of Andechs on its hill above the eastern shore, famous for its beer brewed by monks. A cold Helles in a beer garden under the chestnut trees is the proper end to a summer day here.
t.pilgrimage church of wies@47.7,10.9:
In a meadow at the foot of the Ammergau Alps, surrounded by fields, cows and a few farmhouses, stands one of the most extraordinary churches in Europe. From the outside, the Wieskirche looks fairly plain, a white building with a modest tower. Step inside and you are hit by a wave of light, colour and movement: white and gold stucco, pastel frescoes, columns and galleries that seem to float, and a ceiling painting of Christ's return that opens the roof into heaven. It is the masterpiece of the Bavarian Rococo, built between 1745 and 1754 by Dominikus Zimmermann, with frescoes by his brother Johann Baptist, and it was listed by UNESCO in 1983.

The church owes its existence to a miracle. In 1738, a farmer's wife at the Wies, the meadow, noticed tears on the face of a battered wooden figure of the scourged Christ, which the monks of nearby Steingaden had discarded. Pilgrims began to arrive in such numbers that a small chapel was soon too small, and the abbey commissioned the great church. Dominikus Zimmermann was so attached to it that he spent his last years living in a house beside it.

The landscape is pure Bavarian Alpine foothills: rolling meadows, dark spruce forests, moors and lakes, with the limestone peaks of the Ammergau Alps rising to the south. The roads here are popular with riders, linking the Romantic Road through Steingaden with Oberammergau, Ettal and the Graswang valley towards Linderhof palace and on to Austria. They are generally smooth and well maintained, with flowing curves through forest and meadow, though summer weekends bring tour buses, cyclists and motorbike traffic in numbers. Neuschwanstein is less than half an hour away to the southwest.

The church has a big car park and a few kiosks and restaurants nearby serving coffee, cake and Bavarian dishes, perfect for a break. For fuel and a bigger choice, Steingaden is three kilometres away and Peiting, about thirteen kilometres, is the nearest larger town. Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon to avoid the crowds and to see the interior in the most beautiful light. Remember that it is a working church; services and concerts take place regularly, and quiet respect is expected.
t.king s house on schachen@47.4,11.1:
This is one of the few royal residences in Europe that you cannot reach by any road, and King Ludwig II of Bavaria would have liked it that way. The King's House on Schachen stands on a high alpine meadow at about 1,866 metres in the Wetterstein mountains, south of Garmisch-Partenkirchen, below the jagged walls of the range that culminates in the Zugspitze. Ludwig had it built between 1869 and 1872 as a mountain retreat, and from the outside it looks like a modest Swiss chalet. Inside, upstairs, is a fantasy: the Turkish Hall, a room of blue, gold and red, with a fountain, peacock-feather fans, divans and stained glass, where the king liked to celebrate his birthday dressed in oriental costume while his servants smoked hookahs.

Getting there means walking. The usual routes start from Schloss Elmau or from Garmisch, via the Partnach gorge or the old royal road through the forest, and take several hours each way, climbing well over a thousand metres. It is a full and demanding day, but the views over the Wetterstein and down to the Reintal are magnificent. Next to the house, an alpine botanical garden displays plants from mountain regions around the world, and a simple mountain hut offers food and beds in season. The house and hut are open only in summer, roughly from June to early October.

For riders, the house is a destination for a day off the bike. Garmisch-Partenkirchen, about eight kilometres away as the crow flies, is a lively resort town with every service, and the surrounding roads are among the best in the Bavarian Alps. The route to Mittenwald and on to the Austrian village of Leutasch climbs through forest and meadow, and from there you can descend to the Inn valley via the steep road to Telfs or loop back via Scharnitz and Seefeld. The road past Walchensee and over the Kesselberg is a classic but has weekend motorcycle restrictions on parts of it, so check the signs.

Weather in the mountains changes fast; afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and snow can fall at any time at this height. Bring proper boots, layers and water if you walk up. Garmisch has fuel, hotels, and beer gardens aplenty; after the climb, a weissbier and a pretzel taste better than anything in the Turkish Hall.
t.linz befestigung schlossberg@48.3,14.3:
Linz is a city that has reinvented itself. For much of the twentieth century it was known mainly for its steelworks and its uncomfortable links with the Nazi period; today it markets itself as a city of culture and technology, with the Ars Electronica centre glowing on the Danube bank at night, the Lentos art museum opposite, and a lively music scene. The Schlossberg, the castle hill above the old town, is where it all began: the Romans had a fort here called Lentia, part of the Danube frontier of the empire, and the Danube Limes is now on the World Heritage list. The castle that stands there now dates largely from the Renaissance, built for Emperor Frederick III, who spent his last years in Linz and died here in 1493. It houses a branch of the Upper Austrian state museum.

From the castle terrace you look down over the roofs of the old town to the Hauptplatz, one of the largest town squares in Austria, with its Trinity Column, and across the Danube to Urfahr and the hills beyond. Johannes Kepler lived and worked in Linz for fourteen years, and Anton Bruckner was organist at the old cathedral. The Pöstlingberg, the city's own hill across the river, is reached by one of the steepest adhesion railways in the world.

Riding into Linz means dealing with city traffic, a busy motorway ring and tram tracks, so park the bike and walk the old town. The riding around the city is excellent, though. North of the Danube, the Mühlviertel is a rolling upland of granite boulders, forests, villages and small farms, with quiet roads full of curves leading towards the Czech border and Český Krumlov. West along the Danube, the B130 and B131 follow the river through the narrow valley towards the Schlögen loop, where the river makes a dramatic hairpin through the forested hills.

Linz has every service imaginable: fuel, workshops, hotels and plenty of restaurants. The city's namesake, the Linzer Torte, a spiced nut pastry with a lattice top and redcurrant jam, is said to be one of the oldest cake recipes in the world. Austrian motorways require a vignette, including for motorcycles, so buy one if you plan to use them. Summer festivals, including the Linz Klangwolke, bring the city to life.
t.eining weinberg wachtturm und heiligtum@:
At Eining, on the Danube in Lower Bavaria, the Roman frontier of Raetia met the river. The Raetian Limes, a stone wall running for over a hundred and sixty kilometres across southern Germany, ended near here at Hienheim on the opposite bank, and from there the Danube itself formed the border all the way to the Black Sea. The Romans built the fort of Abusina at Eining, whose stone foundations are among the best preserved in Bavaria, and on the Weinberg, a hill nearby, they built a watchtower and a sanctuary, where soldiers worshipped their gods. Unusually, two separate World Heritage frontiers touch here: the Raetian Limes on land and the Danube Limes along the river.

A short distance upstream, the Danube cuts through a narrow gorge of white limestone cliffs, the Weltenburg Narrows, one of the most beautiful river landscapes in Germany. At the entrance to the gorge stands Weltenburg Abbey, a Benedictine monastery with a dazzling baroque church by the Asam brothers and a brewery that claims to be the oldest monastery brewery in the world. Boats run through the gorge between Weltenburg and Kelheim, where the Befreiungshalle, a huge round hall built by King Ludwig I to commemorate the wars against Napoleon, crowns a hill above the town.

Bad Gögging, right next to Eining, is a spa town with thermal baths, and the Romans also had baths here. Abensberg, a few kilometres to the south, is famous for its white asparagus and for the Kuchlbauer tower, a colourful, whimsical tower designed in the style of the artist Friedensreich Hundertwasser for a local brewery.

The riding in this part of Bavaria is pleasant, on country roads through farmland, hop gardens and forests, with gentle hills and the Danube valley. The Hallertau, the largest hop-growing region in the world, lies just to the south, and in late summer the hop poles are covered in green. Petrol and food are easy in Neustadt an der Donau, seven kilometres away, or in Abensberg. Watch for tractors, cyclists on the Danube cycle route and speed cameras. Try a beer from one of the many local breweries, with a Bavarian snack like Obatzda, a cheese spread, and fresh pretzels.
t.idrijska bela belca water barrier on the:
Deep in a wooded gorge above Idrija, where the stream called Idrijska Bela tumbles over pale limestone, stands one of the strangest pieces of old engineering in Slovenia: a klavže, a water barrier built of massive dressed stone blocks across the narrow valley. Its job had nothing to do with power or flood control. Idrija's mercury mine, one of the two largest in the world for centuries, devoured timber for its shafts and smelters, and the forests close to town were soon exhausted. So the miners built these dams on mountain streams, let water build up behind them, piled cut logs in the bed below and then opened the gates. The released flood swept the timber all the way down to Idrija, where it was caught at a rake across the river.

The barriers date from the eighteenth century and were used well into the twentieth, and the walk along the Idrijska Bela to reach them is one of the loveliest short hikes in the region, through beech forest along water of an almost unreal turquoise. The mine itself, together with the Spanish mercury town of Almadén, is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and Idrija's old miners' houses, its castle and the giant wooden water wheel called the Kamšt make the town worth an hour on their own. Idrija lace, made with bobbins, is still produced, and the local dish is žlikrofi, little stuffed dumplings that every inn serves with its own sauce.

For a rider this corner of western Slovenia is excellent. The road from Idrija down to Ajdovščina and the Vipava valley climbs and twists through forest, with a mix of tight hairpins and faster sections, and the road north-east towards Logatec and Ljubljana is just as much fun. Surfaces are generally good, traffic is light outside weekday commuting hours and the scenery shifts from deep green gorges to the high karst plateau. Expect wet roads; this is one of the rainiest parts of the country.

There is nothing at the barrier itself except the forest and the sound of water, so park sensibly at the trailhead and take some food and water with you. Idrija, about seven kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants, and it is small enough to cross on foot after the walk.
t.pelmo croda da lago@46.4,12.1:
Monte Pelmo is the mountain that looks like a throne. Its huge limestone mass, rising to 3,168 metres, has two summits linked by a great curved basin, and the people of the Cadore call it the Caregon del Padreterno, the armchair of God. It stands alone between the valleys of the Boite and the Fiorentina, and in 1857 it became the first major Dolomite peak to be climbed, by the Irish naturalist John Ball. Across the valley, the jagged towers of the Croda da Lago rise above the little Lago Federa, and the two together form one of the components of the Dolomites World Heritage site.

The area is wonderful for walking, but for riders it is pure joy. The Passo Giau, at 2,236 metres, links Selva di Cadore with the road near Cortina d'Ampezzo, and it is one of the finest passes in the Dolomites: a long sequence of hairpins climbing through larch forest to open meadows, with the Cinque Torri, the Nuvolau and the Tofane all around the summit. The Passo Staulanza, lower and gentler, runs past the foot of the Pelmo from Selva towards Zoldo, with the north face of the mountain looming over the road. Both are busy on fine summer weekends, with cyclists, cars and plenty of other bikes, so the early morning is the time to ride them. Snow can linger near the tops into June and come back in October.

Selva di Cadore is a small village with old wooden barns, and on a boulder below the Pelmetto, the smaller neighbour of the Pelmo, footprints of dinosaurs from more than two hundred million years ago were found in 1985; a cast is displayed in the village museum along with a much older story, the remains of a Mesolithic hunter found at Mondeval, not far away.

For fuel, Cortina d'Ampezzo is the obvious choice, as are Caprile and Alleghe to the south-west; the high villages may have little or nothing. Rifugi on the passes serve proper mountain food: canederli, polenta with mushrooms or cheese, and strudel. Be prepared for weather: afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and temperatures at the passes can be fifteen degrees lower than in the valleys, so pack a warm layer even on a hot day.
t.misumi west port@32.6,130.5:
At the tip of the Uto Peninsula in Kumamoto, where the land narrows towards the islands of Amakusa, there is a small Meiji-era harbour that looks almost unchanged since it was finished in 1887. Misumi West Port was designed by the Dutch engineer Rouwenhorst Mulder as part of Japan's rapid modernisation after it opened to the West, and its long stone quays, drainage channels and carefully fitted granite blocks were built by Japanese stonemasons using their traditional skills. For a while it was a busy export port for coal from the Miike mines across the bay, but when the railway reached another harbour its importance faded, which is precisely why it survived. It is now part of the World Heritage site of Japan's Meiji industrial revolution.

The port is a quiet place, with a few restored buildings from the period, including an old customs and an inn, and the view across the narrow strait to the green hills of Amakusa. The water is calm, the light soft, and on a warm day you hear little but gulls and the creak of moored boats. Unzen, the volcano on the Shimabara Peninsula, stands across the water to the west, and it was near Shimabara, at Hara Castle, that Christian peasants rose in rebellion in 1637 and were crushed by the shogunate, a story that runs through the whole region.

For riders, this is the gateway to one of the best coastal routes in Kyushu. From Misumi, the Amakusa Five Bridges hop from island to island across the sea, and beyond them, roads wind along the coast of the Amakusa islands past fishing villages, terraced fields and small churches that recall the hidden Christians who kept their faith in secret for centuries. The roads along the Uto Peninsula itself and on towards Kumamoto are easy, scenic and well surfaced. Remember Japan drives on the left, and speed limits are low and enforced.

There are small shops and a station at Misumi, and fuel is available along the main roads on the peninsula, with larger towns like Uki and Kumamoto city further inland. Seafood is the obvious meal here: fresh sashimi, octopus and sea bream in the little restaurants around the port and on Amakusa.
t.palu di livenza santissima@46.0,12.5:
At the foot of the Cansiglio plateau, where the Friulian mountains meet the plain, the river Livenza is born from springs of cold, clear water that rise from the limestone, and a little sanctuary, the Santissima, stands right by the source, surrounded by water. Not far away, in a marshy basin called the Palù di Livenza, archaeologists found the remains of a prehistoric pile dwelling settlement, with wooden posts, tools and pottery preserved in the wet ground for thousands of years. It is one of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps listed by UNESCO, a series of more than a hundred sites in six countries that tell the story of farming communities living on the edges of lakes and marshes from the Neolithic to the Bronze Age.

Polcenigo, the village next door, is one of the prettiest in Friuli, with old houses along a stream, a ruined castle on the hill and, a short walk away, the Gorgazzo spring, a deep, flooded cave in the rock filled with water of an intense blue, explored by divers to great depths. The water that flows from these springs keeps the rivers cool and clear all year round, and the air near them is noticeably fresh even in summer.

For riders, this area is an excellent base. The road from Aviano up to Piancavallo climbs the mountain in a long series of hairpins to a ski resort with views over the plain all the way to the Adriatic on a clear day, and the Cansiglio plateau, reached from Polcenigo or Fregona, is a vast beech forest with meadows and grazing deer, crossed by quiet, winding roads. To the west, the Prosecco hills around Valdobbiadene and Conegliano offer more curves among the vineyards. Traffic is light during the week but increases at weekends, when many people come up from the plain. Remember that Aviano is home to a large American air base, so you will see a lot of jets in the sky.

Caneva, Sacile and Aviano have fuel, shops and restaurants, and Polcenigo has a few trattorias and cafés. Try frico, a Friulian dish of fried cheese and potatoes, and the local wines, and if you are there in September, look out for the traditional fair of Polcenigo, the Sagra dei Sest, a celebration of woven baskets and local crafts.
t.fort site and civil settlement of reinau:
Out here on the eastern edge of Württemberg, where the Jagst valley widens into rolling farmland below the Ellwangen hills, the Romans drew a line across the map and then built it in stone. The fort at Rainau-Buch, which the ride labels Reinau-B, sat just behind the Raetian Limes, the frontier that ran from the Rhine toward the Danube. What you find today is a grassy rectangle with low reconstructed wall footings, the outline of a bath house, and the traces of the civilian village that grew up outside the gate, where traders, families and off-duty soldiers lived the way garrison towns always do.

The ground explains why the frontier ran here. It is open, gently rising country with long sight lines, good for watching and signalling. A few kilometres away the Limes Gate at Dalkingen, a showpiece gateway the Romans built across the frontier wall, now sits under a modern glass shelter, and it is worth the short detour if the protective building is open. The Bucher Stausee, a small reservoir right beside the fort site, gives the place a lakeside feel in summer, with walkers, a few anglers and swallows working the water at dusk.

The riding around here is relaxed rather than dramatic. Country roads loop between Rainau, Westhausen and Hüttlingen through wheat, maize and patches of spruce, with gentle climbs, plenty of open bends and village speed limits that come up quickly, so keep an eye out for the yellow signs. The A7 motorway runs close by, which makes the place easy to reach and easy to leave, but the better way in is via the minor roads from the Jagst side. Spring and early autumn are the sweet spots; on hot summer afternoons the farm traffic and the tractors are out in force.

For practical things, Westhausen and Hüttlingen are both towns of several thousand people with fuel and a bakery or two, and Ellwangen, about six kilometres away, is the real centre: a handsome small town with a castle on the hill, the pilgrimage church of Schönenberg looking down on it, cafés around the old market and every service you need. It is a good place to take a long lunch before heading west along the frontier toward the Swabian Forest. The fort itself has no facilities beyond paths and information boards, so bring water if you plan to walk the circuit of the Limes park.
t.vojsko idrijca water barrier@46.0,13.9:
The water barriers of the Idrijca are among the strangest industrial monuments in Europe: massive stone and timber dams built across a narrow mountain river not to store water for drinking or power, but to float logs. Locals call them klavže, and the biggest have been nicknamed the Slovenian pyramids for their huge, carefully cut blocks. They lie in the deep, wooded gorge below the Vojsko plateau, a short ride from the town of Idrija.

The reason they exist is mercury. Idrija's mine, opened at the end of the fifteenth century, was for centuries one of the largest sources of mercury in the world, and the smelters burned enormous quantities of wood. The forests upstream were cut, the logs piled behind the dams, and then the gates were opened and the flood carried the timber down the gorge to the town. The mine and the town are now a World Heritage site together with Almadén in Spain, and the old miners' houses, the castle and the shaft buildings make a fine short walk.

Riding up here is a good test. The roads from Idrija towards Vojsko and along the Idrijca are narrow, twisty and often in deep shade, with mossy edges, damp corners and occasional loose stones from the steep slopes above. There are hairpins, tight sections with no centre line and very little traffic. The plateau of Vojsko itself is a high, open landscape of scattered farms and meadows with views across the forested ridges towards the Julian Alps. In wet weather or early spring, take it slowly; the shade means patches stay damp long after the rain stops.

The Idrijca is clear and cold, flowing over pale limestone, and the forest is mostly beech and spruce. In summer it smells of resin and wet stone, and in autumn the whole valley turns copper. During the Second World War these forests hid partisan hospitals; Franja, the most famous, is in a gorge not far away near Cerkno.

Fuel, food and coffee are in Idrija, about nine kilometres away. While you are there, order žlikrofi, small dumplings filled with potato and herbs that are a protected local speciality, and look into a lace shop: Idrija bobbin lace is another tradition that grew up around the mine, made by miners' wives to bring in extra money.
t.city fortress of palmanova@45.9,13.3:
From the air Palmanova is a perfect nine-pointed star, and even from the saddle you can feel the geometry. The roads come in through monumental gates, cross the moats and ramparts, and run dead straight to a vast hexagonal piazza in the middle, where the whole town seems to stop and look at itself. It is one of the purest examples of an ideal Renaissance city ever built, and it sits on the flat Friulian plain between Udine and the Adriatic like a diagram that somebody forgot to take back.

The Venetian Republic founded it in 1593 as a fortress against the Ottomans and the Habsburgs, who were both pressing on its eastern border. Every detail was designed for defence: the bastions, the angles of fire, the radial streets that let troops reach any part of the walls quickly. Napoleon's engineers later added an outer ring of fortifications, which is why the earthworks look so layered. In 2017 Palmanova joined the World Heritage list as part of the Venetian Works of Defence, alongside places like Bergamo and Zadar.

Riding here is flat-land riding: straight, fast provincial roads through maize fields and vineyards, with the Julian Alps visible on a clear day to the north and the lagoons a short way south. The A4 motorway passes close by, but the back roads towards Aquileia, Cividale or the Collio wine hills are much more fun. Coming through one of the three gates, Porta Udine, Porta Cividale or Porta Aquileia, is a small event in itself: stone arches, a tunnel through the ramparts, and suddenly you are inside.

Walk up onto the bastions if you can. The grassy ramparts and the moats are now a park, full of birds and quiet paths, and from the top the star shape becomes readable. In the evening the piazza fills with people taking their passeggiata, and the cafés around it are the best place to sit with an espresso or a glass of Friulano and watch the light fade on the arcades.

Palmanova is a small town, but it has fuel just outside the walls, shops, bakeries and restaurants. Cervignano del Friuli, about ten kilometres south, is larger and close to Aquileia, whose Roman ruins and great mosaic floors in the basilica make an excellent second stop on any ride through this corner of Italy.
t.kalkalpen wilder graben@47.8,14.4:
Wilder Graben translates as the wild ravine, and the name fits the country south of the Enns valley in Upper Austria, where the Kalkalpen National Park protects a great tangle of limestone mountains, gorges and forest. This is the Reichraminger Hintergebirge, a maze of steep valleys with clear green streams at the bottom and almost no settlements at all. It is one of the largest forested areas in Austria, and parts of its old beech woods belong to the World Heritage site of ancient beech forests across Europe.

You will not ride into the gorge itself; the interior of the park is closed to motor traffic and reserved for hikers and cyclists. What you get instead is the ride around it. The Enns valley road between Steyr and Altenmarkt follows the river through a narrow, wooded valley, part of the old Eisenstrasse, the iron road that carried ore and finished goods from the Styrian Erzberg to the blacksmiths and markets downstream. The curves are smooth and flowing, with frequent changes of rhythm as the valley twists, and traffic is usually light outside weekends. Side roads climb out of the valley to high farms and small passes, narrower and steeper, with views of grey limestone walls above the forest.

The iron industry left its mark everywhere: old hammer mills, workers' houses, chapels and the ruin of Losenstein castle perched above the Enns. Inside the park, a former forest railway built to carry timber out of the Hintergebirge is now a cycle track running through tunnels and over bridges along the Grosser Bach, a sign of how the region has shifted from extraction to protection.

The nature here is the main attraction. The streams run cold and turquoise over white gravel, fed by springs from the karst. Chamois live on the cliffs, golden eagles nest on high crags, and the forest is home to lynx, which have been reintroduced to the area, and the rare white-backed woodpecker. In autumn the beech woods blaze orange and yellow against the pale rock.

Reichraming, about six kilometres away, is a small village with a few inns and basic shopping. For fuel, Grossraming and Losenstein are close, and Steyr, a larger historic town at the confluence of the Enns and Steyr rivers, has everything. The nearest town of five thousand or more listed here is Micheldorf, about twenty-three kilometres south-west.
t.parco archeologico nazionale dei massi d:
Several thousand years of people have been scratching pictures onto the rocks of Val Camonica, and the oldest are thought to be roughly eight thousand years old. The valley runs north from Lake Iseo in Lombardy, following the Oglio river up to the Tonale pass, and its glacier-polished sandstone slabs turned out to be an ideal canvas. The Camuni, an Iron Age people, carved thousands of figures: hunters, deer, warriors, ploughs, huts, dancing figures and a swirling sun-like motif that is now the emblem of the Lombardy region, the Rosa Camuna. In 1979 this became Italy's first World Heritage site.

The Massi di Cemmo, near Capo di Ponte, are two giant boulders carved with stylised figures, the daggers, sun disks and animals of a late Copper and Bronze Age world. They are among the best-known single stones in the valley, and the park around them is a quiet and rather moving place, with green meadows and old chestnut trees. The better-known rock-art parks are a few minutes away, and they involve walks on wooded paths where slabs of rock appear, covered in carvings that are easiest to read in raking light early or late in the day.

Val Camonica is a long, busy valley, and the main road, the SS42, can be slow with local traffic and trucks, but the real attraction for riders is what leaves it. From Edolo, the road climbs to Aprica, and from here the Mortirolo and the Gavia, two of the hardest and most famous Alpine passes in cycling, are within reach, with the Gavia reaching just over two and a half thousand metres. Both are narrow and steep with variable surfaces, both are closed by snow for much of the year, and both reward careful riding with big views and thin air. The Tonale pass up the valley is wider and easier.

For fuel, Darfo Boario Terme at the southern end of the valley is large enough to have several stations, and smaller towns along the SS42 usually have at least one. Capo di Ponte has bars and trattorie, and local dishes tend to be hearty, with polenta, cured meats and casoncelli pasta. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms to the mountains, so start early and keep an eye on the sky.
t.lavagnone@45.4,10.5:
Lavagnone does not look like much, and that is rather the point. South of Lake Garda, behind Desenzano, the landscape is a rumple of low hills left by the glacier that once filled the lake basin, and in a hollow among them lies a small peat basin that was once a shallow lake. Around four thousand years ago, in the Bronze Age, people built houses on timber piles at its edge, and when the water level fell and the peat built up, the wood was preserved in the mud like a time capsule.

The site is one of a group of prehistoric pile dwellings in and around the Alps that were listed by UNESCO in 2011. Excavations here turned up houses, pottery, tools and even wooden objects that normally do not survive, including a very old wheel, among the earliest known in Europe. You cannot see the houses today, because the interest is below ground, but there is a small protected area and information, and the basin gives a sense of how people lived at the water's edge long before the Romans arrived.

The riding in the area is not at the same level as the mountains to the north, but it is pleasant. The moraine hills around Desenzano, Solferino and San Martino della Battaglia are lined with vineyards, cypresses and country lanes with short, bendy climbs and good views, and the battlefields of 1859, where French and Piedmontese forces fought Austria, have monuments and a tower. Traffic on the main roads can be heavy, especially at weekends in summer, so the quiet lanes inland are better. Late spring and early autumn avoid the worst of the crowds.

Desenzano del Garda, four kilometres away, is a busy lakeside town with plenty of fuel, restaurants and cafes, and it is a good base for the day. The local white wine, Lugana, is made on the clay soils south of the lake and goes well with lake fish. If you want the Garda shore itself, the western road north from Salò runs through long tunnels and under steep cliffs with views over the water, and it is a classic run for riders, if a busy one.
t.the palaces of king ludwig ii of bavaria:
Neuschwanstein is the castle that everybody has seen before they arrive, and it is almost impossible to see it freshly. Ludwig II, the king of Bavaria, had it built from 1869 as a private retreat in the style of a medieval knight's castle, with towers, turrets and rooms painted with scenes from the operas of Wagner, whom he adored. It stands on a rocky spur above the Pöllat gorge, with the Alpsee lake and the plain below. Ludwig lived in it only a few months before he was declared unfit to rule and died in mysterious circumstances in Lake Starnberg in June 1886, at the age of forty. The castle was opened to the public within weeks.

The palaces associated with Ludwig, which include Linderhof and Herrenchiemsee, have been put forward as a group for World Heritage status and were recently listed. For all the glamour, the king's story is melancholy, a solitary man building dreams while the state's finances groaned, and the castles were his escape. Hohenschwangau castle, below, was his childhood home, a yellow neo-Gothic palace where his father had lived.

For a rider, the Allgäu is one of the best regions in Germany. The roads climb through meadows and forest, with views of the Alps and the Bavarian lakes, and the Romantic Road, which runs north to south through the region, ends close to here. A short ride over the border into Austria takes you to Reutte, the Plansee and the Hahntennjoch, a high and twisting road with big views. The roads around the castle itself are crowded in summer, with coaches, cars and walkers on the road, so early starts, before nine, are essential, and the parking is a long way down the hill.

Füssen, four kilometres away, is a charming old town with a monastery, a baroque old centre and plenty of fuel, food and hotels. A ride to Linderhof, through the Ammergau Alps, goes via the Ettal monastery, where the monks make a well-known herbal liqueur and beer, and gives a different, quieter view of the king's world. In winter the roads can be icy and many passes close, so check conditions before you set out.
t.kunzing amphitheater und vicus@48.7,13.1:
Künzing sits on the Danube in Lower Bavaria, in a broad, fertile plain known as the Gäuboden, and in Roman times it was a place with a name, Quintana. The Romans built a fort here in the second century, one of the posts on the river frontier of the province of Raetia, and a civilian settlement, a vicus, grew up beside it, with houses, workshops and even an amphitheatre. The Danube Limes in Germany, Austria and Slovakia was listed by UNESCO in 2021, and Künzing is one of the places where it is easiest to grasp what daily life along the frontier was like.

The fort itself lies under fields and the modern village, but the museum, built over excavated Roman buildings, shows what was found, including pottery and everyday tools. The most unusual part is that the museum is built over the dig, so you can see the foundations of Roman buildings exactly as they were uncovered. The amphitheatre, which held a few thousand spectators, is a grassy bowl, and gives an idea of how the soldiers and their families spent their free time.

The surrounding region is gentle and green, with fields of maize and sugar beet, and wooded hills rising to the north into the Bavarian Forest. The Danube road is easy but not exciting, and a better ride goes up into the hills, where narrow roads wind through spruce woods and villages with onion-domed churches, and where in autumn the colours are spectacular. At Osterhofen, a few kilometres away, the Asam Basilica is a masterpiece of Bavarian rococo, designed by the brothers Cosmas Damian and Egid Quirin Asam in the 1720s, with gilded plaster, frescoes and a theatrical interior that comes as a surprise in a village church.

Passau, about twenty kilometres upstream, where three rivers meet, is a good place for a lunch stop, and the old town is a delight. Fuel, bakeries and cafes are found in Osterhofen and Künzing, and the local beer is excellent. A Bavarian lunch of pork roast with dumplings, followed by a coffee and cake, is a fine way to recover. The museum is open in the season and closes in winter, so check the dates.
t.watchtowers wp 13 13 to 13 15@49.1,10.5:
Dinkelsbühl looks like a stage set, and the people who live there have worked hard to keep it that way. The old town, with its ring of walls, towers and gates, its half-timbered houses and the huge Gothic church of St George, survived the wars and the bombing that destroyed so many German towns, and it is one of the best preserved medieval towns on the Romantic Road. Each July the Kinderzeche, a festival that recalls the story of local children who saved the town during the Thirty Years' War, fills the streets with costumes and music.

The watchtowers on our list are older by more than a thousand years. Here, in Franconia, the Raetian Limes, the eastern part of the German frontier, left the forested hills of the Odenwald and Taunus behind and ran across open farmland. In the second century a stone wall, locally called the Devil's Wall, was built along part of it, while in other places a palisade and ditch marked the line. The watchtowers, numbered by early surveyors, stood a few hundred metres apart. The Limes was listed by UNESCO in 2005, and the line can still be followed in places as a low bank in the fields.

The countryside is quiet and pastoral, with orchards, hop gardens, cornfields and villages with onion-domed churches, and the riding is relaxed. The Romantic Road runs through, along the Wörnitz valley, and the surrounding lanes are narrow, lightly used and a pleasure for an easy day. The surface is generally good, but there are tractors, cyclists and the occasional slow farm vehicle. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, and midsummer afternoons can be hot and thundery.

Dinkelsbühl, ten kilometres away, has several fuel stations on its outskirts and a lot of cafes in the old town. Try a Franconian pork roast with dumplings and red cabbage, or a plate of local carp when it is in season, and finish with an Eisbecher, the German ice cream sundae. Parking is easier outside the walls, and walking round the town takes only a short time, so there is no need for hurry.
t.fort site and civil settlement of weisse:
Under the modern town of Weißenburg, in Franconia, lie the remains of a Roman fort called Biriciana, and it holds one of the best finds of the frontier. The fort was built in the second century to guard the line of the Raetian Limes, and a civil settlement grew up next to it, and in the third century it had a bathhouse that is the best preserved Roman bath north of the Alps. The walls of the baths still stand to a good height, with the heating system, the changing rooms and the pools, and a modern building protects them. Next to the baths is a museum, which holds a hoard of silver and bronze objects found in 1979 during building work, including statuettes of gods that were buried in a pit, probably to hide them.

The Roman Limes in this area was listed by UNESCO in 2005, together with the fort at Pfünz, to the south. Weißenburg itself is a pleasant small town, with a ring of medieval walls and gates, half-timbered houses and a handsome town hall. Above it, the Wülzburg fortress, a Renaissance star-shaped fortification, dominates the skyline, and a Roman sentry would have approved of the view.

The riding in the surrounding Altmühl Valley Nature Park is lovely, with limestone cliffs, juniper heaths and winding roads that follow the river. Not far to the east, the Fossa Carolina, a ditch that Charlemagne ordered to be dug in 793 to link the Danube and Rhine systems, is one of the oldest canals in Germany, and it is worth a short detour. The Franconian Jura is a quiet region, and the roads offer wide views, moderate gradients and clean asphalt.

Weißenburg has plenty of fuel, cafes and restaurants, and the Franconian cuisine is hearty, with roast pork, sausages and dumplings, and good local beer from small breweries. In spring, white asparagus is a regional passion, and it appears on menus in all kinds of ways. Nuremberg is about fifty kilometres to the north. Check opening times for the baths and museum, since they close in winter on some days.
t.pale di san martino san lucano dolomiti@:
The Val di San Lucano is a deep, shadowed gash in the southern Dolomites, and the point here lies near Rivamonte and Voltago, in the Agordino, the upper valley of the Cordevole river. The big, pale walls on either side belong to the Pale di San Martino group, one of the nine sets of mountains included in the Dolomites World Heritage listing of 2009, and their sheer rock faces rise more than a thousand metres above the narrow valley floor.

The Dolomites are made of an old coral reef, uplifted and carved by ice, and that is why the rock has the bleached, crenellated look that painters and climbers have loved for generations. In the San Lucano valley the cliffs are especially steep, with names such as the Torre Trieste and the Spiz di Agner, and this part of the range is known more to serious climbers than to casual visitors. It is wilder and quieter than the Cortina or Val Gardena side, with chamois, roe deer, and forests of spruce and larch that glow yellow in October.

The riding is a pleasure. From Agordo the side road winds up the valley with a good surface and long views of the cliffs, but it is narrow and sometimes shaded, so ice and damp lie late on the corners. Higher up the asphalt ends at a car park and the rest is a footpath. Back on the main road, the Passo Duran and the Forcella Staulanza are within reach for a longer day, and the sweeping roads towards the Passo Cereda and Primiero reward patience with a mix of hairpins and open views. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in July and August, and snow can close the high passes from about November to May, so check before setting off.

Agordo, the valley's main town, a few kilometres north, has fuel, bakeries and cafes, and Sedico, lower down towards Belluno, is bigger and has more choice; the villages of Rivamonte and Voltago are very small. Local food leans towards polenta, cured meats and mountain cheeses, and the hotels and refuges of the valley are used to hungry walkers. The best time for riding is June and September, when the roads are dry and the light is clean, and the cliffs turn pink at the end of the day, the well-known glow the Ladin people call the enrosadira.
t.villa zeno@45.7,12.6:
Andrea Palladio designed Villa Zeno at Cessalto in the middle of the sixteenth century, and it stands among the flat fields of the lower Piave plain, about five kilometres from the little town of Ceggia and not far from the Livenza river. It is one of the villas of the Veneto that were collectively inscribed on the World Heritage list, and it is quite different from the grand Palladian pieces near Vicenza: an agricultural house, plain and practical, with a broad central block and a pair of long service wings.

Palladio, the stonemason's apprentice who became the most imitated architect in Europe, built country houses for Venetian families who had turned from sea trade to farming as the Republic's fortunes shifted. The Zeno were one of those families, and the villa sat at the centre of a working estate. Palladio then published his designs in a book, I quattro libri dell'architettura, in 1570, which carried his ideas to England and later to the American colonies. Thomas Jefferson was one of his keenest readers, and half the porticoed houses of the English-speaking world owe him something.

The countryside is the opposite of dramatic. The plain between Treviso, Portogruaro and the lagoon is dead flat, crossed by drainage ditches, straight roads and rows of poplar, with maize and vines on both sides. It is not a place for corners, but it is good for a relaxed day, on quiet minor roads with the occasional farm tractor and a very long view. Fog settles here in winter and can last all day, and in summer the air is humid and mosquito-ridden near the water. Spring and early autumn are the best times.

Ceggia, with about five thousand people, has fuel and a few bars, and San Stino di Livenza is a bit larger, so the way is easy. For something better than a roadside coffee, head towards Treviso, a handsome walled city of canals, or towards the Prosecco hills north of Conegliano, where the roads finally begin to climb and twist. Venice itself is about forty minutes away, but you will not want to ride there.
On the flat shore of the Ariake Sea in Kyushu, in the city of Omuta, a set of brick buildings, steel headframes and tidal docks tells the story of how Japan became an industrial power. The Miike coal mine and the port that served it were inscribed by UNESCO in 2015 among the sites of Japan's Meiji industrial revolution, and the centre of Omuta is a few kilometres away, with a city of about a hundred and thirty thousand people spread around it.

Coal here had been dug on a small scale since the sixteenth century, but in the Meiji period the government took control, and in 1889 the Mitsui company bought the mine. The engineer Dan Takuma designed a new port at Miike, completed in 1908, with a lock gate to deal with the Ariake Sea's huge tides, some of the largest in Japan, and a railway to bring the coal from the pits. For decades Miike was one of the biggest mines in the country, and it supplied energy for the new factories and ships. The mine closed in 1997, and since then the buildings have become a heritage site, but the story has a darker side. Prisoners, and in the Second World War Korean, Chinese and Allied prisoners of war, were forced to work here, and in 1963 an explosion at the Mikawa pit killed more than four hundred men, one of Japan's worst mining disasters. The site is a reminder that industrial progress had a human price.

On the bike, the roads of the Chikugo plain are flat and straightforward, with canals, rice fields and pylons, and traffic can be heavy around Omuta and Kurume. The more interesting riding lies further afield, in the mountains of Kyushu to the east, and at the coast near Yanagawa, with its network of canals and boats. Summers are hot and humid, with typhoons from August to October, and winters are mild. At low tide the Ariake Sea retreats for kilometres, leaving a wide mud flat where mudskippers hop around.

Omuta has all services, with petrol stations, supermarkets and many places for ramen and fried chicken. The nearby town of Tamana is a quieter place with hot springs, and Setakamachi-takayanagi is smaller. Visit the museum in Omuta for a clear account of the mine's history, and check opening days before you set out, as some buildings are viewed only from outside.
t.pestenacker@48.1,10.9:
Pestenacker is a field in Bavaria with a secret under it. Around five and a half thousand years ago, Neolithic farmers built a settlement on the damp ground near the Lech, and the waterlogged soil preserved timber, tools and household remains that would have rotted elsewhere. It belongs to the family of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, inscribed by UNESCO in 2011, a group that also includes the Roseninsel in Lake Starnberg to the south. What you see at the surface is modest, since most of the evidence is below ground, so the interest here lies in imagining.

The area is flat and rural, part of the Lech valley and the Fünfseenland edge, with fields of maize and barley, tidy villages and church spires with onion domes. The nearest small town of any size is Geltendorf, with about five thousand people, and Landsberg am Lech lies not far to the west, a handsome old town on the river with a wide market square and plenty of cafés. Both have fuel and supplies. Weil and Egling, closer to the site, are small.

For a rider, this is easy, relaxed country. Smooth farm roads with long straight sections and gentle bends link the villages, and on clear days, especially when the warm Föhn wind blows, the Alps stand along the southern horizon like a painted backdrop. Traffic is mostly local and agricultural, so expect tractors in harvest time and cyclists on summer weekends. Mornings in May and September are best, when the light is clear and the fields are green or golden.

The landscape's best secrets are the quiet ones. The Neolithic people who lived here farmed wheat and barley, kept cattle, and hunted in the surrounding forest, and they left behind a record of everyday life instead of monuments. Read about them before you come, bring a map and a flask, and let the flat, calm country do the rest. Afterwards, a stop in a village inn for a Bavarian lunch of roast pork and dumplings is a fine way to end the visit.
t.passau boiotro kastell@48.6,13.5:
Passau stands at a meeting of three rivers, and the Romans noticed. The Inn, the Danube and the small, dark Ilz flow together under the cathedral hill, and the Inn bank opposite, where the Innstadt lies today, was the site of the Roman fort of Boiotro, which guarded the Danube frontier, the Limes, and commanded the river crossing. The name suggests the Boii, the Celtic people who once lived in this region, and the Roman fort stood in a long line of defences along the river, from here down to Oberranna in Austria.

The old town on the peninsula, at the confluence, is a beauty of baroque facades, narrow lanes and arcades. St Stephen's Cathedral holds one of the largest church organs in the world, with nearly eighteen thousand pipes, and a summer organ concert is a memorable thing. The Veste Oberhaus, a fortress on the hill across the Danube, gives the best view of the three rivers, which the locals say are three colours: the Danube blue, the Inn green and the Ilz black.

Passau is a city of about fifty thousand, with fuel, restaurants and shops all over, though parking in the centre is limited, so use the car parks along the river. Across the border, only a few kilometres away, Austria begins, with the pleasant town of Schärding on the Inn. The student population keeps the cafés lively, and the beer garden culture is strong, with a Bavarian roast and a pretzel the standard fare.

The riding here is a gentle combination of river and forest. The Danube valley road toward Linz is lovely, with wooded hills pressing in on both sides, and the Bavarian Forest rises just to the north, with long climbs and sweeping views. The Danube cycle path is popular, so expect plenty of cyclists in summer. Spring is cool and fresh, while autumn brings fog and amber leaves. Winter floods occasionally cover the riverside streets, so check before you plan to park near the water.
t.watchtowers wp 13 41 to 13 45@49.1,10.7:
South of Gunzenhausen the old frontier of the Roman Empire ran across the countryside in a ruler-straight line, and the numbered watchtowers are the markers for that line. This is the Raetian Limes, the stretch that, from the second century onward, was built from timber and then stone to protect the province of Raetia from the Germanic tribes to the north. The numbers 13/41 to 13/45 simply describe a cluster of tower sites on the surveyor's map. Most of them have been reduced by farming and time to low mounds and gentle banks in the fields, so what you actually find is landscape rather than masonry.

That landscape is the pleasant part. The ground here is the southern end of the Franconian Lake District, with fields of rape and barley, small woods, drainage ditches and the shining surfaces of the Altmühlsee and the Kleiner Brombachsee close by. The Altmühlsee is an artificial lake created in the 1980s to manage water, and today it is a reserve of great importance for migrating birds, which makes the area fine for a slow morning with binoculars. Muhr am See is a small lakeside village with a neat shoreline and a number of campsites.

For the motorcyclist, roads here are an easy rhythm of long straights and mild bends, with farm traffic, cyclists and families on holiday in July and August. The surface is generally good, and views open across the lakes and farmland. Few spots demand much concentration, so this is a day for letting the mind wander towards the Romans, who simply marched across this country and drew a line on it, which the men posted in a draughty tower would have found far less relaxing than we do now.

Gunzenhausen, six kilometres away, is the logical stop. It has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and ice cream, a historic town centre with half-timbered houses and a good riverside promenade along the Altmühl. A little further south, Weißenburg has Roman baths and a museum that give the line some real substance. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with the lakes quiet and the fields in good colour.
t.watchtowers wp 13 46 to 13 49@49.1,10.7:
The numbers here, 13/46 to 13/49, belong to a surveyor's grid, but the line they follow is the old Raetian frontier, which the Romans built across Bavaria in the second century. East of the town of Gunzenhausen it was turned from a simple timber palisade into a proper stone wall, a rarity in the Roman north. The locals later called this wall the Teufelsmauer, the Devil's Wall, because they could not imagine human hands had built something so straight and so long. Folk stories said that the devil had built it overnight, and that he had run out of time just before dawn.

Today the wall has mostly gone, robbed for farm buildings and village churches over the centuries. A few stretches survive as low humps in the fields, grassy ridges where a plough has changed course. It takes some imagination to read them, but I find the quiet useful: you stand on a mild rise in a field of wheat, with swallows overhead and a village church tower in the distance, and the empire feels very long ago and, because of that, strangely close. The Roman army needed a long tradition of building and logistics to do this far from home, and they left behind little else except the bones of their buildings.

The riding is a lowland pleasure. Roads around Gunzenhausen cross the Altmühl valley and run among cherry orchards and low woods. The corners are long, the climbs are short, and cycle routes follow many of the same roads, so be ready to meet riders with panniers. Franconian villages are neat, with sandstone churches and a Gasthaus on the corner that serves a very decent schnitzel and a local beer brewed within a few miles. Bratwurst in a roll is the right lunch.

Gunzenhausen is only a few kilometres away, with fuel, supermarkets and a pleasant old centre of half-timbered houses along the Altmühl. Muhr am See is closer and quieter, with cafés on the shore of the Altmühlsee. Summer weekends are crowded around the lakes, so aim for a weekday or early morning.
t.watchtowers wp 15 27 to 15 47@48.9,11.6:
Up in the hills above the Altmühl valley, west of Neustadt an der Donau and the Danube, the old Raetian frontier crossed some of its prettiest country. The numbers 15/27 to 15/47 cover a long stretch of the line, and because that line follows the ridges and plateau edges, the landscape is a mixture of fields, juniper-dotted limestone slopes and sheltered woods. The Altmühl itself is a slow river that has cut a deep, winding valley through Jurassic limestone, and the whole district is a nature park, known for fossils from the quarries at Solnhofen.

Riedenburg, the nearest proper town, sits at the base of the cliffs and is dominated by the Rosenburg castle above it, which has a falconry display in season. Essing, a few kilometres downstream, is a tiny village under a rock face with one of Europe's longest wooden footbridges crossing the canal, a lovely piece of carpentry that appears in many a photograph. Burg Prunn, a medieval castle on a ledge above the river, once held a famous manuscript of the Nibelungenlied. Nearby Kelheim marks the point where the Altmühl joins the Danube.

The roads here are a pleasure. The route follows the river for much of the time, a gentle meander with trees and cliffs close at hand, then climbs out onto the plateau where views open across fields and woods. Corners are rolling rather than tight, and the surface is mostly smooth, apart from some patchy repairs. On sunny weekends the valley is busy with cyclists and canoeists, so the morning is best, and midweek is better. Pass with care, and remember that deer cross at dusk.

Riedenburg has fuel, a supermarket and several cafés by the river, and Neustadt an der Donau is larger and has everything. Wherever you stop, ask for the local beer, which in Bavaria is as much a part of the landscape as the limestone. The Limes itself is quiet and unmarked in many places, so go for the country first and the Romans second.
t.villa almerico capra@45.5,11.6:
The Villa Almerico Capra, known as La Rotonda, stands on a small hill above Vicenza, and it is one of the most copied buildings in the history of architecture. Andrea Palladio began it in the 1560s for a retired papal official, Paolo Almerico, who wanted a place for entertaining and for looking at the view rather than for farming. The plan is a perfect square, with a round hall under a dome at the centre, and each of the four sides has an identical portico with Ionic columns and a flight of steps, so that the house presents the same face to every direction. The idea was that the building should be an ornament to the landscape, and the landscape an ornament to the house.

The influence was enormous. Thomas Jefferson borrowed from it for Monticello, and Lord Burlington built Chiswick House in London on the same idea, and a long line of English country houses and American mansions carry its echo. Palladio's buildings in and around Vicenza were listed by UNESCO in 1994, and the city is full of them, from the Teatro Olimpico, one of the oldest surviving indoor theatres in Europe, to the Basilica in the main square. The interior of La Rotonda is open only on certain days, and the grounds are often open when the house is not, so check the days before you go.

The hill is part of the Berici Hills, a low range of limestone covered with olive groves, vineyards and cherry trees, with villas and small churches tucked in the folds. Monte Berico, the pilgrimage hill above the city, has a large basilica and a lovely view. In spring the cherry blossom is white on the slopes, and in autumn the vines are red and gold.

For a rider, the Berici Hills offer pleasant, winding lanes with gentle climbs and views over the plain, and the traffic is moderate, though cyclists are numerous. The surface is mostly good. Vicenza, under two kilometres away, has fuel stations, restaurants and bars, and the neighbouring villages of Arcugnano and Torri have small shops. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and a plate of baccalà alla vicentina, salt cod stewed in milk, is the local speciality.
t.basilica and monastery of st anthony ora:
Padua, in the Veneto, has one of the great pilgrimage churches of Europe, and it is the grave of a Portuguese friar. Anthony of Padua was born in Lisbon, joined the Franciscans and became a famous preacher, and he died near Padua in 1231 at the age of thirty-six. He was made a saint within a year, one of the fastest canonisations in history, and construction of the great basilica began soon after. The Basilica of Saint Anthony, which the people of Padua simply call il Santo, is a church of many domes, partly Romanesque and partly Gothic with a hint of Byzantine, and it holds the saint's tomb in a side chapel, where pilgrims press their hands against the marble.

The basilica holds treasures of art, including the bronze figures of the high altar by Donatello, who spent ten years in Padua, and an equestrian statue of the condottiere Gattamelata outside, the first great bronze horse of the Renaissance. The monastery next to it has cloisters worth a visit. Padua also has the Scrovegni Chapel, painted by Giotto in the early fourteenth century, whose blue ceiling and frescoes mark a turning point in Western art, and the university, founded in 1222, where Galileo taught for eighteen years.

The great oval square called Prato della Valle is a few minutes' walk away, with a ring of statues around a green island and a canal. It is a pleasant place to sit with a spritz, the local aperitif. The city is full of arcades, cafés and markets, and the air in the evening smells of coffee and woodsmoke.
