Riding in the centre of Padua needs patience, since much of the old town is a restricted traffic zone, and it is best to park outside the walls and walk. The surrounding plain is flat and fast, with traffic on the ring roads, and the nearby Euganean Hills offer a lovely twisty alternative. Fuel is easy to find, and Ponte San Nicolò and Mandriola have supermarkets and cafés. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the basilica is crowded on the saint's feast day, 13 June.
t.mietsu naval dock@33.2,130.3:
The Mietsu Naval Dock lies on the Saga Plain, where the Chikugo river flows into the Ariake Sea. It is a place that easily gets overlooked: a modest dry dock and a few stone structures among reeds and creeks. Yet UNESCO listed it in 2015 among the sites of Japan's Meiji industrial revolution, and the reason is the Saga domain's ambition. In the 1850s, under its daimyo Nabeshima Naomasa, Saga set about learning Western shipbuilding, cannon casting and steam technology faster than almost any other domain in Japan, and Mietsu was where the navy was trained and its ships were built and repaired.

The setting is lovely in a flat, watery way. The Ariake Sea has one of the largest tidal ranges in Japan, and at low tide the mudflats stretch for kilometres, home to mudskippers and wading birds, while the plain is laced with old irrigation channels. The land here is farmland, with rice, wheat and seaweed beds offshore, and the light has a hazy softness, particularly in the evening. Nearby Yanagawa is famous for its canals, where flat-bottomed boats glide through the old castle town, and for its steamed eel on rice. Ōkawa, only four kilometres from the dock, has been known for centuries for fine furniture and woodwork.

For a rider the roads here are flat, straight and quiet. This is not a place for tight bends, but a place for easy cruising, with the occasional bridge over a creek and long views over fields. In summer it is hot and humid, and the Ariake can sit under a warm haze, while typhoons occasionally bring heavy rain. Spring and autumn are much better, and the early morning has the best light on the water.

Fuel and food are no problem. Ōkawa, with nearly forty thousand people, and Saga city, a few kilometres away with some 165,000, have plenty of pumps, convenience stores and restaurants. Saga is also known for its beef and its karatsu-style pottery tradition, and the ride to Sakitsu in Amakusa or to Misumi takes you onwards to the islands of Kyushu's west coast, with ferries, shrines and sea views waiting.
t.kolica na igu@46.0,14.5:
The Ljubljana Marsh is a wide, flat plain of peat and wet meadow south of the city, drained since the eighteenth century by canals, and it hides one of the most interesting stories in European prehistory. Some five thousand years ago people built houses on stilts here, at the edge of lakes that have since vanished, and the remains of their villages lie preserved in the peat. The pile dwellings near Ig are part of the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, shared with five other countries.

The most famous find was made near Ig in 2002: a wooden wheel, together with its axle, dated to about 3150 BC, which makes it the oldest wooden wheel ever found. It is on display in the Ljubljana city museum, and the find started a lively debate about where the wheel was first invented. Archaeologists believe the wheel was part of a cart used by people who lived and farmed on the marsh, and that the lake edge was a place of busy trade.

Today the marsh is a landscape of reed beds, ditches, small birch woods and fields, and a haven for birds, including storks, lapwings and the elusive corncrake. The Gruber Canal, dug in the late eighteenth century to drain the marsh, still threads through the area. Morning mist often lies on the plain, with the dark hump of Krim mountain, over a thousand metres high, rising to the south. Ig is a modest village at its edge, with the Iški Vintgar gorge a short ride away for those who prefer cool rock and water to open fields.

Riding across the marsh is easy and flat, with long straight roads, cycle paths and the odd tractor, but the beauty here is in the light and the wide sky. Be careful on summer evenings, when mist and mosquitoes arrive together, and in winter fog can reduce visibility quickly. Weekends bring joggers, cyclists and families. Spring, with blossom and bird song, and autumn, with mist, are the best seasons. Fuel is available in Ig and Škofljica, and Ljubljana has every service, only a dozen kilometres away. The route then runs south to the Snežnik forest and the Dinaric plateaus, with the sort of long wooded climbs and empty roads that make Slovenia a rider's country.
t.idrijska bela putrih s water barrier on@:
The Klavže at Idrijska Bela are a surprising piece of engineering, a huge stone wall built across a narrow gorge in the eighteenth century, with a gate in the middle. The idea was brilliant and simple. The mercury mine at Idrija, one of the largest in Europe, needed vast quantities of timber for its shafts and furnaces, and the forests were in the hills, far from the town. So the woodcutters piled logs behind the barrier, the gate was opened and the stored water carried the logs in a rush down the stream to the mine. Such water barriers, called klavže in Slovenian, were used here for generations, and the one named after Putrih is among the grandest.

The barrier belongs to the heritage of the Idrija mercury mine, which UNESCO listed in 2012, along with the Spanish mine of Almadén. The town itself is a charming place, and has a distinctive tradition of bobbin lace, taught in the local school, and a dish of small dumplings called žlikrofi, filled with potato and herbs and served with meat sauce. The mine was a source of wealth for the Habsburg monarchy, and it carried a high human cost, since mercury poisoning was a constant risk for the miners.

The setting is dramatic: a deep, narrow valley with beech and fir forest, the clear water of the Belca stream and a path that leads along the water to the stone walls. The place is quiet and cool, and in spring the stream runs high. The walk is short and well kept, and the huge wall rising from the gorge is an impressive sight, even more so when you think of the labour that built it.

Riding here is a delight. The roads around Idrija climb and fall through forest, with curves that are tight enough to be fun and a surface that is generally good. The route from Ljubljana via Logatec is a classic, and the way on toward Cerkno and the Soča valley is just as good. Traffic is usually light, but forestry trucks use the narrow roads. Early autumn, with colour in the beeches and fewer visitors, is a splendid time. Winter can bring ice in the shaded gorges, so take care.

Idrija, about eight kilometres away, is the place for fuel, food and a bed, and the cafe tables in the main square are a good place to enjoy a cup of coffee and a slice of local cake. There is little in the small villages along the way.
t.roman walls in mirje@46.0,14.5:
In the middle of Ljubljana, on Mirje street, a long stretch of reconstructed wall recalls the Roman town of Emona. The Romans founded Emona in the early first century AD, on a grid of streets beside the Ljubljanica river, as a frontier outpost and trading town on the road between Italy and the Danube. It had walls, gates, forums, baths and a population of several thousand. Later, the town was sacked by Huns and other invaders, and its stones were reused for centuries, so that very little survived above ground.

What you see on Mirje today is the work of the architect Jože Plečnik, who in the 1930s rebuilt a section of the wall as a landscaped monument, with a pyramid-shaped gate, a garden and a path. It is not a reconstruction in the strict sense, more an artist's act of remembering, and it is typical of Plečnik's way of weaving the past into the daily life of the city. His work in Ljubljana, including the Triple Bridge, the market colonnade and the National Library, was listed by UNESCO in 2021.

Ljubljana is a small, friendly capital of about two hundred and seventy thousand, with a car-free historic centre, a castle on a hill and cafes along the river. The light in the evening on the water, with willows and bridges, is lovely. The food has Alpine, Balkan and Italian influences, and a plate of local sausages, a bowl of jota, a hearty bean and sauerkraut soup, or a cake of prekmurska gibanica, layered with poppy seeds, apples and curd, is a good introduction.

For a rider, the city is easy: traffic is calm, parking is usually available on the edge of the centre and the bike is best left at a car park before walking in. Fuel stations are plentiful around the ring road. The real riding starts outside, on the great passes to the north and west. The Vršič pass, with its fifty hairpins, is a famous one, and the Soča valley beyond is considered one of the finest in Europe. The long ride to Palmanova in Italy crosses the Karst and the border, where the landscape changes quickly from forests and farms to plains and vineyards.
t.church of st francis of assisi@46.1,14.5:
Ljubljana's Church of Saint Francis of Assisi stands in the Šiška district, north-west of the old centre, and it is one of the buildings by Jože Plečnik that UNESCO listed in 2021. Plečnik was born in Ljubljana in 1872, trained in Vienna under Otto Wagner, and worked in Prague, where he renovated the castle for the first Czechoslovak president, before returning to his home city in 1921. He spent the next decades remaking Ljubljana in his own style, with bridges, markets, a library and gardens, mixing classical forms with a personal, almost playful imagination. The church in Šiška, built in the late 1920s, is among his strangest and most original buildings.

From the outside the church looks a bit like a fortress, with a massive brick belltower rising beside a plain nave, and inside you find a wide hall with a flat ceiling and rows of pillars, lit from small windows. Plečnik used humble materials, brick, concrete and wood, but arranged them with such care that the effect is solemn and warm at once. It is a church for the neighbourhood, a place where people still come to worship, so be quiet and respectful.

Šiška was once a village outside the city and still keeps a slightly bohemian air, with a lively cultural centre and a mixture of old houses and new apartment blocks. Nearby, the wooded hill of Rožnik rises above the city, and the park of Tivoli, with its long avenues and Plečnik's promenade, makes a pleasant walk. In the evening, the cafes fill up, and the whole city feels relaxed, with cyclists everywhere.

The rides from here start easily. South, the road heads onto the Ljubljana Marsh and the quiet lanes around Brezovica and Dobrova, and north, a few kilometres away, the Karavanke mountains are the doorway to Austria through the Ljubelj pass, which climbs steeply on the way to Carinthia and the lakes near Klagenfurt, such as the Keutschacher See. The pass road has tight bends and can be busy with trucks, so allow extra time. Summer and the start of autumn suit it best, while winter puts snow and ice on the higher section.

Fuel is easy in the city, with stations on all the ring roads, and parking is easy around Šiška except in the centre. Slovenia requires an e-vignette for use of motorways, so check it before getting on the fast roads, and enjoy a coffee and a slice of potica, the walnut roll that every Slovene grandmother claims to make best.
t.garmisch partenkirchen@47.5,11.1:
Garmisch-Partenkirchen lies in a wide Alpine valley in Bavaria, close to the Austrian border, with the Wetterstein range rising behind it and the Zugspitze, at 2,962 metres the highest mountain in Germany, standing at the end of the valley. The town is really two, Garmisch and Partenkirchen, joined together for the 1936 Winter Olympics, and each still has its own character. Partenkirchen, the older part, has a Roman history, as it stood on the road across the Alps, and its main street, with painted houses, is the more charming.

The setting is dramatic, with gorges nearby, including the Partnach gorge, where a path runs through a narrow rocky channel behind a thunderous waterfall, and the cable car and cog railway take visitors up the Zugspitze. The composer Richard Strauss lived here from the 1900s until his death in 1949, and the surrounding valley, the Werdenfelser Land, is known for wood carving, painted farmhouses and strong local traditions. In winter it is a major ski centre, and in the summer, cows with large bells graze in the meadows.

For riders, it is a gateway. The German Alpine Road, a long scenic route running about four hundred and fifty kilometres from Lake Constance to the Königssee, passes here, and the roads in every direction are superb. West, the Fern pass leads to Tyrol in Austria, with lakes, forests and Alpine views. East, the road runs past Ettal Abbey, a Benedictine monastery founded in the fourteenth century, with a great baroque dome, and then to Oberammergau, famous for its Passion Play, held every ten years. North, the Kesselberg road climbs to the Walchensee, a deep green lake among the mountains.

Be aware of noise rules and speed limits. Bavaria and Tyrol both enforce restrictions on motorcycles on some roads, with local noise limits and weekend or daily bans in some places, so check before you go. Summer weekends are busy, and the best times are weekdays and autumn, when the larch trees are golden.

Garmisch-Partenkirchen is a town of twenty-six thousand, with fuel stations, restaurants and plenty of places to stay. Try a plate of Weisswurst, the Bavarian white sausage, with sweet mustard and a soft pretzel, or a hearty bowl of Kaiserschmarrn, a shredded pancake with plum compote, after a long day in the mountains.
t.passau altstadt kastell@48.6,13.5:
Passau sits at the point where three rivers meet, in the far east of Bavaria, close to the Austrian border: the Danube, which is a cold greenish-blue here, the Inn, which arrives milky green from the Alps, and the Ilz, a small, dark river that stains the water black from the peat of the Bavarian Forest. On a still day you can see all three colours running side by side at the tip of the old town, which is why people call it the City of Three Rivers, and sometimes the Bavarian Venice.

The Romans knew the site well, since it stood on the northern frontier of the empire, along the Danube limes. The fort of Batavis, on the old town hill, guarded the crossing, and another fort, Boiotro, stood across the Inn. Fragments of the walls and finds from the forts are held in local museums, and the Roman past lies under the later city, which grew rich on the salt trade, brought down the rivers and traded here, and as the seat of a powerful prince-bishop. In the baroque old town, the cathedral of Saint Stephen has the largest cathedral organ in the world, with nearly eighteen thousand pipes, and organ concerts are held at midday in summer.

The old town is a narrow peninsula of steep lanes and pastel houses, with arcades and small squares, and the town hall tower looks over the Danube, with flood marks on its wall showing the levels of past floods. The riverside paths are part of the long Danube cycle route, and boat trips leave from the quays. A walk up to the Veste Oberhaus, the fortress above the Danube, rewards you with a view of the confluence.

For riders, Passau is the starting point of some excellent roads. The Danube valley above, in Austria, forms great loops, such as the famous Schlögener Schlinge, a few dozen kilometres upstream, and the hills of the Bavarian Forest to the north have winding roads through spruce woods. Across the border, the Czech village of Holašovice, a perfectly preserved South Bohemian baroque village, is on the ride. Traffic in town is dense and parking limited, so use a car park on the edge and walk in.

Passau has fuel stations on the main roads and plenty of cafes and restaurants. Try a Bavarian pork roast with dumplings, or a pretzel and a mug of the local wheat beer, in a beer garden by the river.
t.watchtowers wp 14 29 to 14 62 including:
Burgsalach is a quiet village of about twelve hundred people on the high limestone plateau of the Franconian Jura, and the old frontier of the Roman Empire ran right across it. This was the Raetian Limes, a different beast from the timber palisade further north. Here the Romans built in stone, and the remains of the wall, which locals long ascribed to the devil and called the Teufelsmauer, still show up as a low line in the fields and woods. The towers along it were numbered by archaeologists, which is why the label is a string of figures rather than a name.

The riding is a pleasure of the minor roads. The area lies between Weißenburg in Bayern and the Altmühl valley, in the Altmühl Jura, a landscape of dry limestone hills, juniper heaths, small beech woods and wide arable fields. The lanes link small villages in gentle curves and easy hills, with little traffic outside the commuting hours. The surface is generally good, although farm tractors leave mud in harvest season, and the wind can sweep across the open plateau. Late spring and early autumn have the best light, with long views across fields to the wooded edges.

Do not expect services at the exact spot. The nearest town of any size is Weißenburg, a little over eight kilometres away, where there is fuel, food and a decent old town ringed by medieval walls. Weißenburg also has the best Roman material in the area, including a bath complex and a museum that displays a treasure hoard dug up there in 1979. If you only have time for one Roman stop in the region, that is the one to pick.

What makes the Limes interesting here is how undramatic it is. There is no monument, only an old boundary line that bends across ordinary countryside and shows that the empire once drew a line in this very field. Take a moment to look along it; the people who built it expected it to last.
t.fort site and civil settlement of gnotzh:
The name Heidenheim, the heathen's home, is old and has nothing to do with the famous city of the same name in Württemberg. This one is a small village on the Hahnenkamm ridge in Middle Franconia, with a big church for its size, and it takes you to a corner of Bavaria where the Roman frontier cuts through gentle farmland. Close to Gnotzheim, a fort and a civil settlement once stood here on the Raetian Limes, the Roman border that ran across southern Germany. Soldiers lived inside the walls while merchants, craftsmen and families huddled outside, and today the site is mostly a quiet field with the odd information board.

The riding is enjoyable if you like rolling country. The Hahnenkamm is a long, wooded ridge, and the lanes over and around it twist through villages with half-timbered farmhouses and church spires. To the north lies the Franconian Lake District, a region of artificial lakes created in recent decades, and the Altmühlsee near Gunzenhausen is the largest, popular with sailors and cyclists. In summer the lake roads can be busy with holiday traffic, while in spring and autumn they are calm and the light over the water is lovely.

For fuel and a proper meal, go to Gunzenhausen, about eight kilometres away, a town of more than sixteen thousand people on the Altmühl river with a good market square. Heidenheim and Dittenheim are small, so do not count on a station in either. Heidenheim's old abbey church is worth a stop, since the monastery was founded in the eighth century by Wunibald, an English-born missionary monk from the circle around Boniface, who helped bring Christianity to the German lands. His sister Walburga later ran the community after his death.

Franconian food is substantial and the beer is good. Look for roast pork with dumplings, or carp in the lake country, a tradition that goes back centuries. If you stay for the sunset, the fields around the fort site turn gold, and for a moment you can imagine the lights of a Roman guard post answering from the next hilltop.
t.straubing ostkastell@48.9,12.6:
Straubing sits on a bend of the Danube in the fertile Gäuboden, the flat, loess-rich farmland that gave Lower Bavaria its reputation for heavy harvests, and the Romans liked it for the same reason. A cavalry fort stood here, on the eastern edge of what is now the town, guarding the river line, and a civilian settlement grew around it. The most remarkable find came in 1950, when workmen digging a cellar uncovered a hoard of Roman parade armour, gilded helmets and masks used by cavalrymen in displays. It is now a prize exhibit in the local museum, and it is one of the finest such finds in Europe.

For a rider the town is a comfortable base. The country round about is flat and agricultural, so the roads are straight, quiet and fast, but a short ride north takes you into the Bavarian Forest, where the hills rise, the woods thicken and the bends begin in earnest. The Danube itself has a long cycle path, so weekends bring plenty of pedal traffic on the riverside lanes. The best months are May to September, and the town's long summer evenings suit a late dinner on the main square.

Straubing is a proper city of over forty-four thousand people, so fuel, food and accommodation are no problem. The old centre has a broad, long market place with a medieval tower at its heart, and the town is known for its August festival, the Gäubodenvolksfest, which in size is second only to Munich's Oktoberfest in Bavaria. If you want quiet, avoid the festival days, when the town fills up and rooms are hard to find.

Parkstetten, to the south-east, is a smaller community with services of its own. The Ostkastell site itself is mostly buried under later buildings, so treat it as a quiet marker of an old border and spend the real time in the museum. Afterwards, ride out to the Danube bank and watch the river slide past, wide and slow and brown, as it has done since the first Roman legions arrived.
t.fort site of eining unterfeld@48.9,11.8:
Eining is the spot where the Danube Limes and the Raetian Limes meet, or more accurately the place where the wall and ditch ran down to the river and gave way to the water as a frontier. The Romans built a fort here called Abusina, on the south bank, with walls that can still be traced in the fields and a small museum nearby. For soldiers posted to the edge of the empire it must have felt like standing at the end of the world, with the river wide and cold in front of them and Germania on the far bank. The name Unterfeld refers to the lower field beside the fort, a plain, practical label for an ordinary piece of land.

The riding here is a pleasure. The Danube in this stretch is hemmed in by limestone cliffs, and just upstream lies the Danube Gorge near Weltenburg, where the river squeezes between white rock walls for several kilometres. A short ferry or road detour takes you to Weltenburg Abbey, said to be among the oldest monasteries in Bavaria, founded in the early Middle Ages and famous for its brewery. The lanes around Eining are quiet, with gentle bends along the river and through hop fields, and on warm weekends the cyclists and canoeists make the area lively.

Neustadt an der Donau and Abensberg, each with around twelve or thirteen thousand people, are the practical choices for fuel and food. Abensberg sits in the Hallertau, the largest hop-growing region in the world, and is known for its beer, with a quirky brewery tower designed by Friedensreich Hundertwasser. Hop gardens line the roads for miles in late summer, and the smell, bitter and green, is hard to miss.

If you enjoy a good story of ordinary lives, spend a while at the fort. The ruins include walls, a gate and traces of a bath house, and with a bit of imagination you can see the whole garrison at their daily chores. Come in late afternoon, when the light on the stones is warm and the river turns pewter.
t.enns legionslager zentralbereich@48.2,14:
Where the little River Enns joins the Danube, about twenty kilometres upstream of Linz, the Romans built their frontier. This was Lauriacum, headquarters of the Second Italic Legion, who were stationed here from the late second century to guard the northern edge of the empire, the province of Noricum, against the tribes beyond the river. Around the fortress grew a civilian town that at its height may have held many thousands of people, and later a bishop is said to have lived here. The modern town of Enns, which takes pride in being the oldest in Austria, grew up beside it, and the legionary camp lay under what is now a mix of fields, streets and suburbs.

You will not find standing walls in the middle of town, and the archaeology is mostly beneath your feet. A museum in the old town and a small archaeological park tell the story, with reconstructed fragments, tombstones and a reconstruction of a part of the camp. The medieval town square is beautiful, dominated by a tall town tower from the sixteenth century, and the pastel houses and arcades have a calm charm. Look for the Roman-era cemetery finds in the museum.

The riding around is easy and pleasant, with the Danube on one side and the Alpine foothills of Upper Austria on the other. Take the river road, the B3, toward Wallsee and Grein, passing orchards, castles and villages, with little traffic and gentle bends. Further south, toward Steyr and the Enns valley, the road climbs into forested hills and the bends get more interesting. Spring blossoms and golden autumn are best, and in summer weekend cyclists share the river paths and sometimes the road.

Enns is a town of about ten thousand people, so you will find fuel, bakeries, cafés and a decent selection of inns, and there is a motorway junction nearby, with a vignette required on the A1. Try a schnitzel or a freshly baked pretzel, or a slice of apple strudel. Mauthausen, the village across the Danube, holds a former concentration camp memorial, a solemn counterpart to the Roman story, and worth visiting with respect. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads at commute times, so plan to ride in the middle of the day.
t.neuschwanstein castle@47.6,10.7:
King Ludwig II of Bavaria began building Neuschwanstein in 1869 as a private dream, a medieval knight's castle with all the comforts of the nineteenth century, including central heating and running water. He never saw it finished, and he lived there for only a handful of months. In 1886 he was declared unfit to rule and removed, and he died a few days later in the Starnberger See, in circumstances that are still debated. Within weeks the castle was opened to the public to pay off his debts, and it has been admired ever since. Walt Disney's designers are said to have taken inspiration from it.

The setting is superb. The castle perches on a rocky ridge above the Pöllat gorge, with the Alps rising behind and the plain of the Allgäu and its lakes stretched in front. Ludwig's boyhood home, Hohenschwangau, lies just below, and the Alpsee shines beside it. The best view comes from the Marienbrücke, a narrow steel bridge over the gorge, a short walk from the castle, but it is crowded in high season, with queues of visitors. Inside, the throne hall and the singers' hall, painted with scenes from Wagner's operas, are elaborate, and only guided tours are allowed.

Riding here is a pleasure, as the Romantic Road and the Alpine edge are two of Germany's great motorcycle areas. From Füssen the road climbs toward the Austrian border and the Fern Pass, with smooth surfaces, long bends and views of snowy peaks. Weekends in summer are crowded with bikes, cars and tour buses, and the police are attentive, so early mornings are better. Rain can come suddenly in the mountains, and in winter the roads can be icy. In spring and autumn the light is soft and the lakes are calm.

The nearest place for fuel and supplies is Füssen, about four kilometres away, a pretty old town with a monastery, a castle and plenty of cafés, and Schwangau itself, a village with hotels and restaurants. Tickets to the castle are timed, and booking in advance is wise, since the walk up from the car park takes some half an hour. Try a Käsespätzle, the Allgäu cheese noodles, or a slice of cake with coffee in the village. Parking for motorcycles is available near the ticket centre, and wet gear can be left in lockers.
t.fort site and civil settlement of unters:
In the fields near Wassertrüdingen, in the soft valley of the Wörnitz and the hills of Middle Franconia, lie the buried remains of a Roman fort that once held an auxiliary unit of several hundred soldiers. Unterschwaningen was one of the larger posts on the Raetian section of the frontier, built in the second century to guard the line and the road behind it. Around it, as at every fort, a civilian settlement grew up, with houses, workshops, bathhouses and a cemetery, and the place must have been noisy and smoky, the roar of a small frontier town. Today the area is mostly farmland, and the outlines are visible only from the air, in dry summers, when crop marks trace the walls.

The area has its own quiet interest. It lies at the edge of the Franconian Heights, in a landscape of gentle ridges and woodland, with hop gardens, meadows and a few small ponds, and the Hesselberg, at over six hundred metres the highest hill in Middle Franconia, rises to the south-west. The Limes is part of the UNESCO site that spans the whole frontier, and a few markers and information boards help walkers visualise the old line.

Riding is calm and enjoyable. The roads here are smooth, with a mix of long gentle curves and village crossings, and the traffic is light apart from agricultural vehicles in the busy seasons. Weekends bring other motorcyclists, and the Altmühl valley, to the east, is a popular destination with a more varied route. Spring and autumn give the best light, and early winter mornings can have frost, so watch for icy patches in shade. Fog is common in autumn.

Wassertrüdingen, three kilometres away, is a small town of about six thousand people, with fuel, a bakery, shops and a handful of inns, and the medieval walled town of Dinkelsbühl, a famous stop on the Romantic Road, lies to the south-west. Try a Franconian dish such as Schäufele, roast pork shoulder with a dumpling, and the regional beer, often a malty lager. Roman remains in this area are mostly under the fields, so do not expect to see walls, and respect private land. A local museum in the region collects finds from the Limes.
t.watchtowers wp 13 51 to 13 53@49.1,10.7:
In the Altmühl country around Gunzenhausen the Roman frontier is a wall rather than a fence. Far to the west it was a timber palisade, earth bank and ditch, but from the edge of the Swabian Alb eastward the Romans replaced it with something sturdier, a stone wall that runs for many kilometres across Bavaria, which locals later nicknamed the Devil's Wall, the Teufelsmauer, because it seemed too big to have been made by men. The watchtowers numbered 13/51 to 13/53 belong to that stone-wall stretch, and they were small square towers of stone or timber that stood just behind the line, with a view over the valley and the next tower in the chain.

Today the traces are modest, fragments of footings, a low bank and ditch among the trees and meadows, but a few spots are marked and reconstructed. The Altmühl itself is a lazy river here, and nearby the Altmühlsee, an artificial lake created in the 1980s as part of a water transfer scheme, attracts sailors, windsurfers and birdwatchers. Gunzenhausen, a town with a Baroque church and a long history, has a museum and the Roman remains of a fort. The whole Limes is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Riding in the Franconian Lake District is easy and generous. The roads wander through hills and villages with half-timbered houses, small vineyards and hop fields, and the lake roads are fast and open. Surfaces are good, with the occasional long climb, and the biggest hazard is slow traffic and tractors in summer. A ride east along the Altmühl valley brings you to Treuchtlingen and Solnhofen, where the quarries produced the limestone that preserved Archaeopteryx. Autumn is beautiful, with mist in the valley, while in July and August the lake is crowded with holidaymakers.

Gunzenhausen is two kilometres away and has fuel stations, cafés and restaurants, and a pleasant old town. A local speciality is carp from the pond country around Franconia, served in autumn, and the local bakeries offer fresh pretzels and cakes. The lake has a long cycle path, and it is a nice place to pause. Remember to follow signs for forest tracks, since vehicles are banned from many, and be considerate to walkers and horse riders on the quiet lanes.
t.watchtowers wp 13 40@49.1,10.6:
Arberg lies in the rolling country of Middle Franconia, where the Altmühl and Wörnitz rivers wander through meadows and the hills are crowned with small woods. The Roman Limes crossed this ground in the second century, and the towers numbered 13/40 belong to the Raetian section, close to the point where the frontier was a stone wall. Today the line is mostly hidden. Farmers have ploughed over it, and trees have grown on the old bank, and in a few places a wooden marker or a stone footing shows where a tower stood. The nearest big fort was at Unterschwaningen, a few kilometres away, and the garrison there sent patrols to the towers.

It is worth saying what a ride to a spot like this really involves. You are not going to a monument but to a place in the landscape, and the pleasure is in the lanes that lead there. The Wörnitz valley is a gentle trough of damp meadows, willow trees and herons, with mill ponds, small churches and farmhouses of half-timber and stone. The hill of the Hesselberg, the highest in the region, rises to the west with a view that on a clear day stretches to the Swabian Alb. Dinkelsbühl, one of the best preserved walled towns in Germany, lies within easy reach to the south-west.

Roads are small and smooth, with gentle curves and a mix of woodland and open field, and the traffic is light. This is not a challenging area for the rider, but a restful one, with views and quiet villages. Tractors and trailers dominate in the harvest season, and the smell of silage and cut hay is strong. Spring blossom and autumn mist are both attractive, while thunderstorms can roll in on warm afternoons. Fog gathers in the valleys in the cold months.

Arberg is a village of a couple of thousand people, four kilometres off, and Wassertrüdingen, eight kilometres away, is the nearest town that offers fuel, supermarkets and a choice of inns. Try a Franconian beer and a Schäufele with potato dumpling, or a slice of cake in a bakery café. Respect the field tracks and forest gates, which are often closed to motor vehicles, and view the Limes line from the public paths. A small information sign may mark the site, and local tourist offices have leaflets about the Limes route.
t.rijeka@45.3,14.4:
Rijeka is a port city that does not try to be pretty, and that is its charm. It lies at the head of the Kvarner Gulf, where the mountains come down steeply to a deep harbour, and it has been a trading city since Roman times. Under the Habsburgs it was Fiume, Hungary's sea gate, and between the wars it was Italian, briefly the plaything of the poet Gabriele D'Annunzio, who occupied it in 1919 and ruled it as a self-styled commandant for fifteen months. Today it is Croatian, and it is the third largest city in the country.

The city is built on industry, and its past includes a torpedo factory that produced the first self-propelled torpedoes in the 1860s, based on a design by a local Austrian naval officer and an English engineer. The buildings along the Korzo, the main pedestrian street, have a faded Habsburg grandeur, and the port still dominates the waterfront, with cranes and cargo ships. Rijeka was European Capital of Culture in 2020, and its old industrial buildings have been turned into galleries and venues. Every winter it hosts one of the biggest carnivals in Croatia, with costumed parades and a good deal of noise.

Above the city, the hilltop of Trsat has a castle and a pilgrimage church, reached by a long staircase of more than five hundred steps from the town. The view over the harbour, the gulf and the islands is worth the climb, and the church has been a place of pilgrimage for centuries.

For riders, Rijeka is the start or end of the Adriatic Highway, the Magistrala, which runs south along the coast through Bakar, Kraljevica and Senj. The first stretch is a beautiful run with hairpins above the sea, but be aware of the bora, a violent cold wind that blows down from the mountains, and which can close the coastal roads and the Krk bridge to bikes. Check forecasts. Summer brings heavy traffic and heat.

Rijeka has more than a hundred and forty thousand people, so fuel and food are easy. Eat fish near the market, and book ahead in summer if you want a room.
t.villa gazzotti grimani@45.6,11.6:
Palladio is the reason most people know the Veneto's villas, and this was one of his first. Villa Gazzotti Grimani stands at Bertesina, just west of Vicenza on the edge of the flat plain, and dates from the early 1540s, when Andrea Palladio was still a stonemason's apprentice turned architect, not yet the man whose Four Books would shape buildings from Virginia to St Petersburg. It was designed for the Gazzotti family and later passed to the Grimani, whose name remained attached. The plan is bold: a centre block with a loggia stacked above a loggia, and a pair of wings that were meant to curve forward but were never completed.

It feels more like a farmhouse that has been given an idea than a palace, and that is the charm. These villas were working estates, grain and wine and silk, and the great hall was where the landowner did business. Palladio's trick was to dress the barn in the clothes of a Roman temple, and the whole area has been protected as a UNESCO site, the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto, since the 1990s.

The riding around here is gentle and honestly not the main attraction. The land is flat, ruled by drainage ditches, poplars and maize fields, and the lanes between Bertesina, Quinto Vicentino and Lisiera are narrow with a lot of tractors and cyclists. The better rewards lie to the north and west, where the Berici hills and then the Asiago plateau begin to climb. In winter, fog can lie thick on the plain for days, and in July the air is heavy enough to feel in your helmet.

Fuel and food are no problem. Vicenza, a city of more than a hundred thousand, is only a few kilometres away, and the old centre is full of Palladio's palaces on the Corso, along with excellent cooking. Try baccalà alla vicentina, the stockfish stewed slowly in milk, which locals defend as fiercely as their football team.

Early or late in the day the stone takes a warm colour from the low sun, and the grass in front is often empty. Tread carefully on the gravel, and check before you go whether the villa is open, since private use and restoration affect visiting.
t.belvedere@45.5,10.7:
South of Lake Garda the mountains step back and the land turns into a theatre of hills. Those are the moraines, left by the glacier that once filled the valley and dropped its load of gravel in a series of curved ridges as it melted. The belvedere on this stretch is part of that gentle amphitheatre, a viewpoint over vineyards and fields on the way between Peschiera del Garda and the old battlefields at San Martino and Solferino, and in clear weather you can see the Alps rising behind the lake.

The country is wine country. Bardolino, Custoza and Lugana grow here, the last a fresh white from the south shore that suits the lake's fish, and the roads between the villages pass farms, cypress rows and country restaurants. Peschiera itself is a fortified town built by the Venetian Republic on an island in the Mincio, its walls part of the Venetian Works of Defence inscribed by UNESCO in 2017. In 1859 the nearby hills saw some of the bloodiest fighting of the Second War of Italian Independence, and the tall memorial tower at San Martino stands as a reminder.

The riding is easy and attractive, if not dramatic. The roads are narrow and winding in the hills, with blind bends, tractor traffic and many cyclists, and the surface can be patchy. Traffic on the lakeshore roads and the roads to Peschiera is heavy on summer weekends, and you will do better to explore the moraine country in the morning. Spring brings blossoms and fresh green, while September has the grape harvest and golden light.

Fuel is easy in Peschiera del Garda, a town of nearly eight thousand with several pumps near the main roads, and the lakeside towns offer more. For a break, stop at a small trattoria for tortellini di Valeggio, the local pasta stuffed with meat or cheese and served in butter and sage.

The ride list continues to Vicenza and Palladio's Villa Almerico Capra, known as La Rotonda, a square house with four porticoes that makes a fitting finish.
t.bande corte carpani@45.4,10.6:
Corte Carpani is the kind of place that the name tells you most about. A corte in this part of Lombardy is a farm courtyard, with a farmhouse, barns and outbuildings arranged around a square, and the old estates in the Mantuan hills often kept the names of the families who owned them for a few generations. It sits among the low moraine hills south of Lake Garda, near the villages of Solferino and Cavriana, in a country of vines, maize, cypress rows and brick farm towers.

The hills themselves are the product of the last Ice Age. A tongue of ice pushed down from the Alps and left curved ridges of gravel, so that the land is a sequence of small, rounded crests with flat plain between them, and the lanes follow the ridge-tops with sudden, wide views. The landscape is also a battlefield. On 24 June 1859, the French and Piedmontese armies met the Austrians here at Solferino, in a day of fighting that left tens of thousands of dead and wounded. A Swiss businessman called Henri Dunant came upon the field by chance, was shocked by the lack of care for the injured, and wrote a book that led to the founding of the Red Cross. There is a museum in Solferino, and the tower on the hill, the Spia d'Italia, gives long views across the battlefield.

The story has a special weight when you remember that the Red Cross began as a Swiss idea, and the quiet of the hills now is a striking contrast. The roads are narrow and the surface is mixed, with farm traffic, cyclists and a few blind corners. Morning mist hangs on the fields in autumn, and in June the poppies are spectacular. Spring and early autumn are best, and the harvest in September brings a rich smell to the vineyards.

Cavriana and Solferino have small shops and cafes, and larger fuel stations are found at Castiglione delle Stiviere and on the main roads towards Mantua and Brescia, so fill the tank beforehand. The local wines, Garda Colli Mantovani, are light and good with a plate of tortelli di zucca, the sweet pumpkin pasta that Mantua loves.

Villa Almerico Capra, the next stop on the ride list, is across the plain to the north-east, and you can ride between the two in half a day.
t.oberstaufen@47.6,10.0:
Oberstaufen is a spa town with a taste for fasting. Its fame comes from the Schroth cure, a regime of dry days, wet days, wraps and very little food that visitors have been putting up with here for generations, and the place wears its wellness reputation with a certain Bavarian shrug. You see it in the clean flower boxes, the Kneipp-style water basins in the park, and the clinic-like hotels. It is also a proper Allgäu town, and a pleasant one, with about seven thousand people, cow bells in the background, and a brewing tradition that makes the fasting look like a very optional part of life.

The setting is the Nagelfluh range, a line of rounded green peaks made of a conglomerate rock that looks like concrete full of pebbles. Hochgrat, at 1,834 metres, is the high point, and a cable car runs up from nearby Steibis. Below the ridge, the countryside is the soft, hilly dairy land that Allgäu is known for, with farms, small chapels, and meadows dotted with onion-domed churches. Cheese is a serious business here, and a slab of Bergkäse with bread is an honest lunch.

For riding, this is a part of the world that rewards a slow day. The roads around Oberstaufen are narrow and well kept, rolling across the hills in long, easy bends, with views toward the Alps, and the border with Austria's Bregenzerwald lies just to the south. Lake Constance is about thirty kilometres to the west, and Lindau, on its island, is a pleasant detour. Be aware of tractors and cyclists on the lanes, and of wet leaves and mud on farm roads after rain.

Fuel and food are easy. There are petrol stations along the main road through town, and cafes, bakeries and inns around the centre. Weather in the foothills changes quickly, with sudden showers and fog on the ridges, so keep a waterproof on top of the luggage. Spring, when the meadows are bright, and early autumn, when the cattle come down from the high pastures, are my choices.
t.dolomiti settentrionali cadorine@46.6,12:
North of Cortina d'Ampezzo, the Dolomites change character. The soft meadows and pine woods of the Ampezzo basin give way to long grey screes, vertical walls and the pale towers that make the range so unmistakable, and the road toward Cimabanche runs through a valley framed by some of the most dramatic rock in Europe. This area belongs to the northern Cadore group in UNESCO's Dolomites listing of 2009, nine separate systems recognised for their landscape and their geology.

The rock itself is the story. Dolomite is a form of limestone rich in magnesium, named for the French geologist Deodat de Dolomieu, who described it in the late eighteenth century. The mountains were once coral reefs in a warm Triassic sea, and fossil shells can still be found high on the cliffs. In the evening, the rock turns pink and orange in a glow the Ladin people call enrosadira, an effect that happens on clear days when the sun is low and has made the range famous.

The history of the area is also layered. Cortina was part of Austria until the end of the First World War, and the front line ran along the ridges above, with soldiers living in tunnels and caves and fighting at altitude through winters. Old trenches, gun positions and open-air museums are all over the mountains. Cortina hosted the Winter Olympics in 1956, and again with Milan in February 2026, and the town is still a fashionable resort.

The riding is excellent. The roads are well maintained and wind through the valleys and over the passes with plenty of bends, wide hairpins and views, and traffic can be heavy in July and August, so mornings and weekdays are better. Passes are generally open from late May until October. The weather changes quickly, and thunderstorms in the afternoon are common in summer.

Cortina, a few kilometres south, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and prices are high. Take a layer for the cold at altitude.
t.promenade along the embankments and brid:
Ljubljana is a small capital with a big reputation for charm, and much of that comes from the river. The Ljubljanica runs through the centre in a shallow curve, with cafes along both banks, willows trailing in the water and bridges at every few steps. The architect Joze Plecnik, who worked here for much of the first half of the twentieth century, shaped the embankments, the market colonnade and the bridges, and his work was listed by UNESCO in 2021 as part of a series of his buildings.

The Triple Bridge, a cluster of three crossings beside the Preseren Square, is the best known, with balustrades and lamp posts that give it a graceful, slightly theatrical look. A little downstream, the Dragon Bridge, from 1901, has fierce green dragons at its corners, and the legend is that the founder of the city killed a dragon here. The covered market along the river is where the locals shop, and the stalls sell cheese, honey, sausage and fruit.

The city centre is closed to most traffic, and the scale is human, so walking is the best way to see it. A funicular carries visitors up to the castle on its hill, where the view takes in the red roofs of the old town and, on a clear day, the Julian Alps and Kamnik Alps beyond. The bridges and river paths are lovely in the early evening, when the light is warm and the cafes fill up.

For riders, Ljubljana is a good base, and the Alps are close. The road north through the Karavanke tunnel leads to Austria, and Klagenfurt is a short ride beyond. Slovenia requires an electronic vignette for motorways, which you can buy online or at petrol stations before the border, and there are heavy fines for riding without one. Fuel is plentiful on the edge of the city, and food ranges from quick snacks to refined dining. Parking in the centre is limited, so use a garage on the outskirts or ask your hotel for advice. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.bad tolz@47.8,11.6:
Bad Tolz grows from the Isar, the river that rushes down from the Alps toward Munich, and the town's main street, the Marktstrasse, climbs a steep slope above the water, lined with painted houses with gabled fronts and carved signs. At the top stands the Kalvarienberg, a hill with a baroque chapel and a view across the roofs to the Alps. The name Bad means spa, and it was the tapping of iodine-rich springs in the nineteenth century that gave the town its status, though the mountains and the old town are the real draw.

Bavaria is full of traditions, and Bad Tolz keeps one of the most colourful: every year on 6 November, the Leonhardifahrt, a procession of decorated wagons pulled by teams of horses, climbs the hill to the chapel of Saint Leonard, the patron saint of livestock. Men in traditional dress, women in dirndls and brass bands fill the streets, and the horses wear garlands and ribbons. The town is also known for its boys' choir, the Tolzer Knabenchor, one of the best in Germany.

For riders, the town sits at the entrance to the Bavarian Alps, and the roads leaving it are among the finest in Germany. To the south, the road leads to Lenggries and the Sylvenstein lake, with views of the Karwendel range, and farther on to the Walchensee and Kochelsee, where the road rises and bends beside deep, green water. The surface is excellent, traffic is heavy on summer weekends, and speed limits are enforced. The Blomberg, a hill with a summer toboggan run, is a popular family outing.

Bad Tolz has about 17,000 people, so there is fuel at several stations, supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants. A weisswurst breakfast, with sweet mustard and a pretzel, is a local ritual. Rooms fill quickly in summer. Early morning is the best time to ride, before the day-trippers arrive from Munich, and the evening light on the mountains is beautiful.
t.watchtower wp 13 40@49.1,10.6:
The Raetian Limes, the eastern part of the Roman frontier in Germany, is different from the Upper Germanic section, because here the Romans built a wall. The remains of the stone wall, which stretches across Bavaria for about a hundred and sixty kilometres, are known locally as the Devil's Wall, the Teufelsmauer, because people long believed that no human could have made it. Watchtower WP 13/40, near the village of Arberg in Middle Franconia, stands along this section, and its foundations can be traced in a field or at the edge of a wood.

Stone towers like this one stood every few hundred metres along the frontier, each housing a handful of soldiers who could signal to their neighbours with fire or flags. The Raetian Limes was built in the later second century, to protect the province of Raetia from the tribes to the north, and was abandoned around 260 AD when Germanic raids overwhelmed the border. Within a few years, the frontier had moved back to the Rhine and the Danube. UNESCO listed the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes in 2005.

The countryside is gentle farmland and low forest, with villages of white and red-roofed houses, church towers, and fields of grain and sugar beet. The region is Franconian, a land of beer, sausages and wine, with a dry humour and a distinct dialect. Arberg is a small place, and the larger town of Ansbach is not far to the north, with a baroque palace.

Riding here is straightforward and pleasant, on quiet country roads with wide views and few cars, a good place for a long day without fuss. The Hesselberg, the highest hill in the area, offers a view over the Franconian plain, and the Altmuhl valley to the south is a favourite for riders. Roads can be wet in spring, and farm traffic is common during harvest. Fuel is available in Arberg's neighbouring towns, and bakeries, butchers and inns provide good food, with Franconian specialities such as roast pork and dumplings. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, and summer afternoons can be hot. Take a moment at the site to imagine the signal fires.
t.cesky krumlov@48.8,14.3:
The Vltava makes a series of tight loops through the south Bohemian hills, and Český Krumlov sits inside one of them like a stone kept in a closed hand. The old town, the castle on its rock above the river, and the bridges and rooftops are all squeezed into the bend. It is a very small place, only about fourteen thousand people, but it has the air of something much larger, because for centuries it was the seat of powerful noble families, first the Rosenbergs and later the Schwarzenbergs and Eggenbergs, who built and rebuilt the castle until it had grown into dozens of buildings around a string of courtyards.

The castle has a famous Baroque theatre, one of the best-preserved in Europe, with its original stage machinery, and a tower that you can climb for the view across the red roofs. The moat is home to bears, a tradition that goes back centuries and that visitors either love or find a bit strange. The painter Egon Schiele, whose mother came from here, lived in the town for a short time and left an art centre in his name.

This is a day trip on the way between Austria and Bohemia, since the ride runs from Schlögen on the Danube, and the road north over the border passes through quiet wooded hills, with small villages and long views across the forests of the Šumava. Surfaces vary, the bends are mostly gentle and traffic can be heavy on weekends. The last stretch into town is narrow and slow, and the old centre is largely closed to cars, so park outside and walk in.

There are fuel stations on the approaches, and the town has more restaurants than you will ever need, many of them offering Czech classics: roast pork, dumplings, goulash, and trdelník, the sweet rolled pastry that is sold on every corner. Afternoons in summer are busy, and the best light and the least crowd come early in the morning or at dusk, when the river lights up under the castle.

Spring and autumn are quieter. If you can, walk down to the river and watch the rafts and canoes go by, because this is also one of the great paddling rivers of Central Europe.
t.nuremberg@49.5,11.1:
Nuremberg wears its history heavily and with some honesty. The old town sits inside a ring of walls on both banks of the Pegnitz, crowned by the Kaiserburg, the imperial castle on its sandstone ridge, where the Holy Roman emperors held court. In the late Middle Ages the city was one of the richest in Germany, a centre of trade, craft and invention, and the home of the painter Albrecht Dürer, whose house you can still visit, as well as of the toy-makers, gingerbread bakers and instrument makers who made it famous.

Most of the old centre was destroyed in the air raids of January 1945 and rebuilt in a careful, simplified version of the original, which gives it a slightly curated feel. The twentieth century has left its mark in other ways too. The Nazi party rally grounds in the south-east of the city are now a documentation centre, and the Palace of Justice, where the war crimes trials were held after 1945, is still a working courthouse. It is an uncomfortable and important place, and a visit adds weight to the idea of the Castle Road, which links the castles and towns of Franconia.

As a place to ride, Nuremberg is a city, with the usual traffic, tram lines and one-way streets, and not somewhere to hurry. The Castle Road itself, coming in from Rothenburg ob der Tauber in the west, crosses gentle Franconian farmland and wooded hills, with easy bends, pleasant villages and a good surface. Heading north from here toward Bamberg is a similar landscape of orchards, half-timbered houses and hop fields. Fuel and food are no problem at all: Nuremberg is a city of half a million, with a station on nearly every main road.

Do not leave without trying the small, finger-sized Nuremberg bratwurst, usually served in sixes on a plate with sauerkraut or potato salad, and the gingerbread known as Lebkuchen, which is a Christmas tradition. The Christkindlesmarkt in December is among the best-known Christmas markets in Europe.

For a short visit, park outside the walls and walk. The centre is compact, and the castle gives a fine view over the roofs.
Bayreuth's Margravial Opera House is the sort of building that makes you wonder how a small provincial court could afford it. It was built between 1745 and 1750 for Margrave Frederick of Brandenburg-Bayreuth and his wife, Wilhelmine, the sister of Frederick the Great, who was a composer, writer and patron and the driving force behind the court's cultural life. The interior, designed by the Italian theatre architect Giuseppe Galli Bibiena and his son Carlo, is a Baroque jewel box of carved and painted wood, with gold and blue tiers, a royal box like a throne and a stage deep enough for elaborate scenery.

It is one of the best-preserved Baroque theatres in Europe, and UNESCO listed it in 2012. Because the interior is made of wood and canvas, with no stone or brick, it is acoustically warm and visually fragile, and the guided tours are timed to protect it. Richard Wagner is said to have been drawn to Bayreuth by the size of this stage, but found the interior too ornate, so he built his own festival theatre on the hill outside town, which is still the home of the summer Wagner festival.

Bayreuth lies in Upper Franconia, on the edge of the Franconian Switzerland, a region of limestone cliffs, caves and small valleys. Riding from the Fichtel Mountains or the Franconian Forest brings long, easy bends, forest, good surface and light traffic, with villages of half-timbered houses and old breweries. Franconia has more breweries per head than almost anywhere in the world, and the local beer is a natural reward at the end of a ride.

The city has over seventy thousand people, so fuel, food and parking are not a problem, though the old town has narrow streets and a pedestrian zone, so use a car park and walk. The local food includes pork roasts, dumplings and the bratwurst of Franconia.

The ride pairs this theatre with Bad Kissingen, the grand spa town to the north-west. In July and August the Wagner festival fills the town, so book ahead if you plan to stay.
t.town of bamberg@49.9,10.9:
Bamberg is built on seven hills, like Rome, and its townspeople are proud of the comparison. The old town survived the Second World War almost unscathed, which makes it unusual in Germany, and its jumble of medieval and Baroque streets, spread between the Regnitz river and the hills, is a World Heritage Site, listed in 1993. At the top of the cathedral hill stands the Kaiserdom, a four-towered Romanesque cathedral that holds the tomb of the Emperor Henry II, who founded the bishopric in the early eleventh century, and his wife Kunigunde. It also holds a mysterious medieval equestrian statue known as the Bamberg Horseman, whose identity is still debated.

On the river below, the old town hall sits on an artificial island in the middle of the Regnitz, joined to both banks by bridges, and its painted facade looks as though it were floating. Nearby, the fishermen's houses of Little Venice line the water, with balconies and small gardens stretching over the stream. The whole town has a lived-in feel, with students, shops and cafés filling the lanes.

Bamberg is also a beer city, famous for its smoked beer, Rauchbier, brewed with malt dried over beechwood fires, which tastes like a smoky sausage to the uninitiated and like heaven to the faithful. The town and the surrounding countryside have a great many small breweries, so a day here is easily turned into an education. Franconian food is hearty, with pork, dumplings and cabbage, and the onion stuffed with meat, a local speciality, is worth a try.

As a place to ride, the surrounding Franconian hills offer winding roads through orchards, forests and small villages, with a gentle gradient and a good surface. The Franconian Switzerland to the east is particularly good for bends. Bamberg itself is busy, with narrow streets and cobbles in the old town, so leave the bike at the edge and walk.

With seventy thousand inhabitants, the town has fuel and every other service you could want. The ride links it to the Margravial Opera House in Bayreuth and on to Bad Kissingen, a good run through the heart of Franconia.
t.city of vicenza@45.5,11.5:
Vicenza is Palladio's town, and almost everything worth seeing is a version of one man's idea of what a building should be. Andrea Palladio, born in Padua and trained as a stonemason, designed palaces, villas and churches in and around Vicenza in the sixteenth century, and his work, with its Roman columns, pediments and strict proportions, shaped architecture across the world, from English country houses to the White House. The city and the villas in its surrounding countryside are together a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and a walk down Corso Palladio feels like a stroll through an architectural textbook.

The centrepiece is the Basilica Palladiana, a great hall with a double arcade of white columns that wraps an older medieval building, set on the Piazza dei Signori. The Teatro Olimpico, a few minutes' walk away, is the oldest surviving enclosed theatre in Europe, a fully built stage set that mimics a Roman theatre, with a wooden stage and painted perspective streets that seem to recede for kilometres. Just outside the city, the Villa Capra, known as La Rotonda, stands on a hill with a dome and four identical porticoes, an extraordinary combination of symmetry and landscape.

For a motorcyclist, Vicenza is a city stop with good surroundings. The centre has a limited traffic zone, so leave the bike outside and walk in. The nearby Berici Hills, to the south, offer winding roads through vineyards, small villages and cypress-lined avenues, much less crowded than the Dolomites. To the north, the road leads up toward Asiago and the Pasubio, where the First World War left trenches, tunnels and memorials, and the roads climb in dozens of hairpins to the high plateau.

Fuel, food and coffee are easy, as the city has over a hundred thousand people. It is known for its goldsmiths and jewellery industry, as well as for baccalà alla vicentina, a dish of dried cod stewed slowly in milk and onions, which is a source of local pride, usually served with polenta. Local wines include Durello and Breganze.

Spring and autumn are lovely, and the lanes of the Berici bring colour. In August the heat is oppressive and the city empties for the holidays.
t.senj@45.0,14.9:
Senj is the town of the bura, and you should know about the bura before you get there. This cold, dry wind falls off the Velebit mountains onto the Adriatic coast in sudden gusts that can exceed a hundred and fifty kilometres an hour, and Senj sits in the worst of it, in a gap where the wind funnels straight down to the sea. Lorries get blown over on the coast road, the authorities close it to motorcycles and high-sided vehicles, and local houses have stones on the roof tiles. If the sea looks white and the flags are flat out, wait it out in a cafe. The bura usually blows from autumn to spring, and in summer it is much calmer.

It was a rough town for a rough job. For much of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Senj was the base of the Uskoks, refugees from the Ottoman advance who became border fighters and, for the Venetians, pirates. They defended the Habsburg frontier from the Nehaj fortress, a square tower built in 1558 on the hill above the town, and raided Venetian shipping with such persistence that it led to a war. The fortress is still there and can be visited, with a view over the channel and Krk island. Senj also has an older distinction. It was a centre of Glagolitic printing, the Croatian alphabet of the early medieval church, and a printing house was working here in the late fifteenth century, one of the earliest in the Slavic world.

The riding on the Adriatic Highway is extraordinary. Heading south from Senj, the road clings to a stark, bare karst coastline, with white limestone slopes falling into blue water and the islands of Rab and Pag low on the horizon. The corners are long and open, the surface is good and the views are almost constant, but the road is narrow in places, with trucks and campervans in summer, and speed controls are frequent. The best time is early morning or late September, when the light is clear and the heat gentler, and the traffic has thinned.

Senj has about five thousand people, so fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and seafood restaurants are all easy. A plate of grilled fish or a bowl of black risotto is the thing to order, and the old town, with its cathedral and narrow lanes, is worth a short walk. Fill up here before heading south, as the coast has long stretches with nothing but rock and sea.
t.verona@45.4,11.0:
Verona is one of those Italian cities where the Romans left such a large footprint that the later centuries had to build around it. The Arena, a first-century amphitheatre, is still used for performances, and each summer the opera festival fills its stone seats with audiences who bring candles and cushions. A few streets away lies the Piazza delle Erbe, once the Roman forum, now an open-air market beneath frescoed palaces and the old watchtower. The Adige river loops around the old town in a tight S-bend, and the stone bridges and ramparts that cross it make a handsome backdrop to evening walks.

The Scaliger family ruled Verona in the Middle Ages, and their fortress, the Castelvecchio, and their ornate Gothic tombs still dominate the city. Shakespeare set Romeo and Juliet in Verona, though he never visited, and the famous balcony of Juliet's house was added in the twentieth century, but visitors queue up to rub the bronze statue's breast for luck anyway. The food is a better draw. Try risotto made with Amarone, the rich red wine of nearby Valpolicella, and, if you are adventurous, pastissada de caval, a slow-cooked horse stew that locals love. The surrounding hills produce excellent wines, including Soave, Valpolicella and Bardolino.

For motorcyclists, Verona has a particular place in the history of the Mille Miglia, the thousand-mile road race that ran from Brescia to Rome and back between 1927 and 1957, passing through the city. The race ended after fatal accidents, but its legacy lives on in a historic regularity event for vintage cars, and the route still draws enthusiasts. North of the city, roads climb into the Lessini hills and toward Lake Garda, with winding bends through vineyards, olive groves and cherry orchards, a fine afternoon ride.

With over two hundred thousand people, Verona has everything: fuel, parking garages, hotels and restaurants. Be careful about the ZTL, the limited traffic zones in the historic centre, which are monitored by cameras, and a fine will follow you home. Park outside the centre and walk or take a taxi. Summer is hot and crowded, particularly during the opera season, so spring and autumn are more comfortable. Evening, when the stone glows warm, is the best time for a stroll.
t.vernal@40.5,-109.5:
The town has about eleven thousand people, with a long main street, a few motels and diners, and a museum of natural history with a collection of dinosaur skeletons, including a life-size model garden with creatures that appear to lurk beside the road. The surrounding country is red and tan rock, sagebrush, and dry river valleys, with the high, snowy Uinta Mountains standing to the north.

Dinosaur National Monument, about thirty kilometres east, is the main reason to come. Its quarry wall, protected beneath a roof, holds the exposed bones of hundreds of dinosaurs, embedded in the rock where they were laid down in a river bar some one hundred and fifty million years ago, and visitors can see and touch the fossils. The monument also protects the canyons of the Green and Yampa rivers, which are popular with rafters. The Uintas, the only major mountain range in the United States that runs east to west, include Kings Peak, the highest in Utah at 13,528 feet.

The road north from Vernal, US 191, climbs over Diamond Mountain and descends to the Flaming Gorge Reservoir, passing a series of geological layers that are visible in the road cuts, each one a different colour, and the Sheep Creek Geological Loop, a side road that shows layers of rock tilted on their sides. The riding is excellent, with long, smooth curves, big views and a quiet road. Summer afternoons bring heat and sometimes thunderstorms, while winter closes the higher roads with snow, so check conditions. Wildlife, including deer, elk and pronghorn, appear at dawn and dusk, and care is needed.

Fuel, food and coffee are all easy in Vernal, with petrol stations, supermarkets and restaurants on the main street, and services thin out beyond. Fill the tank before heading into the mountains, since stations are far apart. Local diners serve big breakfasts and burgers, and the ice cream at the old drug store is a local tradition.

Take the time to stand beside the dinosaur quarry wall, if you can. It is a humbling sight, and a reminder of the age of the land you are about to ride through. Early morning is the best time to start, with cool air and long shadows.
t.svolvaer@68.2,14.6:
The Svolværgeita, the Svolvær Goat, is a pair of rock horns on a peak above the town, and climbers jump the gap between them for the thrill of it. That is the sort of place Svolvær is. It is the largest town in the Lofoten islands, with some four thousand people on the island of Austvågøya, and it sits on the edge of a harbour surrounded by jagged mountains that rise straight out of the sea.

Lofoten has been a fishing centre for more than a thousand years. Every winter, from about January to April, vast shoals of cod come south from the Barents Sea to spawn, and fishermen from across northern Norway used to gather here for the season. The fish is hung on tall wooden racks to dry in the cold, salty air, becoming stockfish, which was a major export to Italy and Portugal for centuries. The racks still stand, and in some places the smell reaches the road. Nearby Kabelvåg has an old fishing village and a small museum.

The road, the E10, is the great ride of the north. It runs west across the islands on bridges, causeways and tunnels, with the mountains pressing in on one side and the sea on the other, and the light changes constantly. The surface is good, the bends are moderate, and the speed limits are low, with cameras on the straighter sections. In summer, the midnight sun lasts from late May to mid-July, and you can ride at any hour with the sky glowing. In winter, snow and darkness change the character of the road, and the northern lights can appear.

Fuel is easy in Svolvær, with several stations, and in Kabelvåg and Leknes. Restaurants serve fresh cod, often in the form of boiled fillets, fish soup or tongues, a local delicacy, and the best meal is whatever came off the boats that morning. Book accommodation ahead in summer, as the islands fill with visitors. Wind and rain can arrive suddenly, so pack warm and waterproof clothing, even in July.
t.leknes@68.1,13.6:
Leknes is the practical heart of Lofoten, a modest town with a lot to be grateful for. It sits on Vestvågøy, the flattest of the larger islands, and has the airport, the biggest supermarkets and the hospital, so everything you forgot to bring can probably be bought here. If you have ridden the long, scenic road from Svolvær, the sight of a proper grocery store is welcome.

The island has something remarkable at Borg, a few kilometres to the east: the Lofotr Viking Museum, built around the foundations of a chieftain's longhouse of the ninth and tenth centuries. The reconstruction is eighty-three metres long, among the biggest Viking buildings ever found, and a guide in costume will explain how a chief lived here, ruling the surrounding fishing communities. It is a reminder that Lofoten was a rich and powerful region long before tourists arrived. Nearby, the beaches at Haukland and Uttakleiv are broad arcs of white sand, with mountains behind and a surprisingly bright blue sea.

The riding on Vestvågøy is gentler than on the neighbouring islands. The E10 and the side roads cross low country, with bends that open to wide views of beaches, lakes and mountains. In the evening light, which is long and golden in summer, the whole island glows. Wind off the Atlantic can be strong, and sudden rain showers are common. In winter, snow and ice make the roads treacherous, and studded tyres are the norm for cars.

Fuel is easy in Leknes, a town of around three and a half thousand, and the supermarkets, bakeries and cafés make it a good place to restock. Local seafood is excellent, and the town has several restaurants. If you plan to camp, Norway's right to roam lets you pitch a tent for a night in the countryside, as long as you keep away from houses and farmland and leave no trace. The dark skies of autumn bring the northern lights, one of the great sights of the north.
t.sandnessjoen@66.0,12.6:
Seven mountains stand in a row along the coast of Alsten island, and the people of Sandnessjøen call them the Seven Sisters. They are jagged, steep and dark, rising straight out of the sea to over a thousand metres, and a Norwegian legend gives each one a name and a story involving trolls and a pursuing suitor. With around five thousand six hundred people, it is the biggest place on this stretch of the coast.

Alstahaug, a few kilometres south, has a history that is well worth knowing. The old church there, from the twelfth century, was the home parish of Petter Dass, a seventeenth-century priest and poet who wrote about the life of the northern fishermen and became a national figure, nicknamed the trumpet of Nordland. His verses were learned by heart in fishing villages for generations, and the local museum celebrates him. The area has been settled since the Stone Age, and the coast is dotted with ancient burial mounds.

The ride along the Helgeland coast is a long chain of ferries and bridges. The Helgelandsbrua, a graceful cable-stayed bridge just over a kilometre long, opened in 1991 and links Alsten to the mainland, replacing a ferry crossing, and the road then runs along the water through tunnels and small villages. The scenery is dramatic, with sea, islands and mountains, and the weather is changeable, with rain, wind and sudden clear light. In June and July, the nights are never dark.

Fuel is easy in Sandnessjøen, which has several stations, and it is the last big stop before the long run north. Restaurants serve fresh fish, and the harbour is lively, with fishing boats and ferries. Check ferry timetables in advance, as they run on a schedule and can fill in summer. Pack waterproofs, since the coast gets plenty of rain, and keep a spare layer. The view of the Seven Sisters in the evening light is worth a pause on the quay.
t.jektvik@66.6,13.3:
The Jektvik to Kilboghamn crossing is part of the Helgeland coastal route, Fv17, and the boat carries cars and bikes over a sound that marks, at its centre, the line of 66 degrees 33 minutes north, so a motorcycle can cross into the Arctic on a ferry deck with a coffee in hand. Beyond the water, the mountains of Meløy and the great Svartisen glacier lie waiting.

Jektvik itself is a tiny community, a few houses, a quay and a ferry waiting room, on a steep shore. The surrounding landscape is brutal and beautiful, with sheer mountains, fjords and a coast broken into thousands of islands. Svartisen, the second largest glacier in mainland Norway, lies to the north-east, and an arm of the ice, Engabreen, reaches almost to sea level. Small boats cross the lake in front of it. Fishing, fish farming and tourism sustain the district, and the people are friendly but spread thin.

The riding on Fv17 is among the best in Norway. The road follows the coast through tunnels and over bridges, with sharp bends, steep climbs and long views of the sea and mountains. The surface is mostly good, but the road is narrow in places, with little room for error. Ferries are an essential part of the route, so check timetables, since they can be infrequent, particularly outside summer. Rain and wind are common, and fog can roll in from the sea.

Food is limited, though the ferry may have a small kiosk. Carry water, snacks and spare layers, and keep your phone charged. In midsummer, the sun does not set, and a late ride across the Arctic Circle in golden light is an unforgettable experience.
t.silvretta high alpine road@46.9,10.1:
Bielerhöhe is the high point of the Silvretta High Alpine Road, a toll road built in the 1950s to link the Montafon valley in Vorarlberg with the Paznaun valley in Tyrol, and the top at about 2,032 metres sits at the edge of the Silvretta reservoir. The lake, a long, deep blue sheet held back by a dam, is surrounded by bare peaks and small glaciers, and the highest of them, Piz Buin at 3,312 metres, rises to the south beyond the water.

The road from the Montafon side is the one to ride, climbing through a long ladder of hairpins from Partenen, with big drops, forest at first and then bare alpine meadows near the top. The surface is excellent, wide enough for coaches, and the corners are tidy and well banked. Tolls apply, which you pay at the booth at the bottom, and the road is open from about June to October, depending on snow. On the Tyrolean side, the road descends more gently to Galtür, which sits in the Paznaun valley, and Ischgl, the ski resort beyond.

The Silvretta group straddles the border of Austria and Switzerland, and the region has a long history of smugglers, herders and mountaineers. Galtür, a small village, suffered a catastrophic avalanche in 1999, and a memorial and a wall of protection stand above the settlement as a reminder. The reservoir is part of a hydroelectric scheme, and a small information centre has displays about the dam and the surrounding nature.

The weather here is changeable, and snow may fall in any month, so carry a warm layer and rain gear. A cafe and restaurant by the lake serve coffee and cake with views, and the walk around the shore is a good way to stretch after the climb. Early mornings are quiet, and the light on the water is superb.
t.augsburg@48.4,10.9:
Augsburg is older than almost everything else on the Romantic Road, and it knows it. The Romans founded a camp here in 15 BC and named it after Emperor Augustus, and for much of the Middle Ages it was one of the richest cities in Europe, thanks to the Fugger and Welser banking families, who lent money to emperors and popes.
