The Fuggerei, a walled quarter of small yellow houses built by Jakob Fugger in 1521, is the world's oldest social housing complex still in use, and the annual rent is famously less than a euro.

The city lies where the rivers Lech and Wertach meet in the Bavarian plain, with about two hundred and sixty thousand people, which makes it the largest place on this road by far. That means everything a rider needs, from fuel and bike dealers to hotels at every price. The old town is a pleasure to walk, with the Renaissance town hall, a golden hall that rises above the square, and the tall Perlach tower beside it. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 gave Lutherans and Catholics in the empire a measure of religious toleration, and the city is still known for it.

Several famous people came from here. Leopold Mozart, the father of Wolfgang Amadeus, was born in Augsburg, and Bertolt Brecht was born here in 1898. Rudolf Diesel developed his engine in the city, working with the machine works that became MAN, and anyone who rides a diesel-powered motorcycle owes a small nod to the place. The canals and water towers of the old water system were recognised by UNESCO in 2019.

The ride in from the south, down the Lech valley, is relaxed, with gentle bends, orchards and Bavarian villages, but the last stretch is suburban. Traffic is heavy at rush hour, so aim to arrive in the late morning or evening, and leave the bike somewhere secure, as in any big city. A coffee and a slice of cake in a cafe near the Rathaus platz is a fine way to end the road.
t.oberjoch@47.5,10.4:
Oberjoch is a village that sits on a saddle, and the saddle belongs to two countries. At 1,178 metres, the pass on the German Alpine Road marks the boundary between the Allgäu in Bavaria and the Tannheimer Valley in Tyrol, and the road crosses it from the town of Hindelang with a steep climb. The pass has a ski resort, a clutch of hotels and a few tidy farmhouses, and it is among the highest villages in Germany.

The German Alpine Road, the Deutsche Alpenstraße, was conceived in the 1930s as a scenic route along the northern edge of the Alps, from Lindau on Lake Constance to Berchtesgaden near the Austrian border, and the stretch through the Allgäu is one of the best. The climb from Hindelang to Oberjoch is a motorcyclist's favourite, a series of hairpins and fast bends through forest, with views of the Allgäu Alps opening up at the top. The surface is good, the corners are well signed, and the traffic can be heavy on summer weekends.

Jungholz, a few kilometres away, is a curious Austrian village that is almost surrounded by Germany and touches Austria at a single point, so tiny that it was long said to be connected by a single mountain peak. It is in effect part of the German customs area, and is an oddity worth a detour. Tannheim, in the valley beyond, has about a thousand people and a lakeside setting at the foot of the mountains.

There is fuel in Hindelang and Sonthofen, the nearest bigger town, about eleven kilometres away, but not at the top. The pass can have snow into May, and it is cold in the morning, even in summer. Fog and rain are frequent, so check the weather before you go. A coffee and a slice of cake at a hotel terrace, with the view over the valley, is a pleasure after the climb.
t.reit im winkl@47.7,12.5:
Reit im Winkl is the snow-sure village at the end of the Chiemgau Alps, a pocket of Bavaria wedged into the corner where Germany meets Austria. At about 700 metres, it sits in a high, green bowl among steep peaks, with the Kaisergebirge, the jagged limestone range of the Tyrolean Kaiser mountains, standing across the border to the south. The snow here is dependable in winter, and the place has produced a number of Olympic skiers.

The German Alpine Road passes through, from Ruhpolding by way of the quiet little lake chain of the Weitsee, the Mittersee and the Lödensee, whose clear water mirrors the forest and the cliffs. The road is smooth, with long bends, gentle gradients and wide views, and it is among the finest stretches in the Bavarian Alps. Cows with bells graze in the meadows, and the farmhouses have carved balconies full of geraniums. It can be busy in summer, so go early.

The village has about two and a half thousand people, with a church, a few shops and many guesthouses. Fuel is available, though for a larger choice, Grassau, about twelve kilometres north, and the Austrian town of Kössen, a short ride away, are good options. The Winklmoosalm, a high plateau above the village, is a great spot for walking, with alpine pastures and mountain huts.

The village is also known for its Gebirgsschützen and for its crafts, and in the main street you can find wood carvings, hand-woven clothes and local cheeses. The food is hearty, with dumplings, roast pork, and Kaiserschmarrn, a torn pancake with raisins and plum compote, that is a classic Alpine dessert. In summer, the evenings are warm, and the smell of hay and wood smoke hangs in the air. In autumn the larches turn gold and the light is superb.
t.bayreuth@49.9,11.6:
Bayreuth is the town where one man's operas became a pilgrimage. Richard Wagner moved here in the 1870s and built a festival theatre on a hill outside the town, designed to his own ideas, with a hidden orchestra pit and a plain brick exterior. The first festival was held in 1876, and every summer since, thousands of people have made the trip to hear his operas. The tickets are so hard to obtain that the waiting list is said to be measured in years.

Long before Wagner, the town had another distinction. The Margravine Wilhelmine, sister of Frederick the Great, made Bayreuth a centre of art and music in the eighteenth century, and built the Margravial Opera House, a masterpiece of baroque theatre in carved and painted wood, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Hermitage, her summer palace and park, with fountains and grottoes, is a short ride from the centre. Franz Liszt, Wagner's father-in-law, died in Bayreuth in 1886 and is buried in the town cemetery.

With about seventy-five thousand people, the city has every service, with fuel stations, bike dealers, hotels and restaurants. The cuisine of Upper Franconia is hearty, with sausages, dumplings, roast pork and local beer, as this part of Bavaria is among the densest brewing regions in the world. The Castle Road, which runs from Mannheim to Prague, passes through here, linking the castles and palaces of the region.

The roads south of Bayreuth lead into Franconian Switzerland, a landscape of limestone cliffs, caves and small valleys, with some of the best riding in southern Germany. The roads are smooth, with tight bends and gentle climbs, and the villages are tidy. In festival season, from late July to August, the city is busy and hotels are full, so book ahead. In spring and autumn it is calmer, and the light is good.
t.wieskirche@47.7,10.9:
The Wieskirche stands alone in a meadow in the Pfaffenwinkel, the priests' corner of Upper Bavaria, with the Ammergau Alps behind it, and it is the finest rococo church in Germany. From the outside it is almost plain: a long, white building with a modest tower and a red roof, set among fields with a few farmhouses nearby. The surprise is on the inside, where the whole space explodes into light, colour and movement, with a ceiling painted as an open sky, stucco curling like clouds and a pulpit and altars glittering with gold.

The story begins in the 1730s with a wooden figure of the scourged Christ that was said to have shed tears, a miracle that drew pilgrims to a farm in this meadow. A church was soon needed to hold them, and the brothers Dominikus and Johann Baptist Zimmermann, a stuccoist and a painter at the height of their powers, built it in the middle of the eighteenth century. Dominikus is said to have been so fond of the church that he built himself a house beside it and spent his last years there. UNESCO recognised it as a World Heritage site in 1983.

The ride to it is part of the pleasure. This is the end of the Romantic Road in spirit, and the lanes that reach the church run through meadows and small woods, with the Alps rising behind, and the bends are gentle. The surface is good, traffic is moderate, though busy on summer weekends when coaches arrive. The best moments are early morning, when the church is quiet and the light enters low through the windows, or late afternoon.

Steingaden, three kilometres away, is a small village with a Romanesque abbey church, and it has cafes and an inn. For fuel, Peiting, thirteen kilometres away, is the larger place, with stations and supermarkets, and Schongau is nearby. Dress respectfully inside, and keep your voice low, since it is still a place of worship. In winter the roads can be icy and the meadows white, a beautiful but cold season, and in spring the fields are bright with flowers.
t.passo falzarego@46.5,12.0:
Falzarego is a pass that rewards the effort of the Dolomites, a bare grey saddle at 2,105 metres between Cortina d'Ampezzo and the high valleys of the Cordevole, ringed by pale, ruined-looking peaks that glow pink at sunset. The mountains here are sheer, jagged and strangely close, with the great cliffs of Lagazuoi and the Tofane on one side and the stacked towers of the Cinque Torri on the other. There is almost no vegetation at the top, only rock, scree and a few huts, and the sky feels very large.

The pass has a grim history. During the First World War, the front line between the Austrian and Italian armies ran straight through these mountains, and soldiers fought for years in tunnels, trenches and galleries blasted into the rock, with many dying from avalanches and cold as well as bullets. The tunnels on Lagazuoi, where each side dug mines under the other, can still be visited, and a cable car runs from the pass to the summit. The road itself was built by the Austrians for military use, and the old fortifications are scattered around the slopes.

The ride up from Cortina is a classic of the Dolomites, with a series of hairpins and long, open bends climbing through larch forest to the bare upper slopes, and then a sweeping descent on the other side toward Arabba and the Marmolada glacier. The surface is generally good, with smooth tarmac, but the road is busy in summer, with cyclists, cars, campers and other motorcyclists, so overtaking needs care. Early morning gives the best light and the emptiest road, and afternoon thunderstorms can build quickly in July and August.

The pass is open from about late spring until the first heavy snow, usually in October, and may close temporarily after storms. It is cold at this altitude even in summer, so keep a warm layer to hand, and give yourself time to walk around a bit, for the views alone.
t.stelvio pass summit@46.5,10.5:
The Stelvio at its summit is a strange mix of mountain and market. At 2,757 metres, it is the second highest paved pass in the Alps, and the car park is crowded with coaches, camper vans, motorbikes and stalls selling sausages, hats and souvenirs. Cold wind blows across the saddle even in July, so keep a jacket in your top box. Ahead the Ortler massif, the highest peak in the eastern Alps at 3,905 metres, rises over the glaciers, and on a clear day it is worth taking a moment to look at it before the stalls draw your attention.

The road itself was built in the 1820s under Austrian rule, designed by the engineer Carlo Donegani to link Lombardy with the Tyrol and bring troops and goods over the mountains. It was a serious piece of engineering for the time, with hairpin after hairpin cut into steep slopes, and it still follows the line he chose. On the northern side, from Prato allo Stelvio, there are close to fifty numbered hairpins, which you can count on the way up or down; on the side toward Bormio, the road is longer and more open, with several tunnels cut into the rock.

Riding it is exciting but demanding. The road is narrow, with low walls and big drops, and the hairpins are tight enough that a loaded touring bike needs real care. Coaches coming the other way take the whole width on corners, so wait until they are clear. Surface quality is usually good but can be damaged by frost heave, and in early summer there may be patches of gravel or meltwater. The best time to ride is early in the morning, before the traffic and before the clouds roll in, or late in the evening when most people have gone. Weekends in July and August are crowded.

The pass is closed in winter, usually from late autumn until late May or June, depending on snow, and it can close for a few days even in summer after a storm. Food at the summit is basic but filling: sausages, sandwiches, strudel and hot chocolate, all priced as you would expect for a place where everything has to be brought up by truck.
t.santa maria val mustair@46.6,10.4:
Santa Maria in the Val Müstair is, strictly speaking, in Switzerland, not Italy, tucked into the far south-east corner of Graubünden a few kilometres from the border at Tubre. The valley is quiet, with meadows, a small river and low houses with painted facades, and the main language is Romansh, a Latin tongue that survives here in several dialects. It sits at around 1,375 metres, so the air is cool and dry, and in spring the fields are full of flowers.

The great thing here is the convent of St John at Müstair, a few minutes down the valley, a UNESCO World Heritage site that dates back to around the year 800 and is traditionally linked to Charlemagne. Its interior holds Carolingian wall paintings, among the largest surviving cycles from that period, along with later Romanesque frescoes layered over them. It is a rare chance to see something that old in near-original state, and well worth half an hour even if you are not usually a museum person. The nuns still live there.

For riders, the valley is both a stop and a hinge. Over the Ofen Pass, the road climbs to about 2,150 metres and then drops toward Zernez and the Engadin, through the Swiss National Park, where cars must stay on the road and wildlife is protected. In the other direction, the Umbrail Pass goes up to the Stelvio road. Between them you have a loop that is hard to beat in the central Alps, though it is a long day if you add Bormio and the Stelvio itself.

The label points to a fuel stop, and there is a small supply in the valley, but pumps are few and Swiss prices are higher than Italian ones, so it makes sense to arrive with a good tank. The nearest bigger towns are on the Italian side, Bormio on one hand and Glorenza on the other. Bring your passport or identity card, since you are crossing an international border, and remember that Swiss speed limits are enforced firmly, with cameras and fines that are large by any standard. Food is simple and good: barley soup, a dense walnut cake from the Engadin and local cheese with dark bread.
t.umbrail pass@46.5,10.4:
Umbrail is the quiet sister of the Stelvio. At 2,501 metres it is the highest paved pass in Switzerland, and yet most people ride past its turning without noticing. It leaves the Stelvio road just below the summit on the Italian side and drops into Switzerland, down to Santa Maria in the Val Müstair, on a road that is narrower, emptier and a good deal slower than its neighbour. There is a Swiss border post near the top, and you should carry your passport.

The history is the same as that of the Stelvio, since both are part of the old trade and military routes between Lombardy and the upper Adige, but the character is different. The Swiss side has fewer coaches, fewer stalls and a much more local feel, with larch and spruce woods lower down and open pasture higher up. The hairpins are still there, tight and steep, but they come in a quieter setting, and you may meet only a few cars, a cyclist or two and sometimes a cow.

For motorcyclists, Umbrail offers an excellent way of making a loop. Ride up the Stelvio from Bormio, cross over to the Umbrail, drop into the Val Müstair and then return via the Ofen Pass and Livigno, or continue on to the Engadin. Whichever way you go, the surface is generally good, though parts of the upper section can be rough after the winter, with patches of broken tarmac and loose stones. In early summer, check that the pass is open, because snow often keeps it closed until June.

Bormio, about nine kilometres from here according to the map, is the sensible place to fill up on the Italian side. In the Val Müstair, small pumps exist but cannot be counted on, so arrive with at least half a tank. Water is not a problem, because there are springs and streams all the way down.

The views from the top are less theatrical than those from the Stelvio, but they have a different charm. You see a broad sweep of bare ridges, dark in the afternoon, and there is a wonderful sense of space. Wind can be strong, and the temperature can be ten degrees lower than in the valley, so layers matter. In early autumn, when the larches start to turn yellow, the whole slope below the pass glows, and the traffic thins out. It is, for many riders, the better of the two passes.
t.espinazo del diablo@23.6,-105.8:
The Espinazo del Diablo, the Devil's Backbone, is a ridge of the Sierra Madre Occidental that the old highway between Durango and Mazatlan followed for decades along its crest, with the ground falling steeply away on both sides, and the narrow road with few barriers seemed to hang between two valleys. At about 2,400 metres, the air is cold and the pine forest thick, and on a misty morning the road disappears into cloud. Truckers called it the most frightening road in Mexico, and the name stuck.

The road has changed. In 2013, a new toll highway, the autopista 40D, opened across the sierra with a series of long tunnels and bridges, including the Baluarte Bridge, a cable-stayed span that is one of the highest in the world, standing about 390 metres above the river. The journey that once took six hours or more is now about half that, and most traffic uses the new road. The old highway remains, and riders who prefer curves to speed can still take it, though it is narrow and sometimes in poor condition.

The country is wild and beautiful. The sierra is covered with pine and oak forest, with deep canyons, waterfalls and small mountain villages, and the air smells of resin. La Ciudad, a lumber town about eighteen kilometres away, sits in the forest, and the logging trucks that rumble through are a reminder of the main industry. Farther west, as the road descends toward the Pacific, the vegetation changes to tropical, with mango trees, banana plants and warm, humid air.

Services are scarce along the high section. La Ciudad has a small supply of fuel and food, but you should not depend on it, and it is wise to fill up in Durango or El Salto before climbing, and carry a little extra if you can. The toll road has fuel stations at intervals. Fog is common, sometimes thick enough to reduce visibility to a few metres, and the road can be icy in winter, so check conditions. Trucks and buses use the old road, and they often take the middle of the bends. The best season is spring or autumn, and the best time of day is mid-morning, when the mist clears.
t.st gilgen@47.8,13.4:
St Gilgen lies at the western end of the Wolfgangsee, a long, deep lake in a cleft between steep wooded hills. It is a village of about a thousand people, but it has the polish of a place that has been welcoming visitors for centuries. The waterfront is tidy, the houses are painted in soft colours, and in summer the lake is busy with sailing boats and paddle steamers.

Mozart's mother, Anna Maria Pertl, was born in this village, and his sister Nannerl later lived here after her marriage. The family house is now a small museum, and the lake itself appears in letters and memories from the Mozart household. The composer himself did not live here, but the connection is so well loved that you will find his name on everything from chocolate to concert posters.

The riding along the lake is more of a pleasure cruise than a challenge. The B158 follows the north shore with a series of gentle curves, with the water on your side and forest on the other, and traffic can be thick, particularly on summer weekends. For a more energetic ride, the road up to the Zwölferhorn cable car and the narrow lanes in the hills behind the village give some height and a little more solitude. Early morning, before the day-trippers arrive, is the best time to see the lake still and glassy.

On the southern shore, directly across the water, lies St Wolfgang, whose pilgrimage church and the Weisses Rössl inn made the lake famous through the operetta. You can reach it by road around the lake, which takes a while, or by boat from St Gilgen, a pleasure in good weather. The ferry is the best way to see the lake from its middle.

St Gilgen is small, so fuel is limited. Salzburg and Hallein are the larger options to the west, and Bad Ischl to the east. Eat at one of the lakeside cafes, where the local fish, grilled or smoked, is good, and the strudel is better. Leave time to walk along the front, because the light on the water around early evening is very fine.
t.bad ischl@47.7,13.6:
Bad Ischl is the town where an Emperor went on holiday and accidentally changed European history. Franz Joseph spent summers here for decades, in a villa given to him and Sisi as a wedding present, and it was from here, in July 1914, that he signed the declaration of war on Serbia that began the First World War. Today the Kaiservilla is a museum with a park, filled with hunting trophies, and a visit gives you a glimpse of how a monarch spent a holiday: shooting chamois and grumbling over paperwork.

The town grew rich on two things, salt and spa water. The salt mines of the Salzkammergut gave the region its name, and in the nineteenth century physicians prescribed brine baths and mountain air to the wealthy of the empire, who responded by building villas, theatres and a famous pastry shop. Konditorei Zauner, on the main street, is still serving cakes and the little chocolate-covered Zaunerstollen to people who remember their grandparents recommending them. Composer Franz Lehár also lived here and wrote some of his operettas in the town.

The setting is a pocket of flat land at the meeting of the Traun and Ischl rivers, with forested hills pressing in on every side. Roads fan out in several directions, which makes Bad Ischl a good base for exploring the lakes, and also a good place for a break. You will find fuel, supermarkets and plenty of cafes; this is a proper small town, not a hamlet, and it copes easily with riders. Parking in the centre can be tight on summer afternoons, so use the larger car parks at the edges.

The nearby roads give a lot of choice: east and south through the Traun valley toward Bad Goisern and Hallstatt, north to Gmunden and the Traunsee, or west toward the Wolfgangsee. The surfaces are mostly good, and the corners are generous, but weekend traffic and caravans can slow things. The best days are weekday mornings in late spring and early autumn, when the beech and maple on the hillsides turn colour.

Take time for a walk by the river and a coffee, because this is a place where things have always been done at a leisurely pace.
t.hallstatt@47.6,13.6:
Hallstatt is the village everyone has seen in photographs, built on a narrow ledge between the steep wall of the Dachstein massif and the dark water of the Hallstätter See. There is hardly any flat ground. Houses climb above each other, the church tower stands on a rock above the lake, and the whole arrangement looks so improbable that you wonder how it ever worked.

It worked because of salt. People have mined salt in the mountain above the village for thousands of years, and the Iron Age culture named after the place, the Hallstatt culture, spread across much of central Europe from about 800 BC. The graves found here, filled with fine bronze and amber, tell of a trading community that was rich by the standards of its time. The salt mine is still there, one of the oldest in the world, and you can ride the funicular up to it and walk in with a helmet and a miner's overall. The village is also a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it has the crowds to prove it.

Be realistic about the visit. In high season the village is a crush of tour buses and photographers, and the narrow lanes can feel like a theme park. Motorcycles are generally parked in the car parks outside the centre, and it is a short walk down to the lake. If you come early in the morning or in the shoulder months, you will find a very different place, quiet and slightly damp, with mist lifting off the water. A small ossuary near the church holds painted skulls, a local custom that is both macabre and rather touching.

The ride in is easy and attractive: the road along the western shore of the lake is narrow with tunnels, fast stretches and cliffs on one side, and the lake on the other. From here you can head south toward Gosau and the Pass Gschütt, a lovely road over a modest saddle, or return north toward Bad Goisern and Bad Ischl.

Fuel is not in the village. Bad Goisern or Bad Ischl is the safer bet, with Gosau as another small option, so fill up before you come in.
t.krimml waterfalls@47.2,12.2:
You hear the Krimml falls before you see them. A low, constant roar rolls down the valley long before the road reaches the village, and on a warm day in early summer, when meltwater from the Hohe Tauern is at its peak, the spray hangs in the air like a fine drizzle. The Krimmler Ache drops about 380 metres in three steps, which makes this the highest waterfall in Austria and one of the highest in Europe.

The falls sit inside the Hohe Tauern National Park, at the very top end of the Pinzgau valley, and the village of Krimml is the doorway to both. A footpath climbs beside the water in a series of switchbacks and viewpoints, with the three drops arriving one after another. Allow a good hour if you only want to see the lower and middle stages, and more if you walk to the top, which is a proper uphill hike in motorcycle boots, so most riders do the first stretch and turn back. There is a modest entrance fee for the path, and the lower section is laid out to be easy for families.

The waterfall has been a tourist attraction for a very long time. In the nineteenth century, travellers from Vienna and beyond arrived to see it, and it was painted and photographed so often that the valley became part of the Romantic image of the Alps. Today, hospitals even use the air here for patients with asthma, because the fine water mist is said to ease the lungs, and the research on the subject has given the falls a second reputation.

On the road, Krimml is the start of the climb to the Gerlos Pass, and it is also the end of the long valley road from Mittersill, the Pinzgau's main town for this stretch. That road is fast and easy, with gentle bends and good views of the Salzach, which begins nearby. At the village, parking is usually found near the falls entrance, and motorcycles are welcome.

Krimml is small, and fuel is not guaranteed. Mittersill, further east along the valley, is the safer choice, and the Gerlos side has a few options in Gerlos itself. After the walk, a bowl of Gulaschsuppe or a plate of Kaiserschmarrn in one of the village inns is exactly right, since the spray cools you more than you expect.
t.gerlos pass@47.2,12.1:
The Gerlos Pass is a handsome, civilised crossing between the Zillertal in Tyrol and the Pinzgau in Salzburg province, and at 1,507 metres it is low enough to be open for most of the year, though not low enough to ignore. It is a toll road, a fact that the locals accept with a shrug, and the money pays for a surface that is smooth, wide and well marked, and for snow clearing that begins early in the winter.

The road was opened in the early 1960s and replaced an old track that was nothing like as friendly. It runs from Zell am Ziller up the Gerlos valley, passes the small ski village of Gerlos, climbs gently to the summit and then drops to Krimml in a succession of tight hairpins above the waterfall valley. The hairpins on the Salzburg side are the best part, with a steep fall away to one side and views of the Krimml falls on a good day. Take them slowly, because gravel washes down in the rain and coach traffic is common in summer.

A reservoir lies close to the summit, the Gerlos lake, dammed for hydroelectric power in the Zillertal scheme. In the morning it can be as still as glass, with the mountains reflected perfectly, and on windy afternoons it takes on a hard blue-grey texture. It is a pleasant place to pause, with a short footpath along the shore and space to park a few bikes. Anglers appear along the shore, patiently, in all weathers.

The Zillertal is a classic Tyrolean valley, with flower-decked farmhouses, brass bands and a local accent that is among the most distinctive in Austria. The Zillertal Tuxer cattle, a small, dark breed, still graze the meadows, and you will often see the farm shops selling smoked ham, hard cheese and schnapps that taste of the mountain. The Zillertal Alps rise to the south, with the glaciers of the Hintertux region standing above the tree line.

Fuel can be found in Gerlos village, though it is small, and the larger services are in Zell am Ziller and Wörgl, which is about twenty-eight kilometres away on the Inn river. Wind can be sharp on the summit, and the temperature feels very different once you are out of the trees, so keep a layer in the pannier even if the valley is warm.
t.schoppernau@47.3,10.0:
Schoppernau is the village where the Bregenzerwald starts to run out of valley. Beyond it the road climbs toward the Hochtannberg Pass, and the mountains that were polite and green in Egg and Bezau become taller and rockier. Houses are still clad in timber, fields are still steep and immaculately mown, but the sense of enclosure is stronger, and the big limestone walls of the Allgäu and Lechquellen mountains look down on the village from all sides.

The most famous son of the village is Franz Michael Felder, born here in 1839, a farmer who taught himself to read, wrote novels and essays in a time when few peasants did, and campaigned for cooperatives and rural reform. He died young, aged only thirty, and is remembered across Vorarlberg as a writer and reformer who gave the region a voice. His story is a quiet counterpoint to the glossy images of mountain tourism, and a small museum in the area keeps his memory alive.

Above the village, the Diedamskopf cable car carries walkers and mountain bikers to open slopes with views over the valley. The Bregenzerach, which runs alongside the road, is a young, clear river here, and in spring it runs fast with meltwater. The air smells of cut hay in summer and woodsmoke in autumn.

For riders, Schoppernau is a step on the way to something bigger. The road from here to Schröcken and the Hochtannberg Pass, about 1,670 metres, is a lovely, wide mountain road with bends that get progressively tighter, and then on to Warth and Lech am Arlberg, a famous ski resort. Beware of the winter: the Hochtannberg can close in heavy snow, and avalanche warnings in the spring are taken seriously. In summer the surface is generally good, but there are patches of repaired tarmac where the frost has bitten.

Schoppernau is small, with fewer than a thousand people, so do not rely on the village for fuel. Check the tank at Bezau or Egg, and if you are in doubt, remember that the nearest large town is far away and across a border. The inns here serve Alpine dairy dishes, including Käsknöpfle, little cheese dumplings, and a drink called Sauser, a young fermented fruit must, when it is in season. Leave a few minutes to listen to the cowbells. They carry well in this valley.
t.poschiavo@46.3,10.1:
Poschiavo is the Italian-speaking surprise on the far side of the Bernina. After the cold, bare grandeur of the pass, you drop through a series of hairpins and arrive in a warm, green valley where the language changes, the houses change and the food changes, even though you are still in Switzerland. The valley, the Valposchiavo, belongs to canton Graubünden, but its people speak a Lombard dialect and its old town looks like a village in Piedmont or Lombardy.

The old centre is a pleasure, a little maze of narrow streets, arcades and small squares around a handsome Catholic church with a tall bell tower. Next to it stands the Protestant church, and the two faiths have lived side by side for centuries, a rare example of peaceful coexistence in a region that had its religious wars. The most striking part of the town is the Spaniola quarter, a group of palazzi built in the nineteenth century by local people who had made their fortunes as confectioners and cafe owners in Spain and returned home to build grand houses with elaborate facades.

The Bernina railway runs through the valley, and the town is a stop on the Bernina Express, which crosses the Alps between Chur and Tirano. A short distance down the valley, at Brusio, the railway makes a complete circle on a stone viaduct to lose height, an engineering feat that is a favourite of photographers. The road keeps close company with the railway, and the ride from Poschiavo to Tirano and the Italian border is delightful, with terraced slopes and warm light.

The ride from the pass to Poschiavo is spectacular, with a descent of hairpins that drop over a thousand metres, and then a gentler run through the valley. The surface is excellent in general, but there are patches of rough tarmac, and the road is busy with buses and cars in summer. The temperature rises as you descend, and it is a good place to take off a layer. In autumn, the chestnut woods turn bronze and the smell of woodsmoke hangs over the villages.

The valley has also gained a reputation for organic farming and local food, and the cafes serve excellent coffee and homemade pastries. Try pizzoccheri, the buckwheat pasta cooked with cabbage, potato and melted cheese, which is the dish of the region, and a glass of local wine from the Valtellina across the border. Poschiavo has fuel stations and shops, and Tirano, about fifteen kilometres to the south in Italy, is the larger town if you need more. Bring your passport if you plan to cross the border.
t.swiss national park@46.7,10.2:
Nowhere else in Switzerland do the rules feel so firm. The Swiss National Park, founded in 1914 and the oldest in the Alps, is a place where the point is to leave things alone: no camping, no picking flowers, no dogs, no leaving the marked paths. For riders, that means a single public road runs through it, the Ofen Pass road between Zernez and the Val Müstair, and the whole experience happens at a steady speed behind a windscreen, with a few official car parks for the walkers who want more.

What you see from the saddle is still remarkable. The forest here is dominated by mountain pine and larch, dark, wiry and twisted at the edges, and it opens onto scree slopes where red deer graze at dusk and chamois pick their way along the rock. Ibex stand on the steeper ridges, marmots whistle from the grass, and golden eagles hang in the thermals. Bearded vultures, reintroduced to the Alps in this region, sometimes pass overhead with a wingspan that makes you check your mirrors twice. Early morning and evening are the best hours for animals.

The park's history is a story of Swiss caution. Local people had logged and hunted this land hard, and a small group of naturalists, backed by early conservationists, persuaded the authorities to lock a patch of valley away from human use. More than a century later it has become one of the most studied pieces of nature in Europe, a laboratory for watching what a landscape does when no one is managing it. The visitor centre in Zernez explains the story, and is worth a stop on a bad weather day.

Practical matters are straightforward. Zernez, with its sleepy centre and petrol station at the junction of the Engadin and the Ofen road, is the sensible place to tank up before you head in. Ride carefully: wildlife on the tarmac is routine, and the bends tighten as you climb. The road is generally open all year, but snow can close it briefly in winter, and the cold is real.

The air up here is clean, sharp and smelling of resin on warm days. If you want a single place to understand why the Alps are more than scenery, this is it, and you do not even need to step off your bike.
t.ofen pass@46.6,10.3:
The Ofen Pass, 2,149 metres at its top, is the lesser-known doorway between the Lower Engadin and the Val Müstair, and it deserves more attention than it gets. The road runs from Zernez through the Swiss National Park, climbing through a dark stand of mountain pine to a high, rocky plateau, and then dropping on the other side toward the quiet Val Müstair, the Swiss corner that feels as much Italian and Tyrolean as it does Swiss.

On the ride, you pass from forest into bare limestone and dolomite, the pale rock giving the mountains a lighter, almost bleached look compared with the dark granite of much of the Alps. The curves are smooth and sustained, with enough room to enjoy a rhythm but a few tight sections that ask for attention, especially in the descent. Traffic is modest, partly because most people prefer the big names, and partly because the road has a reputation for strict speed enforcement within the park. It is wise to keep to the limit.

At the foot of the Müstair side, the road meets the junction for the Umbrail Pass, which climbs to the Stelvio road, the great Italian classic. You can continue that way if you want to make a bigger day of it, but the Val Müstair deserves a stop on its own. In the village of Müstair, the Benedictine convent of St John, a UNESCO World Heritage site, holds some of the best-preserved Carolingian wall paintings in Europe, traditionally linked to the time of Charlemagne. The nuns still live there, and the museum is a quiet, intelligent place.

The valley also has a flavour of its own: Romansh is spoken here, the farmhouses are broad and painted, and the rye bread and barley soup of the Grisons are everywhere. Nearby Livigno, across the Italian border, is a duty-free town and a popular fuel stop for riders, with cheaper petrol and large queues in summer. On the Swiss side, Zernez and Santa Maria in Val Müstair are the places you can count on.

Do not expect pumps at the top. Snow can close the road on rare occasions in winter, and summer storms roll up the valley in the afternoon, so aim for a morning crossing, when the air is crisp and the animals are still out.
t.henningsvaer@68.2,14.2:
Henningsvær is a fishing village scattered over a few small islands off the south coast of Austvågøya in the Lofoten Islands, and it is often called the Venice of Lofoten, though a better comparison would be a sheltered harbour with bridges and a big mountain looking over its shoulder. The houses stand on stilts at the water's edge, the old fish factories and warehouses line the quay, and the jagged peak of Vågakallen rises behind. In winter the racks outside are hung with cod to dry in the cold air, as they have been for a thousand years, and the smell of that trade is part of the place. The cod fishery here begins in January and runs until April, and it is the reason Lofoten was settled at all.

The village has a few unusual things to show. One is the football pitch, laid on a rocky outcrop with the sea on all sides, a sight that appears in photographs from above all over the world. Another is the climbing: the steep rock walls around the village are well known among climbers, and the harbour area holds galleries, small cafés and the odd bookshop. In summer it is busy, with tourists strolling the lanes and cafés spilling onto the water.

The road to get there is a side road, Fv816, which leaves the main E10 and runs for about fifteen kilometres across low bridges and between small hills, with the sea on either side. It is a pleasant, easy ride, with mild bends and good views, though the wind can be strong. Traffic is heavy in summer, with campervans and coaches, and the village has narrow lanes with little parking. Come early or late in the day, and keep to the speed limit, which is low and watched. Winter brings snow and ice, and the days are very short.

Fuel is not available in the village. Svolvær, the main town on the island, has pumps and supermarkets, and Kabelvåg, on the way, also has some services. Eat fish: fresh cod, stockfish stew, or fish soup. Rooms book out in summer, so book ahead, and carry a windproof layer at any season, because the weather turns quickly in the islands.
t.vrsic pass@46.4,13.7:
Vršič is the highest road pass in Slovenia, at 1,611 metres, and it comes with fifty hairpins, each numbered with a little sign. Twenty-four of them are on the north side, from Kranjska Gora, and twenty-six on the south side toward Trenta, and some are still cobbled, which is memorable on a motorcycle in the wet. The road crosses the Julian Alps through a landscape of grey limestone towers, scree slopes and larch woods, and you feel the weight of the peaks pressing in from every side.

The road has a sombre history. It was built during the First World War, around 1915 and 1916, by Russian prisoners of war who were forced to work on it for the Austro-Hungarian army, which needed supply routes to the Isonzo front. In March 1916 an avalanche killed many of the prisoners, and the Russian Chapel, a small wooden church on the northern side, stands where they were buried. It is a beautiful, quiet place, and worth a stop for a moment of reflection. The road still carries the name Russian Road in some accounts.

The riding is intense rather than fast. The hairpins are tight and steep, the surface varies from smooth tarmac to rough patches and cobbles, and drainage grates and loose gravel add to the interest. Traffic can be heavy in summer, with campervans, cyclists and sightseers, and the narrow bends make overtaking difficult. Weekday mornings are best. The pass is closed in winter, usually from late autumn until spring, because of snow and avalanche risk, so check before you go. Weather in the mountains turns quickly, and a warm morning can end in cold rain.

At the top there is a small car park, a mountain hut and a few stalls, with views of the surrounding peaks such as Prisojnik and Mojstrovka. Hot soup and strudel are the correct reward. The high mountain air smells of pine and rock, and the cool breeze is welcome.

Kranjska Gora, about four kilometres below on the north side, has petrol stations, and Bovec in the Soča valley serves the south. Fill the tank at either before you climb, and take the descent slowly; the brakes will thank you.
t.trenta@46.4,13.8:
Trenta is the upper valley of the Soča, the river that runs emerald green out of the Julian Alps, and arriving here from the Vršič hairpins feels like being let out into a quiet room. The mountains rise on both sides, the road runs gently beside the water, and the villages are small clusters of stone and wooden houses scattered among meadows and larch woods. It lies inside Triglav National Park, Slovenia's only national park, and the whole area has the air of a protected landscape: clean, calm and generously green.

The valley's most famous visitor was Julius Kugy, a mountaineer and botanist from Trieste, who spent much of his life exploring these peaks in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and wrote lovingly about them. A monument to him stands in the village. There is also a small botanical garden devoted to Alpine flora, and a visitor centre explains the geology and wildlife of the park. Chamois and ibex live on the high slopes, and the river holds marble trout, a native fish with a distinctive pattern.

The Soča itself is the star. It rises from a spring high in the mountains and flows through narrow gorges and wide gravel beds, and its colour, a clear turquoise-emerald, comes from limestone dust and the cold water. In places you can stop beside a bridge and look down into pools so clear that you can count the stones. The air is cool and fresh, with a smell of pine and river stones, and in autumn the larches turn gold.

The road through the valley is a delight, a gentle descent after the intense hairpins of the pass, with smooth surfaces and easy bends, though it narrows in places and caravans can slow you. In wet weather the valley collects cloud and rain, and in summer there is heavy traffic on weekends. Early morning gives the best light and the most solitude.

Facilities are limited. A few guesthouses and small cafés serve trout, polenta and hearty soups, but shops are few. Fuel is in Kranjska Gora, on the far side of the pass, or in Bovec down the valley, and it is wise to fill up there before you cross. Bring cash, as small places may not take cards, and give yourself time to linger.
t.red canyon overlook@40.9,-109.4:
The Red Canyon Overlook is where the red rock of the Uinta country opens beneath your boots. A short walk from the parking area leads to a rim hundreds of metres above the Flaming Gorge Reservoir, and below you the walls of Red Canyon fall in layers of rust, orange and cream to the green water, with ponderosa pine and juniper clinging to the ledges. It is a classic western view, dry, bright and big, and it is quiet even on a busy summer day.

The name Flaming Gorge comes from John Wesley Powell, the one-armed Civil War veteran who led an expedition down the Green River in 1869 and described the glowing red cliffs at the head of the canyon. The river was later dammed, and the lake that rose behind the dam stretches for dozens of miles, drowning some of the canyon and turning the area into a recreation spot for anglers and boaters. The rim of Red Canyon, however, still gives a sense of the original scale, and the rocks are part of the same ancient sedimentary layers that make up much of the Colorado Plateau.

The surrounding country is part of the Ashley National Forest, and wildlife is plentiful. Mule deer and pronghorn graze in the meadows, and bighorn sheep live on the canyon walls. Ospreys and bald eagles fish in the lake, and in the evening, you can hear coyotes. The air is dry and smells of sage and pine, and the night sky here is spectacular, since light pollution is minimal.

The road through the area, a scenic byway, passes through open sagebrush country and pine forest, with smooth surfaces, long bends and gentle gradients, and it is a relaxed ride. Traffic is light for most of the year, though weekends in summer bring more campers and boat trailers. Weather can change quickly, with afternoon thunderstorms and strong winds, and snow arrives early in the high country, closing some roads in winter. The best months are late spring to early autumn, with September especially pleasant.

Services are scarce. The tiny town of Manila, about twenty-seven kilometres away, has a few basics, but larger supplies and reliable fuel are in Vernal to the south or Rock Springs to the north, so check your tank before you come. Bring water, sunscreen and a windproof layer, since the rim is exposed.

Walk to the edge of the overlook, hold the railing, and let your eyes follow the cliff down to the water. It is further than it looks.
t.flaming gorge dam@40.9,-109.4:
Flaming Gorge Dam is a curve of concrete wedged into a red canyon on the Green River, and on a hot day the water that spills from its base is startlingly cold and green. The dam was built in the early 1960s as part of a plan to store water in the upper Colorado River basin, and it rises roughly five hundred feet from bedrock, a smooth arch that looks small against the surrounding cliffs. It created the long reservoir that now bears the gorge's name, and it supplies hydroelectric power as well as water for farms and cities far downstream.

A visitor centre by the dam explains how it was built, and in season guided tours take you inside, down into the workings of the dam. A short walk lets you look from above at the river below, which is now a famous trout fishery, with big rainbow and brown trout that thrive in the cold, clear water released from the lake. The stretch of river below the dam draws anglers from all over the country, and drift boats float through the canyon, past cliffs the colour of rust.

The ride here is lovely. The Flaming Gorge-Uintas byway runs through pine forest and sagebrush, with long, easy bends and views across the reservoir, and drops into the canyon to the dam with a series of gentle switchbacks. The road surface is mostly good, but watch for gravel in corners, wildlife on the road at dawn and dusk, and the sudden gusts that sweep across the lake. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms, and snow can close higher sections from late autumn. Early morning gives the best light on the red rock.

Do not expect many services. A small community, Dutch John, lies near the dam, and Manila, about twenty-seven kilometres away, has a few shops, but larger supplies are in Vernal or Rock Springs, so arrive with a decent tank. Bring water and snacks, and a jacket, because the canyon can be cool even in summer.

The area is a good example of how much the American West has been reshaped by water engineering. The dam is impressive, but the quiet moments, watching the river run clear below, are better.

Take your time at the viewing area, and look up at the cliffs from the base. They are taller than the dam, and older than anything built on them.
t.many parks curve@40.4,-105.6:
Many Parks Curve is a hairpin on Trail Ridge Road with a viewpoint so good that the engineers who built the road clearly wanted you to stop. From the overlook, at roughly 9,600 feet, the land opens up below like a book: the broad, flat valleys, which early settlers called parks, lie in a row with forested ridges between them, and beyond them the Continental Divide rises in a long line of snow-streaked summits. The word park in this part of Colorado means a high, open grassy basin, and from here you see several at once.

The geology is the glacial kind. During the ice ages, glaciers carved the valleys below, leaving long ridges called moraines, which show as dark, forested lines running through the meadows. Moraine Park, directly below the viewpoint, is a classic example. In autumn, elk gather in the meadows during the rut, and the sound of bull elk bugling carries up the slope, a thrilling sound on a still evening. The hillsides here are covered in lodgepole pine and aspen, and in late September the aspens turn gold in patches.

The road itself is a masterpiece of mountain engineering, the high point of Rocky Mountain National Park's scenic drive, and it was completed in the early 1930s. It climbs from Estes Park through a series of bends and switchbacks, with generous guard walls and constant views, and gradients that are steady rather than steep. The surface is generally smooth, but the road is busy in summer, with cars, tour buses and cyclists, and the park may require timed-entry reservations in peak season, so check the rules before you go. Weather can change fast, with thunderstorms in the afternoon, and snow can fall in any month at the higher elevations.

Trail Ridge Road is closed by snow for much of the year, typically from mid-October until late May, so plan accordingly. There are no services at the curve itself, only a parking area and a viewpoint, so fill the tank in Estes Park, about nine kilometres away, where you will find petrol stations, supermarkets and restaurants. Carry layers and water, since the altitude and wind can make it feel cold even on a sunny day.

Look for the long ridges in the meadows below, and the thin line of the river winding between them. It is a view that rewards a long look.
t.rock cut@40.4,-105.7:
Rock Cut is a place where the road runs into a cliff and the cliff loses. The engineers blasted a deep trench through a ridge of ancient Precambrian rock here, high on Trail Ridge Road at more than twelve thousand feet, and the trench left steep walls on either side, with the highway squeezed between them. You stop at the car park nearby, climb a short paved path and step out onto the alpine tundra, with the world dropping away on all sides and the wind pulling at your jacket.

The tundra is the real subject. Above the treeline, the land is covered with a thin carpet of tiny plants that grow close to the ground to survive the cold, the wind and the short growing season, and in July they burst into flower: moss campion, alpine forget-me-not, sky pilot and paintbrush. The plants are fragile, and a footprint can damage them for years, so stay on the paths. Yellow-bellied marmots whistle from the rocks, pikas squeak in the boulder fields, and herds of elk may graze the slopes in summer. Overhead, the sky is a deep, hard blue, and clouds can drop in within minutes.

The road is the highest continuous paved road in the United States, and Rock Cut is one of the places where you feel it. The ride up from Estes Park is a smooth, steady climb, with long bends, views over valleys and peaks, and increasingly bare, rocky terrain as you leave the forest. At the top, the wind can be cold and strong, and summer thunderstorms can bring lightning, hail and sudden temperature drops, so start early and keep an eye on the sky. The air is thin, and the altitude can make you light-headed or breathless, so go slowly and drink water.

Trail Ridge Road is closed by snow for much of the year, usually from mid-October to late May, and snow can fall in any month. There are toilets at Rock Cut but no other services, and you should fill up in Estes Park, about fourteen kilometres below, where there are petrol stations and shops. Bring warm gloves and a windproof jacket, even in July.

Walk the short path onto the tundra, stand still and listen to the wind. It is a quiet and very big place.
t.alpine visitor center@40.4,-105.8:
The Alpine Visitor Center sits at about 11,800 feet, near the high point of Trail Ridge Road, and it feels like a base camp on the roof of the park. The building is a stone-and-timber lodge with a cafeteria, a gift shop and a view out across the alpine tundra to the peaks of the Never Summer Mountains and the Continental Divide. In clear weather the air is brilliantly sharp, and in poor weather the building is a welcome shelter, with the windows rattling in the wind and the smell of hot coffee and soup inside.

The setting is Fall River Pass, where the road crosses a high, bare saddle between valleys, and the landscape is pure tundra, treeless, windswept and crossed by snowfields that linger into summer. A steep staircase of stone steps rises from the building to a trail leading up the ridge, a climb of a few hundred feet that leaves most people gasping at this altitude, and the view from the top is worth the effort. Elk, marmots and pikas live nearby, and in summer bighorn sheep sometimes graze near the road. The wildflowers in July are a carpet of tiny colours, and the light, with so little atmosphere above you, is clear and strong.

The ride up here, on the highest continuous paved road in the country, is memorable. The highway climbs from Estes Park through forest and then out onto the tundra, with long bends and wide views, and on the way down to Grand Lake on the west side the road descends into a very different landscape of forest and meadows. The surface is mostly good, but the altitude and weather matter: thunderstorms build rapidly in the afternoon, snow can fall in July, and the wind at the top is constant. Altitude sickness is possible if you are not acclimatised, so take it slowly and carry water.

The visitor center is open only in the summer season, generally from around Memorial Day to mid-October, depending on snow, because the road itself closes in winter. Do not expect fuel on the pass. Estes Park, about twenty-one kilometres to the east, is the place to fill the tank, with supermarkets, restaurants and cafés, and Grand Lake on the west side has more modest services. Dress in layers, bring gloves and a windproof jacket, and check road conditions before you set out.

Grab a hot drink, sit by the window and watch the clouds cross the tundra. It is a fine place to rest.
t.milner pass@40.4,-105.8:
Milner Pass is where Trail Ridge Road crosses the Continental Divide, at 3,279 metres, and it does it so quietly that you could miss it. There is a modest sign, a small parking area, and a little tarn called Poudre Lake lying right beside the road. Rain that lands on the east side of the sign heads for the Cache la Poudre and eventually the Platte; rain on the west side ends up in the Colorado. Standing there in a riding jacket, still ringing from the climb, it feels like a very large idea for a very small place.

The riding on either side is the reason you came. From the east you have already done the big work above the treeline, with the tundra running off in every direction and the road cut into the slope with a low stone wall as the only comfort. Milner sits just below that, back among spruce and fir, so the character changes: tighter, shadier, and often a few degrees colder than you expected. Heading west the road drops toward the Kawuneeche Valley, where the infant Colorado River winds through meadows that are a good bet for elk at dawn and dusk. Look across to the Never Summer Mountains and you can see a long pale scar along the slope. That is the Grand Ditch, dug by hand and horse in the late nineteenth century to carry headwater snowmelt over the divide to farmland on the plains.

Plan around the season. Trail Ridge Road closes with the first serious snow, usually somewhere in October, and does not reopen until late May, after crews have carved a canyon through drifts that can be several metres deep. In between, the pattern is reliable: clear mornings, building cloud by noon, thunder in the afternoon. Be over the top before lunch if you can. It is cold up here even in July, so keep a warmer layer in the bag, and remember the park charges an entrance fee and can limit entry at busy times.

Nothing here sells petrol. Estes Park, about 25 kilometres east, is the sensible place to fill the tank before you climb, and on the west side Grand Lake and Granby are your options on the way down. Fill up before the park, because the pass itself is all scenery and a few picnic tables, and the pit toilets at the pull-out are about as luxurious as it gets.
t.nederland@40.0,-105.5:
Nederland is a mountain town that has never entirely decided whether it is a ski-resort suburb, a hippie holdout or a mining camp that kept going. The answer is probably all three. It sits at about 2,500 metres where Boulder Canyon spills into the high country, at the edge of the Barker Reservoir, with the Indian Peaks on the horizon. Once you ride in from the canyon, the first thing you register is how cold the air has become, even in summer.

The name is old and slightly odd. In the 1870s a Dutch company bought a local mine, and the settlement became Nederland, Dutch for the Netherlands. The silver of nearby Caribou had drawn miners and mill workers here, and Nederland lived as a processing and supply place for them. Today the town is better known for its eccentricities than for its silver. A few days every March brings Frozen Dead Guy Days, a festival built around a man preserved in dry ice in a shed up the valley, and the town also has an old carousel hand-carved and restored by locals. I mention these because a rider doing laps on the Peak to Peak Highway should know the place has a sense of humour.

The riding in and out is the draw. Coming up from Boulder, Highway 119 climbs Boulder Canyon in a long run of tight, rocky bends alongside the creek, which suits a middleweight bike and a rider who has not eaten recently. Past town, the Peak to Peak Scenic Byway runs north and south along the Front Range at over 2,500 metres, with a view of snow on the high peaks, long open curves, and not much else. Weekends bring cyclists, tourists and heavy bikes in numbers, so mid-week is better. Winter can close sections, and ice lingers in canyon shadows into spring.

Nederland has a handful of coffee shops, bakeries and a few gas stations, so it is a natural place to refuel, eat and warm up before turning on to the higher parts of the byway. Boulder, about twenty kilometres down the canyon, has everything else. Altitude cuts engine power slightly, and the weather can turn in a few minutes, so pack a layer.
t.fuscher torl@47.1,12.8:
Fuscher Törl is where the Grossglockner High Alpine Road stops being a pleasant drive and becomes a stage set. At 2,428 metres, this high saddle gives the first big view over the whole Glockner range, with the Fuscher valley falling away behind you and ranks of rock and snow ahead, and the tiny shapes of cars and cyclists crawling up the hairpins far below. It is a place where most riders cut the engine, take off their gloves, and simply look.

The road was a major engineering feat. It was built in the early 1930s, with thousands of workers employed during the Depression, and opened in 1935, at a time when mass motoring was only beginning. It is still run as a toll road, and the fee is part of the day's cost, so have a card or cash ready at the gate. A short, steep side road starts at the Törl and climbs to the Edelweissspitze, at about 2,570 metres, where a viewpoint offers a still wider panorama, with more than thirty peaks over three thousand metres in sight on a clear day.

The riding on the northern ramp is superb. From the toll gate at Ferleiten the road climbs in broad, well-surfaced hairpins, with a gradient that never tires, and the vegetation falls away from forest to meadow to bare rock. Traffic can be heavy in summer, especially at weekends and in the middle of the day, so start early. Weather matters greatly: the road is open only from about May to early November, and fog, cold rain, or snow can arrive in any month. A warm layer and waterproof gloves are not optional.

A restaurant and a small museum beside the road offer coffee, soup, and the sort of cake that Austrians treat as a serious matter. Marmots live in the rocks nearby, and are used to people, so you will probably see one. Keep your speed down near the cafes, where pedestrians cross without warning.
t.hochtor@47.1,12.8:
Hochtor is the summit of the road. At 2,504 metres, a short tunnel of three hundred metres or so cuts under the ridge, and it marks the border between the provinces of Salzburg and Carinthia and the highest point on the Grossglockner High Alpine Road. On the northern side lies the long ascent from the Fuscher valley; on the southern, a descent past the Gamsgrube and toward the Pasterze glacier, with Austria's highest peak, the Grossglockner at 3,798 metres, rising to the west.

Long before the road, there was a route. The Romans used the Hochtor as a crossing, and archaeologists have found a bronze statuette of Hercules and other offerings near the pass, evidence that travellers have thanked the gods for safe passage here for two thousand years. Medieval traders, pilgrims, and smugglers followed the same line, carrying salt and wine, and the little chapel at Heiligenblut, below on the south side, was built by people who had to cross the mountains on foot. Its tall Gothic spire, framed by the Glockner, is one of the most photographed views in Austria.

The south ramp is a delight. After the tunnel, the road drops in a long series of curves with fast, open views, and the surface is excellent. The hairpins are more spread out than on the north side, and the road swings around cirques and past waterfalls, with the glacier visible below. Take care on the descent, because brakes work hard, and in summer afternoons, thunderstorms can strike with little warning. Snow can lie on the ground in July, and the road may close for weather at any time.

Fuel is not available on the high road itself, and Heiligenblut, about five kilometres from the pass, is the first place on the south side with services. Zell am See, on the north, is the bigger town, and Rauris is a smaller valley town to the east. A toll is charged for the road, with a lower rate if you go early in the day or late. The restaurants and refuges at the top and near the glacier serve hot food, and a coffee with a view of the ice is a fine way to recover your composure.
t.lake iseo pause@45.7,10.0:
Lake Iseo is the quiet one among the big Lombard lakes, and the western shore, where this pause sits, shows why. The road runs close to the water between cliffs and small villages, with Monte Isola, Europe's largest lake island, rising green in the middle of the lake. Fishing boats and ferries cross to its villages, and in summer the sound of engines drifts over the water. The surroundings are less polished than Lake Como, with working harbours and unfussy cafés, and many riders find that a relief.

The lake has had its moments of fame. In 2016 the artist Christo laid a walkway of floating yellow pontoons across the water from the shore to the island, and hundreds of thousands of people walked on the lake in a couple of weeks. Today the pontoons are gone, but the memory remains, and locals still talk about it. South of the lake is Franciacorta, a wine area known for its sparkling wines made in the traditional method, with neat vineyards and cellars that welcome visitors.

The riding on the western shore is dramatic but demanding. The road is narrow and winding, with many tunnels cut through the rock, and the surface can be rough at the edges. Lorries and buses use it, so keep to your side and take care in the dark tunnels, where sunglasses should come off before you enter. In summer the traffic grows slow, and the best time is early morning or late evening, when the road is calmer and the light on the water is soft. In winter, the shaded sections can be damp and cold.

The villages along this stretch, such as Tavernola Bergamasca and Predore, have small harbours with benches and cafés where you can stop for a drink or a swim from the stony shore. The water is clean, and in summer it is warm enough for a quick dip. Local menus often feature lake fish such as sardines dried or grilled, along with polenta and cheeses from the valleys.

Fuel is available in Iseo, about five kilometres away, a town of five thousand people at the southern end of the lake, and in Sarnico at the other end. The smaller villages have limited services. Parking for bikes is easy at the harbours, though it can fill up on summer weekends.

The wind on the lake, called the Ora in the afternoon, can freshen the air and ruffle the surface, and it is a pleasant counterpoint to the heat.
t.trento food@46.1,11.1:
Trento is the real beginning of the Dolomites, even though the famous peaks are still a good way north. The city lies in the Adige valley, ringed by steep mountains that rise abruptly from the valley floor, and the light that falls on its walls is distinctly alpine, while the cooking and the architecture have a southern ease. It is a university city with about eighty thousand people, and the cafés on its piazzas are full of students and cyclists.

The city is best known for the Council of Trent, held between 1545 and 1563 in response to the Reformation and one of the most important church councils in history. Its decisions shaped Catholic practice for centuries, and the cathedral and the nearby churches still bear its mark. In the centre, the Piazza Duomo has a fountain of Neptune and frescoed houses, and the Castello del Buonconsiglio, once the residence of the prince-bishops, stands at the edge of the old town with its towers and painted halls. The modern MUSE science museum, designed by Renzo Piano, adds a contemporary note beside the river.

As a food stop, Trento rewards a little attention. The cuisine of the Trentino is a meeting of Italian and Austrian traditions. Canederli, bread dumplings often served in broth or with melted butter, appear on many menus, along with polenta, speck and cheeses from mountain dairies. Apple strudel is a regional pride, and the local wines include Teroldego, a deep red from the nearby Rotaliana plain, and sparkling Trentodoc, made in the traditional method on the slopes above the city.

For a rider, the city is an urban pause between road sections, with the Adige valley road carrying fast traffic and the mountain passes beginning to the east and west. Fuel is plentiful, with stations on the approach roads and ring road, and there is parking for motorcycles in several areas near the centre. Zones of limited traffic apply in the old town, so leave the bike outside and walk in.

The weather is usually warm and bright in summer, with mountains standing sharply on both sides, and in autumn, fog can lie along the river in the morning. Evening is lively, with aperitivo hour spilling onto the squares, and a spritz or a glass of Trentodoc is a good way to mark the end of a long day.
t.peak to peak highway@40.0,-105.5:
The Peak to Peak Highway runs along the eastern front of the Rockies, linking Black Hawk in the south to Estes Park in the north, and it follows the old route between mining camps and mountain towns. It is a scenic byway for good reason. The road stays between about 2,400 and 2,800 metres, running through pine and aspen forest with the peaks of the Continental Divide standing white on the western horizon, and every few kilometres a gap in the trees gives you a view of Longs Peak, the Indian Peaks or a glittering lake.

Along the way, you pass small mountain communities that grew from the gold and silver rushes of the 1860s. Nederland, near the middle, is a quirky town with an arts and music scene and an annual festival devoted to a frozen corpse, called Frozen Dead Guy Days, which is exactly as strange as it sounds. Farther along, the villages of Ward and Allenspark keep a rustic, mining-camp feel, with log buildings and cafés that serve hearty meals to riders and hikers.

The riding is outstanding. The curves are long and flowing, the surface is mostly smooth, and the gradients are gentle, so it is a joy for a relaxed day. Aspens turn gold in late September, and the road is at its busiest then, when leaf-peepers and bikers share the lanes, but even in summer it is a joy. Weather changes quickly at altitude. Thunderstorms build in the afternoon, often with hail, and temperatures can drop sharply, so bring layers and a rain suit. Wildlife is common, including elk, mule deer and the occasional black bear, and they sometimes cross the road at dawn and dusk.

Boulder, about twenty-one kilometres from the nearest point, is the large town with the services and the university, and it is also a lively place for food and coffee. Nederland has a small supply of fuel and a few cafés, but prices are higher and hours can be short. It is better to fill up in Boulder or at another larger town before you start.

The Boulder Canyon road, which connects the plains to Nederland, is a good way to reach the highway, and it follows a creek between granite walls with tight bends and a few tunnels. Watch for cyclists, who use the canyon road in large numbers, and for rockfall after storms. Take your time and enjoy the climb.
t.trail ridge road@40.4,-105.7:
Trail Ridge Road is the highest continuous paved highway in the United States, rising to 3,713 metres in Rocky Mountain National Park, and for a few kilometres it runs above the treeline across open alpine tundra. The road was completed in the early 1930s, and it was designed to give visitors the experience of walking in the high country without the walking. Today it carries traffic from Estes Park on the east side to Grand Lake on the west, and it is open only for part of the year. Snow closes it from mid-October, usually until late May, and early or late storms can shut it for days.

The scenery changes as you rise. Below, you ride through lodgepole pine and subalpine fir, then spruce thinning into twisted trees, and finally the tundra itself, a world of low plants, lichen-covered rocks and wide sky. The tundra is fragile, and tiny flowers bloom in the short summer. Elk graze in the meadows at lower levels, and marmots and pikas whistle among the rocks. At the Alpine Visitor Center, you can stand beside snowfields in July and look across mountain ranges that fade into blue.

Riding here needs respect for altitude and weather. The air is thin enough that engines lose power and riders may feel light-headed, so go slowly and drink water. Temperatures at the top can be near freezing even in summer, and wind is fierce, so a warm jacket, gloves and a windproof layer are essential. Thunderstorms build over the high peaks by early afternoon, and lightning is a real hazard on the open ridge, so plan to cross early in the day. The road has steep drops on one side and tight hairpins, but the surface is excellent and the speed limit is modest. Entry to the national park requires a fee or a pass.

Estes Park, about nineteen kilometres from the entrance, is the nearest town with fuel, food and lodging, and Granby on the western side is another. The visitor centre has a café and shop, but hours are limited.

An older gravel road, Fall River Road, climbs the mountain on a one-way route, and it is a worthwhile adventure for those with the right bike and a spare afternoon. Trail Ridge, though, is the grand tour, and on a clear morning there is hardly a better road in North America.
t.estes park food@40.4,-105.5:
Estes Park sits in a high mountain valley at about 2,300 metres, at the gateway to Rocky Mountain National Park, and it has been a holiday town for well over a century. The main street runs beside the Big Thompson River, lined with shops, ice cream parlours and restaurants, and the mountains rise on every side, with the great bulk of Longs Peak to the south. In autumn, herds of elk wander through the town during the rut, grazing on lawns and golf courses, and the males bugle in the evenings, a sound you do not forget.

The landmark above the town is the Stanley Hotel, a white colonial-style building opened in 1909 by F. O. Stanley, an inventor who made his fortune with the Stanley Steamer motor car. The hotel inspired Stephen King's novel The Shining after King stayed there in 1974, and it embraces its reputation with ghost tours. You can wander the grounds and the lobby even if you do not stay, and the view of the mountains from the porch is lovely.

The town also carries a darker memory. In July 1976, a flash flood tore through the Big Thompson Canyon, which carries the road from the plains to Estes Park, killing well over a hundred people. The canyon road is still one of the main ways in, a winding route beside the river through steep walls, and a memorial stands along it. Take it gently, watch for rockfall and keep an eye on the sky, because storms still gather above the canyon.

As a food stop, Estes Park gives plenty of choice. Many places serve burgers, steaks and local trout, along with breakfasts of pancakes and green chile, and coffee shops and bakeries are scattered along the main street. In summer the town is crowded, with tourists filling the pavements and traffic crawling, so patience helps. Parking for motorcycles is usually available in side streets and public lots.

Fuel is plentiful, and the town has about six thousand people, so repairs and supplies are easy. Lyons and Boulder lie to the east and are the other places to fill up on the way up from Denver. Bring layers, because even in summer evenings are cool at this altitude.

Plan to arrive early or late to avoid the worst of the traffic, and keep your eyes open for elk. They are large and unpredictable, and they have the right of way.
t.trieste@45.7,13.8:
Trieste is at the end of Italy, where the Adriatic ends and the Karst plateau begins, and it has a faintly melancholy beauty that comes from having once been something bigger. Under the Habsburgs it was the empire's main seaport, and the grand Piazza Unità d'Italia, open to the sea on one side, is the largest sea-facing square in Europe. The city had writers, too: James Joyce taught English here, Italo Svevo wrote about its middle class, and Rilke wrote part of the Duino Elegies at the nearby castle. Trieste is also a coffee capital, with Illy based here, and its cafes have their own vocabulary for the different ways of serving it.

The wind has a name, the bora, a cold, violent gust from the north-east that can top a hundred and fifty kilometres an hour, and in the old town ropes are strung along the streets to help pedestrians. For a motorbike, the bora is a serious hazard, particularly on the coast road and the viaducts on the Karst, so check the forecast. On calm days, the light on the gulf is sweet, and the white castle of Miramar stands on a rock above the water.

Above the city, the Karst plateau is a different country, with stone walls, sumac that turns scarlet in autumn, and small villages. The old tram that climbs to Villa Opicina, a rack-and-adhesion line, is a curiosity. In the villages, farmers occasionally hang a leafy branch, the frasca, to announce that they are selling their own wine and ham, a tradition known as osmiza. The road continues into Slovenia, to Ig, near Ljubljana, where the long day ends at a prehistoric pile-dwelling site in the marshes, part of a UNESCO listing. Note that Slovenia requires a vignette for motorways, which you can buy online or at the border.

Fuel is easy in Trieste and on the approach roads, and prices may be lower across the border. Eat a plate of jota, a bean and sauerkraut soup, and seafood from the gulf, with a glass of Terrano or Vitovska. Carry your passport, and leave the bike in a secure place in the city.
t.venice@45.4,12.3:
You cannot ride a motorbike in Venice, and that is the best thing about it. The city is built on over a hundred small islands in a shallow lagoon, linked by about four hundred bridges, and there are no roads, only canals and narrow lanes. Cars and bikes stop at Piazzale Roma or at the parking islands, and everything else moves on foot or by water. So the ride begins on the mainland, at Mestre or Tronchetto, with the bike left in a guarded garage and a vaporetto to carry you in.

The old republic grew rich on trade with the East, and its palaces along the Grand Canal, the Basilica of San Marco with its golden mosaics and the Doge's Palace still show it. The lagoon is a delicate world of mudflats and salt marsh, with herons and flamingos in winter, and it is under pressure from tides: acqua alta, the high water, floods the lower parts of the city on autumn and winter days, and a system of sea barriers has been built to hold it back.

The long day's ride heads north through Treviso to the Prosecco hills between Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, which were added to the UNESCO list in 2019. The ridges here are steep and narrow, with vines planted on terraces that must be worked by hand, and the Strada del Prosecco winds along them, with a series of tight bends, stone farmhouses and small wineries. The surface is mostly good, with some steep sections, and the best months are September and October, when the harvest takes place and the leaves turn.

Fuel is easy on the mainland, but not in the old city, so fill the tank in Mestre before you go. Eat cicchetti, small snacks served at the bar, and a plate of sarde in saor, sweet and sour sardines. A spritz, an aperitivo made with Prosecco and bitter liqueur, is the local drink, though if you are riding, it is wise to wait. Visit the old city in the early morning or evening, when the crowds are lighter, and be prepared to walk.
t.tatei jaramara@21.5,-105.3:
