Tatei Haramara, Our Mother the Sea, is the Wixarika name for the Pacific, and the place sacred to the community lies on the coast of Nayarit, near San Blas. Pilgrims walk or travel from the mountains each year to make offerings to the sea goddess, who brings rain, and the coast is part of the long ritual route that also includes the desert of Wirikuta. It is a working shoreline of beaches and rocky points, where the sea is strong and the surf can be heavy. Visitors who come here should remember they are guests at a sacred place and treat offerings and ceremonies with respect.

San Blas, about a kilometre and a half away, is a small, slow, humid port with a lot of history. In the eighteenth century the Spanish built a shipyard and naval base here from which they supplied their colonies in California, and the ruins of the fort of San Basilio and an old customs house stand on a hill above the town. The American poet Longfellow wrote about the bells of San Blas, whose church is a ruin in the plaza. The mangrove estuaries around the town are rich in birds, and boat trips run to the freshwater spring of La Tovara, through tunnels of roots and over water so clear you see fish below.

Be ready for the insects. The sand flies of San Blas, known as jejenes, are infamous, especially at dawn and dusk and on windless days, and they leave painful, itchy bites. Repellent helps and so does staying away from the beach at those times, but the locals say you get used to them. The heat and humidity are heavy from May to October, and the rainy season brings storms.

The road to San Blas is a pleasure for motorcyclists. From Tepic, it drops from the cool highlands toward the coast through a series of curves, with forest, lava fields and tropical vegetation, and the air gets warmer with every kilometre. The surface is generally fine, but trucks, loose gravel and the occasional cow call for attention. Fuel is available in San Blas and Tepic. The seafood is excellent, particularly the shrimp and the fish, served grilled or in empanadas. Winter, from December to March, is the most comfortable season.
t.islas marias@21.6,-106.5:
The Islas Marias lie about a hundred kilometres off the coast of Nayarit, in the Pacific, and for more than a century they were a federal prison colony, one of the most notorious in Mexico. The archipelago has four islands, of which Maria Madre is the largest, and the penal colony operated there from 1905 until it closed in 2019. The prisoners lived in a relatively open regime, working farms and workshops, and the writer Jose Revueltas, who spent time there in the 1930s, wrote about it with powerful effect. The islands are now designated as a nature reserve and a UNESCO biosphere reserve, with tourism slowly being developed.

You cannot ride there, of course, since the only way across is by boat. The usual route runs from the coast near San Blas, and sailing times, permits and arrangements are set by the authorities, who changed the rules several times in recent years, so check before planning. What you can do is ride the coast of Nayarit and imagine the dark line of the archipelago on the horizon. The ride out to the sea along the road from Tepic through San Blas has the quality of a pilgrimage, which is fitting because the Wixarika people regard the Pacific as the home of Tatei Haramara, the sea goddess.

The islands are notable for their wildlife. Isolated for a long time, they hold several species found nowhere else, including a distinct raccoon, a rabbit and a parrot, and the surrounding waters are rich in marine life. Humpback whales pass through in winter, and dolphins and turtles are regular visitors. The forests are tropical dry forest, thick and green in the wet season and brown in the dry.

The coast of Nayarit, where the ride begins, is a world of mangroves, beaches and small fishing villages. The best season for travel is from November to April, when the weather is dry and the sea calm. In summer and early autumn, hurricanes threaten the Pacific coast, and the boat crossings are suspended when weather turns bad. Fuel and supplies are available in San Blas and Tepic, and the roads are generally good.

The sense of distance is the point. A place you can see only in the mind, on the far side of a restless sea, tells you something about what the coast has always meant to the people who live along it.
t.the works of joze plecnik in ljubljana h:
Joze Plecnik is the architect who gave Ljubljana its face. Born in the city in 1872, he trained in Vienna and worked in Prague, where he remodelled the castle for the new Czechoslovak republic, and in 1921 he returned to his home town as a professor. Over the next three decades he reshaped the capital with bridges, markets, squares, colonnades and a library, and he did it with a classical sensibility that mixed Greek and Roman forms with local materials and an unmistakable wit. His works in Ljubljana are on the UNESCO list.

The Triple Bridge is probably his best-known creation. A simple stone bridge crossed the Ljubljanica at the centre of the old town, and Plecnik added two pedestrian bridges alongside it in the 1930s, so that the central span fans out into a wide, balustraded promenade that opens onto the Preseren Square. The riverside market, with its long colonnade of columns, stands nearby, and the National and University Library, with its brick facade, stone and horse-head door handles, is a short walk away. Inside, a dark staircase leads to a bright reading room, a deliberate journey from darkness to light.

Plecnik also designed the Zale cemetery, a group of chapels and courtyards at the edge of the city, and he laid out riverbanks and promenades that make the city a pleasure to stroll. His style is very personal and not easy to classify, and this is part of its appeal.

Riding in Ljubljana is manageable. The old town is largely closed to cars, with a pedestrian zone, so park at the edge and walk. Traffic is moderate, tram lines do not exist, and cyclists are numerous. Fuel is available at stations on the ring road, and the motorway network leads quickly out of the city. Within an hour you can be in the Julian Alps, where the road over the Vrsic pass climbs through fifty hairpins, or on the Karst plateau toward the Adriatic.

Cafes line the Ljubljanica, and the food is a pleasant mix of Central European and Mediterranean, with sausages, štruklji dumplings and good local wine. Spring is lovely, with the river banks in bloom, and autumn is golden.
t.green promenade along vegova street@46.0:
Vegova Street is one of the quieter corners of Plecnik's Ljubljana, and the green promenade that runs beside it was one of the places where he turned a piece of ordinary city into something calm and ordered. The area lies in the district between the old town and the university, where the new National and University Library stands, and the planting, avenues of trees, paths and small spaces have been laid out with the same care he gave to the grand squares. It is a modest thing, but modest is what makes it special.

Plecnik spent years on the library, which opened in 1941, and its design is among his most inventive. The outside is a strict block of brick and stone with little decoration, and the interior carries a sense of drama, with a dark entrance hall and a grand stair of black marble, then a bright, high reading room with large windows. The building is meant to be a journey from ignorance to knowledge, and many visitors feel that. The library is open to the public, and a short visit is possible.

Ljubljana began as the Roman colony of Emona in the first century, and Plecnik also reworked a stretch of the Roman wall, south of here at Mirje, into a small garden with a gate and pillars. A walk between the two is a good way to see how he treated old stones. The area has a quiet charm that tourists often miss.

For motorcyclists, the central area is a pleasure to walk but not to ride, so find parking on the edge, perhaps near the main roads, and spend a morning on foot. The city has fuel stations at its edges, on the ring road and main routes. Afterwards the ride to Palmanova, in Italy, is easy and rewarding, heading southwest through the Vipava valley and over the border, past vineyards and stone villages. The weather in Ljubljana is mild, with warm summers and cold winters, and the best months are April to June and September to October.
t.koper@45.6,13.7:
Koper is Slovenia's seaport, a small walled town on a peninsula in the north of the Adriatic, and it spent centuries as a Venetian city. The Venetians called it Capodistria, and ruled it from the late thirteenth century until 1797, and the old centre shows it clearly. Narrow stone lanes lead to the main square, where the Praetorian Palace, a pink-and-white Gothic and Renaissance building, stands beside the Loggia and the cathedral. The bell tower can be climbed for a view over the red roofs to the bay. A short coast of only forty-six kilometres is all that Slovenia has, and it is made the most of.

The port beside the town is a working one, with ships, cranes and cars waiting for export, and it connects Central Europe with the Mediterranean. For riders, the coast is a pleasant meeting of land and sea, with salt pans at Secovlje, the pretty seaside town of Piran a few kilometres west, and the Istrian hills inland, covered with olive groves and vineyards. Local olive oil is excellent, and the wine of the region, particularly the dark red Refosk and white Malvasia, is worth trying. Seafood is fresh and served simply.

The ride toward Snežnik leads you inland, up onto the Karst plateau and into the forests of Notranjska. The road climbs from the coast in a series of bends, with views back to the sea, and soon the landscape changes to a high, rocky plateau of limestone, scrub, and pine, with stone walls and small villages. In winter, the bora, a cold, strong wind from the northeast, can blow with great force and close roads to light vehicles. Check the forecast. Beyond the Karst, tall beech and fir forests clothe the mountain of Snežnik, which holds a fine castle in the woods and is home to bears and lynx.

Fuel is available in Koper and in Ankaran, three kilometres away, and the prices are usually better than in neighbouring Italy. Restaurants are scattered along the coast, serving fish, pasta and prosciutto. In summer, the town is busy and parking is tight, so arrive early. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding the Karst. Take warm layers, since the plateau is much cooler than the coast.
t.ljubljana@46.1,14.5:
Ljubljana is a small capital with a big sense of itself, and it sits in a basin ringed by hills, with a castle on a steep wooded rise at the centre. The old town huddles beneath it along the green Ljubljanica River, which bends through the middle, and cafe terraces cover the banks. Dragons are the city's symbol, appearing on the Dragon Bridge, a green-copper and concrete span of 1901, and on the coat of arms, and they are said to derive from the legend of Jason and the Argonauts, who supposedly founded the city after killing a dragon in the marsh. The tale is a charming fiction. In reality, the Romans founded Emona here, and the Habsburgs later ran the town as the capital of Carniola.

In 2016, Ljubljana was named European Green Capital, and the centre has been largely closed to cars, with pleasant walks, cycle lanes and a spread of parks. The Tivoli park, on the edge of the centre, is a large green space with avenues and a mansion. Funicular and path lead up to the castle, where a view of the town and the Alps awaits on a clear day. The Central Market, with fruit, cheese and honey, is the best place for breakfast.

For a motorcyclist, the city is a gateway to the Julian Alps, and the day's route leads northwest to the Idrijska Bela valley, where a great barrier of stone blocks was built to hold back torrent water and debris. The Slovenian mountains have a long tradition of such works. Roads in the region are good, with sinuous curves, small villages and glimpses of high peaks. Be mindful of speed cameras, which are frequent, and fines can be heavy. A vignette is required on the motorways, and the Slovenian one is sold at petrol stations and online.

Fuel is plentiful on the ring road and the motorways, and food is good. Try the Carniolan sausage, buckwheat porridge called ajdovi žganci and the cream cake of Bled, if you detour north. The best months for riding are May to September. Alpine passes close in winter.
t.trnovo bridge@46.0,14.5:
Trnovo Bridge is a modest, lovely thing that sums up Plecnik's way of working. In the 1930s, he rebuilt a small bridge over the Gradaščica stream in the Trnovo district of Ljubljana, at the foot of the hill where the church of St Francis of Assisi stands, and he made it wide, wider than the street it joined, so that it became a small square as much as a crossing. The bridge is lined with pillars and balustrades of pale stone, and he planted two rows of birch trees along its edges, a gentle, living touch in the middle of the city. The pyramids at the corners are a nod to Egyptian forms, which he used with a sense of play.

Close by, the church of St Francis, built by Plecnik in the 1920s, is another curiosity. Its facade has a round tower, a brick body and a bold, unusual interior, with an arrangement of columns and light that is entirely his own. It is worth stepping in. The neighbourhood around, Trnovo, is a village-like quarter with small houses and gardens, as if the city had been left out of it.

The stream, the Gradaščica, was once a trouble to the district, flooding often, and Plecnik also helped to channel it, laying paths along the banks. It is a tranquil place now, a good spot for a coffee and an unhurried half hour. The Ljubljanica river and its Plecnik works lie a short walk away, and the castle is visible over the roofs.

Riding in this part of the city is straightforward but slow. Streets are narrow, and some are one-way. Park on the edge of the old town and walk, and Trnovo is a short stroll from the centre. Fuel stations are near the ring road. The ride leads on to the Italian city of Palmanova, a star-shaped fortress town of the late sixteenth century, and the road there crosses the Karst and the Friulian plain, a long, pleasant day. The weather is mild in spring and autumn, and the light on the river in the evening is lovely.
t.munich@48.1,11.6:
Munich is closer to the Alps than any other German city of its size, and on a clear day with a warm southerly wind called the Föhn, the mountains seem to sit at the end of the street. The wind brings a sharp clarity and headaches for the sensitive, and the locals are used to both. The city lies on the Isar, a river that once ran milky green with glacial water and is now lined with gravel banks where people sunbathe, barbecue and swim in summer. Munich's centre is compact and cheerful, with the twin onion-domed towers of the Frauenkirche, the Rathaus on Marienplatz with its mechanical clock figures, and the Viktualienmarkt for food.

The history here is Bavarian through and through: the Wittelsbach dynasty ruled from the city for centuries and left behind palaces and the vast English Garden, one of the largest urban parks in the world. Beer is a big part of the identity, and the Hofbräuhaus is only one of many beer halls where a litre mug is the normal measure. The Oktoberfest, held on the Theresienwiese from mid-September to early October, draws millions of visitors. The city is also home to BMW, whose museum and showroom, a futuristic building near the Olympic park, is a destination for any motorcyclist, since the company has made motorcycles for more than a century.

Riding out of Munich is a pleasure once you clear the suburbs. The roads south lead to the Alpine foothills, with lakes like the Starnberger See and the Tegernsee and a succession of green hills with cows and onion-domed churches, and the mountains rise on the horizon. To the north and west, the Bavarian plain is flat and agricultural, with straight roads and wide skies. Traffic is heavy at rush hour, and weekend trips toward the Alps can produce long queues. An early start, before the day-trippers wake, makes a big difference.

Fuel is easy in a city of well over a million people. The streets near the centre are crowded, with trams, cyclists and a low-emission zone, but a motorcycle is a good way to move through them. Cafes serve strong coffee and the classic Bavarian breakfast of weisswurst, pretzels and sweet mustard before noon. The air has a fresh, slightly resinous smell in spring, and the light in autumn is gentle and golden.
t.bled@46.4,14.1:
Bled looks like a stage set for an alpine fairy tale, and it has the grace to be real. A small glacial lake, deep green and still, is ringed by forested hills, with the pale wall of the Julian Alps rising behind it. On a rocky islet in the middle stands a white church with a baroque steeple, the Church of the Assumption, reached by traditional wooden boats called pletna, which are rowed by hand, and on a cliff on the north shore a castle looks down on the water. The castle is first mentioned in 1004, when the emperor gave the lands to the bishop of Brixen, and it claims to be the oldest in the country. The view from the terrace, with the island and the mountains, is the one on every postcard.

Bled grew as a spa in the nineteenth century, when a Swiss naturopath came to the lake and began prescribing cold water cures, and later Yugoslavia's President Tito had a villa on the shore. The local speciality is the kremšnita, a thick square of custard and whipped cream between layers of flaky pastry, and it is the thing to order with coffee on the lakeside terrace. Going round the lake on foot takes about an hour and a half, and the swimming in summer is clean and cool.

For a rider, Bled is the gateway to the best high roads in Slovenia. A few kilometres away the Vintgar gorge, with its wooden walkway above a rushing river, is a pleasant stop. From the Sava valley the road climbs to the Vršič Pass, at about 1,611 metres, with fifty hairpins, some of them cobbled, that were built by Russian prisoners of war during the First World War, and a little chapel in their memory stands beside the road. The cobbled corners are slippery when wet and need care, and the road may be closed in winter. The Triglav National Park, with the mountain that appears on the national flag, is the backdrop.

Bled is a town of about five thousand and has fuel, shops and plenty of rooms, though the summer weekends can be crowded. Motorways in Slovenia require an e-vignette, which motorcyclists can buy online or at a station, so arrange it before entering. Mornings in September are crisp and clear, with mist on the water.
t.davos@46.8,10.0:
Davos sits in a high, broad valley in the Graubünden Alps at about 1,560 metres, and it calls itself the highest city in Europe, a claim that depends on how you count. The dot is a few kilometres off, in the mountains toward Zernez, probably near the Flüela Pass, where the road climbs to over 2,300 metres between rock and tarn, and the landscape is bare and bright. It is a very different place from the town, which is known for the World Economic Forum in January and for the long ski runs on the Parsenn.

Davos was a health resort long before it was a place for skiers and politicians. In the nineteenth century, doctors prescribed its dry, sunny mountain air for tuberculosis, and sanatoria were built on the hillsides. Thomas Mann stayed here in 1912 while visiting his wife, and the visit inspired his novel The Magic Mountain, which turns the town into a closed world of illness and ideas. Today, the grand sanatorium buildings have been turned into hotels and clinics, and the lake and the old church are good places for a quiet walk.

The Flüela road climbs from Davos through a narrow valley and over the pass at about 2,383 metres, then drops in tight bends toward Susch in the Lower Engadine. Beyond that, Zernez is the gateway to the Swiss National Park, the only national park in the country, founded in 1914, where ibex, red deer, marmots and golden eagles live without being disturbed. The road is narrow and sometimes steep, and it can be closed by snow for part of the year, so check before you go. Alpine weather can change within minutes, even in summer.

The riding here is some of the best in Switzerland, with crisp tarmac, good visibility and a series of rewarding bends. Speed limits are strictly enforced, with cameras in many valleys.

Fuel is easy in Davos and Zernez, and you will find cafes serving Bündner specialities like barley soup and nut cake. The Engadine is Romansh-speaking, and you may see signs in that language, which is one of the four national languages. Summer weekends are busy, and early morning is the quietest time to be on the road.
t.bernina@46.4,10.0:
Alp Grüm is the nearest name to the dot, a tiny station on the Bernina railway where a few red trains stop each hour, and a small restaurant clings to the hillside above a view that stops conversation. Across the valley, the Palü glacier hangs below the peak of Piz Palü, and the ice breaks into blue crevasses above a dark lake. At about 2,090 metres, the air is thin and clear, and the sense of being above everything is complete.

The Bernina Pass, a short climb north, tops out at 2,328 metres and links the Engadine with the Italian-speaking valley of Poschiavo. The road is open all year, which is rare for a pass of this height, but snow can fall in any month and the weather turns fast. On the way down to Poschiavo the road swings through a series of broad hairpins, and the vegetation changes from bare rock to larch, then chestnuts and even palm trees near the Italian border. Ride it in the morning, when the light is soft and the traffic light.

The railway is as famous as the road. The Bernina line, part of the Rhaetian Railway, crosses the pass without a rack, climbing steep gradients and passing the Lago Bianco, a white lake that takes its colour from glacial silt. Further down, near Brusio, the track makes a complete spiral on a circular viaduct, a pretty sight that has been featured on thousands of postcards. The line is on the UNESCO list.

Poschiavo, about ten kilometres from here, is a quiet town of about three and a half thousand people, with old houses, a long main square and a mix of Italian and Swiss flavour. It has fuel and cafes, and is the place to try a plate of pizzoccheri, buckwheat noodles with cheese and cabbage. Up here at the station, fuel is not available, so carry enough for the pass.

A small glacier garden near Cavaglia shows giant potholes ground out by meltwater, an easy stop on the way down. Wear a warm layer even in summer, because the wind off the ice is cold.
t.poschiavo@46.2,10.1:
The label says Poschiavo, but the dot actually falls on the Italian side of the border, about twenty-five kilometres south, in the lower Valtellina near Teglio and the Aprica Pass. It is the long, wide valley of the Adda river, running east to west between the Rhaetian Alps to the north and the Orobie Alps to the south, and the hillsides are stitched into terraces, held up by dry-stone walls, that grow the Nebbiolo grapes known here as Chiavennasca. Wines from the Sassella and Inferno zones are strong, mineral and underrated.

Teglio gives its name, or so the people there insist, to pizzoccheri, the dark buckwheat noodles tossed with cabbage, potato, butter, garlic and slices of local Casera cheese, a dish designed for cold mountain evenings and capable of ending any argument about dinner. There is also an old palace in town, Palazzo Besta, with a Renaissance courtyard and painted rooms that make a surprisingly grand stop for a village of this size.

Aprica, a few kilometres on, sits on a gentle pass at around 1,170 metres that links the Valtellina with the Val Camonica. The climb from the valley floor is a series of wide, easy bends through chestnut and spruce, and the descent on the far side is rapid and enjoyable. The ski resort here is more a family affair than a glamour spot, and in summer it is quiet, with hotels half-empty and cafes keen to see a motorcycle. A little to the east lies the Mortirolo, a brutally steep climb beloved of cyclists, and a good road for riders who like narrow tarmac and hairpins that tighten without warning.

For fuel and food you are in good hands. Aprica has stations and supermarkets, and Tirano, the larger town down the valley, has everything, along with the station where the Bernina Express begins its climb into Switzerland. It is the natural place to cross the border toward Poschiavo, by way of the old customs post at Campocologno, and to ride up the Brusio spiral on the way.

Weather in the Valtellina is generally mild and dry, with warm afternoons from May through September, while the high passes take longer to clear in spring. Autumn is the time for grape harvest, when the terraces turn gold and red and the smell of crushed fruit drifts from the cellars.
t.wurzburg@49.8,10.0:
Würzburg lies on the Main in Lower Franconia, in the middle of a landscape of vineyards, and it is the northern start of the Romantic Road, the touring route that runs through Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg to Füssen in the Alps. The city has around a hundred and thirty thousand inhabitants, a university that dates back to the fifteenth century and a great Baroque palace, the Residenz, built in the eighteenth century for the prince-bishops by the architect Balthasar Neumann. Its staircase has a ceiling fresco by Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, said to be the largest in the world, and the whole building is a World Heritage site.

Most of the city was destroyed in a single air raid in March 1945, and it was rebuilt, sometimes faithfully, sometimes plainly. Even so, the old bridge over the Main, lined with stone statues of saints, is a good place to sit with a glass of local wine and look at the Marienberg fortress on its hill above the river. The wine is Franconian, mostly dry Silvaner, and is sold in a squat, round-bellied bottle called a Bocksbeutel that you will recognise at once.

From here, the Romantic Road heads south through the Tauber valley, a gentle landscape of fields and half-timbered villages, and then to Rothenburg ob der Tauber, a medieval walled town that is almost too perfect, with its towers, cobbled lanes and gabled houses. Dinkelsbühl is another well-preserved walled town, and Nördlingen, the end of this stage, sits in the middle of a giant circular basin called the Ries, a crater made by a meteorite impact about fifteen million years ago. The town's medieval wall can be walked in its entirety, and the tower of the church of St George, nicknamed the Daniel, offers a view across the crater.

The riding is relaxed. The roads are mostly good, with gentle curves and wide views, and the speed limits are generally observed. Tourist traffic is dense in Rothenburg, so arrive early or late. Autumn is a good time, with the vines turning gold, and early summer has the best light.

Fuel is easy in Würzburg and in every town on the way, and there are cafes and inns everywhere. Try a Franconian roast with dumplings and a glass of the local wine.
t.fussen@47.6,10.7:
Füssen is the southern end of the Romantic Road, a sunny little town on the Lech river, a stone's throw from the Austrian border and with the Alps standing straight above its rooftops. It has about fourteen thousand people and a history stretching back to the Romans, who built a road here, the Via Claudia Augusta, to carry troops over the Alps. The old town is tidy, with arcaded streets and painted facades, and the river tumbles over a small waterfall at the edge of the centre.

Above the town stands the High Castle, once a summer residence of the bishops of Augsburg, with remarkable trompe l'oeil paintings on its inner courtyard walls that make flat surfaces look like carved stone. Next to the castle lies the Abbey of St Mang, a Baroque monastery whose church stands over the grave of an early saint. Füssen was also a major centre of lute and violin making from the fifteenth century, and a small museum in the monastery tells the story.

Four kilometres east, the real crowd-puller sits on its crag: Neuschwanstein, the fairy-tale castle that King Ludwig II began building in 1869 as a romantic retreat, and which he never finished. He died in 1886, and within weeks the castle was opened to visitors, who have not stopped coming since. Tickets are timed and sell out in summer, so book ahead, and expect crowds and a steep walk from the car park. Beside it, the yellow castle of Hohenschwangau is where Ludwig grew up, and the lakes, the Alpsee and Forggensee, are lovely.

For riders, the roads in the surrounding area are excellent. The Tegelberg road, the lanes around the lakes and the passes into Tyrol, such as the Gaichtpass and Fernpass, offer winding, scenic riding with sweeping views. In summer, the area is very busy, with coaches and tourists, and parking near the castles is limited and expensive. Early morning is the best time.

Fuel is easy in Füssen, with stations on the road to Austria, and cafes and restaurants of every kind. A Bavarian meal of roast pork with dumplings, a wheat beer on a terrace by the river, and a slice of cake is the natural end to the road.
t.zernez@46.7,10.1:
Zernez is a small village in the Lower Engadine, at about fifteen hundred metres, and the gateway to Switzerland's only national park. The Inn river runs through the valley, a cold green stream fed by glaciers, and the surrounding mountains are dark with larch and pine. The village has an unusual look for the Alps, with white houses decorated with sgraffito, patterns scratched in plaster, and small windows set deep into thick walls, typical of Engadine architecture. Most of the older buildings date from after 1872, when a fire destroyed much of the village, and the rebuilt streets are wider than most in the valley.

The Swiss National Park, founded in 1914, is the oldest in the Alps and has the strictest rules: no camping, no picking flowers, no dogs and no leaving the marked paths. The visitor centre in Zernez explains the park's wildlife, which includes red deer, ibex, chamois and marmots, and, more recently, bears wandering in from Italy. The park's other claim to fame is that it has been left to nature for over a century, giving scientists a rare view of what happens when humans stop interfering.

The road through the park is the Ofen Pass, which climbs from Zernez to about 2,150 metres before descending into the Val Müstair. It is a fine ride, with smooth curves through thick pine forest, and a high, open section with big views. Traffic is moderate, speed limits are low and enforced, and the pass is open year-round in principle, though snow and ice can cause delays. Wildlife can appear on the road, and deer are common at dusk. At the bottom, the Val Müstair has a Romansh-speaking population and a remarkable Carolingian convent at Müstair, a UNESCO World Heritage Site with frescoes from the ninth century.

The nearest towns of any size are Davos, over the Flüela Pass, and the Italian resort of Livigno, through a tunnel.

Try a slice of Engadiner Nusstorte, a rich walnut and caramel tart that is the valley's signature, with a cup of coffee, at one of the bakeries.
t.orlicke mountains@49.9,14.3:
Two rivers meet a short ride south of Prague, and this point sits right beside the meeting. The Vltava, the great river of Bohemia, swings through the villages of Vrané and Davle on its way north to the capital, and at Davle it takes in the Sázava, which has come all the way from the Highlands to the east. The label calls this a return to the Orlické Mountains, but the Orlické range is far away on the Polish border; here you are in the green gorge country just south of the city, in the middle of what Czechs think of as their riverside weekend.

The valley is steep, wooded and narrow, and the roads follow the water. Expect twisty, tree-lined tarmac with plenty of corners, short climbs and sudden views over the river, and also expect cyclists, walkers and weekend traffic on a sunny Saturday. Take it easy through Všenory and the small settlements, where houses crowd the road. The best time is a weekday morning, when the light catches the water and the road is almost empty.

The Vltava here is tamed by a chain of dams and locks, built in the twentieth century to control flooding and to make power, and the river is wider and calmer than it was. Boats move slowly up and down, and the shores are lined with small wooden cottages called chata, a Czech obsession; city people retreat to them at the weekend to fish, garden and drink beer. That tramping culture, born between the wars, is as much part of the landscape as the rocks.

Near Davle stands the old monastery of Sázava, a short ride upstream, founded in the eleventh century and a centre of Slavic liturgy in its early days. It is an interesting detour if you have time. Fuel is easiest in Prague's southern suburbs, since the villages here are small, though there are stations on the main road. Look out for riverside pubs where you can sit with a plate of fried cheese and watch the barges, and a weekend rush when parking disappears.
t.kokorinsko@49.6,14.6:
This corner of Central Bohemia is farmland, ponds and gentle hills, the kind of country that Prague residents drive through without noticing and riders learn to love. The point lies between Votice, Sedlčany and the village of Kosova Hora, roughly halfway between the capital and the Šumava forests to the south. The sandstone towers of Kokořínsko are far to the north, so think of this as the quiet middle of the country, the part that gets less attention.

The landscape is a patchwork. Large fields of wheat, barley and rape run to the horizon, and every few kilometres there is a pond, once dug for carp and still stocked for the Christmas table. Czech families eat carp on Christmas Eve, a tradition that keeps these medieval fishponds alive. Villages come with a little church, a pub, and often a baroque statue or two on the green.

The riding is relaxed. Roads rise and fall in long, easy swells, passing through woods and over small streams, with enough corners to keep things interesting and not enough traffic to cause trouble. Surfaces vary by village budget, from smooth to patched and potholed, and farm vehicles can leave mud on the tarmac in harvest time. You can see a long way on a clear day, and the air smells of cut hay and wet earth.

Votice is a town of four and a half thousand and has fuel and a couple of places to eat, while Sedlčany, a little over seven thousand, is the bigger stop, about ten kilometres off. The lakes of the Vltava cascade, including the long Orlík reservoir, are not far to the west, and the castle of Konopiště, the former home of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, lies to the north-east near Benešov. Both make good detours. Come in late spring or early autumn, when the light is soft and the fields are at their best.
t.trafoi@46.6,10.5:
Trafoi is a village of a few dozen houses in the Ortles Alps of South Tyrol, at about 1,540 metres, on the northern approach to the Stelvio Pass, and it sits under one of the great mountain faces of the Alps. The Ortler, at 3,905 metres the highest peak in the region, rises above the village in a wall of ice and rock, and it was first climbed in 1804 by a local hunter, Josef Pichler, on the orders of an Austrian archduke. The glaciers hang right over the valley, and on a clear morning the sight is so large that the village looks like a toy.

The history here is of pilgrims and soldiers. A small pilgrimage site, the Three Holy Springs, lies above the village at the foot of the mountain, said to have been the place where the Virgin Mary appeared to a shepherd boy in the sixteenth century, and a chapel marks the spot. During the First World War the front line between Austria and Italy ran across these peaks, with troops fighting in ice caves and carrying guns up to the summits, and you can still find traces of trenches and barracks along the Stelvio road.

For riders, Trafoi is the foot of the famous climb. From here the road to the pass, the highest paved road in the Eastern Alps at 2,757 metres, rises in a series of forty-eight numbered hairpins on this side, many of them tight and steep, with sheer views and a wall of rock above. It is generally open from late May or June to October, depending on snow, and closed in winter, so check before you go. The surface is good but the road is very busy on summer weekends, with cyclists, coaches and fast sports bikes, and weather at the top can change within minutes, with cold, fog and even snow in July.

In the village, a few hotels and cafés serve apple strudel, hot chocolate and hearty South Tyrolean food such as dumplings and speck. Come early in the day, bring a warm layer, and give the hairpins respect.
t.hagi proto industrial heritage ohitayama:
Hagi is a castle town at the western end of Honshu, on a delta between the Hashimoto and Matsumoto rivers, and the place where Japan's modern history began in earnest. The Mori clan, who were stripped of most of their lands after losing at Sekigahara in 1600, were sent here to a poor corner on the coast, and they spent the next two and a half centuries nursing a grievance. In the 1860s, men from Hagi and the surrounding domain of Choshu led the movement to topple the shogun, and several later became leaders of the new Japan.

The site called Ohitayama belongs to an earlier chapter. It was a tatara ironworks, where iron was smelted in the old Japanese way, in a clay furnace fed with charcoal and iron sand, and the remains of this proto-industrial site are part of the UNESCO listing of Meiji industrial heritage. In the 1850s, the domain tried to build Western-style cannons and ships, and Ohitayama is where some of the early experiments took place. The place is in hills, in woodland, and it takes some finding.

The ride toward it goes into the mountains above the Sea of Japan coast, with narrow roads through cedar and bamboo forest, small farms, and the occasional view down to the sea. The surface is generally good, but the lanes are narrow and shaded, with leaf litter and damp patches, and some roads are only one lane wide with passing bays. Wild boar and deer are common, and dusk is the time to be careful. The sections close to the site may have limited signage, so check the route in advance and have a map downloaded.

Hagi, fifteen kilometres away, is a city of nearly forty-four thousand, with fuel, shops and a pleasant old quarter of samurai houses and whitewashed walls. Fill the tank in town before you go up. Hagi is also known for its pottery, with soft, pale glazes, and for the sweet summer oranges that grow in its gardens. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the summer humidity is heavy.
t.sites of japan s meiji industrial revolu:
Hagi sits on a small delta where the sea meets two rivers, and around it you can follow the arc of an extraordinary change. The old castle town, with its mud walls and low-roofed samurai houses, is on one side, and on the other, on the edge of the mudflats, stands a chimney. It is the reverberatory furnace at Ebisugahana, built in the 1850s by the Choshu domain to cast iron cannon in the Western manner, using Dutch books as a guide. The experiment was crude, but it shows how fast the clan was learning, and the furnace, a stump of brick, is now part of the UNESCO listing of Japan's Meiji industrial revolution.

The town's other great site is the school of Yoshida Shoin, a young teacher who taught only for a year or two in the 1850s and was executed in 1859 at the age of twenty-nine. Among his students were men who later led the overthrow of the shogun and built the modern state, including Ito Hirobumi, Japan's first prime minister. The small wooden classroom, in the grounds of the Shoin shrine, is tiny and plain, and the effect is memorable, since it is hard to believe that so much came from so little.

For a rider, Hagi is a pleasant, easy town. The streets in the castle quarter are narrow and lined with walls, often marked with the orange of summer citrus branches leaning over, and there are parking lots at the edge. The ride in from the Sea of Japan coast is gentle, with the surface good and the traffic light, and the Hagi shoreline has a quiet, sandy air that is very different from the busy industrial coasts of the Pacific.

Fuel is plentiful in Hagi, with several stations on the main road. Look for the local pottery, soft in colour and prized by tea masters, and try the fresh squid for which the Sea of Japan is known. Spring brings pleasant weather and autumn the clearest light. In winter, winds from the north can be cold and sharp, with grey skies and some snow.
t.mazatlan@23.2,-106.4:
Mazatlan is a Pacific port on the coast of Sinaloa, with a long beach, a historic centre and a seafront promenade, the malecon, which stretches for more than twenty kilometres and counts among the longest in the world. It has a population of about three hundred and eighty thousand, a fishing and shrimping fleet, a ferry to Baja California and a reputation for fun. Old Mazatlan has restored plazas, a cathedral from the nineteenth century and a lovely opera house, and the street food, especially the shrimp, is excellent. Pacifico beer has been brewed here since 1900, and the carnival, held before Lent, is among the largest in Mexico.

The seafront has some surprises. On the headland of Cerro del Crestón stands a lighthouse, said to be one of the highest natural lighthouses in the world, a steep climb rewarded by a view over the city and the ocean. On the rocks below the malecon, cliff divers launch into the surf for tips, and the beaches fill with families at weekends. In winter, humpback whales can be seen offshore.

For motorcyclists, the road east from Mazatlan is the draw. Highway 40 climbs into the Sierra Madre Occidental toward Durango, crossing the Tropic of Cancer, and the stretch known as the Espinazo del Diablo, the Devil's Backbone, runs along a narrow ridge with drops on both sides. It is a legendary road with hundreds of curves, tunnels and sweeping views, and the Baluarte Bridge, opened in 2012, is a cable-stayed span over 390 metres above the canyon floor, one of the tallest of its kind in the world. The climb takes you from tropical heat to pine forest, and fog and rain can reduce visibility. Trucks are slow on the grades, and rockfalls occur.

Mazatlan has fuel everywhere, and the road has stations at intervals, but fill before the climb. Tolls are collected on the new highway, and an older free road runs alongside in sections. Start early to avoid the afternoon storms in summer. The best season is winter and spring, when the days are warm and dry. Allow a full day to enjoy the road, and eat a plate of fresh shrimp at the end.
t.gardena pass@46.6,11.8:
Gardena Pass, or Passo Gardena in Italian and Grödner Joch in German, climbs to 2,121 meters in the heart of the Dolomites, linking the Val Gardena with the Val Badia. The road crosses a high saddle between the huge grey cliffs of the Sella massif and the Puez-Odle range, and the view from the top is one of those scenes that make people stop and fall silent. The Dolomites were inscribed by UNESCO in 2009, valued for their pale limestone towers and for the way the rock changes color from white to pink to deep red at sunrise and sunset, a glow the local people call enrosadira.

This is Ladin country, and the Ladin language, a Romance tongue related to Romansh, is still spoken in the valleys, alongside Italian and German. Signs often appear in all three languages. Selva, in the Val Gardena, and nearby Ortisei are known for their wood carving, a tradition that produced religious figures and toys for centuries, and a skilled carver can turn a block of linden into a saint in an afternoon. The food is a mix of Tyrolean and Italian, with dumplings, speck, polenta and apple strudel on every menu.

For riders, the Sella Ronda circuit is one of the great loops in the Alps. It links four passes, Gardena, Campolongo, Pordoi and Sella, around the great limestone block, and the full circuit takes a few hours with stops. Gardena itself has smooth surfaces, a series of hairpins on both sides and views of the cliffs from nearly every bend. It is a popular road, and on summer weekends traffic is dense with bikes, cars and cyclists. Some mornings in summer the passes are closed to motor vehicles on set days as part of a program to give cyclists the roads, so check the schedule locally.

The season is short. The passes usually open in late spring and close with the first heavy snow in autumn, and early mornings in June or September are best, when the air is clear and crowds are thin. Weather can change within an hour, with thunderstorms in summer afternoons.

Fuel is available in Selva and Corvara, both a short ride from the summit, and mountain huts near the top serve strong coffee and warm food. Bressanone, a bigger town, lies farther away to the north.
t.lake carezza@46.4,11.6:
Lake Carezza, Karersee in German, is the Dolomites' most famous small piece of water, a pool of improbable emerald and sapphire that sits in a bowl of dark spruce beneath the jagged teeth of the Latemar. It lies at about 1,500 metres on the Great Dolomites Road, close to Nova Levante, and it is small enough to walk around in ten minutes. That is part of its charm and part of its problem: in summer, the walkway is crowded, and the best time to see it is early morning, when the water is still and the Latemar is reflected perfectly in it.

The road past is a pleasure. The Great Dolomites Road runs from Bolzano to Cortina d'Ampezzo, and the section over the Karer Pass climbs from the Val d'Ega through dense forest in long, well-banked bends, with the pale towers of the Rosengarten appearing between the trees. The tarmac is excellent, the gradients are friendly and the views are the main danger, as are the tour buses and cyclists. Soraga, a small village farther down the Fassa valley on the far side, is where the road eventually comes out of the mountains. Summer weekends bring heavy traffic, and an early start is wise. Spring and early autumn are quieter, and in October the larches turn gold.

The lake has a legend, as every Dolomite lake does. The story goes that a water nymph lived in the lake and fell in love with a young man, and a wicked sorcerer, hoping to win her, disguised himself as a merchant but was foiled, and in his rage he tore a rainbow from the sky and shattered it into the water, which is why the lake is so many colours. Locals tell it with a smile, and the rainbow explanation is more fun than the scientific one, which involves light and mineral particles.

The Great Dolomites Road itself dates from the early twentieth century, when tourism was growing and a road was built to link the region's valleys, and its engineers did a remarkable job. The mountains here are made of pale dolomite rock, formed from ancient coral reefs, which glows pink and orange at sunset, a phenomenon called the enrosadira. The air is crisp and smells of resin.

Fuel is available in Nova Levante and Bolzano, so fill the tank before the pass. Parking at the lake is paid and fills quickly, and the shore is protected, so stay on the path.
t.gosausee@47.5,13.5:
Gosausee lies at the end of the Gosau valley, in the Dachstein mountains of Upper Austria, in a bowl of limestone cliffs that rise nearly two thousand metres above the water. On a calm morning the lake is a mirror, and the great glacier on the Hoher Dachstein, the highest peak in the range at almost three thousand metres, is reflected upside down in the deep green water. It is one of the most photographed views in the Salzkammergut, and with good reason: the combination of dark forest, grey rock, white ice and blue sky is hard to beat. The lake lies at about nine hundred and thirty metres, and the air is cool and clear, even on hot days.

The valley beyond is a well-trodden path for walkers, with a circuit round the lake and a trail up to the Hintere Gosausee, a smaller, wilder lake, and to the Dachstein glacier. The Gosau valley has given its name to a type of geological formation, the Gosau Group, a layer of Cretaceous sediments full of fossils, which geologists around the world know. It is a place where history is written in the rock, and farmers have lived on the mountain meadows for centuries.

For riders, the road to the lake is a short, rewarding run. From the village of Gosau the road winds up the valley, with a few bends and a gentle gradient, passing farms and pasture, and ends at a car park beside the lake, where a fee is charged. It is part of a greater loop through the Salzkammergut, which crosses the Gschütt Pass, at about nine hundred and sixty metres, a smooth, easy road, and continues to Hallstatt, with its famous salt mine and the lakeside village of painted houses on the water. Summer weekends can be crowded, especially around Hallstatt, so aim for weekday mornings.

Gosau is small, with limited fuel, so fill up in a larger town such as Bad Goisern or Abtenau before the valley. The lakeside cafe serves simple food, and the mountain inns offer dumplings and strudel. The best months are June to October, with autumn light spectacular, and the lake sometimes freezes in winter.
t.krimml@47.2,12.2:
Krimml sits at the very top of the Salzach valley in Pinzgau, where the Hohe Tauern close in and the river is still a loud young thing. The village is small, under a thousand people, and it exists largely because of water: the Krimml Falls drop in three stages for something like 380 metres, which makes them the highest in Austria and among the tallest in Europe. You hear them before you see them, a low roar that gets into the car park, and in the afternoon the spray hangs in the trees like fog.

Most riders park the bike and walk the path beside the falls, which is steep but well built and takes a couple of hours with photo stops. It is worth doing in your boots if you can stand it, because the upper viewpoints are where the scale finally makes sense. The falls are part of Hohe Tauern National Park, and the cold, mineral smell of the place stays in your jacket for the whole ride afterwards.

The road starting here is the Gerlos Alpine Road, a toll road, so keep a few euros or a card handy at the booth. It climbs out of the Krimml gorge in a series of tight, well-surfaced bends, with trees close on both sides, then opens into higher meadows toward the pass. Traffic can be heavy with tour buses and campervans on summer weekends, so an early start pays: the light is soft on the cliffs before ten, and you get the hairpins mostly to yourself.

Fuel is the one practical thing to sort before you leave the valley. Krimml itself is tiny, and the next real choice is Neukirchen am Großvenediger, about eight kilometres back down the valley, where the Großvenediger glacier peak stands over the town. If you are riding up toward Gerlos with less than half a tank, turn around and fill there; the pass section is short, but it is no place to start counting kilometres.

Weather up here changes in an hour. A morning of clear sky can give way to cloud sitting on the road by lunchtime, and even in July the shade near the falls is properly cool. Pack the rain layer, and remember that the pass is open year-round but can see snow outside summer. When you leave, the climb is the best part of the day, and you will be glad you came up on this side of the mountain.
t.gerlos@47.2,12.0:
Gerlos is a ski village strung along a high Tyrolean saddle, roughly 1,200 metres up, between the Zillertal to the west and the Salzach valley to the east. It is the sort of place that is busiest in February, and in summer feels pleasantly half asleep, with farmhouses and chalets, cows with bells, and a handful of cafés that serve strudel to people in leathers at an unhurried pace. The nearest town of any size is a long way off, so think of it as a stop for coffee and a stretch rather than a place to do errands.

The pass itself, the Gerlos Pass, tops out a little above the village at a bit over 1,500 metres, and it has been a crossing for centuries, used by farmers, drovers and smugglers long before anyone paved it. The modern road was built as an alpine toll route in the 1960s, which explains why the gradients are gentle and the corners wide. It is a road made for steady riding, not for heroics. You can lean the bike into the long bends and watch the view change from forest to open pasture to the green water of the Durlassboden reservoir lower down the Zillertal side.

That reservoir deserves a pause if the light is good. It was built for hydropower, as so many valleys here were, and the dam wall is a surprisingly dramatic piece of engineering in an otherwise soft landscape. Gmünd and the Gerlos stream pour down toward Zell am Ziller, the town of the Gauderfest and the Zillertal brewery, where you can find real fuel stations and food. For the practical rider, the lesson is simple: fuel in Zell or back at Neukirchen, not in the village.

The descent into the Zillertal is one of the nicer stretches of tarmac in Tyrol, with a few hairpins and then long open curves through forest. Be wary of wet leaves in autumn and of tour coaches in July, and watch for cyclists, who treat this pass as a training run. If you are heading on toward Innsbruck or the Brenner, you will drop into the valley in good time for lunch; if you are turning around, you have the pleasure of riding the same road in the opposite direction, which always feels like a different road.
t.warth@47.3,10.2:
Warth is a high Walser village on the Vorarlberg side of the Arlberg, a cluster of wooden chalets and ski lifts at the end of the Lech valley's road. It sits at around 1,500 metres, a short ride from Lech, and it has a reputation among skiers as one of the snowiest places in the Alps; locals will tell you that winter can bring metres at a time. In summer it is quiet and rather beautiful, with the meadows steep above the road and the cowbells carrying across the whole valley.

The Walser story is the interesting part. These were people from the upper Valais in Switzerland who migrated eastward in the Middle Ages, taking up high, difficult land that no one else wanted, and building villages like Warth, Mittelberg and Schröcken. They kept their own dialect for centuries, and the farmhouses still show the careful, practical style of mountain people who knew how to survive a long winter. You can see it in the wooden walls and the low roofs, and in the way the village faces the sun.

The riding is all about the Hochtannberg Pass, which runs between Warth and Schröcken at about 1,676 metres. The road is wide, well kept and generous, with long bends and fine views down toward the Bregenzerwald on one side and the Lech on the other. It tends to close in winter, sometimes for days at a time because of avalanche risk, and even in late spring or early autumn it can be cold and wet. Check conditions before you commit. On a clear summer morning, the pass is one of the pleasantest roads in Vorarlberg, and a good place to practise the art of holding a steady line.

For fuel, do not rely on Warth. Lech is six kilometres away and busy with chic hotels, but the nearest large town is Oberstdorf, across the border in Germany, about eighteen kilometres off. Fill up in Bezau or before you set out, and then you can enjoy the pass without arithmetic.

Take a coffee at one of the village cafés and look at the mountains: the Biberkopf and the peaks around the Lechquellen are close, and on a clear day the light on the snow patches is remarkable. It is a good place to end a day of riding, though a cold one if the wind comes from the north.
t.tirano@46.2,10.2:
Tirano is where the Alps run out of snow and start thinking about wine. The town of about eight thousand sits in the Valtellina, the long east-west valley of the Adda, in Lombardy, at the foot of the Bernina Pass, and its mood is distinctly Italian: arcaded streets, warm stone, an espresso at every corner. It is the southern terminus of the Bernina Express, the railway that climbs over the pass from Switzerland, and the station square has red Swiss trains next to Italian ones, a peculiar and pleasing sight.

The town's great monument is the Basilica of the Madonna di Tirano, a Renaissance pilgrimage church built in the early sixteenth century on the spot where the Virgin is said to have appeared in 1504. It is a handsome, spacious building with a great façade, standing at the edge of the town, with a tall bell tower and a square that is almost always full of people. The Valtellina is also a wine country, with steep terraces of Nebbiolo vines, here called Chiavennasca, walled with dry stone and facing south, and the reds that come from them are some of the best in Lombardy. Order a glass with bresaola, the air-dried beef the valley is known for, and a plate of local cheese.

The Bernina Pass road climbs from Tirano on the Italian side in a series of hairpins through the border village of Campocologno, then past the Brusio spiral viaduct, where the railway makes a full circle, and over the pass at about 2,330 metres. The road is wide, smooth and well engineered, with fine views of the Palü glacier and the Bernina range. Switzerland's border posts are manned, so carry your passport or ID.

Fuel, supermarkets and repair shops are all easy in Tirano, and fuel is usually cheaper here than in Switzerland, so use it. Summer can be hot and humid in the valley, while the top of the pass is cold and sometimes foggy. The pass is generally open through the year, though snow can interrupt it in winter. As a place to end a day, Tirano is warm, generous and easy, and a long table outside a trattoria is the right finish.
t.mustair@46.6,10.4:
Müstair is a village at the far eastern end of Switzerland, tucked into the Val Müstair, a high green valley that looks toward Italy and has more in common with South Tyrol than with Zurich. Romansh is still spoken here, along with German and Italian, and the pace of life is gentle, with farms, barley fields and old houses with painted fronts. The great glory is the Benedictine Convent of St John, which tradition says was founded around 775 by Charlemagne, and which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Inside the church, the ninth-century Carolingian frescoes cover the walls in rows of painted scenes, some of the oldest of their kind in Europe, and the effect is quietly overwhelming.

The ride to get here is one of the best in eastern Switzerland. The Ofen Pass, at about 2,150 metres, climbs through the Swiss National Park, the country's only national park, founded in 1914 and strictly protected. There are no stops allowed off the road other than at designated parking places, no dogs and no camping, and you should obey this, because rangers do. The forest of mountain pine and larch is thick and aromatic, and red deer, chamois and marmots are common, particularly in the early morning. The road itself is wide and flowing, with smooth bends and good views.

Fuel in the valley is thin, so check your range. The sensible approach is to fill the tank in Zernez before the pass or across the border in the Italian town of Mals, a short ride from Müstair, where prices are often lower. The village of Tubre, just over the frontier in Italy, is the nearest settlement on the other side, and the border is usually a quick formality, though you should carry your documents. The Umbrail Pass, a side road leading to the Stelvio, is a fine temptation for the next day.

Food in the valley is simple and good: barley soup, rye bread, cured meat and the walnut tart of Graubünden. The convent has a small museum and a shop. Weather can change quickly in this region, with cold and rain even in summer, and the pass is closed in winter. Late summer and early autumn are a good time, when the larches turn and the air is crisp. Müstair is a quiet place to finish, and it rewards anyone who stays longer than an hour.
t.a i lofoten@67.9,13.0:
Å is the last village on the Lofoten road, at the very end of the E10, and it has the shortest name in Norway. The village is a collection of red and ochre fishing huts, called rorbuer, on rocky shores, with drying racks for cod and a small harbour. About a hundred people live here, and Reine, a few kilometres back, is a little larger. The mountains behind are steep and jagged, and the sea is deep blue, with the outer islands of Værøy and Røst visible on clear days. Beyond Å, the road simply stops, and the sea goes on.

The village is a living museum of the old fishing life. The Norwegian Fishing Village Museum preserves buildings from the nineteenth century, including a cod liver oil factory and a bakery that still makes cinnamon rolls that are famous across the islands. The smell of fish and tar hangs in the air, and the racks of drying cod, which turn to stockfish after months in the wind, are a regular sight from February to May. In summer, the racks are empty, and the village is busy with visitors.

The ride along the E10 through Lofoten is one of the great drives of northern Europe. The road crosses bridges, passes through tunnels and runs along the coast, with views of peaks, beaches and fishing villages. The surface is excellent, but the road is narrow in places, and in summer, caravans and camper vans slow the traffic, so be patient. Weather changes quickly: sunshine can turn to rain in minutes, and wind can be strong on the bridges. The best months are June to August, with the midnight sun, but September has clear air and the first northern lights.

Fuel is available at several points along the route, including Sørvågen and Reine, but not at Å itself, so top up in advance. A cafe at the old bakery and a few restaurants serve fresh fish, including stockfish and cod tongue, a local delicacy. Rorbu cabins can be rented, though they are popular, so book ahead. A walk up the nearby rocks, at the end of the day, gives you a view of the village and the sea, and a sense of having come to the end of the road.
t.kranjska gora@46.5,13.8:
Kranjska Gora is the last real town in the Upper Sava valley, a ski resort in winter and a base for hikers and cyclists in summer, tucked so close to the Italian and Austrian frontiers that you can see both countries on a clear afternoon. It is a small place, about fourteen hundred residents, with pastel chalets, a main street of cafes and shops, and the Julian Alps going straight up behind it. The tall wall of Triglav's neighbours dominates the sky, and the fields around the village are neat, green and full of hay racks.

This is the foot of the Vršič Pass, the highest road pass in Slovenia at roughly sixteen hundred metres, and most riders come here for the road alone. Its hairpins are numbered, fifty of them, with twenty-four on the north side and twenty-six on the south, and on the northern ramp several of them are paved in cobbles. The cobbles can be slick in rain and awkward on a heavy bike, so take them slowly and in a low gear. The upper part of the road is narrow, with rock walls and little shoulder, and in summer you will share it with campervans and cyclists. Come early or late for the best of it.

The road itself has a sad origin. It was built during the First World War by Russian prisoners of war, working for the Austro-Hungarian army that was fighting the Italians on the Isonzo front. In March 1916 an avalanche killed many of them, and the little wooden Russian Chapel on the north side of the pass, built by their comrades, still stands among the trees. Stopping there is worth a minute, and flowers are often laid at the door. The road remains a quiet memorial to the men who made it.

Practical matters are simple here. There is fuel in Kranjska Gora, and it is wise to take it, because the pass has none. Restaurants in town serve Slovenian dishes such as jota, a sour-turnip and bean stew, and a sweet called potica. The pass is closed or restricted in winter, usually from late autumn until spring, so look at conditions before planning. Close by is Planica, where ski jumpers fly farther than anywhere else in the world, and the nearby lakes at Jasna are among the most photographed in the valley.
t.most na soci@46.2,13.7:
Most na Soči is a small village at a place where water gathers. Here, the emerald Soča river meets the Idrijca, and the combined flow is held back by a dam built in the late 1930s, which created a long and beautifully coloured reservoir. The lake stretches back into the hills between Tolmin and Kanal, and the water often takes on a milky turquoise that makes a long photo stop worthwhile. The houses cluster around the old bridge, which gives the place its name, since most simply means bridge.

The Soča valley is well known to riders for the river itself, a clear, alpine stream that runs through narrow gorges and wide gravel flats in tones of blue and green found almost nowhere else. The ride from Tolmin leans along the water on gentle curves, with views of forested slopes, small side valleys, and a few old stone bridges. The road surface is usually good and the curves are easy, making it a relaxed afternoon ride rather than a technical one, and the valley is rarely too crowded outside July and August. In summer, expect kayakers and rafters, and in spring, meltwater turns the river even more luminous.

The valley has a darker history, too. During the First World War it was the Isonzo front, where Italian and Austro-Hungarian armies fought twelve battles in two and a half years, and the hills above are still marked with trenches, tunnels and cemeteries. The nearby town of Kobarid has a museum devoted to the war, and Ernest Hemingway wrote about the retreat from here in A Farewell to Arms. When you look at the peaceful water you should keep that in mind.

For fuel, go to Tolmin, about three and a half kilometres away, a modest town with stations and shops, since Most na Soči itself is very small. Cafes and guesthouses by the water serve local food: trout from the river, cheese from the highlands, and a dish of frika, a crisp potato and cheese cake that is a mountain staple. The nearest big city is Nova Gorica, well down the valley toward Italy. Spring and early autumn are the loveliest times, with softer light and fewer visitors.
t.manila utah@41.0,-109.7:
Manila is a very small town in the north-east corner of Utah, a few hundred people strung along a highway beside a high desert reservoir, and it is the sort of place where a stop for fuel and a sandwich becomes a conversation with the person at the counter. Check your tank before you arrive: in a town this size, supplies are limited, and the next big town is a long way off.

What brings people here is Flaming Gorge. The Green River was dammed in the early 1960s at the Flaming Gorge Dam, and the reservoir stretches back for ninety miles or so into Wyoming, a long blue ribbon between sagebrush hills and red sandstone walls. John Wesley Powell named the canyon during his 1869 river expedition, for the glowing red cliffs he saw at sunrise. The water is extremely clear and cold, the fishing for trout and kokanee is famous, and the whole reservoir is part of a national recreation area.

Behind the lake rise the Uinta Mountains, one of the few major ranges in the United States that run east to west, and the highest in Utah, topped by Kings Peak at over thirteen thousand feet. The scenic byway climbs from the reservoir into the forested slopes, with pine, aspen and some big switchback views. Riding here is relaxed and fast, with broad curves, good tarmac and light traffic outside summer weekends. Watch for deer at dusk and for cattle on open range. Weather is changeable: even in July, the high sections can be cold and wet, and the passes close with snow for the winter.

A short ride from the town is Sheep Creek Geological Loop, a side road through a canyon where tilted layers of rock show a billion years of Earth's history in colourful bands. The surrounding country, Browns Park, was once a hideout for outlaws, including Butch Cassidy's crew, because the state borders met nearby and lawmen were slow to follow. In autumn, aspen turn gold across the Uintas, and the air is crisp and clear. The best months are late May to early October.
t.grand lake@40.3,-105.8:
Grand Lake is the largest natural lake in Colorado, and the little town on its shore is the western doorway to Rocky Mountain National Park. At around eight thousand seven hundred feet, it is a village of boardwalks and wooden storefronts, with canoe rentals, ice cream shops and souvenir stalls strung along the water, and it is surrounded by dark forest and high peaks. The lake is cold and deep, and the surface is often dotted with sailing boats in summer.

The Ute people have a legend about the lake, saying that it was the scene of a tragedy in which a war party lost its women and children on a raft in a storm, and that the mist that rises from the water at dawn is their spirits. Whatever the truth, the setting is moving. The Kawuneeche Valley, which runs south from the town, is the upper valley of the Colorado River, which at this point is little more than a small stream winding through meadows, a very long way from the great river that carves the Grand Canyon.

Most riders arrive via Trail Ridge Road, the highest continuous paved road in the United States, which reaches over twelve thousand feet and runs for miles above the tree line, among tundra and rock. It is typically open from late May to mid-October, and it can be closed at any time by snow. The descent to Grand Lake is a long run through spruce forest, past moose meadows, and the last stretch along the valley is relaxed and level, with elk, and with a very good chance of seeing a moose if you look carefully in the willows.

The town has restaurants and basic services, but the main supplies are at Granby, about twenty kilometres away, or Estes Park on the east side, so it is best to arrive with fuel in hand. Cold, wind and thin air at the top of the ridge are real, so dress warmly. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and a road at that altitude is no place to be caught in lightning, so start early. In the evening, the light on the lake, with the peaks turning pink, makes up for a long day.
t.obergurgl@46.9,11.0:
Obergurgl sits at the head of the Ötztal in Tyrol, at about 1,900 metres, and it is often described as the highest church village in Austria. A cluster of timber-trimmed hotels and a modest church are wedged into a bowl of snowfields and peaks, with the Gurgler Ferner glacier and a ring of three-thousand-metre summits behind. It is the kind of place where the road simply runs out of valley, except that in summer it does not: the Timmelsjoch High Alpine Road continues up and over into South Tyrol.

There is a pleasing bit of scientific history here. In 1931, the Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard and his assistant landed their pressurised balloon on the Gurgler glacier after the first manned flight into the stratosphere, having started from Augsburg. A small monument in the village recalls the landing. In the decades since, Obergurgl has turned from a poor mountain farming settlement into a polished ski resort, but the old chapel and farmhouses give it more soul than many of its neighbours.

The riding is the main draw. The road up the Ötztal from the valley bottom climbs steadily through Sölden and on to Obergurgl and Hochgurgl in long, flowing bends, then the Timmelsjoch road tightens into hairpins above the treeline. The pass, at around 2,500 metres, is reached through open, rocky landscape, and the surface is excellent. The high road is closed by snow in winter, and typically opens in early summer and shuts again in autumn, with a toll for the privilege. On sunny weekends the road is busy with bikes and sports cars, so a weekday morning is a delight.

For services, the village has cafes and hotels and a good choice of restaurants, so lunch is easy: Tyrolean classics such as Kaspressknödel soup or Tiroler Gröstl come with a view. Fuel is less certain at this altitude, and the safe plan is to fill up in Sölden, about eleven kilometres down the valley, or Merano on the Italian side. Temperatures can drop sharply in the shade and with altitude, so pack warm layers. After the descent into the Passeier valley, the climate changes entirely, to vines, apples and Italian coffee.
t.bruck an der glocknerstrasse@47.3,12.8:
Bruck is a small village in the Salzach valley, on the edge of the Pinzgau, and for most riders it has one job: it is the doorstep to the Grossglockner High Alpine Road. Zell am See and its lake lie a few kilometres to the east, the broad glacier-carved valley runs on to the west, and above it, to the south, the main ridge of the Hohe Tauern rises in long, dark flanks with ice on top. At about 750 metres, the village is warm and green in summer, with farmhouses, hay meadows and the sound of church bells.

The high road itself, which you join a short way up the side valley toward Fusch and Ferleiten, is one of the great engineering projects of the twentieth century in the Alps. Construction began in 1930, in the middle of an economic depression, as a way to give work to thousands of unemployed men, and it opened in 1935. Around fifty kilometres of road, with some thirty-six hairpins, climb to a crossing at 2,504 metres near the Hochtor, designed so that cars could cross the main Alpine ridge at a gentle gradient. A toll is charged, and it is not small, but riders usually agree it is worth it.

The road is open in summer only, with opening dates that vary from year to year, typically from late spring to early November, and it can close at short notice for snow, even in the middle of the season. Early starts pay off, because by midday the traffic of buses, camper vans, cyclists and bikes can slow things to a crawl. Weather also tends to cloud up in the afternoon. Check forecasts and webcams before you set off, and bring warm layers, because the top is often near freezing even in July.

At Bruck, you will find fuel, a supermarket, a bakery and a few small guesthouses, and the larger town of Zell am See, only four kilometres away, has anything else you might need. Try a Kaiserschmarrn, the shredded pancake that Austrian mountain restaurants do with real pride, at one of the cafes on the way up. It is a gentle start to a very big day.
t.franz josefs hohe@47.1,12.8:
Franz-Josefs-Höhe is a balcony hung at 2,369 metres on the southern flank of the Grossglockner. A short spur from the main high road leads to a vast car park, a visitor centre and a long terrace, and from the rail you look straight across at the Grossglockner itself, the highest mountain in Austria at 3,798 metres, and down onto the Pasterze, the country's longest glacier. The summit is a pyramid of dark rock and ice, the glacier a grey, crevassed river sliding between lateral moraines. It is among the most famous views in the Alps.

The place is named for Emperor Franz Joseph I, who visited the area in 1856 with his wife Elisabeth, and rode up to look at the glacier. A century and a half later, the ice has changed beyond recognition. The Pasterze has shrunk dramatically, retreating several kilometres and thinning by many tens of metres, and the old viewpoints now look down on a lake and rubble rather than ice. Signs along the path show where the surface once stood, and it is hard to avoid a moment of silence. A cable car once brought visitors down to the ice, and a path still runs along the slope.

The detour from the main road is a few kilometres of broad, well-surfaced bends, climbing past meadows and bare rock, and it is as pleasant a ride as any on the route. You will probably share it with tour buses and campervans, so patience helps. Wildlife is better than you might expect: marmots whistle from the rocks near the car park, and ibex sometimes appear on the slopes. The air is thin and cool, and the light can change in minutes as cloud sweeps across the peak.

There is a cafe and restaurant at the terrace, serving hot drinks and Austrian dishes, and a shop, though prices reflect the view. Fuel is not available here, so arrive with enough from the valley, from Heiligenblut or beyond. The best time to come is early in the morning, before cloud builds on the peak and before the crowds arrive, and on a clear day the summit sometimes carries a little banner of snow blown from the ridge. Wear warm gloves, even in summer.
t.heiligenblut@47.0,12.8:
Heiligenblut is the village that every picture of the Grossglockner seems to include. The Gothic church of St Vincent, with its slender spire, stands on a knoll at the head of the Mölltal, and behind it the great snow cone of the mountain rises above forested slopes, the whole composition so tidy that it looks like a painting. At about 1,300 metres, the village is the last settlement on the Carinthian side before the high road climbs toward the glacier, and it has been a pilgrimage stop for centuries.

The name means holy blood, and the legend behind it is a good one. A Danish nobleman called Briccius, so the story goes, was travelling home from Constantinople with a vial of Christ's blood when he was caught in an avalanche in the mountains, and the relic was later found, miraculously preserved, under the snow. The church was built to house it, and a small shrine inside holds an elaborately carved Gothic altar and a relic container. It is worth stepping in, even if you are not religious, because the stonework and carved wood are lovely.

The ride into Heiligenblut from the north, over the Hochtor and down through a series of hairpins, is one of the Alps' great descents, and arriving here feels like a reward. Coming the other way, the climb starts with a few gentle turns before the valley tightens and the bends pile up. The road can be crowded in midsummer, but quieter in the early morning or in September, when the larches turn gold and the first snow dusts the peaks. Weather changes fast; thunderstorms are common in July and August afternoons.

The village is small, about a thousand people, but serves visitors well. There are guesthouses, cafes, a few shops and restaurants serving Carinthian specialities such as Kasnudeln, a cheese-filled pasta, and Almkäse from nearby pastures. Fuel here is limited, and it is wise to rely on the bigger places in the valley, Lienz in East Tyrol being the nearest sizeable town, about twenty-four kilometres away. If you can, spend the night. The mountain at dusk, with the last light on its summit, is better than any photo.
t.chief joseph scenic byway point 2@44.7,-:
The ground is a patchwork of sagebrush, juniper, dry gullies and eroded bluffs in shades of red, yellow and grey, laid down by volcanic activity long before the first people arrived. The Absarokas are volcanic in origin, made of old lava and ash flows, and so they have a very different look to the granite peaks of nearby ranges, with dark, crumbling ridges and jagged tops.

This is cattle country, with ranches strung along the creeks, and the roads are quiet, with only a few vehicles an hour in most seasons. The riding is relaxed and rolling, with long straights and easy bends, and the surface is mostly good, though patched in places by winter frost. The main risk is wildlife. Mule deer and pronghorn cross the road without warning, especially at dawn and dusk, and a collision on a motorbike is a serious matter.
