Cattle guards, metal grids across the road, can be slippery when wet, so cross them upright and at moderate speed.

The sense of space is the main thing. Distances here are large, and a day of riding may take you past just a few small settlements. Fuel is not available in this section, and the last reliable pumps are in Cody, which lies about thirty-five kilometres behind. Stock up before leaving, bring water, and carry a rain jacket, since the sky can change in minutes. Cell service fades away in the foothills, so tell someone where you are headed.

Historically, the area was a corridor for the Crow and Shoshone peoples, and then for trappers and prospectors. The Nez Perce passed through in 1877 and baffled the army by crossing country that cavalry believed impassable. A scatter of homestead cabins and old corrals reminds you how hard the ranching life was.

The light in the late afternoon is the best of the day, warming the bluffs to copper and throwing long shadows across the sage. The smell of dry sagebrush after rain is the unforgettable thing about this country, sharp and clean, and well worth stopping for.
t.chief joseph scenic byway point 3@44.8,-:
The road climbs here into real mountains. The name is old and its origins are disputed, so treat any single story with care, but the place itself is easy to understand: a high, windy shoulder of the Absaroka Range with dark forest, bare grassy slopes and a view that stretches back toward the Bighorn Basin.

This is the best riding on the byway. The road climbs and falls in steep grades, and the descent down the west side, called Dead Indian Hill, is a series of tight switchbacks on a steep slope, with a grade that tests brakes and nerve. Take it in a low gear, use engine braking, and watch for gravel in the bends. Traffic is light, but vehicles towing trailers and campers need space. Good tyres and healthy brakes matter more than horsepower here, and a fully loaded touring bike will have work to do.

At the bottom lies Sunlight Basin, a broad, ranching valley with the creek running through it, and the Sunlight Creek bridge crosses a deep gorge, high above the water. The view from the pull-out is worth the stop, and it is not for those who dislike heights. The basin has a scattering of lodges and ranches, and a small store, with limited supplies. Fuel is scarce, so make sure the tank is full before you leave Cody, and carry spare if you can.

The wilderness here is serious. Grizzly bears live in the Absarokas, and so do black bears, elk, moose and wolves, and the road passes through country with all of them. Do not leave food in the open, carry bear spray when walking away from the bike, and make noise in the brush. In the evening, elk move down to the meadows, and the sound of bugling in September is unforgettable.

Weather in the mountains is changeable. Snow can fall in any month, and the road may close for days in winter. The best time to ride is from late June to September, when the road is clear and the wildflowers are blooming. Dress in layers, as the temperature drops quickly when the sun disappears.
t.trail ridge road point 4@40.4,-105.8:
Fall River Pass sits at 11,796 feet, and the Alpine Visitor Center perched beside it, at just over 12,000 feet on the ridge, is the highest of its kind in the national park system. This is the rooftop of the drive. The forest ended some time ago, and what is left is the tundra, a low, wind-clipped world of tiny cushion plants, lichens and flowers that bloom in a few weeks of summer. It looks like grass, but it grows only a few centimetres per year, and a single footprint can leave a scar that lasts decades. Please stay on the paths.

Trail Ridge Road, which crosses the Continental Divide for about eleven miles above the tree line, is the highest continuous paved road in the United States, topping out at 12,183 feet. It was built in the 1930s, opened in 1932, and replaced the older Fall River Road, a narrow gravel track that still runs one way uphill in summer. The modern road is a wonder of engineering, sweeping across the high ridge with wide views in every direction, and it is open only from about late May to mid October, depending on the snow.

Riders feel the altitude. Bikes run lean, and so do lungs. The wind can be fierce, with gusts strong enough to move a loaded motorcycle, and sudden weather, including hail, sleet or snow, can arrive in the middle of summer. Thunderstorms build over the ridge by early afternoon, and lightning is a real danger on an exposed road, so start early and be off the high ground by noon. Take warm gloves, a windproof jacket and a spare layer.

The visitor centre has a gift shop, a cafe serving coffee, hot chocolate and soup, and a stone-walled terrace with a view of the tundra. Elk and bighorn sheep are often seen grazing on the tundra, and marmots and pikas squeak from the rocks. Pikas are small relatives of rabbits that live only in cold rocky places and are now threatened by warming.

Take a moment to look at the view. On a clear day you can see across to the Never Summer Mountains, the Mummy Range and the long line of the Continental Divide. It is a landscape of great simplicity, and it is easy to see why people come back.
t.trail ridge road point 5@40.4,-105.8:
At Milner Pass the Continental Divide runs right across the road, and a modest sign says so. The elevation is 10,758 feet, which is lower than the high ridge of the road but still above most of the Rockies' passes, and the setting is a quiet mountain lake, Poudre Lake, with a boardwalk, a pine forest and a trail climbing to the Divide. It is a spot where you can stand on a line that decides the fate of rain: water falling on the east side finds its way to the Atlantic by way of the Mississippi, while that on the west joins the Colorado River and ends up in the Pacific, or at least tries to.

The origin of the Colorado is not far off. Just to the west, in the Kawuneeche Valley, the river starts as a small stream, and by the time it reaches Grand Lake it is already a respectable creek. The Never Summer Mountains, a jagged volcanic range, line the western horizon, with snowfields that live up to the name. The Lava Cliffs, a short way east along the road, are an exposed wall of volcanic rock from an eruption some twenty-eight million years ago.

The descent west from the high ridge is long and impressive. The road drops in steady bends through spruce and fir forest, with wide views of the Kawuneeche Valley below, where moose wade in the willows and elk graze in the meadows at dusk. The surface is good, though rough in patches after winter, and traffic is lighter on this side. A rider with a few hours to spare will find it an easy, relaxing descent after the strain of the high tundra.

The nearest stations are in Grand Lake, about twenty-nine kilometres to the south, and in Estes Park on the east side. Water is available at the visitor centres, and a toilet building stands at the pass. The wind can be cold, even in July, so bring a warm layer.

In September the aspens on the lower slopes turn gold, and the moose become more visible. The view from the boardwalk, with the lake still and the divide above, is worth the stop. Take a quiet moment before moving on.
t.trail ridge road point 6@40.3,-105.8:
Grand Lake is a small, relaxed town on the north-east shore of a big, deep glacial lake, the largest natural lake in Colorado, at about 8,400 feet. Boardwalks run along the main street, with wooden storefronts, ice cream shops and bait stores, and a cluster of old log buildings dating from the early days of the town. The lake itself is a dark, cold blue, ringed by forest, with the Never Summer Mountains standing behind. Boats, kayaks and paddle boards fill it in summer, and the local yacht club claims to be one of the highest in the world.

The history of the place is a rich mixture. The Ute and Arapaho people used the area for hunting, and the Ute held the lake sacred, telling of spirits living in its mists. The first white settlers arrived in the 1860s, and the town grew up around mining claims and then tourism. Today it is the western gateway to the national park, and a sleepy contrast to Estes Park on the other side of the mountains.

For riders, Grand Lake is a welcome end to the high-altitude section. The long descent from the Continental Divide brings you through the Kawuneeche Valley, a broad, flat-bottomed valley with the Colorado River as a modest stream beside the road. Moose are often seen here, especially at dawn and dusk, so keep your speed down and your eyes open. The road is smooth, with long, easy curves. Beyond the town, Highway 34 continues to Granby and the large reservoirs of the Colorado-Big Thompson project, which carries water under the Divide to the eastern plains.

There is fuel in Grand Lake, and Granby, about twenty kilometres away, has a larger selection of stations, shops and motels. Local restaurants serve burgers, trout and huckleberry pie, and a walk along the boardwalk is a pleasant way to stretch after the ride. The town can be crowded on summer weekends, and parking is limited.

Weather here is milder than on the ridge, though evenings are cool, and snow can fall in any month. The best season is late June to early October. At night the sky is very dark, and the stars over the lake are brilliant. A short stroll along the shore at dusk, with loons calling and the mountains turning pink, is a gentle end to a day on the high road.
t.near lyons on the way back@40.2,-105.3:
Red rock and running water define Lyons. The small town sits where the North and South St. Vrain creeks meet and run out of the foothills onto the plains north of Boulder, and it is ringed by cliffs of pinkish-red sandstone. That stone, quarried here since the nineteenth century, built much of the University of Colorado campus in Boulder and countless houses and walls across the region. The town itself is built of it too, giving the main street a warm, solid look.

Lyons has seen hard times. In September 2013, days of extraordinary rain sent floods roaring down the St. Vrain canyons, cutting the town off, destroying homes and tearing away highways. The roads into the mountains were closed for months and rebuilt, and the town recovered with remarkable community spirit. Today it is lively again, known for music, especially the bluegrass and folk festivals at a venue beside the river, and for outdoor sports: climbing, fishing, tubing and cycling.

For riders, Lyons is the gateway to some excellent mountain roads. US 36 climbs northwest up the North St. Vrain to Estes Park and the edge of Rocky Mountain National Park, a lovely road of long, flowing curves between cliffs and meadows. Colorado 7 follows the South St. Vrain canyon up to the Peak to Peak Highway, twisting through a narrow, rocky gorge with the creek alongside. Both are popular with motorcycles on weekends, and both get busy with cars heading for the national park, especially in summer and autumn.

On the way back, this stretch near Lyons is where the mountains open onto the plains, and the change is sudden: one moment you are in a canyon of red rock and pine, the next you are rolling out onto flat farmland with Longmont and the urban corridor spread out ahead. The descent is a good time to cool off and enjoy the light as the sun drops behind the peaks. Watch for cyclists on the canyon roads, deer at dusk, and loose gravel on the shoulders.

Lyons has cafes, restaurants and a brewery or two, and fuel is available in town or in Longmont, a large city about fifteen kilometres east. Summer afternoons often bring thunderstorms over the foothills, so plan the climb in the morning and the return before the clouds build.
t.near selva di cadore@46.5,12.1:
Passo Giau, at 2,236 metres, is one of the great passes of the Dolomites, and many riders say it is the best. It links Cortina d'Ampezzo with Selva di Cadore and the Fiorentina valley, climbing through larch forests and high meadows to a broad, grassy saddle surrounded by spectacular peaks: the jagged tower of Ra Gusela, the Nuvolau, the Averau and, a little further, the famous Cinque Torri. To the south, the huge rock faces of Monte Pelmo and the Civetta rise above the valleys.

The climb from Selva di Cadore is the dramatic one, with about thirty hairpins on a narrow road with steep gradients, and it is a regular climb in the Giro d'Italia, so you will share it with cyclists, many of them suffering. The surface is generally good, but the bends are tight, and in summer it is busy with cars, motorcycles and cyclists. From the Cortina side, the road climbs through forests from Pocol, with gentler gradients and wider views. The pass is usually open in summer, but snow can close it from late autumn to spring, and afternoon thunderstorms are common.

The area has a long history. During the First World War, the front line between Italy and Austria-Hungary ran through these mountains, and the Cinque Torri and the surrounding peaks are dotted with trenches, tunnels and fortifications, some restored as an open-air museum. Much further back, at Mondeval, a high plateau above Selva di Cadore, archaeologists found the grave of a Mesolithic hunter, about eight thousand years old, buried with his tools; a small museum in Selva tells his story.

At the top of the pass there is a refuge with food and drink, and on a sunny day the terrace is packed with riders, cyclists and walkers enjoying the view. Selva di Cadore and Colle Santa Lucia are small, quiet villages with a few hotels and restaurants, and Cortina, about nine kilometres away as the crow flies but further by road, has every service.

Fuel is not available on the pass, so fill up in Cortina or in the larger valleys before you climb. Arrive early in the morning, when the light is soft and the road is quiet, and you will understand why this pass is so loved.
t.near poschiavo@46.4,10.0:
The Bernina Pass, at 2,328 metres, crosses the high Alps between the Engadine and the Valposchiavo in south-eastern Switzerland, and it is a place of water and ice. On the broad, rocky summit lie two lakes, Lago Bianco and Lago Nero, separated by a low ridge that is also a great continental watershed: water from one side flows to the Inn and the Danube and eventually to the Black Sea, while water from the other flows to the Adda, the Po and the Adriatic.

To the west, the Bernina massif rises in a wall of glaciers and snowy peaks, with Piz Bernina, the highest summit in the eastern Alps, and the beautiful ridges of Piz Palü. The Morteratsch glacier flows down from them into the valley, though it has retreated dramatically in recent decades, and signs along the trail mark where the ice once stood. A cable car from the pass road climbs to Diavolezza, with a stunning view over the glaciers.

The pass is also famous for its railway. The Bernina Express crosses the pass on a narrow-gauge line that climbs without rack assistance, one of the steepest adhesion railways in the world, and it is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, along with the Albula line. Its red trains wind past the lakes and down to Alp Grüm and Poschiavo, and the circular viaduct at Brusio, further south, is one of the most photographed railway structures in the Alps.

The riding is magnificent. The road from Pontresina climbs through larch forests and open moors to the summit, with long curves and wide views, and the descent to Poschiavo on the Italian-speaking side drops in a series of hairpins into a deep valley, with a change of climate and culture: chestnut trees, Italian food and a warmer feel. The pass is usually open year-round, but snow can close it briefly in winter. Watch for cyclists, tourists and trains.

Fuel is available in Pontresina and Poschiavo, and Livigno, just across the border in Italy, is a duty-free zone where fuel is cheap, so many riders detour there to fill up. Tirano, at the bottom of the valley, is the nearest large town. Stop at the summit, walk to the edge of Lago Bianco and watch the red train pass against the white glaciers.
t.svolv r@68.2,14.6:
Svolvær is the main town of the Lofoten Islands, far north of the Arctic Circle, and it sits on a tight cluster of rocky islets and harbours beneath steep, jagged mountains that rise straight from the sea. It has about four thousand people, a busy harbour full of fishing boats and ferries, and colourful wooden buildings on stilts along the water, including the red and yellow rorbuer, old fishermen's cabins now used for tourist accommodation.

Above the town, a pinnacle of rock called the Svolværgeita, the Svolvær Goat, rises from the mountainside with two horns at the top, and climbers sometimes leap from one horn to the other, a jump of about a metre and a half with a long drop below. The mountains around Svolvær are steep and rugged, with trails to summits offering views over the islands and the sea.

For centuries, Lofoten has lived from the sea. Every winter, huge shoals of cod, called skrei, come here from the Barents Sea to spawn, and fishermen have come from all over Norway to catch them. The fish are hung on wooden racks to dry in the cold air, producing stockfish, which has been exported to Europe for over a thousand years. You will see the racks everywhere, empty in summer and full in spring. Nearby, in Kabelvåg, the old fishing village has a large wooden church, often called the Lofoten Cathedral, and an aquarium and a museum telling the story of the fisheries. During the Second World War, British commandos raided Svolvær in 1941, destroying fish oil factories and capturing German soldiers.

The riding in Lofoten is spectacular. The E10, the main road, runs the length of the islands, connected by bridges and tunnels, with views of mountains, fjords, beaches and villages. It is narrow in places, with tight bends and single-lane bridges, and it is busy with tourists in summer. The weather is changeable, with rain, wind and fog, even in summer, but when the sun shines, the light is magical. From late May to mid-July, the midnight sun never sets.

Svolvær has fuel, food and every service, and the harbour has restaurants serving fresh fish. Try bacalao, a stew made from dried and salted cod, a dish that came back to Lofoten from the countries that bought its fish.
t.near reine@67.9,13.0:
Near the southern end of the Lofoten Islands, the road crosses a series of bridges and islets into Reine, a tiny fishing village of a few hundred people, with red and white cabins scattered along the shore of a fjord, and granite peaks rising straight from the water all around. It is often called one of the most beautiful villages in the world, and when you see it on a clear day, you will not argue.

Above the village, the peak of Reinebringen offers one of the most famous views in Norway, over Reine, the fjords and the mountains. The path up was once steep and dangerous, but Nepalese Sherpas built a stone staircase of nearly two thousand steps, and now it is a hard but safe climb. Nearby, the village of Hamnøy and the island of Sakrisøy, with its yellow cabins, are favourite spots for photographers, especially in winter, when the peaks are covered in snow and the northern lights dance overhead.

At the very end of the road, beyond Reine, lies the village of Å, with a stockfish museum and old fishermen's cabins, and beyond that, the Moskstraumen, one of the strongest tidal currents in the world, a whirlpool that inspired Edgar Allan Poe and Jules Verne to write about the maelstrom. Ferries run from Moskenes, near Reine, to Bodø on the mainland, across the open sea.

The riding is beautiful but demanding. The E10 is narrow, with tight bends, tunnels and single-lane bridges, and it is busy with tourists in summer, many stopping on the bridges to take photos. The wind can be strong, especially on the bridges and exposed stretches, and the weather changes quickly. Watch for sheep, cyclists and campervans.

Services are limited at this end of the islands. There are small shops and cafés in Reine and the nearby villages, but fuel is scarce, and Leknes, further east, is the main service town. Fill up before heading south. Find a spot on the rocks, look at the reflections of the peaks in the still water, and you will understand why people travel so far to see this place.
t.near davos@46.8,10.0:
Flüela tops out at 2,383 metres, a wide, bare saddle between the Schwarzhorn and the Weisshorn, and the first thing you notice when you get there is the silence. The road from Davos has climbed through the Flüela valley, first through pine and larch, then out onto open pasture, and now you are in a stony world of scree, snowfields and two small dark lakes beside the road. The old hospice at the top, a solid stone building, has served travellers for generations and still serves coffee, soup and cake to riders who arrive cold.

The pass links Davos, in the Prättigau and Landwasser valleys, with Susch in the Lower Engadine, and it has been used since the Middle Ages, when mule trains carried goods between the two regions. The modern road was built in the 1860s, and it has always been a seasonal route: in winter heavy snow and avalanches close it, typically from November to May, although the canton tries to keep it open as long as possible, and closures can happen at short notice. Since the Vereina rail tunnel opened in 1999, with a car-carrying train between Klosters and the Engadine, the pass has become a summer road for those who want to ride it for its own sake.

The riding is good rather than technical. On the Davos side, the climb is steady and well surfaced, with long bends and a few hairpins, and the road is wide enough for comfortable overtaking. On the Engadine side, the descent to Susch is steeper and more twisting, with a series of hairpins through the forest and views down into the Lower Engadine. Watch for cyclists, who love this pass, and for cattle and sheep on the open pasture. The weather can change quickly: snow can fall at the top even in July, and fog can roll in from the valleys.

The landscape around the pass is wild and empty, and it is a good place for spotting wildlife: marmots whistle from the rocks, ibex graze on the high slopes, and golden eagles hunt overhead. The Schwarzhorn, to the south, is a popular walk from the top of the pass, with views over the whole of Graubünden. For fuel and food, Davos is about ten kilometres away with every service, and Zernez and Susch, on the Engadine side, have stations and restaurants. Zernez is also the gateway to the Swiss National Park, the oldest in the Alps.
t.near teglio@46.2,10.1:
Teglio gave the Valtellina its name, so the locals say, and it also gave Italy one of its most satisfying dishes. Pizzoccheri, short, flat ribbons of buckwheat pasta cooked with potatoes and cabbage, then layered with melted Valtellina Casera cheese and garlic butter, were born in this hilltop village, and there is an academy here dedicated to defending the recipe. After a morning on the passes, a plate of it will fuel you for the rest of the day, or put you to sleep, depending on your constitution.

The village sits on a sunny terrace on the north side of the valley, high above the Adda river, with the Orobie Alps on the other side. Its finest building is the Palazzo Besta, a Renaissance palace with a frescoed courtyard, built by a powerful local family in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Around it, the slopes are covered in terraced vineyards held up by thousands of kilometres of dry-stone walls, where Nebbiolo grapes, known here as Chiavennasca, are grown for the Valtellina Superiore wines. One local speciality, Sforzato, is made from grapes dried for months before pressing, giving a rich, strong red.

At about 1,170 metres, it is not a high pass, and the road is broad, well surfaced and busy, with long, sweeping bends through forest and views over the valley. Aprica itself is a ski resort strung out along the road at the top, with hotels, restaurants and shops, quiet in summer. Just to the east, the narrow road over the Mortirolo, one of the most feared climbs in professional cycling, offers a much more technical alternative for riders who like steep gradients and tight hairpins.

The Valtellina is a long, deep valley, and in summer it can be hot and hazy in the bottom, so the best riding is in the morning or the late afternoon. Traffic on the main road along the valley floor can be heavy, especially on weekends, with trucks and tourists heading for the passes. For fuel and supplies, Tirano, about nine kilometres east, is the main town, and it is also the end of the famous Bernina Express railway from St. Moritz. Aprica and the villages on the valley floor also have fuel stations, bars and restaurants.
t.near estes park@40.4,-105.6:
Trail Ridge Road begins its climb here, a few miles west of Estes Park, and by the time you reach this stretch of US 34, you have entered Rocky Mountain National Park and left the town far below. The road winds up through forests of ponderosa pine and Douglas fir, past meadows where elk graze, and around curves that open up views of the Continental Divide. Around Many Parks Curve, a parking area on a tight bend gives one of the best early views: a series of mountain meadows, or parks, spread out below, with Longs Peak, the highest summit in the park, towering over them to the south.

Trail Ridge Road was completed in the early 1930s, and it was designed to give motorists a spectacular drive with gentle grades and wide curves. It is the highest continuous paved road in the United States, reaching more than 12,000 feet, and about eleven miles of it run above the treeline, through alpine tundra. It links Estes Park, on the east side of the park, with Grand Lake on the west, and it follows in part an old trail used by the Ute and Arapaho peoples to cross the mountains.

Down in the meadows, the elk are a major attraction, especially in autumn, when the bulls bugle to attract mates, a strange, high-pitched call that echoes through the valleys. They can be found in large numbers in Moraine Park and Horseshoe Park, just off the road, and they often wander onto the road and into the town of Estes Park itself. Keep your distance, since they can be aggressive during the rut, in September and October.

For riders, the lower part of the road is a gentle introduction, with good surface, steady grades and smooth curves. Summer weekends are crowded, and the park has used a timed-entry reservation system during the busiest months, so check the current rules before you go. The road is usually open from late May to mid-October, depending on snow. Estes Park, about nine kilometres east, is a busy gateway town with fuel, food and lodging, and is the last place to fill up before the climb. The Stanley Hotel, on a hill above the town, inspired Stephen King to write The Shining after he stayed there in the 1970s.
t.near estes park@40.4,-105.7:
Up here, near the treeline, the trees give up. Around Rainbow Curve and on toward Forest Canyon Overlook, the spruce and fir that lined the lower road shrink into twisted, stunted shapes called krummholz, bent and sheared by the wind, and then disappear altogether, leaving a vast, open world of tundra, rock and sky. The views are enormous: deep glacial valleys, the jagged peaks of the Continental Divide, and on a clear day the plains stretching away to the east. You are above 11,000 feet, and the air is thin and cold.

The alpine tundra is one of the most fragile environments in the park, and it is protected with care. Plants here grow slowly, with a growing season of only a few weeks a year, and a single footstep can damage them for decades, so stay on the paths. In summer the tundra is covered in tiny wildflowers, alpine forget-me-nots, moss campion and sky pilot, and you might see marmots sunning themselves on rocks, pikas collecting grass for the winter, and bighorn sheep or elk grazing on the high slopes. Ptarmigan, whose feathers turn white in winter, are almost invisible against the rocks.

Forest Canyon Overlook, a short walk from the road, looks down into a deep valley carved by glaciers, with the Big Thompson River at its bottom and the peaks of the Divide above. Further on, the road reaches its highest point, at 12,183 feet, and the Alpine Visitor Center, at the top of a steep cirque, has exhibits, food, toilets and views across the park.

The riding is spectacular but demanding, not because the road is technical, but because of the conditions. The curves are smooth and the grades gentle, but there are no guardrails in places, the drops are steep, and the weather can change in minutes. On summer afternoons, storm cells build over the Divide with lightning, hail and strong winds, and you do not want to be on the exposed tundra when lightning strikes. Snow can fall at any time of year, and the road is closed from mid-October to late May. The altitude can also cause headaches, breathlessness and fatigue, so take it easy, drink plenty of water, and ride early in the day. Fuel is not sold inside the park, so fill up in Estes Park or Grand Lake.
t.near vik@65.2,12.1:
Sømna is a low, green coastal district on the Helgeland coast, south of Brønnøysund, with flat farmland, lakes and a shoreline broken into small bays, islets and skerries. It is unusual country for Norway: there are no great mountains here, and the farms spread out across open land under a huge sky, with the sea glinting on one side and the distant peaks of Vega and the coastal islands on the horizon. The village of Vik is the main settlement, a small place with a church, a school and a few shops.

This stretch is part of the Kystriksveien, the Coastal Route that follows the Helgeland coast for hundreds of kilometres from Steinkjer to Bodø, using roads, bridges and ferries to link a chain of islands, fjords and small communities. It is one of the great slow rides of Norway, and Sømna is one of its gentler interludes, where you can relax after the ferries and the mountains further south.

The landscape has been farmed for a very long time, and the soil here is better than in most of coastal Norway, which is why the farms have lasted and why the district looks so much softer than its neighbours. Today the area is known for dairy farming and for its quiet beaches, some of them white sand, which are surprisingly warm to walk on in high summer, even if the water stays cold.

The riding is easy and relaxed, with gentle curves, long straights and good surface, and very little traffic outside the summer weeks. The wind can be strong on the open coast, and the weather changes quickly. The best time is a clear evening in June or July, when the sun is low and the light across the farmland and the sea is soft and golden. To the north, the mountain of Torghatten, with its famous hole through the middle, comes into view as you approach Brønnøysund.

Vik has a small shop, and Brønnøysund, about twenty kilometres north, is the larger town with fuel, cafes, hotels and all services. There is little in between, so plan your stops. The ferry crossings on the Kystriksveien follow fixed timetables, so check them before setting off.
t.br nn ysund@65.5,12.2:
Brønnøysund likes to call itself the middle of Norway, and if you measure along the long coast from the Swedish border in the south to the Russian one in the north, it has a fair claim. It is a small, pleasant coastal town on a narrow strait, with a harbour full of boats, a few streets of shops and painted wooden houses, and a view across a sea studded with islands. Most Norwegians know the name for a different reason: the Brønnøysund Register Centre, the national registry for companies and other official records, is based here, and every business in the country has its paperwork filed in this small town.

The landmark everyone comes to see lies just south of town. Torghatten is a mountain with a hole right through it, a tunnel about 160 metres long and over thirty metres high, carved by waves and frost when the sea stood much higher after the last ice age. Local legend tells a better story: a troll called Hestmannen shot an arrow at a girl he desired, and a troll king threw his hat into the arrow's path to save her, and the hat turned to stone with the hole in it. There is a footpath up to the hole from the car park, steep but short, and the view through it toward the sea is extraordinary.

The town sits on the Kystriksveien, the Coastal Route along the Helgeland coast, and from here the road goes north toward the ferry crossings and the islands, with Vega, a UNESCO World Heritage archipelago known for its eider-down tradition, reachable by boat. The riding around Brønnøysund is easy and relaxed, with good roads, light traffic outside summer and long views over the sea. The bridge over the strait to Torget, the island with Torghatten, is a beautiful arch with a fine view back to town.

Brønnøysund has all services: fuel, shops, cafes, restaurants and hotels, as well as a hospital and an airport. It is a good place to rest, eat and plan the ferries ahead, which run to timetables and can fill up in summer. The harbour is a pleasant place for a coffee in the evening light, and the shops sell local fish and seafood. The weather can be wet and windy, but on a clear summer evening the light over the islands is magical.
t.sandnessj en@66.0,12.6:
The first thing you notice approaching Sandnessjøen is the mountain range behind it: seven peaks in a row, rising steeply from the island of Alsten, known as De syv søstre, the Seven Sisters. Legend says they were troll maidens turned to stone by the rising sun, and they dominate every view of the town. Sandnessjøen itself is a busy coastal town and the main centre of the Alstahaug area, with a harbour serving fishing boats, the offshore industry and the Hurtigruten coastal ships.

The Helgeland Bridge, a long and elegant suspension bridge, connects Alsten to the mainland at Leirfjord, and riding across it gives you a wide view over the fjords and islands. It opened in 1991 and replaced a ferry crossing. The town is also on the Kystriksveien, the Coastal Route, and from here the route continues north by ferry and road through a landscape of islands and mountains toward the Arctic Circle.

History lives just south of town at Alstahaug, where Petter Dass, the priest and poet, served in the late seventeenth century. He wrote verse about the people and nature of northern Norway, especially a long poem called The Trumpet of Nordland, which is still read today, and he is remembered as one of the great figures of Norwegian literature. The old stone church at Alstahaug, from the Middle Ages, and a modern museum dedicated to him, built into the landscape, make a fine short visit.

The riding around Alsten is easy, with a coastal road around the island, gentle curves and fine views of the Seven Sisters and the sea. There is a road along the western side of the mountains, quiet and scenic. The surface is generally good, but the wind can be strong on the bridge and the exposed parts of the coast. The peaks can be climbed by hikers in summer, all seven in a day if you are fit, and on clear days the view from the top is spectacular.

Sandnessjøen has all services, including fuel, food and beds. A night here, a walk along the harbour and an early start for the ferries ahead is a sound plan. The fish and seafood in the town are excellent, and in summer the evening light over the islands to the west lasts all night.
t.near vagaholmen@66.6,13.3:
Somewhere on the water between Kilboghamn and Jektvik, the ferry on the Coastal Route crosses the Arctic Circle, and a small globe-shaped marker on a rocky islet tells you so. This part of Rødøy municipality is where Helgeland stops being gentle: the mountains close in, the fjords grow steep and dark, and the coast breaks into hundreds of islands with steep sides. Vågaholmen, the main settlement, is a small village with a harbour, a shop and a few houses, about ten kilometres north of here on the road toward the next ferry.

The geography is the story. Rødøy is a scattered municipality of islands and narrow strips of land along the mainland, and most of the people live in small communities along the shore. The island of Rødøy itself has a famous mountain called Rødøyløva, the Rødøy lion, which from the sea looks like a crouching lion. The area has an old church on Rødøy and remains of settlement going back thousands of years, and fishing was always the basis of life here.

The riding on this stretch is short and sweet. The road between the ferries is narrow and twisting, with tight bends, short climbs and a surface that varies. Traffic depends on the ferry timetables: you get a small group of cars after each boat, then nothing for an hour. The views are spectacular, with steep peaks across the fjords, and on a clear day you start to see the ice of Svartisen, Norway's second-largest glacier, further north. Weather changes fast, and the wind on the ferries can be cold even in summer.

This is a section where planning matters. The ferries follow timetables, and missing one can mean waiting an hour or more, so check before you leave. Services are sparse: small shops in the villages, but fuel only in a few places, and the nearest larger towns are Ørnes to the north and Mo i Rana inland. The ferries usually have a cafe on board, which is a good place for a waffle and a coffee. In midsummer the sun stays up all night here, just north of the circle, and the light on the islands is unforgettable.
t.near inndyr@67.1,14.0:
The outer coast of Gildeskål, north of the village of Inndyr, is one of those quiet stretches of northern Norway where the Coastal Route stops showing off and simply follows the shore. Sandhornøya, the island just north, is dominated by the steep peak of Sandhornet, and the road skirts the water between fjords, small farms and islands, with Bodø about twenty kilometres further on. The landscape is a mix of white beaches, green fields, rocky headlands and mountains rising directly from the sea.

Gildeskål has a long history. Its old church, a medieval stone building from the twelfth century, is one of the oldest in northern Norway, and it sits close to the newer church near Inndyr, together a reminder that this coast was settled, wealthy and connected to the rest of Norway long before the roads came. Fishing and farming have supported people here for centuries, and today salmon farming is an important industry, with farms in many of the fjords.

The riding is easy and pleasant. The road follows the shore with gentle curves and short climbs, and the surface is generally good. Traffic is light, apart from the stretches close to Bodø. In summer the midnight sun hangs over the sea to the north, and the light on the beaches and islands at night is soft and golden. The weather can change quickly, with fog rolling in from the sea or wind picking up on exposed parts, and the temperature rarely gets very warm even in July.

A short ride north brings you to Saltstraumen, near Bodø, the strongest tidal current in the world, where huge volumes of water squeeze through a narrow strait between the fjords every six hours, forming whirlpools that can be several metres across. Time your visit to coincide with the peak flow, and watch from the bridge or the rocks below. It is an extraordinary sight, and the fishing is famous.

Inndyr has a small shop and some services, but fuel and the full range of shops, cafes and hotels are in Bodø, the largest town in Nordland, about twenty kilometres away. Bodø is also the port for the ferries to Lofoten, which makes it a natural base for the next stage of the journey.
t.near kabelvag@68.2,14.2:
Henningsvær is the fishing village that turns up in half the photographs of Lofoten, and for once the pictures do not lie. It sits on a cluster of small islands at the tip of a long peninsula, joined to the main island by a pair of bridges, with brightly painted houses, drying racks for stockfish, a busy harbour and a backdrop of jagged peaks across the water. On one of the islands there is a football pitch, laid out on the rock and surrounded by the sea, which became famous after drone photographs of it went around the world.

The village grew on the Lofoten fishery, the great winter cod fishery that has drawn fishermen to these islands for over a thousand years. Every winter, the skrei, the spawning cod from the Barents Sea, come to the waters around Lofoten, and in the old days thousands of fishermen came from all over northern Norway to catch them, living in the rorbuer, the red fishing cabins on the shore. The fish were dried on wooden racks to make stockfish, which was exported to Europe, and the trade made Lofoten rich. In late winter and spring, the racks in Henningsvær are still hung with fish.

Today the village is also a centre for artists and climbers, with galleries, cafes and climbing schools, and in summer it can be busy. The road out from the E10 follows the shore along the base of the mountains, with tight bends, narrow sections, and a few single-track bridges, and it ranks among the most beautiful short rides in Lofoten, especially in the evening light. Traffic in summer is heavy, so take it slowly and be patient.

The weather in Lofoten changes constantly, and it can be wet, windy and cold even in July. But the light, when it comes, is extraordinary, and the midnight sun from late May to mid-July means you can ride and walk at any hour. In winter, the northern lights are common.

Henningsvær has cafes, restaurants and shops, and Kabelvåg and Svolvær, about fifteen to twenty kilometres away, have fuel, hotels and all services. Kabelvåg is also home to the large wooden church known as the Lofoten Cathedral, and an aquarium and museum about the fishery.
t.bad endorf@47.9,12.3:
Bad Endorf is a spa town in the Chiemgau, a few kilometres west of the Chiemsee, and on a long day to Berchtesgaden it is the kind of place where you top up the tank and keep moving. That is not an insult. The town is tidy and functional, with fuel, bakeries and supermarkets, and it sits in some of the most pleasant rolling country in southern Bavaria, so the stop costs you nothing in scenery.

The spa side of things comes from iodine-rich brine found deep underground, which the town turned into a thermal bath in the twentieth century. You will not have time for a soak on a ride day, but it explains the slightly genteel air of the centre. What is far more interesting from the saddle is the landscape around it. This is glacial country: the great Inn glacier of the last ice age left behind a scatter of lakes and hills when it melted, and the result is a soft patchwork of meadows, woods, moors and small lakes like those of the Eggstätt lake district just south-east of town.

Rimsting, a few minutes away, sits on the western shore of the Chiemsee, the largest lake in Bavaria. From Prien, a little further, boats run out to Herreninsel, where King Ludwig II built his unfinished copy of Versailles. It is a half-day excursion rather than a quick stop, but worth knowing about if you ever come back with time to spare.

The roads around Bad Endorf are a mixture of smooth state roads and narrow farm lanes, often lined with fruit trees and passing through hamlets where the tractors are bigger than the houses. Expect cow muck on the tarmac after the cattle have crossed, especially in the mornings. On a clear day the Chiemgau Alps fill the southern horizon, the Kampenwand and Hochfelln standing out above the foothills, and the ride south towards Traunstein and the German Alpine Road gives you increasingly dramatic views. Summer weekends bring traffic and the occasional police control around the lakes; on a weekday morning in May or September you will have the lanes nearly to yourself, and the air will smell of cut grass and woodsmoke.
t.near grunwald@48.0,11.5:
It is one of the wealthiest suburbs in Germany, a place of large villas hidden behind hedges, and also home to the Bavaria Film studios at Geiselgasteig, where films and television series have been made for over a century. The studio tour is a classic Munich day out, with sets from famous productions such as Das Boot.

Grünwald has a small medieval castle, perched above the Isar, which served the Wittelsbach dukes as a hunting seat. The river below is a playground for Munich: on summer weekends, wooden rafts carrying groups of revellers, a brass band and a lot of beer float down from Wolfratshausen to Thalkirchen, a tradition that goes back to the timber rafts that once supplied the city. The riverbanks are lined with gravel beaches, forests and walking paths.

As a starting point for rides south to the Alps, this area is ideal. It lies outside the city centre, with easy access to the roads south through the Isar valley and the forests of the Munich gravel plain. The quiet road through Straßlach and down towards Wolfratshausen and Bad Tölz is a pleasant way to warm up, avoiding the motorway, with forests, fields and occasional glimpses of the mountains on the horizon. From Bad Tölz, the German Alpine Road leads east towards Tegernsee, Schliersee and beyond.

There is fuel and food in Grünwald and the surrounding towns, and plenty of beer gardens for the end of the day. On a clear day, the Alps are visible from the high bank, especially when the föhn wind blows, bringing warm, dry air and unusually clear views, a phenomenon that Munich people both love and blame for headaches. Early morning on a summer weekend is the best time to leave, before the traffic builds up and the day-trippers head for the lakes.
t.milevsko@49.5,14.4:
Milevsko is a quiet South Bohemian town on the rolling uplands between the Vltava and the Lužnice, and you will probably not have heard of it. It deserves a little more credit than a passing fill-up, though, because on its edge stands one of the oldest monasteries in Bohemia: a Premonstratensian abbey founded in the late twelfth century, with a Romanesque basilica that has survived, much altered, through wars, fires and the long communist decades. The monastery grounds are calm and green, and walking around the old walls takes only a few minutes.

The town itself is modest, with a square, a few churches and the services you would expect in a place of about nine thousand people: fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and pubs where a Czech lunch of soup and goulash costs very little. It is a practical stop on the long day to Český Krumlov, roughly halfway between Prague and the south.

What makes this part of the ride worth it lies west of town. The Vltava here has been dammed into a long chain of reservoirs, and the Orlík reservoir winds through a deep, forested valley like a Scandinavian fjord. The Žďákov Bridge, a huge steel arch, carries the road high above the water, and the view from it takes some beating anywhere in Bohemia. On the shore stand two famous castles: Orlík, a white romantic château perched on a rock above the lake, and Zvíkov, an older, rugged royal castle at the meeting of the Vltava and the Otava, often called the king of Czech castles.

The roads around Milevsko are typical of the Czech countryside: narrow, sometimes patched, winding through fields, forests and villages, with little traffic outside the main routes. They can be a joy on a dry day, but watch out for tractors, potholes and loose gravel at junctions. Czech law requires dipped headlights at all times, and there is a zero-tolerance policy on alcohol for drivers and riders, so save the beer for the evening. In summer, the reservoirs fill with holidaymakers; in spring and autumn, the roads are quieter and the forests smell of resin.
t.stelvio@46.6,10.5:
The village of Stelvio, Stilfs in German, clings to a steep slope above the Val Venosta in South Tyrol, a cluster of old houses and narrow lanes high above the valley floor, and most people who pass the turn-off have their eyes on something bigger. A few kilometres up the valley, at Prato allo Stelvio, begins the most famous mountain road in Europe: the climb to the Passo dello Stelvio, at 2,757 metres, with its numbered sequence of forty-eight hairpins stacked one above the other on the northern face of the mountain.

The road was built by the Austrian Empire in the 1820s, to link Lombardy, then under Habsburg rule, with Tyrol, and it was an extraordinary feat of engineering for its time. It became a front line in the First World War, when Italian and Austro-Hungarian troops fought at altitude among the glaciers, and traces of trenches and fortifications can still be found near the pass. Today it is a place of pilgrimage for riders, cyclists and drivers, and on summer weekends the top of the pass resembles a fairground, with sausage stands, souvenir shops and crowds.

The climb from Prato is a serious undertaking. The hairpins are tight, steep and often crowded with cyclists, cars and buses, and the road is narrow in places, with stone walls and steep drops. Above Trafoi, the views of the Ortler, the highest mountain in South Tyrol, and its glaciers are spectacular. From the top, you can descend south to Bormio or take the Umbrail Pass into Switzerland, one of the highest road passes in the country, down into the Val Müstair. The pass is typically closed from autumn to late spring, often from early November to late May or June, depending on the snow, so check before you go.

For food, the villages of the Val Venosta offer hearty Tyrolean fare, such as speck, dumplings and apple strudel, as the valley is famous for its apples. Prato allo Stelvio has fuel and services. Be aware that the weather at the top can be much colder than in the valley, with snow possible even in summer, so carry warm layers.
t.garda@45.6,10.7:
Garda is the town that gave the lake its name, and it sits on the eastern shore, on a gentle bay sheltered by the headland of Punta San Vigilio and the hill of the Rocca, where a castle once stood. It is worth saying straight away that if your ride is a western shore ride, you are on the opposite side here; the lake is long and narrow, and the car ferry between Torri del Benaco, just north of Garda, and Toscolano Maderno on the western shore is the quickest way to get across. The crossing itself, with the mountains rising on both sides, is a lovely break.

The town is charming, with a long lakeside promenade lined with palm trees, cafés and restaurants, and a small old centre of narrow lanes and Venetian-style palazzi. The eastern shore is known as the Riviera degli Olivi, for its olive groves, and the area produces excellent olive oil, as well as Bardolino wine, a light red made in the hills just to the south. Lunch on the lakefront, with a glass of Bardolino and fish from the lake, is an easy pleasure.

The western shore, across the water, is more dramatic. The Gardesana Occidentale, the road along the western shore, runs through dozens of tunnels carved into the cliffs, with views over the lake. Above Campione del Garda, the Strada della Forra, which climbs through a narrow gorge to Tremosine, is often described as one of the most spectacular roads in the world, and it featured in the opening chase of the James Bond film Quantum of Solace. It is narrow, twisty and spectacular, with overhanging rock walls.

On the eastern shore, the road above Garda climbs onto the slopes of Monte Baldo, with fine views over the lake. Traffic around the lake can be very heavy in summer, especially on weekends, and the lakeside roads are slow, so plan to ride early in the morning or in the evening. Fuel and services are available in Garda and the surrounding towns. Come in May or late September if you can, when it is mild and far less crowded.
t.schrobenhausen on the way back@48.6,11.2:
In spring, the sandy fields around Schrobenhausen are covered with long, ridged rows under black plastic, and from April to June the whole region revolves around a single vegetable: white asparagus. Schrobenhausener Spargel is among the best-known asparagus in Germany, protected by an origin designation, and the town even has a museum devoted to it. If you are passing in season, the restaurants serve it in every possible form, classically with boiled potatoes, ham and hollandaise sauce.

The town has a well-preserved medieval wall, with towers and a moat, enclosing the old centre. The painter Franz von Lenbach, famous for his portraits of Bismarck and other notables of the German Empire, was born here in 1836, and his birthplace is now a small museum. The river Paar flows past the town, and the countryside around is gentle, with fields, woods and small villages.

To the north lies the Donaumoos, once the largest fen in southern Germany, which was drained and settled at the end of the eighteenth century under the Elector Karl Theodor. The landscape is flat, with straight roads and drainage channels, and the peat soils have been sinking ever since, as the drained peat decomposes. It is a strange, quiet landscape, with big skies and fields stretching to the horizon.

For a swim on the way back to Munich, there are several quarry and gravel lakes in the area, some with small beaches and kiosks, and the water is clear and refreshing in summer. Choose an official bathing spot, as some lakes are private or used for fishing only. The roads around Schrobenhausen are generally quiet and flat, with gentle curves through the fields and woods, and the ride back to Munich takes about an hour. Fuel, supermarkets and restaurants are available in town, and in May a warm plate of the local asparagus is reason enough to stop twice.
t.near germering@48.1,11.4:
West of Munich, the city fades into a belt of comfortable suburbs, Germering, Planegg, Gräfelfing, set among fields and patches of forest on the flat gravel plain that stretches towards the Alps. The ride ends among them, near the forest of the Kreuzlinger Forst, and it is a convenient finish for rides that have gone south to the Grossglockner and the Allgäu.

It is not a dramatic place, but it is a peaceful one. The Würm, a small river flowing out of Lake Starnberg, winds through Planegg and Gräfelfing, with meadows and paths along its banks. To the west, Fürstenfeldbruck has one of the most magnificent Baroque churches in Bavaria, the abbey church of Fürstenfeld, with a lavishly decorated interior. To the south-west, the Ammersee and Lake Starnberg are popular with Munich people for sailing, swimming and beer gardens.

The Grossglockner High Alpine Road, the goal of the overnight ride, is one of the most spectacular mountain roads in Europe, climbing to more than 2,500 metres at the Hochtor tunnel, with views of the Grossglockner, Austria's highest mountain, and the Pasterze glacier. It was built in the 1930s, and it is a toll road, typically open from May to October. The Allgäu, to the south-west, is a landscape of green hills, lakes and mountains, with excellent riding on quiet roads.

Coming back to Munich after a long weekend, the motorways can be congested, especially the A8 from Salzburg and the A96 from Lindau, so it is worth timing your return carefully. Once in the western suburbs, the roads are calmer, though Germering's streets are busy with commuters. There are fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants in Germering and the neighbouring towns, and Munich's beer gardens are close enough for an evening celebration. Order a Mass, sit under the chestnuts and let the hum of the motorway fade out of your ears.
t.halfing on the way back@48.0,12.3:
After a weekend on the Grossglockner, with its glaciers, hairpins and thin, cold air, there is something deeply satisfying about stopping in the soft green hills of the Chiemgau and lowering yourself into a lake. The point lies near Halfing, a village between Rosenheim and the Chiemsee, and within a few kilometres there are several lakes that make ideal swimming stops on the way back to Munich.

The closest is the Simssee, a long, narrow lake to the south-west, with reedy shores, meadows running down to the water and public bathing spots where families from Rosenheim come on summer weekends. A little further east lies the Eggstätt-Hemhof lake district, a cluster of small lakes in woods and moorland, left behind by the melting Inn glacier, protected as a nature reserve. Some of the lakes, such as the Langbürgner See and the Hartsee, are wonderfully clear, with a greenish tint and gently shelving shores. Swimming is allowed at designated spots, which are well signed.

Halfing itself is a typical Upper Bavarian village, with a church, a few inns and farmhouses with wooden balconies covered in geraniums. The countryside around is a gentle patchwork of meadows, woods and moors, with views south to the mountains of the Chiemgau Alps on clear days. The smell of cut grass, the clang of cowbells and the sound of church bells in the evening make it feel like the Bavaria of postcards.

The roads here are quiet and winding, with good surfaces, but they are narrow in places, and you will share them with tractors, cyclists and the occasional herd of cows. On summer weekends, the lakes are busy, and parking near the bathing spots can be tight, so arrive early or late. For fuel, Bad Endorf, about six kilometres away, and Rosenheim are the best options. After the swim, a beer garden lunch with a Brotzeit, a plate of cold meats, cheese and bread, completes the picture before the last stretch home on the A8.
t.grunwald@48.0,11.5:
It is a quiet, wealthy area of villas and forests, and for riders coming back from the Tegernsee and the Sudelfeld it is a pleasant, low-key finish, close enough to the city but still among trees.

The plateau has been inhabited for a very long time. In the forest near Grünwald, the Römerschanze is an earthwork on the edge of the Isar bluff, used as a fortified site in prehistoric and later times, and Roman roads crossed the river nearby. Upstream, at Schäftlarn, a Benedictine abbey sits beside the river, with a Baroque church and a long tradition of brewing, and its beer garden is a popular spot for walkers and cyclists following the Isar paths.

The Tegernsee and Sudelfeld ride is a classic Munich day out. The Tegernsee is a beautiful lake surrounded by mountains, with a monastery and brewery at Tegernsee town and elegant villas around the shore. From there, the German Alpine Road continues over the Sudelfeld pass road to Bayrischzell, a curving mountain road that is extremely popular with motorcyclists, and as a result it has a history of accidents, noise complaints and frequent police controls. Ride it with respect.

Coming back to Munich, the roads through the Isar valley and the forests south of the city are calm and pleasant, especially in the evening. The B11 and the Isartal roads are lined with trees, and the views over the valley are lovely. Grünwald, Pullach and the surrounding villages have fuel and shops, and there is no shortage of beer gardens for a final drink. On summer evenings, the river below is full of swimmers, kayakers and people grilling on the gravel banks, a scene of very Bavarian contentment.
The Rottal, in Lower Bavaria, is a land of rolling hills, small woods and wide fields, with farmhouses scattered across the slopes and onion-domed church towers rising above the villages. It is far from the famous Alpine scenery of the south, and few tourists come here, but it has a quiet, pastoral beauty that many riders find refreshing. Johanniskirchen is a small village in the hills between the Vils and the Rott, on the way back towards Munich, and the lanes around it are as calm as any in Bavaria.

This is traditional farming country, and the Rottal was once famous for horse breeding, producing a sturdy warmblood used for farm work and cavalry. Nearby Arnstorf has a moated castle and a fine Baroque church, and the small towns of the region have markets and inns serving hearty Lower Bavarian food: roast pork with dumplings, sausages and local beer.

For a swim, the best-known spot in the area is the Rottauensee, a reservoir on the Rott near Postmünster, about twenty kilometres south, with beaches, meadows and a path around the shore, popular with families in summer. There are also smaller ponds and lakes in the hills, some with bathing spots, though many are private or used for fishing. Further south-east, the spa towns of the Bavarian Bäderdreieck, Bad Füssing, Bad Griesbach and Bad Birnbach, offer thermal pools if you prefer warm water.

The roads in the Rottal are quiet and winding, rising and falling over the hills, with good surfaces and very little traffic, ideal for relaxed riding. Watch out for tractors, mud on the road after harvesting and the occasional deer at dusk. Johanniskirchen is small, with few services, so fill up in Arnstorf, Eggenfelden or Pfarrkirchen. The ride back to Munich takes about two hours, through the hills and across the flat plains of the Isar valley.
t.pilsen@49.7,13.4:
In 1842, a Bavarian brewer named Josef Groll brewed a new kind of beer in the town brewery of Plzeň: a clear, golden lager, crisp and hoppy, made with the soft local water, Saaz hops and pale malt. It was an instant success, and the style, named after the town, became the most imitated beer in the world. The original is still brewed here as Pilsner Urquell, and a tour of the brewery, with its historic cellars and a glass of unfiltered beer straight from the oak barrel, is the obvious thing to do. Save it for the end of the day, though; the Czech blood alcohol limit for riders is zero.

Pilsen is the fourth-largest city in the Czech Republic, an industrial centre with a handsome historic core. The main square is dominated by the Gothic cathedral of St. Bartholomew, whose tower is the tallest church tower in the country, and you can climb it for views over the city. The Great Synagogue, built in the late nineteenth century, is one of the largest synagogues in the world. The city was also the birthplace of the Škoda Works, the engineering firm founded by Emil Škoda, which made everything from locomotives to weapons.

In May 1945, Pilsen was liberated by the US Army, while the rest of the country was liberated by the Soviets, and the city celebrates the event every year with a festival of parades and military vehicles. Under communism, the American role was officially played down, and the festival has a special significance today.

For lunch, Pilsen has countless pubs and restaurants serving Czech food: svíčková, beef in a creamy vegetable sauce with dumplings, goulash, roast pork and fried cheese. Prices are low and portions generous. The roads around Pilsen are good for riding, winding through the hills, forests and villages of western Bohemia, with castles at every turn. The city itself has fuel and all services, though traffic can be heavy.
t.monticelli brusati@45.6,10.1:
Franciacorta is Italy's answer to Champagne, and Monticelli Brusati sits in the middle of it. Sparkling wine made by the classic method, second fermentation in the bottle, has been the business of these low hills between Brescia and Lake Iseo since the 1960s, and the result is a landscape of tidy vineyards, cypress-lined drives and cellar doors, with old stone villages tucked into the folds of the land.

It is a good place to fill the tank before the mountains. Monticelli itself is small, so if the pumps in the village are shut, Rodengo-Saiano, a few minutes south, is the reliable alternative. Rodengo also has the great Olivetan abbey of San Nicola, with three cloisters and frescoed halls, a surprisingly grand building in a wine village.

North of here the hills drop to Lake Iseo, the least known of the big Lombard lakes and in many ways the most charming. Monte Isola, in the middle of it, is the largest inhabited lake island in Europe, with fishing villages and almost no cars. The road along the eastern shore, towards Lovere, runs through tunnels and along the water's edge with fine views.

The ride towards Passo San Marco takes you west and north, through Bergamo's valleys and up Val Brembana, where the roads narrow and climb steeply through forests and old mining villages. The pass itself crosses to the Valtellina with a long series of hairpins on the northern side.

Round Monticelli the roads are narrow, winding and well surfaced, with gentle gradients and little traffic, though weekend wine visitors can slow things down. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the vineyards are green or golden and the air is fresh. Save the tasting for the evening; the carabinieri are not sentimental about bubbles.
t.marco@45.8,11.0:
Dante may have ridden past here. In the twelfth canto of the Inferno he compares a steep, broken descent in hell to a great landslide on the Adige south of Trento, and most scholars believe he meant the Lavini di Marco, the chaos of boulders and bare rock above this village. The slope has another secret: in the 1990s, scientists found hundreds of dinosaur footprints preserved in its limestone slabs, and a path now leads up to them.

Marco is a quiet village in the Vallagarina, the stretch of the Adige valley between Trento and Verona, just south of Rovereto. The valley is broad and busy, with the motorway, the railway and the river running side by side, but the slopes on either side rise steeply into the mountains. Brentonico, on a plateau above, is the gateway to Monte Baldo, a long ridge with alpine meadows and views over Lake Garda.

Rovereto, a few minutes north, is a lively town with a fine modern art museum, the MART, and a huge bell, the Campana dei Caduti, cast from the bronze of First World War cannons and rung every evening in memory of the dead of all wars. The front line ran through these mountains between 1915 and 1918, and trenches and forts can still be found on the heights.

Food is the reason to stop. The local wine is Marzemino, a light red that Mozart mentions in Don Giovanni, and the trattorie serve canederli, bread dumplings, and polenta with local cheese. Mori, next door, has bakeries, cafés and fuel.

From Mori the road climbs over the low Passo San Giovanni to Torbole on the north shore of Lake Garda, a short ride with a view of the lake that hits you all at once. In the other direction, small roads climb to Brentonico and the Monte Baldo plateau, with tight bends and steep grades.
t.near planegg@48.1,11.4:
The end of a Bavarian lakes day usually means the Würm valley, and this finish lies on its edge, between Planegg, Krailling and Neuried, where Munich's south-western suburbs meet the forests. The Würm flows north out of Lake Starnberg through a gentle valley of meadows and villages, and the Forstenrieder Park, a large forest of beech and spruce, stretches to the east. It is a pleasant, green corner of the city's fringe.

Planegg has a small pilgrimage chapel in the woods, Maria Eich, built around an oak tree in which a statue of the Virgin was placed in the eighteenth century, and it remains a place of quiet devotion. Next door, Martinsried is home to Max Planck institutes and a biotech campus, a hive of research in a suburban setting.

The ride back from Kochelsee and Walchensee takes you over the Kesselberg, a short, steep pass with tight hairpins between the two lakes. It is a classic motorcycle road, but because of accidents and noise, one direction has been closed to motorcycles on weekends and public holidays during the riding season. Check the signs and current rules before you plan the route, and ride it the way you are allowed to.

Lake Starnberg is the obvious place for a last swim. It is large, deep and clear, with public bathing areas along the shore, and on a hot day the water is cool and refreshing. King Ludwig II drowned in its shallows in 1886 in mysterious circumstances, and a cross in the water marks the spot.

The Würm villages keep their beer gardens under chestnut trees, and the order of the evening is not complicated: park, a litre of something cold, a pretzel the size of a steering lock. Refuel on the way in, while you still care.
t.near heiligenblut@47.1,12.8:
At 2,428 metres, Fuscher Törl is the high balcony of the Grossglockner High Alpine Road, a saddle on the northern side where the road loops around a ridge and the whole of the Fusch valley drops away below. A stone monument stands here in memory of the men who built the road, designed by the architect Clemens Holzmeister, and from the terrace you look across a sea of peaks to the summit of the Grossglockner itself, at 3,798 metres the highest mountain in Austria.

The road was built between 1930 and 1935 under the engineer Franz Wallack, partly to give work to thousands of unemployed men during the Depression, and it was designed from the start as a scenic route for tourists. It climbs from Fusch in the north and Heiligenblut in the south through more than thirty hairpins, crossing the main ridge of the Alps in a tunnel at Hochtor. A side road from Fuscher Törl, cobbled and steep, climbs to the Edelweissspitze, the highest point you can reach on the road, with a view over dozens of three-thousand-metre peaks.

On the southern side, a branch road leads to the Kaiser-Franz-Josefs-Höhe, where the Pasterze, the largest glacier in Austria, lies at the foot of the Grossglockner. It has shrunk dramatically in recent decades, and signs along the path show where the ice reached in past years. Marmots whistle from the rocks, and ibex graze on the slopes.

The road is a toll road, open roughly from early May to late October or early November, depending on snow, and closed at night. Weather can change quickly, with snow possible even in summer, and the temperature at the top can be twenty degrees lower than in the valley.

Fill up in the valleys before you climb; Zell am See, Bruck and Heiligenblut are the nearest options. There are restaurants at several points along the road, including Fuscher Törl.
t.near canazei@46.5,11.8:
Passo Pordoi, at 2,239 metres, is the highest point of the Great Dolomites Road, which runs from Bolzano to Cortina d'Ampezzo through the heart of the Dolomites. The pass sits between the Sella group, a massive fortress of rock with sheer walls, and the Marmolada, the highest mountain in the Dolomites, with its glacier. From the top, a cable car climbs to the Sass Pordoi, nearly three thousand metres high, with a view over the whole range.

The Great Dolomites Road was completed in 1909, when this region was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and it was built to open the valleys to tourists. The Pordoi is a legend of the Giro d'Italia, and a monument at the top honours Fausto Coppi, the great Italian cyclist whose name the race still gives to its highest summit each year. A German war cemetery, just below the pass, holds the remains of thousands of soldiers killed in the First and Second World Wars.

The road climbs from Canazei in the Val di Fassa through dozens of hairpins, then drops to Arabba in the Livinallongo valley. It is one of the four passes of the Sella Ronda, the circuit around the Sella group that is a classic for both riders and skiers.

The valleys are home to the Ladin people, who speak a language descended from Latin and have their own culture and traditions. The food is a mix of Italian, Austrian and Ladin influences: canederli, speck, polenta and apple strudel.

The Pordoi is normally kept open through the winter, though storms can shut it for a day or two. Summer weekends are crowded with cars, coaches and hundreds of cyclists grinding up the hairpins, so be patient on the overtakes. Canazei and Arabba are the fuel stops at either end, and the huts at the top serve a fine plate of polenta with mushrooms when the wind gets up.
t.near corvara in badia@46.5,11.9:
Passo Campolongo, at 1,875 metres, is the gentlest of the four Sella passes, a short, easy climb through meadows and larch forests between Corvara in Alta Badia and Arabba in Livinallongo. It is the link that completes the Sella Ronda, and its broad, grassy saddle is a place to pause and look at the peaks around: the Sassongher, a pyramid of rock above Corvara, and the massive walls of the Sella group to the west.

Alta Badia, on the northern side, is a valley of Ladin villages, wooden farmhouses and alpine pastures, and it has become one of the great food destinations of the Alps, with several restaurants holding Michelin stars. The local dishes are simpler but no less delicious: turtres, fried pastries filled with spinach or sauerkraut, and canederli, bread dumplings with speck.

Livinallongo del Col di Lana, on the southern side, is named after a mountain that saw some of the fiercest fighting of the First World War. In 1916, Italian troops dug a tunnel under the Austrian positions on the summit and blew it up with tons of explosives, leaving a crater that is still visible. The front line ran through these mountains, and trenches, tunnels and forts can still be found.

The riding is pleasant and easy, with gentle bends and good surfaces, and the views are superb. In summer, the road is busy with riders doing the Sella Ronda, and cyclists are numerous.

Corvara and Arabba both have fuel and plenty of places to sleep. If the day is going well, take the small detour to a hut on the pastures above the pass, where turtres come hot from the pan and the Sella walls glow orange in the evening.
t.pei enberg@47.8,11.0:
Peißenberg owes its existence to coal. For more than a century a deep mine worked the seams of pitch coal under the town, and when it closed in 1971 the place had to reinvent itself. You can still see traces of the mining past in the old shaft buildings and a small museum, but the modern town is a pleasant, unpretentious market centre in the rolling foothills between the Ammersee and the Alps.

The real draw lies just above it. The Hoher Peißenberg, a lone hill of almost a thousand metres, rises from the moraine country with a pilgrimage church on top and a meteorological observatory that has been recording the weather since 1781, making it one of the oldest mountain weather stations anywhere. The road to the summit is short and steep, and on a clear day the panorama runs along the whole wall of the Bavarian Alps from the Allgäu to the Karwendel, with the Zugspitze unmistakable to the south. It is a superb spot for a photo or simply a pause.

Riding around Peißenberg is a pleasant mix of small roads through meadows, forests and villages with onion-domed churches. To the west, the Ammer river has cut a deep, wooded gorge, and the roads towards Rottenbuch and Wieskirche lead into the classic Pfaffenwinkel landscape, so named for its density of monasteries and churches. Surfaces are good, but on weekends cyclists and day trippers are out in force, and the narrower lanes demand patience.

Peißenberg has fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, so it makes a natural top-up before heading south into the Ammergau and towards Plansee. Weilheim, a few kilometres away, is the larger town if you need more. The inn on the summit of the Hoher Peißenberg is a classic Bavarian stop for coffee and cake with a view.
t.near votice@49.6,14.6:
The hills around Votice belong to the Central Bohemian uplands, a rumpled country of fields, fishponds and small forests between Prague and Tábor. Votice itself is a modest market town with a square, a church and a few thousand inhabitants, a quiet place where the main event of the day might be the arrival of the bus. It has a bakery, shops and fuel, which is all a rider really needs from it.

The local landscape, though, has a legend attached. A short ride south-east rises Blaník, a forested hill that every Czech knows: according to folklore, an army of knights sleeps inside it, waiting to ride out and save the nation in its darkest hour. Smetana included the story in his cycle Má vlast, and the hill has a lookout tower on its summit. Even without the legend, the countryside around it is lovely, with long views over gentle ridges and small villages.

The roads here are narrow and winding, rising over low hills and dipping into valleys with ponds and mills. Surfaces vary a lot, from fresh asphalt to patched and broken stretches, and village roads can have potholes deep enough to be a problem on a sports bike. Watch for tractors and for cars overtaking on blind crests. The D3 motorway runs nearby, handy for a quick escape back towards Prague, but the minor roads are where the pleasure lies.

Benešov, the nearest larger town, has more choice of fuel and food, and its château of Konopiště, once the home of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, whose murder in Sarajevo triggered the First World War, is worth a stop if you have time. In Votice, a coffee on the square and a look at the old houses make a gentle pause before heading on into the rolling uplands.
t.near moosinning@48.3,11.8:
North-east of Munich, the land flattens into a wide plain of fields, drainage ditches and scattered villages. This is the Erdinger Moos, once a vast marsh, drained over the past two centuries and now home to farms, gravel pits and, a few kilometres away, Munich's international airport. Moosinning is one of the villages on its edge, quiet and practical, with a church, a few farms and modern housing.

The riding here is not dramatic, but it has a certain calm charm. Roads run straight between fields of maize and wheat, then curve gently through villages and over small streams. The Isar flows to the north, with riverside woods and gravel banks. On a clear day, the Alps appear as a pale blue line on the southern horizon, a promise of what is to come. Watch for agricultural traffic, especially in harvest season, and for strong crosswinds on the open plain.

Erding, the nearest town, is worth a stop. Its old centre has a pretty square and a tall city tower, and it is home to a famous wheat beer brewery, Erdinger, whose name you have probably seen on bottles worldwide. Nearby, the huge Therme Erding thermal spa draws visitors from all over Bavaria. If you are heading towards the German Alpine Road, though, you will probably want to keep moving south.

For fuel, Erding and the larger villages along the main roads have stations, and bakeries offer pretzels and coffee. The airport area also has services but can be busy. Moosinning is a good place to take a short break, check the route and enjoy the open landscape before turning towards the mountains, where the roads become much more interesting.
t.prittriching@48.2,10.9:
Prittriching lies on the Lechfeld, the broad gravel plain that the River Lech built as it flowed north from the Alps towards the Danube. The village is small and agricultural, with a church, farms and a few modern houses, and the countryside around it is flat and open, given over to fields of maize, wheat and potatoes. It is a quiet place with a long view in every direction.

The Lechfeld has a place in European history. In 955, somewhere on this plain south of Augsburg, Otto the Great defeated the Magyar horsemen who had been raiding central Europe for decades, a victory that helped secure his position and led to his coronation as emperor a few years later. Nothing marks the exact spot, but the open landscape makes it easy to imagine the clash of armies.

On the bike, things are relaxed. Roads are straight and smooth, linking villages across the plain, and the Lech, with its chain of reservoirs and riverside woods, runs to the west. Wind can be strong on the open fields, and farm machinery is common, particularly at harvest time. On a clear day, the Alps rise on the southern horizon, a hint of the mountain roads to come.
