Prittriching has a village inn and a bakery, which can be a good stop for a simple Bavarian meal or coffee. For fuel, the nearby towns of Königsbrunn and Landsberg am Lech are the best bets. Landsberg is especially worth a visit for its medieval old town, perched on the steep bank of the Lech with a weir and colourful houses. From the Lechfeld, the route heads south towards the German Alpine Road, where flat fields give way to mountains and lakes.
t.near au in der hallertau@48.5,11.7:
Tall green walls of hops line the roads around Au in der Hallertau in late summer. The Hallertau is the largest continuous hop-growing region in the world, and its vines climb wires strung between poles about seven metres high, giving the landscape a strange, almost theatrical look. Au, a small market town with a castle and a church, is one of its centres, and the smell of hops at harvest time, from late August into September, is unforgettable.

The hops grown here go into beers all over the world, and many local breweries make the most of their proximity. The landscape is gently hilly, with fields, woods and villages, and the hop gardens add a vertical dimension to the countryside. In winter, the bare poles and wires stand like a grid across the fields, waiting for the next season.

Riding through the Hallertau is a pleasure. The roads roll over hills and through valleys, with good surfaces and moderate traffic. The curves are gentle but frequent, and the landscape changes constantly, from open fields to hop gardens and forests. Be careful of farm vehicles, especially during harvest, when tractors and trailers transport the hops to drying kilns.

Au in der Hallertau has fuel, shops and inns, making it a good place for a break. Mainburg, a few kilometres north, is the other main centre of the region, and the hop museum in Wolnzach to the west explains the history and culture of hop growing. From here, the route continues south towards Munich and the Alps, on the way to the Grossglockner, Austria's highest mountain road.
t.near donauworth@48.7,10.8:
Donauwörth stands where the Wörnitz flows into the Danube, a meeting of waters that made the town important for trade and crossings since the Middle Ages. Its main street, the Reichsstraße, is lined with colourful gabled houses, churches and the old town hall, and it was once part of an important trade route between Nuremberg and Augsburg. Today it is a stop on the Romantic Road, the tourist route that runs from Würzburg to Füssen.

The town has an eventful history. It was a free imperial city, and a religious dispute here in the early seventeenth century helped spark tensions that led to the Thirty Years' War. More recently, it has become an industrial centre, home to a big helicopter factory, and the Käthe Kruse doll workshop, famous across Germany, also has its base here.

The surrounding landscape is varied. To the north lies the Ries, a huge crater formed by a meteorite impact about fifteen million years ago, with the walled town of Nördlingen at its centre. To the south, the Danube valley opens out, with floodplain forests and gravel pits. The roads offer a mix of fast main routes and winding minor roads through the hills and valleys, with good surfaces and moderate traffic.

Donauwörth has no shortage of fuel, supermarkets or places to eat, so it is an easy place to refuel and eat. The Reichsstraße has cafés and beer gardens, perfect for a break. The riverside promenade and the island in the Wörnitz, with its old houses and mill, make a lovely short walk. Beyond, the ride heads south towards the Allgäu, whose green hills and mountain roads are a highlight of any Bavarian tour.
t.near zajecov@49.8,13.9:
For decades the Brdy hills south-west of Prague were off-limits: a large military training area closed to the public, with forests that grew wild and roads that only soldiers used. In 2016 much of it was opened and became a protected landscape area, and the hills around villages like Zaječov have quietly become one of the more interesting places to explore in central Bohemia.

The Brdy are a long, forested ridge of old rocks, rising above the surrounding farmland. The forests are mainly spruce and beech, with clearings, peat bogs and streams, and they are full of roe deer, boar and many birds. The region also has an industrial past, as iron ore was mined and smelted here for centuries, and the ironworks at nearby Komárov were famous for their cast iron. Small museums and old buildings tell this story.

Zaječov itself is a small village at the foot of the hills, with a church and a few farms. The roads around it are narrow and winding, climbing into the forest and dropping into valleys, with very little traffic. Some forest roads remain closed to motor vehicles, so follow the signs carefully. Surfaces can be rough and covered in leaves or gravel, especially after rain.

There are no real services in Zaječov, so fill up in Hořovice, the nearest town, which has fuel stations, shops and a château. A picnic in the forest is a good alternative to a restaurant. Onward, the way heads south towards the Šumava, the great forest on the border with Bavaria, where the roads become even wilder and the landscape more remote.
t.near tuntenhausen@47.9,12.0:
The twin towers of Tuntenhausen's pilgrimage church rise above the meadows between Bad Aibling and Rosenheim, visible from miles around. For centuries, pilgrims have come here to venerate an image of the Virgin, and the church, rebuilt in the seventeenth century, is richly decorated inside with stucco and paintings. It is a quiet place, surrounded by farms and fields, with the Alps rising on the southern horizon.

The landscape here is the Alpine foreland, a land of rolling hills, meadows, forests and lakes, shaped by the glaciers that flowed out of the mountains during the Ice Ages. The views from the hills around Tuntenhausen stretch south to the Wendelstein, the Kaisergebirge and the Chiemgau Alps, a magnificent panorama on a clear day. The meadows are dotted with farms, and the villages have onion-domed churches, typical of Upper Bavaria.

The roads roll over the hills and through the villages, with gentle curves, good surfaces and moderate traffic. They are a fine warm-up for the mountain roads to come, and the views of the Alps are a constant companion. Watch for agricultural vehicles, cyclists and cows being moved between pastures. The weather can change quickly, with thunderstorms common in summer.

Tuntenhausen has a village inn, and fuel and food are easily found in Bad Aibling or Rosenheim. Bad Aibling is a spa town with a thermal bath and a pleasant centre, and Rosenheim is a lively market town on the Inn. The German Alpine Road continues east towards Berchtesgaden, with lakes, passes and the mountains ever closer.
t.near ebersberg@48.1,12.0:
The Ebersberger Forst is one of the largest continuous forests in the lowlands of Germany, a vast expanse of spruce, beech and oak east of Munich, crossed by straight roads and tracks. It was once a royal hunting ground, and it is still full of roe deer, boar and many birds. The town of Ebersberg sits on its edge, with a large church that holds a relic said to be the skull of Saint Sebastian, the object of a pilgrimage for centuries.

Ebersberg is a pleasant market town with a lake, an old centre and views over the surrounding countryside. A wooden lookout tower on the Ludwigshöhe hill above the town gives a wide panorama over the forest and, on clear days, the Alps. The landscape around is a mix of forests, meadows and small villages, part of the rolling Alpine foreland.

From the saddle it is relaxed and pleasant. The roads through the forest are straight and fast, but speed limits are enforced, and wildlife can be a hazard. The roads around the town and towards the south are more winding, with gentle curves and views of the Alps. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads towards Munich, especially at rush hour. In autumn, the forest is beautiful, with the beeches turning gold.

Fuel, groceries and somewhere to eat are all easy in Ebersberg. A beer garden or a café by the lake is a pleasant place for a break. The German Alpine Road and the Walchensee lie to the south, with the mountains growing closer with every kilometre.
t.near penzberg@47.8,11.4:
Penzberg was a coal town until 1966, when its mine closed after more than a century of operation. The miners' houses, the old headframe and a museum recall that past, but Penzberg's real surprise is cultural: its museum houses a remarkable collection of works by Heinrich Campendonk, a member of the Blue Rider group of painters, with his colourful, dreamlike paintings and glass works. It is an unexpected treasure in a small town at the edge of the Alps.

The landscape around Penzberg is a mix of meadows, forests, moors and lakes, with the Alps rising to the south. A short ride away lie the Osterseen, a chain of small, clear lakes in a moorland nature reserve, and the larger Starnberger See and Kochelsee. Beyond Kochel, the road climbs the Kesselberg to the Walchensee, one of the most beautiful lakes in Bavaria, with deep turquoise water surrounded by mountains.

The riding here is excellent. The roads roll through the meadows and forests, with gentle curves and views of the mountains, and the Kesselberg road, with its hairpins, is a classic. Note that the Kesselberg has had weekend and holiday restrictions for motorcycles in one direction because of noise and accidents, so check the signs. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, and the roads are popular with cyclists.

Penzberg has fuel stations, shops and restaurants, making it a good place to fill up before heading into the mountains. A visit to the Campendonk museum is a fine way to spend a rainy hour. The Walchensee and Kochelsee loop continues south into the mountains.
t.near dinkelscherben@48.3,10.6:
West of Augsburg, the land rises into a quiet country of wooded hills and valleys, protected as the Augsburg Western Forests nature park. Dinkelscherben is a small market town in the valley of the Zusam, with a church, a few shops and inns, and it makes a peaceful stop on a ride through the Swabian countryside, far from the busy roads around the city.

The forests here are a mix of spruce, beech and oak, with clearings, meadows and small streams. The valleys are green and gentle, with villages, farms and chapels, and the hills offer views over the surrounding countryside. The region has a long history of farming, and the villages have retained their traditional character, with half-timbered houses and onion-domed churches. Augsburg itself, a short ride east, is one of the oldest cities in Germany, founded by the Romans, and home to the Fuggerei, the oldest social housing complex in the world still in use.

On the bike, things are pleasant. The roads wind through the forests and valleys, with gentle curves, good surfaces and light traffic. They are a fine warm-up for the mountain roads to come, and the landscape is varied and green. Watch for agricultural vehicles, cyclists and wildlife, especially at dawn and dusk.

Dinkelscherben has fuel, shops and inns, so it makes an easy pause. A Swabian lunch, perhaps Käsespätzle or Maultaschen, is a hearty choice. The Ammergau and the Plansee lie to the south, with the Alps rising ever higher as you approach.
t.near starnberg@48.0,11.3:
On the evening of 13 June 1886, King Ludwig II of Bavaria, the builder of Neuschwanstein, drowned in the shallow waters of the Starnberger See, together with his psychiatrist, a day after being deposed and declared insane. The circumstances have never been fully explained, and theories of murder or suicide still circulate. A cross in the water off Berg, on the eastern shore, marks the spot, and a votive chapel stands on the hill above. Across the lake, at Possenhofen, his cousin Elisabeth, the future Empress Sisi of Austria, spent her childhood summers.

The Starnberger See is a large, deep lake south of Munich, surrounded by villas, parks and villages, with the Alps rising beyond the southern shore. Starnberg itself is a wealthy town at the northern end, with a lakeside promenade, boats and cafés. The lake has been a playground for Munich's elite since the days of the kings, and its shores are lined with mansions and gardens.

The riding around the lake is pleasant but often busy. The roads follow the shores, with curves and views over the water, but traffic can be heavy, especially on summer weekends, and speed limits are strictly enforced. The roads away from the lake, into the hills and villages, are quieter and more rewarding, with views of the Alps. Watch for cyclists, who are numerous.

Starnberg has plenty of fuel stations, shops, cafés and restaurants, making it a convenient stop. A coffee on the promenade, watching the boats, is a pleasant break. The Grossglockner and the high Alps lie far to the south, over the mountains into Austria.
t.near herrsching am ammersee@48.0,11.1:
On a hill above the Ammersee, the onion-domed church of Andechs Monastery has drawn pilgrims for centuries, but many modern visitors come for something else: the beer. The Benedictine monks of Andechs brew some of the most celebrated beers in Bavaria, and the beer garden next to the monastery, with its view over the countryside, is famous. The climb from Herrsching through the Kiental, a narrow wooded valley, is a pleasant walk for those who want to earn their beer; riders, of course, take the road and leave the beer for later.

Herrsching itself is a lakeside town on the eastern shore of the Ammersee, with a promenade, a beach and a pier where the paddle steamers call. The Ammersee is a large lake, less fashionable than the Starnberger See, but equally beautiful, with reed beds, forests and villages around its shores. On clear days, the Alps rise beyond the southern end of the lake, and the sunsets over the water are spectacular.

The roads wind around the lake and climb into the hills, with gentle curves and views over the water and the mountains. The climb to Andechs is short but steep, with tight bends. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, especially around the monastery, and the roads are popular with cyclists. Watch for pedestrians in the villages and near the monastery.

Herrsching covers the basics without fuss: a pump, a supermarket, a few places to eat. The monastery has a restaurant serving hearty Bavarian food, including roast pork and pretzels, and its own cheese. The Allgäu foothills lie to the south-west, with green hills and mountain views.
t.near petershausen@48.4,11.6:
North of Munich, the land rolls gently through the valleys of the Glonn and the Ilm, a quiet country of fields, forests and villages known as the Dachauer Hinterland. Petershausen is one of its towns, with a railway station linking it to the city, and a church and old farmhouses. It is a practical place, and the surrounding countryside is pleasant, with meadows, woods and onion-domed churches.

A few kilometres south lies Dachau, a town with an old centre, a castle and an artists' colony that flourished in the late nineteenth century. Its name, however, is forever linked to the concentration camp built there in 1933, the first in Nazi Germany and the model for many others. The memorial site, on the grounds of the former camp, is a sombre and important place to visit, with an exhibition, the reconstructed barracks and memorials of different faiths. Allow time for it if you plan to stop.

The riding around Petershausen is relaxed. The roads roll over the hills and through the villages, with gentle curves, good surfaces and moderate traffic. The landscape is green and pastoral, a pleasant contrast to the busy roads around Munich. Watch for agricultural vehicles and cyclists, and for the occasional sharp bend at a farm corner.

Petershausen has fuel, shops and inns, making it a good place for a short break. A Bavarian lunch in a village inn, with a view of the church tower, is a pleasant way to pass an hour. The Grossglockner and the high Alps lie far to the south, beyond Munich.
t.near bad feilnbach@47.8,12.0:
Bad Feilnbach is a spa town at the foot of the Wendelstein, the striking rocky peak that rises above the Inn valley south of Rosenheim. Its speciality is moor baths, using peat from the surrounding bogs, and visitors have come for its healing treatments for over a century. The town is quiet and green, with meadows, orchards and farmhouses, and the mountain looms over everything.

The Wendelstein has a cog railway and a cable car to its summit, where an observatory and a chapel sit on the rocks, with views over the Alps and the plain. Below it, the Jenbach valley has waterfalls and gorges, and the meadows around Bad Feilnbach are dotted with farms and chapels. To the south, the Tatzelwurm road climbs through a narrow valley to the Sudelfeld, a winding mountain road popular with riders, which leads over to Bayrischzell.

As for the riding, it is excellent. The roads wind through the meadows and climb into the mountains, with tight curves, steep grades and spectacular views. The Sudelfeld road is famous and busy, and it has seen speed limits, noise controls and weekend restrictions for motorcycles in recent years because of complaints from residents, so check the signs. Weather can change quickly in the mountains, with thunderstorms common in summer.

Bad Feilnbach has inns and cafés, and fuel and supplies are easily found in Bad Aibling or Rosenheim. A coffee and cake on a terrace with a view of the Wendelstein is a classic Bavarian pleasure. The Grossglockner lies to the south, beyond the Inn valley and the Kitzbühel Alps.
t.near miesbach@47.8,11.9:
In 1882, a wire strung on poles between Miesbach and Munich carried electricity over a distance of fifty-seven kilometres, one of the first long-distance power transmissions in history, a demonstration organised by the engineer Oskar von Miller and the French physicist Marcel Deprez. It powered a small pump driving an artificial waterfall at an exhibition in Munich. The achievement helped launch the age of electricity, and Oskar von Miller went on to found the Deutsches Museum.

Miesbach is a pleasant market town in the Bavarian Oberland, between the Tegernsee and the Schliersee, with an old centre, a church and a lively market. The surrounding landscape is the Alpine foreland at its most beautiful, with green hills, meadows, forests and farms, and the mountains rising to the south. The Miesbach breed of cattle and the local cheeses are part of the region's pride, and the traditional costume, the Tracht, is still worn on festive occasions.

The roads roll over the hills and wind through the valleys, with gentle curves, good surfaces and views of the mountains. The roads to the Tegernsee and the Schliersee are popular and can be busy on weekends, but the quieter roads through the hills offer more relaxed riding. The Taubenberg, a hill north of the town, has an inn with a view over the Alps. Watch for agricultural vehicles, cyclists and cows.

In Miesbach you will find fuel and food within a few hundred metres of each other. A coffee in the town square, followed by a short walk through the old centre, is a pleasant break. The Sudelfeld Pass lies to the south, through the Schliersee and Bayrischzell.
t.bruckmuhl@47.9,11.9:
The Mangfall flows out of the Tegernsee and winds north through a deep, wooded valley before turning east towards Rosenheim and the Inn, and Bruckmühl sits on its banks, a modest industrial town with a church, a few factories and modern homes. The valley's springs supply a large part of Munich's drinking water, which is famously pure, and the forests along the river are protected to keep it that way.

The town itself is practical rather than beautiful, but the surrounding countryside is lovely. The Mangfall valley is green and wooded, with meadows, farms and small villages, and the river is clear and fast-flowing. To the south, the land rises towards the Alps, with the Wendelstein and the mountains of the Mangfall range on the horizon. The views from the hills around Bruckmühl are superb on a clear day.

From the saddle it is pleasant. The roads follow the river and climb over the hills, with gentle curves, good surfaces and moderate traffic. The roads towards the Tegernsee, Miesbach and Bad Aibling offer varied riding, with views of the mountains. Watch for agricultural vehicles, cyclists and the occasional sharp bend. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads towards Rosenheim and Munich, especially at rush hour.

Bruckmühl has fuel stations, shops and inns, making it a convenient stop. A Bavarian lunch in a local inn, perhaps with a view of the river, is a pleasant break. The Tegernsee and the Sudelfeld Pass lie to the south, with the mountains growing closer and the roads more winding.
t.near rottach egern@47.7,11.7:
At the southern end of the Tegernsee, Rottach-Egern sits where the lake meets the mountains, and it has long been one of the most comfortable addresses in Upper Bavaria. Painted houses, carved balconies and well-kept gardens line the shore, and in summer the lake is busy with sailors and swimmers. The Wallberg rises steeply behind the village, and on a clear day its summit looks close enough to touch.

This is a sensible place to fill the tank before heading deeper into the hills. There are filling stations around the lake and in the neighbouring towns of Tegernsee and Bad Wiessee, and once you climb south towards the Achen Pass and the Austrian border, choices thin out. The road south from Rottach runs past Kreuth and Wildbad Kreuth before climbing gently through forest to the Achenpass and on to the Achensee in Tyrol. It is a lovely ride, more flowing than technical, with good surface and long views over pasture and pine.

Be aware that the Tegernsee valley is a magnet on sunny weekends. Day-trippers from Munich pour in, and the lakeside roads can crawl. Early mornings are far better, and police take noise and speed seriously here; the residents are not shy about complaining. Ride with a light hand on the throttle through the villages and you will be fine.

The area has a long monastic history. The Benedictine abbey at Tegernsee, founded in the eighth century, was one of the great centres of learning in southern Germany, and its brewery still produces the Tegernseer beer you will see on every menu. Save that for the evening. For now, the lake's clear water, the smell of cut grass and the first ridges of the Mangfall mountains are a fine way to start a day in the Bavarian Alps.
t.near navis@47.5,11.2:
Navis lies in a long, quiet side valley that branches east from the Wipptal, the great Brenner corridor south of Innsbruck. Down on the main valley floor the motorway and the railway carry an endless stream of traffic towards Italy; turn off at Matrei or Steinach and climb into Navis, and within minutes the noise is gone. What remains is a scattered farming village strung along the valley for several kilometres, with steep meadows, wooden barns and a church that seems to keep watch from its slope.

The road in is narrow and climbs with purpose, the kind of Tyrolean byway where you meet a tractor or a delivery van and both of you tuck in tight. Surface is generally good but patched in places, and the edges can carry gravel after storms. It is a dead-end valley for vehicles, so you are riding it for its own sake: for the climb, the views back across the Wipptal to the Stubai peaks, and the stillness at the top. Go gently through the hamlets; children, dogs and cattle all share the road.

The alpine pastures above it are still worked in summer. Hikers use Navis as a base for the Tuxer Alps, and on a fine day you will see them heading for the huts on the ridges.

Do not count on a filling station in the valley. Fill up in the Wipptal, at Matrei or Steinach, or in Innsbruck before you leave the city. The Brenner route itself has a toll on the motorway, but the old Brenner road alongside it is free and a pleasant alternative. Weather comes in quickly at this altitude, so carry a layer even in July; afternoon thunderstorms are common in high summer.
t.near schwabmunchen@48.1,10.7:
South of Augsburg the land flattens into the Lechfeld, a broad gravel plain shaped by the Lech river as it runs north from the Alps. Schwabmünchen is the market town of this stretch, a practical place with a long main street, a handful of churches, and all the shops and services a rider needs. It is not a postcard town, and it does not pretend to be, but it makes a reliable pause between Augsburg and the Allgäu.

History runs deep on this plain. In 955 the Lechfeld was the scene of the battle in which Otto the Great defeated the Magyar raiders, ending decades of incursions into German lands. Nothing much on the ground marks it today, just wide fields, but it is worth knowing as you ride across that this flat country once decided the future of central Europe.

The riding here is about moving efficiently rather than leaning. Roads are straight or gently curved, generally well surfaced, and run through farmland, small woods and villages with maypoles in the square. On a clear day, looking south, the line of the Alps appears on the horizon like a promise, and that view grows as you head towards Landsberg, Kaufbeuren and the high roads of the Allgäu. Wind across the plain can be gusty, and in late autumn morning fog lies thick in the hollows.

Schwabmünchen has fuel, bakeries and cafés, so it is a good place to take on supplies before the hillier roads. The Lech itself, with its weirs and turquoise water, is never far to the west if you want a quieter ride parallel to the main routes. Think of this stretch as the overture: calm, steady, building towards the mountains.
t.near arnstorf@48.5,12.8:
Arnstorf is a small market town in the Rottal, the gently rolling country of Lower Bavaria between the Isar and the Inn. It is farming country through and through: maize, wheat, hop gardens here and there, big Bavarian farmsteads and onion-domed churches on every rise. The Rottal is also famous for horse breeding, and you may see paddocks of the sturdy Rottaler horses along the lanes.

The town has a fine little centre with a castle, the Schloss Arnstorf, owned for centuries by a noble family and still standing at the heart of the place. The market square is the kind where you will find a bakery, a butcher selling warm Leberkäse rolls at midday and an inn with a beer garden under chestnut trees. That is exactly what a food stop at the end of a long day should be.

Riding into the Rottal is relaxed and pleasant. The roads roll over low hills in long bends with good sightlines, and traffic is light away from the main routes between Pfarrkirchen, Eggenfelden and Landau. Surfaces are generally good, though farm vehicles drop mud in wet weather, especially at field entrances. This is not mountain riding, but there is real satisfaction in linking the small roads that thread between the villages, with the land opening and closing around you.

As a finish, Arnstorf is quiet and unpretentious. Fuel is available in town and in the larger neighbours, and the Rottal spa towns of Bad Birnbach and Bad Griesbach are not far if you want a warm thermal bath to ease the stiffness of a long ride. Order something hearty, a Schweinsbraten with dumplings and a local wheat beer if you are done for the day, and watch the evening settle over the fields.
t.near dobris@49.7,14.2:
Dobříš is a small town in Central Bohemia, about forty kilometres south-west of Prague, set on the edge of the Brdy, a long range of forested hills. The town is best known for its Rococo chateau, built in the eighteenth century for the Colloredo-Mansfeld family, with formal French gardens and an English-style park. After the Second World War, the chateau served for decades as a retreat for Czechoslovak writers, and it is now open to visitors again.

The surrounding landscape is dominated by forests and ponds. The Brdy hills were a closed military area for much of the twentieth century, and as a result they remain largely wild and undeveloped. In 2016, a large part of the area became a protected landscape area and was opened to the public. Ponds and small reservoirs dot the countryside around Dobříš, and some are used for swimming in summer.

The riding around Dobříš is pleasant, with quiet roads winding through forests and farmland, and a few short climbs into the hills. Surfaces vary from smooth to rough, and some smaller roads are narrow and patched. Traffic is generally light away from the main road to Prague.

Dobříš has fuel, shops and restaurants, making it a convenient stop. If you are looking for a swim, ask locally about the best ponds, as conditions and access vary. The Vltava and the Slapy reservoir are also not far to the east, offering more opportunities for water and scenery.
t.near kozlany@49.9,13.6:
Kožlany is a small town on the high, rolling plateau north of Plzeň, and if the name rings a faint bell it is because Edvard Beneš was born here in 1884. The man who would become Czechoslovakia's second president, and who led the government in exile during the Second World War, grew up in a farming family in this quiet corner of western Bohemia. A memorial in the town marks the connection.

The country around it is wide and open, a patchwork of big fields, scattered woods and villages built around a pond and a church. To the south, the land drops towards the deep, wooded valley of the Berounka, which loops and twists its way towards Prague through some of the prettiest scenery in the region. Castles perch above it here and there, and the river is popular with canoeists in summer.

Riding up here is calm and rewarding. The roads cross the plateau in long, gentle curves, with surfaces that range from good to bumpy and patched, and traffic is usually light. Dropping down into the Berounka valley gives you something more interesting, with tighter bends and short, steep descents through forest. Watch for tractors and for gravel at junctions, and be ready for village speed limits, which are enforced.

As a photo stop, the appeal is the sense of space: big skies, golden fields in summer, and the gentle geometry of Bohemian farmland. Fuel and food are available in Kralovice nearby and in Plzeň, a short ride south. If you have time, Plzeň's brewery, birthplace of the original pilsner lager, is a worthwhile detour, though best saved for after the ride.
t.near sedlcany@49.7,14.4:
Sedlčany sits in the Central Bohemian uplands south of Prague, in a landscape of low hills, forests, fields and fishponds. The town itself is modest, with a market square, a Gothic church and a scattering of shops and cafés, but the countryside around it is the real attraction.

To the west, the Vltava carves a deep, winding valley, flooded in stretches by the dams of the Vltava cascade. The Slapy and Orlík reservoirs create long, fjord-like lakes between steep wooded banks, and their shores are lined with holiday cabins and campsites. Castles and chateaux are scattered through the area, including Orlík, perched above the water, and Vysoký Chlumec on its rocky hill, home to a well-known brewery.

The riding here is among the best close to Prague. Roads wind through forests and along valley sides, with plenty of bends, short climbs and descents, and views over the water. Surfaces vary, and some minor roads are narrow and rough, so take care. Traffic is light on weekdays but can increase on summer weekends when Praguers head to their cottages.

Sedlčany has fuel, food and basic services. As a scenic stretch, it offers a taste of rural Bohemia at its most relaxed, with quiet roads, gentle landscapes and a sense of being far from the city, even though Prague is only an hour away.
t.near sazava@49.9,14.8:
Sázava is a small town on the river of the same name, east of Prague, best known for its monastery, one of the oldest in Bohemia. The Benedictine abbey was founded in the eleventh century by Saint Procopius, a hermit, and for a time it was a centre of Slavonic liturgy before Latin replaced it. Today, the monastery is a museum, with a Gothic church, Romanesque remains and medieval frescoes.

The Sázava river winds through a deep, wooded valley here, and it is popular with canoeists, campers and swimmers in summer. There are several places along the river where people swim, and campsites with access to the water. Check conditions locally, as currents and water levels vary.

The town also has a long tradition of glassmaking, and the old Kavalier glassworks was once one of the most important in the country. The surrounding countryside is a mix of forest, fields and small villages, with plenty of quiet roads to explore.

The riding here is pleasant, with roads following the river valley and climbing onto the surrounding plateau. Bends are frequent, and some roads are narrow and rough. Traffic is generally light. Fuel and food are available in Sázava and nearby towns. As a high point, the plateau above the valley offers views over the forested hills and the winding river below.
t.postupice@49.7,14.8:
Postupice is a straggling village in the hills east of Benešov, the kind of place where the church tower is the tallest thing for miles and the pub is the second most important building. Around it the Posázaví uplands fold into small valleys with ponds in the bottoms and woods on the crests, and the roads between the hamlets climb and drop in short, satisfying pulls.

The high ground here is not dramatic, but it gives you a long look across Central Bohemia. On a clear evening you can pick out wooded ridges in every direction, and to the south-east the twin humps of the Blaník hills. Velký Blaník holds one of the best-loved Czech legends: inside the mountain, so the story goes, sleeps an army of knights led by Saint Wenceslas, waiting to ride out and save the nation in its darkest hour. Plenty of Czechs will tell you, with a wry smile, that the knights have overslept on several occasions.

Closer at hand, Konopiště, just outside Benešov, was the country seat of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, whose assassination in Sarajevo in 1914 set off the First World War. The chateau is stuffed with his hunting trophies, many thousands of them, and its park and rose garden make a pleasant break if you are passing.

The riding is quiet and twisty in a low-key way. Lanes are narrow, often bumpy and patched, with blind crests and the odd farm dog that considers motorcycles a personal insult. Traffic is light enough that you can relax into it. Late in the day, with low sun raking across the fields and the smell of hay in the air, this is Bohemian back-country at its most likeable.
t.near benesov@49.8,14.8:
Benešov is a busy little county town about forty-five minutes south-east of Prague, and for most riders its name is shorthand for one thing: Konopiště. The chateau sits in a wooded park just west of the centre, a Gothic castle remodelled in the late nineteenth century for Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Habsburg throne. He was an obsessive hunter, and the corridors are lined with an almost unsettling quantity of antlers and trophies. The rose garden, the deer park and the lake below the castle are calmer company.

The town itself is practical rather than pretty, with a railway junction, supermarkets and a modest square. Its practical side is what matters at the end of a ride: fuel stations on the edges of town, places to eat, and an easy run back to Prague on the D1 motorway if you want to be home quickly. Remember that Czech motorways require an electronic vignette, motorcycles included.

The country around Benešov is the Posázaví, the land of the Sázava river, and it is made for unhurried riding. Minor roads swing through mixed forest, past fishponds fringed with reeds, and up over low ridges where the view opens across a rumpled quilt of fields. Corners are frequent but rarely tight, and surfaces range from fresh to tired. Weekend traffic is light away from the main roads, though cyclists like these lanes too.

If you are finishing here, the old road towards Prague through Poříčí nad Sázavou and along the river makes a gentler alternative to the motorway, with the water glinting through the trees and campsites and riverside pubs along the banks. It is a pleasant way to let the day unwind.
t.kumamoto@32.8,130.7:
Kumamoto is the big city of central Kyushu, with a population of around 680,000, and its centrepiece is a castle. Kumamoto Castle was built in the early seventeenth century by the warlord Kato Kiyomasa, who was a master of fortification, and its great stone walls curve upward in a flare that is said to defeat any attempt to climb them. In April 2016 a pair of powerful earthquakes badly damaged the castle and brought down parts of its walls and roofs, and restoration work has been long and careful. The scale of the damage, and the care of the repair, are part of the city's character now.

The city has other claims on your attention. Suizenji, a landscape garden laid out in the seventeenth century, recreates the Tokaido road in miniature, with a small mound representing Mount Fuji. The local food is distinctive: thick, garlicky tonkotsu ramen, and basashi, thinly sliced raw horse meat, which is a regional specialty. The city's bear mascot, Kumamon, is everywhere, on trains, signs and souvenirs, a marketing success that has made the red cheeks famous across Japan.

As a place to start a motorcycle ride, Kumamoto is convenient. Fuel stations are everywhere, parking for bikes is manageable if you book a hotel with space, and the roads east toward Aso quickly leave the city behind. Getting out takes patience, though, because the central streets are busy with trams, buses and commuters, and the ring roads are slow at rush hour. Early on a weekend morning, you can be out of the suburbs and among the rice fields in under half an hour.

The route heads for the Aso caldera, one of the largest in the world, and the landscape changes steadily, with farmland giving way to ridges, grassland and then the volcanic bowl itself. Spring and autumn offer the best conditions, with clear air and moderate temperatures, while summer can be hot and humid, with heavy rain in June and July. Stock up on water, eat a proper breakfast, and enjoy the feeling of heading for the mountains.
t.rock springs@41.6,-109.2:
Rock Springs is a coal town that ended up on the world's busiest east-west railroad, and it has the odd mix of origins you would expect. The Union Pacific arrived in the late 1860s, the mines dug into the surrounding desert, and workers came from dozens of countries, which is why the town's old tales mention such a long list of nationalities. It also has a darker chapter: in 1885 white miners attacked their Chinese coworkers in a massacre that is remembered in local history, and the place does not hide from it.

The country around the town is high desert, roughly nineteen hundred metres up, a landscape of sagebrush, buttes and big pale cliffs that feels enormous even by Wyoming standards. The Red Desert to the north is one of the largest unfenced areas left in the lower forty-eight, and it holds a herd of wild horses along with the Killpecker Sand Dunes, among the largest active dunes in North America. A loop on the White Mountain road to the north takes you past wild horses with a fair chance of seeing them on a quiet morning. Rain is scarce and sunshine reliable, though the wind is something else and can be fierce across the Interstate and the open highways. Crosswinds on a loaded bike deserve respect. Winter turns the highway into a closed-road gamble, so ride from late spring to early autumn.

Rock Springs is large enough to have everything: fuel, motels, supermarkets, motorcycle-friendly diners and a historic district with brick buildings from the boom years. It is the sensible place to sort out gear before you head south toward Flaming Gorge, where the road leaves the interstate hum behind and begins to climb through sagebrush and then, at last, pine.

Green River lies about twenty-three kilometres west, and between them they make a good pair, one big and busy, the other quieter and tied to the river. Fill up here, eat well, and use the open desert light in the evening to plan tomorrow's climb into the Gorge country.
t.green river@41.5,-109.5:
The river that gives this town its name is also the reason the town matters. John Wesley Powell, the one-armed Civil War veteran, launched his two famous expeditions down the Green and Colorado Rivers from here in 1869 and 1871, and a small island in the middle of town, Expedition Island, marks the spot where his boats slid into the current. It is worth a short walk across a footbridge, because the sight of this wide, green water in the middle of the high desert is a small shock.

Green River is smaller and quieter than Rock Springs, a county seat with around twelve thousand residents, railroad roots and a trona industry that digs a salt used in glass and detergents from the ground nearby. The rock around the town is the prize for geologists: the Green River Formation holds some of the world's best fossil fish, preserved by the thousands in ancient lake beds, and you will see them sold in shops across the region. Towers of sandstone, Castle Rock and Tollgate Rock, rise at the edge of town and give it a frontier-fort silhouette.

For riders, the town is the doorway to the Flaming Gorge Scenic Byway. The first stretch south is straightforward highway across open sagebrush, with wide views and a tendency for the wind to push sideways. As you reach the reservoir area the terrain tightens, the red rock walls appear and the corners begin to matter. Mornings are cool even in summer, and by afternoon the desert heat builds, so an early start is rewarded. Watch for pronghorn near the road and for livestock that has wandered.

Services are no problem here. There is fuel, groceries, a number of diners and plenty of motel rooms, and the downtown, while modest, has a few old brick storefronts worth a glance. If you want a better look at the water, the river path near the island is a quiet place for a sandwich. Rock Springs is just a short ride east if you need anything bigger, but most riders find this is the better place to start the day.
t.manila@41.0,-109.7:
Manila is a very small town at a very big view. It sits on the Utah side of the state line, only a few hundred metres south of the Wyoming border, on the western rim of Flaming Gorge Reservoir, and if you blink on the highway you might miss it. A few hundred people live here, a handful of motels and cafés serve the visitors, and the real attraction lies just beyond the last building, where the land drops into a long blue arm of water between red cliffs.

The dam that made the lake was built across the Green River in the early 1960s, and the reservoir backs up for about ninety miles. John Wesley Powell passed through here in 1869 and gave the canyon its name for the flaming red of its walls. The rock is part of the Uinta Mountain uplift, and the layers get older and redder as you go south. The Sheep Creek Geological Loop a short distance away reveals tilted layers in a deep canyon, and in late summer the kokanee salmon spawn in the creeks nearby, which draws bears and bird-watchers alike. The viewpoint at Red Canyon is the one to remember.

The ride here is the best part of the day. Highway 191 climbs from the desert with long, flowing bends through juniper and sagebrush and then into pine and aspen as you reach altitude. The surface is generally good, the grades are steady rather than steep, and the views over the water come in sudden, generous flashes. Wildlife is common: mule deer, pronghorn, bighorn sheep on the cliffs and the occasional moose. Snow can arrive early and linger, so the season is roughly late May to early October. Temperatures swing widely, so pack layers.

Services in a town of this size are limited, so arrive with a decent tank. The larger places are Green River and Rock Springs to the north and Vernal to the south, and it is wise to top up before leaving either. Manila itself is for a coffee, a photograph and a long look at the water.
t.near estes park@40.3,-105.7:
Trail Ridge Road begins its climb here, a few miles west of Estes Park, and by the time you reach this stretch of US 34, you have entered Rocky Mountain National Park and left the town far below. The road winds up through forests of ponderosa pine and Douglas fir, past meadows where elk graze, and around curves that open up views of the Continental Divide. Around Many Parks Curve, a parking area on a tight bend gives one of the best early views: a series of mountain meadows, or parks, spread out below, with Longs Peak, the highest summit in the park, towering over them to the south.

Trail Ridge Road was completed in the early 1930s, and it was designed to give motorists a spectacular drive with gentle grades and wide curves. It is the highest continuous paved road in the United States, reaching more than 12,000 feet, and about eleven miles of it run above the treeline, through alpine tundra. It links Estes Park, on the east side of the park, with Grand Lake on the west, and it follows in part an old trail used by the Ute and Arapaho peoples to cross the mountains.

Down in the meadows, the elk are a major attraction, especially in autumn, when the bulls bugle to attract mates, a strange, high-pitched call that echoes through the valleys. They can be found in large numbers in Moraine Park and Horseshoe Park, just off the road, and they often wander onto the road and into the town of Estes Park itself. Keep your distance, since they can be aggressive during the rut, in September and October.

For riders, the lower part of the road is a gentle introduction, with good surface, steady grades and smooth curves. Summer weekends are crowded, and the park has used a timed-entry reservation system during the busiest months, so check the current rules before you go. The road is usually open from late May to mid-October, depending on snow. Estes Park, about nine kilometres east, is a busy gateway town with fuel, food and lodging, and is the last place to fill up before the climb. The Stanley Hotel, on a hill above the town, inspired Stephen King to write The Shining after he stayed there in the 1970s.
t.near herrsching am ammersee@48.0,11.2:
On a hill above the Ammersee, the onion-domed church of Andechs Monastery has drawn pilgrims for centuries, but many modern visitors come for something else: the beer. The Benedictine monks of Andechs brew some of the most celebrated beers in Bavaria, and the beer garden next to the monastery, with its view over the countryside, is famous. The climb from Herrsching through the Kiental, a narrow wooded valley, is a pleasant walk for those who want to earn their beer; riders, of course, take the road and leave the beer for later.

Herrsching itself is a lakeside town on the eastern shore of the Ammersee, with a promenade, a beach and a pier where the paddle steamers call. The Ammersee is a large lake, less fashionable than the Starnberger See, but equally beautiful, with reed beds, forests and villages around its shores. On clear days, the Alps rise beyond the southern end of the lake, and the sunsets over the water are spectacular.

The roads wind around the lake and climb into the hills, with gentle curves and views over the water and the mountains. The climb to Andechs is short but steep, with tight bends. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, especially around the monastery, and the roads are popular with cyclists. Watch for pedestrians in the villages and near the monastery.

Herrsching covers the basics without fuss: a pump, a supermarket, a few places to eat. The monastery has a restaurant serving hearty Bavarian food, including roast pork and pretzels, and its own cheese. The Allgäu foothills lie to the south-west, with green hills and mountain views.
t.selva di cadore@46.4,12.1:
Selva di Cadore is a quiet village on the road between two big names, in the Fiorentina valley, with Monte Pelmo on one side and the great wall of the Civetta on the other. It is not a place that most people choose as a destination, and that is part of its appeal. A handful of houses, a church, a few hotels and a ski lift sit in a green bowl, and above them the Pelmo, with its flat, throne-like summit, dominates the view. The mountain is known locally as the throne of God, and when the light catches it at the end of the day, it is easy to see why.

The village belongs to the Ladin cultural area, and the neighbouring Colle Santa Lucia, only a couple of kilometres away, is one of the Ladin-speaking communities that keep their language and traditions alive in the face of Italian and German. The Dolomites were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009, and this part of the range, with its high walls and its pale rock, is one of the finest.

The riding is excellent in both directions. Heading east from Selva, the road climbs towards Passo Giau, at 2,236 metres, with long sequences of hairpins through meadows and then open rock, and the summit area is a high saddle with a cluster of huts and spectacular views. It is one of the finest passes in the Dolomites and the road, though narrow in places, is well surfaced. From there you can continue to Passo Falzarego and loop back via Cortina or the Livinallongo valley. In the other direction, the road climbs over Passo Staulanza, below the Pelmo, and down to the Zoldo valley. Traffic is moderate, though weekends in July and August bring more bikes and cyclists.

Weather in these mountains can change quickly, with morning sunshine turning to afternoon thunderstorms, and snow can close the higher passes from autumn to late spring. At the top of the Giau, the wind can be cold even in summer, so bring a windproof layer.

There is little in the village itself, though there are a couple of cafes and small shops, and local dishes such as casunziei, a stuffed pasta with beetroot, or polenta with mushrooms are worth trying. Fuel is limited, and the larger town of Cortina d'Ampezzo, about twelve kilometres away, has stations and plenty of services, so fill there before heading for the high passes.

Late June brings flowers to the pastures, and September offers crisp air and golden larches on the slopes.
t.near rottach egern@47.7,11.8:
At the southern end of the Tegernsee, Rottach-Egern sits where the lake meets the mountains, and it has long been one of the most comfortable addresses in Upper Bavaria. Painted houses, carved balconies and well-kept gardens line the shore, and in summer the lake is busy with sailors and swimmers. The Wallberg rises steeply behind the village, and on a clear day its summit looks close enough to touch.

This is a sensible place to fill the tank before heading deeper into the hills. There are filling stations around the lake and in the neighbouring towns of Tegernsee and Bad Wiessee, and once you climb south towards the Achen Pass and the Austrian border, choices thin out. The road south from Rottach runs past Kreuth and Wildbad Kreuth before climbing gently through forest to the Achenpass and on to the Achensee in Tyrol. It is a lovely ride, more flowing than technical, with good surface and long views over pasture and pine.

Be aware that the Tegernsee valley is a magnet on sunny weekends. Day-trippers from Munich pour in, and the lakeside roads can crawl. Early mornings are far better, and police take noise and speed seriously here; the residents are not shy about complaining. Ride with a light hand on the throttle through the villages and you will be fine.

The area has a long monastic history. The Benedictine abbey at Tegernsee, founded in the eighth century, was one of the great centres of learning in southern Germany, and its brewery still produces the Tegernseer beer you will see on every menu. Save that for the evening. For now, the lake's clear water, the smell of cut grass and the first ridges of the Mangfall mountains are a fine way to start a day in the Bavarian Alps.
t.near manching on the way back@48.7,11.5:
South of Ingolstadt on the Danube plain, the ground is so flat that the horizon becomes the main landscape feature. This stop lies between Manching and Ingolstadt, in a region once covered by the great Donaumoos, a peat bog drained in the eighteenth century under the Bavarian elector Karl Theodor, who wanted farmland and settlers. The road network that crosses the old moor is neat, straight and carefully ditch-lined, with fields of maize, wheat and sugar beet standing behind.

Manching has a history much older than the roads. The Celts built a huge fortified settlement here, an oppidum, in the last two centuries before Christ, one of the largest in Europe, with ramparts that ran for kilometres. Today the town is better known for its military airfield and aerospace industry, but the Celtic past still lingers in the museum, which is worth a look if you like objects with stories. Ingolstadt, seven kilometres away, is a large city with over a hundred thousand people, home to Audi, a medieval wall, and the claim to be where the Bavarian beer purity law was issued in 1516.

For a rider, this is a start, not a destination. Fuel and food are easy in Manching, and Ingolstadt has everything you could need. The roads near the Danube are good for covering ground quickly, but they are also busy with commuters, so a morning start before the traffic builds is a good plan. The Danube floodplain nearby has paths and beech woods if you want to walk for ten minutes before you mount up.

The reward for a start like this comes later, when the road turns south and the first hills of the Alpine foreland rise ahead. The contrast makes the mountains look taller than they are. Check your luggage, fill the tank and enjoy the rare luxury of flat tarmac, because you will want to remember it when the hairpins begin.
t.near castello dell acqua on the way back:
The Orobie Alps rise steeply on the southern side of the Valtellina, and this part of the valley, around Chiuro and the side valleys that drop into it, is one of the least visited corners of Lombardy.

Valtellina's terraced vineyards are a sight in themselves. Over centuries, farmers built stone walls up the steep slope to create narrow shelves for vines, and the terraces now extend for dozens of kilometres, a landscape so remarkable that it is protected as a heritage site in its own right. The grape is Nebbiolo, known locally as Chiavennasca, and the wines, with names such as Sassella and Grumello, are elegant and long-lived. Teglio, nearby, is the home of pizzoccheri, buckwheat pasta cooked with cabbage, potato, butter and cheese, which is perfect after a cold ride.

The roads into the side valleys are often steep, narrow and twisty, with hairpins that climb through woods and meadows to small mountain villages. In autumn the larches turn gold and the whole slope glows, and in spring the meadows are covered with wildflowers. Surfaces can be broken by frost and rock fall, so watch for gravel on the corners, and expect cyclists, because the valley is a favourite training ground. The big names, such as the Stelvio and Mortirolo, are not far away, which makes this a fine base.

Sondrio, fourteen kilometres away, has the fuel, shops and restaurants that a rider needs. The town is the capital of the province, with a handsome old centre and a castle, and is also the place to taste bresaola, the air-dried beef that is a speciality of the valley, and bitto, a strong cheese made in the high pastures. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and good light, while in summer the valley can be very hot and the traffic heavier.
t.near mengkofen on the way back@48.8,12.5:
Straubing lies a little to the northeast, and this stop sits in the great grain country around it, the Gäuboden. It is some of the most fertile land in Bavaria, a broad plain between the Danube and the Bavarian Forest covered in deep loess soil laid down by wind in the ice age, and the locals call it the breadbasket of the state. The villages of Leiblfing, Mengkofen and Geiselhöring each have a church with an onion dome and a ring of large farms. In summer the fields stand tall and golden, and the whole area smells of dust and warm straw.

For riders, this is a place of long straight roads and wide horizons. The land is flat, with scarcely a bend, and the surface is good, so progress is easy but a little monotonous. The most important thing is to watch the wind and the farm traffic: tractors with wide trailers appear without warning, and in harvest season the roads can be littered with chaff. Visibility is good, and you can see a long way ahead, but patience is a virtue.

Geiselhöring is the largest place nearby, with nearly seven thousand people, a railway station and the usual shops, bakeries and fuel stations. Mengkofen, a bit smaller, also has services, and Leiblfing, though tiny, has an inn. For a more substantial stop, Straubing, with its handsome old town and tall city tower, is only a short ride away, and every August hosts the Gäubodenfest, one of the biggest folk festivals in Bavaria.

The swim marker suggests a quiet lake or river bank nearby, and the Danube and Isar both lie within a few kilometres, along with a number of gravel pit lakes that have become local bathing spots. Be careful of currents on the rivers and ask a local about safe places. On a hot afternoon, a dip and a nap in the shade of an alder are an excellent way to end a day on the plain.
t.near nederland@40.1,-105.5:
Nederland is a mountain town that has never entirely decided whether it is a ski-resort suburb, a hippie holdout or a mining camp that kept going. The answer is probably all three. It sits at about 2,500 metres where Boulder Canyon spills into the high country, at the edge of the Barker Reservoir, with the Indian Peaks on the horizon. Once you ride in from the canyon, the first thing you register is how cold the air has become, even in summer.

The name is old and slightly odd. In the 1870s a Dutch company bought a local mine, and the settlement became Nederland, Dutch for the Netherlands. The silver of nearby Caribou had drawn miners and mill workers here, and Nederland lived as a processing and supply place for them. Today the town is better known for its eccentricities than for its silver. A few days every March brings Frozen Dead Guy Days, a festival built around a man preserved in dry ice in a shed up the valley, and the town also has an old carousel hand-carved and restored by locals. I mention these because a rider doing laps on the Peak to Peak Highway should know the place has a sense of humour.

The riding in and out is the draw. Coming up from Boulder, Highway 119 climbs Boulder Canyon in a long run of tight, rocky bends alongside the creek, which suits a middleweight bike and a rider who has not eaten recently. Past town, the Peak to Peak Scenic Byway runs north and south along the Front Range at over 2,500 metres, with a view of snow on the high peaks, long open curves, and not much else. Weekends bring cyclists, tourists and heavy bikes in numbers, so mid-week is better. Winter can close sections, and ice lingers in canyon shadows into spring.

Nederland has a handful of coffee shops, bakeries and a few gas stations, so it is a natural place to refuel, eat and warm up before turning on to the higher parts of the byway. Boulder, about twenty kilometres down the canyon, has everything else. Altitude cuts engine power slightly, and the weather can turn in a few minutes, so pack a layer.
t.near stelvio@46.5,10.5:
The village of Stelvio, Stilfs in German, clings to a steep slope above the Val Venosta in South Tyrol, a cluster of old houses and narrow lanes high above the valley floor, and most people who pass the turn-off have their eyes on something bigger. A few kilometres up the valley, at Prato allo Stelvio, begins the most famous mountain road in Europe: the climb to the Passo dello Stelvio, at 2,757 metres, with its numbered sequence of forty-eight hairpins stacked one above the other on the northern face of the mountain.

The road was built by the Austrian Empire in the 1820s, to link Lombardy, then under Habsburg rule, with Tyrol, and it was an extraordinary feat of engineering for its time. It became a front line in the First World War, when Italian and Austro-Hungarian troops fought at altitude among the glaciers, and traces of trenches and fortifications can still be found near the pass. Today it is a place of pilgrimage for riders, cyclists and drivers, and on summer weekends the top of the pass resembles a fairground, with sausage stands, souvenir shops and crowds.

The climb from Prato is a serious undertaking. The hairpins are tight, steep and often crowded with cyclists, cars and buses, and the road is narrow in places, with stone walls and steep drops. Above Trafoi, the views of the Ortler, the highest mountain in South Tyrol, and its glaciers are spectacular. From the top, you can descend south to Bormio or take the Umbrail Pass into Switzerland, one of the highest road passes in the country, down into the Val Müstair. The pass is typically closed from autumn to late spring, often from early November to late May or June, depending on the snow, so check before you go.

For food, the villages of the Val Venosta offer hearty Tyrolean fare, such as speck, dumplings and apple strudel, as the valley is famous for its apples. Prato allo Stelvio has fuel and services. Be aware that the weather at the top can be much colder than in the valley, with snow possible even in summer, so carry warm layers.
t.near ponte di legno@46.3,10.5:
Ponte di Legno takes its name from the wooden bridge that once crossed the Oglio river here, and it is the last proper village before the road leaves the Val Camonica and heads up into the high mountains. It sits at about 1,260 metres, and it is surrounded by the peaks of the Adamello and Ortles-Cevedale groups, with the Tonale Pass just to the east and the Gavia pass to the north. The village is a ski and walking resort, and it keeps a handsome old centre of stone houses beside a modern strip of hotels and cafes. The nearby hamlets of Temù and Vezza d'Oglio are smaller still.

For a rider, this is where preparation counts. The Gavia Pass, at 2,621 metres, is one of the highest paved roads in Italy, and it has a reputation. The road from the Ponte di Legno side is narrow, with steep gradients, tight hairpins, little or no barrier in places and sections of rough surface. It is closed in winter, usually opening in late spring or early summer after snow clearing, and it can close again at the first autumn snowfall. Check conditions before you go. The Giro d'Italia has crossed it, famously in 1988 in a blizzard.

Ponte di Legno has fuel stations and shops, and since the pass has no supplies at the top, fill up and take some water. The village is also a convenient place for a hot lunch before or after the climb, and local cooking features polenta, cured meats, cheese and berries from the woods. The nearby Stelvio National Park, one of Italy's largest, protects chamois, ibex and golden eagles, and in the early morning you may see wildlife on the road verges.

Weather is the constant theme. Mornings tend to be clearest, and afternoon cloud and thunder build over the mountains in summer, so start early. Even in July, it can be near freezing at the top, so carry layers. The ride finishes here with the sort of tiredness that comes from concentration and altitude, and a quiet evening in the village feels earned.
t.near galtur@46.9,10.1:
Galtür stands at about 1,600 metres at the head of the Paznaun valley, and the first thing you notice is a concrete wall. It is long, curved and tall, and it was built after the avalanche of February 1999, when a wall of snow roared down into the village and killed thirty-one people. The wall now shields the centre, and a museum beside it, the Alpinarium, tells the story of the disaster and, more broadly, of living under snow. It is a serious place, and a thoughtful stop even for riders who normally only want coffee.

The village itself has recovered with quiet dignity. The church, the old farmhouses and the gardens still have the look of a high mountain community, and the rhythm of the place is set by the seasons: ski traffic in winter, hikers and riders in summer, and a lull in November when everything shuts for a rest. The Trisanna river runs beside the village, a pale grey-green stream fed by glaciers that you can see from the road in clear weather.

The riding here is the eastern half of the Silvretta High Alpine Road. Coming from the Bielerhöhe, you descend a gentler, wider road than the Montafon side, with longer straights between the bends and big views down the valley. Out of the village, the road continues toward Ischgl and Landeck along the Trisanna, a fast, pleasant run with a few tunnels and some tight stretches where the valley closes in. In the evening the shadows lengthen early, so you may be riding in cold air long before sunset.

It is worth remembering how remote Galtür feels. It has a population of under eight hundred, and though it is not a small village in tourist terms, with plenty of beds, it is a long way from any large town. Ischgl is nine kilometres down the valley and has services, but anything bigger means a drive to Landeck or over the border. Check your fuel before committing to the high road.

Eat at one of the traditional inns if you can. Tyrolean dishes like Kaspressknödel, cheese dumplings in broth, are the right size for the end of a cold day, and the beer, brewed somewhere down the valley, is honest and cold.
t.near solden@46.9,11.0:
Sölden lies at about thirteen hundred metres in the Ötztal, a long Tyrolean valley that runs south from the Inn into the high, glaciated mountains on the Italian border. In winter it is one of Austria's big ski resorts, and in summer it is a base for hikers, cyclists and riders heading for the Timmelsjoch. The village is a bit loud and a bit brash, with large hotels and plenty of apres-ski, but the setting is genuinely impressive, with peaks above three thousand metres on all sides and a river running clear and fast below.

The valley has a famous visitor in the museum record. In 1991 hikers found a mummified man in the ice of the nearby Similaun, a Copper Age hunter who had lain there about five thousand years. Known as Ötzi, he is now displayed in Bolzano, but the Ötztal still takes pride in the find, and the story gives an extra dimension to the quiet peaks above the village. Sölden also appeared in a James Bond film, which locals will mention if you give them a chance.

Riding out from here is the point. Ride south and the road climbs through Zwieselstein and Obergurgl, which is among the highest parish villages in Austria, then goes over the Timmelsjoch at about 2,474 metres into Italy. It is a toll road and closes in winter, normally opening in early summer and staying open until the first heavy snow in autumn. The bends are well engineered and wide, the surface is good, and the road switches from forest to bare rock in a matter of minutes. Tourists and cyclists share it, so be patient on the lower sections.

Sölden has several filling stations and plenty of food, from simple bakeries to heavy Tyrolean fare of Kasspatzln and dumplings. The valley also offers the Aqua Dome thermal spa at Längenfeld, which will do wonders for tired shoulders after a long day in the saddle.

Mornings are calmest, and crowds thin out by evening. Early in the season, you may find snow banks beside the road at the top, while in September the larches turn gold and the light is superb.
t.near zernez@46.8,10.1:
Zernez is a small village in the Lower Engadine, at about fifteen hundred metres, and the gateway to Switzerland's only national park. The Inn river runs through the valley, a cold green stream fed by glaciers, and the surrounding mountains are dark with larch and pine. The village has an unusual look for the Alps, with white houses decorated with sgraffito, patterns scratched in plaster, and small windows set deep into thick walls, typical of Engadine architecture. Most of the older buildings date from after 1872, when a fire destroyed much of the village, and the rebuilt streets are wider than most in the valley.

The Swiss National Park, founded in 1914, is the oldest in the Alps and has the strictest rules: no camping, no picking flowers, no dogs and no leaving the marked paths. The visitor centre in Zernez explains the park's wildlife, which includes red deer, ibex, chamois and marmots, and, more recently, bears wandering in from Italy. The park's other claim to fame is that it has been left to nature for over a century, giving scientists a rare view of what happens when humans stop interfering.

The road through the park is the Ofen Pass, which climbs from Zernez to about 2,150 metres before descending into the Val Müstair. It is a fine ride, with smooth curves through thick pine forest, and a high, open section with big views. Traffic is moderate, speed limits are low and enforced, and the pass is open year-round in principle, though snow and ice can cause delays. Wildlife can appear on the road, and deer are common at dusk. At the bottom, the Val Müstair has a Romansh-speaking population and a remarkable Carolingian convent at Müstair, a UNESCO World Heritage Site with frescoes from the ninth century.

The nearest towns of any size are Davos, over the Flüela Pass, and the Italian resort of Livigno, through a tunnel.

Try a slice of Engadiner Nusstorte, a rich walnut and caramel tart that is the valley's signature, with a cup of coffee, at one of the bakeries.

t.near st anton am arlberg@47.1,10.2:
St Anton is the village where alpine skiing as the world knows it was invented, or at least codified. In the 1920s, the local ski teacher Hannes Schneider, building on the Arlberg technique, taught generations of skiers to turn on steep slopes, and his school became famous across Europe. Today, the village of fewer than two thousand people sits at the head of the Stanzer valley in Tyrol, at about 1,300 metres, with the great ridge of the Arlberg massif rising on all sides. In winter it is one of the liveliest ski resorts in the Alps, famous for its steep terrain and noisy, lively après-ski.

Summer is quieter, and for riders, perhaps better. The valley is green, the high meadows are full of flowers, and the streets are calmer, with a few shops open, a clutch of good restaurants, and cafes with terraces. The old railway station is a handsome landmark, and the Arlberg rail tunnel, finished in 1884, opened the region to the world. The road tunnel beneath the pass, nearly fourteen kilometres long, opened in 1978 and carries the main traffic, and a toll is charged to use it. Most riders choose the old road over the pass, which is free and much prettier.

The village has fuel, shops and plenty of places to eat, and it is the best base for the surrounding roads. Going west, the pass road climbs to the Arlberg Pass and then to Lech and Zürs. East, the road runs down the valley to Landeck, about twenty-three kilometres away, with the Inn valley beyond. Tyrol's food is hearty, with Kaiserschmarrn, a shredded pancake with raisins and fruit compote, Tiroler Gröstl, a pan of potatoes, bacon and egg, and Kasspatzln, small cheese dumplings. After a day's riding, they are exactly right.

The weather here is mountain weather. Mornings can be clear and cool, and afternoons bring cloud and thunderstorms, especially in July and August. Snow can come early in autumn and linger late in spring, and the high roads are closed in winter. Be ready for cold at the passes, even if it is warm in the village.

Parking in the centre is easy outside the ski season, and a walk along the main street, with the mountains above, is a good way to stretch. The cable car to the Valluga, a high summit, offers wide views.
t.near lech@47.2,10.2:
Lech sits in a high bowl of the Lech valley in Vorarlberg, at around fourteen hundred and fifty metres, with grey limestone peaks of the Arlberg on every side. It is known mainly as a ski resort, one of the most exclusive in Austria, and in winter the narrow village fills with fur coats and champagne, but in summer it is quiet, green and full of cowbells. The village was settled in the fourteenth century by Walser people, German-speaking farmers from the Valais in Switzerland who moved to high valleys across the Alps, and their wooden houses and chapel give it character. The river Lech, which rises nearby and flows north into Bavaria, is one of the last wild rivers in the Alps, with gravel banks and braided channels in its lower reaches.

For riders, Lech is the end of a fine road. The Flexenpass, at around seventeen hundred and seventy metres, links the Klostertal with the Lech valley, and the road is carved into the rock on the steep slope, passing through galleries and tunnels built to protect it from avalanches. The ascent from Stuben has tight hairpins and a pleasing rhythm, and the views from the top over the Rote Wand and the green basin below are superb. The surface is good, and traffic is moderate, though weekends can bring a convoy of cars and bikes. The pass is closed in winter, usually until late spring, and sudden avalanche closures can happen even in early summer, so check conditions.

North of Lech, the road continues along the river toward Warth and the Hochtannberg Pass, with long views and gentle bends, a route that combines mountain scenery with smooth tarmac. Weather in the Arlberg is changeable, with cold air, fog and showers in the afternoon, so carry a waterproof.

Fuel in Lech itself is limited, so fill up in Bludenz or Landeck, or in the valley below, and use the village for lunch. Austrian mountain cooking, with Kässpätzle, cheese dumplings in a pan with fried onions, is the thing to order. The best months are late June to September.

t.near salo@45.6,10.6:
Salò is a lakeside town on the western shore of Lake Garda, tucked into a deep bay that protects it from the worst of the wind. It has a long, elegant promenade, a cathedral with a Gothic facade and the kind of old arcades that make you want to sit with a coffee. The town is known for the violin maker Gasparo da Salò, who worked here in the sixteenth century and is considered one of the founders of the modern violin. For a very different reason, it is also remembered as the seat of the Italian Social Republic, Mussolini's puppet state, from 1943 to 1945.

With around eight thousand people, Salò has everything a rider needs: petrol stations, supermarkets, bakeries and plenty of places to eat by the water. The nearby town of Roè Volciano has more shopping and services. The Gardesana Occidentale, the road along the west shore, begins here and runs north, a famous route with tunnels carved into the cliffs and views over the water. Early in the day it is a joy; at weekends and in summer, it fills with cars, campervans and cyclists, and a leisurely pace is the only sensible one.

Garda is Italy's largest lake, formed by a glacier, and its climate is mild enough that lemon trees, olives and oleander grow along the shore. The wind pattern is well known: the Peler blows from the north in the morning, and the Ora arrives from the south in the early afternoon, making the lake a favourite for sailors and windsurfers. Spring can bring surprising squalls, and storms in summer build quickly over the mountains at the north end, so keep an eye on the sky.

The route that leaves Salò toward the hills behind the lake offers a quiet alternative. Narrow roads climb through olive groves and small villages, with a very different feel from the busy shore. The food is lake fish, such as lavarello and trout, with olive oil from the local groves, which is among the lightest in Italy. Start here early, have a proper breakfast on the front, and watch the first light turn the lake silver before the day's traffic begins.
t.near kranjska gora@46.5,13.8:
Kranjska Gora is the last real town in the Upper Sava valley, a ski resort in winter and a base for hikers and cyclists in summer, tucked so close to the Italian and Austrian frontiers that you can see both countries on a clear afternoon. It is a small place, about fourteen hundred residents, with pastel chalets, a main street of cafes and shops, and the Julian Alps going straight up behind it. The tall wall of Triglav's neighbours dominates the sky, and the fields around the village are neat, green and full of hay racks.

This is the foot of the Vršič Pass, the highest road pass in Slovenia at roughly sixteen hundred metres, and most riders come here for the road alone. Its hairpins are numbered, fifty of them, with twenty-four on the north side and twenty-six on the south, and on the northern ramp several of them are paved in cobbles. The cobbles can be slick in rain and awkward on a heavy bike, so take them slowly and in a low gear. The upper part of the road is narrow, with rock walls and little shoulder, and in summer you will share it with campervans and cyclists. Come early or late for the best of it.

The road itself has a sad origin. It was built during the First World War by Russian prisoners of war, working for the Austro-Hungarian army that was fighting the Italians on the Isonzo front. In March 1916 an avalanche killed many of them, and the little wooden Russian Chapel on the north side of the pass, built by their comrades, still stands among the trees. Stopping there is worth a minute, and flowers are often laid at the door. The road remains a quiet memorial to the men who made it.

Practical matters are simple here. There is fuel in Kranjska Gora, and it is wise to take it, because the pass has none. Restaurants in town serve Slovenian dishes such as jota, a sour-turnip and bean stew, and a sweet called potica. The pass is closed or restricted in winter, usually from late autumn until spring, so look at conditions before planning. Close by is Planica, where ski jumpers fly farther than anywhere else in the world, and the nearby lakes at Jasna are among the most photographed in the valley.
